en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Birth Stories in the Minor Collection.
(First Part) Introduction to the Composition Beneficial [teaching],
immeasurable, and spanning thousands of millions of births;
Having paid homage at the feet of that Great Seer by whom the world was guided by the Lord of the World,
having made the añjali-gesture toward the Dhamma,
and having honored the Saṅgha— the vessel of all veneration.
By the power of the merit arising from paying homage to the Triple Gem and other such deeds,
having severed all calamities through that influence,
[the teachings] were taught by the Radiant One, occasioned by various specific causes.
In the past, the Great Seer [taught] the *Apaṇṇaka* and other Jātaka stories,
in which the Teacher, the Leader, desiring to bring the world across, fully matured the infinite requisites for enlightenment over a long period of time.
By those who compiled them all together into a single collection,
that which is known as the *Jātaka* was chanted by the Dhamma-reciters.
Desiring the long endurance of this *Buddhavaṃsa*, [one should preserve it].
Having been entreated by the Elder Atthadassī—
who dwells in non-association, who always lives in purity,
who is likewise a friend of the Buddha, whose mind is tranquil, and who is wise— he approached him.
By Buddhadeva, a monk of pure intellect who arose within the Mahīṃsāsaka lineage and was skilled in the methods [of exposition],
[this work was composed] regarding the inconceivable power of the Great Beings' conduct.
While illuminating this commentary on the meaning of the Jātaka,
which follows the oral tradition of the Mahāvihāravāsins—
I shall speak it; may the virtuous ones kindly grasp what I say.
As for this commentary on the meaning of the Jātaka, it is described by showing these three origins— the distant origin, the not-distant origin,
and the proximate origin— so that those who hear it may understand it starting from its ultimate source.
Since it is indeed well understood, we shall therefore explain it by first showing those introductory causes (*nidāna*).
In this regard, first of all, the delimitation of those introductory causes must be known.

For the narrative course that occurred from the time the Great Being made his resolution at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha until he passed away from his existence as Vessantara and was reborn in the Tusita heaven—this is [the scope].
The "distant cause" (dūrenidāna) refers to the period from the time he passed away from the Tusita heaven until his attainment of omniscience at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

The "not-so-distant cause" (avidūrenidāna) refers to the narrative sequence that occurs from the time he descended from the Tusita heaven until his attainment of omniscience at the seat of enlightenment.
The "proximate cause" (santikenidāna), however, is found in each specific location while he was dwelling in those various places.
1. The Discourse on the Remote Past.
Herein, this is what is called the "Remote Past": It is said that four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons ago, there was a city named Amarāvatī.
There dwelt a brahmin named Sumedha, who was [learned] in both...

Well-born on the mother’s side and on the father’s side, of pure descent back through seven generations, unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth, handsome, pleasing, and inspiring confidence, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion;
he, without engaging in any other work, mastered the craft of a brahmin. While he was still in his childhood, his parents...

They passed away. Then the treasurer-minister brought forth the register of income, opened the storehouses filled with gold, silver, gems, pearls, and other treasures, and having explained the wealth down to the seventh generation of ancestors—saying, "This much, prince, belonged to your mother; this much to your father;
this much to your grandfathers and great-grandfathers"—he said, "Take possession of this."
He said: The wise Sumedha thought, "When my father, grandfather, and their ancestors departed for the next world, they did not take even a single kahāpaṇa with them;
it is fitting that I, however, should take this wealth and provide the means for my own departure.
Having informed the king and caused the drum to be beaten throughout the city, he gave alms to the great multitude and went forth as an ascetic.
He went forth. To clarify this matter, the story of Sumedha should be told here.
Although this story has indeed been recorded continuously in the *Buddhavamsa*, it is not very clear because it was presented merely as a sequence of verses.
Therefore, we shall relate it here, interspersing it with explanatory remarks that clarify the connection between the verses.
The Story of Sumedha:

At the conclusion of four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand eons, there was a city named Amaravatī, also known as Amara, which was never devoid of ten sounds. With reference to this, it is said in the *Buddhavamsa*:
“During four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand eons...”
“Amara is the name of the city, beautiful to behold and delightful;
it is never devoid of ten sounds and is well-supplied with food and drink.
Regarding that, “never devoid of ten sounds” means [it resounds] with the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of kettledrums...

It was never devoid of these ten sounds: the sound of kettledrums, the sound of lutes, the sound of flutes, the sound of cymbals, the sound of conchs, and tenthly, the sound of [people saying], "Eat! Drink! Feast!
Taking only a portion of those sounds—
“‘The sound of elephants, the sound of horses, and the drums, conchs, and chariots—eat and drink! Proclaim this with food and drink!
Having spoken this verse in the *Buddhavaṃsa*—”
“The city was complete in all its parts, where every task was accomplished;
it was endowed with the seven treasures and crowded with various people;
prosperous like the city of the gods, it was a dwelling for those who perform meritorious deeds.”
“In the city of Amarāvatī, there was a brahmin named Sumedha,
who possessed a vast accumulation of many millions and owned abundant wealth and grain.
He was a reciter of the scriptures, a keeper of the mantras, and one who had mastered the three Vedas.”
“Having reached perfection in the marks, in history, and in his own Dhamma,” it was said.
Then one day, that wise Sumedha, having gone into seclusion on the terrace of the excellent upper palace and sitting with his legs crossed in the *pallaṅka* posture, reflected:
“O Wise One, the taking of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in a new existence is suffering; likewise, in whatever place one is born, [there is suffering].”
"The breaking up of the body is certain, and I am subject to birth, subject to aging, subject to sickness, and subject to death.
For one such as I, it is fitting to seek the great Nibbāna—the deathless, cool, blissful state that is without birth, aging, or sickness.
Having necessarily been liberated from existence, there must be a single path leading to Nibbāna. Thus it was said.
“Seated in seclusion, I then reflected thus:
‘Rebirth is indeed suffering, as is the dissolution of the body.
Subject to birth, subject to aging, and subject to sickness, I was then [in that state].’”
“I shall seek the unaging, deathless, secure state of Nibbāna.
“What if I were now to cast aside this putrid body, filled with various kinds of filth,
and go forth, indifferent and free from desire?”
“There must exist that path; it is not impossible for me.
I shall seek that path for the sake of complete liberation from existence.
After that, he thought even further: “Just as in the world there is indeed what is called happiness, which is the opposite of suffering...”
Since this exists, there must also exist its opposite, namely non-becoming (*vibhava*).
And just as when heat exists, its pacification, which is cold, also exists, so too there must exist *nibbāna*, which is the pacification of the fires of passion and the other defilements.
And just as there is a wholesome, blameless state that is the opposite of evil and base states...
It is indeed so: just as when there is evil birth, there must also be what is called "non-birth" (ajāti), namely Nibbāna, because it transcends all forms of birth.
Therefore it was said:
"Just as when suffering exists, that which is called happiness also exists;..."
While existence thus exists, non-existence must also be desired.
Just as when heat exists, its opposite, coolness, is found;
so too, while the threefold fire exists, Nibbāna must be desired.
“Just as when evil exists, the beautiful also exists;
even so, while birth exists, the unborn should be sought.
He further reflected: “Just as if a man were submerged in a heap of excrement and [saw] from afar a place covered with five-colored lotuses...”
Upon seeing a great lake, it is appropriate to search for that lake, thinking, "By what path should one go there?

That one does not search for it is not the fault of the lake. In the same way, while the great lake of the deathless Nibbāna exists for the washing away of the stains of defilements, the failure to seek it is not the fault of the great lake of the deathless Nibbāna. And just as when one is surrounded by thieves...
If a man does not flee even though a path of escape exists, it is not the fault of the path; it is the fault of the man alone.

In the same way, for a person who is surrounded and seized by defilements, the failure to seek the auspicious path leading to Nibbāna—even though that path exists—is not the fault of the path; it is the fault of the individual alone. And just as...
If a man afflicted by disease does not seek out treatment for his ailment from a physician who is available and capable of curing him, it is not the fault of the physician;

it is the fault of the man himself. In the same way, if a person afflicted by the disease of the defilements (*kilesa*) does not seek out a teacher who is available and skilled in the path that leads to the pacification of those defilements, the fault lies with him alone.
"Not [the fault] of the teacher who destroys the defilements. Therefore it was said:
"Just as a man who has fallen into excrement, upon seeing a pond filled [with it], does not seek out that pond—this is no fault of the pond."
“Thus, while the pond of the Deathless exists for washing away the stains of defilement, one does not seek that pond; there is no fault in the pond of the Deathless.
Just as one besieged by enemies, when a path for escape exists...”
That man does not flee; it is no fault of the straight path.
"Thus, though obstructed by defilements while the auspicious path exists, he does not seek that way;
it is no fault of the auspicious straight path."
"Just as a man who is diseased, though a physician is present,
does not have that disease treated— this is no fault of the physician.
So too, one who is afflicted and oppressed by the diseases of the defilements..."
"He does not seek out that teacher; there is no fault in him, the leader.

He thought further: "Just as a man of a decorative nature, having cast off a corpse clinging to his neck, goes on happily, even so must I, casting off this putrid body, enter the city of Nibbāna without looking back."
Just as men and women, having voided excrement and urine in a cesspool,
do not carry it away on their laps or wrap it in their garments and go, but rather, loathing it, discard it without regard and depart; even so,
I too shall discard this putrid body without regard and enter the deathless city of Nibbāna.

It is fitting. Just as sailors abandon a dilapidated ship without looking back and go on their way, so too shall I, abandoning this body which is leaking from nine openings, enter the city of Nibbāna without looking back.
And just as a man, while traveling the road with thieves carrying various kinds of jewels, [considers] himself...
Out of fear of losing his jewels, he abandons that [treacherous] path and takes the safe road; in the same way, this body made of flesh is like a thief who plunders one's jewels.
If I were to harbor craving for this, the jewel of the noble path and the wholesome qualities would be lost to me.
Therefore, it is right for me to abandon this body, which is like a thief, and enter the city of Nibbāna. Thus it was said:
“Just as a person, loathing a corpse tied around his neck,
might set it free and go away happy, independent, and self-mastered; even so,
[one should abandon] this putrid body, a heap of various corpses.”
Having cast it away, I would go forth, indifferent and without desire:
"Just as men and women, having discarded excrement in a place for filth,
go away indifferent and without desire."
“In this very way, having cast off this body filled with various kinds of filth,
I shall depart, just as one leaves a hut after having voided excrement.
Just as an old boat, leaking and taking on water,”
“Carpenters abandon [a boat] and go away, indifferent and having no further need for it.
In the same way, I shall abandon this body— with its nine openings and constant flow—
and depart, just as owners leave behind a worn-out boat.”
“Just as a man traveling with thieves, taking his goods along,
might see the danger of having his goods stolen and so depart after casting them away;
even so is this body, like a great thief.”
"Having abandoned this, I shall go away for fear of the destruction of my wholesome roots. Thus,
after the wise Sumedha had reflected on this matter connected with renunciation through various kinds of similes,
he distributed his immeasurable mass of wealth among the poor, the destitute, and others, in the manner described below, within his own residence.
Having given a great gift and abandoned both sensual pleasures of the objects and sensual pleasures of the defilements, he departed from the City of the Immortals (Amaranagara).
All alone, he established a hermitage at the foot of a mountain named Dhammika in the Himalayas;

there, having constructed a leaf-hut and a walking-path, he dwelt in a state free from the five faults of the hindrances, as described in the passage beginning with, "When the mind is thus concentrated."

Endowed with eight qualities of cause, he entered the ascetic life (*isipabbajjā*) in that hermitage, having discarded his garment— which possessed nine defects— in order to acquire the power known as the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*),

and having donned a bark robe (*vākacīra*) endowed with twelve qualities. Having thus gone forth, he abandoned that leaf-hut (*paṇṇasālā*) which was filled with eight defects, [and took up] that which was endowed with ten qualities.
Having gone to the foot of a tree and abandoned all varieties of grain, he lived on naturally fallen fruit and applied himself to striving by means of sitting, standing, and walking.
Within seven days, he became an attainer of the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Thus he reached the power of direct knowledge as he had desired. Therefore it was said:
“Having thus reflected, I gave away wealth amounting to many hundreds of millions to those who had protectors and those who were protectorless, and then I went to the Himalayas.
Not far from the Himalayas is a mountain named Dhammika.”
“My hermitage is well-constructed, my leaf-hut is beautifully arranged.
There I fashioned a walking path, free from five defects and endowed with eight qualities;
I brought forth the power of direct knowledge.”
“There I discarded my cloth garment, which had come to possess nine faults;
I donned a bark robe, which possessed twelve virtues.
I abandoned the leaf-hut, which was beset by eight faults.”
I approached the foot of the tree, which was endowed with ten qualities.
"The grain that had been sown and planted, I abandoned without remainder;
I took instead the fruit that grows spontaneously, possessing manifold virtues."
“Right there I applied myself to striving— sitting, standing, and walking—
and within seven days internally I attained the powers of direct knowledge.
Regarding this, by means of the passage beginning, “My hermitage is well-prepared, my leaf-hut is well-constructed,” the wise Sumedha—
The hermitage, the leaf-hut, and the walking-path are described as if they were built with his own hands. This, however, is the meaning here:

when Sakka, Lord of the Devas, saw the Great Being set out, having descended into the Himalayas with the thought, "Today I shall enter Mount Dhammika," he addressed the divine son Vissakamma: "Dear one, this wise Sumedha intends to go forth into the homeless life."
“Having departed, build a dwelling place for him. Accepting his words, he constructed a delightful hermitage, a well-guarded leaf-hut, and a charming walking path.
Then the Blessed One, referring to that hermitage which had been brought forth by the power of his own merit, said to Sāriputta on Mount Dhammika:
“My hermitage is well-constructed, my leaf-hut is beautifully built;
there I constructed a walking path, free from the five defects,” he said.
In this context, “well-constructed by me” means it was well-constructed by me. “My leaf-hut is beautifully built” means that even my hut with a roof of leaves was well-constructed.

"Free from the five faults": there are these five faults of a walking path (caṅkama): stiffness and unevenness, trees growing inside, being overgrown with thickets, being too narrow, and being too wide.
For when one walks on a walking path where the ground is stiff and uneven, the feet ache, blisters arise, the mind does not attain one-pointedness, and the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) fails.
However, when the ground is soft and even, one attains a comfortable dwelling and the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) succeeds.

Therefore, the state of being hard and uneven ground should be understood as the first fault. If there is a tree at the end, in the middle, or at the side of the walking path, the forehead or head of one who is walking may strike it through negligence;
thus, having a tree within [the path] is the second fault. [If the path is] covered by a thicket of grass, creepers, and so forth...
While walking back and forth on the *caṅkama* at the time of darkness, one may step on or kill living beings such as snakes, or be bitten by them and thus fall into suffering;
this concealment by thickets is the third fault.
Furthermore, when walking on a *caṅkama* that is too narrow—measuring either one *ratana* or half a *ratana* in width—one may stumble at its edge and break one's nails or fingers.
Being too narrow is the fourth fault. When walking on a walkway that is too wide, the mind wanders and one does not attain one-pointedness;

thus, being too wide is the fifth fault. As for the walkway itself, it should be one and a half *ratanas* in width, with a side-walk of one *ratana* on both sides, sixty cubits in length, with a smooth surface and evenly scattered sand.
It was appropriate, like the walking path of the Elder Mahinda, the illuminator of the Island, at Cetiyagiri;
such it became. Therefore he said: "There I had a walking path constructed, free from the five defects.
"Endowed with eight qualities" means endowed with the eight kinds of happiness of a recluse (samaṇa). These eight are called the happinesses of a recluse: [list follows].
The absence of possession of wealth and grain; the state of seeking blameless alms-food; the state of consuming alms-food with a sense of relief;
the absence of the defilement of oppressing the country when dealing with royal families that seize wealth, essences, head-money, kahāpaṇas, and so forth;
the state of having no desire or lust for requisites; the state of being fearless during a bandit’s plunder; and the state of not associating with kings or high ministers.
"Unobstructed state in the four directions. This is what is meant:

"Just as it is possible for one dwelling in that hermitage to experience these eight kinds of ascetic happiness, so may they build that hermitage endowed with these eight qualities. "He brought forth the power of direct knowledge":
later, while dwelling in that hermitage, having performed the preliminary work for the *kasiṇas*, he [attained] the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).

For the purpose of producing the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), I began the insight meditation (*vipassanā*) on [the aggregates] as impermanent and suffering, and brought forth the power of insight that had reached full strength.

The meaning is: "Having constructed that hermitage so that it was suitable for the power of insight intended for those higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), I made it such that while dwelling there, I would be able to bring forth that power."
"He abandoned his robe there, having fallen into nine faults"—herein is this sequential account:

it is said that at that time, having constructed a delightful hermitage adorned with walkways and caves, covered with flowering and fruit-bearing trees, possessing pools of sweet water, free from terrifying wild beasts and birds, and suitable for seclusion;
and having placed a support-board at both ends of the decorated walkway—
Having prepared a level slab of earth the color of green mung beans for a sitting mat in the middle of the walking path, he arranged within the leaf-hut the requisites of an ascetic—
such as a mass of matted hair, bark garments, a triple staff, and a water pot— and in the pavilion, water jars, water-conch shells, and water basins;
and in the fire-hut, charcoal pans, wood, and so forth— in this way, whatever was conducive to the benefit of those who have gone forth.
Having fashioned all of those things, the divine son Vissakamma inscribed the words on the wall of the leaf-hut, "Whoever desires to go forth,
let them take these requisites and go forth," and departed for the world of the gods. Then the wise Sumedha, following a mountain cave at the foot of the Himavat mountains,
looked about for a comfortable place suitable for his own dwelling.
Having seen the delightful hermitage, built by Vissakamma at the river’s bend and granted by Sakka,
he went to the end of the walking path; not seeing any footprints, he thought, "Surely the renunciants, having sought alms in the village ahead and being weary from their journey,
must have entered the leaf-hut and are sitting there," and after waiting a short while, [he saw] "exceedingly..."

“They are taking their time; I shall find out,” he thought. Opening the door of the leaf-hut, he entered and, looking here and there, read the letters inscribed on the great wall. Thinking, “These are my own requisites;
having taken these, I shall go forth,” he cast off the pair of garments he was wearing. Therefore he said: “I cast off the garment.”
"Having entered there," Sāriputta, "I discarded my cloth in that leaf-hut.
By saying 'having seen nine faults,' he indicates that one discards the cloth having seen nine defects.
For nine defects appear regarding the cloth for those who have gone forth into the ascetic life. Among these, its high cost is one defect."
There is one aspect: that it arises dependent on others; another: that it becomes quickly soiled through use—for what is soiled must be washed and dyed;
another: that it decays through use—for when it is worn out, it must be sewn or provided with patches;
and yet another: that it is difficult to obtain through further seeking, as in the case of the ascetic life of renunciation.
Its lack of beauty is one [disadvantage], and its being common property for enemies is another.

For it must be guarded in such a way that enemies do not seize it. Its being an object of adornment for one who uses it is one [advantage], and its being a burden on the shoulder and a source of weariness for one who carries it about is another.
"I wore bark-cloth," Sāriputta, "is what I said; having seen these nine faults, I abandoned my garment and wore bark-cloth.
The meaning is that I took up the bark-cloth made by weaving muñja grass, pulling it out strand by strand, for the purpose of wearing as an undergarment and an upper robe.
'Possessing twelve qualities' means being endowed with twelve benefits. For in bark-cloth there are twelve [benefits]..."
The benefits: it is inexpensive, beautiful, and allowable—this is first; it can be made with one's own hands—this is second;
through use it wears out slowly, and even when washing it there is no great trouble—this is third;
even when worn out by use, there is no need for sewing—this is fourth; and for one seeking another, it is easy to make.
The fifth is its suitability for the renunciation of a forest-dweller; the sixth is the state of depriving adversaries of their enjoyment;
the seventh is the absence of any occasion for adornment for one who uses it; the eighth is its lightness when worn; the ninth is the state of having few desires regarding the requisite of robes;
the tenth is its being righteous and blameless in its production through speech; and the eleventh is even when the bark-fiber robe is lost...
"The twelfth is the state of being free from longing.
He abandoned the leaf-hut, which was beset by eight defects. How did he abandon it?
It is said that, having taken off his pair of fine garments and put on a red bark-cloth robe—which hung upon the robe-rack like a garland of *anoja* flowers—he donned it.

Over that, having put on another bark garment (*vākacīra*) the color of gold, and having placed a deerskin (*ajinacamma*) complete with its hooves upon it like a carpet of *punnāga* flowers, he arranged it over one shoulder;
then, having bound his mass of matted hair (*jaṭāmaṇḍala*), he inserted a metal pin (*sārasūci*) into his topknot (*cūḷā*) to keep it steady;
and having hung a coral-colored water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*) from a carrying-net (*sikkā*) resembling a lattice of pearls, [he stood] at the three...
Taking his crooked carrying-pole at the appropriate places, hanging a water-jar from one end and an ankus,
a hatchet, a staff, and other tools from the other, placing a load of bundles upon his shoulder, and grasping a walking-stick with his right hand,
he emerged from the leaf-hut and paced back and forth on the great sixty-cubit walkway, surveying his own appearance.
“My heart’s desire has reached its fulfillment; indeed, my renunciation shines forth!
This so-called renunciation is praised and extolled by all wise men, beginning with the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas. The fetters of the household life have been abandoned by me;
I have gone forth into homelessness. I have attained the supreme renunciation; I shall practice the duty of a recluse, and I shall attain [the goal].”

Filled with enthusiasm, thinking, "The bliss of the paths and fruits," he unloaded his pack-animal and sat upon a stone slab the color of green mung beans in the middle of the walkway like a golden statue.
Having spent the day there, at evening time he entered the leaf-hut and lay down on a wooden mattress beside a bed of *bida* leaves. After allowing his body to warm up, at the powerful dawn...

Having awakened, he reflected upon his own arrival: "Seeing the peril in the household life, I abandoned immeasurable wealth and boundless treasures, entered the forest, and went forth as one seeking renunciation. From this moment on, it is not fitting for me to walk in negligence.
For the flies of wrong thoughts devour one who wanders having abandoned seclusion; now, I must cultivate seclusion."
It is appropriate. For I have gone forth having seen household life as an impediment;

yet here is this pleasant leaf-hut, with its floor smoothed the color of ripe *veluva* fruit, its white walls the color of silver, its thatched roof the color of pigeon’s feet, and its split-bamboo couch the color of variegated rugs—a dwelling place comfortable for living.
"I do not perceive any household prosperity greater than this," he said. While searching for the faults in the leaf-hut, he saw eight faults.
For there are eight disadvantages in the use of a leaf-hut: first, the disadvantage of having to seek out materials and the labor involved in assembling the building supplies;
second, the necessity of repeatedly replacing the grass, leaves, and clay whenever they fall away.
The state of having to look after belongings is the second; the fact that a dwelling is obtained for one who is senior is the third;
the lack of one-pointedness of mind when being awakened at an improper time is the fourth; the state of making the body delicate through protection from cold and heat is the fifth;
and the state of concealing censure, thinking that anyone who has entered a house might be capable of doing some evil, is the sixth.
The sixth [disadvantage] is the state of making it one's own by claiming "it is mine. The seventh is the so-called presence of a house, which means living with a companion.
The eighth is the state of being shared with many, due to its commonality with things such as bedbugs, cockroaches, and house-lizards.
Having seen these eight disadvantages, the Great Being abandoned the leaf-hut. Therefore he said: "Filled with eight faults..."
"I abandoned the leaf-hut.
He says this to declare that, having rejected the [leaf-hut] roof, he has approached the foot of a tree endowed with ten qualities.
Herein, these are the ten qualities: (1) little exertion is one quality; it requires merely approaching [the tree].
For there is no sense of ownership there; lack of maintenance is the second [reason], for even if it is not properly swept, whether it has been swept or not, it remains comfortable for use.

The state of being beyond reproach is the third; one does not conceal blame, for one feels shame when committing evil there—thus, the state of not concealing blame is the fourth; like living in the open air, it does not stiffen the body.
The fifth is the state of the body being unpropped up; the sixth is the absence of making it one's own;
the seventh is the rejection of a home as a dwelling place; the eighth is the absence of taking it out, thinking "I will look after this" or "Go away," as one would with a house shared by many;
the ninth is the state of delight while dwelling [there]; and [the tenth is] because the lodging at the foot of a tree is easily available wherever one goes.
"Having seen these ten qualities—the tenth being the state of non-attachment—I have come to the foot of a tree," he said.
Having observed these many reasons, the Great Being entered the village for alms on the following day.
Then, in the village he reached, the people gave him alms with great enthusiasm. He finished his meal...
Having completed his hermitage and returned to sit down, he reflected: "I did not go forth thinking, 'I shall not obtain food.
This so-called 'succulent food' increases pride, intoxication, and the arrogance of man. There is no end to the suffering rooted in food.
What if I were to abandon food produced from sown and planted grain and subsist instead on wild fruits that grow spontaneously?"

“...might it come to pass. Rising from that place, he acted accordingly, striving and exerting himself, and within seven days he produced the eight attainments and the five direct knowledges. Therefore it was said:
“The grain that had been sown and planted, I abandoned without remainder;”
“I took ripe fruit endowed with manifold virtues.
There, sitting, standing, and walking, I applied myself to the supreme effort;
within seven days, I attained the power of direct knowledge.”
While the ascetic Sumedha was thus passing his time in the bliss of meditative attainment after attaining the power of direct knowledge, a Teacher named Dīpaṅkara appeared in the world.

At the moments of his conception, birth, enlightenment, and turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the entire ten-thousandfold world system trembled, quaked, and shook violently, and a great roar resounded. Thirty-two...
The preliminary signs appeared. While the ascetic Sumedha was passing his time in the bliss of meditative attainment, he neither heard that sound nor saw those signs. Therefore it is said:
"Thus, for me who had attained success and mastery in the Teaching..."
The Conqueror named Dīpaṅkara arose as a leader of the world.
“While he was arising, being born, awakening, and teaching the Dhamma, I,
absorbed in the delight of jhāna, did not perceive the four signs.”

At that time, the Ten-Powered Dīpaṅkara, surrounded by four hundred thousand whose taints were exhausted, traveling by stages on his alms-round, reached the city named Ramma and resided there in the Sudassana Great Monastery. The inhabitants of the city of Ramma heard:
"It is said that the Lord of Recluses, Dīpaṅkara, having attained supreme perfect enlightenment and set in motion the excellent Wheel of Dhamma, has arrived here by stages..."
Having heard that while wandering on his alms-round he had reached the city of Ramma and was staying at the Sudassana Great Monastery, she had clarified butter, fresh butter,
and other medicinal requisites, as well as robes and coverings, prepared; then, with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in her hands,
inclining, leaning, and tending toward the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, she approached the Teacher, paid homage, and—

Having worshipped with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, they sat to one side; after hearing the teaching on the Dhamma and inviting [the Buddha] for the following day’s meal, they rose from their seats and departed.
On the next day, having prepared a great almsgiving and decorated the city, they adorned the path by which the One of Ten Powers would arrive.
In the places where the ground had been broken by water, they threw earth to level the surface,
scattered sand the color of silver plates, strewn parched grain and flowers, raised banners and streamers of various colors,
and set up plantain trees and rows of full water-jars. At that time, the ascetic Sumedha— his own...
Having risen from the hermitage and traveling through the air above those people, he saw them joyful and delighted, and thinking, "What could be the reason for this?
he descended from the sky and stood to one side. He questioned the people:
"O sirs, for whom are you decorating this road? Thus it was said.
“In a border region, having invited the Tathāgata,
they cleanse the path for his arrival with joyful minds.
At that time, I departed from my own Sakka realm.”
Shaking off my bark garments, I then traveled through the sky.
Seeing the people filled with Vedic knowledge, joyful, delighted, and overjoyed,
I descended from the heavens and immediately questioned the men.
“With hearts joyful, elated, and full of rapture, the great multitude asks:
‘Whose path is being cleared? The straight way, the path of travel?
The people replied, “Venerable Sumedha, you do not know: Dīpaṅkara, the One of Ten Powers, is seeking perfect enlightenment.”
“Having set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, while wandering on his alms tour, he has reached our city and is staying at the Sudassana Great Monastery.
We have invited that Blessed One, and we are now decorating the path by which that Buddha, the Blessed One, will arrive.
The ascetic Sumedha thought: “In this world, even the mere sound of the word ‘Buddha’ is difficult to find.”
“Not only should there be the appearance of a Buddha, but it is also fitting for me to adorn the path of the One Possessed of Ten Powers together with these men. He said to those men:
“Sirs, if you are adorning this path for the Buddha, give me one opportunity as well; I too shall adorn the path together with you. They replied, “Very well.”
Having accepted it and knowing that "the ascetic Sumedha possesses psychic power," they observed a spot where the water had receded and gave it to him, saying, "May you adorn this place.
Seizing upon the joy inspired by the Buddha as his mental object, Sumedha thought:
"I am able to adorn this place with my psychic power; however, being adorned in such a way will not satisfy my mind."
"Today it is fitting for me to perform manual service," he thought, and having brought some soil, he scattered it over that spot.
While that place was still unadorned, Dīpaṅkara the Ten-Powered One—

surrounded by four hundred thousand great beings who possessed the six supernormal powers and had exhausted all taints, and while the deities were honoring him with celestial perfumes, garlands, and other offerings— [passed by].
While celestial music was playing and humans were honoring him with human perfumes, garlands, and other offerings,
he set out upon that decorated and prepared road, stretching himself like a lion upon a slab of emerald with the infinite grace of a Buddha.
The ascetic Sumedha opened his eyes and beheld the One Possessed of Ten Powers as He approached along the decorated road.
He beheld his own person, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, graced with the eighty minor characteristics,
surrounded by a fathom-wide aura of radiance, emitting dense, six-colored Buddha-rays— like various streaks of lightning in the sky,
appearing as interlacing garlands and paired clusters— possessing the supreme form.
Having observed this, he thought: "Today it is fitting for me to sacrifice my life for the One of Ten Powers. Let not the Blessed One tread upon the mud;

rather, let him walk as if treading upon a bridge of jeweled slabs, crushing my back along with the four hundred thousand who have destroyed their taints. That shall be for my welfare and happiness for a long time."

Having loosened his hair and spread out a black antelope skin, a circle of matted locks, and bark garments upon the mud, he lay down on the surface of the mud like a bridge made of jeweled slabs. Thus it was said:
“They answered me when asked: ‘The Buddha is unsurpassed in the world;’”
“A Victor named Dīpaṅkara, a leader of the world, has appeared;
his path is being cleared—the straight way for traveling.
Having heard the word “Buddha,” joy arose in me at that very moment.
Uttering "Buddha, Buddha," I experienced a surge of joy.
Standing there, with a heart both delighted and stirred, I reflected:
"I shall plant seeds here; let not this opportune moment pass me by."
“If you would clear it for the Buddha, grant me a single space;
I too shall clear the straight path, the way of travel.
They then granted me the space to clear that straight path.
Thinking, "Buddha, Buddha," I then cleared the path.
While my place was not yet finished, the Great Sage Dīpaṅkara,
together with four hundred thousand [monks] who possessed the six supernormal knowledges and were like him, [arrived].
The Conqueror proceeded along the straight path with those who were stainless and whose taints were destroyed.
"Welcoming processions took place, and many drums resounded;
humans and gods, filled with joy, raised shouts of 'Well done!'"
“Devas see humans, and humans also see deities;
both of them, with palms joined in reverence, follow after the Tathāgata.
Devas with celestial music and humans with human music [honor him].”
Both of them, avoiding [the path], followed after the Tathāgata. The gods,
having ascended into the sky, scattered divine mandārava flowers, lotuses,
and pārichattaka trees in every direction.
“Men on the surface of the earth are casting up campaka, salala, nīpa, nāga, punnāga,
and ketaka flowers in every direction. There,
having loosened my hair, I [threw down] my bark garment and my hide.”
Having spread myself out upon the mud, I lay down face downwards:
"May the Buddha, together with his disciples, walk over me;
let him not step upon the mud—this will be for my welfare."
Thus, while still lying on the surface of the mud, he opened his eyes again and, beholding the splendor of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the One of Ten Powers, thought thus:
"If I so desired, I could enter the city of Ramma as a junior member of the Saṅgha after having burned away all my defilements.
However, it is by concealing my identity that I shall burn away my defilements and attain Nibbāna."

"There is nothing further to be done. What if I, like the Ten-Powered Dīpaṅkara, were to attain supreme perfect enlightenment, board the ship of the Dhamma, and after ferrying the great multitude across the ocean of saṃsāra, subsequently pass into parinibbāna? This would be fitting for me.
Then, having brought together the eight qualities and made the aspiration for Buddhahood, he lay down. Thus it was said:
“As I lay upon the ground, such was the thought in my mind:
‘If I so desired, I could today burn away my defilements.
What need have I for this disguise of anonymity, when the Dhamma has been realized right here?’”
"Having attained omniscience, I shall become a Buddha in the world with its devas.
'What need have I for this single person who has crossed over and perceives his own strength?
Having attained omniscience, I shall ferry across the world with its devas.'"
"By this service rendered to the Supreme Person,
having attained omniscience, may I deliver the vast multitude of beings.
Having cut off the stream of saṃsāra and shattered the three realms of existence,"
“Having boarded the ship of the Dhamma, I shall ferry across the world with its gods.
For one who aspires to Buddhahood, it is said:
“Human birth, the perfection of gender, the cause, and the sight of a Teacher;”
"Renunciation, perfection of qualities, the requisite capacity, and zeal—
through the convergence of these eight factors, the resolution succeeds.
For it is only while remaining in a human existence that the aspiration of one who aspires to Buddhahood succeeds, and not otherwise.

The aspiration of a nāga, a supaṇṇa, or a deity succeeds. Even among human beings, the aspiration succeeds only for one established in the male gender, not for a woman, nor for a paṇḍaka, a napuṃsaka, or a hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka).
Even for a man, within that particular existence, [the aspiration succeeds] only for one who is endowed with the causes for attaining arahantship.

A resolution succeeds for one [who possesses the necessary conditions], but not for another. Even for one who possesses the causal factors, a resolution succeeds only when made in the presence of a living Buddha;
it does not succeed for one making a resolution near a shrine or at the foot of the Bodhi tree after the Buddha has attained Parinibbāna.
Furthermore, even for one making a resolution in the presence of Buddhas, it succeeds only for one who stands within the marks of the renunciant (pabbajjāliṅga).
It succeeds for one who has gone forth, not for one remaining in the garb of a householder.

Even among those who have gone forth, it succeeds only for one who possesses the five higher knowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) and has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), and not for one devoid of these perfections of virtue (*guṇasampadā*).

Furthermore, even for one endowed with such virtues, it succeeds only for one who has perfected his service by having sacrificed his own life for the Buddhas, and thus possesses the requisite of service (*adhikāra*).

Not for another. Even for one who possesses the necessary qualification, success belongs only to him who has great desire, energy, effort, and inquiry for the sake of the qualities that constitute a Buddha, and not for another.
Herein, this is an illustration of the greatness of desire: suppose it were thus: "Whoever [could fill] the entire interior of the world-system..."
One who is able to cross over and reach the far shore by swimming with the strength of one's own arms through water that has become a single expanse reaches Buddhahood.
Or again, one who is able to reach the far shore by walking on foot after filling and trampling the entire interior of a world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) covered with thickets of bamboo reaches Buddhahood.
Or again, one who [is able to do so] with the entire interior of a world-system...
“Whoever is capable of reaching the far shore by walking on foot across a place strewn continuously with spears after striking down those spears, he attains Buddhahood.

Or again, whoever is capable of reaching the far shore by treading with their feet upon the entire interior of the Cakkavāḷa filled with glowing embers, he attains Buddhahood. Whoever [is capable] of even one among these...

He does not consider his own task difficult; rather, he is endowed with great desire, energy, effort, and inquiry, thinking, “Having crossed over this, or having gone through it, I shall reach the further shore.
For such a person, the aspiration succeeds, but not for another. The ascetic Sumedha, however, having combined these eight qualities—
Having made the resolve for Buddhahood, he lay down.
Then the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara arrived and, standing at the head of the ascetic Sumedha as if opening a jeweled lion-window,
opened his eyes endowed with the fivefold clarity and gazed upon the ascetic Sumedha lying on the surface of the mud.
Having seen him, [he thought], "This ascetic has made a resolution for Buddhahood and lies here; will this aspiration of his succeed, or will it not?

Sending forth his knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*), he investigated and, knowing that "after four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) plus one hundred thousand aeons have passed from now, one named Gotama will become a Buddha," he remained standing right where he was.
In the midst of the assembly, he declared: “Do you see this ascetic of fierce penance lying on the surface of the mud?
“Yes, venerable sir,” they replied. “This one has made the aspiration for Buddhahood and lies here;
his wish shall be fulfilled. At the end of four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons from now, he will become known as Gotama.”
He will become a Buddha. In that existence, his residence will be the city named Kapilavatthu;
his mother will be the queen named Māyā, his father the king named Suddhodana; his chief disciple will be the elder named Upatissa, his second disciple the elder named Kolita;
his attendant will be named Ānanda; his chief female disciple will be the elder nun named Khemā, and his second female disciple—

“There will be a nun named Uppalavaṇṇā; having attained mature knowledge, she will make the Great Renunciation, exert herself in the Great Struggle, receive milk-rice at the foot of the Nigrodha tree, eat it on the bank of the Nerañjarā River, ascend the seat of enlightenment, and attain full awakening at the foot of the Assattha tree. Thus it was said.
“Dīpaṅkara, the knower of the world, the receiver of offerings,
standing at my head, spoke these words:
‘Behold this ascetic, the matted-hair ascetic of fierce austerities!’”
"In an immeasurable aeon from now, a Buddha will appear in the world.
Having gone forth from the delightful city called Kapila, the Tathāgata,
after exerting himself in striving and performing difficult austerities..."
“Having sat at the foot of the Ajapāla tree, the Tathāgata will take his meal there and proceed to the Nerañjarā River.
On the bank of the Nerañjarā, that Conqueror will eat the milk-rice.”
By the prepared noble path, he will approach the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Then, having circumambulated the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to the right,
the unsurpassed one of great glory will awaken at the foot of the Assattha tree.
‘His mother who gave him birth shall be named Māyā;
his father shall be named Suddhodana, and he himself shall be Gotama.
Free from taints, devoid of passion, with peaceful minds and concentrated, he shall be.’
Kolita and Upatissa shall be the foremost disciples;
one named Ānanda shall be the attendant who will serve that Conqueror.
Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā shall be the foremost female disciples.
“Taintless and free from passion, with peaceful minds and concentrated, the enlightenment of that Blessed One is called ‘Assattha.
Upon hearing this, the ascetic Sumedha was filled with joy, thinking, “It seems my aspiration will indeed be fulfilled. The great multitude...
Having heard the words of Dīpaṅkara Dasabala, he was filled with joy and satisfaction, thinking, "The ascetic Sumedha is indeed the seed of a Buddha, the sprout of a Buddha.

And this thought occurred to him: "Just as a man crossing a river, being unable to ford it at a straight landing-place, crosses at a lower landing-place, even so we [should follow] Dīpaṅkara Dasabala..."

They made this aspiration: "If we do not attain the fruits of the Path within this Dispensation, may we be capable of realizing the fruits of the Path in your presence when you become a Buddha in the future.
The Fortunate One Dīpaṅkara, having praised the Bodhisatta and honored him with eight handfuls of flowers, circumambulated him and departed.
Those four hundred thousand who had exhausted their taints (khīṇāsava), having honored the Bodhisatta with perfumes and garlands and having circumambulated him, departed.
Likewise, the devas and humans, having honored and paid homage to him, departed.
When they had all gone, the Bodhisatta rose from his bed and, thinking, "I shall search for the perfections (pāramiyo)," stood upon the heap of flowers.
Having folded his legs crosswise, he sat down. When the Bodhisatta was thus seated, the deities of the entire ten-thousandfold world system assembled, and having offered their applause, they said:
"Noble Sumedha ascetic, when the ancient Bodhisattas sat cross-legged with the thought, 'I shall investigate the perfections,' certain portents known as omens appeared."
"All these signs have appeared today; without doubt you will become a Buddha. We know this:
'Whosoever these marks are seen upon him, he is certainly a Buddha. Therefore, exerting firm energy, apply yourself!
Thus they extolled the Bodhisatta with various kinds of praise. Hence it is said:
“Having heard these words of the Peerless Great Sage, humans and gods were filled with joy, thinking, ‘This one, it is said, is the seed of a Buddha.
Shouts of acclamation arose; they clapped their hands and laughed.”
With palms joined in reverence, the ten thousand worlds together with their devas pay homage,
saying: "If we fail to fulfill the teaching of this Lord of the World,
in a future time we shall stand face to face with him."
"Just as people crossing a river, having lost their raft,
take hold of a foothold at a lower ford and cross over the great river— even so,
if we all were to release this Conqueror, [we too would cross over]."
"In a future time, we shall stand face to face with him.
"Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings,
having proclaimed my deed, raised up his right foot."
“Those sons of the Conqueror who were there all circumambulated me;
men, nāgas, and gandhabbas, having paid homage, departed.
Even as the Leader of the World was passing beyond my sight, together with his Saṅgha,”
With a heart joyful and elated, I then rose from my seat.
"I am happy through happiness, delighted by rapture;
drenched with joy, I then sat cross-legged."
“Sitting cross-legged, I then reflected thus:
‘I have attained mastery in jhāna and reached perfection in the higher knowledges (abhiññā).
In this world-system of a thousand worlds, there are no seers equal to me.’”
"Unrivaled among those with psychic powers, I obtained such bliss as this:
'While I sat cross-legged, the inhabitants of the ten thousandfold world-system raised a great cry:
"Surely you will become a Buddha!"'"
‘Those signs which appeared formerly when the Bodhisattas sat upon their excellent thrones, those very signs appear today.
The cold has vanished, and the heat is stilled.’
Those [signs] are visible today; surely you will become a Buddha.
The ten-thousandfold world system is silent and undisturbed;
those [signs] are visible today; surely you will become a Buddha.
“Great winds do not blow, and the rivers do not flow;
those [signs] are visible today—surely you will become a Buddha.
All flowers, whether born on land or born in water, are blooming at this very moment.”
"Today all these trees have blossomed; surely you will become a Buddha.
Whether creepers or trees, they are now laden with fruit;
today all have borne fruit; surely you will become a Buddha."
“As long as the jewels dwelling in the sky and those on the earth shone, those same jewels shine today; surely you will become a Buddha.
As long as human and divine musical instruments resounded,”
"Those very same beings rejoice; surely you will become a Buddha.
Even now, various flowers rain down from the sky;
they rain down today as well—surely you will become a Buddha."
"The great ocean rolls back, and the ten-thousandfold world system trembles;
all the heavens resound with joy: 'Surely you will become a Buddha.
Even in the ten-thousandfold world system of hells, the fires are extinguished at that very moment."
"Today the fires have been extinguished; surely you will become a Buddha.
The sun has become cloudless, yet all the stars are visible;
even they are visible today; surely you will become a Buddha."
‘At that time, water welled up from the earth without being drawn up;
even now it wells up from the earth—surely you will become a Buddha.
The hosts of stars shine forth, the constellations in the circle of the sky.
"Visākhā is joined with the moon; surely you will become a Buddha.
'Creatures dwelling in holes and caves are emerging from their own abodes;
today they have abandoned their lairs; surely you will become a Buddha.'"
“Discontent does not arise for beings; they remain content for the time being.
Since all these are content today, you will certainly become a Buddha.
Illnesses are pacified therein, and hunger is destroyed.”
"These signs are appearing today; surely you will become a Buddha.
'At that time, passion becomes thin, hatred and delusion perish;
all these are now gone away—surely you will become a Buddha.'"
“Then there was no fear, yet today it is seen;
by this sign we know for certain that you will become a Buddha.
Dust does not rise upward, yet today it is seen.”
"By this mark we know: you will certainly become a Buddha.
An unpleasant odor departs, and a pleasant fragrance wafts forth;
that fragrance spreads today—certainly you will become a Buddha."
‘All the gods appear, with the exception of those who are formless;
all of them are visible today, so surely you will become a Buddha.
As far as there are places called hells, they all are visible right now.’
"Today all these things are visible; surely you will become a Buddha.
Walls, doors, and rocks—these were not obstacles then;
having become like space today, surely you will become a Buddha."
“Death and rebirth do not exist at that moment;
those [marks] are now visible—surely you will become a Buddha.
Exert firm energy; do not turn back, but press forward!”
“Let us know this too: you will certainly become a Buddha.
Having heard the words of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara and the deities of the ten thousand world-systems, the Bodhisatta became even more resolute and thought:
“The Buddhas are indeed those whose words are never in vain; there is no falsehood in the Buddhas.”
The alteration of the narrative: For just as the falling of a clod of earth thrown into the air is certain,
the death of one who is born is certain, the rising of the sun when dawn has broken is certain, the roaring of a lion emerging from his lair is certain,
and the delivery of the burden by a woman heavy with child is an inevitable occurrence, even so the word of the Buddhas is indeed certain and unfailing.
“Surely I shall become a Buddha. Therefore it was said:
“Having heard the word of the Buddha, Both the ten-thousandfold world-system was filled with joy;
Thrilled, elated, and overjoyed, I then reflected thus.”
“The Buddhas’ words are free from duplicity; the Conquerors’ words are never in vain.
There is nothing false in the Buddhas; surely I shall become a Buddha.
Just as a clod of earth thrown into the sky will surely fall to the ground,” so it was said.
In the very same way, the word of the Best of Buddhas is permanent and eternal.
Just as death is certain and constant for all beings,
so too the word of the Best of Buddhas is permanent and eternal.
“Just as when the night has ended, the rising of the sun is certain;
even so, the word of the Best of Buddhas is certain and eternal.
Just as the roaring of a lion who has left his lair is certain;”
In the same way, the word of the Best of Buddhas is firm and eternal.
Just as the laying down of the burden for those who have taken it up is certain,
so too the word of the Best of Buddhas is firm and eternal.

Thus, having made the firm resolve, "I shall certainly become a Buddha," and seeking to investigate the qualities that constitute a Buddha, he thought, "Where indeed are these qualities that make a Buddha?
Are they above, or below, in the cardinal directions, or in the intermediate directions?

Gradually searching the entire realm of phenomena (*dhammadhātu*), he first [encountered] the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), which had been practiced and cultivated by the ancient Bodhisattvas.
Having seen this, he exhorted himself thus: "O wise Sumedha, from this day forward you must fulfill the perfection of giving first.

Just as an overturned water-jar pours out its water completely until nothing remains and does not draw it back in, even so, without looking back at wealth, fame, children, wife, or even your own limbs and members, [you must give] to those who approach as supplicants."
“Sitting at the foot of the Bodhi tree, by giving away everything desired, without exception, you will become a Buddha.
Thus he firmly established his resolve upon the first perfection, that of generosity. Therefore it is said:
“Come now, I shall search here and there for the qualities that make a Buddha.”
Above, below, and in the ten directions, as far as the realm of phenomena extends—
searching therein, I then beheld the first perfection of giving,
that great path practiced by the great seers of old.
“First, having firmly undertaken this,
go forth to the perfection of giving, if you wish to attain enlightenment.
Just as a jar that is completely full, when turned upside down— ”
"Just as one vomits water until nothing remains, without guarding anything back,
so too, upon seeing beggars— whether low, high, or middling—
give your gift completely, like a jar turned upside down."
Then, thinking to himself, "The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot be limited to these alone," he investigated further.
Seeing the second perfection, that of virtue (*sīla-pāramī*), this thought occurred to him: "O wise Sumedha, from now on you must fulfill the perfection of virtue as well.
For just as the yak-ox, disregarding even its own life, protects only its tail-hair—"
"In this way, from now on, disregarding even your own life and guarding only your virtue, you shall become a Buddha.
Thus he made a firm resolve, strengthening the second perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī). Therefore it is said:
"These qualities of a Buddha will not be merely so many;"
“I shall search for other qualities as well, those factors that ripen enlightenment.
While searching, I then beheld the second perfection, that of virtue (sīla),
which had been practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
“First, you must firmly undertake this second one;
go forth to the perfection of virtue if you wish to attain enlightenment.
Just as a yak’s tail, when caught upon anything—”
There he meets his death, yet he does not let his tail be disturbed.
“In the same way, fulfill the precepts in the four stages;
always guard your virtue as the yak guards its tail.”

Then, thinking to himself, "There must be more qualities that make one a Buddha," as he investigated further, he saw the third perfection, renunciation (*nekkhammapāramī*), and thought: "O wise Sumedha, from this time forth you should fulfill the perfection of renunciation as well.
For just as a man who has lived for a long time in a prison does not feel any affection for it..."

“Just as one who is weary of a place desires only to leave it, even so you too, having regarded all states of existence as a prison-house, being weary of all states of existence and desiring liberation, turn toward renunciation; in this way you will become a Buddha.
Thus he made firm his resolve, strengthening the third perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*). Therefore it is said:
“It will not be merely these that shall constitute the qualities of a Buddha;
I shall seek others as well—those qualities that ripen into enlightenment.
While searching, I then beheld the third perfection: renunciation.
“Practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old:
‘First, you must firmly undertake this third [perfection];
go forth to the perfection of renunciation, if you wish to attain enlightenment.’”
“Just as a man long imprisoned in a dungeon,
afflicted by suffering, does not conceive lust for it but seeks only release;
even so, you should view all states of existence as if they were that very dungeon.”
“Be intent upon renunciation for the sake of liberation from existence.
Then, thinking to himself, “The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot be limited to these alone,” he examined further.
Seeing the fourth perfection, the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*), he thought: “O wise Sumedha, from this point forward, you must also fulfill the perfection of wisdom.”
You should fulfill it. Without omitting anyone among those who are inferior, middling, or superior, you should approach all wise men and ask your question.

For just as an alms-collecting bhikkhu, by wandering for alms in succession through families—without omitting any, whether lowly or otherwise—quickly obtains enough to sustain himself, so too you, by approaching all wise men and asking your question, [will quickly attain your goal].
“By asking [these questions], you will become a Buddha”—thus he made firm his resolve, establishing the fourth perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramitā*). Therefore it is said:
“These qualities of a Buddha will not be merely these many;
I shall seek others as well, those qualities that bring enlightenment to fruition.”
“Searching, I then beheld the fourth perfection of wisdom,
practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old. Therefore,
you too, having firmly undertaken this fourth [perfection],”
Go to the perfection of wisdom if you desire to attain enlightenment.
Just as a monk, while wandering for alms, does not avoid families— whether low, high, or middling—
and thus obtains his sustenance, so too [should one proceed].
“In this very way, by constantly questioning wise people at all times,
you will reach the perfection of wisdom and attain full enlightenment.
Then, as he reflected further, thinking, “The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot be limited to just these,” he continued his investigation.
Having seen the fifth perfection, that of energy, he thought: "O Wise Sumedha, from this time forth you must fulfill the perfection of energy as well.

For just as Sīha, the king of beasts, possesses firm energy in all postures, so too, by being one whose energy is firm and unshrinking in all existences and in all postures, you shall become a Buddha."
Having made the fifth perfection, energy, firm, he resolved. Therefore it was said:
"These qualities of a Buddha will not be merely these many;
I shall seek others as well, those qualities that ripen enlightenment."
“Searching, I then beheld the fifth perfection of energy,
practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old. ‘Therefore, you too,
having made this fifth one firm, undertake it;’”
Go to the perfection of energy if you wish to attain awakening.
Just as the lion, the king of beasts, whether sitting,
standing, or walking, is always unflagging in energy with a mind ever-exerted.
“In the same way, you must exert firm energy throughout all existences;
having reached the perfection of energy, you will attain full enlightenment.
Then, as he reflected further, thinking, “It cannot be that there are only these qualities that make one a Buddha,” he investigated even more deeply.
Having seen the sixth perfection of patience, he thought: "O wise Sumedha, from this time forth you should fulfill the perfection of patience as well.
Whether treated with honor or with contempt, you should remain patient.
For just as when they cast both the pure and the impure upon the earth, the earth feels neither affection nor resentment, but remains patient and enduring."
“‘He indeed consented, saying: "In this way, you too, being one who endures both honor and dishonor, will become a Buddha.
Thus, having made firm the sixth Perfection of Forbearance, he resolved. Therefore it was said:
'These alone shall not be all the qualities of a Buddha...'"
“I will investigate others as well, those qualities that ripen enlightenment.
While investigating, I then beheld the sixth perfection, patience,
which had been practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
“First, having firmly undertaken this sixth [precept],
with a mind free from doubt therein, you will attain full enlightenment.
Just as that which is called ‘earth’ [holds] both the pure and the impure...”
“He endures everything when it is cast upon him, and he does not harbor resentment toward you.
In the same way, you too must endure both honor and dishonor from all;
having reached the perfection of patience, you will attain supreme enlightenment.”

Then, thinking, "The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot be limited to these alone," as he investigated further, he saw the seventh perfection, Truth (sacca-pāramī), and this thought occurred to him: "O wise Sumedha, from now on you must fulfill the perfection of truth as well.
Even if a thunderbolt were to fall upon your head, you must not, for the sake of wealth or other interests, knowingly speak a falsehood through desire or other such motives."

“Do not utter what is called a lie. For just as the star Osadhītārakā, in all seasons, does not abandon its own path of travel and go by another path, but travels only by its own path, even so you too, by abandoning truth and never committing what is called a lie, will become a Buddha.
Thus he made firm his resolve, strengthening the seventh perfection of truth. Therefore it is said:
“It will not be merely these that constitute the qualities of a Buddha;
I shall seek others as well—those qualities that ripen into enlightenment.
While searching, I then beheld the seventh perfection: Truth.
“Practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old:
‘Having firmly undertaken this seventh [precept] for now,
and being free from duplicity of speech therein, you shall attain full enlightenment.’”
“Just as the plant known as Osadhi, acting as a scale for the world including the gods,
does not deviate from its course at the proper time of the seasons or the rains;
even so, you too must not deviate from the course of truths.”
“Having gone to the perfection of truth, you will attain full enlightenment.

Then, as he reflected further, thinking, “It cannot be that there are only these qualities that make one a Buddha,” and seeing the eighth, the perfection of determination (*adhiṭṭhānapāramī*), it occurred to him:
“O wise Sumedha, from this time forth, you must also [practice] the perfection of determination.”
"You shall fulfill it. In whatever you resolve, you shall remain unshakable in that resolution.

For just as a mountain, though struck by winds from all directions, neither trembles nor wavers but remains exactly where it stands, even so you too, remaining unshakable in your own resolution, shall become a Buddha"—thus he spoke regarding the eighth perfection of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī*).
He made a firm resolution. Therefore it was said:
“These are not the only Buddha-qualities there will be;
I shall search for others as well, those qualities that ripen into enlightenment.”
“Searching, I then beheld the eighth perfection of determination (adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī),
which was practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
‘Therefore, you too, having firmly undertaken this eighth [perfection],’”
Remaining unshakable therein, you shall attain perfect enlightenment.
"Just as a rocky mountain, immovable and well-established,
Does not tremble before violent winds, but stands firm in its own place."
“In the same way, you too must always remain unshakable in your resolve;
having reached the perfection of resolve, you shall attain full enlightenment.
Then, as he reflected further, thinking, “The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot be limited to just these,” he continued his investigation.

Having seen the ninth perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī*), this thought occurred to him: "O Wise Sumedha, from this point forward you should fulfill the ninth perfection of loving-kindness as well.
You should maintain a single-minded attitude toward both those who wish you harm and those who wish you well.
For just as water, indeed, pervades both wicked people and virtuous people alike, making its coolness exactly the same for all, even so..."

“You too, by maintaining a single-minded state of loving-kindness toward all beings, will become a Buddha. Thus he made firm his resolve, strengthening the ninth perfection of loving-kindness. Therefore it is said:
“These qualities of a Buddha will not be merely these many;”
“I shall investigate other qualities as well, those factors that ripen enlightenment.
While investigating, I then beheld the ninth perfection, loving-kindness (*mettā*),
which had been practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
“First, having firmly undertaken this ninth [precept],
be peerless in loving-kindness if you wish to attain enlightenment.
Just as water, indeed, [is the same] toward both good and evil people...”
"It spreads coolness equally and blows away dust and impurity.
In the same way, you too should cultivate loving-kindness equally toward both the harmful and the beneficial;
having reached the perfection of loving-kindness, you will attain supreme enlightenment."

Then, thinking, "The qualities that make one a Buddha cannot be limited to these alone," as he investigated further, he beheld the tenth perfection, equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*), and this thought occurred to him: "O Wise Sumedha, from now on you must fulfill the perfection of equanimity as well.
Whether in pleasure or in pain, you must remain perfectly neutral. For just as the earth, even when [covered with] filth..."
"Even when impurities are thrown into it, it remains neutral; even so, you too, remaining neutral amidst pleasure and pain, will become a Buddha.
Thus he made firm his resolve by strengthening the tenth perfection, equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*). Therefore it is said:
"These shall not be merely these many qualities of a Buddha..."
“I shall seek out other qualities as well, those states that ripen into enlightenment.
While searching, I then beheld the tenth perfection, equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī),
which had been practiced and cultivated by the great seers of old.
“First, having firmly undertaken this tenth precept,
and becoming firm like a scale, you will attain full enlightenment.
Just as the earth, indeed, treats both the impure and the pure alike;”
“He remains equanimous toward both of these, free from aversion and attachment.
In the same way, you too should always remain like a balance scale toward pleasure and pain;
having reached the perfection of equanimity, you will attain full enlightenment.”
Then he reflected: “In this world, the qualities that bring about Buddhahood—the factors for maturing enlightenment that must be fulfilled by Bodhisattvas—are only these;
there are no others apart from the ten perfections (pāramīs).
These ten perfections do not exist above in the sky, nor below in the earth, nor in the directions such as the east; they exist only within the very flesh of my own heart.”
"Established. Having thus seen that they were established in their hearts, he resolved with firm determination;
and repeatedly contemplating them, he contemplates them in direct and reverse order: taking the end, he brings it to the beginning;
taking the beginning, he places it at the end; taking the middle, he brings it out from both ends; and taking hold of both ends...

He pours it out in the middle. The relinquishing of external goods is called the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramī*); the relinquishing of limbs is called the near-perfection of giving (*dāna-upapāramī*);
and the relinquishing of life is called the ultimate perfection of giving (*dāna-paramatthapāramī*).

Thus, as if turning the oil of a machine, he makes Mount Meru his head and [fills] the great ocean of the world-system with the ten perfections, the ten near-perfections, and the ten ultimate perfections.
And as he was thus reflecting upon the ten perfections, this great earth— though it is two hundred and forty thousand yojanas in thickness—
trembled, quaked, and shook violently under the majesty of his Dhamma, like a bundle of reeds trampled by an elephant,
or like a field of sugarcane being pressed. It revolved like a potter’s wheel or an oil-pressing wheel, uttering a great roar.
And I wandered about as if [in a dream]. Therefore it was said:
“Only so many things in this world are those factors that ripen enlightenment;
there is nothing beyond these. Stand firm therein.”
“As he comprehends these phenomena— each with its own essential nature, inherent tendency,
and characteristic— the earth of the ten-thousandfold world system trembles through the power of that Dhamma.
The earth shakes and roars like a field of sugar-cane being pressed.”
“As if an oil-lamp were being whirled, so does the earth tremble.
When the great earth shook, the inhabitants of the city of Ramma were unable to stand their ground;
like great sāla trees struck by the winds at the end of an eon, they fell down repeatedly in a swoon, while clay pots and other vessels rolled about.
Striking one another, they were reduced to powder and dust. The great multitude, terrified and trembling, approached the Teacher and said:
"What is this, Blessed One? Is this a serpent-demon (*nāga*), or is it one among the spirits, *yakṣas*, or deities?
Indeed, we do not know this; moreover, this entire great multitude is afflicted. What indeed has happened to this world?"
"Will this result in evil, or will it be auspicious? Tell us the reason for this," he said.
Then the Teacher, having heard their conversation, said: "Do not fear, do not worry; you have no cause for fear on this account.
He whom I have today prophesied as the wise Sumedha, saying, 'In the future he shall become a Buddha named Gotama'—"

"He contemplates the ten perfections; as he contemplates and churns the ten perfections, by the power of his Dhamma, the entire ten-thousandfold world system shakes and resounds all at once. Thus it was said:
"As far as the assembly gathered for the Buddha’s meal distribution..."
Trembling there, she fell unconscious and lay upon the ground:
“Thousands of jars and many hundreds of pots were crushed and pounded there,
clashing violently against one another.”
“Agitated, thirsty, and terrified, their minds bewildered and distressed, the great masses of people gathered together and approached Dīpaṅkara, asking:
‘What will happen to the world? Will it be auspicious or evil?’”
“The entire world is distressed; dispel that, O Visionary One!
Then Dīpaṅkara, the Great Sage, reassured them:
“Be confident, do not fear this trembling of the earth.”
“Today I have prophesied: ‘He shall become a Buddha in the world.
He now comprehends the Dhamma, that which was practiced by the Conquerors of old.
As he comprehends the Dhamma, he will reach the stage of a Buddha without exception.”
"Therefore this earth, together with its ten thousand worlds and its gods, has trembled.
Having heard these words of the Tathāgata, the great multitude was joyful and delighted;
taking flowers, perfumes, and ointments, they departed from the city of Ramma, approached the Bodhisatta, honored him with the flowers and other offerings, paid homage, and circumambulated him.

He entered Ramma-nagara itself. The Bodhisatta, too, having reflected upon the ten perfections (pāramīs) and having made his effort firm, rose from the seat where he sat with resolute determination. Thus it is said:
“Having heard the word of the Buddha, my mind was instantly extinguished.”
All of them approached me and once again paid homage.
Having undertaken the qualities of a Buddha and made my mind firm,
I then rose from my seat after paying reverence to Dīpaṅkara.
Then, as the Bodhisatta was rising from his seat, the devas of the entire ten-thousandfold world-system gathered together;
having honored him with celestial garlands and perfumes and having paid homage to him, they said:

"Noble Sumedha ascetic, today at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, the Ten-Powered One, you have made a great aspiration. May it be fulfilled for you without obstacle; let there be no fear for you."
“May there be no trembling, nor may even the slightest ailment arise in your body; quickly fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs), may you realize perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi).
Just as trees that bear flowers and fruits blossom and bear fruit in their proper season, even so, without overstepping the right time, may you quickly touch the supreme enlightenment,” and so forth.
They recited auspicious verses of praise; having thus offered their praise, they each departed for their own celestial abodes.

The Bodhisatta, too, being extolled by the deities, strengthened his resolve and made a firm determination, thinking: "Having fulfilled the ten perfections, I shall become a Buddha at the conclusion of four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons."
Having ascended into the sky, he went back to the Himālaya itself. Therefore it was said:
“Divine and human flowers—both gods and humans alike— Sprinkle him with flowers as he rises from his seat.”
“Both gods and humans alike proclaim your well-being:
‘May you obtain that great boon you have desired, just as you wish!
May all perils be averted; may sorrow and disease perish!’”
“May there be no obstacles for you; quickly touch supreme enlightenment.
Just as when the proper season has arrived, flowering trees burst into bloom, even so, O Great Hero, may you blossom with the wisdom of a Buddha.”
“Just as all those who were perfectly enlightened fulfilled the ten perfections,
even so may you, O Great Hero, fulfill the ten perfections.
Just as all those who were perfectly enlightened awakened at the seat of enlightenment...”
In that very way, O Great Hero, awaken to the enlightenment of the Conqueror.
Just as all those who were perfectly enlightened set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma,
even so, O Great Hero, set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
“As the moon on the full-moon night shines forth completely pure, even so do you,
O one of fulfilled mind, shine throughout the ten thousandfold world-system.
As the sun, released from Rāhu, outshines all with its heat.”
In that same way, having liberated the worlds, you shine with glory.
"Just as whatever rivers flow toward the great ocean,
so may the worlds, together with their devas, flow toward you."
“Praised and extolled by them, having undertaken ten qualities and fulfilling those qualities, he then entered the forest.
The Story of Sumedha is concluded.
The inhabitants of Ramma-nagara also, having entered the city, gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
The Teacher, having taught the Dhamma to them and established the great multitude in the refuges and other precepts, departed from Ramma-nagara;
and thereafter, remaining for as long as his lifespan lasted, he performed all the duties of a Buddha and, in due course—
