He attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without remainder. Whatever needs to be said regarding this matter should be understood entirely according to the method already stated in the *Buddhavaṃsa*. For it is said there:
“Then, having fed the Leader of the World together with his Saṅgha...”
They went for refuge to that Teacher, Dīpaṅkara.
“The Tathāgata established some in the going for refuge;
others he established in the five precepts, and others in the tenfold morality.”
“To some he gives the state of recluseship, the four supreme fruits;
to some he gives the peerless states, the analytical knowledges.
To some the Bull among Men gives the eight excellent attainments.”
The Great Sage bestows the three types of clear knowledge and the six supernormal powers upon anyone [who is worthy].
By means of that practice, he instructs the multitude of people;
by that means, the teaching of the Lord of the World became widespread.
“Mahāhanu, Sabhakkhandha, and Dīpaṅkara by name—
these deliver many people and liberate them from miserable rebirths.
Seeing those capable of being awakened, even at a distance of a hundred thousand yojanas,”
Approaching in an instant, the Great Sage awakened him:
"At the first realization, the Buddha awakened one hundred koṭis;
at the second realization, the Protector awakened ninety koṭis."
“And when the Buddha taught the Dhamma in the abode of the gods,
there was a third realization for ninety thousand koṭis.
There were three assemblies under the Teacher Dīpaṅkara.”
The first assembly consisted of one hundred thousand times ten million [beings].
Later, when the Conqueror had retired to solitude at Nāradakūṭa,
a hundred million [beings] who were free from taints and devoid of impurities gathered together.
“At the time when the Great Hero, the Great Sage,
was offering alms to ninety thousand koṭis on the Sudassana mountain of stone,
I at that time was a matted-hair ascetic practicing fierce austerities.”
Wandering through the sky, he had reached the further shore of the five higher knowledges.
There was the realization of the Dhamma by ten or twenty thousand;
those who attained realization were beyond counting, numbering one or two.
“Extensive, well-known, prosperous,
and flourishing was the teaching of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara at that time, having been thoroughly purified.
Four hundred thousand [monks], possessing the six direct knowledges and great psychic power,”
They always attend upon Dīpaṅkara, the knower of the world.
"Whoever at that time abandons human existence,
being trainees who have not yet attained the mind [of arahantship], they become objects of reproach."
“The well-flowered Pāvacana shines forth in the world of gods, through the Tathāgatas, the Arahants, those with taints destroyed and stainless.
There was a city named Rammavatī, and a kshatriya named Sudeva.”
The mother of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara was named Sumedhā.
Sumaṅgala and Tissa were his two chief disciples,
and the attendant of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara was named Sāgata.
“Nandā and Sunandā were his chief female disciples;
the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Pipphalī.
Dīpaṅkara, the Great Sage, was eighty cubits in height.”
He shines like a lamp-tree, like a king of sal trees in full bloom.
For a hundred thousand years was the lifespan of that Great Sage;
remaining for that long, he delivered many people.
“Having kindled the True Dhamma and having brought across the great multitude of people,
he— like a blazing mass of fire— has attained Nibbāna together with his disciples. That psychic power, that fame, and those wheel-treasures upon his feet...”
"All that has vanished; are not all conditioned things empty?
Then, after the passing of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, once an incalculable aeon had elapsed, a Teacher named Koṇḍañña appeared.
He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand koṭis.

In the second [assembly] there were one thousand koṭis, and in the third ninety koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a wheel-turning monarch named Vijitāvī, gave a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus numbering one hundred thousand koṭis, headed by the Buddha.
The Teacher, having prophesied to the Bodhisatta, "You will become a Buddha," taught the Dhamma. He [the Bodhisatta] [listened to] the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma...

Having heard this, he handed over the kingdom and went forth. Having mastered the three Piṭakas and attained the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), he was reborn in the Brahma-world without ever falling away from his jhāna.
As for the Buddha Koṇḍañña, however, his city was named Rammavatī; his father was the kshatriya Sunanda, his mother was Queen Sujātā, and [his son] was Bhadda.
Subhadda was his second chief disciple; Anuruddha by name was his attendant; Tissā and Upatissā were his two chief female disciples;
the Sāla-kalyāṇī was his Bodhi tree; his body was eighty-eight cubits in height; and the measure of his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
After Dīpaṅkara, there was a Leader named Koṇḍañña.
“Of infinite splendor, immeasurable fame, unfathomable, and invincible.
After that, having passed one incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyya*), four Buddhas appeared in a single aeon:
Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, and Sobhita. There were three assemblies during the time of the Blessed One Maṅgala. Among them—
At the first assembly, there were one hundred billion monks; at the second, one thousand billion; and at the third, ninety billion.
It is said that his half-brother, Prince Ānanda, went into the presence of the Teacher with a retinue numbering ninety billion for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
The Teacher delivered a graduated discourse to him, and he, together with the assembly...
He attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).

The Teacher, surveying the past conduct of those sons of good family and seeing the supporting condition for their supernaturally produced bowls and robes, extended his right hand and said, "Come, monks.
At that very moment, they all became endowed with proper deportment, wearing supernaturally produced bowls and robes like great elders of sixty years' standing.
Having made the offering and paid homage to the Teacher, they surrounded him. This was his third assembly of disciples.
Whereas the bodily radiance of other Buddhas extended only for a distance of eighty cubits all around, the bodily radiance of that Blessed One constantly pervaded the ten-thousandfold world system.

He stood there. The trees, the earth, the mountains, the oceans, and so forth—even down to the mortars and other utensils—became as if covered with golden plates. His lifespan was ninety thousand years.

During that time, the moon, the sun, and the other celestial bodies were unable to shine by their own light, and the distinction between night and day was not perceived. By day, through the light of the sun...

Beings wandered about constantly by means of the Buddha’s radiance alone; they discerned the distinction between night and day through flowers blooming in the evening and through birds and other creatures crying out at dawn.
But does this majesty not belong to other Buddhas as well? It does not fail them; for they too, if they so desire—

They might illuminate a world-system of ten thousand worlds, or even more, with their radiance. However, by virtue of the Blessed One Maṅgala’s former aspiration, his bodily radiance—unlike that of others which is limited to a fathom—remained at all times pervading a world-system of ten thousand worlds.
It is said that while he was practicing the conduct of a Bodhisatta, existing in an existence such as that of Vessantara, together with his children and wife...

He dwelt on a mountain resembling Mount Vaṅka. Then, a certain yakkha named Kharadāṭhika, having heard of the Great Being’s inclination toward generosity, approached him in the guise of a brahmin and asked the Great Being for his two children.
The Great Being, with a joyful heart, saying, "I give these two children to the brahmin," shook the earth as far as its watery boundaries, giving both children away.
He gave them. Standing at the edge of the walkway leaning against a support-board, the yakkha devoured the two children like bundles of roots even as the Great Being was looking on.
When the Great Man looked at the yakkha and saw its mouth—just as it opened—vomiting streams of blood like a mass of flames, not even a hair’s breadth of dejection arose in him.
It did not arise. However, as he thought, "Truly, my gift was well-bestowed," a great rapture and joy arose within his body. He made this aspiration:
"By the result of this, may rays of light issue forth from my body in this very manner in the future.
Based on that aspiration, when he became a Buddha, rays of light issued forth from his body.
They pervaded that much space.

Furthermore, he has another past deed: it is said that in his time as a Bodhisatta, upon seeing the stupa of a certain Buddha, he thought, "It is fitting for me to sacrifice my life for this Buddha," and according to the method of wrapping a torch around a staff—
Having wrapped his entire body [in fine cloth], he filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [pieces]—adorned with a crest-jewel the size of a gem—with clarified butter;
having lit a thousand wicks therein, he took it upon his head, wrapped his entire body in flames, and spent the whole night performing circumambulations of the Cetiya.
Thus, even as he exerted himself until the rising of the sun, he remained there.
Not even a breath of heat reached the pores of his skin; it was as if he had entered the interior of a lotus.
Indeed, this Dhamma protects him who protects himself. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives according to Dhamma; Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness.”
“This is the blessing when the Dhamma is well-practiced: one who lives according to the Dhamma does not go to an evil destination.
Through the outflow of this very deed, the radiance from the Blessed One’s body remained pervading the ten-thousandfold world system.
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having become a brahmin named Suruci, approached [the Buddha] with the thought, “I shall invite the Teacher.”
Having heard the sweet discourse on the Dhamma, he said, "Venerable sir, please accept my alms tomorrow.
The Buddha asked, "Brāhmaṇa, how many bhikkhus do you require? He replied, "And how many, venerable sir, are in your retinue of bhikkhus?
At that time, it was the very first assembly of the Teacher, so he said, "One hundred thousand times ten million. "Venerable sir..."
“Accept alms from me at my house together with all of them. The Teacher consented.

Having invited [them] for the following day, the brahmin went home and thought: “I am able to provide so many bhikkhus with rice porridge, food, robes, and so forth, but how will there be a place for them to sit?”
That thought produced heat upon the stone throne of Paṇḍukambala, which stood eighty-four thousand yojanas above, belonging to the king of the gods.
Sakka, wondering, "Who indeed desires to displace me from this place?", surveyed with his divine eye and saw the Great Man.
He then perceived that a brahmin named Suruci had invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
He thought, "It would be fitting for me to go there as well and take a portion of the merit.
Assuming the guise of a carpenter, with axe and adze in hand, he appeared before the Great Man.
Seeing him, the Great Man asked, "What work will you do? Is there anything that needs to be done for wages?"
He said, "I have no craft that I do not know; whatever house or pavilion anyone has built, I know how to build it.

"In that case, I have work for you. "What is it, noble lady? "For tomorrow, I have invited one hundred thousand times ten million bhikkhus; you shall build a sitting pavilion for them. "I would indeed build it, if I were to receive wages..."
“Will you be able to give it? “I shall be able to do so, dear father,” he replied. “Very well, I will do it,” he said, and having gone there, he looked upon a certain spot;
that area, measuring twelve or thirteen yojanas, became level like a *kasiṇa* disk.
He then thought, “Let a pavilion made of the seven precious gems arise in this much space,” and as soon as he looked, the earth [responded].
Having split open, the pavilion rose up. Upon its pillars made of gold were water-pots made of silver;

upon those made of silver, those made of gold; upon pillars of jewels, those made of coral; upon pillars of coral, those made of jewels; and upon those made of the seven precious gems, there were likewise water-pots made of the seven precious gems.
Then [he thought], "Let a network of small bells hang down throughout the interior of the pavilion."
He looked out, and at the very moment of his looking, a network of small bells hung down;
when stirred by a gentle breeze, a sweet sound issued from it like that of a five-fold musical ensemble, as if it were the time for the performance of celestial music.
He thought, "Let garlands of perfumes and flower-garlands hang down here and there," and the garlands hung down. [He thought of] those numbering one hundred thousand crores...
He thought, "Let the seats and the pedestals for the monks spring up from the ground," and at that very moment they sprang up.
He thought, "Let a water-jar appear in every corner," and the water-jars appeared.
Having created all this, he went into the presence of the brahmin and said, "Come, noble sir; having looked at your pavilion, [look at] mine..."
"Give me wages," he said. The Great Man went and looked at the pavilion;
even as he was looking, his entire body became suffused without interruption by five-colored rapture. Then, as he gazed upon the pavilion, this thought occurred to him:
"This pavilion was not made by any human being, but rather by means of my own aspiration and my own virtue."
“Surely the abode of Sakka must have become hot; therefore, this pavilion must have been caused to be built by Sakka, the king of the gods.
He thought, “It is not fitting for me to give alms in such a pavilion for only a single day; I shall give them for seven days.
For no matter how great an external gift may be, it is unable to bring satisfaction to the Bodhisattvas.
But when one has cut off the adorned head, gouged out the anointed eyes, or torn out the heart-flesh and given them away,
there arises what is called joy based on the generosity of the Bodhisattvas. For even in our own Bodhisattva’s *Sivi Jātaka*,
he distributed five hundred thousand kahāpaṇas every day at the four gates and in the middle of the city.
While he was giving that gift, it was unable to produce the joy of renunciation within him.
However, when Sakka, King of the Devas, approached in the guise of a brahmin and begged for his eyes, then, even as he was plucking them out and giving them away, laughter arose;
there was not even a hair’s breadth of change in his mind. Thus, through the power of giving, the Bodhisattas find no satiety.

There was no such thing as a lack of means. Therefore, that Great Being, thinking, "It is fitting for me to give alms for seven days to monks numbering one hundred thousand crores," had the Saṅgha of monks, headed by the Buddha, seated in that pavilion and gave for seven days the gift known as *gavapāna*.
*Gavapāna* refers to [the pouring of] milk from large, large jars (*kolamba*).
Having filled [the vessels] and placed them on the hearths, when the milk had been cooked until thick and solid, they added a small amount of rice;
this food, prepared with boiled honey, sugar-candy powder, and clarified butter, is what is called [the meal]. However, humans alone were unable to serve it;
even the gods served it at intervals. Furthermore, the monks were able to occupy a space measuring twelve or thirteen yojanas.
It was simply not enough. However, those monks sat down according to their own respective supernatural powers.
On the final day, having had the bowls of all the monks washed and filled with ghee, fresh butter, honey, molasses, and other medicinal requisites, he gave them along with the three robes;
the robes and garments received by the most junior monk of the Saṅgha were worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
The Teacher, offering words of appreciation, reflected, "This man has given such a great gift; who indeed will he become?
As he investigated, he saw that "in the future, at the conclusion of two incalculable eons plus one hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will appear.
Having seen this, he addressed the Great Man: "After this much time has passed, you—"
“You will become a Buddha named Gotama,” he prophesied. Having heard this prophecy, the Great Man thought, “I shall indeed become a Buddha;
what need have I for the life of a householder? I shall go forth.

Abandoning such magnificent prosperity as if it were a globule of spittle, he went forth in the presence of the Teacher, mastered the word of the Buddha, and attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Having attained the various meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he was reborn in the Brahma-world at the end of his lifespan.
The city of the Blessed One Maṅgala was named Uttara;
his father was a kshatriya named Uttara, and his mother was Queen Uttarā. Sudeva and Dhammasena were his two chief disciples, and Pālita was his attendant.
Sīvalī and Asokā were his two chief female disciples; his Bodhi tree was the Nāga tree; and his body was eighty-eight cubits in height.
When that Blessed One passed away after remaining for ninety thousand years, ten thousand world-systems simultaneously became one vast darkness.
Among all the world-systems, the humans experienced great...
There was weeping and lamentation:
“After Koṇḍañña, the Leader named Maṅgala appeared;
having destroyed the darkness in the world, he upheld the Dhamma-faring.”
Thus, after that Blessed One had passed away into *parinibbāna* having enveloped the ten-thousandfold world-system in darkness, at a later time, a Teacher named Sumana arose.
He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand times ten million (*koṭisatasahassa*) monks;
in the second, on the Golden Mountain (*Kañcanapabbata*), ninety thousand times ten million; and in the third...
There were eighty thousand crores. At that time, the Great Being was a Nāga king named Atula, possessed of great psychic power and majesty.

Hearing that "a Buddha has appeared," he departed from the Nāga realm surrounded by his kinsmen and, having caused a presentation of divine musical instruments for that Blessed One who was accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand crores of monks, he distributed a great almsgiving and offered pairs of garments to each individual.
Having given [the gift], he established himself in the Refuges. The Teacher also prophesied of him: "In the future, you shall become a Buddha.
That Blessed One’s city was named Khema; his father was King Sudatta, his mother was named Sirimā, and his two chief disciples were Saraṇa and Bhāvitatta.
His attendant was named Udena, and his two female lay disciples were Soṇā and Upasoṇā.
His chief female disciple was Nāgarukkha, his Bodhi tree was the Nāga-tree, his body was ninety cubits in height, and the measure of his lifespan was ninety thousand years.
"After Maṅgala, the Leader named Sumana appeared;
peerless in all qualities, supreme among all beings."
In a later period, a teacher named Revata appeared. He too had three assemblies of disciples.
In the first assembly, there was no counting; in the second, there were one hundred thousand koṭis of bhikkhus; likewise in the third.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a brahmin named Atideva, heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma and established himself in the refuges.
Placing his hands in anjali at his head, he praised that Teacher for his abandonment of the defilements and made an offering with his upper robe.
He, too, prophesied of him, "You shall become a Buddha. Furthermore, the city of that Blessed One was named Dhaññavatī;
his father was the khattiya named Vipula, and his mother was the queen named Vipulā; [his son was] Varuṇa...
Brahmadeva and [another] were the two chief disciples; his attendant was named Sambhava; Bhaddā and Subhaddā were the two chief female disciples;
his Bodhi tree was the Nāga-tree; his body was eighty cubits in height; and his lifespan was sixty thousand years.
After Sumanas, the Leader named Revata appeared.
“Matchless, peerless, incomparable, supreme is the Jina.
Later than him, a Teacher named Sobhita arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples:
in the first assembly there were one hundred koṭis of bhikkhus; in the second, ninety koṭis; and in the third, eighty koṭis.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a brahmin named Ajita, heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, established himself in the refuges, and gave a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. He too prophesied of him: "You will become a Buddha.
That Blessed One’s city was named Sudhamma, and his father was also named Sudhamma.
The king was Sudhamma; the queen was also named Sudhammā. The two chief disciples were Asama and Sunetta. The attendant was named Anoma.
The two chief female disciples were Nakulā and Sujātā. The Bodhi tree was a Nāga-tree.
His body was eighty-eight cubits in height, and the lifespan was ninety thousand years.
“After Revata, there was a leader named Sobhita;
he was concentrated, with a peaceful mind, peerless and without equal.
After his time, once one incalculable aeon had passed, three Buddhas appeared within a single aeon.
Anomadassī, Paduma, and Nārada. The Blessed One Anomadassī had three assemblies of disciples.
In the first assembly there were eight hundred thousand bhikkhus; in the second, seven; and in the third, six.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was a single yakkha general, possessed of great psychic power and great majesty, [surrounded by] many hundreds of thousands of koṭis.
He was the lord of the *yakkhas*. Having heard that "a Buddha has appeared," he came and gave a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
The Teacher also prophesied of him: "In the future, you will become a Buddha.
Now, for the Blessed One Anomadassi, there was a city named Candavatī; his father was a king named Yasavā, and [his mother] was named Yasodharā.
His mother was Nisabhā, his two chief disciples were Anoma and Varuṇa, his attendant was named Upaṭṭhāka, and his two chief female disciples were Sundarī and Sumanā.
His Bodhi tree was the Ajjuṇa tree, his body was eighty-eight cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
After Sobhita, there was another Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds.
“Anomadassī of immeasurable fame, radiant and difficult to surpass.
Subsequently, in a later period, a Teacher named Paduma arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples.
In the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand koṭis of bhikkhus; in the second, three hundred thousand; and in the third—
In a forest devoid of villages, there were two hundred thousand bhikkhus dwelling in a great woodland grove.
At that time, while the Tathāgata was residing in that woodland grove, the Bodhisatta, having become a lion, saw the Teacher having entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
With a mind full of faith, he paid homage, performed a circumambulation, and, filled with joy and gladness, let out a lion’s roar three times.

Having roared for seven days, without abandoning the joy inspired by the Buddha as its object, and without departing from his range even while in that state of rapture and bliss, he remained in attendance, having renounced his life. At the end of the seven days, the Teacher emerged from cessation;
looking at the lion, he thought, "He will also clear his mind toward the Saṅgha of monks and pay homage to the Saṅgha. Thus, the Saṅgha of monks...
"Let him come," he thought. At that very moment, the monks arrived. Sīha developed serene confidence in the Saṅgha.
The Teacher, observing his mind, prophesied: "In the future, you will become a Buddha.
For the Blessed One Paduma, however, there was a city named Campaka; his father was King Asama, his mother was Queen Asamā, and [his brother] was Sāla.
Upasāla and two other chief disciples, Varuṇa by name as the attendant, Rāmā and Surāmā as the two chief female disciples,
the Bodhi tree named Soṇarukkha, a body eighty-eight cubits in height, and a lifespan of one hundred thousand years.
After Anomadassi, there was another Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds.
"Named Paduma, peerless and without equal.
Later, a teacher named Nārada appeared. He too had three assemblies of disciples:
in the first assembly there were one hundred thousand times ten million bhikkhus; in the second, ninety thousand times ten million; and in the third...

There were eighty thousand crores. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having gone forth as an ascetic and attained mastery over the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments, gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha and performed worship with red sandalwood.
He, too, prophesied of him: "In the future, you will become a Buddha. Of him—
The Blessed One’s city was named Dhaññavatī; his father was a kshatriya named Sudeva, and his mother was named Anomā.
His two chief disciples were Saddhasāla and Jitamitta; his attendant was named Vāseṭṭha; his two chief female disciples were Uttarā and Phaggunī;
his Bodhi tree was named Mahāsoṇa; and his body was eighty-eight cubits in height.
“The lifespan was ninety thousand years.
Following Paduma, there was a perfectly enlightened Buddha, the supreme among bipeds,
named Nārada by name, peerless and without equal.”

After the time of the Buddha Nārada, once an incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyya*) had passed, one hundred thousand aeons ago, in a single aeon, there arose a single Buddha named Padumuttara. He too had three assemblies of disciples.
In the first assembly, there were one hundred billion monks; in the second, on Mount Vebhāra, there were ninety-nine billion.

In the third [calculation], there were eighty thousand koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a great ṛṣi named Jaṭila, gave a gift of robes to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. He, too, prophesied of him: "In the future, you will become a Buddha.
However, during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, there were no so-called *titthiyas*; all gods and humans [revered] only the Buddha.
They went for refuge. His city was named Haṃsavatī; his father was the kṣatriya Ānanda; his mother was Queen Sujātā;
Devala and Sujāta were his two chief disciples; Sumana was his attendant;
Amitā and Asamā were his two chief female disciples; the Salala tree was his Bodhi tree; and his body was fifty-eight cubits in height.
His bodily radiance extended twelve yojanas all around, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
"After Nārada, there appeared a Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds;
the Conqueror named Padumuttara, unshakable like the ocean."
After a further period of seventy thousand eons had passed, two Buddhas were born in a single eon: Sumedha and Sujāta.
Sumedha also had three assemblies of disciples: in the first assembly, in the city of Sudassana, there were one hundred and ten million who had destroyed the taints;
in the second, ninety million; and in the third, eighty million.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been a young brahmin named Uttara, released his eighty crores of wealth which had been set aside as a hoard and gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Having heard the Dhamma, he established himself in the refuges, went forth from the household life, and was ordained.
The Blessed One also prophesied of him: "In the future, you shall become a Buddha. This was concerning the Blessed One Sumedha.
There was a city named Sudassana; his father was a king named Sudatta, and his mother was also named Sudattā.
His two chief disciples were Saraṇa and Sabbakāma; his attendant was named Sāgara; his two chief female disciples were Rāmā and Surāmā.
His Bodhi tree was the Mahānīpa tree, his body was eighty-eight cubits in height, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.
“After Padumuttara, there was a leader named Sumedha, a sage difficult to approach, of fierce majesty, the most excellent in all the world.
After him, a Teacher named Sujāta arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples.
At the first assembly there were six million monks; at the second, fifty thousand; and at the third, forty thousand.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been a wheel-turning monarch, heard that "a Buddha has arisen," and having approached and heard the Dhamma, he offered the kingdom of the four great continents, together with the seven treasures, to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
Having given [this], he went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher.

The inhabitants of the entire kingdom, taking up the office of *raṭṭhuppāda* (steward), constantly offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. The Teacher also prophesied of him:
"In the future, you shall become a Buddha. The city of that Blessed One was named Sumaṅgala.
His father was King Uggata, his mother was named Pabhāvatī, his two chief disciples were Sudassana and Sudeva, his attendant was named Nārada,
his two chief female disciples were Nāgā and Nāgasamālā, and his Bodhi tree was the Mahāveḷu (Great Bamboo) tree.
It is said that this tree had small openings and a dense trunk, with great branches extending upward like a bundle of peacock feathers.
He shone forth. The body of that Blessed One was fifty cubits in height, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.
"In that very Maṇḍa-kappa, there was a Leader named Sujāta;
with a jaw like a lion's and shoulders like a bull's, he was immeasurable and difficult to approach."
In a later period, one hundred and eighteen aeons ago from now, three Buddhas—Piyadassī, Atthadassī, and Dhammadassī—appeared in a single aeon. Piyadassī also had three assemblies of disciples:
in the first there were one hundred and ten koṭis of bhikkhus, in the second ninety koṭis, and in the third eighty koṭis.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was a young brahmin named Kassapa who had mastered the three Vedas.
Having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he built a monastery at the cost of one hundred thousand million pieces of wealth and established himself in the refuges and the precepts.
Then the Teacher prophesied of him: "In the passing of eighteen hundred aeons, you shall become a Buddha. Of that Blessed One...
There was a city named Anoma; his father was King Sudinna, and his mother was Queen Candā.
Pālita and Sabbadassī were the two chief disciples, and Sobhita was the attendant. Sujātā and Dhammadinnā were the two chief female disciples.
The Kakudha tree was his Bodhi tree; his body was eighty cubits in height, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.
“After Sujāta, the Self-Existent One, the Leader of the World, difficult to approach, unequaled and peerless, Piyadassī of great renown [appeared].
After him, a Teacher named Atthadassī arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples.
In the first assembly there were eight million nine hundred thousand bhikkhus; in the second, eight million eight hundred thousand; and likewise in the third.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a powerful ascetic named Susīma, brought a mandārava flower parasol from the deva-world and honored the Teacher;
he, too, prophesied of him: "In the future, you shall become a Buddha. Of him—
The Blessed One’s city was named Sobhita; his father was King Sāgara; his mother was named Sudassanā;
his two chief disciples were Santo and Upasanto; his attendant was named Abhaya; his two chief female disciples were Dhammā and Sudhammā;
his Bodhi tree was the Campaka tree; his body was eighty cubits in height; and the radiance of his body extended all around.
He remained pervading an area of one league at all times, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
"In that very Maṇḍa-kappa, Atthadassī, the Bull among Men,
having destroyed the great darkness, attained supreme enlightenment."
In a later period, a Teacher named Dhammadassī appeared. He too had three assemblies of disciples:
in the first there were one hundred koṭis of bhikkhus, in the second seventy koṭis, and in the third eighty koṭis.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become Sakka, king of the devas, performed worship with celestial fragrant flowers and celestial musical instruments.
He, too, prophesied of him: "In the future you will become a Buddha. That Blessed One had a city named Saraṇa;
his father was King Saraṇa, his mother was Sunandā, and his two chief disciples were Paduma and Phussadeva.
His attendant was named Sunetta, and his two chief female disciples were Khemā and Sabbanāmā. The Bodhi tree was the Rattaṅkura tree.
He is also called Bimbisāra; his body was eighty cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
“In that very aeon of adornment (maṇḍakappa), the greatly renowned Dhammadassī, having dispelled that darkness, shone forth among the world of devas.”
In a later period, ninety-four aeons ago from now, in one particular aeon, there arose a single Buddha named Siddhattha.
He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred and ten billion bhikkhus;
in the second, ninety billion; and in the third, eighty billion. At that time, the Bodhisatta possessed great majesty...
Endowed with the power of higher knowledge, he became an ascetic named Maṅgala and, having brought a large jambu fruit, gave it to the Tathāgata.
After the Teacher had consumed that fruit, he prophesied to the Bodhisatta: "In the ninety-fourth aeon hence, you will become a Buddha.
The city of that Blessed One was named Vebhāra, and his father was named Jayasena.
The king was named Suphassa; Sambala and Sumitta were the two chief disciples; Revata was the attendant;
Sīvalī and Surāmā were the two chief female disciples; the Kaṇikāra tree was his Bodhi tree;
his body was sixty cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
“After Dhammadassi, there was a leader named Siddhattha, who, having destroyed all darkness, rose up like the sun.
Subsequently, at a time ninety-two aeons ago from this, there were two Buddhas in a single aeon: Tissa and Phussa.
They were reborn. The Blessed One Tissa had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred koṭis of bhikkhus;
in the second, ninety koṭis; and in the third, eighty koṭis.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been born as a noble of great wealth and great fame named Sujāta, went forth into the ascetic life and attained great supernormal power.
Hearing that "a Buddha has appeared," he took divine mandārava, paduma, and pāricchattaka flowers and honored the Tathāgata as he proceeded through the midst of the fourfold assembly;
he formed a canopy of flowers in the sky. The Teacher also prophesied of him: "In ninety-two aeons from now, you shall become a Buddha.
That Blessed One had a city named Khema, and his father was Janasandha.
His name was Khatthiya; his mother was named Padumā; Brahmadeva and Udaya were his two chief disciples; his attendant was named Samaṅga;
Phussā and Sudattā were his two chief female disciples; the Asana tree was his Bodhi tree; his body was sixty cubits in height;
and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
“After Siddhattha came one who was peerless and without equal, of infinite virtue and immeasurable fame, Tissa, the leader of the world.
After him, a Teacher named Phussa arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples.
At the first assembly there were six million monks; at the second, fifty thousand; and at the third, thirty-two thousand.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been a kshatriya named Vijitāvin, renounced great sovereignty and went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher.
Having mastered the Three Piṭakas, he preached the Dhamma to the multitude and fulfilled the perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī). He too—
He likewise prophesied to him, saying, "You shall become a Buddha. That Blessed One had a city named Kāsī;
his father was King Jayasena, and his mother was Sirimā. His two chief disciples were Surakkhita and Dhammasena;
his attendant was Sabhiya; his two chief female disciples were Cālā and Upacālā; his Bodhi tree was the Āmalaka tree; and such was his physical body.
He was fifty-eight cubits in height, and the lifespan was ninety thousand years.
"In that very Maṇḍa-kappa, there was an unsurpassed Teacher;
incomparable, peerless, Phussa, the leader of the world."
In a later period, ninety-one aeons ago from now, the Blessed One named Vipassī appeared. He too had three assemblies of disciples:
in the first assembly there were six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus; in the second, one million; and in the third, eighty thousand.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was a Nāga king named Atula, possessed of great psychic power and great majesty.
Having offered it, he gave a great golden throne inlaid with the seven precious gems to the Blessed One. He, too, prophesied of him:
"In the ninety-first aeon from now, you shall become a Buddha. That Blessed One’s city was named Bandhumatī;
his father was King Bandhuma, his mother was Bandhumatī, and Khaṇḍa and Tissa were his two chief disciples.
His attendant was named Asoka; his two chief female disciples were Candā and Candamittā; his Bodhi tree was the Pāṭali tree;
his body was eighty cubits in height; the radiance of his body remained pervading seven yojanas at all times;
and his lifespan was eighty thousand years.
“After Phussa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, supreme among bipeds, named Vipassī, the possessor of vision, arose in the world.
Following him, thirty-one aeons ago, there were two Buddhas: Sikhī and Vessabhū. Of Sikhī as well—
The Blessed One had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly there were one hundred thousand bhikkhus; in the second, eighty thousand;

and in the third, seventy-seven thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been a king named Arindama, offered a great almsgiving including robes to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and [constructed] a [stūpa] adorned with the seven treasures.
Having given the elephant-treasure and having established the standard for elephants, he gave him allowable goods. He too prophesied of him:
"In thirty-one aeons from now, you will become a Buddha. That Blessed One’s city was named Aruṇavatī;
his father was the kṣatriya Aruṇa, his mother was Pabhāvatī, and his two chief disciples were Abhibhū and Sambhava. His [attendant] was Khemaṅkara.
His attendant was Nāmupaṭṭhāka, and his two chief female disciples were Sakhilā and Padumā. His Bodhi tree was the Puṇḍarīka tree.
His body was seventy cubits in height, and the radiance of his body remained pervading three yojanas. His lifespan was seventy thousand years.
After Vipassi, another Sambuddha, the supreme among bipeds, appeared:
“The Victor named Sikhī was peerless, without a rival.
After him, a Teacher named Vessabhū arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples.
In the first assembly there were eighty thousand bhikkhus; in the second, seventy thousand; and in the third, sixty thousand. At that time...
The Bodhisatta, having been King Sudassana, gave a great almsgiving including robes to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha;
he then went forth into homelessness in his presence and, being perfected in conduct and virtue, was filled with reverence and joy toward the Jewel of the Buddha.
The Blessed One also prophesied of him: "In thirty-one aeons from now, you shall become a Buddha. Furthermore, of him...
The Blessed One’s city was named Anoma; his father was King Suppatīta, and his mother was Yasavatī.
His two chief disciples were Soṇa and Uttara; his attendant was Upasanta; and his two chief female disciples were Dāmā and Samālā.
His Bodhi tree was the Sāla tree; his body was sixty cubits in height, and his lifespan was sixty thousand years.
“In that very same Maṇḍakappa, peerless and without rival, there arose in the world a Victor named Vessabhū.
Subsequently, in this kappa, four Buddhas were born: Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and [Gotama].
"O Blessed One, ours. The Blessed One Kakusandha had only one assembly of disciples; therein there were forty thousand bhikkhus.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been King Khema, gave a great almsgiving of robes and other requisites, as well as medicinal ointments and the like, to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and [honored] the Teacher.
Having heard the teaching of the Dhamma, he went forth. The Teacher also made a prediction concerning him. Now, for the Blessed One Kakusandha, there was a city named Khema;
his father was a brahmin named Aggidatta, and his mother was a brahmin woman named Visākhā.
His two chief disciples were Vidhura and Sañjīva; his attendant was named Buddhija; and his two chief female disciples were Sāmā and Campakā.
His chief female disciple was Mahāsirī, his Bodhi tree was the Sirīsa, his body was forty cubits in height,
and his lifespan was forty thousand years. After Vessabhu,
there arose another Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds.
“Named Kakusandha, immeasurable and difficult to approach.
After him, a Teacher named Koṇāgamana arose. He too had one assembly of disciples;
therein there were thirty thousand bhikkhus. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been King Pabbata, surrounded by a host of ministers...

Having gone into the presence of the Teacher and heard his teaching of the Dhamma, he invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and after providing a great almsgiving, he gave fine woolen cloths, Chinese silk, Koseyya silk, kambala wool, and dukūla cloth, as well as golden sandals, and went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher.
He too made a prediction concerning him. The Blessed One’s city was named Sobhavatī.
His father was a brahmin named Ahosiyaññadatta, his mother was a brahmin woman named Uttarā,
his two chief disciples were Bhiyyasa and Uttara, his attendant was named Sotthija, his two chief female disciples were Samuddā and Uttarā,
his Bodhi tree was the Udumbara, his body was thirty cubits in height, and his lifespan was thirty thousand years.
“After Kakusandha, there arose a Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds, a Conqueror named Koṇāgamana, the eldest in the world, a bull among men.
After him, a Teacher named Kassapa appeared. He too had one assembly of disciples; therein—

There were twenty thousand bhikkhus. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been a young brahmin named Jotipāla who had mastered the three Vedas and was renowned both on earth and in the sky, was a friend of Ghaṭīkāra the potter.
Together with him, he approached the Teacher, heard a discourse on the Dhamma, went forth, and applied himself with energy.
Having mastered the Three Piṭakas, he beautified the Buddha’s dispensation through his perfection in the prescribed and customary duties.
He, too, gave him a prediction. That Blessed One’s birthplace was called Bārāṇasī;
his father was a brahmin named Brahmadatta, and his mother was a brahmin woman named Dhanavatī. Tissa and Bhāradvāja were his two chief disciples, and Sabbamitta was [his attendant].
His attendant was Nāmudā, his two chief female disciples were Anulā and Uruvelā, his Bodhi tree was the Nigrodha tree, his body was twenty cubits in height,
and his lifespan was twenty thousand years. After Koṇāgamana,
there appeared another Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds.
“Kassapa by clan, the King of Dhamma, the Illuminator.
Now, in the same kappa in which Dīpaṅkara, the Ten-Powered One, appeared, there were three other Buddhas as well.
There was no prophecy concerning the Bodhisatta from their presence; therefore, they have not been mentioned here. In the Commentary...
However, in order to show all the Buddhas starting from that aeon, this was said:
“Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, and also Saraṇaṅkara;
Dīpaṅkara the Fully Enlightened One, and Koṇḍañña, the supreme among bipeds.”
“Maṅgala and Sumana, Revata and Sobhita the Sage;
Anomadassī, Paduma, Nārada, and Padumuttara.
Sumedha and Sujāta, Piyadassī of great renown;”
Atthadassī, Dhammadassī, Siddhattha, the Leader of the World;
Tissa, Phussa, and the Sambuddha Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū;
Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa—these were the Leaders.
“These were the Fully Awakened Ones, free from passion and composed;
like suns arisen, they dispelled the great darkness;
having blazed like masses of fire, they have gone out together with their disciples.”
In this regard, our Bodhisatta arrived after performing services in the presence of twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṅkara, over four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons.
However, from the time of the Blessed One Kassapa onwards, there has been no other Buddha except for this Perfectly Enlightened One. Thus, [regarding] those beginning with Dīpaṅkara...
But the Bodhisatta, who had received his prediction in the presence of twenty-four Buddhas,
[recited]: “Human birth, the perfection of gender, the cause,
the sight of the Teacher, Renunciation, the perfection of virtues, service, and zeal;”
“Through the combination of eight qualities, the resolution succeeds.
Having combined these eight qualities and having made his resolution at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha, he exerted himself with the thought:
“Come now, let me search here and there for the qualities that make a Buddha. While searching, he then beheld: first, the perfection of giving.

The qualities that constitute a Buddha, such as the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) and the rest, were seen by him; and while fulfilling them, he proceeded all the way until his existence as Vessantara.

And as he was coming, those benefits which have been described for Bodhisattvas who have made their formal resolution (*abhinīhāra*)—“Thus, men endowed with every limb, destined for enlightenment; — [were realized].
Throughout the long course of saṃsāra, even for hundreds of millions of eons,
they are not reborn in the Avīci hell, nor likewise in the Lokantara hells;
their thirst is parched, they suffer no hunger or thirst, and they do not become Kālakañjaka spirits.
“Small creatures do not arise in an evil state;
when they are born among humans, they are not born blind.
They have no deficiency of hearing, nor do they become mute.”
They do not go to the female state, nor are they hermaphrodites or eunuchs.
These men do not belong to the mundane realm; they are destined for enlightenment.
Freed from the immediate transgressions, they maintain a pure range of conduct in every respect.
“They do not practice wrong view, seeing the efficacy of kamma;
even while dwelling in the heavens, they are never reborn in the realm of non-percipient beings.
Among the gods of the Pure Abodes, the cause [for such rebirth] does not exist.”
“True men, inclined toward renunciation and detached from existence after existence, practice deeds for the welfare of the world and fulfill all the perfections.
Having attained these benefits, he came [here]. And while fulfilling the perfections, during his time as the brahmin Akitti and during his time as the brahmin Saṅkha...
There is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of giving during the time of King Dhanañcaya, the time of Mahāsudassana,
the time of Mahāgovinda, the time of King Nimi, the time of Prince Canda, the time of the merchant Visayha, the time of King Sivi,
and the time of Vessantara. However, it was exclusively in the *Sasapaṇḍita Jātaka*—
“Seeing him who had approached for alms, I surrendered my own self;
there is no one equal to me in giving—this is my perfection of giving.
Thus, for one who makes such a sacrifice of self, the perfection of giving becomes what is called the ultimate perfection (*paramattha-pāramī*). Likewise, during the time of Sīlavara:
There is no measure for the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of virtue during the time of Campeyya the Nāga King,
Bhūridatta the Nāga King, Chaddanta the Nāga King, Prince Jayaddisa, and Prince Alīnasattu. However, it is stated with absolute certainty in the Saṅkhapāla Jātaka:
“Even when pierced by stakes and even when crushed by spears, I did not become angry with Bhojaputta; this is my perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramī*).
Thus, for one who practices self-sacrifice, the perfection of virtue becomes what is called the ultimate perfection (*paramatthapāramī*). Likewise, during the time of Somanassa Kumāra...

There is no limit to the number of times he fulfilled the perfection of renunciation by abandoning great sovereignty during his time as the elephant-keeper youth and his time as the wise Ayoghara Paṇḍita.
However, in the Cūḷasutasoma Jātaka, it is stated categorically:
"Great sovereignty, come into my hands, I cast away like a globule of spittle."
"Nothing clings to one who has renounced;

this is my perfection of renunciation (*nekkhammapāramī*)."—Thus, for him who renounced the kingdom out of detachment, the perfection of renunciation became a perfection in the ultimate sense (*paramatthapāramī*).
Likewise during the time of the wise Vidhura, the time of the wise Mahāgovinda, and the time of the wise Kuddāla.
There is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of wisdom during his time as the wise Araka, his time as the wanderer Bodhi, and his time as the wise Mahosadha.
However, it was specifically during his time as the wise Senaka in the Sattubhasta Jātaka that he said:
“Discerning with wisdom, O Brahmin, I liberated the brahmin from suffering.”
“There is no one equal to me in wisdom; this is my perfection of wisdom.
Thus, for him who showed the snake that had entered inside his own belly, the perfection of wisdom became known as the *paramattha-pāramī* (the ultimate perfection).

Likewise, there is no measure for the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of energy (*vīriya-pāramitā*) and the others. However, in the case of the *Mahājanaka-jātaka*, it is stated with absolute certainty: [that there is no limit].
“Failing to see the other shore in the midst of the waters, all those men were destroyed;
there was no change in my mind—this is my perfection of energy.
Thus, the perfection of energy that arose while crossing the great ocean became known as a perfection in the ultimate sense. In the *Khantivādijātaka*:
“Though they were hacking at me as if I were insentient with a sharp axe, I felt no anger toward the King of Kāsi; this is my perfection of patience.

Thus, for one who endures great suffering as if it were insentient, the perfection of patience becomes what is called the ultimate perfection (*paramattha-pāramī*). As stated in the *Mahāsutasoma Jātaka*:
“Protecting my word of truth, even at the cost of my own life, I liberated one hundred kṣatriyas; this is my perfection of truth.
Thus, for one who protects truth by sacrificing their life, the perfection of truth becomes what is called the ultimate perfection (*paramatthapāramī*). As it says in the *Mūgapakkha Jātaka*:
“Neither my mother nor my father are dear to me, nor is great fame dear to me;
omniscience alone is dear to me, therefore I have resolved upon this vow.

Thus, for one who resolves upon a vow even at the cost of giving up his life, the perfection of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-pāramitā*) becomes known as the ultimate perfection (*paramattha-pāramī*). In the *Ekarāja-jātaka*:
“‘No one terrifies me, nor do I fear anyone at all;
supported by the power of loving-kindness, I then delight in the forest.

Thus, for one who practices loving-kindness without regard even for life, the perfection of loving-kindness (mettā-pāramitā) becomes what is called the ultimate perfection.”—In the *Lomahaṃsa Jātaka*:
“I make my bed in the charnel ground, using a human skeleton as my pillow;
when the village children come near, they show me no small variety of forms.
Thus it was, even while the village boys were causing him pleasure and pain by spitting on him and the like, and by offering garlands, perfumes, and other such things.
For one who does not overstep equanimity, the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramitā) becomes what is called the ultimate perfection (paramattha-pāramī). This is the summary here;
however, this matter in detail should be taken from the Cariyāpiṭaka. Having thus fulfilled the perfections while established in the Vessantara existence, he said:
“This earth is insentient, Unaware of pleasure or pain;”
“By the power of my gift, even she shook seven times.
Having thus performed such great meritorious deeds as the shaking of the great earth, at the end of his life-span, passing away from there, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
Thus, from the time he was at the feet of Dīpaṅkara until his rebirth in the city of Tusita, this much [time passed].
It should be understood that this place is called "having a distant origin.
The discourse on the distant origin is finished.
2. The discourse on the not-distant origin.
While the Bodhisatta was still dwelling in the Tusita heaven, that which is called the "Buddha-proclamation" (buddhakolāhala) arose. For three proclamations arise in the world:
the proclamation of an aeon (kappakolāhala), the proclamation of a Buddha (buddhakolāhala), and the proclamation of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavattikolāhala).
In this regard, when a hundred thousand years have passed, thinking "the emergence of an aeon will occur," the gods of the sense-sphere realm known as the Lokabyūhas—

With their veins showing, their hair disheveled, their faces weeping, wiping away tears with their hands, dressed in red garments and wearing extremely hideous attire, they wandered along the public roads proclaiming:
“Sirs, after the passing of one hundred thousand years from now, the end of the eon will occur;
this world will be destroyed, and even the great ocean will dry up.”
“This great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will burn up and perish;
until the destruction of the world reaches as far as the Brahma-world, friends, cultivate loving-kindness; friends, cultivate compassion, gladness, and equanimity.
Serve your mother; serve your father; be respectful toward the elders of the family.”
This is called the "clamor regarding the eon. Furthermore, after the passing of a thousand years, a Sammasambuddha will arise in the world;
thus the world-protecting deities wander about proclaiming, "Sirs, after the passing of a thousand years from now, a Buddha will arise in the world.
This is called the "clamor regarding the Buddha. After the passing of a hundred years, a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti Rāja) will arise.
Deities wander about proclaiming, "Venerable sirs, at the end of one hundred years from now, a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) will appear in the world.
This is known as the "clamor of the Wheel-turner. These three clamors are great.
Upon hearing the sound of the clamor concerning a Buddha among them, the deities of the entire ten-thousandfold world-system assemble together.
Knowing that "a being named so-and-so will become a Buddha," they approach him and make their request.

And they make their request when the preliminary signs have appeared. At that time, however, all the deities assemble in a single world-system together with the Four Great Kings, Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Sunimmita, Vasavatti, and Mahābrahmā;
having gathered in one world-system, they go into the presence of the Bodhisatta in the Tusita heaven and say: "O Noble One..."

“While you were fulfilling the ten perfections, you did not do so aspiring for the attainment of Sakka, nor the attainment of Māra, nor the attainment of Brahmā, nor the attainment of a wheel-turning monarch;
rather, you fulfilled them aspiring for omniscience for the sake of delivering the world.
Now, dear sir, is the time for your Buddhahood; dear sir, this is the moment for your Buddhahood,” they entreated.

Then the Great Being, without yet giving his promise to the deities, performed what is called the five great observations (*pañcamahāvilokana*) by way of observing the time, the continent, the country, the lineage, the mother, and the limit of the lifespan. Therein, he first observed the time, thinking: "Is it the right time, or is it not the right time?
In this regard, a period when the lifespan has increased beyond one hundred thousand years is not considered the right time. Why is that?
For at that time, birth, aging, and death are not perceived among beings. And there is no teaching of the Dhamma by the Buddhas that is exempt from the three characteristics.
When they speak of "impermanence, suffering, and non-self," people think, "What is it they are saying?
and thus consider it neither worth hearing nor worth believing. Consequently, there is no realization (abhisamaya); and in its absence, [the teaching] is not conducive to liberation.
The Dispensation does not exist; therefore, that is not the right time. Even a time when the lifespan is less than a hundred years is not the right time.

Why? Because at that time, sentient beings have defilements in abundance; and advice given to those with abundant defilements does not remain in its proper place, but quickly vanishes like a line drawn with a stick upon water.
Therefore, that too is not the right time. However, from [a lifespan of] one hundred thousand years...
The period of life beginning from below one hundred years and extending upwards from one hundred years is called "the time. And at that time, it was the era of a hundred-year lifespan.
Then the Great Being perceived that "the time for rebirth has arrived.

Thereafter, surveying the continent, he looked upon the four continents together with their surrounding islands and perceived the continent, seeing that "Buddhas are not born in the three continents; they are born only in Jambudīpa."
Then, looking for a suitable location, he thought, "Jambudīpa is indeed great, measuring ten thousand yojanas; in which region, then, do Buddhas take birth?
He saw the Middle Country (Majjhima-desa). As for the Middle Country:
"To the east is the town named Gajaṅgala; to its west is Mahāsāla; beyond that are the bordering districts."
Within these limits is the center. To the eastern direction lies the river named Sallavatī; beyond that are the bordering districts—this is the center within those limits.
To the southern direction lies the market town named Setakaṇṇika; beyond that are the bordering districts—this is the center within those limits.
To the western direction lies the brahmin village named Thūṇa; beyond that are the bordering districts—this is the center within those limits.
"From here to the middle. To the north is the mountain named Usīraddhaja; beyond that are the bordering provinces;

from here to the middle"—this is the region described in the Vinaya. It is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference. In this region, Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas [arise].
The chief disciples, the eighty great disciples, universal monarchs, and other highly influential kshatriyas, brahmins, householders, and great landowners will arise.
He reached the conclusion: "This city named Kapilavatthu shall be my place of birth.
Then, surveying the family, he considered: "Buddhas are not born into the merchant class or the servant class; they are born into a family esteemed by the world..."
Furthermore, he is born into only two types of families: either a kshatriya family or a brahmin family. Now, the kshatriya family is esteemed by the world;
I shall be born there. King Śuddhodana shall be my father. Thus he discerned the family. Then, looking for a mother, [he reflected]:
“The mother of a Buddha is not one who is lustful, addicted to liquor, or a gambler. For a hundred thousand aeons...”
However, one who has fulfilled the perfections possesses the five precepts unbroken from birth onwards.
This queen named Mahāmāyā was such a person; [the Bodhisatta] saw: "She shall be my mother, but how long will her lifespan be? It is ten months and seven days more."
Having thus performed these five great observations and saying, "The time for my Buddhahood has come, friends," he gave his promise while gathering the deities together.

Then, dismissing those deities with the words, "Go, you," he entered the Nandana Grove in Tusitapura, surrounded by the Tusita deities. For indeed, the Nandana Grove exists in all the worlds of the gods.

There, deities wander about, reminding him of the sphere of wholesome karma performed in the past, saying, "Pass away from here and go to a happy destination; pass away from here and go to a happy destination.
Surrounded by these deities thus reminding him of his wholesome deeds, as he wandered there, he passed away and took rebirth in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā.

To clarify this, here is the sequential account: At that time, it is said, the festival of the Āsāḷhi constellation was proclaimed in the city of Kapilavatthu, and the great multitude was enjoying the festivities.

Queen Mahāmāyā, too, from the seventh day prior to the full moon, abstaining from intoxicants and adorned with garlands, perfumes, and finery, was enjoying the festival celebrations when, on the seventh [day]...
Rising early in the morning, having bathed with scented water, having bestowed four hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and given a great almsgiving,
adorned with all her ornaments, and having eaten excellent food, she resolved upon the factors of the Uposatha. Then,
entering the decorated bedchamber and lying down upon her royal couch, as she was falling asleep, she saw this dream:
"Indeed, the four Great Kings, having lifted her up along with her bed, carried her to the Himālayas and set her down on a surface of mind-made stone sixty yojanas wide,
beneath a great sāla tree seven yojanas high, and stood to one side. Then their queens came,
led the queen to Lake Anotatta, and bathed her in order to remove the impurities of human birth."
Having had her dressed in celestial garments, anointed with perfumes, and adorned with celestial flowers, they then led her to a silver mountain not far from there.
Inside it was a golden palace; having prepared a celestial couch there with its head toward the east, they laid her down upon it.
Then the Bodhisatta, having become a noble white elephant, [appeared] on a golden mountain not far from that place.
There was; having wandered there, descended from that place, and ascended the Silver Mountain, he came from the northern direction,
took a white lotus with his trunk which was the color of a silver garland, let out a trumpeting cry, entered the golden celestial palace,
circumambulated his mother’s bed three times keeping it to his right, and appeared as if entering her womb by splitting open her right side.
"Thus it was. In this way, he took rebirth under the constellation Uttarāsāḷha.
On the following day, the queen, having awakened, related that dream to the king.
The king summoned about sixty-four eminent brahmins and, on a ground smeared with green cow-dung and adorned with auspicious honors such as parched grain, [prepared] costly...
Having prepared seats, he filled golden and silver bowls with excellent milk-rice (pāyāsa) prepared with ghee, honey, and sugar for the brahmins seated there;
having covered them with golden and silver lids, he gave them to them.
Furthermore, he satisfied them with other gifts such as unwashed garments and tawny cows. Then, when they had been satisfied with all their desires—
Having had the dream reported, he asked, "What will come of it? The brahmins said, "Do not worry, Great King.
A fetus has been conceived in the womb of your queen; moreover, it is a male fetus, not a female one. You will have a son.
If he dwells at home, he will become a universal monarch (cakkavattī); if he leaves the home life..."
“Having gone forth, he will renounce the world; he will become a Buddha in the world, one who removes the veil of ignorance.

At the very moment the Bodhisatta took rebirth in his mother’s womb, the entire ten-thousandfold world system shook, trembled, and quaked all at once. Thirty-two omens appeared in the ten directions—ten...
An immeasurable radiance pervaded thousands of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). As if desiring to behold his glory, the blind regained their sight,
the deaf heard sounds, the mute spoke, the hunchbacked became straight-limbed, the lame regained the ability to walk on their feet,
all beings who were in bondage were released from their fetters and chains, and in all the hells...
The fire was extinguished; hunger and thirst were stilled in the realm of the hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*); fear ceased among the animals; the disease of all beings was pacified;
all beings became speakers of kind words; horses neighed with sweet tones, elephants trumpeted, and all musical instruments emitted their respective sounds even without being struck;
and the hand-drums and other instruments of humans sounded even without being beaten.
The ornaments resounded, all directions became serene, a soft and cool breeze blew bringing happiness to sentient beings,
an unseasonable rain fell, water welled up and overflowed from the earth, birds abandoned their flight through the sky,
rivers stood still without flowing, the waters of the great ocean became sweet, and everywhere indeed—
Its surface was covered with five-colored lotuses; all kinds of flowers, both land-born and water-born, blossomed;
on the trunks of the trees, trunk-lotuses bloomed; on the branches, branch-lotuses bloomed; and on the creepers, creeper-lotuses bloomed;
and even on the dry ground, having split the surfaces of the rocks, stalked-lotuses known as *daṇḍapaduma* emerged, seven upon seven, one above another.
In the sky, hanging lotuses known as *olambaka-padumāni* appeared; showers of flowers rained down from all sides; celestial musical instruments resounded in the air;

and the entire ten-thousandfold world system became like a loose cluster of garlands, like a tightly bound bouquet of garlands, or like a decorated throne prepared with garlands—completely draped in garlands, with waving yak-tail fans, and perfumed with flowers, incense, and fragrances.
She attained the highest degree of beauty.
Thus, for the Bodhisatta who had taken rebirth,
four sons of gods with swords in hand stood guard from the moment of conception, in order to ward off any misfortune for both the Bodhisatta and his mother.
They took her. However, no lustful thought arose in the Bodhisatta’s mother toward men;
she attained the pinnacle of gain and the summit of glory, being happy and with an unwearied body.
And she saw the Bodhisatta within her womb like a yellow thread wound around a clear jewel. For a womb inhabited by a Bodhisatta is indeed like the interior of a shrine.
It exists such that it cannot be inhabited or utilized by any other being;
therefore, seven days after the Bodhisatta is born, the Bodhisatta’s mother passes away and is reborn in the Tusita heaven.
Furthermore, unlike other women who give birth while standing, sitting, or lying down—even before or after the ten months have passed—it is not so with the Bodhisatta’s mother.
Having carried the Bodhisatta in her womb for ten months, she gives birth while still standing; this is the natural law regarding the mother of a Bodhisatta.

Queen Mahāmāyā also, having carried the Bodhisatta in her womb for ten months like oil in a vessel, with her pregnancy fully matured and desiring to go to her father’s home, informed King Suddhodana: "I wish, O Lord, to go to my family's home..."
“...to go to the city of Devadaha. The King, accepting with the words “Very well,” had the road leveled from Kapilavatthu as far as the city of Devadaha;

having had it adorned with plantain trees, full water-pots, banners, flags, and so forth, he had the Queen seated in a golden palanquin and sent her off with a great retinue, carried by a thousand ministers. But of the two—
Between the two cities, there was a grove of auspicious sal trees called Lumbinīvana, inhabited by the residents of both cities; at that time,
from its roots up to its topmost branches, the entire grove was in full bloom, and amidst the branches and the flowers,
swarms of five-colored bees and various flocks of birds [hummed] with sweet voices.
They moved about warbling. The entire Lumbinī grove was like a forest of *cittalatā* creepers;
it became like a well-prepared drinking circle for the majestic king. When the queen saw it, the desire to sport in the *sāla* grove arose in her mind.
Taking the queen with them, the ministers entered the *sāla* grove. She went to the foot of the auspicious *sāla* tree and [grasped] a *sāla* branch.
Desiring to grasp it, the branch of the *sāla* tree bent down like the well-polished tip of a bamboo cane and came within reach of the Queen’s hand.
She extended her hand and seized the branch. At that very moment, the winds born of her karma began to stir.
Then, having screened her with a curtain, the great multitude withdrew. While she remained standing, holding the *sāla* branch, for her—
The emergence from the womb took place. At that very moment, four Great Brahmās with purified minds arrived carrying a golden net;
having received the Bodhisatta in that golden net and placed him before his mother, they said, "Be joyful, O Queen! A son of great power has been born to you."
But unlike other beings who emerge from the mother’s womb smeared with repulsive impurities,
the Bodhisatta does not do so. Rather, like a preacher descending from a Dhamma-seat or a man descending from a ladder,
he stands with both hands and both feet outstretched, free from anything born of the mother’s womb.
Untainted by any impurity, pure and stainless, he emerged from his mother’s womb shining like a precious gem placed upon a cloth of Kāsi silk.
Nevertheless, for the sake of honoring both the Bodhisatta and the Bodhisatta’s mother,
two streams of water issued forth from the sky and brought warmth to the bodies of both the Bodhisatta and his mother.

Then, having been received by the Brahmās standing with a golden net, the Four Great Kings took him from their hands upon a deerskin rug that was auspiciously esteemed and pleasant to the touch; from their hands, men took him upon a cushion of fine linen.
Having been released from the hands of the men and set down upon the earth, he [faced] the eastern direction.
He looked out, and thousands of world-systems became a single open space. There, gods and humans, worshipping with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, said:
"Great Being, there is no one else here equal to you; how could there be anyone superior?
Having thus surveyed the ten directions—the four cardinal points, the four intermediate points, below, and above—he, by himself...

Seeing no one equal to him, he took seven steps toward the northern direction with the thought, "This is the north," while Mahābrahmā held a white parasol over him, Suyāma wielded a yak-tail fan, and other deities followed behind him, carrying the various insignia of royalty in their hands.
Then, standing on the seventh step, he uttered this bold proclamation: "I am the foremost in the world," and so forth.
He let out a lion’s roar.
For in three of his existences—the existence as Mahosadha, the existence as Vessantara, and this present existence—the Bodhisatta uttered speech immediately upon emerging from his mother’s womb.
It is said that in the existence as Mahosadha, as soon as he had emerged from his mother’s womb...
Sakka, the king of the gods, came, placed a piece of sandalwood essence in his hand, and departed; he emerged having taken it in his very fist.
Then his mother asked him, "Dear son, what have you brought? "Medicine, mother," he replied.
Because he had come having taken medicine, they gave him the name "Osadhadāraka" (Medicine Boy). Having taken that medicine...
They placed him in a basket, and for those who came one after another—such as the blind and the deaf—that very thing became medicine for the pacification of all their diseases.
Then, because of the words that arose, "This is a great medicine! This is a great medicine!
his name became "Mahosadha. Furthermore, when he emerged from his mother’s womb during his existence as Vessantara, his right hand...
Stretching out his hand and saying, "Is there anything in the house, mother? I shall give a gift," he went out.
Then his mother, saying, "My son, you were born into a wealthy family," placed her palm against her son's hand and set down a purse containing a thousand pieces of gold.
It was on this very occasion that he uttered this lion’s roar. Thus it is said:
In three of his existences, the Bodhisatta uttered speech immediately upon emerging from his mother’s womb.
And just as at the moment of conception, thirty-two omens appeared at the moment of his birth.
Furthermore, at the very time our Bodhisatta was born in the Lumbinī grove, at that same moment Rāhulamātā...
The Queen, the Elder Ānanda, the minister Channa, the minister Kāḷudāyī, Kaṇḍaka the king of horses, the Great Bodhi Tree, and four treasure-pots were born together.
Among them, one was a quarter-league in size, one was half a league, one was three-quarters of a league, and one was a full league. These seven are known as the "co-natives."
The inhabitants of both cities took the Bodhisatta and went to the city of Kapilavatthu itself.
On that very day, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, the hosts of gods, joyful and delighted, cried out, "A son has been born to the great King Suddhodana in the city of Kapilavatthu;
this prince, having sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree, will become a Buddha," and they performed such acts as the waving of their garments.

They played. At that time, a forest-dwelling ascetic named Kāḷadevīla, a follower of King Suddhodana who had attained the eight meditative absorptions, having finished his meal, went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven for his midday rest.
While sitting there for his rest, he saw those deities playing and asked, "For what reason do you play with such joyful minds? This [joy] is mine as well."
“Tell me the reason,” he asked. The deities said, “Venerable sir, a son has been born to King Suddhodana;
having sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree and become a Buddha, he will set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
We are joyful for this reason, thinking that we shall behold his infinite Buddha-play and hear his Dhamma. The ascetic [heard] their words...
Having heard this, he quickly descended from the world of the gods, entered the royal palace, and sat upon the prepared seat.
He said, "It is said, Great King, that a son has been born to you; I shall see him. The king had the prince, adorned and prepared for the occasion, brought forward to pay homage to the ascetic;
however, the Bodhisatta’s feet turned back and rested upon the ascetic’s matted locks.
Indeed, for the Bodhisatta, in that particular existence, there was no one else worthy of being saluted.
For had they, out of ignorance, placed the Bodhisatta’s head at the feet of the ascetic, the ascetic’s head would have split into seven pieces.
Thinking, "It is not right for me to destroy myself," the ascetic rose from his seat and extended his joined palms in reverence toward the Bodhisatta.
Having seen that marvel, the king paid homage to his own son.
The ascetic recollected eighty eons—forty eons of the past and forty eons of the future.
Having observed the perfection of the Bodhisatta’s marks, he reflected and investigated, wondering, "Will he become a Buddha, or will he not?"
Knowing, "He will undoubtedly become a Buddha," he smiled, thinking, "This is a marvelous man.
Then, reflecting, "Shall I or shall I not have the opportunity to see him when he has become a Buddha? he perceived: "I shall not;
for I will pass away in the interval, at a time when even a hundred Buddhas or a thousand Buddhas, though they were to go there, would be unable to awaken him."
Seeing this, she thought, "I shall be reborn in the formless realm," and weeping, she said, "I shall not have the opportunity to see such a marvelous man become a Buddha;
alas, a great loss will be mine!
When people saw her, they asked, "Our noble lady just now laughed and now weeps again. Why is this, venerable one? What has happened to us?"
“Will some obstacle arise for the noble son? they asked. “There is no obstacle for him;

he will undoubtedly become a Buddha,” [the seer] replied. Then they asked, “Why then do you weep? He said, “I weep because I shall not be able to see such a person once he has become a Buddha, thinking, ‘Oh, what a great loss this will be for me! Thus I grieve for myself.”
Then, reflecting, "Will anyone among my kinsmen be able to see this one who has become a Buddha, or will they not?
he saw his own nephew, the boy Nālaka. He went to his sister's house and asked, "Where is your son Nālaka?
"He is at home, noble sir," she replied. "Call him here," he said; having had him summoned, he brought him into his presence.
When the prince had arrived, he said to him: "Dear one, a son has been born into the family of the great king Suddhodana;
he is a sprout of a Buddha, and after thirty-five years have passed, he will become a Buddha. You shall be permitted to see him; therefore, go forth into homelessness this very day.
Although the boy was born into a family possessing seven hundred and eighty million pieces of wealth, he thought, "My maternal uncle will not involve me in what is unbeneficial."
Having thought thus, he immediately had yellow robes and an earthen bowl brought from the marketplace;
having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the yellow robes, he said, "My renunciation is for the sake of that Supreme Person in the world," and extending his joined palms toward the Bodhisatta,
he paid homage by prostrating himself on his five limbs and took the bowl.
Having placed [the bowl] in his bag and slung it over his shoulder, he entered the Himālayas and practiced the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
He approached the Tathāgata who had attained supreme enlightenment and requested the Nāḷaka method of practice.
Returning again to the Himālayas, he attained *arahantship* and, practicing the austere method (*ukkaṭṭhapatipadā*), spent seven months there.
Having lived out his lifespan, he attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue while standing beside a single mountain of gold.
On the fifth day after the Bodhisatta’s birth, having bathed his head and thinking,
"We shall perform the naming ceremony," they anointed the royal palace with four kinds of fragrant scents, scattered flowers with parched grain as the fifth, and [prepared] unbroken milk-rice.
Having had food prepared, they invited eight hundred brahmins who had mastered the three Vedas, seated them in the royal palace, fed them with excellent food,
and having rendered great honor, they had their physical marks examined, wondering, "What indeed will happen?
Among them were Rāma, Dhaja, Lakkhaṇa, and the counselor Koṇḍañña, as well as Bhoja, Suyāma, and Sudatta.
