“At that time there were these eight brahmins who, possessing the sixfold knowledge, interpreted the mantra.”—These very eight brahmins were the examiners of the marks. On the day of the conception, even the dream was interpreted by them alone.
Among them, seven persons, raising two fingers, gave a twofold interpretation:

“Endowed with these marks, one who dwells at home becomes a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), and one who goes forth becomes a Buddha,” they declared, describing the entire majesty and power of a wheel-turning monarch.
Among them, however, the youngest in age—a young brahmin named Koṇḍañña by clan—having observed the perfection of the Bodhisattva’s excellent marks, said: “Of this...
"There is no reason for him to remain in the midst of a household; he will certainly be a Buddha whose veil is rolled away," he declared this categorical prediction, raising only a single finger.

For this being, who had performed his duties and was in his final existence, having surpassed the other seven men in wisdom, [was endowed with these marks] "for one who possesses these characteristics in the midst of a household..."
"There is no possibility that he will not become a Buddha; he will undoubtedly become a Buddha"—thus he saw only one single destiny.

Therefore, raising a single finger, he made this prediction. Then, when they were choosing a name for him, because he would bring about the accomplishment of the welfare of the whole world, they gave him the name "Siddhattha" (Accomplished Purpose).
Then those brahmins, having gone to their own homes, addressed their sons: "Dear ones, we are old;

whether or not we shall live to see the son of King Suddhodana attain omniscience, once that prince has attained omniscience, you should go forth into his dispensation. Those seven men [lived] for as long as their lifespan lasted.
Having stood there, they departed according to their respective karmic destiny; only the young man Koṇḍañña remained free from illness.
As the Great Being grew up, he made the Great Renunciation and, proceeding by stages, went to Uruvelā. There, having formed the thought, "How delightful indeed is this region!
It is truly fit for a son of noble family who seeks to strive in spiritual exertion," he established his mind upon it.
When they had arrived there and heard that "the Great Man has gone forth," they approached the sons of those brahmins and said this:
"It is said that Prince Siddhattha has gone forth; he will undoubtedly become a Buddha.
If your fathers were free from illness, they would have gone forth today. If you also should desire it..."
"Come, I shall go forth following that man. They were all unable to become of one mind;
three persons did not go forth. With the brahmin Koṇḍañña as their leader, the other four went forth.
Those five persons became known as the Pañcavaggiya Theras.
Then the king asked, "What did my son see that he would go forth? [The charioteer replied,] "Four portents.
"Which ones, and which ones? "An aged man, a sick man, a corpse, and one who has gone forth.
The king said, "From now on, do not allow such people as these to approach my son; for my son—"
“In the state of Buddhahood there is no such action;

rather, I wish to see my son exercising sovereignty and lordship as king over the four great continents surrounded by two thousand islands, traveling through the sky surrounded by a retinue measuring thirty-six yojanas in circumference. Having spoken thus, regarding these four kinds...
To prevent the arrival of omens within the prince’s line of sight, he established a guard at intervals of one *gāvuta* in each of the four directions.
On that day, however, among the eighty thousand kinsmen assembled at the auspicious site, each one pledged his own son, saying:
"Whether he becomes a Buddha or a king, we shall each give one son..."
“We shall give them. If he becomes a Buddha, he will wander surrounded and attended by kshatriya ascetics alone;
if he becomes a king, he will wander surrounded and attended by kshatriya princes alone.
The King also appointed for the Bodhisatta nurses endowed with the most excellent beauty and free from all defects. The Bodhisatta...
He prospers with an infinite retinue and great splendor and majesty.
Now, on one occasion, there was for the king a festival known as the "Blessing of the Sowing. On that day, they decorated the entire city like a celestial mansion of the gods;
all the slaves, laborers, and others were dressed in new garments and adorned with perfumes, garlands, and the like.
They gathered at the royal palace. For the king’s work, a thousand plows were yoked.
On that day, however, seven hundred and ninety-nine plows, together with their oxen, reins, and traces, were adorned with silver;
but the king’s own guiding plow was adorned with red gold. Even the horns, reins, and goads of the oxen [were likewise adorned].
They were indeed adorned with gold. The king, having set out with a great retinue, took his son and departed.
At the site of the work, there was a *jambu* tree with thick foliage and spreading shade.
Having had a bed prepared for the prince beneath it and a canopy inlaid with golden stars fastened above, [he enclosed it] with a screen wall.

Having had the area surrounded and guards stationed there, the king, adorned with all his ornaments and surrounded by a host of ministers, went to the place where the plowing was to take place. There, the king took up a golden plow;

the ministers took up one hundred and seven silver plows minus one; and the farmers took up the remaining plows. Having taken them up, they plowed here and there. But the king [plowed] from this side to the other...
He goes, or he comes from the further shore to this side. At that place there was great prosperity.
The nurses sitting around the Bodhisatta, thinking, "We shall see the king's prosperity," stepped out from within the curtain.
The Bodhisatta, looking here and there and seeing no one, rose up quickly, folded his legs crosswise, and [focused on] the mindfulness of breathing.
Having taken hold of it, he produced the first *jhāna*. The nurses, while moving about among the food and snacks, delayed for a short while.
The shadows of the other trees had turned back, but the shadow of that tree remained standing all around it in a circle.
Thinking, "The noble son is alone," the nurses hurriedly lifted the curtain and were entering inside when they saw the Bodhisatta on his bed.
Having seen him sitting cross-legged and having witnessed that miracle, they went and informed the king: "Your Majesty, the prince is sitting thus;
while the shadows of other trees have turned back, the shadow of the rose-apple tree remains perfectly circular.
The king came with great haste, and seeing the miracle, he paid homage to his son, saying: "This is your second salutation, my dear."
Then, in due course, the Bodhisatta reached the age of sixteen years.

The King had three palaces built for the Bodhisatta, suitable for the three seasons—one with nine stories, one with seven stories, and one with five stories—and he provided him with forty thousand female dancers.
Thus the Bodhisatta lived like a god, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs.
Surrounded by a retinue of adorned dancers and entertained by instrumental music performed by women, he dwelt in those palaces according to the seasons, enjoying great prosperity.
His queen, the mother of Rāhula, was his chief consort.
While he was thus experiencing such great prosperity, one day this conversation arose within the circle of his kinsmen:
The thought arose: “Siddhattha wanders about merely addicted to play; he does not learn any craft. When war is imminent, what will he do?

The King had the Bodhisatta summoned and asked: “Dear son, your kinsmen say that Siddhattha wanders about merely addicted to play without learning any craft. What do you consider appropriate in this matter?”
“Your Majesty, there is no need for me to practice my craft; have the drum beaten in the city to demonstrate my skill, announcing:
‘On the seventh day from now, I shall display my craft to my kinsmen. The king did so.
The Bodhisatta, having assembled archers skilled in shooting at moving targets and those skilled in shooting at stationary targets, stood in the midst of the great multitude before the other archers.
He demonstrated twelve kinds of crafts that were not shared even by his kinsmen; this should be understood according to the method presented in the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka.
At that time, the assembly of his kinsmen became free from doubt.
Then one day, desiring to go to the pleasure grove, the Bodhisatta addressed his charioteer, saying, "Yoke the chariot."

He replied, "Very well," and having adorned a magnificent, supreme chariot with every ornament, he yoked to it four auspicious Sindhava horses, the color of white lotus petals, and announced its readiness to the Bodhisatta.
The Bodhisatta ascended the chariot, which resembled a celestial palace, and set out toward the park. The deities [thought], "Of Prince Siddhattha..."

"The time for his full awakening is near; we shall show him a preliminary sign," they said, and having conjured a son of the gods who was decrepit with old age, with broken teeth, grey hair, a crooked and bent body, and holding a staff while trembling, they showed him to him.
Both the Bodhisatta and the charioteer saw him. Then the Bodhisatta asked the charioteer: "My good man, what is this?"

"Is this man's hair not like that of others? Having asked this according to the method found in the *Mahāpadāna Sutta*, and having heard his reply, he was moved with a heart full of agitation, thinking:
"Alas, what a wretched thing is birth, for where there is birth, aging is perceived!
He turned back from that very spot and ascended the palace once more. The king asked: "For what reason has my son returned so quickly?"
He asked, “What did they say when they saw the old man, O King? “They said, ‘Having seen the old man, he will go forth into homelessness.
Why do you destroy me? Quickly prepare theatrical performances for my son; while enjoying such prosperity, he will not turn his mind toward renunciation.
Having said this, he increased the guard and stationed them at intervals of half a *yojana* in every direction.
On another day, as the Bodhisatta was going to the pleasure garden in the same manner, he saw a diseased man created by the deities.
Having questioned him in the same way as before, his heart was filled with agitation; he turned back and ascended to the palace.
The king also, having questioned him and made arrangements in the manner described above, increased the security once more within a radius of three *gāvutas* on all sides.
He established a guard over the area. On another day, as the Bodhisatta was going to the park in the same manner, he saw a person created by the deities who had passed away;
having questioned him in the same way as before, his heart was filled with agitation, and he turned back again and ascended to the palace.
The king also, having questioned him and made arrangements in the manner described above, increased [the guard] once more.
He established a guard over an area measuring one *yojana* on all sides.

Furthermore, on another day, while going to the pleasure grove, he saw a renunciant—well-robed and well-clad—who had been manifested by the deities in that very same manner; seeing him, he asked the charioteer, "Who indeed is this, my good man?
Although the charioteer was unable to explain the appearance of a Buddha or the virtues of the renunciant due to the absence of a Buddha in the world, [he nevertheless described him].
Or perhaps he did not know; rather, through the power of the deity, [the deity] said, "This one is indeed a renunciant, O gods," and praised the virtues of the renunciant life.
The Bodhisatta, having conceived a longing for the renunciant life, went to the park on that very day.
However, the Dīgha-bhāṇakas say: "He went after seeing four omens on a single day."
Thus, having spent part of the day there and bathed in the Maṅgala lotus pond, he sat down on the Maṅgala stone slab when the sun had set, desiring to have himself adorned.
Then his attendants, taking various colored garments, diverse kinds of ornaments, garlands, perfumes, and ointments, stood surrounding him on all sides. In that [moment]...
At that moment, Sakka’s seat became hot. Thinking, “Who indeed wishes to displace me from this position?
he investigated and, perceiving the Bodhisatta’s desire to adorn himself, addressed Vissakamma:
“Friend Vissakamma, today at the hour of midnight, Prince Siddhattha will go forth on the Great Renunciation; this is his [ornament]—”
“This is the final adornment; having gone to the garden, adorn the Great Man with celestial ornaments.
Having consented, saying “Very well,” he approached at that very moment through the power of the deity.
Assuming the appearance of a barber, he took a turban-cloth from the barber’s hand and wrapped it around the head of the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta—
By the mere touch of his hand, he recognized: "This is no human; this is a son of the gods.
As soon as the head was wrapped with the cloth, a thousand lengths of cloth rose up in the form of a crest-jewel made of precious gems. As he wrapped it again, another thousand lengths rose up;
thus, as he wrapped it ten times, ten thousand lengths of cloth rose up. "The head is small, yet the cloths—"
One should not wonder, "How did so many [lotuses] emerge? For among them, the largest was the size of an *āmalaka* flower, while the remaining ones were the size of *kusumbhaka* flowers.
The head of the Bodhisatta became like a *kuyyaka* flower, covered as if by its filaments.
Then, while all the musicians displayed their respective skills,
while the brahmins honored him with words such as "Victory and Joy," and while the bards, minstrels, and others celebrated with various auspicious speeches and hymns of praise,
he mounted his excellent chariot, which was adorned with every ornament. At that moment, Rāhula’s mother—
Upon hearing that she had given birth to a son, King Suddhodana sent a message saying, "Announce my joy to my son.
When the Bodhisatta heard this, he said, "Rāhu is born; a bond is born. The king asked, "What did my son say?
and having heard those words, he declared, "From now on, let my grandson's name be Rāhula-kumāra alone."
The Bodhisatta, too, having mounted his excellent chariot, entered the city with great glory, exceeding delightfulness, and radiant splendor.

At that time, a noble maiden named Kisāgotamī, who was on the upper terrace of the palace, beheld the beauty of the Bodhisatta’s form as he circumambulated the city; filled with joy and gladness, she uttered this inspired utterance:
“Truly extinguished is that mother; truly extinguished is that father;
truly extinguished is that woman whose husband is such as this.
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta thought: “The heart of a mother who sees such a physical form as this—”
‘The fire goes out; the father’s heart goes out; the mother’s heart goes out!
Now, when what has gone out is it said that the heart has gone out? Then, his mind having become dispassionate toward the defilements, this thought occurred to him:
“When the fire of lust has gone out, it is said to have gone out; when the fire of hatred has gone out, it is said to have gone out.”

When the fire of delusion is extinguished, it is called "extinguished" (*nibbūta*); when all the fevers of the defilements, such as pride and views, have been extinguished, it is called "extinguished.
This man has informed me of what must be heard; for I wander seeking *nibbāna*.
It is fitting that this very day I should abandon the household life, go forth, and seek *nibbāna*.
"Let this be the teacher's fee for her," she said, and having removed it from her own neck, she sent a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand pieces to Kisāgotamī.
She, filled with joy, thought, "Prince Siddhattha has sent me this gift because his heart is bound to me."
The Bodhisatta, too, having ascended his own palace with great splendor and majesty, lay down upon his royal couch.

At that very moment, women adorned with every ornament, highly skilled in dancing and singing, possessing a beauty like that of celestial nymphs, surrounded him while holding various musical instruments;
providing him with delight, they set to work with their dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
Because his mind was dispassionate toward the defilements, the Bodhisatta took no delight in the dancing and other performances and fell asleep for a moment.
Those women thought, "He for whose sake we employed the dancing and other arts has now fallen asleep; why should we continue to weary ourselves now?
Thus, they overwhelmed the instruments they had been holding and lay down, as did the lamps fed with fragrant oil.

They were meditating. The Bodhisatta, having awakened and sitting cross-legged upon the back of his bed, saw those women sleeping after they had laid aside their musical instruments—some with saliva trickling down, their limbs drenched in mucus;
some gnashing their teeth, some grinding them, some muttering incoherently, and some with mouths wide open.
Some were stripped of their garments, their private parts exposed in a state of loathsome nakedness.
Seeing this transformation in them, his mind became even more intensely detached from sensual desires.

To him, that great terrace—which had been like the well-adorned palace of Sakka—now appeared like a raw charnel ground filled with discarded and various kinds of filth; so too did the three realms of existence appear to him.
They appeared like a house on fire; he uttered an exclamation, “Alas, we are beset! Alas, we are overwhelmed!
and his mind inclined exceedingly toward the life of renunciation.
Thinking, “It is fitting for me to go forth on the Great Renunciation this very day,” he rose from his bed and approached the door.
Having gone there, he asked, "Who is here? Channa, who was lying down with his head upon the threshold, replied, "I am Channa, noble son.
[The Prince] said, "Today I desire to go forth on the Great Renunciation; prepare a horse for me.
He replied, "Very well, Your Majesty," and taking the horse-trappings, went to the stable while fragrant oil lamps were burning.

Seeing the royal horse Kaṇḍaka standing on a delightful stretch of ground beneath a canopy of *sumana* cloth, [the Bodhisatta] thought, "Today it is fitting that I should saddle him," and he saddled Kaṇḍaka.
Even as he was being saddled, Kaṇḍaka understood: "This saddling is exceedingly tight;
it is not like the saddling used on other days when going for excursions to the pleasure gardens and such."
“Today my noble son will desire to go forth on the Great Renunciation.
Then, with a joyful heart, he let out a great laugh. That sound would have spread throughout the entire city, but the deities suppressed that sound and did not allow anyone to hear it.

The Bodhisatta, having sent Channa away and thinking, "I shall first see my son," rose from his sitting-couch and went to the dwelling place of Rāhula’s mother; he opened the door of the inner chamber.
At that moment, a lamp of scented oil was burning within the room, and Rāhula’s mother was lying on a bed strewn knee-deep with jasmine, mallika, and other flowers.
She fell asleep with her hand placed upon her son’s head. The Bodhisatta, standing still with his foot placed upon the threshold, looked down and thought:
“If I remove the queen’s hand and take my son, the queen will wake up;
thus there will be an obstacle to my departure. Only after becoming a Buddha shall I return and see my son. From the palace roof...
He descended. As for what is stated in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*—“At that time, Prince Rāhula was seven days old”—this is not found in the other commentaries;
therefore, this [other version] alone should be accepted.
Thus, having descended from the palace roof and approached the horse, the Bodhisatta spoke as follows: “Dear Kaṇḍaka, you...”
“Today, for one night, save me; by relying on you, having become a Buddha, I shall save the world together with its devas.
Then, leaping up, he mounted the back of Kaṇḍaka.
From the neck upward, Kaṇḍaka was eighteen cubits in length, endowed with a corresponding height, possessed of strength and speed, all-white like a polished conch shell.
Thus, had he laughed or made even the sound of a footfall, his voice would have spread throughout the entire city.
Therefore, by her own supernatural power, the deity suppressed the sound of his laughter so that no one could hear it, and at every step as he walked, she held out the palms of her hands.
The Bodhisatta was seated upon the middle of the horse’s back.
Having had the horse Channa seize its tail, he arrived near the great gate at the hour of midnight. At that time,

however, the king, thinking, "In this way, the Bodhisatta will not be able to exit by having the city gates opened at any time whatsoever," had it decreed that each of the two gate-leaves must be opened by a thousand men.
The Bodhisatta was endowed with strength and power; he possessed the strength of ten thousand million elephants by the count of elephants, and of ten thousand million men by the count of men.
He thought: "If the gate is not opened, today, while seated on Kaṇḍaka’s back, I shall take hold of his tail and [depart] together with Channa who stands holding it."
“Pressing against his thighs, I will leap over the eighteen-cubit-high wall and pass through.
Channa also thought: “If the gate is not opened, I will place the noble son upon my shoulder, wrap Kaṇḍaka with my right hand around his belly, hold him between my knees, leap over the wall, and—”

“I shall pass over it. Kaṇḍaka also thought: “If the gate is not opened, I will lift my master, even as he sits upon my back, together with Channa who stands holding onto his tail, and having leaped over the wall, I shall pass over it.
If the gate were not opened, [he would have done] exactly as he had intended.
One of those three men would prepare the way. Then the deity dwelling at the gate opened the door.
At that very moment, Māra, thinking, "I shall turn the Bodhisatta back," arrived and stood in the air, saying: "My dear sir, do not go out!
On the seventh day from now, the Wheel-Treasure (cakkaratana) will appear to you, [ruling] over the two thousand minor islands that surround it."
“You shall rule over the four great continents; turn back, dear sir! “Who are you? “I am Vasavattī.
“Māra, I know of the appearance of my Wheel-Treasure. I have no need for kingship; having made the ten-thousandfold world-system resound, I shall become a Buddha,” he said.
Then Māra thought, “From this moment on, you shall have neither thoughts of sensual desire nor thoughts of ill will...”
"Or, when he is reflecting, I shall know whether he entertains thoughts of sensual desire or thoughts of ill will. Thus, seeking an opportunity, Māra followed him like a shadow that never departs.

The Bodhisatta, however, having cast away the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch that had come into his hands as if it were a globule of spittle, without looking back, departed from the city with great honor on the full moon day of Āsāḷha while the constellation Uttarāsāḷha was in the ascendant. Having departed, he...
Furthermore, he became desirous of looking back at the city.
As soon as this thought arose in his mind, the great earth—as if saying, "Great Being, you have not performed the act of looking back"—split and turned like a potter's wheel.
The Bodhisatta stood facing the city, looked back at it, and [in that moment]...
Having shown the site of the Kaṇḍakanivattana Cetiya on a portion of the earth and having turned Kaṇḍaka toward the path to be traveled,
he set forth with great honor and sublime majesty and splendor. At that time, it is said,
deities held sixty thousand torches in front of him, sixty behind him, sixty on his right side, and sixty on his left side.
Sixty other deities held immeasurable torches at the rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-mukhavaṭṭi*).
Other deities, as well as *nāgas*, *supaṇṇas*, and others, proceeded while making offerings with divine perfumes, garlands, powders, and incense.
With *pāricchattaka* flowers and *mandārava* flowers, it was as if there were torrents of rain falling from thick clouds.
The sky became continuous [with light], celestial songs resounded, and six million eight hundred thousand musical instruments played on all sides;
it was like the time of thundering clouds within the belly of the ocean, or like the roar of the sea within the belly of Mount Yugandhara.
Traveling with such splendor and majesty, the Bodhisatta, in a single night, passed beyond three kingdoms and reached a distance of thirty yojanas.
He reached the bank of the Anomā River. "But why was the horse unable to go further than that?

"It was not so; he was not able. For he was capable of returning by early morning after traversing the entire circuit of a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), as if crushing the rim of a wheel fixed at its hub, and then eating the meal he had prepared for himself. At that time...

However, as his body was covered up to the region of his thighs by perfumes, garlands, and other offerings dropped from the sky by devas, nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others who stood above him, it became excessively cumbersome for him as he pulled them along while cutting through the mass of garlands; therefore, he traveled only about thirty yojanas.
Then, standing on the riverbank, the Bodhisatta asked Channa: "What is the name of this river?"
“It is ‘Anomā,’ O King. “Then our renunciation too shall be ‘Anomā’ (Unprecedented),” he said, giving the signal to the horse by nudging him with his heel.
The horse leaped into the air and landed on the far bank of a river eight usabhas in width.
The Bodhisatta dismounted from the horse’s back and, standing upon the sandy shore which resembled a silver plate, addressed Channa:
“‘Friend Channa, take my ornaments and Kaṇḍaka and go; I shall go forth,’ he said. ‘I too, O Lord, will go forth,’ replied Channa.
The Bodhisatta, having refused him three times, saying, ‘It is not right for you to go forth;
go now,’ and having handed over the ornaments and Kaṇḍaka, reflected: ‘These [ornaments] of mine...’”

“Hair is not suitable for a recluse. Since there was no one else fit to cut the Bodhisatta’s hair, he thought, “I shall cut it myself with a sword,” and taking a sword in his right hand and grasping his topknot together with the tuft of hair on his crown with his left hand, he cut them;
the hair, being only two finger-breadths long, curled toward the right.
They grew back to that same length for as long as they lived, and their beards were proportionate to that; thus, there was never again any need to shave their hair or beards.
Taking his topknot along with his turban, the Bodhisatta said, "If I shall become a Buddha, let it stay in the air;
if not, let it fall to the ground," and he threw it into the sky. It—
Having traveled to a place one *yojana* in extent, the crest-jewel stood suspended in the air.

Sakka, the king of the gods, beheld it with his divine eye, received it in a golden *caṅkoṭaka* basket one *yojana* in size, and established it in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as the shrine known as the Cūḷāmaṇi Cetiya.
“Having cut off his topknot, which was scented with the finest perfumes, the Supreme Person tossed it up into the sky.”
“Vāsava, with his thousand eyes, accepted them upon his head with a most excellent golden casket.
Then the Bodhisatta thought, “These Kāsika garments are not suitable for me as an ascetic.
At that moment, Ghaṭīkāra Mahābrahmā, who had been his old friend during the time of Kassapa Buddha and had remained untouched by decay for an entire interval between Buddhas, [appeared].
With a friendly disposition, he thought: “Today my companion has gone forth on the Great Renunciation;
I shall go taking his requisites for a recluse.
“The three robes and the bowl, the razor, the needle, and the girdle;”
“With this water-strainer, these eight [requisites] belong to the bhikkhu who is devoted to yoga.

Having brought these eight requisites of a recluse, he gave them [to him]. The Bodhisatta, having donned the robe that is the banner of the Arahants and assumed the supreme garb of one gone forth, said, “Channa, convey my words to my parents and wish them good health,” and then dismissed him. Channa—
Having paid homage to the Bodhisatta and circumambulated him, he departed.
But Kaṇḍaka, standing there listening to the words of the Bodhisatta as he consulted with Channa, thought, "I shall never see my master again.
As he passed beyond the range of sight, unable to endure his grief, his heart burst and he died.
In the realm of the Thirty-three, he was reborn as a son of the gods named Kaṇḍaka.
Channa had previously experienced only one sorrow, but now, oppressed by a second sorrow due to the death of Kaṇḍaka, he went into the city weeping and lamenting.
The Bodhisatta, having gone forth, stayed for seven days in that very region in a mango grove called Anupiya.
Having spent his time in the happiness of the renunciant life, he traveled thirty yojanas on foot in a single day and entered Rājagaha.
Having entered, he went for alms from house to house in regular succession.

The entire city was thrown into a state of agitation by the sight of the Bodhisatta’s form, like the city of Rājagaha when it was entered by Dhanapālaka, or like the city of the gods when it was entered by the Lord of the Asuras.
He arrived. The king’s men went and reported, "Your Majesty, a being such as this is wandering for alms in the city;
we do not know whether he is a god, a human, a nāga, or a supaṇṇa—what indeed is he?
Standing on the terrace of his palace, the king saw the Great Man and, struck with wonder and amazement, commanded his men: "Go, sirs, investigate."
"If he is a non-human being, he will depart from the city and vanish;
if he is a deity, he will go through the air; if he is a nāga, he will descend into the earth and depart;
if he is a human being, he will consume the alms-food as received."
The Great Being, having gathered the mixed food and knowing, "This is sufficient for my sustenance," departed from the city by the very gate he had entered.
Sitting down in the shade of Mount Paṇḍava facing the east, he began to consume the food.
Then his intestines turned inside out, as if they were about to emerge from his mouth.
Then, because such food as this had never before been seen even with his eyes in that state of existence, he was repelled by that loathsome food and admonished himself thus:

"Siddhattha, although you were born into a family where food and drink were easily obtained, in a place where one eats three-year-old *gandha-sāli* rice with various choice flavors, yet upon seeing a single rag-robe wearer (*paṃsukūlika*), you thought: 'When indeed shall I too...'"
"Having become such as this, I shall go for alms and eat; will that time ever come for me?
Having thought thus, he set out. "Now, what is this you are doing? Having thus exhorted himself by himself, he remained free from agitation and consumed his food.
The king’s men, having witnessed this occurrence, went and reported it to the king.

Upon hearing the messengers’ words, the king departed from the city with haste and went into the presence of the Bodhisatta. Even at the mere sight of his deportment, he was filled with faith and entrusted all his sovereignty to the Bodhisatta.
The Bodhisatta said, “Great King, for me there is no need for either sensual pleasures of the objects (*vatthukāma*) or sensual pleasures of the defilements (*kilesakāma*).”
"Or rather, there is no need; I have gone forth desiring supreme perfect enlightenment," he said.
Although the king entreated him in many ways, failing to win his consent, he took a formal promise from him, saying: "Surely you will become a Buddha;
when you have become a Buddha, you must first come to my realm. This is the summary here; the detailed account is as follows.
However, this should be understood by consulting the *Pabbajjā-sutta* together with its commentary, which begins: "I shall proclaim the going-forth, how the Visionary One went forth.
The Bodhisatta, having given his promise to the king, wandered on by stages until he reached Āḷāra Kālāma and Udaka.

Having approached Rāmaputta and attained his meditative absorptions (samāpatti), and [realizing] "this is not the path to enlightenment," he did not even adorn himself with that cultivation of absorption.
Desiring to exert the Great Struggle (mahāpadhāna) in order to demonstrate his own strength and vigor to the world including its devas, he went to Uruvelā;
thinking, "How delightful indeed is this region of land," he took up residence right there.

"Exert the Great Struggle. Then those five who had gone forth, led by Koṇḍañña, while wandering for alms through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, arrived there at the place where the Bodhisatta was.
As he was exerting the Great Struggle for six years, they thought, "Now he will become a Buddha;
now he will become a Buddha," and [they served him] with tasks such as sweeping the monastery courtyards.

Attending upon him with the performance of his duties, they remained in his presence. The Bodhisatta, thinking, "I shall perform austerities that have reached the ultimate limit," passed the time even on a single sesame seed or grain of rice;
he even completely cut off all food, and though the deities offered nourishment through the pores of his skin, he rejected it.
Then, because of that lack of food, his body—having reached the extreme limit of emaciation—changed from its golden color to a dark hue.

The thirty-two marks of a Great Man became obscured. At times, while practicing breathless meditation (*appaṇaka-jhāna*), overcome by great pains and losing consciousness, he would fall at the end of his walking path. Then, some...
The deities said, "The ascetic Gotama has passed away," while some said, "This was merely the dwelling-place of an Arahant.
Among them, those who thought he had passed away went and informed King Suddhodana, saying, "Your son has passed away. [The king asked:
"Did my son pass away after becoming a Buddha, or without having become one? [They replied: "He was unable to become a Buddha."
"He fell right there on the ground of exertion and passed away. Upon hearing this, the king rejected it, saying, "I do not believe it;
for my son, there can be no passing away until he has attained enlightenment. Why did the king not believe it?
Because he had witnessed the miracles at the foot of the rose-apple tree on the day he was made to pay homage to the ascetic Kāḷadevī.
When the Bodhisatta regained consciousness and arose, those deities went and announced, "Your son is well, Great King.
The King replied, "I already know that my son will not die.
To the Mahāsatta, who was performing austerities for six years, it was as if he were merely making a knot in the air. He thought, "This practice of austerities..."
“there is no path to enlightenment,” he began to consume substantial food. Having wandered for alms among the villages and market towns, he took nourishment;
then his thirty-two marks of a Great Man became manifest, and his body turned the color of gold.
The monks of the Group of Five [said], “Even though this man practiced austerities for six years, he did not attain omniscience...”
"He was unable to penetrate [the truth]; now that he wanders for alms among villages and the like, taking coarse food, what will he be able to achieve?
He is one who indulges in abundance and has abandoned his striving. Our seeking for excellence from him is like one wishing to bathe his head who calculates the drops of dew;
what use have we for him? Thus, having abandoned the Great Man, he returned to his own [place].
Taking their own bowls and robes, they traveled a road of eighteen *yojanas* and entered Isipatana.
Now at that time, in the village of Senā at Uruvelā, a girl named Sujātā had been born in the house of a householder of the Senā clan;
having reached maturity, she made a vow under a banyan tree: "If [I may obtain] a husband from a family of equal status..."
"Having gone there, I shall obtain a son in my first pregnancy; year after year, I will perform a ritual offering by giving away a hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. Her aspiration was fulfilled.
When the sixth year of the Great Being’s practice of austerities had come to an end, on the full moon day of Visākha, she desired to perform the ritual offering and prepared beforehand.
Having caused a thousand cows to graze in a grove of *laṭṭhi* and *madhuka* trees, he had five hundred cows drink their milk;
then their milk was given to two hundred and fifty, and so on, until finally eight cows drank the milk of sixteen.
Thus, desiring the thickness, sweetness, and nutritive essence (*ojas*) of the milk, he performed this succession of milk-transfers.

She gave [the child] a name. On the full moon day of the month of Visākha, thinking, "I shall perform the offering ceremony early in the morning," she rose at the break of dawn during the night and had those eight cows milked. The calves did not come to the udders of the cows;
however, as soon as the new vessels were brought to the udders, streams of milk flowed out by their own nature. This was a marvel.
Having seen this, Sujātā took the milk with her own hands, placed it in a new vessel,
and began to cook it over a fire lit by her own hand.
As that milk-rice was cooking, large bubbles rose up and moved about, turning to the right.
Not even a single drop fell outside, and not even a trace of smoke rose from the hearth.
At that time, the four World-Protectors arrived and took up their guard over the hearth;
Mahābrahmā held the parasol, and Sakka kindled the fire by fanning the embers. The deities [were present] throughout the four great continents, each surrounded by two thousand islands.

By means of their own divine power, they gathered the nourishing essence suitable for both gods and humans—just as one might extract honey by pressing a honeycomb bound with sticks—and placed it therein.

For at other times, the deities place the essence morsel by morsel into the mouth; however, on the day of the Enlightenment and on the day of the Parinibbāna, they place it directly into the cooking pot.
They were throwing [the offerings] in. On that very day, Sujātā, having witnessed many wonders manifest there, addressed her maidservant Puṇṇā:
"Mother Puṇṇā, today our deity is exceedingly well-pleased;
in all this time, I have never before seen such a wonder. Go quickly and attend to the place where the deity resides."
She, saying "Very well, noble lady," accepted her words and went to the foot of the tree in great haste.
The Bodhisatta, having seen five great dreams during that portion of the night and reflecting upon them, reached the firm conclusion:
"Without doubt, today I shall become a Buddha. At the end of that night, having attended to his physical needs, he—
Waiting for the time to go on his alms-round, he arrived early in the morning and sat down at the foot of that tree,
illuminating the entire tree with his own radiance. Then Puṇṇā came and saw the Bodhisatta sitting at the foot of the tree,
gazing toward the eastern world-system, and the entire tree was [illuminated] by the rays of light issuing from his body.
[She was] golden-hued. Having seen her, it occurred to her: "Today our deity has descended from the tree and is likely sitting down to receive the offering with her own hands.
Overcome with excitement, she came running swiftly and reported this matter to Sujātā.
Upon hearing her words, Sujātā became joyful in heart and thought: "From this day forward, in place of my eldest daughter..."
"Stay," she said, and gave her daughter all the ornaments suitable for her.

Since it was fitting that on the day she would attain Buddhahood she should receive a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, she conceived the thought, "I shall place the milk-rice in a golden bowl," and had a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand brought out; therein—
Desiring to put the milk-rice (pāyāsa) [into the bowl], she looked toward the cooking vessel.
All the milk-rice turned back like water on a lotus leaf and settled in the bowl; it filled only a single bowl.
She, recognizing that bowl, covered it with another golden bowl, wrapped it in white cloth, adorned her body with all her ornaments, and [took] that bowl...
Placing it upon his own head, he went to the foot of the Nigrodha tree with great majesty;
beholding the Bodhisatta and being filled with intense joy, perceiving him as a "tree deity," he proceeded by bowing lower and lower from the spot where he had seen him,
removed the bowl from his head, uncovered it, and [poured] water scented with perfumed flowers from a golden pitcher.

Having taken the Bodhisatta, he approached and stood before him. The clay bowl given by the Great Brahmā Ghaṭīkāra had not left the Bodhisatta’s side for so long, yet at that moment it vanished from sight;
not seeing the bowl, the Bodhisatta extended his right hand and received the water. Sujātā brought the milk-rice together with the bowl to the Great Being.
He placed it in his hand; the Great Man looked at Sujātā. Perceiving his gesture, she said, "Noble sir, this has been offered by me to you;

take it and go as you please. Having paid homage, she added, "Just as my own heart's desire has been fulfilled, may yours likewise be fulfilled," and she took a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [pieces] from beneath some old leaves.
Having become indifferent as if it were something else,
he departed. The Bodhisatta also, rising from his seat, circumambulated the tree clockwise, took the bowl,
and went to the bank of the Nerañjarā River— the bathing place where many thousands of Bodhisattas had descended on the day of their full enlightenment.
There is a place called Suppaṭṭhitatittha; having placed his bowl on its bank, he descended and bathed.
Then, having put on the robe of an Arahant—the dwelling-place of many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas—he sat down facing the east.

Having formed forty-nine lumps, each the size of a single standing palm fruit, he consumed all that honeyed milk-rice, which was entirely free of water. For this very reason, when he had become a Buddha...
While dwelling on the seat of enlightenment for seven times seven days, there was food for him for forty-nine days.
During that time, there was no other food, nor bathing, nor washing of the face, nor cleansing of the body;
he passed the time through the bliss of meditative absorption, the bliss of the Path, and the bliss of the Fruit. Having consumed that milk-rice, [he set aside] the golden bowl...
Having taken it, he said, "If I am able to become a Buddha today, let this bowl go against the current;
if I am not able, let it go with the current," and he threw it into the river's flow.
Cutting through the current, it went to the middle of the river and, from that very central spot, traveled for a distance of eighty cubits like a horse endowed with great speed.
Going against the current, he submerged himself in a whirlpool and went to the abode of the Naga King Kāḷa.
Making a "kili-kilī" sound, he struck the alms-bowls used by the three Buddhas and stood at the very bottom of them all.
Hearing that sound, the Naga King Kāḷa thought, "Yesterday one Buddha was born, and today another."
Having said, "He has been reborn," he rose up, uttering praises in many hundreds of verses.
Indeed, for him, the time spent ascending to fill the sky to the extent of one yojana and three gavutas above the great earth was as if it were either today or yesterday.
The Bodhisatta, having passed the day’s rest in a grove of flowering *sāla* trees on the riverbank, at the time of evening [began to gather] the flowers...
At the moment he was released from the stalk, he set out toward the Bodhi tree, stretching himself like a lion along a path eight usabhas wide that had been adorned by the deities.
Nagas, yakkhas, supaṇṇas, and others honored him with divine perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
they performed divine music and the like, and the ten-thousandfold world system became one in fragrance, one in garlands, and one in shouts of "Well done!"
At that time, a grass-cutter named Sotthiya, coming along the opposite path carrying grass, recognized the demeanor of the Great Being and gave him eight handfuls of grass.
The Bodhisatta took the grass, ascended the seat of enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa), and stood on the southern side facing north. At that moment, the southern world-system (cakkavāḷa) sank down.
It was as if it had reached down to the Avīci hell below, and as if it had leaped over the northern Cakkavāḷa and reached up to the peak of existence above.

The Bodhisatta, thinking, "I suspect this will not be the place for attaining full enlightenment," moved clockwise toward the western direction and stood facing the east; then, [he beheld] the western Cakkavāḷa.
Sinking down, it was as if it had reached the Avīci hell below; leaping over the eastern world-system, it was as if it had reached the peak of existence above.
In every place where it stood, the great earth became depressed and elevated, like the wheel of a great cart whose rim has been trodden upon and which is now resting upon its hub. The Bodhisatta—
Thinking, "This too will not be the place for attaining full enlightenment," the Bodhisatta circumambulated it, went toward the northern quarter, and stood facing south.
Thereupon, the northern world-system sank down as if reaching the Avīci hell below, while the southern world-system rose up as if reaching the peak of existence above. The Bodhisatta—
Thinking, "I suppose this place will not be the spot for attaining full enlightenment," the Great Being circumambulated it and, having gone to the eastern quarter, stood facing the west.
However, in the eastern quarter lies the seat of the cross-legged posture (pallaṅka) for all Buddhas;
that place neither trembles nor shakes. The Great Being [thought], "This is the immovable place never abandoned by all Buddhas."
Knowing them to be "the place for the destruction of the cage of defilements," the Bodhisatta took those grasses by their tips and shook them;

at that very moment, they became a couch fourteen cubits long. Those grasses also arranged themselves into such a form that no painter or weaver, however skilled, would be capable of depicting it even in a painting. The Bodhisatta—
Placing the mass of awakening behind him and facing forward with a firm mind, he resolved:
"Let only skin, sinews, and bone remain;
let the flesh and blood in my body dry up entirely."

Thinking, "I shall not break this cross-legged posture until I have attained supreme perfect enlightenment," he sat down, having folded his legs in the invincible *pallaṅka* which was truly indestructible even by a hundred simultaneous thunderbolts.
At that time, Māra the son of a deva thought, "Prince Siddhattha wishes to transcend my domain;
I will not allow him to transcend it. He went to the presence of the Māra-force, reported this matter, and proclaimed the cry of Māra.
Having caused his name to be proclaimed, he set forth taking the Māra-force with him.
That army of Māra extended twelve yojanas in front of him, twelve yojanas to the right and to the left, and stood behind him as far as the limits of the world-system (cakkavāḷa);
it was nine yojanas in height, and the sound of its loud shouting reached from a thousand yojanas away.

It resounded like the sound of the earth-trembling drum. Then Māra the son of a deity, having mounted the elephant named Girimekhala—who was one hundred and fifty leagues in height—and having manifested a thousand arms, seized various weapons.
Among the rest of Māra’s retinue as well, not two persons took up the same weapon; they assumed various complexions and various facial expressions.
They approached, overwhelming the Great Being.
However, the devas of the ten thousand world-systems stood by, uttering praises of the Great Being. Sakka, the king of the gods, stood there blowing his victory-conch, the Vijayuttara;
it is said that this conch was one hundred and twenty cubits long. Once—
Having plunged into the wind and trumpeted for four months, it became silent after making its sound.
The Great Black Naga King stood there praising [the Bodhisatta] with more than a hundred verses, while the Great Brahmā stood holding a white parasol.
But when the hosts of Māra approached the seat of enlightenment, not even one among them was able to remain; they were driven back from their very positions face-to-face.
They fled. The Naga king Kāḷa, having submerged himself into the earth, went to his own Naga abode, Mañjerika, five hundred yojanas away, and lay down covering his face with both hands.
Sakka, placing the Vijayuttara conch upon his back, stood at the rim of the Cakkavāḷa. Mahābrahmā, holding the white parasol, stood at the edge of the Cakkavāḷa.
He went straight to the Brahma-world. Not even a single deity was able to remain;
the Great Man sat all alone. Māra also said to his own retinue: "Sons, there is no other man equal to Siddhattha, the son of Suddhodana.
We shall not be able to give him battle face-to-face; let us give it from behind."
The Great Being, too, looked toward the three directions and saw that they were empty because all the deities had fled.
Then, seeing the army of Māra overwhelming him from the northern direction, he thought:
"This great multitude exerts such immense effort and prowess directed against me alone; in this place, I have neither mother, nor father, nor brother..."
"Since I have no other kinsman or relative, these ten perfections alone have been like a long-time retinue to me;
therefore, it is right that I should shatter this army by making the perfections my shield and striking with the essence of the perfections themselves.
Thus he sat, reflecting upon the ten perfections.
Then Māra the son of a deva, thinking, "I shall cause Siddhattha to flee by this very means," raised up a whirlwind.
At that very moment, winds of the eastern and other directions arose, shattering mountain peaks measuring half a yojana, one yojana, two yojanas, and three yojanas in size, uprooting forests,
thickets, trees, and the like, and reducing villages and towns on all sides to dust and fragments.
Although she was capable of doing so, her power was neutralized by the majesty of the Great Being’s merit; thus, upon reaching the Bodhisatta, she was unable to move even the hem of his robe.
Thereupon, thinking, "I shall kill him without drowning him in water," she unleashed a great rain.
By its power, clouds consisting of hundreds and thousands of layers arose one above the other and rained down.

The earth was pierced by the force of the downpour of rain. Although a great cloud approached from above the forest trees and other vegetation, it was unable to moisten even a spot the size of a dewdrop on the Great Being’s robe.
Thereupon, he raised a shower of stones. Massive mountain peaks, smoking and blazing, came through the air.
Upon reaching the Bodhisatta, they turned into divine garlands and bouquets. Then he unleashed a rain of weapons.
Single-edged and double-edged swords, spears, arrows, razor-tipped shafts, and the like—smoking and blazing—came through the air and, upon reaching the Bodhisatta, became celestial flowers.
Then he unleashed a rain of embers. Embers the color of *kiṃsuka* flowers came through the air and...
They became divine flowers and scattered at the feet of the Bodhisattva. Then he raised a rain of hot ashes (*kukkuḷa*).
The extremely hot, fire-colored hot ashes came through the air and fell at the feet of the Bodhisattva, having become divine sandalwood powder.
Then he raised a rain of sand. The exceedingly fine sand was smoking and blazing.
Having come through the air, they fell at the feet of the Bodhisatta as celestial flowers.
Then he caused a rain of mud to arise. That mud, smoking and blazing, came through the air and fell at the feet of the Bodhisatta as celestial ointment.
Then, thinking, "By terrifying him with this, I shall cause Siddhattha to flee," he created darkness.
He raised it up. That great darkness, as if endowed with four limbs, reached the Bodhisatta and vanished like the gloom dispelled by the radiance of the sun.
Thus did Māra [attack] with these nine showers of wind, rain, stones, blows, glowing embers, hot sand, mud, and darkness.
Failing to frighten the Bodhisatta away, he commanded his retinue, saying, "What, you fellows! Stay! Seize this Prince Siddhattha!
Kill him! Drive him away! Then, mounting the back of the elephant Girimekhala and taking up his discus weapon, he approached the Bodhisatta and said, "Siddhattha, rise from this cross-legged seat!"
"This does not belong to you; it belongs to me alone," he said. Having heard his words, the Great Being replied:
"Māra, neither have you fulfilled the ten perfections (pāramitā), nor the secondary perfections (upapāramitā), nor the ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramitā);

neither have you renounced the five great sacrifices (mahāpariccāga), nor practiced for the welfare of relatives (ñātatthacariyā), nor for the welfare of the world (lokatthacariyā), nor the practice of wisdom (buddhicariyā)."
“All these have been fulfilled; they have all been fulfilled by me alone. Therefore, this couch does not belong to you; it belongs to me alone.
Enraged and unable to endure the force of his anger, Māra hurled the discus-weapon at the Great Being.
As he was reflecting upon his ten perfections (*pāramitā*), it remained suspended above him like a canopy of garlands. Indeed, that discus-weapon possessed a razor-sharp edge.
On another occasion, when he was angry, it would go along cutting through solid stone pillars as if they were mere bamboo shoots;

but now, while he stood there as a canopy of garlands, the rest of Māra’s retinue, thinking, "He will now rise from his cross-legged seat and flee," hurled down massive mountain peaks. These too [were cut by] the Great Being...
As he was reflecting upon the ten perfections, they took on the form of a flower garland and fell to the ground.

Deities standing at the rim of the world-system stretched out their necks and raised their heads, looking on and thinking, "Alas, that body of Prince Siddhattha, which had attained the pinnacle of beauty, is lost! What indeed will he do now?"

Then the Great Being said, "On the day of the full awakening of Bodhisattvas who have fulfilled the perfections, the seat upon which they sit is mine alone," and addressed Māra, who stood there: "Māra, who is your witness that you have given this gift?
Māra stretched out his hand toward his own host and said, "These people here are my witnesses."
At that moment, the sound raised by Māra’s retinue crying out, “I am witness! I am witness! was like the roar of the earth quaking.
Then Māra said to the Great Being, “Siddhattha, who is witness to the fact that you have given this gift?
The Great Being replied, “As for your own gift, sentient beings are witnesses; but as for mine in this case—”

"In this matter, there is no conscious witness whatsoever; let alone the gifts I gave in my other existences, even this insentient great earth is a witness to the fact that I gave the Great Gift of the Seven Hundreds while dwelling in the Vessantara existence.
Having thus spoken, he extended his right hand from within the folds of his robe and said, "In the Vessantara existence..."
"Standing here, am I not a witness to my having given the great gift of seven hundred [measures]?

he said, extending his hand toward the great earth. The great earth roared with a hundred cries, a thousand cries, and a hundred thousand cries—as if overwhelming the host of Māra—proclaiming, "I was your witness then!"

Then, as the Great Being was reflecting upon the Vessantara gift, thinking, "Siddhattha, you have given a great gift, a supreme gift," the elephant Girimekhala, one hundred and fifty leagues in height, knelt upon the earth on his knees. Māra’s assembly fled in every direction;
there were none who went along the same path, for they scattered their head-ornaments and their garments.
And having abandoned him, they fled in every direction, right before his eyes.
Then the hosts of devas, seeing Māra’s army fleeing, cried out, “Māra has been defeated! Prince Siddhattha has won!

Let us perform a victory offering!”—and thus the nāgas proclaimed it to the nāgas, the supaṇṇas to the supaṇṇas, the devas to the devas, and the brahmas to the brahmas; with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands, they [proceeded].
They went to the presence of the Great Being at the seat of enlightenment.
And when they had thus departed, [the Buddha declared]:
"This is indeed victory for the Glorious Buddha, and defeat for Māra the Evil One."
Delighted, the hosts of nāgas then proclaimed victory for the Great Sage at the seat of enlightenment:
“This is indeed the victory of the glorious Buddha, and the defeat of Māra the Evil One!
Delighted, the throngs of supaṇṇas also proclaimed victory for the Great Sage at the seat of enlightenment.
“Victory indeed belongs to the glorious Buddha, and defeat to Māra the Evil One!
Thus did the throngs of gods, filled with joy, proclaim the victory of the Great Seer at the seat of enlightenment.
“Victory indeed belongs to the glorious Buddha, and defeat to Māra the Evil One!”
"Then, on the seat of enlightenment, the hosts of Brahmas, filled with joy, also proclaimed victory to the Tathāgata.
The remaining deities in the ten thousand world-systems stood by, honoring him with garlands, perfumes, and ointments, and uttering various kinds of praises.
Thus, even before the sun had set, the Great Being, having shattered the army of Māra, [sat down].
Being honored as if by sprouts of the Bodhi tree falling over his robe like red coral shoots, he recollected his past lives during the first watch of the night;
having purified his divine eye during the middle watch, he applied his knowledge to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) during the last watch.
Then, [he contemplated] the twelvefold formula of conditions by way of the forward and reverse order of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa*).
As he contemplated [the dependent origination] in forward and reverse order, the ten-thousandfold world-system, bounded by the waters, shook twelve times.

When the Great Being, having caused the ten-thousandfold world-system to resound, penetrated the knowledge of omniscience at the time of sunrise, the entire ten-thousandfold world-system became adorned and prepared. At the eastern rim of the world-sphere...
The rays of the raised banners and streamers strike the western rim of the world-sphere;
likewise, those raised on the western rim strike the eastern rim, those raised on the southern rim strike the northern rim,
and those raised on the northern rim [strike the southern rim].

They struck the rim of the southern world-system; moreover, the banners and flags raised upon the surface of the earth stood reaching as far as the Brahma-world, while those fastened in the Brahma-world descended and were established upon the surface of the earth.
In the ten thousand world-systems, flowering trees put forth blossoms, and fruit-bearing trees became laden with the weight of clusters of fruit.
In the trunks, trunk-lotuses blossomed; on the branches, branch-lotuses; on the creepers, creeper-lotuses;
in the sky, hanging lotuses; and having split the surfaces of the rocks, stalk-lotuses sprang up, seven upon seven, one above the other.
The ten-thousandfold world system, turning like a loosened cluster of garlands, became like a well-spread carpet of flowers.

And it was as if [the world] were a single mass of light. In the intervals between world-systems, the eight thousand *yojana* voids that had never before been illuminated even by the radiance of seven suns became a single expanse of light. The great ocean, eighty-four thousand *yojanas* deep, became sweet water;
rivers ceased to flow; those blind from birth saw forms; and those deaf from birth heard sounds.
The birth-born snakes crawled on their bellies, and those bound in fetters and the like broke free and fell down.

Thus, being honored with immeasurable splendor and majesty, and while many kinds of marvelous phenomena were manifesting, the Great Being, having penetrated the knowledge of omniscience, uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) common to all Buddhas:
“Through many births in saṃsāra, I have wandered without finding [peace];”
Seeking the house-builder, one undergoes birth again and again through suffering.
"O house-builder, you are seen! You shall build no more houses;
all your rafters are broken, and the ridgepole is shattered."
“The mind has reached the unconditioned; it has attained the destruction of craving.
Thus, from the Tusita heaven down to this attainment of omniscience at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), this extent should be understood as the "not-so-distant past" (avidūrenidāna).
The account of the not-so-distant past is concluded.
3. The Introduction Concerning Proximity As for the introduction concerning proximity:

it is stated, “The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park,” or “He was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Gabled Hall. Thus, while he was dwelling in various such locations, in that [context]...
"It is obtained right at that spot," so it is said. Nevertheless, even though this was stated thus, it should nevertheless be understood from the very beginning as follows:
After the Blessed One had uttered an inspired utterance (udāna) while seated upon the Victor’s Throne (jayapallaṅka), this thought occurred to him:
"For four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons, I have run about for the sake of this throne."
For so long a time, for the sake of this very couch, I have given away my head with its ornaments after cutting it from my neck;

I have given away my well-anointed eyes and even extracted the flesh of my heart; sons like Prince Jālī, daughters like Princess Kaṇhājinā, and wives like Queen Maddī have been given away to be slaves for others; this couch of mine is a couch of victory.
"And this excellent couch. Seated here, my intentions shall be fulfilled; I will not rise from here until then.
Thus, entering into meditative attainments numbering many hundreds of thousands of millions, he sat right there for seven days. It was with reference to this that it was said:
"Then the Blessed One sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, experiencing the bliss of liberation."
Then, a reflection arose in some deities: "Surely there must still be some duty to be performed by Siddhattha, for he does not yet relinquish his attachment to the cross-legged posture.
The Teacher, knowing the reflection of those deities, ascended into the air and displayed the Twin Miracle in order to quell their thoughts. For it was at the Great Seat of Enlightenment—
The miracle performed at Katapa, the miracle performed at the assembly of kinsmen, and the miracle performed at the assembly of Pāṭikaputta—
all were like the Twin Miracle at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree. Thus,
having stilled the thoughts of the deities by means of this miracle, the Teacher slightly shifted from his cross-legged posture toward the east.
Standing in the northern direction, he spent seven days gazing with unblinking eyes at the Bodhi tree and the seat upon which he had realized omniscience, thinking:

"On this very seat, indeed, I have penetrated the knowledge of omniscience. That place is the site where he attained the fruit of the perfections fulfilled over four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons.
Thus, it became known as the Animisa Cetiya.
Then, having constructed a walking path between the place of the throne and the spot where he stood, he spent seven days walking back and forth on that jeweled walkway extending from east to west;
that place became known as the Ratanacaṅkama Cetiya.
During the fourth week, however, deities constructed a Jewel House in the northwestern direction from the Bodhi tree.
There, sitting cross-legged, he spent seven days investigating the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, and specifically the *Samantapāsādikā* (The Universal Foundation) with its infinite methods.
The masters of the Abhidhamma, however, say that what is called the "Jewel House" was not made of the seven precious gems.
“However, because it is the place where the seven treatises were contemplated, it is called the ‘Jewel House’ (Ratanaghara).
Since both these designations are appropriate here, both should indeed be accepted.
From that time on, that place became known as the Ratanaghara Cetiya. Thus, for four weeks right near the Bodhi tree,”
Having spent five weeks at the foot of the Bodhi tree, he approached the Goatherd’s Banyan tree.
There too, reflecting upon the Dhamma and experiencing the bliss of liberation, he sat down.
At that time, Māra the son of the gods thought: “Though I have followed him for so long, seeking an opening, I have found none in him.”
"I have indeed seen some lapse; now he has escaped from my power," he thought.
Overcome with dejection, he sat down on the high road and, reflecting upon the sixteen causes, drew sixteen lines upon the ground:
"I did not fulfill the perfection of giving as he has; therefore, I was not born equal to him"—thus he drew one line. Likewise...

“I did not fulfill the perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī), the perfection of renunciation (nekkhammapāramī), the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī), the perfection of energy (vīriyapāramī), the perfection of patience (khantipāramī), the perfection of truth (saccapāramī), the perfection of determination (adhiṭṭhānapāramī), the perfection of loving-kindness (mettāpāramī), and the perfection of equanimity (upekkhāpāramī) like this person;
therefore, I was not born equal to him,” he wrote in the tenth letter. Likewise, “I [did not fulfill] the uncommon...”
“I did not fulfill the ten perfections that serve as the decisive support for the penetration of the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of beings;
therefore, no one like me has ever been born. Thus he drew the eleventh letter. Likewise:

“Unlike him, I did not fulfill the perfections that serve as the decisive support for the uncommon knowledge of the underlying tendencies and latent dispositions, the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion, the knowledge of the Twin Miracle, and the unobstructed knowledge.”
"I did not fulfill the ten perfections that serve as the proximate cause for the penetration of omniscient knowledge;
therefore, no one like me has ever been born. Thus he drew the sixteenth line. In this manner, he sat drawing sixteen lines upon the great highway for these reasons.
At that time, the three daughters of Māra—Taṇhā, Arati, and Ragā—looking about and thinking, "Our father is not to be seen;
where indeed is he now?", saw him sitting there, overcome with dejection and scratching the ground.
They went to their father's side and asked, "Father, why are you suffering and dejected? "Daughters, this great ascetic..."
"He has escaped my power; though I have watched him for all this time, I was unable to find a flaw in him, and therefore I am pained and dejected.
"If that is so, do not worry; we shall bring him under our own control and take him away.
"It is impossible, mothers; no one can bring this man under their control, for he is a person established in unshakable faith."
“Father, we women shall now bind him with the snares of passion and bring him back; you need not worry,” they said.
They approached the Blessed One and said, “O ascetic, let us serve your feet. But the Blessed One paid no heed to their words;
he did not even open his eyes to look at them, for his mind was liberated through the unsurpassed destruction of the substrata of existence (*anuttare upadhisaṅkhaye vimuttamānaso*).
He sat there, experiencing only the bliss of seclusion.
Again, the daughters of Māra thought, "The inclinations of men are indeed diverse;
some have affection for maidens, some for those in the first stage of life, and some for those in the middle stage of life. What if we were now to [tempt him] in various ways?"
Thinking, "We shall entice him with forms," each one manifested a hundred bodies by means of the appearance of maidens and so forth;

having become maidens, those who had not yet given birth, those who had given birth once, those who had given birth twice, middle-aged women, and mature women, they approached the Blessed One six times and said, "O ascetic, let us serve your feet. But the Blessed One did not [consent].
He performed a mental act of resolve, just as one who is liberated through the destruction of the substrata (upadhi) in the unsurpassed state. However, some teachers say:
"Having seen them approaching in their state as great women, the Blessed One resolved: 'In this very way, let these women have broken teeth and grey hair!
This is not to be accepted; for the Teacher does not perform such a resolution. The Blessed One...

But then, regarding his own abandonment of the defilements, he said: “Go away! Seeing what do you strive thus? Is it fitting to act in such a manner before those who are not free from lust and the like?
But for the Tathāgata, lust has been abandoned, hatred has been abandoned, and delusion has been abandoned. And concerning this, he spoke:
“For him whose victory is never lost, and whose victory no one in the world can undo—”
“How can you lead by means of any path that Buddha whose range is infinite, who is trackless?
For him in whom there is no ensnaring, clinging craving to lead him anywhere—
that Buddha whose range is infinite, who is trackless, how can you lead him by means of any path?”

Speaking these two verses from the *Buddhavagga* of the *Dhammapada*, he taught the Dhamma. Having said, "It seems our father spoke the truth: 'The Arhat, the Sugata in the world, cannot be led astray by passion,'" and so forth, they went into the presence of their father.
The Blessed One, having spent seven days there, went to the foot of the Mucalinda tree.
There, when a seven-day storm arose, the Naga king Mucalinda encircled him seven times with his coils in order to ward off the cold and other discomforts.

Spending seven days experiencing the bliss of liberation as if dwelling in his own Gandhakuṭī, free from all constraints, he approached the Rājāyatana tree; there too, he sat down while still experiencing that very bliss of liberation.
At this point, the seven weeks were completed. During this interval, he neither washed his face nor attended to the care of his body.
He had no need for food; he passed his time solely through the bliss of jhāna and the bliss of the fruit [of the path].
Then, on the forty-ninth day, at the end of those seven weeks, as he was sitting there, the thought arose in him, "I shall wash my face.
Sakka, lord of the devas, brought a *agada* gourd and gave it to him; the Teacher—
He consumed it, and by that his body became radiant. Then Sakka himself provided him with a nāga-vine tooth-stick and water for rinsing the mouth.
Having chewed that tooth-stick and rinsed his mouth with the water from Lake Anotatta, the Teacher sat down right there at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree.
At that time, two merchants named Tapussa and Bhallika, traveling from the country of Ukkala to the Middle Country with five hundred carts,
were stopped by a deity who was a blood relative of their own. Encouraged by her to provide food for the Teacher,
they took some parched grain and honey-cakes and said, "Venerable Sir, please accept these from us."
"May the Blessed One accept this food out of compassion," they said, and having approached the Teacher, they stood there.
On the very day of receiving the milk-rice, because his bowl had vanished, the Blessed One thought, "Tathāgatas do not receive food in their hands; in what, then, shall I receive it?
Then, knowing his mind, four [deities] from the four directions...
The great kings offered bowls made of sapphire, but the Blessed One declined them. Again, they offered four bowls made of emerald-colored stone.

Out of compassion for all four sons of the gods, the Blessed One accepted all four bowls, stacked them one upon another, and resolved, "Let there be one," whereby all four became a single bowl at the rim.
Becoming visible lines, they attained oneness by means of a medium measurement.
The Blessed One, having accepted food in that excellent stone bowl and having partaken of it, gave a blessing of thanksgiving.

The two brothers, the merchants, went for refuge to the Buddha and the Dhamma and became lay followers (*upāsaka*) by the formula of the two refuges. Then, [the Blessed One said] to them: "One of us..."
To those who said, "Venerable sir, please give us a portion to be worshipped," he stroked his own head with his right hand and gave them the hair-relics.
They placed those relics inside a golden casket in their own city and established a shrine over them.
The Perfectly Enlightened One also rose from there, went back once more to the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, and sat down at the foot of the banyan.

Then, as soon as he had sat down there, while reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma he had realized, there arose in him—following the custom of all Buddhas—the state of mind characterized by a reluctance to teach the Dhamma to others, thinking: "This Dhamma has been realized by me."
The thought arose [in the Blessed One]. Then Brahmā Sahampati, thinking, "Alas, the world is perishing! Alas, the world is being destroyed!
took with him the Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Sunimmita, Vasavatti, and Mahābrahmās from ten thousand world-systems and went into the presence of the Teacher.
He requested the teaching of the Dhamma by means of the method beginning with the words, "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma."
The Teacher, having given him his promise, reflected, "To whom indeed should I first teach the Dhamma?
Thinking, "Āḷāra is wise; he will quickly understand this Dhamma," he formed that thought.
But looking further, he perceived that Āḷāra had died seven days prior, and he directed his attention toward Udaka. He [then] perceived that Udaka, too, had died the previous evening.

Knowing, "The monks of the group of five have been very helpful to me," he directed his attention toward the group of five and, reflecting, "Where are they living now? he perceived, "They are at the Deer Park in Isipatana near Bārāṇasī.
Thinking, "I shall go there and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma," he remained for several days in the vicinity of the seat of enlightenment.
Having dwelt wandering for alms, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha he thought, "I shall go to Bārāṇasī.
On the fourteenth day, at the time of dawn when the night had brightened, he took his bowl and robe very early and set out on the eighteen-yojana journey.
On the way, having seen an Ājīvika named Upaka, he declared to him his state as a Buddha.
On that very day, in the evening, he went to Isipatana.
When the five elder monks saw the Tathāgata approaching from afar, they said, "Friends, here comes the ascetic Gotama,
who has turned back to a life of abundance, with his body full, his senses robust, and his complexion golden."
"We shall not perform prostrations and other marks of respect toward him; however, since he is born of a great family, he deserves the offering of a seat, so we shall prepare a mere seat for him.

Thus they made an agreement. The Blessed One, through his knowledge capable of discerning the mental movements of the world including its devas, reflected, "What indeed are these people thinking? and thus he understood their thoughts. Then—
Having condensed the loving-kindness that was capable of pervading all gods and humans without distinction, he pervaded them with loving-kindness directed toward specific individuals.
Touched by the Blessed One’s loving-kindness, they were unable to maintain their prior agreement when the Tathāgata approached;
they performed all the duties such as bowing down and rising from their seats, and [realized] his state as a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.
Not knowing him, they addressed him merely by name and with the term "friend.
Then the Blessed One, making them understand his state as a Buddha by saying, "Bhikkhus, do not address the Tathāgata by name or with the term 'friend';
the Tathāgata, bhikkhus, is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One," [spoke] while he was seated on the prepared seat.
Seated upon the sublime Buddha-throne while the constellation Uttarāsāḷha was in conjunction, surrounded by eighteen koṭis of Brahmās,
he addressed the five elder monks and taught the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. Among them, the Elder Aññā Koṇḍañña,
directing his knowledge according to the course of the teaching, [attained realization] at the conclusion of the sutta, along with the eighteen koṭis of Brahmās.

He established himself together with the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). The Teacher, having entered the rains retreat right there, sat in the monastery itself on the following day while instructing the Elder Vappa; the other four went out for alms.
The Elder Vappa attained the fruit of stream-entry that very morning. By this same method, on the next day he instructed the Elder Bhaddiya, and on the next day the Elder Mahānāma.

On the following day, having established everyone in the fruit of stream-entry, the Teacher gathered the five men together on the fifth day of the fortnight and taught the *Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta*. At the conclusion of the teaching, all five elders were established in the fruit of arhatship.
Then the Teacher, perceiving the spiritual potential (*upanissaya*) of the young man Yasa, [proceeded].
Having seen him depart from his home in the middle of the night out of world-weariness, she called out to him, "Come, Yasa!
and that very same night established him in the fruit of stream-entry; on the following day, she established him in arahantship.
Furthermore, she ordained his forty-four companions through the "Come, monk" formula and led them to the attainment of arahantship.

Thus, when sixty-one arahants had arisen in the world, the Teacher, having completed the rains retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, dispatched sixty bhikkhus to various directions, saying, "Wander, O bhikkhus, on tour.
He himself, proceeding toward Uruvelā, converted thirty youths of the Bhaddavaggiya group in a cottonwood grove along the way.
Among them, the last to attain was a stream-enterer, and the first was an arahant.
He became a non-returner (*anāgāmī*). Having ordained all of them by the mere formula "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*), he sent them out in various directions.

Then, going to Uruvelā, he displayed three thousand five hundred miracles. Having converted the three brothers, the matted-hair ascetics (*jaṭila*) headed by Uruvelakassapa, along with their retinue of one thousand matted-hair ascetics, by ordaining them through the "Come, monk" formula, he seated them at Gayāsīsa and [taught] the discourse on the Simile of the Burning Fire (*Ādittapariyāya-sutta*).
Having established them in arahantship and surrounded by those one thousand arahants,
[the Teacher] went to Rājagaha, thinking, "I shall fulfill the promise given to King Bimbisāra," and arrived at the Laṭṭhivana Grove on the outskirts of the city.
