When the king heard from the park-keeper that "the Teacher has arrived," he went to meet the Teacher, surrounded by twelve hundred thousand brahmins and householders.

Having approached, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the Tathāgata—which emitted a mass of radiance like a canopy of golden cloth upon their wheel-marked soles—and sat down to one side together with the assembly.
Then, this thought occurred to those brahmins and householders: "What now, is it that the Great Ascetic [will ordain] Uruvelakassapa?"

“Is it you who practice the holy life, or is it Uruvela Kassapa who does so under the Great Ascetic? The Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in their minds, addressed the Elder with a verse:
“What did you see, O dweller of Uruvela, that you abandoned the fire, claiming yourself to be emaciated?”
“I ask you this matter, Kassapa: how have you abandoned the fire-sacrifice?
The Elder, having understood the Blessed One’s intention, replied:
“In forms, sounds, and likewise tastes, and in women who are desired—these are what they call sacrifices.”
"Having understood that this is the stain among acquisitions, therefore he did not delight in sacrifice or offering.

Having spoken this verse, in order to manifest his status as a disciple, he placed his head at the feet of the Tathāgata and said, "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my Teacher; I am his disciple," and then [clapped] one hand, two hands, and three hands.
Having risen into the air seven times to the height of seven palm trees, he descended, paid homage to the Tathāgata, and sat down to one side.
Seeing that miracle, the great multitude thought: "Aho! How majestic are the Buddhas!
Even Uruvelakassapa—who was considered an 'Arahant' despite being so firmly entrenched in his views—has broken the net of his wrong views and been tamed by the Tathāgata."
He spoke only of the Teacher’s virtues. The Blessed One said, “It is not only now that I am taming Uruvela Kassapa; in the past, too, he was tamed by me.
Having spoken thus, and having related the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka on this occasion, he proclaimed the Four Noble Truths.
The King of Magadha, together with eleven *nahutas* of followers, was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti*).

One hundred thousand people declared themselves lay followers (*upāsaka*). While still seated in the presence of the Teacher, the king proclaimed the five assurances, went for refuge, and invited him for the following day;
then, rising from his seat, he circumambulated the Blessed One and departed.
On the following day, all the inhabitants of Rājagaha, numbering eighteen koṭis, both those who had seen the Blessed One and those who had not, [assembled].
People desiring to see the Tathāgata set out from Rājagaha for the Laṭṭhivana Grove early in the morning.
The road, three *gāvutas* long, was insufficient; the entire Laṭṭhivana Grove became packed without any gaps.
The great multitude, beholding the Blessed One’s physical form which had attained the pinnacle of beauty, could not find satiety. This is indeed what is called "the ground of excellence."
For on such occasions, the entire splendor of the Tathāgata’s material body—including its various marks (*lakkhaṇa*) and minor characteristics (*anubyañjana*)—should be described.

As the great multitude, beholding the body of the One Possessing Ten Powers which had thus attained the pinnacle of physical beauty, crowded the park and the road without any gaps, there was not even space for a single bhikkhu to emerge. On that day, it is said...
The Blessed One made his seat appear hot for Sakka, thinking, "May the Lord not go without food.

Sakka, reflecting on this, understood the reason; he then manifested himself in the form of a young brahmin, descended before the One of Ten Powers while reciting praises concerning the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and having created space by means of his divine power—
“The Tamed One, together with those formerly matted-hair ascetics who were tamed; the Liberated One, together with those formerly matted-hair ascetics who were liberated;
the Blessed One, with the color of refined gold, entered Rājagaha.
The Released One, together with those formerly matted-hair ascetics who were released, was utterly free.”
With the color of refined gold, the Blessed One entered Rājagaha.
“Crossed over together with those who have crossed over— the former matted-hair ascetics— liberated together with those who are liberated,
with the color of refined gold, the Blessed One entered Rājagaha.”
“Ten-dwelling, ten-powered, knower of the ten Dhammas, endowed with the ten [virtues];
surrounded by a retinue of a thousand, the Blessed One entered Rājagaha.
Reciting these verses in praise of the Teacher, he walked ahead. At that time, the great multitude beheld the youth’s splendor of form.

Having seen him, he thought, "This young man is exceedingly handsome, and indeed, he has never been seen by us before," and he asked, "Where does this young man come from, or to whom does he belong? Hearing this, the young man said:
"The wise one who is self-controlled in every way, pure and without rival;"
“The Arahant, the Sugata, is in the world; I am his attendant.
Having spoken this verse, the Teacher set out upon the path prepared by Sakka and, surrounded by a thousand bhikkhus, entered Rājagaha.
After the King had given a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he said: “Venerable Sir, without the Three Jewels...”
“I will not be able to go [to the city]; whether it be at the right time or not the right time, I shall come into the presence of the Blessed One.

The Lāṭṭhivana grove is indeed too far away; however, this grove of ours called Veḷuvana is neither too far nor too near, it is well-suited for coming and going, and it is a dwelling fit for a Buddha.
May the Blessed One accept this from me. Thus he spoke, pouring water scented with flowers and perfumes from a golden pitcher.
Taking water the color of a jewel, he offered it into the hand of the One Possessing Ten Powers while dedicating the Veḷuvana monastery.
At the acceptance of that grove, the great earth shook, as it was thought: "The roots of the Buddha’s dispensation have been planted.
Indeed, in Jambudīpa, there is no other monastery except Veḷuvana that was accepted by causing the great earth to shake. It was the same in the island of Tambapaṇṇi.
Except for the Mahāvihāra, there was no other place on earth where a dwelling had been taken by shaking the ground.
Having accepted the Veḷuvana monastery and offered words of thanksgiving to the king, the Teacher rose from his seat and, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, went to Veḷuvana.
At that time, two wanderers named Sāriputta and Moggallāna were residing near Rājagaha.
They dwelt there seeking the Deathless. Among them, Sāriputta, seeing the Elder Assaji entering for alms, approached him with a clear mind;
having heard the verse beginning, "Those phenomena that arise from a cause," he was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
He then recited that very same verse to his own companion, the wanderer Moggallāna. He too—
He was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Both men, having looked upon their own retinue, went forth in the presence of the Blessed One together with their followers.
Among them, Mahāmoggallāna attained Arahantship in seven days, while the Elder Sāriputta did so in half a month.
The Teacher appointed both of them to the position of chief disciples. On the very day the Elder Sāriputta attained Arahantship...
He convened an assembly of disciples.
While the Tathāgata was dwelling in that very Veḷuvana monastery, King Suddhodana heard:
"It is said that my son, having practiced austerities for six years and attained supreme perfect enlightenment, has set in motion the excellent Wheel of Dhamma."
Having heard that [the Buddha] was dwelling at Veḷuvana, dependent on Rājagaha, he addressed a certain minister:
"Come, my good man, go to Rājagaha with a retinue of a thousand men and, speaking in my name, say: 'Your father, the Great King Suddhodana, desires to see you';
then, taking my son with you, return. He replied, "So be it, Your Majesty," and accepted the king's command.
Having accepted it with his head, surrounded by a thousand men, he quickly traveled sixty yojanas and entered the monastery at the time of the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse,
while the Ten-Powered One was seated in the midst of the fourfold assembly. Thinking,
"Let the message sent by the king wait for now," he stood at the edge [of the assembly] and, having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, remained just as he was.
Having attained arahantship together with a thousand men, he requested the going-forth.
The Blessed One extended his hand, saying, "Come, monks," and at that very moment they all became as if sixty-year-old elders, wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power.
From the time they attained arahantship, however, the noble ones (ariyas) remain indeed equanimous; thus he—
He did not report the message sent by the king to the One of Ten Powers.
The king, thinking, “Neither does he go nor is the message heard,” dispatched another minister in the same manner, saying, “Come, sir, you go.
He too, having gone and attained Arahatship along with his retinue in the same way as before, remained silent. The king, by this very...
In accordance with custom, he dispatched nine ministers accompanied by a retinue of a thousand men;
yet, having all completed their own business, they remained right there in silence.
Finding that not even a single message was brought back to report, the king thought: "Because these many people lack affection for me..."
They did not respond even to a mere command, [thinking], "Who indeed will carry out my word? Looking over the entire royal army, he saw Kāḷudāyin.

It is said that this minister was the king’s accomplisher of all aims, an intimate and most trusted confidant, born on the same day as the Bodhisatta, a playmate from childhood, and a friend. Then the king addressed him.
“Dear Kāḷudāyi, desiring to see my son, I sent nine thousand men;
yet not even a single man has returned to report even a mere message. Indeed, the threat to life is difficult to discern;
while I am still alive, I wish to see my son. Will you be able to show my son to me? “I shall be able, Your Majesty.”
“If I am permitted to go forth,” he said. “Dear son, whether you go forth or not, show my son to me.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” he replied, and taking the king’s message, he went to Rājagaha.

Standing at the edge of the assembly during the Teacher’s time for preaching the Dhamma, he heard the Dhamma; together with his retinue, he attained the fruit of Arhatship and was established in the state of an *ehibhikkhu*.
Having become the Teacher, the Buddha spent his first rains retreat at Isipatana;
having completed the rains and performed the *pavāraṇā*, he went to Uruvelā and dwelt there for three months, training the three brothers who were matted-hair ascetics.

Surrounded by a retinue of one thousand bhikkhus, he went to Rājagaha on the full moon of the Phussa month and stayed there for two months. At this point, five months had elapsed since his departure from Bārāṇasī.
The entire winter had passed. Seven or eight days had elapsed since the arrival of the Elder Kāḷudāyin.
On the full moon day of the month of Phagguna, he thought: "Winter has passed; the spring season has arrived.
People have harvested their crops and cleared the roads with space on both sides; the earth is covered with green grass."
“The forest groves are in full bloom, the roads are fit for travel; it is time for the One of Ten Powers to perform an act of kinship.
Then, having approached the Blessed One, he said:
“Now, O Venerable Sir, the trees are leafless, bearing fruit and having shed their foliage;”
“They shine forth like those possessed of radiance; it is the time for the Great Heroes, the Aṅgīrasas… ‘Neither too cold nor too hot, neither too famine-stricken nor parched;
the earth is lush and green—this is the time, O Great Sage.’”
With sixty verses, he praised the journey for the sake of the Ten-Powered One’s departure for his native city.
Then the Teacher asked him, “Udāyin, why do you praise the journey with such a sweet voice?
“Venerable Sir, your father, the Great King Suddhodana, desires to see you; please show favor to your kinsmen. “Very well.”
“Udāyī, I shall provide for my kinsmen; announce this to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus that they will fulfill the duties of those traveling.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Elder announced it to them.
The Blessed One [set out] with ten thousand noble sons dwelling in Aṅga and Magadha, and ten [thousand] dwelling in Kapilavatthu.
Surrounded by all twenty thousand bhikkhus whose taints were destroyed, he departed from Rājagaha and traveled a *yojana* each day.
Thinking, “I shall reach Kapilavatthu, sixty *yojanas* from Rājagaha, in two months,” he set out on his journey without haste.
The Elder, for his part, thought, “I shall inform the King that the Blessed One has departed.”
Having ascended into the air, he appeared in the king’s residence. Seeing the Elder, the king was filled with joy;
he had him sit upon a magnificent couch, filled his bowl with various kinds of choice food prepared for himself, and gave it to him.
The Elder rose and made a gesture as if to depart. "Sit down and eat, dear sir," the king said. [The Elder replied,] "I shall go to the presence of the Teacher."
“I shall eat, Great King. “But where is the Teacher, dear sir?
“He has set out on a journey with a retinue of twenty thousand bhikkhus for the purpose of seeing you, Great King. With a joyful heart, the king said:
“After you have partaken of this, until my son reaches this city, provide him almsfood from right here.”

“Take it,” he said. The Elder consented. The king served the Elder, rubbed his bowl with scented powder, filled it with the finest food, and placing it in the Elder’s hands, said, “Give this to the Tathāgata.
While everyone was looking on, the Elder threw the bowl into the air and, rising himself into the sky, [offered] the alms-food...

Having brought it, he placed it in the Teacher’s hand. The Teacher consumed it. By this means, the Elder brought food day after day, and the Teacher likewise consumed his almsfood on the very path back from the king’s palace.
At the conclusion of each meal, the Elder would reflect on the virtues of the Buddha, thinking day after day: "Today the Blessed One came for so much; today for so much."
Through this discourse, the entire royal family developed faith in the Teacher even before seeing him.
For that very reason, the Blessed One placed him in the foremost position, saying: "Bhikkhus, among my disciples, the bhikkhus who inspire confidence in families, Kāḷudāyī is the foremost."
The Sākiyas, thinking, "Now that the Blessed One has arrived, we shall see our foremost kinsman," gathered together and,
while searching for a place for the Blessed One to stay, observed that "the Nigrodha Sakka’s park is delightful.
Having had all the preparations for its maintenance carried out there, they went out to meet him with perfumes and flowers in their hands.
First, they sent forth the very young sons and daughters of the city, adorned with every ornament;

after them, the princes and princesses; and immediately following them, the King himself, honoring the Blessed One with perfumes, flowers, powders, and other offerings, took hold of him and proceeded to the Nigrodha Monastery. There, the Blessed One was surrounded by twenty thousand arahants whose taints were destroyed.
He sat down upon the excellent Buddha-throne that had been prepared. The Śākyas, being of a proud nature and stiff with pride, thought:
"Prince Siddhattha is younger than we; he is our junior, our nephew, our son, and our grandson.
Having so reflected, they said to the youngest of the royal princes, "You all pay him homage; we shall sit behind you."
While they were thus sitting without having paid homage, the Blessed One, observing their disposition, thought: "My kinsmen do not pay homage to me;

well then, I shall now cause them to pay homage. Having attained the fourth jhāna as a basis for direct knowledge, and emerging from it, he rose up into the air and, as if scattering the dust from his feet upon their heads, performed at the foot of the Kaṇḍama tree a miracle similar to the Twin Miracle.

He performed a miracle. Having seen that marvel, the king said: "Blessed One, on the day of your birth, when you were brought for Kāḷadevala to pay homage, I paid homage to you even after seeing your feet turn around and rest upon the head of the brahmin;
this was my first act of homage. On the auspicious day of the plowing ceremony, while you lay upon the couch of glory in the shade of the rose-apple tree..."
“Even though I saw that the shade of the rose-apple tree did not shift while you were seated, I nevertheless bowed at your feet; this was my second salutation.
Now, having seen this miracle never before witnessed, I bow at your feet once more; this is my third salutation.
But when the king had thus paid homage, not even a single Sākiyan was able to remain standing without bowing to the Blessed One.
There was no one who did not; everyone indeed paid homage.
Thus, having caused his kinsmen to pay homage, the Blessed One descended from the sky and sat upon the prepared seat.
When the Blessed One was seated, the assembly of kinsmen reached its peak, and they all sat down with one-pointed minds. Then a great cloud...
A rain of lotuses fell. Water of copper-colored hue flowed below with a roar;

it drenched only those who wished to be drenched, while not even a single drop fell upon the bodies of those who did not wish to be drenched. Seeing this, everyone was struck with a sense of wonder and amazement and raised the cry:
"Oh, how marvelous! Oh, how extraordinary! The Teacher said, "It is not only now that this has happened for me..."
At this occasion—"When there is a gathering of kinsmen, the rain falls like a lotus; it has rained even in the past"—he related the Vessantara Jātaka.
Having heard the teaching on the Dhamma, they all rose, paid homage, and departed.
Not a single king or royal minister went away without saying, "Please accept our alms tomorrow."
On the following day, the Teacher entered Kapilavatthu for alms, surrounded by a retinue of twenty thousand bhikkhus.
No one went out to invite him, nor did anyone take his bowl. Standing at the city gate (indakhīla), the Blessed One reflected:
"How indeed did the Buddhas of the past conduct themselves when walking for alms in their own native cities? Did they follow a fixed order among the noble families?"
“Did they go directly to the houses, or did they practice the alms-round from door to door? Then, seeing that not even a single Buddha had ever gone out of sequence, he thought:
“I too must now uphold this lineage and this tradition;
and in the future, my disciples, training in accordance with me alone, will fulfill the conduct of the alms-round. Thus, from the house situated at the end of the row...

Starting from there, he went for alms from house to house in regular succession. Hearing that "the noble Prince Siddhattha is indeed wandering for alms," the great multitude of people opened the latticed windows of their palaces—whether two-storied or three-storied—and busied themselves with looking on.
Queen Rāhulamātā also thought, "The noble son, it is said, is in this very city with great royal splendor, [riding] in golden palanquins and the like..."
Having reflected thus, "Now, having shaved off his hair and beard, clothed in saffron robes, and with an alms-bowl in hand,
he wanders for alms; does he indeed shine?", she opened the lion-window and looked out,

[beholding] the Blessed One illuminating the city streets with the radiance of his body, which blazed with various colors, endowed with a fathom-wide halo, and resplendent with the eighty minor marks.
Having seen him shining with the incomparable splendor of a Buddha, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, [he gazed] from the crown of the head down to the soles of the feet:
“With glossy, dark-blue, soft, and curled hair; with a forehead like the stainless surface of the sun;”
The lion among men, whose abode is the pleasant grove of Yuttatuṅga, is spread with a network of rays.
With excellent wheels marked upon his reddish, beautiful feet, his long heels adorned with the marks of excellence,
and his heels graced by the chowries in his hands— this indeed is your father, the lion among men.
“The Sakyan prince, the granter of boons, delicately nurtured, with a body beautiful and distinguished by the marks;
this hero among men has come for the welfare of the world—he indeed is your father, a lion among men.
With long, well-proportioned, and well-formed ears, cow-eyed, and with deep-blue eyes.”
With a face as dark-blue as a rain-cloud, he is indeed your father, the lion among men.
With a complexion like full-blown sandalwood, beloved even by gods and men, a true elephant among men;
with the graceful gait of a lordly elephant in rut, he is indeed your father, the lion among men.
“With a smooth, deep, and sweet voice, a tongue red like vermilion and well-proportioned,
and twenty even, white teeth— this indeed is your father, a lion among men.
Born of the Khattiya caste, a sovereign of the foremost lineage, his feet are worshipped by gods and humans.”
With a mind established in virtue and concentration—this indeed is your father, the lion among men.
With a neck well-rounded, curved, and beautifully shaped, with a jaw like a lion’s and a body like that of the king of beasts;
with a most excellent complexion and the hue of refined gold—this indeed is your father, the lion among men.
“With hair as deep blue-black as the color of collyrium, with a forehead as pure as a strip of gold,
and with a face as bright and clear as the white medicinal herb— this indeed is your father, a lion among men.
Moving along the path of the wind like the moon, his form augmented by a host of stars.”
“Standing amidst his disciples, this Lord of Ascetics is indeed your father, that lion among men.
Having thus praised him with these ten verses known as the *Narasīhagāthā*, he reported to the king: “It is said that your son is now wandering for alms.
With a heart moved by agitation, the king hurriedly adjusted his garment with his hand.
Having gone out and proceeded with haste, he stood before the Blessed One and said: "Venerable sir, why do you put us to shame?
For what purpose do you wander for alms? Do you think, 'It is impossible to obtain food for so many bhikkhus'?
"This is our family custom, Great King. "But, venerable sir, is it not ours [as well]?"
The lineage known as the Mahāsammata kṣatriya clan is such that not even a single kṣatriya therein was ever called a "beggar.
"Great King, this so-called royal lineage is your own lineage; however, for us, there is the lineage of the Buddhas, beginning with Dīpaṅkara, Koṇḍañña... [and] Kassapa.
These and other Buddhas, numbering many thousands, were beggars; it was solely by means of begging that they lived."
“...make a livelihood,” he said while standing right there in the middle of the street:
“One should rise up and not be negligent; one should practice the Dhamma of good conduct.
One who lives by the Dhamma sleeps happily, both in this world and in the next.”
He spoke this verse. At the conclusion of the verse, the king was established in the fruit of stream-entry:
“One should practice the Dhamma well, and not practice what is ill-conducted;
one who practices the Dhamma sleeps happily, both in this world and in the next.”

Upon hearing this verse, however, he was established in the fruit of a once-returner (*sakadāgāmiphala*). Having heard the *Mahādhammapāla-jātaka*, he was established in the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
At the time of his death, while reclining on a magnificent couch beneath a white parasol, he attained *arahantship*.
For the king, there was no need for the practice of striving through dwelling in the forest; for he had already realized the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*).
Then, taking the Blessed One’s bowl, she escorted the Blessed One together with his retinue up to the Great Palace and served him with excellent hard and soft foods.
At the conclusion of the meal, the entire harem came and paid homage to the Blessed One, with the exception of Rāhula’s mother. She, however, said, "Go, pay homage to my noble son."
Although she was being urged by her attendants, she said, "If I possess any virtue, the noble son will come to me of his own accord;
I shall pay homage to him only when he has arrived," and so she did not go.
The Blessed One, having had the king take his bowl, went together with the two chief disciples to the princess's bedchamber.
Having gone there, he said, "The princess may pay homage as she wishes; nothing should be said to her," and then sat down on the prepared seat.
She came with great haste, grasped his ankles, and placing her head upon the back of his feet, paid homage according to her heart's desire.
The king spoke of the princess’s excellence in qualities, such as her affection and great respect for the Blessed One: "Venerable sir..."
When my daughter heard that you had put on saffron-colored robes, from that time forth she began to wear saffron-colored robes herself;
having heard of your practice of eating only one meal a day, she became a single-meal eater;
having heard that you had abandoned large beds, she lay down only on a small plank bed; and having heard of your abstinence from garlands, perfumes, and such things—

"Having understood that she had become free from garlands and perfumes, even when her own kinsmen sent word to the Saṅgha saying, 'We shall look after her,' she did not look upon even a single relative.
Thus my daughter is endowed with such virtues, O Blessed One.
"It is not surprising, Great King, that this princess, now being protected by you, should protect herself once her knowledge has matured; but this was so even previously."
"Unprotected, wandering at the foot of the mountain while your knowledge is not yet mature, you must guard yourself," he said;
and having related the Candakinnarī Jātaka, he rose from his seat and departed.
On the second day, however, while the auspicious ceremonies for Prince Nanda’s entry into the consecration hall and his marriage were taking place,
Having gone to his house and having had the prince take the bowl, [the Elder], desiring to ordain him, uttered a blessing and rose from his seat and departed.
Janapadakalyāṇī, seeing the prince departing, said, "May you return quickly, noble son," and she looked back with her neck extended.
He too, being unable to say to the Blessed One, "Take the bowl," [remained silent].
He went to the monastery itself, and though he was unwilling, the Blessed One ordained him. Thus, having gone to Kapilavatthu, the Blessed One ordained Nanda on the third day.
On the seventh day, Rāhula’s mother, having adorned the prince, sent him into the presence of the Blessed One, saying, "Look, dear son..."
"This ascetic, surrounded by twenty thousand monks, golden-hued and possessing the form of a Brahmā—this is your father.
He possessed great treasures, but since the time of his renunciation, we have seen none of them.
Go and ask for your inheritance, saying: 'Father, once I have received the consecration, I shall become a Wheel-turning Monarch.'"
“I have need of wealth; give me wealth. For a son belongs to his father’s property.

And the prince, having gone into the presence of the Blessed One and regained his affection for his father, stood there joyful and delighted, saying, “May you have a pleasant shade, O ascetic,” and speaking many other words appropriate to himself. The Blessed One, having finished his meal—
Having expressed his appreciation, he rose from his seat and departed. The prince, however, followed after the Blessed One, saying, "Give me my inheritance, ascetic! Give me my inheritance, ascetic!

The Blessed One did not cause the prince to turn back, nor was the retinue able to turn him back as he went along with the Blessed One. Thus, he went right to the monastery together with the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One thought: “The wealth that this youth desires belongs to his father; it is subject to the cycle of existence and fraught with suffering.
Come now, I shall give him the sevenfold noble wealth obtained at the seat of enlightenment, and make him the heir to the supramundane inheritance.
Thus he addressed the Venerable Sāriputta: “In that case, Sāriputta, you [should instruct] Prince Rāhula...”
“Please let him go forth. The Elder ordained him. But once the prince had been ordained, an excessive sorrow arose within the king.

Unable to endure it, he informed the Blessed One and requested this boon: “It would be well, venerable sir, if the noble ones would not ordain a son who has not been permitted by his mother and father.
The Blessed One granted him that boon, and on the following day—

Having taken his morning meal at the royal residence, the King sat to one side and said, "Venerable sir, when you were practicing austerities, a certain deity approached me and said, 'Your son has died.
Not believing her words, I rejected them, saying, 'My son will not die until he has attained enlightenment. When this was said, [the Venerable Ānanda asked], "What now?"
“You will believe me, for even when you were previously shown bones and told, ‘Your son is dead,’ you did not believe it.
On this occasion, the Blessed One related the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka. At the conclusion of the discourse, the king was established in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
Thus, having established his father in the three fruits, the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, returned once more to Rājagaha.

Having gone there, he dwelt in the Bamboo Grove. At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, taking merchandise with five hundred carts, went to the house of his dear friend the merchant in Rājagaha;
having heard there of the appearance of the Buddha, the Blessed One, at the time of the powerful dawn, through the power of a deity, he entered by means of an opened gate.
Having approached the Teacher and heard the Dhamma, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
On the following day, after giving a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, he obtained the Teacher’s consent to come to Sāvatthī.
Along the way, at intervals of forty-five yojanas, he gave one hundred thousand pieces of gold at each stage for every yojana.
Having caused a monastery to be built at Jetavana after purchasing it for eighteen crores of gold with a layer of ten million pieces, he commenced the new construction work. In its center,
he had a fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi) built for the One of Ten Powers, and surrounding that,

he constructed individual residences and dwellings for the eighty great elders, consisting of single-storied and double-storied gabled houses, *haṃsavaṭṭaka* pavilions, long halls, maṇḍapas, and so forth.
Having caused a delightful monastery to be built on a beautiful stretch of land through the gift of eighteen crores— comprising various dwellings, lotus ponds, walking paths,
night-quarters, and day-quarters— he dispatched a messenger for the sake of the Teacher’s arrival.
Having heard the messenger’s words, the Teacher departed from Rājagaha surrounded by a great community of monks and proceeded by stages.
He arrived at the city of Sāvatthī.
Meanwhile, the Great Merchant, having prepared the festival for the monastery, on the day the Tathāgata was to enter Jetavana,
adorned his son with all ornaments and sent him forth together with five hundred youths, all likewise dressed in finery.
He sent [them]. He, together with his retinue, took five hundred banners resplendent with cloth of five colors and stood before the One of Ten Powers.
Behind them, the two daughters of the treasurer, Mahāsubhaddā and Cūḷasubhaddā, went forth with five hundred young maidens, carrying full water-jars. Behind them was the treasurer’s wife.
Adorned with all her ornaments, she went forth together with five hundred women, each carrying a bowl filled with offerings.
Following behind them all, the Great Merchant himself, dressed in new garments, approached the Blessed One together with five hundred merchants, all likewise dressed in new garments.
The Blessed One [stood] before this assembly of lay followers.

Having done so, surrounded by the great community of monks, making the forest groves appear as if stained tawny by the pouring of liquid gold through the radiance of his own body, he entered the Jetavana monastery with the infinite grace of a Buddha and the peerless splendor of a Buddha.
Then Anāthapiṇḍika asked him: "Venerable sir, how should I conduct myself in this monastery?"
"Therefore, householder, give this monastery to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus from the four quarters, both present and future.
"Very well, Bhante," the Great Merchant replied. Taking a golden water-pot, he poured water into the hand of the One Possessing Ten Powers and gave it, saying:
"I give this Jetavana monastery to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus from the four quarters, both present and future."
Having accepted the monastery, the Teacher gave a blessing of thanksgiving:
“It wards off cold and heat, as well as predatory beasts,
And snakes, mosquitoes, the chill, and even rains.”
“Then, when fierce wind and heat arise, one is struck by them;
[the gift of a dwelling] is for the sake of shelter, for the sake of comfort, and for the purpose of meditating and practicing insight.
The gift of a monastery to the Saṅgha has been praised as supreme by the Buddha.”
Therefore, a wise person, clearly perceiving their own welfare,
should have delightful monasteries built and cause those who are learned to dwell therein;
and they should provide them with food, drink, clothing, and lodgings.
“One should give with a serene mind to those who have become upright;
they will teach him the Dhamma that removes all suffering,
by knowing which Dhamma here, he attains final Nibbāna, free from taints.”
He spoke on the benefits of a monastery. From the second day onward, Anāthapiṇḍika began the festival for the monastery.
Visākhā’s festival for her palace was completed in four months, but Anāthapiṇḍika’s festival for the monastery concluded after nine months.
During the monastery festival as well, eighteen koṭis were offered as gifts. Thus, in a single instance—
He renounced wealth amounting to four hundred and fifty million for the monastery.

Furthermore, in the past, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, a merchant named Punabbasumitta purchased that very site with bricks of gold and had a monastic complex measuring one *yojana* built there. During the time of the Blessed One Sikhī—
A merchant named Sirivaḍḍha purchased that very spot with a spread of gold ploughshares and built a monastic complex (saṅghārāma) measuring three gavutas in size.

During the time of the Blessed One Vessabhu, a merchant named Sotthija purchased that same spot with a spread of golden elephant tracks and built a monastic complex measuring half a yojana in size. [During the time] of the Blessed One Kakusandha...
In the time of the Buddha Kāla, a merchant named Accuta purchased that very spot with a layer of gold bricks and built a monastery there measuring one *gāvuta* in extent.

In the time of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, a merchant named Ugga purchased that same spot with a layer of golden tortoises and built a monastery there measuring half a *gāvuta* in extent. In the time of the Blessed One Kassapa...
In ancient times, a merchant named Sumaṅgala purchased that very spot with a layer of gold bricks and constructed a monastic dwelling (saṅghārāma) there measuring sixteen karīsas.

However, in the time of our Blessed One, a merchant named Anāthapiṇḍika purchased that same spot with ten million kahāpaṇas and constructed a monastic dwelling there measuring eight karīsas. Indeed, this is that place.
It is indeed the place never abandoned by all Buddhas.

Thus, from the attainment of omniscience at the Great Seat of Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa) until the couch of the Great Parinibbāna, in whatever place the Blessed One dwelt, this is called the "Proximate Introduction" (santikenidāna). By means of it, we shall describe all the Jātakas.
The Introduction (Nidānakathā) is finished.
1. Ekakanipāta 1.
Apaṇṇakavagga 1.
Apaṇṇakajātaka Commentary (Apaṇṇakajātakavaṇṇanā)
The Blessed One delivered this "Incontrovertible Teaching on Dhamma" while residing at the Great Monastery of Jetavana near Sāvatthī.
But with reference to whom did this discourse arise? It was concerning five hundred lay followers of other sects who were friends of the merchant [Anāthapiṇḍika].
For one day, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika [encountered] his own five hundred friends who were disciples of other sects.
Taking many garlands, perfumes, and ointments, as well as ghee, oil, honey, molasses, cloth, and coverings, and having them brought along, he went to Jetavana.
Having paid homage to the Blessed One and honored him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, he distributed the medicines and garments to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Avoiding the six faults of sitting, he sat down to one side. Those followers of other sects also...
Having paid homage to the Tathāgata, they sat down right beside Anāthapiṇḍika, gazing upon the Teacher’s face, which was as beautiful as the full moon,
adorned with the primary and secondary marks, encircled by a fathom-wide aura, and from which thick Buddha-rays issued forth in dense,
interlocking clusters like garlands upon garlands.
Then, on the surface of the ruby-stone, the Teacher— roaring like a young lion uttering a lion’s roar,
thundering like a rain-cloud, pouring down the celestial Ganges as it were, and weaving a garland of jewels as it were—
delivered a sweet discourse on the Dhamma, variegated with various methods, in a Brahma-voice endowed with the eight qualities, which was worth hearing and delightful.

Having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, their hearts filled with confidence, they rose, paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, and—breaking their refuge in other sects—went for refuge to the Buddha.

From that time forth, they went regularly to the monastery together with Anāthapiṇḍika, carrying perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands; there they listened to the Dhamma, gave gifts, and observed the precepts.
They performed the Uposatha ceremony.
Then the Blessed One returned from Sāvatthī once again to Rājagaha.
When the Tathāgata had departed, they broke that refuge and went back to the refuge of other sectarians, re-establishing themselves in their own original positions.
The Blessed One, having spent seven or eight months there, returned once more to the Jeta Grove. Anāthapiṇḍika again took them and went into the presence of the Teacher;
having honored the Teacher with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, he paid homage and sat down to one side.
They too, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Then, while the Tathāgata was on his alms-round...
After he had departed, [the monk] broke his taken refuge and again took refuge in another sect; he then reported to the Blessed One that he had returned to his original state.

The Blessed One, as if opening a jewel casket filled with various scents and fragrant with divine perfumes through the power of his well-spoken words uttered continuously for immeasurable millions of eons, opened his lotus-like mouth and spoke in a sweet voice.
Calling out, he asked, "Is it true, lay followers, that you have broken the three refuges and gone for refuge to other sectarians?
When they were unable to conceal the truth and replied, "It is true, Blessed One," the Teacher said, "Lay followers,
from the Avīci hell below up to the peak of existence above, and across the immeasurable world-systems in the horizontal directions— "
“There is no one equal to the Buddha in qualities such as virtue; how much less could there be anyone superior? This is declared in such discourses as:
“Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed—the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them...
Whatever wealth there is, whether here or in the world beyond... [and so on]... the foremost indeed for those with confidence. Thus it is made known.
Having proclaimed the virtues of the Triple Gem, [the Teacher said]:
"There are no lay followers, whether male or female, who have gone for refuge to the Triple Gem endowed with such supreme qualities and yet are reborn in the hells and other woeful states.
Rather, having been liberated from rebirth in the lower realms, they arise in the world of the devas and experience great prosperity; therefore, you must not break such a refuge as this."
"It was improper for those going to take refuge in other sects," he said.

And here, for the purpose of showing that for those who have gone for refuge to the Three Jewels by way of liberation and by way of supremacy, there is no rebirth in the states of misery, these suttas should be cited:
"Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, they shall not go to the plane of misery..."
Having abandoned the human body, they will fulfill the host of devas.
"Whoever has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, they shall not go to the plane of misery;
having abandoned the human body, they will fulfill the host of devas."
“Whoever has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha will not go to a plane of misery;
having abandoned the human body, they will fulfill the host of devas.
Indeed, many go for refuge to mountains and forests.”
“Grove-deities, tree-deities, and shrine-deities—people driven by fear [take refuge in these].
But this is not a secure refuge; this is not the supreme refuge.
By coming to this refuge, one is not released from all suffering.”
“But whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha,
sees the Four Noble Truths with right wisdom:
suffering, the origin of suffering, and the transcendence of suffering.”
And the Noble Eightfold Path, which leads to the stilling of suffering.
"This indeed is the secure refuge, this is the supreme refuge;
having come to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering."
Furthermore, the Teacher did not teach them only this much Dhamma; rather, he taught:

"O lay followers, the meditation subject called recollection of the Buddha, the meditation subject called recollection of the Dhamma, and the meditation subject called recollection of the Saṅgha bestow the path of stream-entry, bestow the fruit of stream-entry, bestow the path of once-returning, and bestow the fruit of once-returning; they bestow the path of non-returning..."

Having taught the Dhamma by means of such methods as, “It gives [the fruit of] stream-entry; it gives the fruit of once-returning; it gives the fruit of non-returning; it gives the path of arahantship; it gives the fruit of arahantship,” he said, “It was unbecoming for you to break such a refuge.
And here, the bestowing of the path of stream-entry and so forth through meditation subjects such as the recollection of the Buddha is called “one thing” (ekadhammo).
“Monks, when developed and cultivated, this one thing leads to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.
What is that one thing? It is the recollection of the Buddha”—thus it should be illustrated by such suttas.
Having thus exhorted the lay followers in various ways, the Blessed One said: “Lay followers, in the past too, humans regarded what was no refuge as a ‘refuge.’”
“Having taken hold by means of a speculative grasp and a mistaken grasp, those who were seized by non-human beings in the wilderness became food for *yakkhas* and met with great destruction;

however, those who took hold of the unerring grasp, the categorical grasp, and the unmistakable grasp attained safety in that very same wilderness,” having said this, he became silent. Then Anāthapiṇḍika...
The householder rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and having praised him and placed his joined palms to his head, spoke thus:
"Venerable Sir, at present it is evident to us that these lay followers have broken their supreme refuge and adopted reasoning;
however, in the past, in the wilderness possessed by non-human beings, those who relied on reasoning met with destruction, while those who held to the unerring [refuge] did not."
“The safety of those people we have taken hold of is hidden from us but manifest to you.
It would be well if the Blessed One were to make this matter manifest to us, like one raising the full moon in the sky.
Then the Blessed One said, “Householder, it was for the very purpose of cutting through the world’s doubts that I fulfilled the ten perfections for an immeasurable time.”
“Listen attentively with an ear applied as if filling a golden tube with lion’s fat; you have penetrated the knowledge of omniscience.

Thus, having stirred up mindfulness in the merchant, he made manifest the cause that had been concealed by his previous existence, just as one might split open the womb of the snow-mountain and bring forth the full moon.
In the past, in the kingdom of Kāsi, in the city of Bārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta. At that time, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in a caravan leader’s family;

after ten months had passed and he emerged from his mother’s womb, he gradually reached maturity and traveled about conducting trade with five hundred carts. Sometimes he went from the eastern region to the western region.
Sometimes [the Bodhisatta] would go from the future back to the past. At that time, there was another son of a caravan leader in Bārāṇasī who was foolish, incompetent, and unskilled in means.
Then the Bodhisatta, having taken very valuable goods from Bārāṇasī, filled five hundred carts and set them ready for departure.
That foolish son of a caravan leader did exactly the same with five hundred carts.
Having filled them and made them ready for departure, he set them down.

Then the Bodhisatta thought: "If this foolish caravan leader’s son goes along with me, the road will not suffice for a thousand carts traveling together, nor will there be enough wood, water, and other supplies for the people."
“Even grass will become difficult for the bound prisoners to find; therefore, it is fitting that either you or I go on ahead.
He summoned him and, having explained this matter, said, “It is not possible for both of us to go together.
Will you go in front, or will you go behind? He thought, “If I go in front, many [will suffer].”
“There are these advantages: I shall travel by a path that has not yet been trodden; the oxen will eat grass untouched [by others];
there will be potherb leaves for people that have not been gathered; the water will be clear;
and I shall sell my goods after setting the price as I please. He said, “Friend, I shall go on ahead. The Bodhisatta also—
He saw many advantages in going behind. For it occurred to him:
"Those going ahead will level the uneven places on the path; I shall travel by the path they have cleared.
When the oxen going ahead have eaten the withered and hard grass, my own oxen will eat the sweet grass that has grown up again. From the place where leaves have been gathered..."

"The vegetables for people's soup will become sweet; by digging a pit in a place where there is no water, they will cause water to appear there, and we shall drink the water from the pits they have made.
Setting a price is like depriving people of their lives; I shall go behind them and [negotiate] according to the price they have set."
“I shall sell my wares. Then, seeing such advantages, he said, “Friend, you go on ahead.
“Very well, friend,” replied the foolish caravan leader; having yoked his wagons, he set out and, passing by inhabited places in succession, reached the entrance of the wilderness.
A "wilderness" (kantāra) is fivefold: a wilderness of robbers, a wilderness of beasts of prey, a wilderness without water, a wilderness of non-human beings, and a wilderness where food is scarce.
Among these, a path frequented by robbers is called a wilderness of robbers; a path frequented by lions and other such creatures is called a wilderness of beasts of prey;
that place where there is no water for bathing or drinking is a wilderness without water.
A wilderness inhabited by non-human beings is called a "non-human wilderness. A wilderness lacking roots, edible plants, and other provisions is called a "foodless wilderness.
Among these five kinds of wildernesses, this particular one was both a waterless wilderness and a non-human wilderness.
Therefore, that foolish caravan leader’s son placed very large jars upon the carts and filled them with water.
He set out upon a wilderness sixty yojanas in extent.
Then, when he had reached the middle of the wilderness, a yakkha dwelling in that wilderness thought,
"I will cause these men to discard the water they have taken, weaken them, and devour them all," and [he conjured] a chariot yoked with entirely white, young oxen.
Having fashioned a beautiful vehicle and being surrounded by ten or twelve non-human beings (amanussa) with bows,
quivers, shields, and weapons in their hands, he— adorned with blue and white lotuses, wearing wet garments and a wet outer cloak like a lordly man—
sat upon that vehicle and traveled toward the opposite direction on wheels smeared with mud. His retinue of non-human beings also [followed].
Going both before and behind, with their hair wet and their clothes wet,
having donned garlands of blue and white water-lilies and holding bundles of red and white lotuses, they went along eating lotus roots and stalks,
with drops of water and mud trickling down from them. And when the headwind blows, those called caravan leaders sit in their vehicles.
Surrounded by their attendants and clearing away the dust, they proceeded ahead. When the wind blew from behind, they went backward in that same manner.
But on this occasion, there was a headwind; therefore, the caravan leader’s son went forward.
Seeing him approaching, the yakkha caused his own vehicle to move off the path and asked, "Where are you going?"

He exchanged greetings with him. The caravan leader, having caused his own vehicle to turn off the path and making way for the carts, stood to one side and said to that yakkha: "Sir, we are indeed coming from Bārāṇasī;
but you, wearing blue and white lotuses as ornaments, holding pink and white lotuses in your hands, and eating lotus stalks and roots—"
"You are coming along smeared with mud, with drops of water trickling down.
Is it raining on the path you have come by, or are there lakes covered with blue lotuses and other flowers? he asked.
Having heard his words, the yakkha replied, "Good sir, what are you saying? Here is the line of a dark forest visible; from that point onwards, the entire..."
“The forest has but a single water source, and the rain falls incessantly; the ravines are filled, and in various places there are lakes covered with lotuses and other plants.
Having said this, as the carts proceeded one after another, he asked, “Where are you going with these carts? “To such-and-such a province,” they replied. “And what is in these various carts?”
“What goods are there? “This and that. “A cart coming from behind is approaching extremely heavily;

what goods are there in this one? “There is water here. “So far, you have done us a favor by bringing water from further away, but from now on there is no need for water; there is plenty of water ahead. [Bring] buckets.”
"Break them, throw away the water, and go on with ease," he said. Having spoken thus, [the yakkha] added, "You go;
we have much to attend to. Then, after going a short distance until they were out of sight, he returned to his own yakkha-city.
That foolish caravan leader, for his own folly, accepted the words of the yakkha and had the jars broken.
Having caused all the water to be discarded without leaving even a single drop behind, he drove the carts forward;
there was not even a small amount of water ahead, and the people grew weary, finding no drinking water.
They traveled until sunset, then unyoked the carts, arranged them in a circle, and tied the oxen to the wheels. There was no water for the oxen either.
There was no rice gruel or cooked food for the people. The weak among the people lay down here and there to sleep.

Toward the end of the night, yakkhas came from the city of the yakkhas and, having brought all the oxen and people to their death, they ate the flesh, leaving only the bones, and departed. Thus it happened to one foolish caravan leader’s son.
Relying on that [treasure], they all met their destruction; their bones, hands, and other remains were scattered in every direction.
Five hundred carts remained exactly as they had been loaded.
The Bodhisatta, for his part, having spent a month and a half from the day the young caravan leader’s son departed—
Departing from the city with five hundred carts, he gradually reached the edge of the wilderness.
There, having filled water-jars and taken a great quantity of water, he had a drum beaten throughout the camp to assemble the people, and said to them:
"Without asking me for permission, you must not use even as much as a pinch of water; in the wilderness there are poisonous trees..."
“Whatever leaves, flowers, or fruits have never been eaten by you before, do not eat them without asking me.
Having thus given this advice to the people, he set out across the wilderness with five hundred carts.
When they reached the middle of that wilderness, that *yakkha* appeared on the path ahead of the Bodhisatta in the same manner as before.
He showed himself. Upon seeing him, the Bodhisatta recognized: "There is no water in this wilderness; it is indeed a waterless wilderness.
And this man is fearless, with bloodshot eyes, and his shadow is not visible.
Without a doubt, the foolish caravan leader’s son who went ahead must have caused all the water to be discarded, exhausted them, and devoured them along with his own followers."
"But he does not seem to know my wisdom or my skill in means," he thought. Then he said to him, "Go ahead;
we are called merchants, and having taken water, we do not discard it unless we see another supply.
However, once we have seen another place, we shall discard what we have here and proceed with our carts made light. Having said this, the *yakkha* went a short distance until he was out of sight.
Having approached, he went back to his own city of the *yakkhas*.
When the *yakkhas* had departed, the people said to the Bodhisatta: "Noble sir, these men, wearing garlands of blue and white water-lilies, have said:
'That line of dark forest is visible; from there onwards, the rain falls continuously.'"

“Taking bundles of white lotuses, eating the roots and stalks, and coming along with our clothes and hair wet, with drops of water trickling down, let us discard the water and travel quickly with lightened carts.
Having heard their words, the Bodhisatta had the carts halted, gathered all the people together, and said: “By you, in this—”
“Has anyone ever heard before that there is a lake or a lotus pond in the wilderness? he asked. “No, venerable sir, we have never heard such a thing,” they replied.
“This is what is called a waterless wilderness. Now some people say, ‘The rain is falling ahead of us behind that row of dark-blue forest.
How far does a rainstorm blow, venerable sir? “About a league, venerable sir.”
“But does the wind from the rain strike the body of even one of you? “No, venerable lady.
“In how great a space is what is called a ‘cloud-head’ perceived? “In a space of three yojanas, venerable lady.
“But has even a single cloud-head been seen by any of you? “No, venerable lady. “In how great a space is what is called a ‘flash of lightning’ perceived?”
“Four or five yojanas away, noble lady. “But has anyone seen a flash of lightning? “No, noble lady.
“And how far can the sound of thunder be heard? “One or two yojanas, noble lady.
“But has anyone heard the sound of thunder? “No, noble lady. “These are not human beings.”
"These must be yakkhas who have come desiring to eat us after having made us weak by causing us to discard our water.
The foolish caravan leader’s son who went ahead was not skilled in means; surely he has been eaten by them after they caused him to discard his water and exhausted him.
The five hundred carts must remain standing exactly as they were loaded."
"Today we shall see them; drive on very quickly, without spilling even a drop of water," he said, and had the carts driven forward.

As he went along, seeing those five hundred carts exactly as they had been loaded, and seeing the bones of oxen and men scattered in all directions, he had the carts unhitched and established his camp with the caravan of carts.
Having had the men and oxen bound and fed their evening meal at the very early hour, he had the oxen laid down in the midst of the men;
then, acting as the leader of the force with sword in hand, he remained on guard throughout the three watches of the night and caused the dawn to rise while still standing there.
On the following day, however, having completed all his duties at dawn, [he attended to] the oxen...
Having fed them, he had the weak carts discarded and took hold of strong ones;
having had the cheap goods discarded and loaded with expensive goods, he went to his intended destination, sold the goods for double or triple their cost,
and taking his entire retinue, returned once again to his own city.
Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, the Teacher said, "In this way, householder, those who previously grasped at speculative views met with great ruin;
however, those who grasped the 'unerring' view were released from the hands of the non-human beings, reached their desired destination in safety, and returned once more to their own place.
Having thus connected these two instances, he concluded this teaching on the unerring Dhamma.
Having attained full enlightenment, he spoke this verse:
"Some say there is one certain position, while others, the logicians, say there is a second.
Having understood this, the wise man should take that which is certain."
In this context, *apaṇṇaka* means categorical, unerring, and leading to liberation. *Ṭhāna* means cause.
For a cause is called a "basis" (*ṭhāna*) because the fruit stands depending upon it;

thus it is termed "basis. Its usage should be understood in such passages as: "the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible. Thus, by the two words "the categorical basis" (*apaṇṇakaṃ ṭhānaṃ*), [the meaning is established].
He illuminates this by showing: "This is that which, because it brings about exclusive benefit and happiness, is practiced by the wise;
it is a one-sided cause, an unfailing cause, and a cause of deliverance. This is the summary here;

as for the detailed classification, however, there are the three goings for refuge, the five precepts, the ten precepts, restraint according to the Pātimokkha, restraint of the sense faculties, purity of livelihood, and the use of the requisites.
All the fourfold purification of virtue as well— guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness,
jhāna, insight, direct knowledge, meditative attainments, the noble path, and the noble fruit— all this is the "unfailing state" (apaṇṇaka-ṭṭhāna);
the meaning is that it is the unfailing practice, the practice leading to liberation.
And because this is the name for the practice that leads to liberation, it is for this very reason that the Blessed One, showing the unerring practice (*apaṇṇaka-paṭipadā*), spoke this sutta:
"Bhikkhus, endowed with three qualities, a bhikkhu has entered upon the unerring practice;
the foundation for the destruction of the taints has been established for him. With which three? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu..."
He is one who guards the doors of the sense faculties, he is moderate in eating, and he is devoted to wakefulness.
And how, monks, is a monk one who guards the doors of the sense faculties? Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk does not grasp at its signs...
[as above] ...In this way, monks, a monk is one who guards the doors of the sense faculties.
“And how, monks, is a monk moderate in eating? Here, monks, a monk reflects wisely before partaking of food:
‘It is neither for amusement, nor for intoxication, nor for the sake of physical beauty and attractiveness... [as in the full formula] ...In this way, monks, a monk is moderate in eating.

“And how, monks, is a monk devoted to wakefulness? Here, monks, during the day, while walking back and forth and sitting, [he purifies his mind of obstructive states]... [as in the full formula] ...In this way, monks, a monk is devoted to wakefulness.”
In this sutta as well, only these three factors are mentioned. Furthermore, this "unerring practice" (apaṇṇaka-paṭipadā) leads all the way to the attainment of the fruit of Arahatship.

In that regard, even the fruit of Arahatship itself is called a "practice," both in terms of dwelling in the attainment of the fruit and in terms of final Nirvana without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna).

"Ekati" refers to certain wise people. Although there is no specific restriction as to who they are by name, it should be understood that this was said with reference specifically to the Bodhisatta together with his retinue.

"The second they call 'speculative'" means that, relative to the first—which is the unerring position and the cause for deliverance—this second is the cause of grasping at speculation, which is not a cause for deliverance.
Regarding the phrase "They said, 'The reasoners,'" the construction here is as follows, together with the preceding line:
"Some wise men, headed by Bodhisattas, accepted the unerring position—the one-sided reason, the non-contradictory reason, the leading-out reason.
But those reasoners who said so, headed by Bālasatthavāhaputta, [accepted] the second position, which is faulty and not one-sided.
They grasped at a cause that was deviant and a cause that did not lead to liberation.

Among them, those who grasped at the incontrovertible point were practicing the bright path (*sukkapaṭipadā*). Those who grasped at the second, the non-liberating cause known as the "grasping of reasoning"—namely, "one must first have water"—were practicing the dark path (*kaṇhapaṭipadā*).
In this regard, the bright course of practice is a course that leads to non-decline, while the dark course of practice is a course that leads to decline.
Therefore, those who have entered upon the bright course of practice are non-declined and have attained safety;
whereas those who have entered upon the dark course of practice are declined and have fallen into ruin and disaster. This was the meaning [conveyed] by the Blessed One to Anāthapiṇḍika.
Having addressed the householders, he further said this: "Knowing this, the wise man should take that which is 'without a wager' (apaṇṇaka).
In this context, "the wise man knowing this" refers to a clansman endowed with that wisdom—named "medhā"—which is vast, pure, and supreme;
[he knows] these two, namely, that which is called "grasping without reasoning" and "grasping with reasoning," both regarding what is without a wager and what is with a wager.
The meaning is: "having understood the advantages and disadvantages, the increase and decrease, and what is beneficial and what is harmful in various situations.

One should take up that which is "unerring" (*apaṇṇaka*); that is, one should take up only that which is unerring, certain, reckoned as the white practice and the practice that does not lead to decline, and is a cause for deliverance.
Why? Precisely because of its certainty and so forth. But one should not take up the other. Why? Precisely because of its lack of certainty and so forth.
For this is indeed called the "unerring path" (apaṇṇaka-paṭipadā), the path of all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and sons of the Buddha.
For all Buddhas, by standing upon this very unerring path and fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs) with firm energy, become known as Buddhas at the foot of the Bodhi tree;
Paccekabuddhas give rise to individual enlightenment (paccekabodhi); and the sons of the Buddha penetrate the knowledge of the disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramiñāṇa).

Thus the Blessed One, having granted those lay followers the three kinds of prosperity of noble families as well as the prosperity of the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure and the Brahma-world,
delivered this "Infallible Dhamma Teaching" (Apannaka-dhammadesanā), which at its conclusion bestows the path and fruit of Arahantship—
known as the "Infallible Practice"— and conversely, which bestows rebirth in the four states of misery and the five low-born families— known as the "Fallible Practice."
Having shown this, he further elucidated the Four Noble Truths in sixteen aspects.
At the conclusion of the teaching on the Four Truths, all five hundred lay followers were established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
Having brought forth and demonstrated this Dharma discourse, and having related two past events, the Teacher connected the narrative to the present context.
Having correlated the Jātaka, he showed: "At that time, the son of the foolish caravan leader was Devadatta;
his retinue was the retinue of Devadatta; the retinue of the son of the wise caravan leader was the retinue of the Buddha;
and the son of the wise caravan leader was none other than myself. Thus he concluded the teaching.
The first is the commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka.
2. The commentary on the Vaṇṇupatha Jātaka:
"Those who are untiring"—the Blessed One delivered this teaching while dwelling at Sāvatthī. But with reference to whom was it spoken?

One monk who had abandoned his energy. It is said that while the Tathāgata was dwelling at Sāvatthī, a certain son of good family living in Sāvatthī went to Jetavana, heard a discourse on the Dhamma from the Teacher, and with a mind full of confidence, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, went forth.
Having received full ordination, when he had been five years ordained, he mastered the two Mātikās and [began] the practice of insight (vipassanā).

Having trained and received a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) according to his own preference from the Teacher, he entered a forest, entered the rains retreat, and although he strove for three months, he was unable to produce even a mere radiance or a mere sign.
Then this thought occurred to him: "The Teacher has spoken of four types of persons; among them, I must be one who is at most a follower of the words."
"I suppose there is neither the Path nor the Fruit for me in this present existence; what use is dwelling in the forest?
I shall go into the presence of the Teacher and dwell beholding the Buddha’s body, which has attained the pinnacle of physical beauty, and listening to his sweet preaching of the Dhamma.
Having said this, he returned once more to Jetavana. Then his friends and companions—
They said, "Friend, you went into the presence of the Teacher after receiving a meditation subject, thinking, 'I will practice the duty of a recluse.
But now, having returned, you are wandering about delighting in company. Has the purpose for which you went forth reached its culmination?
Have you been born without further rebirth? [He replied: "Friends, it is because I have not attained either the path or the fruit."
“I have come here having abandoned my energy, thinking, ‘I must become a person incapable [of progress].
“Friend, you have done what is improper, in that you have abandoned your energy after going forth in the teaching of a Teacher of firm energy; you have done what is unbecoming.
Come, let us show him to the Tathāgata. Taking him with them, they went into the presence of the Teacher.
Seeing him, the Teacher said: "Monks, you have brought this monk here against his will; what has he done?
They replied, "Venerable Sir, this monk, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation and practicing the duties of a recluse, has come back having abandoned his energy.
Then the Teacher said to him: "Is it true, as they say, that you..."
“Bhikkhu, have you abandoned your energy? “It is true, Blessed One.

“But why, bhikkhu, having gone forth in such a teaching as mine, do you not let yourself be known as ‘one of few wishes,’ or ‘contented,’ or ‘secluded,’ or ‘aroused in energy,’ but instead let yourself be known as ‘a bhikkhu who has abandoned his energy’? Were you not formerly energetic?”
"It was so; by relying on the energy exerted by you alone, the people and oxen in five hundred carts obtained water in the desert wilderness and became happy. Why do you now slacken your energy?
At these words, that bhikkhu was encouraged.
Having heard that, the bhikkhus requested of the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, at present this bhikkhu’s state of having slackened his energy is manifest to us;

however, previously, by means of his energy alone, he enabled oxen and humans to obtain water in the desert wilderness and thus attain happiness—this was hidden [from us] and known only to your omniscient knowledge."

“It is clear; tell us this reason of ours as well. “Then listen, monks,” the Blessed One said, rousing mindfulness in those monks and making manifest that reason which had been concealed by another existence.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling the kingdom in Bārāṇasī in the country of Kāsi, the Bodhisatta [was born] into a caravan leader’s family.
Having taken rebirth and reached maturity, he traveled about engaging in trade with five hundred carts.
On one occasion, he entered a desert wilderness sixty yojanas in extent. In that desert, fine sand could not remain in the hand when grasped by the fist;
from the time the sun rose, it became as hot as a heap of glowing embers. It was not...
It is possible to cross it. Therefore, those who set out upon it take firewood, water, sesame seeds, rice, and other provisions in carts;

traveling by night, they turn the carts around at the break of dawn, erect a pavilion at the head of the path, complete their meal preparations early, spend the day sitting in the shade, and when the sun has set, they take their evening meal.
Having eaten, when the ground had become cool, they would yoke their carts and set out; their journey was exactly like a voyage across the ocean.
It is necessary to have one known as a land-pilot, who brings the caravan across by means of the "star-sign.
That caravan leader, traveling through that wilderness by this very method at that time, covered fifty-nine yojanas.
Having traveled some distance, [the caravan leader] thought, "Now, in just one night, we shall emerge from this desert wilderness.
Having eaten his evening meal, used up all the wood and water, and yoked the carts, he set out.
But the pilot, having had a seat spread on the first cart, lay down looking at the stars in the sky, saying, "Drive this way, drive that way! and so forth.
Thus, exhausted from not having slept for such a long time, he fell asleep;
he did not notice that the oxen had turned back and were following the very path they had come. The oxen traveled throughout the entire night.
At the time of dawn, the pilot woke up, observed the constellations, and said, "Turn the wagons back! Turn them back! Having turned the wagons back, they were arranged in their proper order.
While they were still working, the sun rose. The people thought, "This is the very place where we encamped yesterday;
even our firewood is exhausted, and now we are lost. Unyoking their carts and arranging them in a circle, they constructed a shelter over them and lay down beneath each of their own carts, lamenting.
The Bodhisatta, thinking, "If I relax my effort, everyone will perish," wandered about at the cool hour of dawn.
Seeing a thicket of *dabbatīṇa* grass, he thought, "These grasses must have sprouted due to the moisture of water beneath.
He had them take up spades and have that spot dug; they dug a pit sixty cubits deep.
While they were digging to that extent and striking away, the spade struck against a rock below; at the mere touch of it, they all abandoned their effort.
But the Bodhisatta, thinking, "There must be water beneath this rock," descended and stood upon the rock.
Leaning over and listening intently, as he applied his mind to the sound, he perceived the sound of water flowing below.
Having heard this, he climbed out and said to his junior attendant, "Dear son, if you abandon your effort, we shall all perish.
While you do not abandon your effort, take this iron bar, descend into the pit, and strike this rock.
Accepting his word, even though everyone else had abandoned their effort and stood still, he exerted his effort.
Not letting go, he descended and struck the rock. The rock split in the middle and fell down;
having blocked the stream, it stood there, and a column of water as thick as a palm trunk gushed forth.
Having all drunk the water and bathed, they split up the remaining axle-trees and other parts, cooked rice gruel and food, and ate.
Having fed the oxen and the sun having set, they tied a banner near a water-pool and went to their desired destination.
There, having sold their goods and obtained a profit double, triple, or quadruple [the cost], they returned to their own dwelling place.
Having remained there for the duration of their lifespan, they departed according to their karma.
The Bodhisatta, too, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, departed according to his own karma.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Fully Enlightened One, immediately upon his awakening, spoke this verse:
“Those who dug in the path through the forest without weariness found water there in a dry place.”
"Thus the sage, endowed with the power of energy, unwearied, finds peace of heart.
In this context, "unwearied" means those who are not indolent and have initiated energy. "In a sandy track" (*vaṇṇupathe*): "sandy" (*vaṇṇu*) refers to sand; the meaning is "on a path of sand.
"Digging" means digging the earth. "In the courtyard" (*udaṅgaṇe*): here *uda* is a particle, and *aṅgaṇe* refers to the courtyards of men.
"In a place for wandering" means on a portion of ground that is not enclosed by a trench. "Therein" means on that path of sand.

"They found water" means they obtained water. For water is called "papa" because it is desirable to drink (*papīyana*); or else, "papa" is increased water (*pavaddham āpam*), meaning a great quantity of water.
Thus is the application of the simile. "Muni": *mona* is said to mean knowledge (*ñāṇa*), or else any one of the forms of bodily silence (*kāyamoneyya*) and so forth;
because he is endowed with that, a person is called a "muni. Furthermore, this [muni] is of many kinds:

the householder muni, the homeless muni, the muni in training (*sekkha*), the muni beyond training (*asekkha*), the muni who is a paccekabuddha, and the muni of munis. Among these, the "householder muni" refers to—
A householder who has attained the fruit and understood the teaching; a homeless sage (*muni*) is one who has gone forth in such a manner;

a trainee sage (*sekkha-muni*) refers to the seven types of trainees; a non-trainee sage (*asekkha-muni*) is one whose taints are destroyed; a private-buddha sage (*paccekabuddha-muni*) is a privately enlightened one;

and a sage-of-sages (*munimuni*) is a perfectly enlightened Buddha (*sammāsambuddha*). In this context, however, it refers to one endowed with the wisdom designated as "sageliness" (*moneyya*), which encompasses all [these categories].
“He should be understood as a ‘muni. “Endowed with the power of energy” means possessed of both energy and the physical strength and the power of wisdom.
“Unwearied” means free from indolence—[thinking]:
“Let there remain only skin, sinew, and bone;”
"Let the flesh and blood in my body dry up entirely"—
because he was endowed with such energy possessed of the four factors, he was untiring.
He found "peace" (santi), which is designated as such because it brings about a state of coolness for both the mind and the physical heart.
The meaning is that he finds and attains the noble Dhamma known as the knowledge of the paths to arahantship, together with the higher knowledges (abhiññā), insight (vipassanā), and the jhānas.
For the Blessed One said:
"Bhikkhus, it is suffering for one who dwells indolent, entangled in evil and unwholesome states; and [great...]".
"He neglects his own true welfare. But one who has aroused energy, monks, dwells happily, secluded from evil unwholesome states, and fulfills his great own welfare;
for by means of the inferior, monks, the attainment of the supreme does not occur."
Thus, by means of numerous suttas, the dwelling in suffering of the lazy one and the dwelling in happiness of the one who has aroused energy have been extolled.

Here too, showing that very dwelling in happiness which is to be attained by the power of energy by a practitioner of insight who has not yet formed a fixed conclusion, [the Blessed One says]: "Thus the sage, endowed with the power of energy, finds for his heart..."

“There is,” he said. This is what is meant: just as those merchants, being untiring, found water while digging in the desert path, so too, a wise bhikkhu who exerts himself without weariness in this Dispensation attains this peace of the heart, which is distinguished by the jhānas and other states.
You, bhikkhu, having previously exerted energy for the sake of mere water...
"Now, why do you slacken your energy in such a liberating dispensation that bestows the paths and fruits?

Having thus shown this teaching of the Dhamma, he proclaimed the Four Noble Truths. At the conclusion of the truths, the monk who had slackened his energy was established in Arahantship, the supreme fruit.
The Teacher, having related two stories and established the connection, identified the Jātaka by showing:
"At that time, this monk who had slackened his energy was the junior attendant who, without relinquishing his effort, split the rock and gave water to the great multitude;
the rest of the assembly has now become the Buddha’s assembly; and the chief caravan leader was [the Buddha himself]."
"But it was I myself who was he," he said, thus concluding the teaching.
This concludes the second commentary, the Vaṇṇupathajātakavaṇṇanā.
3. Serivavāṇijajātakavaṇṇanā (The Commentary on the Serivavāṇija Jātaka)
“If you should fail in this” is a teaching on the Dhamma that the Blessed One gave while dwelling at Sāvatthī concerning a certain monk who had slackened his energy.
Having seen that monk brought before him by the monks in the same manner as before, the Teacher said:
“Bhikkhu, having gone forth in such a Dispensation as this, which bestows the paths and fruits, you are now slackening your energy; [you are wasting] that which is worth a hundred thousand.”
“You will grieve for a long time, like the merchant of Seriva who was deprived of his golden bowl.
The monks requested the Blessed One to clarify the meaning of this, and the Blessed One made manifest the cause that had been concealed by the passage of time.
In the past, five aeons ago, the Bodhisatta was a merchant in Kacchapuṭa in the kingdom of Seri. He [was accompanied] by one named Seriva...
