While traveling for the sake of trade with a certain merchant named Lolakacchapuṭa, he crossed the river named Nīlavāha and, upon entering the city named Ariṭṭhapura, divided the city streets among themselves.
He wandered about selling his wares in the street allotted to him, while the other took the street allotted to himself. Now, in that city, there was one...
The merchant’s family had fallen into decay; all the sons and brothers had perished, and the wealth was exhausted.
Only a single daughter remained with her grandmother, and the two of them lived by working for hire for others.
However, in their house, a golden bowl that had formerly been used by the Great Merchant remained placed among the other vessels for a long time.
Being handled, it became soiled with dirt that they did not even recognize its state as a golden bowl.
At that time, a greedy merchant, wandering about crying out, "Baskets! Baskets!", arrived at that house door.
Seeing him, the young girl said to her grandmother, "Mother, buy me one ornament. "Mother, we..."
“Wretched women! What shall we give to receive this? [The merchant replied,] “We have this bowl, but it is of no use to us;
let us give this away and take [the other]. She had the merchant summoned, seated him on a chair, gave him that bowl, and said, “Noble sir, take this and give something to your sister.
The merchant, taking the bowl in his very hand, said, “A golden bowl—”

Thinking, "It will be so," he turned it over, drew a line with a needle on the back of the bowl, and having recognized its golden nature, thought, "I shall take this bowl away without giving anything for these [coins]. Saying, "What is this worth?
Even half a māsaka is not its price," he threw it on the ground, rose from his seat, and departed by the path taken by those who had entered and left. By one [who followed], the path...
"The other may enter," [she thought]. The Bodhisatta entered that street and, wandering about crying out, "Water-jars!
Water-jars!", arrived at that very door of the house.
Again, the young girl spoke to her grandmother in the same manner. Then the grandmother said to her, "Daughter, the merchant who came first..."
“Having thrown the bowl on the ground, he has gone; now, having given what, shall we take it back? she said.
“Mother, that merchant was harsh of speech, but this one is pleasant to look upon and gentle in conversation; perhaps he might take it back.
“Mother, in that case, call him. She called him. Then, after he had entered his house and sat down, [she gave] that bowl to him.
They gave it to him. Having realized that it was a golden bowl, he said, "Mother, this bowl is worth a hundred thousand; I do not have any goods in my possession worth a hundred thousand.

"Noble sir, the merchant who arrived first came and went away after throwing it on the ground, saying, 'This is not even worth half a māsaka. But this golden bowl must have arisen through your own merit."
“We give this to you; give us something in exchange and take it and go.

At that moment, the Bodhisatta gave all the five hundred kahāpaṇas and the merchandise worth five hundred coins that were in his hands, and having requested only this much—“Give me this balance-beam, this pouch, and eight kahāpaṇas”—he took them and departed.
He departed. Having gone quickly to the riverbank, he gave eight kahāpaṇas to the ferryman and boarded the boat.
Then the greedy merchant went back to that house again and said, "Bring that bowl; I will give you something.
She rebuked him, saying, "You [would not give] even half a māsaka for our golden bowl worth a hundred thousand."
"He did not do so; however, a righteous merchant, who was like your own master, gave us a thousand pieces of money and took it away.
Upon hearing this, she thought, "I have been deprived of a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand;
alas, this has caused me a great loss! A powerful grief arose within her, and being unable to maintain her mindfulness, she fell unconscious.

Having sacrificed his own hand-held kahāpaṇas and his bundle of goods right there at the door of his house, and casting off his lower and upper garments, he took a balance-beam and made it into a club;
then, following in the footsteps of the Bodhisatta, he went to the riverbank.
Seeing the Bodhisatta departing, he said, "O boatman, turn back the boat! The Bodhisatta—
But he forbade him, saying, "Dear one, do not turn back. Even for the other, as he watched the Bodhisatta departing, a powerful sorrow arose;
his heart grew hot, blood gushed from his mouth, and his heart burst like the mud at the bottom of a pond.
Having conceived malice toward the Bodhisatta, he met his death right there. This is...
First was Devadatta’s binding of enmity toward the Bodhisatta. Having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, the Bodhisatta departed according to his karma.
After delivering this teaching on the Dhamma, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having attained full awakening, spoke this verse:
“If one violates here the fixed course of the True Dhamma...”
"You will long regret it, like the merchant Seriva.

In this context, "If you fail here in the fixed course of the True Dharma" means that you have failed in this teaching—the path of stream-entry known as the fixed course of the True Dharma. If you have failed, by relinquishing your effort, you shall not attain [the goal].
The meaning is "you do not obtain. "For a long time you will regret" means: this being so, you will grieve and lament for a long duration and thus regret;

or else, because the Noble Path has been missed due to the abandonment of energy (*ossatthavīriyatā*), you will regret—that is, you will suffer—experiencing various kinds of suffering after having arisen in the hells and other realms for a long night.
This is the meaning here. How so? Just like the merchant named Seriva—this merchant called "Seriva" is used as an example.

This is what is meant: just as in the past a merchant named Seriva, having obtained a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [pieces], failed to exert effort to secure it and thus fell away from it and regretted it, even so are you.
"In this teaching, if you do not attain the Noble Path— which is like a golden bowl prepared for you— due to a slackening of your energy,
you will fall away from it and suffer for a long time. But if you do not abandon your energy,
you will obtain the ninefold supramundane Dhamma within my teaching, just as the wise merchant obtained the golden bowl."

Thus the Teacher, bringing the matter to its conclusion by means of Arahantship, showed this teaching of the Dhamma and proclaimed the Four Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who had slackened his energy was established in Arahantship, the supreme fruit.

The Teacher, having related two past events and joined the connection, identified the Jātaka and concluded the instruction, saying: "At that time, the foolish merchant was Devadatta, while the wise merchant was none other than myself.
This is the third commentary on the Serivavāṇija Jātaka.
4. Commentary on the Cūḷaseṭṭhijātaka:
"Even with a little, the wise man... The Blessed One gave this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Jīvakambavana near Rājagaha, concerning the Elder Cūḷapanthaka.
In that regard, first the account of Cūḷapanthaka’s birth must be told. It is said that in Rājagaha, within a family of wealthy merchants...
Having formed an intimacy with her own slave, the daughter, fearing that others might also learn of this deed, spoke thus:
"We cannot remain in this place; if my parents discover this fault, they will cut us to pieces.
Let us go and live in a foreign land," and taking his essential belongings, she departed.
Having departed through the main gate, they both went to a place where others would not know them, thinking, "We shall live wherever we find ourselves.
While they were living in one place, through their cohabitation, a fetus was conceived in her womb.
When the pregnancy had reached maturity, she consulted with her husband, saying, "My pregnancy has matured; [we are] separated from our kinsmen and relatives..."
“At this stage, leaving the womb would be a source of suffering for both of us; let us go to our own family home.
He thought, “If I go, I shall not live,” and so he let the days pass, thinking, “We will go today,” or “We will go tomorrow.
She thought, “This fool, because of the greatness of his own fault, does not dare to go.”
"Parents are indeed exclusively beneficial; whether he goes or not, it is fitting for me to go.
When he had departed from the house, she put away the household belongings, informed her neighbors that she was going to her own family home, and set out on the road.
Then that man, having returned home and not seeing her, asked his neighbors;
hearing that she had gone to her parents' house, he pursued her with speed and caught up with her on the way. At that very spot, she too gave birth to a child.
He asked, "What is this, my dear? She replied, "Husband, a son has been born. He asked, "What shall we do now?"
“The purpose for which we were going to our family home has been accomplished along the way;
having gone there, what would we do? Let us turn back. With one mind, they both turned back.
Because that child was born on the road, they gave him the name Panthaka. Not long after that, she conceived another pregnancy.

Everything should be detailed in the same manner as before. Furthermore, because that child was born on the road (*paṇtha*), they gave the first-born the name "Mahāpanthaka" (Great Roadling) and the other the name "Cūḷapanthaka" (Little Roadling).
Taking both children with them, they returned to their own dwelling place.
While they were living there, this boy Mahāpanthaka heard other boys calling their own fathers "little father" and "great father," and their uncles "noble father" and "noble mother.
He asked his mother, "Mother, other boys call them 'little father' and 'great father,' and they also call them 'noble father' and 'noble mother. Do we have no relatives? "Yes, dear, we do not."
“There are no kinsmen here; however, in the city of Rājagaha you have a grandfather named Dhanaseṭṭhi, and there you have many kinsmen.

“Why do you not go there, mother? Without telling her son the reason for her not going, she said to her husband as her sons continued to press her again and again: “These children distress me excessively.”
"What will our parents do when they see us? Will they eat us raw? Come, let us show the children their grandfather's family.
"I shall not be able to appear before them in person, but I will lead him there. "Very well, noble sir;
by whatever means possible, it is right that the children should see their grandfather's family. Thus, both men [took] the children...
Taking them, he reached Rājagaha by stages; having stayed overnight in a certain hall at the city gate, he informed the parents that the mother of the children had arrived bringing the two boys.
Upon hearing this message, they said, "For those wandering in *saṃsāra*, there is no such thing as 'no son' or 'no daughter'; they [belong] to us..."

“They are great offenders; they cannot remain within the range of our sight. However, having taken this much wealth, let both of them go to a comfortable place and live there; as for the children, let them send them here.
The merchant’s daughter took the wealth sent by her parents, placed it in the hands of the messengers who had come for the children, and sent them away. The children—

They were growing up in their grandfather’s family. Among them, Cūḷapanthaka was still very young, but Mahāpanthaka would go with his grandfather to hear the Dhamma discourse of the One of Ten Powers.
As he constantly listened to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, his mind inclined toward the going forth.
He said to his grandfather, "If you agree, I would like to go forth."
“What do you say, dear? Since I have gone forth for the sake of the entire world, your own going forth is truly auspicious.
If you are able, go forth, dear. Having thus consented, he went into the presence of the Teacher.
The Teacher asked, “Great merchant, have you obtained a boy? “Yes, venerable sir; this boy is my grandson, and he says, ‘I will go forth in your presence.’”
“...so he says,” he replied. The Teacher commanded a certain alms-collecting bhikkhu, “Ordain this boy.
The Elder, having instructed him in the meditation subject of the five aggregates (the *pañcakkhandha-kammaṭṭhāna*), ordained him.
Having mastered much of the Buddha’s word, when he had reached full age, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*). Having been fully ordained, through wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*)—
While performing his duties, he attained arahantship.
Spending his time in the bliss of jhāna, the bliss of the Path, and the bliss of the Fruit, he thought, "Could this bliss indeed be given to Cūḷapanthaka?
Thereupon, he went to the presence of the Elder Merchant and said, "Great Merchant..."
“If you agree, I shall ordain Cūḷapanthaka,” he said. “Please ordain him, venerable sir,” they replied.
The Elder ordained the boy Cūḷapanthaka and established him in the ten precepts.
However, as soon as he had been ordained, the novice Cūḷapanthaka proved to be dull-witted.
"Just as a fragrant red lotus may be in full bloom at dawn, its fragrance unabated;
behold Aṅgīrasa shining forth, blazing like the sun in the sky.
He was unable to learn this single verse in four months. It is said that during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, he...
Having gone forth and become wise, he engaged in playful mockery at the time when a certain slow-witted bhikkhu was receiving a scriptural recitation (*uddesa*).
That bhikkhu, being ashamed because of that mockery, neither received the recitation nor practiced it.
Due to that kamma, this man became dull-witted even after going forth; every word he grasped, as he was grasping the words one after another, [was lost].
It was lost. As he strove to master this very verse, four months passed by.
Then Mahāpanthaka said to him, "Cūḷapanthaka, you are incapable in this dispensation;
you have not been able to learn even a single verse in four months. How then will you bring your purpose in going forth to its ultimate fulfillment?"
"Get out of here! he said, and threw him out of the monastery. Because of his affection for the Buddha’s teaching, Cūḷapanthaka did not desire the state of a householder.
At that time, Mahāpanthaka was the distributor of meals.
Jīvaka Komārabhacca, having taken many perfumes and garlands, went to his own mango grove; there he honored the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma, and rose from his seat.
Having paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, he approached Mahāpanthaka and asked, "Venerable sir, how many bhikkhus are there in the presence of the Teacher?

"About five hundred bhikkhus," he replied. "Venerable sir, tomorrow, taking five hundred bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, please accept almsfood at our residence. "Lay follower, there is a bhikkhu named Cūḷapanthaka..."
"I am slow and my nature has not yet matured; therefore, excluding him, I accept the invitation for the rest," said the Elder.
Upon hearing this, Cūḷapanthaka thought: "The Elder accepts the invitation for so many monks while excluding me;
undoubtedly, my brother's heart has turned away from me."
"What will become of it? What use have I now for this teaching? I shall live as a householder, performing meritorious deeds such as giving.
On the following day at dawn, thinking "I shall become a householder," he set out. The Teacher, surveying the world at the very time of dawn, saw this circumstance;
having arrived there first, he stood at the gatehouse on the path where Cūḷapanthaka was traveling.
While walking back and forth, he stood still. As Cūḷapanthaka was going home, he saw the Teacher, approached him, and paid homage.
Then the Teacher said to him, "Cūḷapanthaka, where are you going at this hour?
"Venerable sir, my brother is driving me out; therefore, I am going to disrobe," he replied. "Cūḷapanthaka, your going forth—"
“Cūḷapanthaka is my own; why did he not come into my presence after being driven out by his brothers? Come! What use is the life of a householder to you?
You shall remain in my presence. Having said this, the Blessed One took Cūḷapanthaka with him, led him to the entrance of the Fragrant Chamber, and seated him there, saying:
“Cūḷapanthaka, facing eastward, take this rag and [regard it as] a dust-remover.”

Having given him a piece of pure cloth prepared through supernormal power (iddhi), saying, "Wipe with this 'dust-remover' and remain right here," he—surrounded by the community of monks—went at the announced time to Jīvaka’s house and sat down on the prepared seat.
Meanwhile, Cūḷapanthaka, looking toward the sun, was wiping that piece of cloth, saying, "Dust-remover! Dust-remover!"
He sat down, and as he repeatedly rubbed that piece of rag, it became soiled.
Then he thought: "This piece of rag was once exceedingly pure, yet by depending on this physical form, it has abandoned its former nature and become thus defiled;
truly impermanent are conditioned phenomena. Thus he contemplated their decay and passing away.
As he established [the meditation], his insight increased. The Teacher, knowing that Cūḷapanthaka’s mind had ascended to insight, said:
“Cūḷapanthaka, do not form the perception that this mere scrap of ragged cloth is defiled and stained with dust;
rather, there is the dust of passion and other defilements within you—remove those! Having said this, he emitted a radiance.
Having cast it off, appearing as if he were sitting before them, he spoke these verses:
“Lust is not called ‘dust,’ nor is it called ‘grime’; this is merely a designation for lust.
Having completely abandoned this dust, O monks, they dwell in the teaching of the One Free from Dust.”
“Hatred is called ‘dust,’ but it is not what is meant by ‘dust. This is a designation for hatred: ‘dust.
Having utterly abandoned this dust, O monks, they dwell in the teaching of one who is free from dust.
Delusion is called ‘dust,’ but it is not what is meant by ‘dust. This is a designation for delusion: ‘dust.’”
“Having utterly abandoned this dust, O bhikkhus, they dwell in the teaching of him who is free from dust.
At the conclusion of this verse, Cūḷapanthaka attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā); through those very analytical knowledges, the three Piṭakas came to him.
It is said that formerly, when he was a king, while performing a circumambulation of the city, [a drop of water] fell from his forehead...
As he sat, he wiped his forehead with a clean cloth, and the cloth became soiled.
Thinking, "In dependence upon this body, even such a pure cloth has abandoned its natural state and become soiled;
impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena," he attained the perception of impermanence. For that reason, the dust-remover itself became the condition for him.
Jīvaka Komārabhacca also offered water for the Teacher’s ablution.
The Teacher covered the bowl with his hand, saying, “Jīvaka, are there not monks in the monastery? Mahāpanthaka replied, “Venerable Sir, there are no monks in the monastery.
The Teacher said, “There are, Jīvaka. Jīvaka said, “In that case, sir, go to the monastery yourself.”
“Find out whether there are monks present in the monastery or not,” he sent a man.
At that moment, Cūḷapanthaka thought, “My brother says there are no monks in the monastery;
I shall demonstrate to him that there are indeed monks in the monastery. He then filled the entire mango grove with monks alone. Some monks...
Some were making robes, some were dyeing them, and some were engaged in recitation;

thus he established a thousand monks, each different from the other. When that man saw so many monks in the monastery, he turned back and reported to Jīvaka, "Venerable sir, the entire mango grove is filled with monks. And the Elder remained right there—
“Having manifested himself a thousandfold, Panthaka sat in the delightful mango grove until the time for his summons was announced.
Then the Teacher said to that man: “Go to the monastery and say, ‘The Teacher calls for Cūḷapanthaka.’”
“Go and say so. Having gone there and being addressed in that manner, he raised a thousand voices, saying, “I am Cūḷapanthaka! I am Cūḷapanthaka!
The man went back and said, “Venerable sir, it seems they are all indeed named Cūḷapanthaka.
[The Buddha said: “In that case, go and take hold of the hand of whichever one says first, ‘I am Cūḷapanthaka,’ while the rest...”
“They shall disappear. He did accordingly, and at that very moment, about a thousand bhikkhus vanished.
The Elder went along with that man. At the conclusion of the meal, the Teacher addressed Jīvaka:
“Jīvaka, take Cūḷapanthaka’s bowl; he will deliver the thanksgiving discourse for you. Jīvaka did so.
The Elder, letting out a lion’s roar like a young lion, agitated the Three Piṭakas and offered words of thanksgiving.
The Teacher rose from his seat, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and went to the monastery.

When the bhikkhus had performed their duties, he rose from his seat, stood at the entrance of the Fragrant Chamber, gave the Sugata’s exhortation to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and taught them a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
Having dismissed the community of monks and entered the Fragrant Chamber, which was perfumed with fragrant scents, he lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture.
Then, in the evening, the monks gathered from here and there in the Dhamma Hall;
sitting as if surrounding a red woolen rug, they began a discourse on the virtues of the Teacher: "Friends,..."
Mahāpanthaka, not knowing Cūḷapanthaka’s disposition, thought, “He cannot learn even a single verse in four months;

he is dull-witted,” and expelled him from the monastery. But the Perfectly Enlightened One, by virtue of his unsurpassed sovereignty over the Dhamma, bestowed upon him, within a single meal, the state of Arahatship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), as well as mastery of the Three Piṭakas through those very same analytical knowledges.
“They have arrived! Oh, how great indeed is the power of the Buddhas!
Then the Blessed One, having understood this conversation taking place in the Dhamma Hall, thought, “It is fitting for me to go today.
Rising from his Buddha-rest, he put on his well-dyed inner robe, fastened his waistband like a flash of lightning, and—
Having donned the Great Robe of the Sugata, which resembled a crimson woolen blanket, he emerged from the fragrant Perfumed Chamber.
Stretching his limbs with the playful majesty of a lion and the stride of an elephant in rut, he proceeded to the Dhamma Assembly with the infinite grace of a Buddha.
Ascending the excellent Buddha-seat well-prepared in the center of the decorated pavilion, he emitted the six-colored rays of a Buddha.
Illuminating the depths of the ocean as he descended, he sat in the midst of his seat like the morning sun upon the peak of Mount Yugandhara.
As soon as the Perfectly Enlightened One had arrived, the community of monks ceased their conversation and became silent.
The Teacher, looking upon the assembly with a gentle heart of loving-kindness, said, "This assembly shines exceedingly; not even one person..."
There is no fidgeting with hands or feet, nor any sound of coughing or sneezing;

out of reverence for the Buddha, they are all respectful and intimidated by the Buddha’s majesty. While I remain seated without speaking even for the duration of a lifetime, they will not initiate the first conversation.
Indeed, it is I alone who must know the proper etiquette for initiating conversation.
"I shall speak first," he said, and addressing the bhikkhus with a sweet, Brahma-like voice, he asked:
"Bhikkhus, about what topic are you gathered here now, and what was the conversation among you that was left unfinished?
"Venerable Sir, we are not sitting here discussing some trivial, worldly talk; it is concerning you alone..."

However, while we were sitting praising his virtues, [we heard that] the Venerable Mahāpanthaka, not knowing Cūḷapanthaka’s disposition, had expelled him from the monastery, saying, "This man is dull;
he cannot learn even a single verse in four months.

But the Perfectly Enlightened One, due to his supreme sovereignty over the Dhamma, [granted him] the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) together with [the realization of the Truth] within a single meal.
“He has granted him Arahatship! Oh, how great indeed is the power of the Buddhas!
When the Teacher heard the monks’ conversation, he said, “Monks, by depending on me, Cūḷapanthaka has now attained greatness among the qualities of the Dhamma;
but in the past, by depending on me, he also attained greatness in wealth. The monks [asked] about the meaning of this.
They requested the Blessed One for the sake of its manifestation. The Blessed One made manifest the cause that had been concealed within a previous existence.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāsi, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a guild-leader’s family;
having reached maturity and obtained the position of guild-leader, he was known as Cūḷaseṭṭhi. He was wise, competent, and skilled in all signs.
He understood. One day, while going to attend upon the king, he saw a dead mouse in the middle of the street;
immediately taking the auspicious moment into account, he said this: "Is it possible for a wise man of good family, having taken this rat, to support a wife and children and engage them in work?
A certain son of a poor family, hearing those words of the merchant, [acted accordingly].
Thinking, “He will not speak without knowing [the truth,” he took the mouse and sold it in a shop for a cat, receiving a *kākaṇika* coin.
With that *kākaṇika*, he bought molasses and took a jar of water.
Seeing some garland-makers returning from the forest, he gave them small pieces of molasses little by little, using his water-skin (*uḷuṅka*).
He gave them water, and they each gave him a handful of flowers.
With that money from the flowers, on the following day he took molasses and a water jar and went once again to the flower garden.
On that day, the florists gave him half-grown flower clusters and departed. Before long, by this means, he obtained eight kahāpaṇas.
Again, on a day of wind and rain, many dry trunks, branches, and leaves were blown down by the wind in the royal garden; the gardener saw no way to clear them away.
He went there and said to the gardener, "If you give me these wood and leaves, I will carry them all out for you."

He said, "Take it, noble sir," and accepted. The junior pupil went to the children's playground, gave them molasses, and in a short while had all the wooden leaves removed and piled up at the gate of the park.
At that time, the royal potter was searching for wood at the park gate for the purpose of firing vessels in the royal household.
Having seen them, he bought them from his hand and took them. On that day, the junior pupil obtained sixteen kahāpaṇas from the sale of wood, as well as five vessels, including a jar and others.
When twenty-four kahāpaṇas had been accumulated, he thought, "I have found this means," and [went] not far from the city gate.
Having placed a single water-scoop in a suitable spot, he served five hundred grass-cutters with water.
They said to him, "Friend, you have been very helpful to us; what can we do for you?
He replied, "When a need arises for me, you shall do it," and as he wandered here and there, he encountered both land-traders and sea-traders.
He formed a friendship with him. The land-trader informed him, "Tomorrow a horse-dealer will arrive at this city bringing five hundred horses.
Having heard his words, he said to the grass-gatherers, "Give me one bundle of grass each today; as long as I have not sold my grass, do not sell your own."
Having agreed, saying "Very well," they brought five hundred bundles of grass and delivered them to his house.
The horse-dealer, unable to find fodder for his horses anywhere in the city, paid him a thousand pieces of money and took that grass.
Then, after a few days had passed, a friend of his who was engaged in sea transport informed him, "A great ship has arrived at the port."
Thinking, "There is this means," he took for a short-term loan a chariot complete with every kind of equipment for eight kahāpaṇas.
Accompanied by great splendor, he went to the harbor;
there, having given a signet ring as a pledge to the boatman, he had a screen erected in a spot not far away and sat down. He then commanded his men: "From outside, among the merchants..."

“When the third signal has arrived, report this to me. Having heard that the ship had arrived, about a hundred merchants from Benares came, saying, “We will take the goods. [The man said: “You will not obtain the goods;
a merchant of such-and-such a place has given his solemn pledge. Having heard this, they went into his presence. The footmen—
By means of the third stratagem, in accordance with their previous understanding, they announced that those [merchants] had arrived.
Those hundred merchants each gave a thousand [pieces of gold] and, having boarded the ship together with him, they again gave a thousand each, dismissed the boatmen,
and made the merchandise their own property.
Cūḷantevāsika, having taken two hundred thousand [pieces of gold], came to Bārāṇasī and thought, "It is fitting that I be grateful.
He had one hundred thousand pieces taken and went into the presence of Cūḷaseṭṭhi.
Then the merchant asked him, "My dear son, what have you done to obtain this wealth? He replied, "By following the method you explained..."
He related the entire story, beginning with the "dead mouse" he had obtained within just four months.

Upon hearing his words, the junior merchant thought, "Now it is fitting to take such a boy as my own," and gave him his daughter who had reached marriageable age, making him the master of his entire household. After the merchant passed away, he— [...in that place...]
He obtained the position of a guild-leader in the city. The Bodhisatta, too, departed according to his karma.
And the Fully Enlightened One, having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, spoke this verse immediately upon his enlightenment:
“Even with a small load, the wise man who is discerning, though he be poor, can still support himself.”
"He raises himself up like a tiny spark blown by the wind.
In this context, "even with a small amount" means even with a little or a trifling amount. "The wise one" means the one possessed of wisdom (*paññavā*).
"With his capital" means with the cost-price of his goods. "Discerning" means skilled in business affairs. "He raises himself up" means having produced great wealth and fame.
Therein, he steadies and establishes himself. How so? Like a small fire being fanned:

just as a wise man, by gradually adding cow-dung powder and other fuels to a small fire and blowing upon it with his mouth, causes it to arise, increases it, and makes it into a great mass of flame—even so does the wise man [deal with] even a slight amount of light.
Having acquired [wealth] through various means and having applied it, one increases both wealth and fame; and having increased them,
one establishes oneself therein, or else, by means of that very greatness of wealth and fame, one exalts oneself—
the meaning is that one makes oneself well-known and prominent.
Thus the Blessed One, having shown this teaching of the Dhamma by saying, "Monks, by relying on me, Cūḷapanthaka has now attained greatness in the Dhamma;
but in the past, he also attained greatness in wealth," and having related two stories and connected the sequence, he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the junior pupil was..."
“Cūḷapanthaka was he, while I myself was Cūḷakaseṭṭhi,” he said, concluding the teaching.
This is the fourth, the Commentary on the Cūḷakaseṭṭhi Jātaka.
5. The Commentary on the Taṇḍulanāḷi Jātaka.
"How much is a stalk of rice worth?"—this was said by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning the Elder Lāḷudāyin.
At that time, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta was the assigner of meals for the Saṅgha.
While he was assigning the tickets for meals early in the morning, sometimes the choice meal would fall to the Elder Lāḷudāyin, and sometimes it did not.

[He was assigned] poor food. On the day that poor food was to be distributed, he threw the voting sticks (salāka) into disorder, saying, "What, does Dabba alone know how to distribute the voting sticks? Do we not know?
While he was throwing the voting sticks into disorder, they said, "Well then, you yourself give the voting stick! From that time on, he [was appointed] for the Saṅgha...

He gave out the voting sticks (*salāka*). While giving them, he did not know whether it was "choice food" or "inferior food," nor whether it was "choice food at such-and-such a previous *vassa* (rainy-season retreat)" or "inferior food at such-and-such a previous *vassa*.
Even when making the mark, he did not observe, "This is the mark for such-and-such a *vassa*. At the time when the bhikkhus were marking their places, [he thought], "In this place, this..."
He draws a line on the ground or on a wall, thinking, "This is the standing place; it is here.

On the following day, when the number of monks at the distribution of voting tickets (salāka) is either fewer or greater than before, the line is lower if there are fewer monks, and higher if there are more.
Not knowing the actual standing place, he distributes the ticket based on his perception of that line.
Then the monks said to him, "Friend Udāyī, a line may indeed be either at the bottom or at the top;
however, the choice of superior food was established in such-and-such a year, and the choice of inferior food was established in such-and-such a year.
As he was arguing back with the monks, he said, "If that is so, why is this line positioned thus? Why should I believe you? [I rely on] this line..."

"I have faith," he said. Then the young novices drove him out from the place where the voting sticks were being distributed, saying, "Friend Lāḷudāyi, because you give the voting sticks, the monks are deprived of their gains;
you are not fit to give them, so go away from here!
At that moment, a great clamor arose at the place where the voting sticks were being distributed. Hearing this, the Teacher [addressed] the Elder Ānanda:
The Blessed One asked, “Ānanda, there is a great clamor at the counting of the voting sticks; what kind of sound is this? The Elder reported the matter to the Tathāgata.
“Ānanda, it is not only now that Lāḷudāyin, through his own foolishness, causes others to suffer loss of gain;
he did so even in the past,” he said. The Elder then requested the Blessed One to clarify the meaning of that matter.
The Blessed One made manifest a cause that had been concealed during another existence.
In the past, in the kingdom of Kāsi, in Bārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta. At that time, our Bodhisatta was his appraiser.
He appraised elephants, horses, and so forth, as well as jewels, gold, and other valuables; having appraised them, he [returned them] to the owners of the goods.
He had the price paid exactly according to the value of the goods. However, the king was greedy; out of his greedy nature, he thought:
"This appraiser, by appraising things in this way, will soon cause the wealth in my treasury to be exhausted.
I shall appoint another appraiser. Opening the lion-window and looking out over the royal courtyard, he saw one...
Seeing a country man, a greedy youth, walking through the royal courtyard, [the king thought], "He will be able to perform my work of appraisal.
Having summoned him, he said, "My good man, will you be able to perform our work of appraisal?
"I shall be able, Your Majesty," he replied. For the sake of protecting his own wealth, the king [entrusted] that youth with the work of appraisal.
He appointed him [to that position]. From that time on, that fool, while appraising elephants, horses, and other goods, would undervalue them and speak according to his own whim.
Because he was established in that office, whatever he said became the official price.
At that time, a horse merchant from the Northern Road brought five hundred horses. The king [sent for] that man...
Having summoned the horses, he had them appraised. He set the value of five hundred horses at one measure of rice.
Having done so, he said, "Give one measure of rice to the horse-dealer," and had the horses tethered in the stable.
The horse-dealer went to the former appraiser and reported what had happened.
"Now, what should be done? he asked. He replied, "Give a bribe to that man and ask him this:
'It is already known that our horses are worth one measure of rice; however, relying on you, we wish to know the value of that measure of rice.
Will you be able to stand before the king and [declare] that measure of rice to be this much...'"
“...to say that it is worth its name? “If you can do so,” he replied. Taking that [price], go to the presence of the king;
I too shall come there.
The horse-dealer, having accepted the Bodhisatta’s words with “Very well,” gave a bribe to the appraiser.
He reported that matter [to the king]. Having received a bribe, he thought, "I shall be able to have the measure of rice valued.
Saying, "In that case, let us go to the royal palace," he took him and went into the presence of the king.
The Bodhisatta and many other ministers also went there. The horse-dealer, having paid homage to the king, said: "Your Majesty, for five hundred horses..."
“We know that one stalk of rice is worth five hundred coins; however, Your Majesty, ask the appraiser what that stalk of rice itself is worth.
The king, unaware of this matter, asked, “Ho, appraiser! What is five hundred horses worth?
“That stalk of rice, Your Majesty,” he replied. “Very well, man! Let the horses [first] value that stalk of rice.”
"Let it be valued. But what is that grain-stalk worth? he asked. That foolish man replied, "That grain-stalk is worth all of Bārāṇasī, inside and out.
It is said that previously, while serving the king, he had set the price of a single grain-stalk at the value of horses.
Then, having received a bribe from the merchant's hand, regarding that grain-stalk...
He set a price for Bārāṇasī, both inside and outside. At that time, however, the enclosure of the city walls of Bārāṇasī was twelve yojanas;
this was its interior, while the territory outside it was three hundred yojanas.
Thus, that fool valued such a vast Bārāṇasī, including both its interior and exterior, at a single measure of rice.
Hearing this, the ministers clapped their hands and laughed, saying, "Previously, we thought the earth and the kingdom were priceless;
yet this kingdom of Bārāṇasī, so great and including its royal retinue, is said to be worth only a single stalk of rice!
Oh, what a perfection of wisdom this appraiser possesses! Where has this appraiser been living for all this time? [He has been living] among us..."
“It is truly worthy of the King! they said, making a jest:
“What is the price of this grain-stalk, O King? Tell us its value in exchange for horses!
This grain-stalk is worth all of Benares, both within and without.”
At that time, the king, feeling ashamed, had that foolish appraiser driven out and gave the place of appraisal to the Bodhisatta alone. The Bodhisatta, too, departed according to his karma.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher spoke of two past events, established the connection, and identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the foolish village appraiser was Lāḷudāyī, while the wise appraiser was none other than myself."
Thus he concluded the teaching with the words, “It was so.
The commentary on the *Taṇḍulanāḷi-jātaka* is the fifth.
6. The commentary on the *Devadhamma-jātaka*.
"Endowed with moral shame and fear of wrongdoing"—this was said by the Blessed One while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who possessed many belongings.
It is said that a householder living in Sāvatthī went forth into homelessness after his wife had died.
When he went forth, he had a cell, a fire-hall, and a store-room built for himself; and in the store-room, [he filled it] with ghee, rice, and other provisions.
Having filled [the bowl], he went forth. After going forth, however, he summoned his own slaves, had food cooked according to his liking, and ate it;
he possessed many requisites, wearing one set of lower and upper robes at night and another during the day.
He lived on the outskirts of the monastery. One day, having brought out his robes, bedspreads, and other belongings—
While he was spreading them out in the courtyard and drying them, a number of monks from the countryside, wandering about the lodgings, went to that courtyard;
seeing the robes and other items, they asked, "Whose are these? He replied, "They are mine, friends.
They said, "Friend, is this robe also yours, is this undergarment also yours, and is this bedspread also yours—is everything yours alone?"
“Yes, it is mine alone,” he replied. “Friend, the Blessed One has permitted only three robes;
yet you, having gone forth in the teaching of a Buddha who is so moderate in his needs, have come to possess so many requisites.
Come, let us take you into the presence of the Teacher. Having said this, they took him and went into the presence of the Master.
The Teacher, seeing them, asked: "Monks, why have you come taking this monk against his will?
"Venerable Sir, this monk possesses many goods and many requisites. "Is it true, monk, that you possess many goods? "It is true, Blessed One.
"But why, monk, have you become one who possesses so many goods? "Is it not [true]?"
“I speak in praise of fewness of desires, contentment, seclusion, and the arousal of energy.
Having heard the Teacher’s words, he became angry and thought, “I shall now conduct myself in this manner!
Casting off his upper robe, he stood in the midst of the assembly wearing only a single garment.

Then the Teacher, supporting him, said: "Is it not true, monk, that formerly you were a seeker of shame and fear of wrongdoing, and even during your time as a water-demon, you lived for twelve years seeking shame and fear of wrongdoing?

Why then, having now gone forth in this so weighty teaching of the Buddha, do you stand here in the midst of the fourfold assembly having cast off your upper robe and abandoned shame and fear of wrongdoing?"
Having heard the Teacher’s words, he established a sense of shame and dread of blame, put on that robe, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side.
The bhikkhus requested the Blessed One to clarify the meaning of this matter;
the Blessed One made manifest the cause that had been concealed by another existence.
In the past, in the kingdom of Kāsi, there was a king named Brahmadatta in Bārāṇasī. At that time, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of his chief queen.
On the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name Mahisāsakumāra.
While he was running about and playing, another son was born to the king, who was named Candakumāra.
They gave him a name. However, while he was running about and playing, the Bodhisatta’s mother passed away, and the king appointed another woman to the position of chief queen.
She became dear and pleasing to the king, and in the course of their living together, she gave birth to a son;
they named him "Sūriyakumāra. Upon seeing his son, the king was filled with joy.
“Bhadde, I grant a boon to your son,” he said. The queen, intending to take the boon at the appropriate time, set it aside.
When her son had reached maturity, she said to the king, “Sire, a boon was granted to my son by you at the time of his birth;
give the kingdom to my son. The king replied, “I have two sons who blaze like masses of fire...”
Having refused him, saying, "They wander about; it is not possible to give the kingdom to your son," he saw that despite this refusal, the man was still entreating him again and again.
Thinking, "This man might even plot evil against my sons," he summoned his sons and said:
"Sons, at the time of Prince Sūriya’s birth, I granted him a boon. Now his mother is asking for the kingdom."
“I am not willing to give him [the kingdom] to you; women are indeed wicked. She might even plot evil against you.
Once you have entered the forest, after my passing, you may rule the kingdom in the city that belongs to our family.

Having said this, he wept and wailed, kissed their heads, and sent them forth. As they were descending from the palace after paying homage to their father, Prince Sūriyakumāra was playing in the royal courtyard.
Having seen that and understood the reason for it, [the Bodhisatta] thought, "I too shall go with my brothers," and set out together with them.
They entered the Himalayas.
The Bodhisatta, having descended from the road and sat down at the foot of a tree, addressed Sūriyakumāra: "Dear Sūriyakumāra,..."
“Having gone to that lake, bathe, drink, and bring water for us as well on lotus leaves.
Now, that lake had been obtained from Vessavaṇa by a certain water-demon, and Vessavaṇa had said to him:
“Except for those who know the divine qualities (devadhamma), anyone else who enters this lake shall be eaten.”

"You obtain [them] when you have entered; you do not obtain them when you have not entered. From that time on, whenever people entered that lake, that *rakkhasa* would question them about the divine qualities (*devadhamma*);
those who did not know them, he would devour. Then Sūriyakumāra went to that lake and, without even investigating, entered it.
Thereupon, the *rakkhasa* seized him and asked, "Do you know the divine qualities?"
Thus he said, "The 'divine qualities' (devadhammā) are the moon and the sun.
Then, saying to him, "You do not know the divine qualities," he made him enter the water and placed him in his own dwelling place.
The Bodhisatta, seeing that he was taking too long, sent Prince Candaka. The rākṣasa seized him as well and asked, "Do you know the divine qualities? "Yes."

“I know that the so-called divine qualities (*devadhammā*) are the four quarters,” he said. The rākṣasa, thinking, “You do not know the divine qualities,” seized him as well and placed him right there.
When the Bodhisatta saw that even he was delaying, he thought, “There must be some obstacle,” and went there himself.
Seeing that both paths were accessible for entry, he thought, "This must be a voice possessed by a *rakkhasa*," and so,
having girded his sword and taken up his bow, he stood ready. When the water-*rakkhasa* saw that the Bodhisatta was not descending into the water,
he disguised himself as a forest worker and said to the Bodhisatta, "O man, you are weary from the road."
"Why do you not descend into this lake, bathe, drink, eat the lotus roots and stalks, adorn yourself with the flowers, and go away as you please?
The Bodhisatta, seeing him, recognized, "This must be a *yakkha*," and said, "My brothers have been seized by you.
"Yes, they have been seized," he replied. "For what reason? "Because I am [the owner] of this lake..."
“I obtain those who have fallen [into the stream],” he said. “But do you obtain all of them? “I obtain everyone except those who know the divine qualities (devadhamma).
“Do you, however, have need for the divine qualities? “Yes, I do.
“If that is so, I shall explain the divine qualities to you. “In that case, please speak; I will listen to the divine qualities.”
The Bodhisatta said, "I would speak on the divine qualities (devadhamma), but my body is defiled.
The yakkha bathed the Bodhisatta, fed him, gave him water to drink, had him adorned with flowers, and had him anointed with perfumes;
then, having spread out a couch in the center of a decorated pavilion, he offered it to him.
The Bodhisatta sat upon his seat, had the yakkha sit at his feet, and said, "In that case, listen attentively with an attentive ear to the divine qualities (devadhamma)," and spoke this verse:
"Those endowed with moral shame and fear of wrongdoing,
established in bright qualities, the virtuous true men in the world— these are called those who possess the divine qualities."

In this context, "endowed with moral shame (*hirī*) and moral dread (*ottappa*)" means being possessed of both moral shame and moral dread. Among these, that which feels shame regarding bodily misconduct and so forth is *hirī*;
this is a designation for modesty (*lajjā*). That which dreads those very same things is *ottappa*;
this is a designation for agitation toward evil. Therein, moral shame originates from within oneself, while moral dread originates from without. It has the self as its dominant influence...
Moral shame (*hirī*) is the authority of the world; moral dread (*ottappa*) is the authority of the world.

Moral shame is established on the nature of modesty; moral dread is established on the nature of fear. Moral shame has the characteristic of having a sense of respect; moral dread has the characteristic of seeing danger and fearing what is blameworthy.
Therein, one arouses moral shame originating from within by means of four reasons: by reflecting upon birth...
We [should act] after reflecting upon our own character, reflecting upon our courage, and reflecting upon our great learning. How so? First, by reflecting on birth:
"This doing of evil is not the work of those endowed with noble birth; it is the work of low-born people such as fishermen and the like.
It is not fitting for one like me, who is endowed with noble birth, to perform this deed. Thus, first, one reflects on birth.
By refraining from evil such as the taking of life, one arouses moral shame (*hiri*). Likewise, by reflecting on one’s own age—thinking, “This performance of evil is a deed fit for the young;

it is not appropriate for one like me, established in middle age, to do such a deed”—one refrains from evil such as the taking of life and arouses moral shame. Likewise, [reflecting that] “this is indeed an evil deed...”

"This is the work of those who are weak by nature; it is not fitting for one like me, endowed with courage, to perform such an act"—reflecting thus on his own courage, he arouses a sense of moral shame (*hiri*) by refraining from evil deeds such as the taking of life. Likewise:
"This evil deed is the work of blind fools, not of the wise; it is not for one like me, a wise man of great learning..."
"This action is not fit to be done"—having thus reflected upon his great learning (*bāhusacca*), he who refrains from evil such as the taking of life arouses moral shame (*hirī*).
In this way, he arouses internally-arisen moral shame by means of four causes.
Having aroused it, and having introduced moral shame into his own mind, he does not commit an evil deed. Thus is moral shame.
It is called "originating internally.
How is it that moral dread (ottappa) originates externally? [One thinks: "If you commit an evil deed, you will become an object of reproach among the four assemblies.
The wise will reproach you, just as they would reproach an impure city-dweller:"
“Shunned by those who possess virtue, how will you fare as a bhikkhu?
Reflecting thus, one does not commit an evil deed through *ottappa* (moral dread) arising from the external. In this way, *ottappa* is said to have an external origin.
How is it that *hirī* (moral shame) has oneself as its governing principle? Here, a certain son of good family regards himself as the governing authority and the elder.
Having reflected, "It is not fitting for one like me—who has gone forth out of faith, who is learned, and who maintains the ascetic practices—to commit an evil deed," he does not do evil.
In this way, moral shame (hirī) is said to be "dominated by oneself. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Making himself alone his master, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless; he preserves himself in purity."

What is meant by moral dread (*ottappa*) as having the world as its governing principle (*lokādhipateyya*)? Here, a certain son of good family, making the world his authority and his elder, does not commit an evil deed. As it has been said:

"Great indeed is this worldly habitation. In this great worldly habitation there are recluses and brahmins who possess psychic power, divine vision, and knowledge of the minds of others; they see even from afar, while those nearby may not be seen."
They know the mind with their own minds, and they will think of me thus: "Look, sirs!
This clansman, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, dwells mired in evil, unwholesome states.
There are also deities who possess psychic power, have the divine eye, and understand the minds of others; they see even from afar.
Though they are nearby, they are not seen; yet they know his mind with their own minds, and they will think of me thus:
"Look, sirs! This clansman, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, dwells mired in evil, unwholesome states.
Thus, making the world itself his master and his chief, he [engages in] the unwholesome.
“He abandons what is unwholesome and develops what is wholesome; he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless; he maintains himself in purity.
In this way, moral dread (ottappa) is called "having the world as its authority.
Furthermore, regarding the statement: “Hiri is established in the nature of shame; ottappa is established in the nature of fear,” here *lajjā* means...
*Hirī* is that which has the nature of shame; it is established with that as its essential characteristic. *Ottappa* is that which has the nature of fear—specifically, the fear of the states of woe;
it is established with that as its essential characteristic. Both of these become manifest in the avoidance of evil.

For instance, just as a certain son of good family, while performing the functions of defecation or urination, might encounter someone for whom he ought to feel shame and thereby come to experience the state of shame; so too do these two qualities function.

Being thus reviled, having descended into a state of self-reproach within himself, he does not commit an evil deed. Another person, being terrified by the fear of the states of misery (*apāya*), does not commit an evil deed.

Herein is this simile: suppose there were two iron balls; one were cold but smeared with excrement, while the other were hot and glowing. In that case, a wise man [would avoid] the cold one because it was smeared with excrement...
One who feels disgust does not take hold [of it], while the other does not because of the fear of burning.
In this context, the non-taking of what is cool and smeared with excrement due to disgust should be understood as the non-committing of evil after having descended into the nature of shame within;
and the non-taking of what is hot due to the fear of burning should be understood as the non-committing of evil out of fear of the states of misery (apāya).
“*Hirī* has the characteristic of having a sense of shame; *ottappa* has the characteristic of seeing fear in what is blameworthy.
This pair also becomes manifest specifically in the avoidance of evil. For a certain person possesses the characteristic of having a sense of shame through four causes:
reflection on the greatness of one’s birth, reflection on the greatness of the Teacher, reflection on the greatness of the inheritance, and reflection on the greatness of one’s fellow celibates.

Having aroused moral shame (*hiri*), one does not commit evil. A certain person, having aroused moral dread (*ottappa*)—which is characterized by the fear of blame and the perception of danger—through four causes: the fear of self-reproach, the fear of reproach by others, the fear of punishment, and the fear of an unhappy rebirth, does not commit evil.
In this context, there are both the reflections on the greatness of one's birth and so forth, as well as the fears of self-reproach and the rest.
These should be explained in detail. Their detailed exposition is stated in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā*.

Regarding the phrase "concentrated in bright states" (*sukkadhammasamāhitā*): indeed, those wholesome states (*kusaladhammā*) that are to be practiced, beginning with this very sense of shame (*hirī*) and fear of wrongdoing (*ottappa*), are called "bright states.

By way of the method of universal inclusion, these comprise all mundane and supramundane states belonging to the four planes. One who is "concentrated" (*samāhitā*) means one who is endowed with them.
The meaning is as follows: "In the world, the peaceful, true persons" (*santo sappurisā loke*). They are "peaceful" (*santo*) because of the tranquility of their bodily actions and so forth;

they are "true persons" (*sappurisā*) because they are beautiful persons who are grateful and mindful of what has been done for them. Furthermore, the "world" (*loka*) is of many kinds: the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*), the world of beings (*sattaloka*), the world of space (*okāsaloka*), the world of aggregates (*khandhaloka*), the world of bases (*āyatanaloka*), and the world of elements (*dhātuloka*).
Among these, it is said: "One world: all beings subsist by nutriment... [and so on]."

In the passage, “The eighteen worlds are the eighteen elements,” the world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*) is spoken of. The worlds of the aggregates (*khandha-loka*) and so forth are included therein.
However, in such passages as, “This world and the other world, the world of devas and the world of humans,” the world of beings (*satta-loka*) is spoken of.
“As far as the moon and sun revolve, shining and illuminating the quarters...”
“To that extent the world extends in a thousandfold way; therein your sovereignty prevails. Here, the world of space (*okāsaloka*) is mentioned.

Among those [three worlds], it is the world of beings (*sattaloka*) that is intended here. For among the world of beings, those such as these true persons (*sappurisa*) are called “divine qualities” (*devadhamma*).

In that regard, there are three kinds of “gods”: gods by convention (*sammutideva*), gods by rebirth (*upapattideva*), and gods by purification (*visuddhideva*). Among these, from the time of the Mahāsammata...
Because they have been designated as "gods" by the world from the beginning, kings, princes, and others are called conventional gods (*sammutideva*).
Those born in the heavenly worlds are called gods by birth (*upapattideva*). But those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) are called pure gods (*visuddhideva*).

And this has been said: “Conventional gods are kings, queens, and princes. Gods by birth are the gods starting from the earth-deities and those higher than them. Pure gods are Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and those whose taints are destroyed.”
"Deva-dhammas" means the qualities (*dhamma*) of these deities. "Are called" (*vuccare*) means they are spoken of.

Since wholesome qualities rooted in moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*) are the causes for the perfection of one's family, rebirth in the world of the deities, and the state of purity, they are termed "deva-dhammas" in the sense of being the cause for all three of those types of deities;
and persons endowed with those deva-dhammas are likewise so called.
“Divine qualities. Therefore, showing those qualities through a teaching focused on the individual, he said: “The peaceful, true persons in the world are called ‘those possessing divine qualities.
Having heard this teaching on the Dhamma, the yakkha, with a clear mind, said to the Bodhisatta: “O Wise One, I [belong] to you...”
“Being pleased, I wish to give one of my brothers; which one shall I bring? “Bring the youngest.
“Wise sir, you know only the divine qualities (*devadhamma*), but you do not practice them. “For what reason?
“Because by setting aside the elder brother and ordering the younger, you fail to perform the duty of honoring the elder. [He asked: “What are the divine qualities?”
"And I, yakkha, know this, and I conduct myself according to it. For it was for his sake that we entered this forest.
Indeed, on his account our mother requested the kingdom from our father;
yet our father, instead of granting her that boon, permitted him to dwell in the forest for the sake of protecting us. That prince, having complied [with our request]..."
"He came with us. Even if it were said, "A single *yakkha* devoured him in the forest," no one would believe it;
therefore, fearing the blame, I commanded that very person. "Excellent, excellent, O wise one!
You know the divine qualities (*devadhamma*) and you conduct yourself according to them. Pleased, the *yakkha* gave his approval to the Bodhisattva and—both... [text continues]
The brothers brought him and gave him to him.
Then the Bodhisatta said to him: "Friend, previously, by means of the evil deed you yourself committed, you were reborn as a *yakkha* who eats the flesh and blood of others;
even now you are doing only evil. This evil deed of yours will not release you from hell and the other realms of suffering."
“He will not grant you leave; therefore, from this moment on, abandon evil and perform wholesome deeds.

And he was indeed able to tame him. Having tamed that *yakkha* and being protected by his arrangements, while living right there, he one day observed the constellations, learned of his father’s death, and taking the *yakkha* with him, went to Bārāṇasī and [seized] the kingdom.
Having taken the vice-regency from Prince Canda and the position of commander-in-chief from Prince Suriya,
he established a shrine for the Yakkha in a delightful place and ensured that the deity received the finest garlands, the finest flowers, and the finest food.
Having ruled the kingdom righteously, he passed away according to his karma.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and displayed it, proclaimed the Truths.
At the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Fully Enlightened One, having related two past events and joined the connection, identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the water-demon was the bhikkhu Bahubhaṇḍika, and Suriyakumāra..."
“Ānanda was Candakumāra, Sāriputta was Jeṭṭhakabhātā, and Mahisāsakumāra was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Devadhamma Jātaka, the sixth.
7. Commentary on the Kaṭṭhahāri Jātaka.
"I am your son, O Great King"—this was said by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning the nobleman Vāsabhakhattiya.
The story of Vāsabhakhattiya will be revealed in the Bhaddasāla Jātaka of the Dvādasakanipāta.
It is said that she was the daughter of the Sakyan Mahānāma, born from the womb of a slave-girl named Nāgamuṇḍā, [and became the wife] of the King of Kosala.

She became the chief queen. She gave birth to a son for the king. However, when the king later discovered her former status as a slave, he deprived her of her position, and he likewise deprived her son, Viṭaṭūbha, of his position.
Both of them lived within the palace itself. The Teacher, having understood this situation, went to the king’s residence at the forenoon hour, surrounded by five hundred bhikkhus.
Having gone there and sat down on the prepared seat, he said, “Great King, where is Vāsabhakhattiyā?
The king related the matter to him. [The Elder asked: “Great King, whose daughter is Vāsabhakhattiyā? “Venerable sir, she is Mahānāma’s.
“Whose daughter did she become when she came here? “Venerable sir, she became mine. “Great King, she is the king’s daughter; she belongs to the king alone.”
"She came [to him] and, depending solely upon the king, obtained a son. For what reason does that son not become the owner of the kingdom belonging to his father?
Formerly, kings—even having obtained a son in the womb of a momentary wood-gatherer—gave the kingdom to that son.
The king requested the Blessed One for the sake of clarifying this matter, and the Blessed One [spoke].
He made manifest a cause that had been concealed during another existence.
In the past, in Benares, King Brahmadatta went to a pleasure garden with great splendor;
while wandering there out of a desire for flowers and fruit, he saw a woman singing in a grove of the park who was splitting wood, and his heart became bound to her.
He entered into a marriage union with her. At that very moment, the Bodhisatta took conception in her womb;
immediately, her womb became heavy as if filled with adamant.
Realizing that she was pregnant, she said, "O King, I am pregnant. The king gave her a finger-ring and said, "If it is a girl..."
"Having released this [child], you may raise him; if he becomes a son, you must bring him to me along with his finger-ring," she said, and then departed.
When her pregnancy was fully mature, she gave birth to the Bodhisatta. While he was running about and wandering here and there, [she...]
While he was playing in the playground, people said, "We have been struck by his father.
Hearing this, the Bodhisatta went to his mother and asked, "Mother, who is my father? "Dear son, you are the son of the King of Bārāṇasī.
"Mother, is there anyone who can bear witness to this? "Dear son, the King gave her this seal-ring [and said], 'If she gives birth to a daughter...'"

"Having released this one, you may support him; if a son is born, you must bring him here along with this finger-ring," she said, and then she departed. "Mother, if that is so, why did you not take me to my father?
Understanding her son's intention, she went to the king's gate and had her presence announced to the king. Summoned by the king, she entered, paid homage to the king, and—
“This, O King, is your son,” he said. Although the king knew it was so, out of shame before the assembly, he said, “This is not my son.
“This seal-ring, O King, do you recognize? “This seal-ring is not mine either.
“Your Majesty, now there is no witness for me other than an act of truth; if this child is yours...”
"Born as he is, let him remain in the air; if not, let him fall to the ground and die.
Seizing the Bodhisatta by the feet, he hurled him into the air. The Bodhisatta sat cross-legged in mid-air and, speaking the Dhamma to his father in a sweet voice, uttered this verse:
“I am your son, O Great King; nourish me, O Lord of Men.
The Deity nourishes others as well—why then does the Deity not nourish his own offspring?
In this context, “I am your son” means I am your son. And a son is of these kinds: one born of the womb (*atrja*), one born of the field (*khettaja*), and one who is a pupil (*antevāsika*).
The term *dinnaka* (given) is fourfold. Among these, one born dependent upon oneself is called *atrāja* (one's own offspring).

One produced on the back of a bed, on a couch, on the breast, and so forth, is called *khetta-ja* (born of the field). One who acquires a craft in close proximity is called *antevāsika* (resident pupil).

One given for the purpose of being reared is called *dinnaka*. Here, however, it is said "son" (*putta*) with reference to the *atrāja*. [He is supported] by the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*).
One who pleases people is a king (*rājā*); a great king is a *mahārājā*. Addressing him, he said, "O Great King.
"Sustain me, O lord of people" means: O lord of people, you who are the eldest among the multitude, sustain me—support, nourish, and cause me to grow.
"Other gods also sustain" refers to other humans such as elephant-trainers and so forth, as well as the vast number of animals such as elephants, horses, and the like.
“The god nourishes. Regarding the phrase “his own offspring” (*sakaṃ pajaṃ*): here, the particle *kiñci* is used both in the sense of censure (*garaha*) and in the sense of favor (*anuggaha*).
When one says, “The god does not nourish me, his own child,” one is censuring him;
when one says, “He nourishes many others,” one is showing favor. Thus, the Bodhisatta, while both censuring and favoring [the god],...
"And furthermore, O King, [look at] your own offspring," he said.
When the King heard the Bodhisatta preaching the Dhamma while seated thus in the air, he stretched out his hand, saying, "Come, dear one!
A thousand hands were then stretched out, each crying, "I myself will support him! I myself will support him! The Bodhisatta—
Without descending into the hands of another, he descended into the hands of the king himself and sat upon his lap.
The king gave him the position of viceroy and made his mother the chief queen. Upon the passing of his father, he became King Kaṭṭhavāhana;
having ruled the kingdom according to the Dhamma, he departed according to his karma.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching to the King of Kosala, the Teacher illustrated it with two examples, established the connection, and identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the mother was Mahāmāyā; the father was the Great King Suddhodana;
and King Kaṭṭhavāhana was none other than myself."
The seventh is the commentary on the Kaṭṭhahāri Jātaka.
8. The commentary on the Gāmaṇi Jātaka:
"Even those who do not hasten... This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who had slackened his energy.
He related [the story]. However, both the present-day narrative and the past-life narrative of this Jātaka will be revealed in the Saṃvara-jātaka of the Ekādasaka-nipāta.
For the narrative in that [Jātaka] and in this one are exactly the same, though the verses differ.
Having stood by the Bodhisatta’s advice, the village headman’s son, although the youngest of a hundred brothers, was surrounded by those hundred brothers.
Seated upon a magnificent couch beneath a white parasol, he surveyed his own glorious success and,
being delighted that "this glory of mine belongs to our teacher," he uttered this inspired utterance:
"Even for those who do not hasten, the hope for fruit is indeed fulfilled."
“I have ripened the holy life; know this thus, O village leader.

In this context, *api* is a mere particle. *Ataramānānaṃ* refers to those wise ones who, standing by the instruction [of the Teacher], do not cross over in haste, do not act with agitation, but perform their work through skillful means.
*Phalāsā va samijjhati* means that the hope for a fruit, according to what was aspired to, is indeed fulfilled. Regarding that fruit...
It is indeed successful through its accomplishment. Alternatively, "fruit of hope" (*āsāphala*) means that the fruit as desired is indeed successful.

Regarding the phrase "I have ripened the holy life" (*vipakkabrahmacariyo*): here, the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*) are called the "holy life" (*brahmacariya*) because they are the supreme conduct;
and it is called "ripened" (*vipakka*) because it has been obtained through the excellence of fame rooted therein—or rather, because of the fame itself.
That which has been accomplished is also called the "holy life" (*brahmacariya*) in the sense of being supreme. Therefore he said, "I am one whose holy life is matured.
"Know this thus, O headman"—in some contexts, even a village man or a village elder is called a "headman" (*gāmaṇī*);
but here he speaks with reference to himself as the foremost among all people. "O headman, you should know this reason thus: by depending on a teacher..."
Having surpassed a hundred brothers, he uttered this inspired exclamation: "I have attained this great sovereignty.
However, seven or eight days after he had ascended the throne, all his brothers departed for their respective places of residence.
King Gāmaṇi, having ruled righteously, passed away according to his karma; the Bodhisatta, too, having performed meritorious deeds, passed away according to his karma.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and shown it, the Teacher proclaimed the Truths.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who had slackened his energy was established in Arahatship. Having related these two accounts and joined the connection, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the village headman’s son was the monk who had slackened his energy, and the teacher was none other than myself."
The eighth: The Commentary on the Gāmaṇi Jātaka.
9. The Commentary on the Maghadeva Jātaka:
"My hair from the noblest part of my body"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Great Renunciation.
He related it; that has already been told below in the Nidānakathā. At that time, however, the bhikkhus were sitting there praising the renunciation of the One of Ten Powers.
Then the Teacher, having arrived at the Dhamma Hall and seated himself upon the Buddha’s throne, addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, about what conversation are you gathered here now? "Venerable sir," [they replied].

When they said, "We did not come for any other talk; we sat here praising renunciation (nekkhamma) to you alone," the Blessed One said, "Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata has gone forth into renunciation; he has indeed gone forth even in the past.
The monks requested the Blessed One to explain the meaning of this matter, and the Blessed One [related] what was concealed by another existence.
He made the cause manifest.
In the past, in the kingdom of Videha at Mithilā, there was a king named Maghadeva, a righteous Dhamma-king.
He spent eighty-four thousand years playing as a prince, and likewise in the vice-regency, and likewise after exercising great sovereignty for a long period of time.
Having passed some time, he addressed his barber one day: "Friend barber, when you see grey hairs upon my head, then inform me.
After the barber had also passed a long period of time, one day, seeing a single grey hair among the king's jet-black locks, he said: "Your Majesty, a grey hair of yours is visible."
He reported this. When [the king] said, "In that case, my friend, pull out that grey hair and place it in my hand," he pulled it out with a golden pair of tweezers and placed it in the king's hand.
At that time, eighty-four thousand years of the king's lifespan still remained.
Nevertheless, upon seeing the grey hair, he felt as though King Death had arrived and was standing right beside him.
Thinking that he was like one who had entered a leaf-hut on fire, he was seized by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and thought:
"O foolish Maghadeva, you have not been able to abandon these defilements until now, even though gray hair has appeared!
As he thus reflected upon the manifestation of gray hair, an internal burning arose within him, sweat broke out from his body, and his garments...
Having been pressed, they reached a state where they had to be removed. He thought, "It is fitting for me to go forth and renounce the world this very day.
Giving a choice village worth a hundred thousand pieces of money to his barber, he summoned his eldest son and said, "Dear son, gray hair has appeared on my head;
I have become old. Furthermore, I have already enjoyed human sensual pleasures."
"Now I shall seek celestial pleasures; it is time for my renunciation.
You take over this kingdom, but as for me, having gone forth, I will practice the duty of a recluse while dwelling in the Makhādeva Mango Grove park," he said.
When he thus expressed his desire to go forth, the ministers approached him and asked, "Your Majesty, what is the reason for your renunciation?"
They asked. The king, taking a grey hair in his hand, spoke this verse to his ministers:
"These hairs grown on my head have appeared as the harbingers of age;
The divine messenger has manifested; it is time for me to go forth."

In this context, "hair of the head" (*uttamaṅgaruha*) refers to the hair. For since it grows on the head, which is the most excellent of all limbs such as the hands and feet, it is called "hair of the head.
"Behold, dear ones, these that have arisen as the stealers of youth":

because they carry away the three stages of life through the manifestation of grey hair, these that have arisen are called "stealers of youth. "Manifested" means produced. "Messengers of the gods" (*devadūta*): the god...

It is called Death; its messengers are the "messengers of the gods" (*devadūtā*). For when grey hairs appear on the head, one stands as if in the presence of the King of Death; therefore, grey hairs are called "the messengers of the god Death.
Alternatively, they are "messengers of the gods" because they are like gods. Just as a goddess, adorned and prepared, standing in the sky [announces], "On such-and-such a day..."
When it was said, "You shall die," it happened exactly so; likewise, when grey hairs have appeared on the head, it is just like the declaration of a deity.
Therefore, grey hairs are called "messengers resembling deities" (*devasadisā dūtā*). They are also called "deity-messengers" (*devadūtā*) because they are messengers from the pure deities.
For all Bodhisattvas, upon seeing an old man, a sick man, a dead man, or one who has gone forth, experience a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Having gone forth, they go into homelessness. As it is said:

“Having seen one who is aged and one who is suffering from illness, and having seen one who is dead with the span of life exhausted, and having seen one who has gone forth clad in saffron robes—therefore, O King, I have gone forth.”
In this manner, because grey hairs act as messengers for the devas of purification, they are called "deva-messengers. By saying,

"The time for my going-forth has come," he shows that it is now his time to take up the ascetic’s insignia— which receives the name "going-forth" in the sense of having departed from the state of a householder.
Having spoken thus, on that very day he abandoned his kingdom and went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*.
Dwelling in that very mango grove of Makhādeva, he cultivated the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) for eighty-four thousand years.

Remaining established in unimpaired meditative absorption (*jhāna*), he passed away and was reborn in the Brahma-world. Then, passing away from there, he was reborn in Mithilā itself as one named Nimi.

Having been a king, he reunited his declining lineage and, having gone forth right there in that mango grove and developed the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), he was reborn once again in the Brahma-world.
The Teacher also said: "Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata has gone forth on the Great Renunciation; in the past as well..."
Having brought forward and shown this teaching on the Dhamma with the words, "He has indeed gone forth," the Blessed One proclaimed the Four Noble Truths.
At the conclusion of the exposition of the Truths, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, and some non-returners.
Thus, having related these two accounts and joined the connection, the Blessed One identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the barber was Ānanda; his son..."
“Rāhula, King Maghadeva was none other than myself.
This concludes the ninth discourse, the Commentary on the Maghadeva Jātaka. 10.
The Commentary on the Sukhavihāri Jātaka.

Regarding the phrase "and that which others do not guard," the Teacher spoke this while dwelling in the Mango Grove at Anupiya, near the city of Anupiya, concerning the Elder Bhaddiya, who was living in comfort.

The Elder Bhaddiya, who lived in comfort, had gone forth as the seventh among the six khattiya princes, with Upāli as the seventh. Among them were the Elder Bhaddiya, the Elder Kimila, and the Elder Bhagu.
The Elder Upāli attained Arahatship; the Elder Ānanda became a Stream-enterer; the Elder Anuruddha acquired the divine eye;
