and Devadatta became an attainer of the meditative absorptions (jhāna). The story of the six Khattiyas will be revealed in the Khaṇḍahāla Jātaka, as far as the city of Anupiya.
Furthermore, during his time as king, the Venerable Bhaddiya made arrangements for his own protection against many [demons].

Reflecting upon how fear arose within himself while he was being protected, even as he rolled about on his great couch on the roof of the excellent palace, and now, having attained *arahatship*, how he is free from fear wherever he dwells—even in the forest and other such places—he uttered this exclamation:
"Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness! Having heard this, [the king...]
The monks informed the Blessed One, saying, "Venerable Bhaddiya has declared final knowledge.
The Blessed One said, "Monks, it is not only now that Bhaddiya dwells in happiness; formerly, too, he dwelt in happiness.
The monks requested the Blessed One to explain the meaning of this matter. The Blessed One made manifest the cause that had been concealed by another existence.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta, having been a wealthy and eminent brahmin of the northern region, saw the peril in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation.
Abandoning sensual pleasures, he entered the Himalayas, went forth as an ascetic, and attained the eight meditative absorptions (samāpatti). His retinue was large, numbering five hundred.
There were hundreds of ascetics. Having departed from the Himalayas during the rainy season, surrounded by his company of ascetics, he traveled through villages, market towns, and other settlements.
Upon reaching Bārāṇasī, he took up residence in the royal park under the patronage of the king.
After staying there for the four months of the rains retreat, he took leave of the king. Then the king said to him, "Venerable sir, you are advanced in years; why..."
“O Himavat, send your resident disciples to the Himalayas and you yourself remain right here,” he requested.
The Bodhisatta, having entrusted five hundred ascetics to his senior disciple, dismissed them, saying, “Go, dwell in the Himalayas with these men;
as for me, I shall remain right here,” and he himself took up residence in that very place.
Now his senior pupil, who had gone forth as a royal renunciant, had abandoned a great kingdom to enter the homeless life;
having performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*, he became an attainer of the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*).
While living with the other ascetics in the Himalayas, on one occasion, desiring to see his teacher, he addressed those ascetics: "You should remain right here without becoming weary."
“I shall return after paying homage to my teacher,” he said. He went into the presence of his teacher, paid homage, and exchanged greetings;
then, having spread out a wooden plank as a mat, he lay down right there in the teacher’s presence.
At that time, the king, thinking, “I will see the ascetic,” went to the park, paid homage, and sat down to one side. The ascetic who was the resident pupil—
Seeing the king, he did not rise; instead, while still lying down, he uttered this inspired exclamation: "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!
The king, displeased that "this ascetic has not even risen upon seeing me," said to the Bodhisatta:
"Venerable sir, this ascetic must have eaten as much as he desired; uttering such an exclamation, he simply makes his bed comfortable."
"Great King, this ascetic was formerly a king just like you.

Thinking, 'In my former life as a householder, even while enjoying the glory of sovereignty and being guarded by many with weapons in hand, I did not obtain such happiness as this,' he utters this inspired utterance (udāna) concerning the happiness of his own renunciation and the happiness of meditative absorption (jhāna). And so it was said.
Having said this, the Bodhisatta spoke this verse in order to deliver a discourse on the Dhamma to the king:
“He who does not protect others, and whom others do not protect—
he indeed, O King, sleeps in happiness, being free from longing for sensual pleasures.”
In this regard, "whom others do not protect" refers to that person whom many other people do not protect.
And "who does not protect others" refers to one who, thinking "I alone shall rule the kingdom," does not protect the many other people.
"That king indeed sleeps in happiness" means, O Great King, that such a person—being alone, without a second, and secluded—is possessed of both bodily and mental happiness.
"Having sacrificed, he sleeps in peace. This is merely a figurative expression for the teaching.
Not only does he sleep in peace, but such a person also goes, stands, sits, and lies down in peace; thus, in all postures, he has attained happiness.
"Without regard for sensual pleasures" means being free from longing for the objects of sense and the defilements of sense-desire, and having abandoned desire and lust for them.
"O Great King, such a person free from craving dwells happily in all postures.
Having heard this teaching of the Dhamma, the king, with a joyful mind, paid homage and returned to his palace; the pupil also paid homage to his teacher and departed for the Himālaya mountains.
But the Bodhisatta, remaining right there, passed away without falling away from his meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
Having done so, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
The Teacher, having brought forth and shown this Dhamma teaching, having related two past instances, and having established the connection, identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the pupil was the Venerable Bhaddiya, and the leader of the group was none other than myself."
The tenth: The Exposition of the *Sukhavihāri-jātaka*.
The first chapter, the *Apaṇṇaka-vagga*.
Its summary (*uddāna*) is as follows:
Apaṇṇaka, Vaṇṇupatha, Seriva, Cūḷaseṭṭhi, Taṇḍula,
Devadhamma, Kaṭṭhavāhana, Gāmaṇi, Maghadeva,
and Vihāri— these ten Jātakas are grouped together.
2. The Chapter on Virtue [11] 1. The Commentary on the Lakkhaṇa Deer-Jātaka:
"There is welfare for those who possess virtue. This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Veḷuvana near Rājagaha concerning Devadatta.
He spoke with reference to this. The account of Devadatta, from the instigation of the plot for assassination up to the point where it will appear in the Khaṇḍahāla Jātaka,
and from the dismissal of Dhanapālaka up to where it will appear in the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka, and up to his entry into the earth,
will appear in the Samuddavāṇija Jātaka of the Twelfth Book (Dvādasanipāta).

For at one time, Devadatta, having failed to obtain his request for five points, split the Saṅgha and, taking five hundred bhikkhus with him, was dwelling at Gayāsīsa. Then the wisdom of those bhikkhus reached maturity.
Knowing this, the Teacher addressed the two chief disciples: "Sāriputta, those five hundred who depend upon you..."
“Those monks, having approved of Devadatta’s views, went along with him; but now their wisdom has reached maturity.
Therefore, go there together with many monks, teach them the Dhamma, awaken those monks to the paths and fruits, and bring them back with you. They went accordingly, taught them the Dhamma, and—
Having awakened them through the attainment of the paths and fruits, on the following day at the time of sunrise, they took those bhikkhus and returned to the Veḷuvana itself.

Upon their arrival, while the Venerable Sāriputta was standing after having paid homage to the Blessed One, the bhikkhus praised the Elder and said to the Blessed One: "Bhante, our eldest brother, the Dhammasenāpati..."
“Surrounded by five hundred bhikkhus, he comes along looking exceedingly magnificent, whereas Devadatta has become one whose retinue has diminished.
“Bhikkhus, it is not only now that Sāriputta looks magnificent as he comes surrounded by his circle of kinsmen;
he looked magnificent even in the past. And it is not only now that Devadatta has fallen away from his following; he had already fallen away from it in the past.”
The monks requested the Blessed One for the purpose of explaining the meaning of that matter; the Blessed One made manifest the cause that had been concealed by another existence.
In the past, in the kingdom of Magadha, in the city of Rājagaha, a certain king of Magadha reigned. At that time, the Bodhisatta—
Having taken rebirth in the womb of a deer, he grew up and lived in the forest surrounded by a thousand deer.
He had two sons, Lakkhaṇa and Kāḷa. When he reached old age, he said, "Sons, I am now old;
you must look after this herd," and he entrusted five hundred deer to each of his sons.
From that time on, those two men protected the herd of deer.
During the harvest season in the kingdom of Magadha, when the fields were crowded with ripening grain, the forest became a place of peril for the deer.
People, in order to kill the deer that ate their crops, dug pits here and there, set up stakes, prepared stone traps, and laid snares and other such devices.

They set snares, and many deer meet their destruction. The Bodhisatta, knowing that it was a time of scarcity due to the failure of crops, summoned his two sons and said: "Sons, this is a time of scarcity; many deer are meeting their destruction.
We, being old, shall spend our time in one place by whatever means possible; as for you..."
“Having captured your herds of deer and entered the forest foothills, you should return when the crops have been harvested.
Having heard their father’s words, they replied, “Very well,” and set out with their retinues. People, however, knew the path by which they traveled:
“At this time the deer ascend the mountain; at that time they descend. They [the people] were there—
There, they would lie in wait in concealed places and kill many deer by piercing them with arrows.
Because of his own slowness, the black deer did not know, "One should go at such a time; one should not go at such a time.
Taking the herd of deer with him, he would pass through the village gate in the forenoon, in the evening, at dusk, and at dawn.
In various places there, many wild animals—both those naturally stationary and those lying in ambush—were brought to destruction by humans.
Thus, through his own stupidity, he caused the destruction of many wild animals and entered the forest with only a few remaining.
But the Lakkhaṇa deer was wise, experienced, and skilled in means; he knew, "At this time one must go, at this time..."
He knew, "One must not go. He did not go even through the village gate;
he did not go by day, nor at dusk, nor at dawn. Taking a herd of deer, he went only at the hour of midnight.
Therefore, without harming even a single deer, he entered the forest. Having stayed there for four months, when the crops...
When the mountains were lifted up, they descended.
Although Kāḷa was returning, he came back all alone, having caused the destruction of the remaining deer in the same manner as before.
Lakkhaṇa, however, without destroying even a single deer, returned to his parents surrounded by five hundred deer.
Seeing his two sons approaching, the Bodhisatta, while conversing with the herd of deer, uttered this verse:
“There is benefit for those of virtuous conduct who live in hospitality;
behold the auspicious sign as they approach, honored by the assembly of their kinsmen.”
"Then we see this dark one, utterly abandoned by his kinsmen.
In this context, "possessing virtue" (*sīlavanta*) refers to those who possess virtue through their pleasant conduct and are endowed with right behavior. "Welfare" (*attha*) means prosperity.

"Those whose livelihood is hospitality" (*paṭisanthāravuttinaṃ*): both the hospitality of the Dhamma and the hospitality of material goods constitute their livelihood; thus they are "those whose livelihood is hospitality," and it is of them [that this is said].

"Of those whose conduct consists of hospitality. Herein, "hospitality in the Dhamma" should be understood by way of instruction and admonition that ward off evil, while "hospitality with material things" should be understood by way of providing a sphere of activity, obtaining gains, nursing the sick, and providing righteous protection.
This is what is meant: for those wise ones who are endowed with proper conduct and established in these two forms of hospitality—
"It is called growth. Now, in order to demonstrate that growth, he spoke the words beginning with "Behold the omen," as if addressing his own mother.

Here is the meaning in brief: behold your own son, endowed with proper conduct and hospitality, coming forward surrounded and honored by a host of kinsmen, having not harmed even a single animal. By her—
However, those who lack the excellence of conduct and hospitality, being slow-witted, we see— even as late as this very day—
that they come alone, utterly destitute of kinsmen, without leaving behind even a single relative such as Kāḷa. Having thus rejoiced over his son,
the Bodhisatta remained for the duration of his lifespan and then passed away according to his karma.
The Teacher also said, "Monks, it is not only now that Sāriputta shines when surrounded by a host of kinsmen; he shone even in the past.
Nor is it only at present that Devadatta has fallen away from his following; he fell away even in the past.
Having thus delivered this Dhamma teaching, and having related two stories, he connected the context and identified the Jātaka.
“At that time, Kāḷa was Devadatta; his retinue was the very retinue of Devadatta; Lakkhaṇa was Sāriputta;
his retinue, however, was the retinue of the Buddha; his mother was Rāhula’s mother; and his father was none other than myself.
Thus ends the first commentary on the Lakkhaṇamiga Jātaka.
[12] 2. The Commentary on the Nigrodhamiga Jātaka:
"One should resort only to the banyan tree. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the mother of the Elder Kumārakassapa.
It is said that she was the daughter of a very wealthy merchant in the city of Rājagaha and had accumulated abundant roots of merit.
With her mental formations thoroughly worn away, she was one in her final existence; like a lamp inside a jar, the necessary condition for Arahantship blazed within her heart.
From the moment she recognized herself [as such], she became dissatisfied with life in the household and, desiring to go forth, said to her parents:
"Mother and father, my mind finds no delight in the life of a householder; I wish to enter the Buddha’s dispensation, which leads to liberation."
“I wish to go forth; please let me go forth. “Mother, what are you saying? This family is very wealthy, and you are our only daughter;
it is not possible for you to go forth. Although she requested again and again, failing to obtain permission to go forth from her parents, she thought:
“Very well; once I have gone to my husband’s family and won over my husband, I shall go forth.”
Having reached marriageable age, she went to her husband’s family and lived as a virtuous and noble-minded woman, devoted to her husband as a deity.
Then, in the course of their living together, a fetus was conceived in her womb; however, she did not realize that a fetus had been established there.
At that time, a festival was proclaimed in that city, and all the inhabitants of the city [prepared for] the festival.
They played, and the city became adorned and prepared like a city of the gods.
Yet, even while such a magnificent festival was underway, she did not anoint her body nor adorn herself; she moved about in her natural state.
Then her husband said to her, "My dear, the entire city is intent upon the festival, but you, however, [do not adorn] your body..."
“Do you not attend to it? “Noble son, my body is filled with thirty-two kinds of filth;

what is the use of this being adorned? For this body was not created by the gods, nor created by Brahmā, nor made of gold, nor made of jewels, nor made of yellow sandalwood, nor produced from the interior of a white, red, or blue lotus, nor filled with the elixir of immortality; rather—”
It was born from a corpse, produced from the union of mother and father; it is subject to the nature of being impermanent, requiring constant covering, rubbing, breaking, and disintegration;
it increases the cemetery; it is seized by craving; it is the source of sorrows, the basis for lamentations, the abode of all diseases, and the recipient of karmic actions;
it is internally putrid and constantly oozing outwards; it is a dwelling place for swarms of worms and has proceeded from the charnel ground.
Ending in death, though present within the range of vision of the entire world—it is said:
“Bound together by bone and sinew, smeared with skin and flesh, the body is concealed by the outer hide; it is not seen as it truly is.”
“Full of entrails, full of stomach, with a covering of the liver-case;
of the heart, of the lungs, of the kidneys, and of the spleen.
Of mucus, of spittle, of sweat, and of fat;”
Of blood, synovial fluid, bile, and fat—
“Then from his nine streams, impurity flows constantly:
eye-secretion from the eyes, ear-secretion from the ears.”
“Mucus flows from the nose, and sometimes one vomits through the mouth;
bile and phlegm are vomited, and sweat and grime flow from the body.
Then his head is hollow, filled with brain matter.”
The fool, led on by ignorance, regards it as beautiful.
“The body has endless dangers;
it is like a poisonous tree, the dwelling place of all diseases, and a mere heap of suffering.”
“If this body were outside, rather than inside,
one would surely take up a staff and drive away the crows and dogs.
Foul-smelling and impure, this body is a corpse, comparable to a heap of filth.”
“Reproached by those who have become eyes, this body is delighted in by fools.
Covered with its own skin, it is a great wound with nine openings;
it oozes from every side, impure and foul-smelling.”
“Noble son, having adorned this body, what will I do? Is not the act of adorning it like applying decorative painting to the outside of a jar filled with excrement?
Having heard her words, the merchant’s son said, “Bhadde, seeing these defects in this body, why do you not go forth [into homelessness]? “Noble son, I—”

“If she obtains the going-forth, let her go forth this very day. The merchant’s son said, “Very well, I shall cause her to go forth,” and having offered a great gift and performed great honors, he led her with a large retinue to the nuns’ quarters.
While causing her to go forth, he had her ordained in the presence of the nuns who were followers of Devadatta. She [received] the going-forth...
Having obtained [this], her aspirations were fulfilled and she became joyful.

Then, as the fetus in her womb reached maturity, seeing the transformation of her faculties, the thickening of the backs of her hands and feet, and the enlargement of her abdominal membrane, the bhikkhunīs asked her: "Noble lady, you are pregnant."
"You appear as if you were possessed by a spirit; what is this? "Noble lady, I do not know that 'this is the cause,' but my virtue is indeed complete.

Then those bhikkhunīs led her into the presence of Devadatta and asked him, "Noble sir, this daughter of good family obtained the going-forth after winning over her husband with great difficulty; but now she is pregnant..."
"It is evident; we do not know whether this fetus was conceived during his time as a householder or after he had gone forth into homelessness.
What shall we do now? Because of his own lack of enlightenment and his absence of patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, Devadatta thought thus:
"A nun belonging to Devadatta’s faction is carrying a fetus in her womb; Devadatta..."
"If I look on with equanimity toward him, blame will arise against me; it is right for me to cause him to leave the order.
Without even investigating, like one rolling down a stone ball, he rushed forward and said, "Go!
Cause him to leave the order! Hearing his words, they rose, paid their respects, and went to the monastery.
Then that young woman said to those bhikkhunīs: "Venerable ladies, Devadatta Thera is not the Buddha, nor did my going forth take place in his presence;

rather, my going forth was in the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One, the foremost person in the world, and it was obtained by me with great difficulty. Do not let it be lost; come, take me [with you]."

“Go to the Teacher at Jetavana. Taking her with them, they traveled the forty-five-league road from Rājagaha and, arriving at Jetavana by stages, paid homage to the Teacher and reported the matter to him.
The Teacher thought: “Although she conceived a child while she was still a householder, nevertheless, ‘Is this ascetic...’”
“‘Gotama is wandering about taking what was abandoned by Devadatta’—this will provide an opportunity for the non-Buddhist sectarians (titthiyas).
Therefore, it is fitting to cut off this talk and to adjudicate this legal matter (adhikaraṇa) in the midst of the assembly including the king.
On the following day, [he addressed] King Pasenadi of Kosala, Mahānāthapiṇḍika, Cūḷanāthapiṇḍika, and Visākhā...
Having summoned the Great Female Lay Disciple (mahā-upāsikā) and other well-known great families, and when the four assemblies had gathered in the evening, he addressed the Elder Upāli:
"Go, you, and clear this young nun's legal case in the midst of the four assemblies.
"Very well, Bhante," the Elder replied, and having gone into the midst of the assembly, he sat upon the seat prepared for him.
Having sat down, he summoned the laywoman Visākhā before the king and entrusted this legal matter to her, saying:

"Go, Visākhā; having ascertained the truth that 'this young woman was ordained in such a month and on such a day,' find out whether this pregnancy occurred before or after [her ordination]. The laywoman accepted, saying, "Very well."
Having had a curtain drawn around her, he observed the hands, feet, navel, belly, and other parts of the young bhikkhunī within the curtain;
then, calculating the months and days, he correctly understood that she had conceived while still a householder.
He went into the presence of the Elder and reported the matter to him. In the midst of the fourfold assembly, the Elder declared that bhikkhunī to be pure.
Having done so, she became pure; then, having paid homage to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and the Teacher, she went back to her own dwelling with the bhikkhunīs.
When her pregnancy had reached maturity, she gave birth to a son of great majesty, who was the fulfillment of the aspiration she had made at the feet of Padumuttara Buddha.
Then one day, as the king was passing near the nuns’ quarters, he heard the sound of a child crying and questioned his ministers.
The ministers, having understood the reason, said, “Your Majesty, a young nun has given birth to a son; this is its cry.
“Ministers, the care of children is indeed a hindrance for nuns; we ourselves shall look after him.”
The king had that boy entrusted to dancing girls and raised him with the same care given to a prince. On the day his name was given, they named him Kassapa.
Because he had been raised with the care due to a prince, they came to know him as Kumārakassapa.
When he reached the age of seven, he went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher; having completed his full year of training, he received full ordination.
As time passed after he had attained this, among the preachers of the Dhamma, he became a distinguished speaker.
Then the Teacher placed him in the foremost position, saying: "Bhikkhus, among my disciples, the bhikkhus who are distinguished speakers, the foremost is Kumāra-Kassapa.
Later, through the Vammika Sutta, he reached Arahantship. His mother, too, was a bhikkhunī who practiced insight meditation.
Having increased [their practice], they attained the supreme fruit. Elder Kumāra-Kassapa became as renowned in the Buddha’s dispensation as the full moon in the midst of the sky.
Then one day, after the meal, when the Tathāgata had returned from his alms-round and given exhortation to the bhikkhus, he entered the fragrant chamber.
The bhikkhus, having received the exhortation, [retired] to their respective night-quarters and day-quarters.
Having spent the portion of the day, at the time of evening, they assembled in the Dhamma Hall and said:

"Friends, because of his own lack of Buddhahood and his absence of patience, loving-kindness, and other such qualities, Devadatta caused both the Elder Kumāra Kassapa and the Elder Nun to be expelled;
however, the Perfectly Enlightened One, through his own sovereignty over the Dhamma and his perfection in patience, loving-kindness, and compassion..."
“Indeed, they have both become conditions for one another,” they said, as they sat there praising the virtues of the Buddha.
The Teacher, arriving at the Dhamma Hall with the grace of a Buddha, sat upon the prepared seat and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
“Venerable Sir, it was a discussion concerning your own virtues,” they replied, and related everything that had occurred. “No,” [the Teacher said].
“Monks, it was not only now that the Tathāgata became the cause and the support for these two; he was so even in the past.
To clarify the meaning of this, the monks requested the Blessed One [to speak further]. The Blessed One then made manifest the reason that had been concealed by another existence.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of a deer.
Upon emerging from his mother’s womb, he was golden-colored;
his eyes were like precious gems, his horns were silver-colored, his face had the hue of a heap of red woolen cloth, and the extremities of his limbs...
His body became like that of a yak’s tail which has been processed with lac-resin; however, his body was large, the size of a young horse.
He lived in the forest surrounded by five hundred deer, known by the name Nigrodha, the King of Deer.
Not far from him lived another deer named Sākha, who also had a retinue of five hundred deer and was likewise golden-colored.

At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī was devoted to hunting; he would not eat without meat, and having interrupted the work of the people, he would assemble all the townspeople and countryfolk and go out for the hunt every day.
The people thought: “This king is interrupting our work; what if we were to [place] deer in the park?”
“Having sown bait, having provided water, and having led many deer into the park, we shall shut the gate and hand it over to the king.
So they all planted fodder for the deer in the park, provided water, secured the gate,
and taking snares and various weapons such as clubs in their hands, they entered the forest and began searching for the deer.
Thinking, "We shall capture the deer when they are in the middle," they surrounded an area of about one *yojana* and,
while narrowing their circle, they encircled the dwelling place of the *nigrodha* and *sākha* deer, placing it in the center. Then, seeing that herd of deer,
they struck the trees, thickets, and the ground with clubs, and having driven the herd out from its thicket, [they took up] swords, spears, bows, and other weapons.
Having brandished their weapons and let out a great roar, they drove that herd of deer into the park, closed the gate, and approached the king, saying:
"Your Majesty, by going on continuous hunts, you are ruining our livelihood;
we have brought deer from the forest and filled your park. From now on, [we shall provide] their meat..."
Having taken their leave of the king with the words, “Eat [this],” they departed.
Upon hearing their words, the king went to the park; while observing the deer there, he saw two golden deer and granted them safety (*abhaya*).
From then on, however, he would sometimes go himself, shoot one deer, and bring it back.
Sometimes his cook would go, pierce them, and bring them back. Upon seeing the bow, the deer were terrified by the fear of death and fled;
yet even after receiving two or three wounds, they became exhausted, fell ill, and met their deaths.
The herd of deer reported this matter to the Bodhisatta. He summoned Sākha and said:
“Friend, many deer are perishing; since they must inevitably die, from now on let them not be struck by arrows.
Let there be a turn for the deer at the place of the Dhamma-pillar. One day let the turn fall to my retinue, and one day to yours.
When the turn arrives, the deer shall go and lie down with its neck placed upon the Dhamma-pillar.”
"This being so, the deer will not become exhausted," he said. "Very well," the other agreed.
From that time on, whenever it was his turn, the deer would go and lie down with his neck resting upon the stone pillar for the Dharma.
When the cook arrived, he would take him while he was still lying there and depart.
Then one day, it was the turn of a pregnant doe in the herd of the Sākha deer.
She approached Sākha and said, "Master, I am pregnant; once I have given birth, two individuals will have to take our turn. Please let my turn pass.
He replied, "It is not possible to let your turn fall to others; you yourself must [take it]."
“You will know your turn; go now,” he said. Not receiving favor from him, she approached the Bodhisatta and reported the matter to him.
Having heard her words, he said, “Very well, you may go;
I shall let your turn pass. He went himself and lay down with his head toward the Dhamma-pillar. The cook—
Seeing him, [the king’s attendants] thought, "The King of Beasts has found safety and is lying on the stone slab; what could be the reason for this?
They went in haste and informed the king.
The king immediately mounted his chariot and, arriving with a great retinue, saw the Bodhisatta and said, "Friend..."
“O King of Beasts, did I not grant you safety? Why then do you lie here?
“Great King, a pregnant doe came and said, ‘Pass my turn to another.
Yet it was impossible for me to transfer the suffering of one’s death onto another; therefore, having given my own life to her, I—”
“Having accepted death as my own portion, I lie here; do not harbor any other fear, Great King,” he said.
The king replied, “Sir, golden-hued king of deer, I have never before seen anyone among humans so endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion;
therefore, I am pleased with you. Arise! I grant safety to both you and her. “By two...”
“If safety has been granted to them, what will the rest do, O King of Men? “I grant safety to the rest as well, my lord.
“Great King, even if the deer in the park alone receive safety, what will the others do? “I grant safety to them too, my lord.
“Great King, let the deer have safety for now; what about the other four-footed creatures?”
“...will they do? “I grant them safety as well, my lord. “Great King, let the four-footed creatures have safety for now;
what will the flocks of birds do? “I grant them safety as well, my lord. “Great King, let the flocks of birds have safety for now;
what will the fish dwelling in the water do? “I grant them safety as well...”
“I grant you safety, my lord. Thus the Great Being, having requested safety for all beings from the king, rose and established the king in the five precepts, saying:

“Practice the Dhamma, Great King! Practicing the Dhamma toward your mother and father, your sons and daughters, the brahmins and householders, and the people of the towns and countryside—practicing with impartiality—you will, at the breaking up of the body, [attain a happy destination].”
"After death, you shall go to a happy destination, to a heavenly world," he said.
Having taught the Dhamma to the king with the grace of a Buddha, and having stayed in the park for a few days, he gave the king his exhortation and entered the forest surrounded by a herd of deer.
Meanwhile, that doe gave birth to a son who resembled a flower-ear. While playing, he approached a branch-deer.
He went away. Then his mother, seeing him departing for that person's presence, spoke this verse as she admonished him: "One should serve only the banyan tree;
one should not dwell near the *sākhā* tree."
"In the banyan tree there is better life than in the branch.
In this context, "one should resort only to the banyan" means, dear one, you or anyone else desiring their own welfare should resort to, associate with, and approach the banyan alone;
one should not dwell near the branch—that is, one should not approach and live in proximity to the branch-deer.
One should not live together with him, nor should one make a livelihood depending upon him.
"Death is better than a banyan tree" means that even death at the feet of King Nigrodha is better, more excellent, and supreme.
"But life with Sākha" means that life in the presence of Sākha is neither better, nor more excellent, nor supreme—this is the meaning.
From that time on, however, the deer who had received the assurance of safety began eating the crops of the people.
The people, thinking, "These deer have obtained safety," were unable either to strike them or to drive them away.
They gathered in the royal courtyard and reported the matter to the king. The king said, "Out of confidence, I granted a boon to Nigrodha, the king of the deer; I—"
“I would rather renounce my kingdom than break that promise; go, for no one in my realm is permitted to strike at the deer,” he said.
When the Nigrodha deer heard this news, he gathered the herd of deer together and, having exhorted them, saying, “From now on, you must not eat the crops of others,” [addressed] the humans...
He had it proclaimed: "From this time forward, let those people who cultivate crops not build fences for the purpose of protecting their harvests;
instead, having plowed the fields, let them bind leaf-marks. From that time on, it is said, the practice of binding leaf-marks arose in the fields.
From that time on, there was no deer whatsoever that would overstep the leaf-mark. This, it is said, was because of the Bodhisatta.
Having received this advice, the Bodhisatta, after thus instructing the herd of deer, lived out his full lifespan and passed away according to his karma along with the deer.
The king also, remaining steadfast in the Bodhisatta’s advice and performing meritorious deeds, passed away according to his karma.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that I am a refuge for the Elder Nun and Kumāra Kassapa; in the past as well..."

Having brought forth this teaching on the Dhamma, "A refuge indeed," and having turned back from the teaching on the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, he related two past events, established the connection, and identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Sākhamiga was Devadatta;
his retinue was Devadatta’s retinue; Migadhenu was the Elder Nun; and the son was Kumārakassapa."
"King Ānanda was none other than myself, while Nigrodha the deer-king was indeed I.
This concludes the second commentary, the Nigrodhamiga Jātaka.
[13] 3. The Commentary on the Kaṇḍi Jātaka.
"Fie on the arrow of the wound!"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the seduction by his former wife.
This will be revealed in the Indriya Jātaka in the Aṭṭhaka Nipāta. However, the Blessed One said this to that bhikkhu:
"Bhikkhu, in the past as well, you met your end because of this woman."

"...cooked over embers from which the flames have been extinguished. To clarify the meaning of this, the bhikkhus requested the Blessed One, and the Blessed One made manifest that which had been concealed by another existence.
From here on, however, without mentioning the bhikkhus' request or the concealment by another existence, we shall say only this: "He brought forth the past. To this extent...

Even though this has been stated, the request and the fact that the cause was concealed by another existence should be understood by applying the analogy of the extraction of sandalwood from the interior of a cloud, in accordance with the method explained below.
In the past, in the kingdom of Magadha, at Rājagaha, the King of Magadha reigned. During the time of the crops for the inhabitants of Magadha...
There is a great danger for deer. They enter the foothills of the mountains in the forest.

There, a certain mountain-dwelling deer, having formed an intimacy with a young doe living near a village, descends from those mountain foothills with her at the time of returning to the village; because his mind is bound to that young doe, he [is caught] by them...
He descended right along with her. Then she said to him, "Sir, you are a wild mountain deer;
the vicinity of a village is full of danger and peril. Do not descend with us. Because his heart was bound to her, he did not turn back but went down together with her.
The inhabitants of Magadha thought, "Now is the time for the deer to descend from the foothills of the mountains."
Having realized this, they stood in a concealed thicket along the path. On the approach to those two as well, a hunter was standing in a concealed thicket.

Having smelled the scent of humans, the doe thought, "A hunter must be standing there," and placing that young deer in front of her, she positioned herself behind him. With a single discharge of an arrow, the hunter—
He struck down the deer right there. The fawn, realizing he had been wounded, leaped up and fled by way of the wind.
The hunter emerged from his hut, skewered the deer, and made a fire;
having roasted the sweet meat over the glowing embers, he ate it, drank water, and [left] the remainder with drops of blood dripping down.
Taking his young ones in his mouth, he went home, comforting them.
At that time, the Bodhisatta had been reborn as a tree deity in that forest grove.
Seeing this occurrence, he thought: "The death of this foolish deer is due neither to his mother nor to his father; rather—"

Indeed, it is by depending on sensual desire (*kāma*) that beings encounter suffering—such as the cutting off of hands and other such punishments—in the happy realms, and various forms of suffering, including the fivefold bonds and so forth, in the miserable realms.
Even the causing of death and suffering to others is censured in this world. That district which a woman traverses and governs is called "governed by women" (*itthipariṇāyaka*).
“Even the countryside itself is censured; those beings who fall under the power of women are likewise censured.
Having thus shown these three grounds for censure in this single verse, the forest deity offered her applause.
While the deities were honoring him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, he proclaimed that grove with a sweet voice and taught the Dhamma with this verse:
“Shame on the arrow that has been shot, the man who has struck so deeply!
Shame on that country where women are the leaders!
And cursed are those beings who have fallen under the power of women.”
In this context, *dhiratthu* is a particle used in the sense of reproach; here, it should be understood as reproach due to the influence of fear and agitation.
For it was while being terrified and agitated that the Bodhisatta spoke thus. One who has an arrow (*kaṇḍa*) is called *kaṇḍī*; he is one possessing such an arrow.

Furthermore, that arrow is called a "dart" (*salla*) in the sense of piercing into [the body]; therefore, regarding the phrase "the dart possessing the arrow": [The rest of the passage continues with grammatical analysis of the terms.]
The meaning is "possessing arrows and shafts. Or, that which has an arrow (*salla*) is called an "arrow" (*sallo*); it is that arrow.
One who pierces deeply, making a large wound-opening and delivering a powerful blow, is a "deep-piercer" (*gāḷhavedhī*); [the weapon] is that deep-piercer.
It is equipped with various kinds of shafts (*kaṇḍa*), with a tip shaped like a lotus leaf, and with an arrow that travels straight; it is that deep-piercer.
"Shame on the man"—this is the meaning here. "Leader" means a ruler or an organizer. "Censured" means reviled.
The rest here is of plain meaning. From now on, however, without saying even this much, we shall explain each point that is not self-evident.
Having thus shown three grounds for censure by means of a single verse, the Bodhisatta—
Having caused the forest to resound, he taught the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher proclaimed the Truths;

at the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher, having related two past events and joined them to the present context, [concluded] the Jātaka.
He brought [the past and present] together. From this point on, however, instead of saying "having related two instances," we shall say only "having connected the sequence.
Even though it is not explicitly stated, it should be understood by applying the method already explained below.

At that time, the mountain-dwelling deer was the dissatisfied bhikkhu; the young doe was his former wife; and as for the deity who taught the Dhamma by showing the defects of sensual pleasures, that was none other than myself.
The Third: The Commentary on the Kaṇḍijaṭaka.
[14] 4. The Commentary on the Vātamigajāṭaka.
"There is indeed nothing worse than flavors," said this while the Teacher was dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātika Tissa.

The Teacher spoke concerning this. It is said that while the Teacher was dwelling at Veḷuvana near Rājagaha, a son of a very wealthy merchant family named Tissa Kumāra went to Veḷuvana one day and, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, desired to go forth.
Having requested the going-forth, he was refused by his parents because they had not given their permission; thus, for seven days—
Having fasted until his meal was cut short, like the Elder Raṭṭhapāla, he obtained permission from his mother and father and went forth in the presence of the Teacher.
After the Teacher had ordained him and dwelt for about half a month at Veḷuvana, he went to Jetavana.
There, this son of good family undertook the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) and wandered for alms from house to house in Sāvatthī.

He passed his time, and when it was said, "This is the Elder named Cūḷapiṇḍapātikatissa," he became renowned and famous throughout the Buddha's dispensation like the full moon in the vault of the sky.
At that time, while a festival of constellations was being celebrated in Rājagaha, the Elder’s parents [remembered] what had occurred during his time as a householder.

There was a set of ornaments; having placed it in a jeweled casket and laid it upon her breast, she wept, saying, "On other festival occasions, our son would play at the festival adorned with these ornaments.
But the ascetic Gotama has taken that only son of ours and gone to the city of Sāvatthī. Where is he sitting now? Where is he standing? Thus she spoke as she wept.
Then a certain beautiful courtesan went to that family and, seeing the merchant’s wife weeping, asked, “Noble lady, why are you weeping?
She told her the matter. [The courtesan asked], “Noble lady, what does your husband love?
“This and that,” she replied. [The courtesan said], “If you give me all the authority in this house, I—”

“I will bring your son back. The merchant’s wife agreed, saying, “Very well,” and after providing him with travel expenses, she sent him forth with a large retinue, saying, “Go, and by your own power bring my son back.
She sat in a covered carriage and went to Sāvatthī; having taken up residence on the street where the Elder went for alms, she [sent word] from the merchant’s family...
When the people arrived, they did not show them to the Elder, but remained surrounded by their own retinue.
As soon as the Elder had entered for alms, they gave him a ladleful of gruel and savory food; having bound him with a craving for flavors, they gradually led him into the house.
While giving him alms, and perceiving that he had come under their influence, they feigned illness.
She lay down in the inner chamber. At the time for the alms-round, the Elder, walking from house to house in regular succession, arrived at the door of that house.
The attendants took the Elder’s bowl and had him sit down in the house. As soon as he was seated, the Elder asked, "Where is the female lay devotee?
"She is ill, venerable sir; she wishes to see you. He [was overcome] by craving for flavors.
Bound by his own undertaking of a vow, he broke it and entered the place where she lay.

She explained the reason for her arrival, seduced him, and having bound him with the craving for sensual pleasure, she caused him to disrobe, brought him under her control, seated him in a carriage, and departed for Rājagaha with a great retinue. This event became widely known.
The bhikkhus, having sat down in the Dhamma hall, initiated a discussion, saying, “It is said that a certain courtesan,
having bound the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātika Tissa with the craving for flavors, has taken him away. The Teacher,
having approached the Dhamma hall and sat upon the decorated Dhamma throne, asked, “Bhikkhus, about what conversation are you sitting here now?”
He said: "They related that occurrence to him. 'Monks, it is not only now that this monk was bound by craving for flavors and fell under its power;
in the past as well, he fell under its power. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, King Brahmadatta had a park-keeper named Sañjaya. Now, there was a certain deer of the wind..."
Having come to that garden and seen Sañjaya, he fled; yet Sañjaya did not threaten him or drive him out.
He returned again and again and roamed about in the garden itself.
The gardener, having gathered various kinds of flowers and fruits from the garden, brought them to the king day after day. Then one day the king asked him: "Good friend, gardener..."
"Do you see anything wonderful in the park? "Your Majesty, I see nothing else;
however, a single wind-horse (vātamiga) has come and is roaming in the park—this is what I see. "Will you be able to capture it?
"If I receive a small amount of honey, Your Majesty, I will be able to bring it even inside the royal palace. The king gave him the honey.
He caused it to be given. Taking it, he went to the garden and, having smeared grass with honey at the place where the deer frequented, he hid himself.
When the deer arrived, ate the honey-smeared grass, and became bound by craving for its flavor, he would not go elsewhere but returned to the garden alone.
The gardener, realizing that the deer was infatuated with the honey-smeared grass, gradually—
He showed himself. Having seen him, the deer fled for several days;
but seeing him again and again, he gained his confidence and gradually began to eat the grass held in the hands of the park-keeper.
Knowing that the deer had gained his trust, the keeper surrounded the path leading as far as the royal palace with mats.

Breaking off branches here and there, he hung a honey-gourd from his shoulder, tucked a bundle of grass under his arm, and went straight into the royal palace, scattering grass smeared with honey before the deer at every step.
Once the deer had entered within, they closed the door. Seeing the men, the deer trembled, seized by the terror of death.
He ran and rushed about within the courtyard of the inner palace. The king, descending from his palace, saw him trembling and thought:
"The wind-deer does not go to a place where it has been seen by humans for seven days; it does not go to a place where it has been threatened for as long as its life lasts.
Yet this very wind-deer, dwelling in such dense thickets, being bound by the craving for flavors, has now come to such a place."
With this verse—“Indeed, O sir, there is nothing more evil in the world than craving for flavors”—he began his teaching of the Dhamma:
“There is surely nothing more evil than flavors, Nor than dwellings or social attachments;
Yet by means of flavors, Sañjaya brought the wind-deer, Who dwelt in the depths of the forest, under his control.”
In this context, *kirā* is a particle used in the sense of hearsay or tradition. *Rasehi* means by flavors cognizable by the tongue, such as sweet, sour, and so forth.
*Pāpiyo* means more evil. Regarding the phrase *āvāsehi vā saṇṭhavehi vā*:

even in dwellings—which are defined as places where one resides permanently—and even in friendships with friends, desire and lust are indeed evil; for through those dwellings or friendships, which are enjoyed with craving and lust, [evil results].

"By a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even a hundred-thousandfold, in terms of its constant consumption and because it lacks the preservation of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) without food, the enjoyment of flavors through desire and lust is indeed more evil.
However, the Bodhisatta, as if this matter had come to him through hearsay, said: "There is surely nothing more evil than flavors; [they are like] dwellings and social attachments..."
Thus he spoke. Now, in order to demonstrate their wretched state, he said, "The wind-deer," and so forth.
Therein, "dependent on thickets" means dependent on a place of dense growth. This is what is meant: behold the wretchedness of tastes;
for instance, this very wind-deer dwelling in a thicket in a forest region was brought under the control of Sañjaya, the park-keeper, by means of sweet flavors.

He brought [him back], and explaining that there is nothing more sinful or more base than the enjoyment of flavors accompanied by desire and lust in every respect, he spoke of the danger of craving for flavors. Having spoken thus, he sent the deer back to the forest itself.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it was not only now that this courtesan, having bound him with craving for flavors, brought him under her control."
Having brought forth this teaching on the Dhamma, “He does so now; he has done so in the past as well,” and having established the connection, he identified the Jātaka:
“At that time, Sañjaya was this courtesan Vaṇṇadāsī, Vātamiga was Cūḷapiṇḍapātika, and the King of Bārāṇasī was none other than myself.”
The Fourth: The Commentary on the Vātamiga-jātaka.
[15] 5. The Commentary on the Kharādiya-jātaka:
"Aṭṭhakkhuraṃ kharādiye. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was difficult to speak to.
The Teacher spoke concerning this. It is said that a certain bhikkhu was difficult to admonish and would not accept instruction.
Then the Teacher asked him, "Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are difficult to admonish and do not accept instruction? "It is true, Blessed One.
The Teacher said, "In the past as well, because of your difficulty in being spoken to, you failed to heed the advice of the wise and, caught in a snare, met your end."
Having said, "He has attained [it]," he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta lived in the forest as a deer, surrounded by a herd of deer.
Then his sister, a female deer, showed him her young son and said, "Brother, this is your nephew."
“Teach this deer-trick to him,” she said, and sent him away. He told his nephew, “Come at such-and-such a time and learn it.
But he did not come at the appointed time. Just as on that first day, so for seven days he failed to give the seven instructions;
and while wandering about without having learned the deer-trick, he was caught in a snare. His mother—
Having approached his brother, he asked, "Brother, why has your nephew been made to learn the art of hunting?
The Bodhisatta replied, "Do not worry about that unadmonishable one; your son has not learned the art of hunting.
Then, wishing once again not to admonish him, he spoke this verse:
“A deer with eight hooves, harsh and wild, crooked and exceedingly crooked—having transgressed the seven times, I cannot bear to instruct him.
In this context, “eight-hoofed” means having two hooves on each foot, thus eight in total. “Harsh and wild” (kharādiye) [refers to its nature].
He addresses him by name. "Miga" (deer) is a term that includes all [animals]. "Vaṅkātivaṅkin" means those that are crooked at the base and excessively crooked at the tip;
one who possesses such horns is "vaṅkātivaṅkī," and thus he is called "vaṅkātivaṅkinaṃ.
"By seven [occasions] having transgressed the time" means having transgressed the exhortation by seven times for the occasion of exhortation. Not...
"I am not able to advise this ill-behaved deer"— this shows that he is unable to advise the ill-behaved deer,
and that even the thought of advising him does not arise in his mind. Then, having killed the ill-behaved deer caught in the snare,
the hunter took the meat and departed.

The Teacher also, saying, “Monk, you were not only difficult to speak to just now; you were difficult to speak to in the past as well,” brought forth this Dhamma teaching, established the connection, and identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the deer who was my nephew was the monk difficult to speak to;
his sister was Uppalavaṇṇā; and the deer who gave the exhortation was none other than myself.”
The fifth: The Commentary on the Kharādiya Jātaka.
[16] 6. The Commentary on the Tipallattha-miga Jātaka:
"A deer with three folds... This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at the Badarika Monastery in Kosambī concerning the Elder Rāhula, who was desirous of training.

He spoke concerning this. For at one time, while the Teacher was dwelling near the city of Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine, many laymen, laywomen, monks, and nuns were going to the monastery for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma;
it was a daytime discourse on the Dhamma. As time passed, however, the laywomen and the nuns...
They did not depart; rather, they became monks and lay devotees. From that time on, there was a regular hearing of the Dhamma at night.
At the conclusion of the Dhamma discourse, the elder monks would go to their respective dwelling places.
The young novices, however, slept together with the lay devotees in the assembly hall. While they were fallen asleep,
Some lay down gasping with wheezing breaths, snoring, and gnashing their teeth; others, having slept for a moment, arose.
Seeing that misfortune, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, having laid down the training rule:
"If a monk should lie down on the same bed with one who is not fully ordained, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)," went to Kosambī.
Thereupon the monks said to the Venerable Rāhula: "Friend Rāhula, a training rule has been laid down by the Blessed One;

now you must find out where your own dwelling place is. Previously, however, those monks—out of reverence for the Blessed One and because of that venerable one’s desire for training—had treated him with great affection whenever he came to his own dwelling place.

Having prepared a small couch, they gave him a robe for the purpose of making a head-covering; however, on that day, out of fear of violating the training rules, they did not even give him a place to stay.

Rāhula the Fortunate thought, "He is my father" regarding the One of Ten Powers, or "He is my preceptor" regarding the General of the Dhamma, or "He is my teacher" regarding Mahāmoggallāna, or "He is my younger father..."
Thinking thus, instead of going to the presence of the Elder Ānanda, he entered the bathroom used by the One of Ten Powers as if entering a Brahma-palace and took up residence there.

For in the bathrooms used by the Buddhas, the door is well-secured, the floor is anointed with fragrant ointments, and fragrant garlands and flower-wreaths are suspended; [this remains so] throughout the entire night.
The lamp was burning. However, the venerable Rāhula did not go to live there because of that hut’s excellence;
rather, having been told by the bhikkhus, "Find a place to stay," he went to live there out of respect for their instruction and a desire to train.
For from time to time, the bhikkhus would see that venerable one coming from afar.
Having seen it, in order to test him, they threw a hand-broom or a refuse-sweeper outside;
when he came back, they asked, "Friend, by whom was this thrown?
Thereupon, when some said, "Rāhula went by this path," that venerable one did not say, "Venerable sirs, I do not know this," but instead put it back in its place.
“Forgive me, venerable sir,” he said, and having asked for forgiveness, he departed. Thus was he desirous of training;
it was solely out of that desire for training that he had come to dwell there. Then, before dawn, the Teacher stood at the door of the privy and coughed;
the Venerable Rāhula coughed in response. “Who is this? “It is I, Rāhula. Having stepped out, [he spoke].
He paid homage and asked, "Rāhula, why are you lying here? "Because there is no place to stay," he replied.
"In the past, Bhante, the monks used to provide for me; but now, out of fear of their own offenses, they do not give me a place to stay.
Therefore, thinking, 'This is a place where I will not disturb others,' I am lying here for that reason."
Then a sense of spiritual urgency arose in the Blessed One, thinking: "If they abandon even Rāhula in this way, what will they do after ordaining other sons of good families?
Then, early in the morning, the Blessed One had the monks assembled and asked the General of the Dhamma: "Do you know..."
“Sāriputta, do you know where Rāhula has stayed today? “I do not know, Bhante.
“Sāriputta, Rāhula has stayed in the restroom today. Sāriputta, if you abandon Rāhula in this way, what will you achieve by ordaining other sons of good families?
For if this is the case, those who have gone forth in this teaching will find no firm footing.”

“From now on, after one or two days have been spent with a person who is not fully ordained in your presence, you must, on the third day, having ascertained their place of residence, have them stay outside.
Having made this supplementary rule (anupaññatti), he laid down the training precept once again.
At that time, the monks seated together in the Dhamma Hall were discussing Rāhula’s virtues, saying: “See, friends!”
"How eager for training this Rāhula truly is! When told, 'Find out where you shall dwell,' he did not even confront a single bhikkhu by saying, 'I am the son of the One of Ten Powers;
you yourselves must depart from my lodging,' but instead took up residence in the privy. While they were thus conversing, the Teacher went to the Hall of Truth.
Having sat down upon the decorated throne, he asked, "Monks, with what talk are you gathered here now?
"Venerable Sir, it is talk concerning Rāhula's desire for training, not any other talk. The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Rāhula desires training;
even when he was reborn in the animal realm in the past, he was likewise desirous of training," and having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in Rājagaha, a certain king of Magadha reigned.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having been reborn in the womb of a deer, lived in the forest surrounded by a herd of deer.
Then his sister brought her young son to him and said, "Brother, please teach this nephew of yours the art of hunting. The Bodhisatta consented, saying, "Very well."
“Go, dear one; having returned at such-and-such a time, you should learn [the art].

He was told this by his maternal uncle, and without letting that appointed time pass, he approached him and learned the art of the deer-trap. One day, while wandering in the forest, he was caught in a snare and let out a cry of being bound.
The herd of deer fled, and [his mother] heard that her son had been caught in a snare.
He reported this. She went to her brother and asked, "Brother, has your nephew been taught the art of deer-illusion?
The Bodhisatta said, "Do not suspect any evil of your son; he has mastered the deer-illusion well, and now he will come back making you laugh," and he spoke this verse:
“A deer with three-fold coils, possessing many wiles, with eight hooves, who drinks at midnight;
breathing out upon the ground through a single nostril—your nephew is worth six times that.
Therein, “deer” refers to the nephew-deer. “Three-fold coils” (*tipallattha*): a “coil” (*pallattha*) is said to be a bed; by both...
"By way of looking straight ahead and lying down"—thus, in three ways it would be "rolled over," or it would have three roll-overs;
hence, "three-fold rolled" (*tipallattha*). "Possessing manifold guile" means having much deceit and much trickery.
"Having eight hooves" means being endowed with eight hooves by virtue of two on each foot. "Arising at midnight."
Having passed the first watch and coming from the forest during the middle watch to drink water, he drinks water at midnight;
thus, he is "one who drinks water at midnight" (*addharattāpāyī*). The meaning is: one who drinks at midnight. I had my nephew, the deer, thoroughly train in the art of hunting.
How so? So that, breathing through one nostril while lying on the ground, [he could perceive] with six...
"He outbids his sister's son by six kalās. This is what is meant:

I indeed had your son train himself in such a way that, having suppressed the wind in one upper nostril and remaining pressed against the ground, he would, while breathing right there on the earth through a single lower nostril, outbid the hunter by six kalās—that is, he would overwhelm him with six portions.
The meaning is "he deceives. By what six [means]? By lying on one side with four legs stretched out;
by scratching grass and dust with his hooves; by causing his belly to swell by thrusting out his tongue; by the discharge of excrement and urine;
and by suppressing the wind.

Another method: by taking up soil with his foot and dragging it toward himself, by pushing it away, by moving it back and forth on both sides, by tossing it upward into his belly, and by dropping it downward—by these six maneuvers, he deceives them by creating the perception that "this one is dead" whenever he has finished eating.
This explains how they were made to learn this deer-trick.

Another method: he caused him to learn it in such a way that, breathing out six times with a single breath, he would "hit the mark" (kalāhiti) by means of the six reasons shown in both methods; "he will hit the mark" (kalāyissati) means he will deceive the hunter.
"Lady" (bhotī) is an address to a sister. "Nephew" (bhāgineyyo) refers to a nephew who deceives in this manner by means of the six reasons.
He explained thus. In this way, the Bodhisatta reassured his sister, demonstrating that her nephew had thoroughly mastered the art of the deer-deceiver.
That young fawn, too, though bound by the snare, did not struggle at all, but simply stretched out its legs upon the ground on its broad side.
Lying down, having struck the ground near his feet with his hooves, having torn up the dust and grass, having discharged excrement and urine,
having lowered his head, having protruded his tongue, having made his body slick with saliva,
and having caused his belly to swell from the retention of wind, he rolled his eyes and let the wind pass through the lower nostrils.
Having suppressed the wind through the upper nostrils and caused his entire body to become rigid, he displayed the appearance of one who was dead.
Blue flies swarmed around him, and crows perched in various places upon him.
The hunter arrived, struck his belly with his hand, and said, "He must have been bound while still very much alive; he has now become putrid. Regarding him...
Having loosened the binding rope, thinking, "Now I shall cut it right here, take its flesh,
and go," he began to grasp the branches and foliage without any apprehension. The fawn, too, stood up, planted all four feet firmly on the ground,
shook its body, stretched out its neck, and with great speed— like a cloud torn asunder by a mighty wind— went back to its mother.
The Teacher also, having delivered this Dhamma teaching—“Monks, it is not only now that Rāhula is desirous of training;
even in the past he was indeed desirous of training”—and having established the connection, he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the young deer who was my nephew was Rāhula;
his mother was Uppalavaṇṇā; and the uncle-deer was none other than myself.”
The sixth [story], the Commentary on the Tipallatthamiga Jātaka.
7. The Commentary on the Māluṅkya Jātaka:
"Whether in black or in white"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning two elderly men who had gone forth.
He related the story. It is said that those two lived together in a forest dwelling in the Kosala country.
One was named Elder Kāḷa, and the other was named Elder Juṇha. Then one day, Juṇha asked Kāḷa, "Venerable Kāḷa, at what time does it become cold?
He replied, "It becomes cold during the dark fortnight. Then one day, Kāḷa asked Juṇha— "Venerable Juṇha..."
“When does what is called ‘cold’ occur? He replied, “It occurs during the moonlight.
Since neither of them was able to resolve their own doubt, they went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage to him, and asked, “Venerable sir, when does what is called ‘cold’ occur?
Having heard their words, the Teacher said, “Monks, even in the past I [resolved this for you].”
"I spoke the question, but because I had entered into a state of mental concentration (*bhavasaṅkhepa*), I did not perceive it," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, at the foot of a certain mountain, a lion and a tiger lived as two companions in a single cave.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having gone forth as an ascetic, was also living on that same mountain slope. Then, one day—
A dispute arose among those companions concerning the cold. The tiger said, "It becomes cold only at nightfall.
The lion said, "It becomes cold only at dawn. Being unable to resolve their own doubt, they both questioned the Bodhisatta.
The Bodhisatta spoke this verse:
“Whether in the dark fortnight or in the bright fortnight, whenever the wind blows;
for cold things are born of the wind—both [trees] stand undefeated.
Therein, “whether in the dark fortnight or in the bright fortnight” means either during the waning half of the month or the waxing half. “Whenever the wind blows” means:
At whatever time the wind blows, whether distinguished as eastern or otherwise, at that time it is cold. For what reason?
Because coldness is born of the wind; for it is only when the wind exists that there is coldness. It is said that here, neither the dark fortnight nor the bright fortnight is a limiting factor.
"Both of you are invincible" means that both of you [are invincible] regarding this question.
"‘Invincible’—thus the Bodhisatta persuaded those companions.
The Teacher also said, "Monks, in the past this question was also told by me to you," and having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, he proclaimed the Truths.
At the conclusion of the Truths, both elders were established in the fruit of stream-entry.

The Teacher, having established the connection, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the black tiger was Kāḷa, the lion was Juṇha, and the ascetic who answered the questions was none other than myself.
This is the seventh commentary on the Māluṭa Jātaka.
[18] 8. The Commentary on the Matakabhatta Jātaka.
“If beings would but know thus,” this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning funeral offerings (matakabhatta).
At that time, people were killing many goats, sheep, and other animals to offer funeral meals in honor of deceased relatives.
They gave it the name "funeral meal. When the monks saw those people acting in that way, they asked the Teacher:
"Venerable sir, at present these people, having brought many living beings to their death, give what is called a 'funeral meal.
Is there, venerable sir, any increase in merit in this? The Teacher said: "Monks, even if one has made the resolve, 'We shall give a funeral meal,' [there is no merit if life is taken]."

"There is indeed no increase whatsoever in the taking of life; formerly, wise men sat in the sky, taught the Dhamma, and having explained the danger in this matter, caused all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa to abandon this practice.
But now, because of the contraction of the world-age (bhavasaṅkhepa), it has appeared once again," he said, and then related a story from the past.

Thinking, "I shall provide a funeral feast," he had a sheep brought and said to his pupils:
"Sirs, take this sheep to the river, bathe it, place a garland around its neck, and [apply] the five-finger mark..."
“Having bathed him and adorned him, bring him back. They replied, “Very well,” and taking him, they went to the river, bathed him, adorned him, and set him on the riverbank.
Seeing his own past karma, the goat thought, “Today I shall be freed from such suffering as this,” and filled with joy, he let out a great laugh like one breaking an earthen water-jar.
Again, thinking, "This brahmin will suffer the same pain that I have suffered after he has had me killed," he gave rise to compassion for the brahmin and wept with a loud voice.
Then those young men asked him, "Friend Eḷaka, you are both laughing and weeping with a great sound; why is this?"
“Why indeed did you laugh, and for what reason did you weep? [The goat replied:
“You should ask about this matter of mine from your own teacher. They took him and went, and reported this matter to the teacher.
Having heard their words, the teacher asked the goat, “Why did you laugh, goat, and why did you weep? The goat [replied] himself—
Having recollected his past deeds through the knowledge of recollecting former births, he said to the brahmin: "Brahmin, in the past I was likewise a brahmin who had mastered the mantras;
thinking, 'I shall give a funeral feast,' I killed a sheep and provided that funeral feast.

"I have undergone the severing of my head; this is my five-hundredth existence standing at the limit.
Thinking, 'Today I shall be freed from such sufferings,' I felt joy and laughed for that reason. But weeping, I thought:

"But this brahmin, having killed me, will suffer the agony of decapitation for five hundred lifetimes just as I have;

Whether you kill me or not, it is impossible for me to escape death today. "O sheep," [the king said].
"Do not fear; I will take charge of your protection and I shall go about with you.
"Brahmin, your protection is but slight, whereas the evil I have committed is great and powerful.
The brahmin released the goat and said to his pupils, "I will not allow anyone to kill this goat."
Having taken him, he wandered along with a goat.
As soon as the goat was let loose, it began to eat leaves, having raised its neck against a thicket growing by a rocky surface.
At that very moment, a lightning bolt struck that rocky surface; a fragment of rock broke off, fell upon the goat’s outstretched neck, and [struck] its head.
"Cut it down! The great multitude has gathered. At that time, the Bodhisatta had been reborn in that place as a tree deity.
Even as the great multitude was looking on, by the power of a deity, he sat cross-legged in the air and, in a sweet voice, said:
"If these beings knew the fruit of such evil, perhaps they would refrain from taking life."
While teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“If beings knew that the arising of birth is suffering,
no living being would kill another living being, for the killer of a living being grieves.”
In that context, "If beings were to know thus" means: if these beings were to know thus. How?

"Birth and its arising are suffering"—if they were to know that birth in various places and the subsequent growth of one who has been born—termed "arising"—are "suffering" because they serve as the basis for the sufferings of aging, sickness, death, association with the unpleasant, dissociation from the pleasant, the cutting off of hands and feet, and so forth.
"One living being does not kill another living being" means: "another..."

“By killing, one receives killing; by oppressing, one receives oppression”—thus, knowing the state of suffering because the arising of birth is a basis for suffering, no living being whatsoever would kill another living being; the meaning is that a sentient being would not kill a sentient being.
For what reason? Because “the killer of a living being grieves,” since [he grieves] by means of whichever of the six methods, such as direct physical action and so forth, he employs.
By some means, through the cutting off of another’s life-faculty,

a person who has taken life experiences great suffering for a long time in these four states of misery— the eight great hells, the sixteen supplementary hells, the various animal wombs, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the world of asuras— while afflicted by sorrow characterized by inward brooding.
He grieves. Just as this sheep grieves out of fear of death, knowing that one will likewise grieve for a long time, no living being should kill another living being;
no one at all should commit the deed known as the taking of life. However, those who are deluded by ignorance and blinded by *avijjā*, failing to see this danger, commit the taking of life.
Thus the Great Being, having exhorted them with the fear of hell, taught the Dhamma. Having heard that teaching of the Dhamma, the people, terrified by the fear of hell, abstained from taking life.
The Bodhisatta, too, having taught the Dhamma and established the great multitude in virtue, departed according to his karma;
and the great multitude, abiding by the Bodhisatta’s instruction, performed meritorious deeds such as giving.
Having done so, he filled the city of the gods. The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and established the connection, identified the Jātaka, saying:
"At that time, I was the tree deity. This concludes the eighth narrative, the Commentary on the Mataka-bhatta Jātaka.
[19] 9. The Commentary on the Āyācitabhatta Jātaka.

"If one is released here, one will be released after passing away"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the ritual offerings made by deities through the power of supplication.

In the past, in a certain village in the kingdom of Kāsi, a householder had promised to perform an offering to a deity dwelling in a banyan tree standing at the village gate.
Having returned safely, he slaughtered many living beings, thinking, “I shall be released from my vow by means of this sacrifice.”
He went to the foot of a tree. A tree deity, standing on a branch, spoke this verse:

In this regard: "If you are released, having passed away, O man—if you are released, if you desire to be released—pass away so that you are released;
do not be bound in the world beyond. For one who is being released is indeed bound:
for just as you wish to be released by killing a living being, one who is thus being released is bound by that evil deed. Therefore...
"The wise are not liberated in this way"—those who are wise men do not become liberated by making such a promise. Why is that?

Because such a form of liberation is actually a bond for a fool; he taught the Dhamma, saying that this so-called "liberation" after having committed the taking of life is nothing but a bond for a fool.
From that time forth, people abstained from such acts of taking life and [practiced] the Dhamma.
