[20] 10. The Commentary on the Naḷapāna Jātaka.

Having seen that the footprint had not been stepped over—this the Teacher spoke concerning the stalks of reed while wandering on tour among the Kosalans, having arrived at the village of Naḷakapāna and staying in the Ketaka grove by the Naḷakapāna lotus pond. At that time, it is said:
After the monks had bathed in the Naḷakapāna lotus pond, they had the novices fetch reed stalks for needle-cases.
Seeing that those stalks were perforated all the way through, they approached the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, we have had the novices fetch reed stalks for needle-cases;
they are perforated from the base all the way to the tip. What is the reason for this?"
They asked. The Teacher said, "Monks, this was my ancient resolve," and having said this, he related a past event.
It is said that formerly that forest grove belonged to a wild hunter. In that lotus pond, there was a water-demon who would devour anyone who stepped into it.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, being the size of a young red deer, was the king of monkeys, surrounded by a retinue of eighty thousand monkeys.
Avoiding the herd, he lived in that forest. He gave this instruction to the troop of monkeys:
"Sirs, in this forest there are poisonous trees and lotus ponds presided over by non-human beings;
if you eat any fruit never eaten before, or drink any water never drunk before, you must ask me about it. They...
Having replied, “Very well,” they went one day to a place where they had never been before.
Having wandered there for much of the day, they saw a lotus pond while searching for water; yet, without drinking the water, they sat down waiting for the arrival of the Bodhisatta.
When the Bodhisatta arrived, he asked, “Why, dear ones, do you not drink the water? [They replied: “Because of you...”
“Let us watch for his arrival. “Very well, dear ones,” said the Bodhisatta; and having stirred the lotus pond and followed the tracks, he saw him only as he was entering, not as he was emerging.
Knowing, “Without a doubt, this place is possessed by non-human beings,” he said, “Well done by you, dear ones, in not drinking the water; this place is possessed by non-human beings.”
The water-demon (*dakarakkhasa*), knowing that they would not descend, assumed a terrifying appearance with a dark blue belly, a pale face, and deep red hands and feet;
having split the water in two, he emerged and said, "Why do you sit here? Descend and drink the water!
Then the Bodhisatta asked him, "Are you a water-demon born right here?"
“Yes, I do. “Do you catch those who have entered the lotus pond? “Yes, I do.
From anyone who enters here, even down to a tiny bird, I let nothing go; I shall devour all of you as well.
“We will not give ourselves to be eaten by you. “But will you drink the water? “Yes, we shall drink the water.”
"And we shall not fall under your power. "Then how will you drink water? "What do you think?

Will they drink by descending [into it]? "Indeed, without descending, even the eighty thousand of us, each taking hold of a single reed-stalk, shall drink the water from your lotus pond just as one drinks through the hollow stalk of a blue lotus; thus..."
“You will not be able to eat it. Having understood this matter, the Teacher, having become fully enlightened, spoke the first two lines of this verse:
“Having seen a footprint that has not crossed over, having seen a footprint that has not descended.”
The meaning of this is as follows: "Monks, that king of monkeys did not see even a single footprint leading out of that lotus pond;

he saw only the footprints of those who had entered. Having seen this—that is, seeing the footprints of those who had entered and no footprints of those who had exited—he realized, 'Surely this lotus pond is possessed by non-human beings. Knowing this, he spoke with his retinue while conversing with him [the ogre]:”
“We will drink water through a reed.
Its meaning is: “We will drink water from your lotus pond through a reed. Again the Great Being said:
“You shall not kill me.”
"The meaning is: 'In this way, you shall not kill me nor my retinue as they drink water through the reed.
Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta had a single reed-stalk brought; he then reflected upon the perfections (pāramitās), performed an act of truth (saccakiriya), and blew into it with his mouth.
The reed became entirely hollow throughout, without leaving even a single knot inside."
In this manner, having had more and more brought, he blew upon it with his mouth and gave it.
Even so, however, it was not possible to finish; therefore, it should not be understood in that way. Instead, the Bodhisatta resolved:
"May all the reeds growing around this lotus pond have a single opening. For the service rendered for the welfare of Bodhisattas—
The resolution for greatness was successful. From that time on, all the reeds that had grown surrounding that lotus pond became hollow.
In this eon, there are four wonders known as the "eonic wonders" (*kappaṭṭhiya-pāṭihāriya*).
What are the four? The mark of the hare on the moon will remain throughout this entire eon; [and as stated] in the *Vaṭṭaka-jātaka*...

the site of Ghaṭīkāra’s dwelling shall remain free from rain for the duration of this entire eon; and the reeds that have grown surrounding this lotus pond shall remain with a single opening for the duration of this entire eon—these are known as the four miracles lasting for an eon (kappaṭṭhiya-pāṭihāriya).
Having thus resolved, the Bodhisatta took a single reed and sat down.

3. Kuruṅga Chapter [21] 1.
Commentary on the Kuruṅgamiga Jātaka.
"This was known to the Kuruṅga deer"—this the Teacher spoke while staying at Veḷuvana concerning Devadatta.

he hurled a stone; he released Dhanapāla; in every way..."
They sat down speaking in dispraise of Devadatta, saying, "He is striving for the destruction of the One Possessing the Ten Powers.
The Teacher, having arrived and sat upon the prepared seat, asked, "Bhikkhus, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
"Venerable Sir, Devadatta is striving for your destruction; we are gathered here discussing his lack of virtue."
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has striven for my death;
in the past, too, he strove for my death, yet he was unable to kill me. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta, having become a kuruṅga deer, lived in a certain...
He lived in a forest region eating wild fruits. At one time, when a *sepaṇṇi* tree was laden with fruit, he ate the *sepaṇṇi* fruits.
Then a certain village-dwelling deer-trapper, having observed the tracks of deer at the foot of the fruit trees, set a trap high up in the tree;
sitting there, he waited for deer to come and eat the fruits as they arrived.
Piercing them with a spear, he made his living by selling their meat.
One day, seeing the footprints of the Bodhisatta at the base of that tree, he set up a platform on that *sepaṇṇi* tree;
having eaten his morning meal, he took his spear, entered the forest, climbed the tree, and sat upon the platform.
The Bodhisatta also, having departed from his dwelling early in the morning, thought,
"I shall eat *sepaṇṇi* fruits," and approached the foot of that tree; however, instead of entering it immediately,
he stood outside while investigating whether there might be some danger, such as hunters setting snares on the trees.
The hunter, realizing that the Bodhisatta had not yet returned, sat upon the platform and, repeatedly throwing *sepaṇṇi* fruits, caused them to fall before him.
The Bodhisatta thought, "These fruits come and fall before me;
could there be a hunter above? Looking up again and again, he saw the hunter, yet acted as if he did not see him.
Having made the offering, he said: "O tree, formerly you caused the fruits to fall straight down like one swinging a hanging ornament;

but today your duty as a tree has been abandoned by you. Since you have thus abandoned your duty as a tree, I too shall go to another tree-root and seek my own food. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Kuruṅga, this is well known to you: that you consider the *sepaṇṇī* fruit to be excellent.
I shall go for another *sepaṇṇī*; those fruits do not please me.
In this context, *ñātaṃ* means “become manifest”; *etaṃ* means “this”; *kuruṅgassa* means “of the kuruṅga deer. As for *yaṃ tvaṃ*:

"O *sepaṇṇi* tree, you who are called 'the best' (*seyyasī*), since you excel, shine forth, and become laden with fruit by dropping your fruits before me, all of that has become evident to the *kuruṅga* deer.
'I do not like your fruit'—thus, though you give me fruit, your fruit is not pleasing to me; stay where you are, I shall go elsewhere."
Thinking, "I shall go," he departed.
Then, while the hunter was still seated on his stool, he hurled a spear and said, "Go! Now I have missed you.
The Bodhisatta turned back and stood there, saying, "O man, even though you have now missed me, what will you do?"
"Furthermore, he has not failed to experience the eight great hells, the sixteen secondary hells, and the fivefold tortures such as binding and other forms of punishment.
Having spoken thus, [Devadatta] fled and went wherever he pleased; the hunter also descended and went wherever he pleased.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has striven for my death; in the past, too, he strove for it."
Having brought forth this teaching on the Dhamma, “And yet he was not able to kill me,” and having established the connection, he identified the Jātaka:
“At that time, the deer-trapper was Devadatta, while I myself was the Kuruṅga deer.

[22] 2. The Commentary on the Dog Jātaka (*Kukkurajātakavaṇṇanā*).

"Those dogs..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the conduct for the benefit of those who know. This will be revealed in the Bhaddasāla Jātaka in the Twelfth Book (*Dvādasakanipāta*). However, having established the present narrative, he brought forth the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, due to a corresponding deed, [was born as a dog].
Having been reborn in the womb of a dog, he lived in the great charnel ground surrounded by many hundreds of dogs.

Then one day, the king mounted a chariot yoked with white thoroughbred horses and adorned with every ornament, went to the pleasure garden, and after sporting there for part of the day, entered the city when the sun had set. His excellent chariot remained exactly as it had been harnessed.
They placed it in the royal courtyard; during the night, while it was raining, it became soaked.
Noble dogs descended from the upper palace and gnawed at its leather covering and its straps. On the following day, they informed the king:
"Your Majesty, dogs entered through the drainage opening and have chewed the leather covering and the straps of the chariot. The king, becoming angry with the dogs, said:
“Kill the dogs wherever they are seen,” he said. From that time on, a great calamity befell the dogs.
Being killed wherever they were seen, they fled and went to the charnel ground, where they approached the Bodhisatta.
The Bodhisatta asked, “You have gathered here in such large numbers; what is the reason? They replied, “It is said that in the royal palace...”
"The leather and the straps of the chariot have been eaten by dogs," they said;
"the king, being enraged, has ordered the slaughter of the dogs, many dogs have perished, and a great terror has arisen. The Bodhisatta thought:
"In the place of protection there is no opportunity for stray dogs; that deed belongs only to the noble-bred dogs within the royal residence."
"It will come to pass. But now there is no fear for the thieves at all; instead, those who are not thieves are receiving death.
What if I were to show the thieves to the king and grant the gift of life to my circle of kinsmen? Having thus reassured his relatives, he said, "Do not be afraid;
I shall bring you safety. Until I see the king, remain right here."
Having reflected upon the perfections (*pāramitā*) and preceded his actions with the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*), he made this resolve:
"May no one dare to throw a clod or a club at me. Having thus determined, he entered the city all alone.
Then, upon seeing him, not even a single being felt anger, nor was there anyone who even looked at him with ill will. The King, having ordered the execution of the dogs, [continued...]
He was seated in the court of justice. The Bodhisatta went right there, leaped forward, and entered beneath the king’s throne.
Then the king’s men began to drag him out, but the king stopped them.
After resting for a short while, he emerged from beneath the seat, paid homage to the king, and said, “Your Majesty, as for your dog...”
“Have them executed,” he asked. “Yes, we shall have them executed. “What is their offense, O King?
“They ate the leather trimmings and the sinews of my chariot. “Do you know who it was that ate them? “We do not know.
“To execute people at the very spot where they were seen, without knowing for certain that ‘these are indeed the thieves who ate the leather’—[is this just?]”
“It is not right, O King. “Because the chariot-hide was eaten by the dogs, he ordered the slaughter of the dogs, saying:
‘Kill every single one you see! “But do your people kill all the dogs, or are there some who do not meet their death?
“There are, Your Majesty; those in our own homes that are of noble breed do not meet their death. “Great King!”
"Just now you said, 'Because the chariot-skin was eaten by dogs, he ordered the slaughter of dogs, saying, "Kill every single one you see!
But now you say, 'In our house, well-bred dogs do not meet with death.
Is it not the case that, this being so, you are following a wrong course out of favoritism and the like?"
"To go along a wrong path is neither fitting nor the duty of a king; indeed, a king ought to be like a scale, seeking only the truth.
Now, noble dogs do not receive the death penalty, while only weak ones do;
if this is so, this is not the slaughter of all dogs, but rather the 'slayer of the weak'. Having spoken thus, he continued:
The Great Being, emitting a sweet voice, spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma to the king:
“Those dogs that are bred in the royal household, of noble lineage and endowed with beauty and strength;”
"We are not to be killed; we are to be killed. This is no slaughter of our own kind by a weak slayer.

In this context, "dogs" refers to those who are hounds. For just as even pungent urine is called "putrid urine," a jackal born on that very day is called an "old jackal," a tender creeper is called a "rotten creeper," and a body with a golden complexion is called a "rotten body."
Just as even a hundred-year-old dog is called a "dog," so too are those dogs, though they are old and possessed of physical strength, still called "dogs.
"Vaddhā" means grown. "Koleyyakā" means born, arisen, and raised in a royal family.
"Vaṇṇabalūpapannā" means endowed with both physical beauty and bodily strength. "Teme na vajjhā" means they are not to be killed.
"These [women] have owners and are protected; they are not to be killed.

We are those who are to be killed"—thus, we have become known as "ownerless" and "unprotected," and therefore "to be killed. "This is not a general slaughter": even this being so, it does not constitute a general slaughter.
However, it is called "the slaughter of the weak" because it consists specifically in the killing of the weak. Indeed, thieves are to be suppressed by kings.
“There are no thieves here. Yet, in this place, there is no danger for the thieves; instead, those who are not thieves meet their death.
Alas! In this world, what is improper prevails! Alas! What is unrighteous prevails!
When the king heard the words of the Bodhisatta, he said: “Do you know, O wise one, by whom the chariot-skin was [stolen] from such-and-such people?”
“Was it eaten? “Yes, I know. “By whom was it eaten? “By the well-bred dogs living in your house.
“How can the fact that they ate it be known? “I shall show you the evidence of their having eaten it. “Show us, wise one.

He performed an offering with a white parasol. Having thus established the king in the five precepts (*pañca-sīla*), he returned the white parasol to the king himself.
Having heard the Bodhisatta’s discourse on the Dhamma, the king granted safety to all beings.
Beginning with the Bodhisatta, he established a regular meal for all the dogs, providing food equal to his own.

Abiding by the Bodhisatta’s advice, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving throughout the span of his life. When he passed away, he was reborn in the world of the devas. This is the "Instruction to the Dog."

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching—“Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata acts for the welfare of his kinsmen;
he has done so in the past as well”—and having established the connection, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the king was...”

Saying, "Very well, Your Majesty," he paid homage to the king, descended from the palace, had a noble Bhoja Sindhava horse brought, and having well-equipped it, he himself donned all his armor, fastened his sword, and mounted the back of that excellent Sindhava steed.
Having departed from the city and moving like a flash of lightning, he first broke through the first military outpost;
having captured one king alive, he returned and delivered him to the army in the city. Going forth again, he broke through the second military outpost, and likewise the third.
In this manner, having captured five kings alive, he reached the sixth military outpost.
When the sixth king was struck and captured, the noble Bhoja horse received a blow; blood flowed, and intense pains set in.
The horseman, realizing he had been struck, laid the noble Bhoja Sindhava at the palace gate, loosened its harness, and began to saddle another horse. At that moment, the Bodhisatta—
Lying on his side with his great ribs exposed, he opened his eyes and, seeing the horseman, thought: "This man is saddling another horse;
this horse will not be able to break through the seventh rampart and capture the seventh king, my own deed will go to waste, this peerless horseman will perish, and the king as well—"
"It will fall into the hands of the enemy; there is no one other than me capable of breaking through the seventh rampart and capturing the seventh king.

Having said this while still lying down, he summoned the horseman and said, "Good horseman, apart from me, there is no one else capable of breaking through the seventh rampart and capturing the seventh king."
“I have no other horse; I will not let the deed I have done go to waste.
Raise me up myself and lead me away,” he said, and spoke this verse:
“Even while lying on my side, pierced through by arrows, I am still stung by shafts.”
"Better indeed is the mare Bhojjha than one who lies on his side; better even is the charioteer.
In this context, "lying on his side" means even while lying on one side. "Pierced by arrows" means being struck by arrows.
"Better indeed is the mare Bhojjha": "mare" refers to a wild colt not born of the Sindhu breed.
"Bhojja" means a well-bred Sindhu horse. Thus, even if pierced by arrows, a mare is better, more excellent, and superior than a well-bred Sindhu horse.
"Harness me alone, O charioteer"—because I am indeed superior even when gone, he says, "Therefore, yoke me alone; arm me."
The horseman raised up the Bodhisatta, bound his wound, and having equipped him with a full set of armor, he sat upon his back.
Having broken through the seventh military outpost and captured the seventh king alive, he delivered him over to the royal army;
they then brought the Bodhisatta as well to the palace gate. The king went out to see him.
The Great Being said to the king: "Great King, do not have the seven kings executed; instead, make them take an oath and release them.
As for the honor that should be given to me and my horseman, give it to the horseman alone.
It is not right to destroy what is called 'given battle' by seizing the seven kings. You too should give alms and guard your virtue."
"Rule the kingdom righteously and justly. When the Bodhisatta had thus given this advice to the king, they removed his armor;

as soon as the armor was removed, he passed away. The king, having performed the funeral rites for him, bestowed great honor upon the horseman and compelled the seven kings to swear an oath that they would not betray him again.
Having sent them each to their respective places and ruled the kingdom with justice and equity, he passed away at the end of his life and went according to his karma.
The Teacher said, "Thus, monk, in the past, the wise exerted effort even in an unsuitable place; even when receiving such a blow as this, they did not slacken.
But you, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, why do you slacken your effort?"
Having spoken thus, he proclaimed the Four Noble Truths; at the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who had slackened his effort was established in the fruit of Arahatship.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and joined the connection, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the king was Ānanda, the horseman was Sāriputta, and I myself was the noble thoroughbred Sindhu horse.
This is the third narrative, the Commentary on the Bhojājānīya Jātaka.
[24] 4. The Commentary on the *Ājaññajātakaya*:
"Whenever..."—this too was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who had slackened his energy.
The Teacher addressed that monk, saying: "Monk, in the past, even when wise men received blows in an improper place..."
Having said, "Exerting their energy, they acted," he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, seven kings surrounded the city in the same manner as described previously.
Then, one chariot-warrior, having yoked two Sindhu-brother horses to his chariot, departed from the city.
Having broken through the six gate-towers, he captured six kings. At that moment, the lead horse received a blow.
The charioteer, driving the chariot, arrived at the palace gate;
he unyoked the lead brother from the chariot, loosened his armor, laid him down on one side, and began to harness another horse. The Bodhisatta—
Having seen him and reflected in the same manner as before, he summoned a charioteer and, while still lying down, spoke this verse:
“Whenever and wherever, at whatever time and in whatever place,
The noble steed exerts its speed, there the wild beasts perish.”
In this context: *yadā yadā* means at whichever time, such as the morning and so forth; *yattha* means in whichever place, whether on the road or at the head of the battle;
*yadā* means at whichever moment; *yattha yattha* means in many battlefields by way of the seven divisions of the army;
and *yadā yadā* means at whichever time, whether at the time of receiving a blow or at the time of not receiving one.
Or: "The thoroughbred (*ājañña*) exerts speed"—the noble stallion, whose nature is to understand the driver’s desired intention, exerts speed, strives, and arouses energy.

"There, the other mares fall away"—while that speed is being exerted, the other mares known as *vaḷava* (wild mares) or *khaḷuṅka* (unbroken horses) fall away and retreat; therefore he said, "Yoke me alone to this chariot."

The charioteer, having raised the Bodhisatta and yoked him to the chariot, broke through the seventh defensive wall and, taking the seventh king with him, drove the chariot toward the palace gate; upon arriving, he unyoked the horse.
The Bodhisatta, lying on one side, gave the king exhortation in the same manner as before and passed away. The king performed the funeral rites for his body.
Having had [the horse] executed, having shown honor to the charioteer, and having ruled the kingdom according to the Dhamma, he departed according to his karma.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction, proclaimed the Truths; at the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu was established in Arahatship.
The Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, King Ānanda was the charioteer, and the horse was the Perfectly Enlightened One."
The Fourth: The Commentary on the Ājañña Jātaka.
5. The Commentary on the Tittha Jātaka:
"From various fords"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a co-resident disciple of the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta).
He spoke concerning a certain monk who had formerly been a goldsmith. For the knowledge of the underlying tendencies (*āsayānusayañāṇa*) belongs only to the Buddhas, not to others.
Therefore, because the General of the Dharma (Sāriputta) lacked this knowledge of underlying tendencies, he did not know the underlying tendencies of his co-resident;
thus, he taught him only the meditation subject of the foul (*asubhakammaṭṭhāna*), which was not suitable for him.
Why was this? It is said that for five hundred successive births he had taken rebirth specifically in a goldsmith’s workshop;
thus, because his mind was so long accustomed to beholding pure gold, the foul (asubha) was not suitable for him.
Unable to produce even a mere sign of meditation there, he spent four months.
The General of the Dhamma, being unable to grant Arahantship to his own co-resident, thought, "Surely this one must be converted by the Buddha;
I shall lead him into the presence of the Tathāgata. Taking him with him early in the morning, he went into the presence of the Teacher.
The Teacher asked, "Sāriputta, why have you come bringing a single bhikkhu? [He replied,] "I..."
“Venerable sir, I gave him this meditation subject, yet after four months he had not produced even a mere sign.
Thinking, ‘He must be one who is to be guided by a Buddha,’ I have brought him here into your presence.
“Sāriputta, which meditation subject did you give to your co-resident? “The meditation subject of the foul (asubha).”
“Bhante,” [he replied]. “Sāriputta, you do not possess the knowledge of the underlying tendencies (*āsayānusayañāṇa*) within your own continuum. Go;
you may return in the evening and go with your co-resident disciple.
Having thus dismissed the Elder, the Teacher had a pleasing robe and lower garment given to that monk, and taking him with him, he entered the village for alms.

Having caused excellent hard and soft food to be served, and having returned to the monastery accompanied by a great assembly of monks, he spent a portion of the day in the Gandhakuṭī. Then, at the time of evening, taking that monk with him, he went on a walking tour of the monastery grounds;
there, in a mango grove, he created a lotus pond and a large cluster of lotuses within it. There too—
Having fashioned a single large lotus flower, he had the monk sit down with the instruction, “Monk, sit here gazing at this flower,” and then entered the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī).
That monk gazed at the flower again and again. The Blessed One caused that flower to reach decay;
while the monk was still looking at it, it reached decay and became discolored. Then, starting from its edges, the petals...
In a mere moment, all the petals fell away. Then the filaments fell, and only the pericarp remained.
Seeing this, the bhikkhu thought: "This lotus flower was just now beautiful and lovely to behold;
now its color has faded, its petals and filaments have fallen, and only the pericarp remains."
"Even for such a lotus as this, old age has arrived; what then will not come upon my own body?

All conditioned phenomena are impermanent. Thus he established insight. The Teacher, knowing that his mind had ascended to insight, while seated in the Fragrant Chamber, emitted a radiance and spoke this verse:
“Cut off your own affection, as one plucks an autumnal lily with the hand;
cultivate only the path to peace, the Nibbāna taught by the Sugata.
At the conclusion of this verse, that bhikkhu attained arahantship and thought, “I am indeed liberated from all states of existence.”
“Thus having completed my residence, with mind fulfilled, my taints destroyed, bearing my final body;
pure in virtue, with faculties well-composed, like the moon released from the mouth of Rāhu.
I have dispelled the great darkness of delusion that spread everywhere, and removed every stain without exception.”
"Creating light and radiance, the maker of splendor, like the thousand-rayed sun in the sky"—with these verses he uttered an *udāna*.
Having uttered it, he went and paid homage to the Blessed One.
The Elder also came, paid homage to the Teacher, and departed taking his own student with him. This was the account that reached the monks.
This became known in the meantime. In the Dhamma Hall, the bhikkhus sat praising the virtues of the One Possessed of Ten Powers:
"Friends, the Elder Sāriputta, due to a lack of knowledge regarding the underlying tendencies and latent dispositions (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*), did not know the disposition of his own co-resident;
but the Teacher, having known it, bestowed upon him Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) in a single day."
“Oh, how great is the power of those called Buddhas!
The Teacher, having arrived and sat down on the prepared seat, asked: “Monks, with what discussion are you sitting here gathered now?
“Not about any other matter, Blessed One; rather, it is concerning your own Dhamma-general, the disciple with whom you lived together.”
“In the discourse on the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies.
The Teacher said, “Monks, this is not surprising that I, having now become a Buddha, know his disposition; even in the past, I knew his disposition. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, Brahmadatta reigned as king. At that time, the Bodhisatta [was] to that king in matters of...
And he taught the Dhamma. At that time, at the bathing ford for the king’s auspicious horse, they were washing a certain mare with a colt.
As the auspicious horse was being led down to the bathing ford by the mare, he felt loathing and did not wish to go down.
The groom went and reported to the king, "Your Majesty, the auspicious horse does not wish to go down to the ford."
The king sent for the Bodhisatta, saying: “Go, wise one, find out for what reason the horse will not step down into the ford when being led there.
The Bodhisatta replied, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and went to the riverbank.
Looking at the horse and perceiving that it was free from disease, he reflected, “For what reason does this horse not step down into this ford? As he pondered, [he saw] first of all—
Thinking, "Someone else must have been bathed here; it is likely because of that he is feeling disgusted and does not descend into the bathing place," he asked the horse-herders, "Ho there!
Whom did you bathe first at this bathing place? "A certain mare, sir."
The Bodhisatta, understanding the horse’s disposition—thinking, “This one, loathing his own swiftness, does not wish to bathe here;
it would be better to bathe him at another ford”—said, “O horse-keeper, even for one who repeatedly eats food prepared with ghee, honey, molasses, and the like, satiety eventually comes.
This horse has bathed many times at this very ford; let him bathe elsewhere as well.”
"Having brought him down to that bathing place, bathe him and give him a drink," he said, and then spoke this verse:
"O charioteer, let the horse drink from various watering places;
For a man who has been waiting long is satisfied even by a drink."
In this context, "by various [means]" (*aññamaññehi*) means by this or that [different method]. "Feed" (*pāyehi*) is a mere heading for the instruction; the meaning is "bathe and feed.

Regarding "of one who has overeaten" (*accāsanassa*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is "by overeating" or "by having eaten too much. "He is satisfied even by milk-rice" (*pāyāsassa pi tappati*):
he is satisfied—that is, satiated—by sweet milk-rice prepared with ghee and other such ingredients; he is nourished and well-fed.
Furthermore, he did not fall prey to the desire to eat again. Therefore, this horse must have reached his limit through bathing at this watering place; let him bathe him elsewhere.
Having heard his words, they led the horse down to another watering place, where they gave him water to drink and bathed him. The Bodhisatta—
Having drunk water and bathed, the horse went into the presence of the king at bathing time.
The king asked, "What is it, dear one? Has the horse bathed and drunk? "Yes, Your Majesty," he replied. "Why did he not wish to do so at first?
"For this reason," he explained, recounting everything. The king remarked, "He truly knows the disposition even of such an animal!"
"Ah, he is wise! Having thus bestowed great honor upon the Bodhisatta, [the king] passed away at the end of his life and went according to his karma.
The Bodhisatta also went according to his own karma.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that I know his disposition; I have known it even in the past. Thus [he spoke]. This...
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma and established the connection, he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the auspicious horse was this very bhikkhu; the king was Ānanda; and the wise minister was none other than myself.
This is the fifth explanation, the Titthajātaka.
[26] 6. The Commentary on the Mahilāmukha Jātaka:
"Having heeded the words of the former thieves"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning Devadatta.
Devadatta won over Prince Ajātasattu and brought about gain and honor for himself. Prince Ajātasattu...
Having had a monastery built by Devadatta at Gayāsīsa, they brought five hundred *thālipāka* offerings daily—consisting of rice cooked with three-year-old fragrant grains and various choice flavors.
Due to this gain and honor, Devadatta’s retinue became great; accompanied by his followers, Devadatta remained right there in the monastery. At that time...
There were two companions living in Rājagaha. Of them, one went forth in the presence of the Teacher, while the other went forth under Devadatta.
They saw each other in various places, and even when they had gone to the monastery, they would see one another.
Then one day, Devadatta’s dependent said to the other: "Friend, why do you sweat every day?"
"While you wander for alms even while being released [from bonds], Devadatta sits right there in the Gayāsīsa monastery and eats fine food with various choice flavors;
such a means as this he does not have. Why do you undergo suffering?
Why do you come to Gayāsīsa at daybreak, drink rice-gruel with curd-rinings, eat eighteen kinds of snacks, and [partake] of various choice flavors?"
"It is not proper to eat fine food. Though he was told this again and again, he became desirous of going;
from then on, he would go to Gayāsīsa, eat there, and return to Veḷuvana at an early hour.
He was unable to conceal it for long, and it became known that "he goes to Gayāsīsa and eats the meal prepared by Devadatta."
Before long, he became well known. Then his companions asked him, "Is it true, friend, that you eat the meal prepared for Devadatta? "Who says such a thing? "So-and-so and so-and-so.
"It is true, friends, that I go to Gayāsīsa and eat there, but Devadatta does not give me the meal; other people do."
“Friend, Devadatta is a thorn to the Buddhas; being immoral, he has gained favor with Ajātasattu and thereby procured his own gain and honor through unrighteous means.

Having gone forth in such a liberating teaching of the Buddha, you eat food procured by Devadatta through unrighteous means. Come, let us lead you into the presence of the Teacher. Thus [he spoke] to that bhikkhu.
They took him and came to the Dhamma Hall.
As soon as the Teacher saw them, he asked, "Bhikkhus, why have you come taking this bhikkhu even though he does not wish it?
"Yes, Bhante; this bhikkhu, having gone forth in your presence, [was led away] by Devadatta through what is contrary to the Dhamma."
“I am eating food,” he replied. “Is it true, monk, that you eat food obtained by Devadatta through an unrighteous means?
“It is not so, Bhante; Devadatta does not give to me, but other people give, and I eat what they give.
The Teacher said, “Do not try to evade this matter, monk. Devadatta is immoral and of bad character; how indeed could you—”
"Having gone forth here, you follow my teaching yet you eat the food of Devadatta;
you are always one who associates, and wherever you see him, you associate with him," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his minister. At that time—
The king had an auspicious elephant named Mahilāmukha, who was virtuous and possessed of good conduct, and he did not harm anyone.
Then one day, toward the end of the night, thieves arrived near his stall and sat down not far from him, deliberating on their thieving spells:
"The breach should be made in this way; the work of breaking through the wall should be done in this way."
One must act; having made the way out, the breaking of the wall, and the path like a ford—level, free from tangles, and free from thickets—it is permissible to carry off the goods.
But when carrying them off, one must kill [the owner] first so that he will not be able to rise up again.
Furthermore, a thief must not be one endowed with virtue and good conduct; he must be harsh and cruel.
"One must be reckless. Having deliberated thus and having taught one another, they departed.
By this very means, coming there on the following day and the day after that, they deliberated for many days.
Hearing their words, he perceived, "They are teaching me," and thought, "Now, by me [must be acted] with severity, harshness, and recklessness."

Thinking, "It must become like that," he became exactly such a person. As soon as the elephant-keeper returned in the morning, he seized him by the trunk, dashed him against the ground, and killed him.
Again and again, in the same manner, he killed every single keeper who arrived.
They reported to the king, "Mahilāmukha has gone mad; he kills every single person he sees. The king [sent for] the Bodhisatta...
He sent [a messenger], saying: "Go, wise one; find out for what reason he has become wicked.
The Bodhisatta went and, having ascertained that there was no physical ailment in his body, reflected: "For what reason has he become wicked? While investigating, he realized:
"Surely, having heard the words of certain people nearby, he became wicked under the impression that 'these people are training me.'"
Having reached a conclusion, he asked the elephant-keepers, "Has anything ever been said by anyone near the elephant stable during the night?
"Yes, master; thieves came and spoke," they replied.
The Bodhisatta went and reported to the king, "Your Majesty, there is no other change in the elephant's body; it was after hearing the talk of the thieves..."

“He has been born wicked! [The king asked,] “What should be done now? [The ministers replied,] “It is fitting to have virtuous recluses and brahmins seated in the elephant stable and have them discourse on the practice of virtue. [The king said,] “Do so, my dear ones.
The Bodhisatta went and, having had the virtuous recluses and brahmins seated in the elephant stable, [he had them deliver] a discourse on virtue.
“Tell me, venerable sir,” he said. Sitting not far from the elephant, they spoke a discourse on virtue, saying: “No one should be touched or killed;
it is fitting to be endowed with virtue and conduct, joined with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion.
Having heard this, he thought, “These people are instructing me; from now on, I must be virtuous,” and so he became virtuous.
It happened thus. The king asked the Bodhisatta, "What is it, dear father, that you have been born virtuous? The Bodhisatta replied, "Yes, Your Majesty.
"Such a wicked elephant, by relying on the wise, has been established once again in his ancient nature," he said, and uttered this verse:
"Having heeded the words of the old thieves, Mahilāmukha wandered about striking [others]."
"For the word of those who are well-restrained, having reflected upon it, the best of elephants stands firm in all virtues.
In this context, "of the ancient thieves" means of the thieves of old. "Having reflected" means having heard; the sense is that he first heard the words of the thieves.
"With the face of a female" means having a face resembling that of a female elephant. Just as a female elephant, when looked at from the front...
It shines when looked at from the front, not from behind; likewise, he too shone when looked at from the front.
Therefore, they gave him the name "Mahiḷāmukha" (The Woman’s Face). *Pothayamānucārī* means one who follows along while striking or killing;

this is indeed the reading. *Susaññatānaṃ* means those who are well-restrained, the virtuous. *Gajuttamo* means the supreme elephant, the auspicious state-elephant (*maṅgalahatthī*). Regarding all qualities...
"Aṭṭha" means he was established in all the ancient virtues. The king, thinking, "He knows even the dwelling place of an animal," bestowed great honor upon the Bodhisattva.
Having lived out his full lifespan, he passed away together with the Bodhisattva according to their respective kamma.
The Teacher said, "Monk, even in the past you associated only with those you had seen; having heard the words of the thieves, you associated with the thieves."
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, "Having heard the words of the righteous, one should associate with the righteous," he established the connection and identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, Mahilāmukha was the monk who served the enemy faction; King Ānanda was [the other king];
and as for the minister, it was I myself."
The Sixth: The Explanation of the Mahilāmukha Jātaka.
[27] 7. The Explanation of the Abhiṇha Jātaka:
"He is not able to swallow a mouthful," this was said by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain lay follower and an elder monk.
He spoke concerning this. It is said that in Sāvatthī there were two friends. One of them went forth into homelessness and went to the other’s house every day.
After giving him almsfood and eating himself, he would go with him to the monastery and sit in conversation until sunset, after which he would enter the city; the other did likewise.
He would follow them as far as the city gates and then turn back. His friendship with those monks became well known among the community.
Then one day, while the monks were sitting in the Dhamma Hall discussing their friendship, the Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now? They replied:
“Indeed, Bhante, it was by her,” they said. The Teacher said, “Monks, these two were not only trustworthy now;
in the past, too, they were trustworthy,” and having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his minister. At that time—
A certain dog went to the stable of the auspicious elephant and ate the grains of rice that had fallen at the auspicious elephant’s feeding place.
Growing up on that very food, he became a trusted companion to the auspicious elephant;
he ate right beside the elephant, and neither of them was able to live without the other. The elephant would take him by the trunk...
Playing by throwing it from one place to another, he would pick it up and set it back down in the jar.
Then one day, a villager gave the elephant-keeper his wages, took the dog with him, and went to his own village.
From that time on, not seeing the dog, the elephant neither ate nor drank nor bathed. They reported this matter to the king.
The king sent for the Bodhisatta, saying, "Go, wise one, and find out for what reason the elephant acts in this manner.
The Bodhisatta went to the elephant stable; perceiving the elephant's dejected state, he thought, "No disease is apparent in its body.
There must be some friend with whom it has a close intimacy; not seeing him, it..."
"I suspect he is overcome with grief," [the king] said, and asked the elephant-keeper, "Does this one have any acquaintance with anyone?
"Yes, master; he has a strong friendship with a certain dog.
"Where is he now? "He was led away by a man. "Do you know his place of residence? "We do not know, master. Thus spoke the Bodhisatta.
Having gone into the presence of the king, he said, “Your Majesty, there is no ailment whatsoever with the elephant;
however, it has a strong friendship with a certain dog, and not seeing him, I suspect it will not eat. Having spoken thus, he recited this verse:
“It is not able to take a morsel, nor a lump of food, nor to chew the *kusa* grass, nor to grind it.”
"I think that from seeing him frequently, the elephant felt affection for the dog.
In this context, *nālaṃ* means "not capable. *Kabaḷaṃ* refers to the first bitter morsel given at the time of eating. *Padātavā* is *padātave*;
the elision of the vowel *ā* should be understood as occurring by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), meaning "to be taken. *Na ca piṇḍaṃ*... [and not a morsel].
Even when given a mouthful of food that had been increased in size, he was unable to swallow it.
He could not even eat the grass given for his fodder. When being bathed, he was unable to even rub his body.
Thus, having reported to the king everything that the elephant was incapable of doing, [they informed him] of his inability.
Declaring the reason he had observed for himself, he said, "I think," and so forth.
Having heard his words, the king asked, "What should be done now, wise men?
[The ministers replied,] "It is said that a certain man has taken our auspicious elephant’s companion, the dog, and gone away; whoever sees that dog in their house, [to them...]"
"O gods, have the drum beaten, proclaiming: 'This is indeed the punishment! The king had it done accordingly.
Hearing of this occurrence, the man released his dog; the dog came running with great speed and went straight to the side of the elephant.
The elephant seized it with its trunk, placed it upon its forehead, wept and lamented, and having lowered it from its forehead, [he spoke] to him...
After eating, he himself also ate. The king, thinking, "He knows the dwelling place of even a beast," bestowed great honor upon the Bodhisatta.
The Teacher said, "Monks, these two were not only trustworthy now; they were trustworthy in the past as well," and he gave this Dhamma teaching.
Having brought it forth, he turned [the discourse] toward the teaching of the Four Noble Truths, joined the connection, and identified the Jātaka.
This turning toward the teaching of the Four Noble Truths exists in all Jātakas;
however, we shall point it out only where its benefit is evident.
At that time, the dog was a lay follower (upāsaka), the elephant was the Elder Mahallaka, King Ānanda, and the wise minister was none other than myself.
This concludes the seventh commentary on the *Abhiṇha-jātaka*.
[28] 8. Commentary on the *Nandivisāla-jātaka*
"One should speak only what is agreeable. The Teacher spoke this while residing at Jetavana, concerning the verbal abuse of the group of six monks (*chabbaggiya*).

At that time, the group of six, while engaged in quarreling, reviled, mocked, and insulted the virtuous monks, and they abused them with the ten grounds for censure. The monks reported this to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One summoned the group of six monks and, having asked, "Is it true, monks? and being told, "It is true," he rebuked them, saying:
"Monks, harsh speech is indeed unpleasant even to animals;
once in the past, an animal defeated a man who was addressing him with harsh words by winning a thousand [coins]. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Gandhāra, at Takkasilā, the King of Gandhāra reigned. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a cow.
Then, while he was still a young calf, a certain brahmin obtained him from those who were giving away cattle as sacrificial gifts;
having named him "Nandivisāla," he placed him in the position of a son and, full of affection, provided him with rice gruel, food, and other necessities.
Having given [him], he nourished him. When the Bodhisatta reached maturity, he thought: "I have been raised by this brahmin with great hardship;
indeed, there is no other ox in all of Jambudīpa who is my equal in strength.
What if I were to display my own power and give it to the brahmin as a means of livelihood? One day, he said to the brahmin: "Go..."

“Brāhmaṇa, go to the merchant Govittaka and say, ‘My ox pulls a hundred overloaded carts,’ and then perform a miracle for him for a thousand [pieces of money]. That brāhmaṇa went to the merchant and initiated the conversation:
“In this city, whose ox is endowed with such strength? Then the merchant—
Having said, "Of such-and-such a person and such-and-such a person," he added, "But in the entire city, there is no one whose oxen are equal to ours.
The brahmin replied, "I have one ox capable of pulling a hundred heavily laden carts.
The householder merchant asked, "Where is such an ox? The brahmin said, "He is in my house. [The merchant said,] "In that case..."
“Indeed, perform a marvel! “Very well, I shall do so,” he replied, and performed a marvel with a thousand [oxen].
He filled a hundred carts with nothing but sand, gravel, and stones, arranged them in a row, and bound them all together with a single axle-fastening rope.
Then he bathed Nandivisāla, applied scented ointment to his five limbs, and fastened a garland around his neck.
Having yoked only a single ox to the pole of his former cart, the merchant himself sat upon the pole, raised his goad, and said, "Go on, you rogue!

Pull, you rogue! The Bodhisatta, thinking, "This man addresses me, who am no rogue, with the word 'rogue'," stood firm with his four feet as motionless as pillars. At that very moment, the merchant gave the Brahmin a thousand [pieces].
He had [the ox] brought back. The brahmin, having lost a thousand [coins], released the ox and went home; overcome by grief, he lay down.
When Nandivisāla returned from grazing and saw the brahmin overcome by grief, he approached him and asked, "Brahmin, why are you sleeping?
"How can I sleep, when I have been defeated for a thousand [coins]? Brahmin, for so long a time..."
"While living in your house, has there ever been any vessel broken by you, or anyone else beaten, or has excrement or urine ever been voided in an improper place? "There has not, dear father.
"Then why do you treat me with false speech? This fault is yours alone; I have no fault. Go [and deal] with him."
"Perform the miracle with two thousand [carts]; do not treat me, who am entirely innocent, with a false accusation.

Having heard his words, the brahmin went and performed the miracle with two thousand [carts], fastening a hundred carts together in the same manner as before, decorating Nandivisāla, and yoking him to the pole of the foremost cart. How did he yoke them?
Having fastened the yoke immovably at the pole, he hitched Nandivisāla by one end;
having wound the other end around the pole with a thong, he placed a wooden staff from the *muṇḍa* tree against both the end of the yoke and the axle-stand, and secured it firmly with that thong.
For when this was done, the yoke could not move either forward or backward, and it became possible [to proceed].
To pull it with only a single ox. Then the brahmin sat upon the yoke, rubbed the back of Nandivisāla, and said, "Go, noble one; draw, noble one!
The Bodhisatta, having pulled back the hundred wagons with a single impulse, placed the wagon standing behind in the position of the wagon standing in front.
The merchant Govittaka, having been defeated, gave two thousand [pieces of gold] to the brahmin.
Other people as well gave much wealth to the Bodhisatta, and all of it came to belong to the brahmin. Thus, by relying on the Bodhisatta, he obtained much wealth.

The Teacher, having rebuked the group of six monks, saying, "Monks, harsh speech is indeed not pleasing to anyone," and having laid down the training rule, spoke this verse after attaining full enlightenment:
“One should speak only what is pleasing, never what is displeasing;
for one who speaks what is pleasing, a heavy burden was lifted,
and he obtained wealth, whereby his heart was gladdened.”

In this context, "one should speak only what is agreeable" means that when speaking with another, one should speak only words that are sweet, pleasing, gentle, soft, and dear—words free from the four faults. "He lifted up a heavy burden" refers to the ox Nandivisāla;
having failed to lift the burden for one who spoke unpleasantly, he later [lifted it] for one who spoke pleasantly and with endearing words.
"He lifted a heavy burden for the brahmin; having lifted it, he dragged it and rolled it away"—this is the meaning.
Here, however, the letter *da* serves as a phonetic conjunction (*byañjanasandhi*) to join the words.

Thus the Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching beginning with "One should speak only what is pleasing," identified the Jātaka: "At that time the brahmin was Ānanda, and Nandivisāla was none other than myself."
The Eighth: The Nandivisāla Jātaka Commentary.
9. The Kaṇha Jātaka Commentary.
"Whichever way the heavy burden... This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Twin Miracle.
He related it. This, together with the descent from the heavens, will be made clear in the Sarabhamiga Jātaka in the Thera-gāthā Nipāta.

However, when the Perfectly Enlightened One, having performed the Twin Miracle and dwelt in the world of the gods for three months, descended at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa on the Great Invitation Day and entered Jetavana with a great retinue, the monks [discussed it] in the Dhamma Hall.
Having assembled, they said, "Friends, the Tathāgata is indeed peerless; there is no one else capable of carrying the burden that the Tathāgata has taken up.
Six teachers, each saying, 'We alone shall perform the miracle! We alone shall perform the miracle!
failed to perform even a single miracle. Oh, how peerless is the Teacher! Thus they spoke of the Teacher.
They sat down engaged in a discussion of his virtues. The Teacher approached and asked, "Bhikkhus, with what kind of discussion are you sitting here gathered now?
"Venerable Sir, we are not discussing any other matter; rather, we are discussing your own virtues in this manner.
The Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, now that I have laid down my burden, who will carry it? Formerly, while I was in the animal realm..."
"Even though I was reborn, I did not find anyone who was my equal," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of a cow.
Then his owners, while he was still a young calf, kept him in the house of a certain elderly woman and [provided for him] from her wages for lodging.
Having determined [the amount], they gave it to her. She, nursing him with rice gruel, food, and other provisions, raised him, treating him as her own son.
He became known by the name "Ayyikākāḷaka" (Blackie the Uncle).

When he reached maturity, he became the color of collyrium and wandered together with the village oxen; he was endowed with virtue and good conduct. The village boys would seize him by his horns, his ears, or even his neck.
They hung from him; they even took hold of his tail and played with him, or sat upon his back. One day he thought, "My mother is in a state of misery;
she raised me with great hardship, placing me in the position of a son.
What if I were to work for wages and free her from this state of poverty? From that time on, he went about seeking employment.
Then one day, a certain son of a caravan leader arrived at a difficult ford with five hundred carts;
his oxen were unable to pull the carts across, and although the oxen were yoked in a continuous line from cart to cart among those five hundred carts, they could not pull even a single cart across.
The Bodhisatta was also there nearby together with the village oxen.
He was moving along. The son of a caravan leader, whose wealth consisted of cattle, was searching for a noble bull capable of pulling these carts through the midst of the herd;
seeing the Bodhisatta, he thought, "This noble bull will be able to pull my carts; who, then, is its owner? and [he addressed] the cowherds.
He asked, "Who indeed, sir, is the owner of this? Having harnessed him to the cart, I will pay you wages once the carts have been unloaded.
They said, "Take him and harness him; there is no owner for him here in this place.
He bound him by the nose with a rope, but though he pulled, he could not even move him. It is said that the Bodhisatta...
“I will go when wages have been declared,” he said, and so he did not go.

The caravan leader’s son, understanding his intention, said, “Sir, once five hundred carts have been unloaded by you, I will give you a thousand kahāpaṇas, making the wage for each cart two kahāpaṇas.
Then the Bodhisatta went there himself. Then the men...
They yoked them to the front carts. Then, lifting him up with a single impulse, he set him down upon dry land.
By this means, he brought all the carts across.
The caravan leader’s son, having made one [man] for each cart and formed five hundred bundles of goods, gave them to him.
He tied [the cart] by the neck. Thinking, "This man does not give me my wages as agreed;
I will not let him go," he went and stood blocking the road in front of the very first cart.
Even though they strove to remove him, they were unable to do so. The caravan leader’s son thought, "He surely knows about his own wages."

Regarding the phrase "the state of deficiency": having placed two [weights] on each cart and tied them together as a bundle weighing a thousand [units], he fastened it around the neck [of Kāḷaka], saying, "This is your fee for crossing the carts.
Taking that bundle of a thousand, he went into his mother's presence.
The village children came to the Bodhisatta, asking, "What is this on the neck of the noble Kāḷaka? He followed after them.
He went into his mother’s presence, fleeing from afar. Because he had unloaded five hundred carts, he appeared exhausted, with bloodshot eyes.
When his grandmother saw the purse of a thousand coins around his neck, she asked the cowherd boy, “Dear, where did you get this?
Having heard the matter, she said, “Dear, why am I...?”
Having said, "Desiring life, why do you endure such suffering for the sake of that meager wage?
she bathed the Bodhisatta with warm water, anointed his entire body with oil, gave him a drink, and fed him suitable food;
then, at the end of her life, she departed together with the Bodhisatta according to their respective kamma.

The Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata is peerless in his burden; in the past as well, he was peerless in his burden. Having spoken thus, and having delivered this Dhamma teaching and established the connection, he, being fully enlightened, uttered this verse:
“Whenever there is a heavy burden, whenever there is a path that is deep to traverse, then they yoke the dark one; and he indeed carries that burden.”
In this context, "wherever the burden is heavy" means that in whichever place the burden is heavy and difficult to bear, other oxen are unable to lift it.
"Where the path is deep" (*gambhīravattanī*): it is called a *vattanī* because they travel (*vattanti*) upon it;
this is a name for the road. It refers to a place where, due to the great extent of water and mud, or because of unevenly cut banks, [the path is difficult].
The meaning is that the path is deep. Regarding the phrase "then they yoke Kaṇha," here *assu* is a mere particle; the meaning is "then they yoke Kaṇha.
When the burden is heavy and the path is deep, then having removed the other oxen, they yoke Kaṇha alone—this is what is meant. Regarding the phrase "he indeed carries that burden," here too...
*Assu* is merely a particle; the meaning is that he bears that burden.
Thus, having shown, "At that time, monks, Kaṇha alone bore that burden," and having established the connection, the Blessed One identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, Mahallikā was Uppalavaṇṇā, but Ayyikā-Kāḷaka was none other than myself."
The ninth *Kaṇhajātakavaṇṇanā*.
[30] 10. The *Munikajātakavaṇṇanā*:
"Do not envy the sage (*muni*)"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning the seduction of a young woman of large stature.
He related it. This will be made clear in the *Cūḷanāradakassapa Jātaka* in the *Terasakanipāta*.
The Teacher, however, asked that bhikkhu, "Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are weary? "Yes, venerable sir," he replied. "On account of what?
"On account of being seduced by a young woman of high birth, venerable sir. The Teacher said, "Bhikkhu, she has brought about your misfortune."
"Even previously, on the day of her marriage, you met your end and became a meal for the great multitude," he said,
and then related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was with a certain householder in a certain village."
He was reborn in that household in a cow-womb by the name of Mahālohita; his younger brother was named Cūḷalohita.
It was upon the basis of those two brothers alone that the burden of the household duties was sustained in that family.
In that family there was a daughter whom a certain son of a respectable family from the city had requested for his own son. Her parents—
Thinking, "There will be a special meal for the guests who come at the time of the maiden's marriage," they gave her rice gruel and food, and raised a pig named Munika.
Seeing this, Cūḷalohita asked his brother, "In this family, the burden of work is carried out depending on us two brothers; yet these people give us only grass, straw, and such."
“They are feeding the pig with rice gruel and solid food; for what reason does it receive this?
Then his brother said to him, “Dear Cūḷalohita, do not envy its food. This pig is eating its death meal.
For at the time of this young woman’s marriage, it will serve as the *uttaribhaṅga* (afternoon refreshment) for the guests who have come.”
"These people are raising this pig; after a few days have passed, those men will come here,
and then you will see them seize that pig by its feet, drag it out from under the bed, put it to death,
and prepare it as a curry and condiment for their guests," and having said this, he spoke this verse:
"Do not envy the monk who eats choice foods;
eat chaff without anxiety—this is the mark of long life.
In this context, "do not envy the monk" means do not give rise to longing for the monk's food, thinking, "This monk eats fine food..."
"Do not envy the sage because he eats [fine food]," nor should you aspire to the state of a sage thinking, "When indeed shall I too become so happy?
For this one eats the food of the sick; "food of the sick" means meals that lead to death. "Carelessly eat the chaff":
being indifferent toward his meal, eat the chaff that you yourself have obtained.
"This is the mark of long life" means this is the cause for the state of long life. Not long after that, those men arrived;
having killed the sage, they cooked him in various ways. The Bodhisatta said to Cūḷalohita, "My dear, have you seen the sage?
"I have seen him, brother," he replied, "the food-fruit of the sage; from eating this..."
“By a hundredfold, by a thousandfold, it is merely a handful of our straw and chaff, yet it is supreme, blameless, and possesses the characteristic of long life.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, saying, “Thus indeed, monk, even in the past you met your end because of this girl,
yet you became a source of superior refreshment for the great multitude,” the Teacher proclaimed the Truths.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the weary monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
The Teacher, having drawn out the connection, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the boar Munika was the weary monk;
the young woman Thullakumārikā was this very person; Cūḷalohita was Ānanda, and Mahālohita was indeed myself."
The tenth: The Commentary on the Munikajaṭaka.
The third chapter: The Kuruṅga Chapter.
Its summary (uddāna) is as follows:
The kuruṅga deer, the dog, the well-bred Bhoja steed, the thoroughbred, the ford, the woman’s face repeatedly, Nandikaṇha, and the Sage’s desire—this is the Kulāvakavagga. 4.108–117.
The Chapter on the Bird’s Nest.
[31] 1. The Commentary on the *Kulāvakajātaka*. Regarding the phrase "The Bird’s Nest":
this was related by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning a bhikkhu who had drunk water without straining it.
It is said that two young bhikkhu friends from Sāvatthī, having gone to a certain region, settled in a comfortable place.
Having stayed there according to their inclinations with the thought, "We shall see the Perfectly Enlightened One," they departed from there once more and set out toward the Jeta Grove.
One of them had a water-strainer in his hand, while the other did not. Both would strain the water together and drink.
One day they fell into a dispute; the owner of the water-strainer refused to give his strainer to the other.
Having strained the water himself, he drank; the other, however, being unable to endure his thirst because he could not find a strainer, drank the water without straining it.
Both of them eventually reached Jetavana, where they paid homage to the Teacher and sat down.
After the Teacher had exchanged greetings with them, he asked, "From where have you come?"
“Venerable sir, we lived in a certain village in the Kosala country, and having departed from there, we have come to see you.

“But have you come together in harmony? The one without a water-strainer said, “Venerable sir, this man quarreled with me on the way and did not give me his water-strainer. The other also said, “This man…”

“Venerable sir, did you knowingly drink water containing living beings without first straining it? “Is it true, monk, that you knowingly drank water containing living beings? “Yes, venerable sir, I drank unstrained water.
The Teacher said, “Monk, in the past, when wise men were ruling in the city of the gods and fled by way of the ocean’s surface after being defeated in battle...”

"Having renounced such great glory, saying, 'We will not commit the slaughter of living beings out of reliance on our sovereignty,' they turned back their chariot after granting life to the young garuḍas," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Magadha, a king of Magadha reigned in Rājagaha. At that time, the Bodhisatta—just as...
In a previous existence, Sakka was born in the kingdom of Magadha in the village of Macala;
likewise, he was now born in that very same village of Macala as the son of a great family. On the day of his naming, they gave him the name "Magha Kumāra.
When he reached maturity, he became known as "the young brahmin Magha. Then his parents [sought a wife] from a family of equal caste...
They brought a daughter for him. As he grew up with sons and daughters, he became a patron of almsgiving and observed the five precepts.
In that village there were exactly thirty-three families; on one occasion, those thirty-three families stood in the middle of the village and performed their communal work.
The Bodhisatta, having cleared away the dust from the ground with his feet at the spot where he was standing, [prepared] that place...
Having made that spot beautiful, he stood there; then another person came and stood in that place.
The Bodhisatta made another spot beautiful and stood there, and yet another person stood there as well.
The Bodhisatta likewise made every spot where anyone was standing beautiful, and at a later time, he had a pavilion constructed in that place.
Having removed even the pavilion, he had a hall built; there, having spread out wooden seats, he placed a water jar.
At another time, those thirty-three people also came to share the same resolve as the Bodhisatta.
Having established them in the five precepts, the Bodhisatta thereafter wandered about performing meritorious deeds together with them.
Performing meritorious deeds together with him, they would rise early in the morning and, with axes, hatchets, and pestles in hand,
would turn stones with pestles at the four great crossroads and other places; they would remove trees that obstructed the axles of vehicles,
level uneven ground, construct bridges, dig lotus ponds, build halls, and give gifts.
They guarded their moral precepts (*sīla*). Thus, for the most part, all the inhabitants of the village remained established in the Bodhisatta’s instruction and guarded their moral precepts.

Then the village headman thought: “Formerly, when these people were drinking liquor and committing acts such as taking life, I used to obtain wealth from them through fines for broken pots, coins, and so forth, as well as through forced labor. But now, with the young man Magha...”
"He keeps them from violating the precepts; he does not allow them to commit acts such as taking life. But now, I shall no longer have them observe the five precepts.
Thus speaking, the enraged man approached the king and said, "Your Majesty, many thieves are wandering about committing village raids and other such crimes.
Upon hearing his words, the king said, "Go, bring them here. He went and [brought] all of them...
Having bound them and brought them back, they reported to the king, "The thieves have been brought, Your Majesty.
Without investigating their case, the king said, "Have them trampled by an elephant. Then, having laid them all down in the royal courtyard, they brought in the elephant.
The Bodhisatta gave them this advice: "You should reflect upon your own virtues, as well as upon the slanderer and the king."
“Cultivate loving-kindness toward the elephant and your own body as being exactly the same. They did so.
Then they brought an elephant to trample them. Even when it was being led toward them, it would not approach;
letting out a great cry, it fled. They brought another elephant, and those [monks] likewise fled.
The king, thinking, "There must be some medicine in their hands," said, "Search for it.
While searching, they did not find it and said, "There is none, Your Majesty. [The king thought: "In that case, they will surely recite some mantra;
ask them, 'Do you have a recitation-mantra? The king's men asked, and the Bodhisatta said, "I do. The king's men...
“There seems to be a spell, O King,” they reported. The king summoned them all and said, “Tell me the spell you know.
The Bodhisatta replied, “Your Majesty, we have no other so-called spell;
however, we thirty-three people do not take life, we do not take what is not given, we do not engage in sexual misconduct, and we do not speak falsehoods.”
"We do not speak [harshly], we do not drink intoxicants, we cultivate loving-kindness, we give gifts, we level the roads, we dig lotus ponds, and we plant sal trees;
this is our mantra, our protection, and our prosperity.
The king, being pleased with them, gave all the household wealth of the slanderer to them and made him their slave.
He gave both the elephant and the village to those very people.

From that time forward, performing meritorious deeds according to their inclination, they summoned a carpenter and began the construction of a great hall (*sāla*), thinking, "We shall have a great hall built at the crossroads. However, because of their lack of desire for women...
They did not grant a share of the sal-tree hall to women. At that time, there were four women in the Bodhisatta’s household: Sudhammā, Cittā, Nandā, and Sujātā.
Among them, Sudhammā conspired with the carpenter, saying, “Brother, make me the chief pillar of this sal-tree hall,” and she gave him a bribe. He replied, “Very well.”
Having accepted it, he first dried the pillar-tree, cut it down, bored it out, completed the pillar, wrapped it in cloth, and set it aside.
Then, after the hall was finished and it was time to install the pillar, he said, "Oh, masters, we have forgotten one thing! "What is that, sir? "We need a pillar."
“Let it be; we shall bring one. “It is not possible now to make one from a tree that has been cut down;
it is necessary to obtain a socket-block that was previously cut, planed, and bored and set aside. “What should be done now?
“If there is a socket-block for sale that someone has finished making and kept in their house, it should be sought out. While they were searching, it occurred to them:
Having seen her in the Sudhammā hall, they could not obtain her for even the price of her root.
When he said, "If you make me the master of the hall, I will give [it]," they replied, "We do not give our daughters to women.
Then the carpenter said to them, "Noble sirs, what are you saying? Apart from the Brahma-world, there is no other place devoid of women."
“There is no name; take the corner-stone. This being done, our work will reach completion.
Saying “Very well,” they took the corner-stone, finished the hall, spread out the wooden seats, set out water-jars, and prepared the rice-gruel and food.
Having surrounded the hall with a wall and fitted it with a door, [they arranged] within the enclosure—
Having scattered sand, they planted rows of palm trees along the outer wall. Citta also had a garden constructed in that place;
there was no flowering or fruit-bearing tree of which it could be said, "Such-and-such a tree is not there.
Nandā also had a lotus pond constructed in that very same place, beautiful and covered with five-colored lotuses. Sujā did nothing at all.

The Bodhisatta, having fulfilled these seven precepts— namely, service to his mother, service to his father, honoring those who are senior in the family, truthful speech, gentle speech, non-slanderous speech,
and the removal of stinginess— declared: “The person who supports his mother and father, Who honors those who are senior in the family,
Who speaks gently and kindly, And has abandoned slander.”
“The man who is intent on the subduing of stinginess, who is truthful, and who has overcome anger—
him indeed the gods of the Thirty-three call a ‘true man.
Having thus attained a state worthy of praise, at the end of his life he became Sakka, the king of the gods, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
He was reborn there, and his three companions were also reborn in that very same place. At that time, the asuras were dwelling in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Sakka, the king of the gods, thought, "What is the use of sovereignty shared with others?

He had the asuras drink divine liquor until they were intoxicated, and while they were in that state, he seized them by their feet and hurled them down to the base of Mount Sineru. They landed right back in the asura realm.
The realm of the asuras, called Asurabhavana, is at the base of Sineru and is equal in size to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
There, like the pāricchattaka tree of the devas, there is an eternal tree named Cittapāṭali.
When the Cittapāṭali tree blooms, they know: "This is not our own deva-world; for it is in the deva-world that the pāricchattaka tree flowers. Then they...
“Jarasakka, having intoxicated us and cast us onto the back of the great ocean, seized our celestial city;
we shall now fight with him and reclaim our own celestial city. Thus they rose up, crawling along Mount Sineru like ants upon a pillar.
When Sakka heard that “the asuras have indeed risen up,” he remained right there on the surface of the ocean.
Having advanced and engaged in battle, being defeated by them, he began to flee across the surface of the southern ocean in his Vejayanta chariot, which was one hundred and fifty yojanas long.
As his chariot traveled with great speed over the surface of the ocean, it entered a forest of *simbali* trees;
along its path of travel, the *simbali* forest was cut away piece by piece, like a forest of reeds, and fell onto the surface of the ocean.
It fell. As the young garuḍas were falling upon the surface of the ocean, they let out a great cry.
Sakka asked Mātali, "Friend Mātali, what is this sound? A most piteous wailing is occurring.
"Your Majesty, the young garuḍas, crushed by the speed of your chariot and falling upon the *simbali* grove, are crying out with a single voice, terrified by the fear of death."
The Great Being said, “Friend Mātali, let them not suffer because of us;
we do not commit the act of killing living beings out of a desire for power. Rather, for their sake, we shall sacrifice our own lives and give ourselves to the asuras.
Turn back this chariot! Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“O Mātali, avoid the nestlings in the *simbala* tree with the front of the chariot-pole!
We would rather give up our lives among the asuras than let these birds become nestless.
Therein, “nestlings” refers to the young of the *supaṇṇas*. “Mātali” is how he addressed the charioteer. “In the *simbala* tree”—look!
This shows that these *simbali* trees are standing hanging down. "Avoid them with the front of the pole" means:
you should avoid them in such a way that they are not struck by the front of this chariot's pole.

"We would gladly give up our lives among the asuras" means: if, while we are giving up our lives for the sake of the asuras, their safety is secured, then we would gladly give up [our lives] with absolute certainty.
"We shall sacrifice our lives among the Asuras. Let these birds not be 'homeless' (vikulāvā);
let these young Garuḍas not be rendered homeless by the destruction and crushing of their nests. Do not hurl suffering upon them;
turn back, turn back the chariot! Having heard his words, the charioteer Mātali—
Having turned the chariot back, he set it on another path toward the world of the gods.
But when the asuras saw him turning back, they thought, "Surely others from other world-systems are coming; having gained strength, the chariot must have been turned back.
Terrified by the fear of death, they fled and entered the asura realm itself.
Sakka, too, having entered the city of the gods, stood in the center of the city surrounded by the hosts of devas from two celestial realms.
At that moment, the Vejayanta Palace, a thousand yojanas in height, rose up, splitting the earth.
Because it arose at the Vejayanta [gate], they gave it the name "Vejayanta. Then Sakka, for the purpose of preventing the asuras from returning, [acted].
He established protection at five places. With reference to this, it was said:
“Between the two cities of Ayujjhana, Fivefold protection was established:
The Uragas, Karoṭapāṇas, and Hārītīs, And the four great [Nāgas] with ten thousand Madanas.”
Because both cities could not be captured by means of war, they became known as "Cities of No Battle," namely the city of the gods and the city of the asuras.
For when the asuras were powerful, the gods would flee and enter the city of the gods;
once the gates were closed, even a hundred thousand asuras would be unable to do anything. When the gods...
When they become powerful, they flee from the Asuras and enter the city of the Asuras;
once the gates are closed, even a hundred thousand Sakkas are unable to do anything. Thus, these two cities are called "invincible.
Between them, at these five locations—beginning with the Uraga—Sakka has stationed a guard. Therein, by the word "Uraga" (serpent)...
