The *nāgas* are included. They are powerful in the water; therefore, their protection is on the first terrace of Sineru.
By the word *karoṭi*, the *supaṇṇas* are included. It is said that their food and drink is called *karoṭi*;
they received that name because of it. Their protection is on the second terrace. By the word *payassahāri*, the *kumbhaṇḍas* are included. [Also] the *dānavas* and *rakkhasas*.
In the second gallery, their protection is provided. By the word *madanayuta*, the *yakkhas* are included;

they are said to be of uneven conduct and fond of battle, and in the third gallery, their protection is provided. "And the four great ones" refers to the four Great Kings (*mahārājāno*), and in the fourth gallery, their protection is provided.
Therefore, if the *asuras*, provoked and with turbid minds, approach the city of the gods...
Of the five terraces of the mountain, it is upon the first that the serpents stand surrounding it;

likewise for the others in their respective places. Having established a guard at these five locations while Sakka, lord of the gods, was enjoying his divine splendor, Sudhammā passed away from that state and was reborn as his very footmaiden, by virtue of the merit she had bestowed upon Kaṇṇikā.
From that [merit], there arose a divine assembly hall named Sudhammā, five hundred yojanas in extent, where Sakka, lord of the devas,
sits upon a golden throne one yojana in size beneath a divine white parasol and performs the duties to be done for both devas and humans.
Cittā, too, having passed away, was reborn as his personal attendant due to the residual result of her work on the pleasure grove.
From her, a pleasure grove named Cittalatāvana arose. Nandā, having passed away, was reborn as his attendant for that tree;
and from the overflow of the lotus pond, a lotus pond named Nandā arose for her.
But Sujā, because she had not performed wholesome deeds, was reborn in a certain forest ravine as a female crane.
Sakka, thinking, “Sujā is not to be seen; where has she been reborn?

and perceiving her with his supernormal knowledge, went there, took her, and returned to the world of the gods. Having shown her the delightful city of the gods, the Sudhamma assembly hall, the Cittalatā grove, and the Nandā lotus pond, he said, “Having performed wholesome deeds, she has been reborn here as my attendant.”
"But you, having failed to perform wholesome deeds, have been reborn in the animal realm; from now on, guard your virtue," he advised her.
Having thus established her in the five precepts, he led her back to that very place and released her.
From then on, she guarded her virtue. After a few days had passed, Sakka wondered, "Is it possible for her to guard her virtue? and went there in the form of a jackal.
Lying on her back, she lay down before him; thinking it was a dead fish, she seized it by the head.
The fish wagged its tail, whereupon she released it, thinking, "I believe it is alive. Sakka said, "Excellent, excellent! You will be able to guard your virtue," and departed.
Having passed away from there, she was reborn in a potter's house in Bārāṇasī.
Sakka, wondering "Where have they been reborn?", realized their state of rebirth there.
Filling a cart with golden plantains (*eḷāluka*), he sat in the middle of the village in the guise of an old man and shouted, "Take the plantains! Take the plantains!
People came and said, "Give them to us, dear sir. He replied, "I give them to those who guard their virtue; you..."
“Guard your virtue! [They replied: “We do not know what is called virtue; give us the price. [He said: “I have no need for a price;
I give only to those who guard their virtue. The people, thinking, “Who is this Eḷāluka? departed.
When Sujā heard of this occurrence, she thought, “It will be brought to me,” and having gone there, she said to him, “Give it to me, dear father.”
He asked, "Mother, do you observe the precepts? "Yes, I observe them," she replied.
"I have brought this specifically for your sake," he said, and having set it down at the door of her house along with a carriage, he departed.
She too, having observed the precepts for as long as she lived, passed away from there and was reborn as the daughter of Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras.

Due to the fruit of her virtue, she became beautiful. When she reached marriageable age, he assembled the asuras, saying, "Let my daughter choose for herself a husband according to her own heart's desire.
Sakka, looking about to see where she had been reborn, learned that she had been reborn there and thought, "If Sujā chooses a husband according to her heart's desire, she will choose me."
Having assumed the form of an asura, he went there. They adorned Sujā, brought her to the assembly place, and said, "Choose a husband according to your heart's desire.
As she looked about, she saw Sakka; her heart was overwhelmed, as if by a great flood, by the love that had arisen even before through the power of past affection.
Saying, "This is my husband," she threw a garland of flowers over him.

Having hurled him, he seized him. The asuras, feeling ashamed, departed, thinking, "Our king, having failed to find a suitable husband for his daughter for so long, has now found one; this very man, though older than her grandfather, is indeed suitable for her.
He brought her to that celestial city and, making her the senior among two and a half million female dancers, lived there for the duration of his lifespan.
Having stood there, he departed according to his karma.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "In this way, Bhikkhu, in the past, when wise men were ruling in the city of the gods, they did not commit the taking of life even at the cost of their own lives; yet you, for your part, [act] in such a manner..."
Having gone forth in the dispensation that leads to liberation, will you drink water that is unstrained and contains living beings?
Having thus rebuked that bhikkhu, the Teacher connected the narrative and identified the Jātaka, saying:
“At that time Mātalisaṅgāhaka was Ānanda, and Sakka was none other than myself.”
The First Explanation: The *Kulāvakajātaka*.
[32] 2. The Explanation of the *Naccajātaka*: "Weeping is charming.
This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who possessed many belongings.
He related the story. The background of the case was exactly as told previously in the *Devadhamma Jātaka*.
The Teacher asked that monk, "Is it true, monk, that you possess many belongings? "Yes, venerable sir," he replied.
"For what reason, monk, have you come to possess so many belongings? Upon hearing this much, he became angry, cast off his lower and upper robes, and said, "By this..."
“Now I shall wander about naked,” he said, and stood before the Teacher stark naked. People cried out, “Shame! Shame!

He fled from there and returned to the lower life as a layman. The monks, having assembled in the Dhamma Hall, spoke in dispraise of him, saying, “How could one act in such a manner right before the Teacher? The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, what is it that you are discussing here?”
“Monks, for what discussion have you been sitting together now? he asked the monks. “Venerable Sir, we were sitting discussing his lack of virtue, saying:
‘Indeed, that monk, having cast aside shame and dread of blame in your presence before the fourfold assembly, stood naked like a village boy while being reviled by the people;
he has returned to the lower life and fallen away from the Dispensation.’”
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that this monk has fallen away from the Jewel of the Dispensation due to a lack of moral shame and fear of wrongdoing;
in the past, he fell away even from the possession of the Woman-Jewel. Having said this, he related a story of the past:
In the first eon, four-footed creatures made the lion their king, fish made the Ānanda-fish their king, and birds made the golden swan their king.
Now, that daughter of the golden swan-king was a beautiful young female swan.
He granted her a boon, and she chose as her husband one who pleased her own heart. Having granted her the boon, the swan-king caused all the birds in the Himalayas to assemble;
various flocks of birds, such as swans, peacocks, and others, having gathered together in one great place—
They gathered together on the surface of the rock. The swan-king summoned his daughter, saying, "Let her come and choose as her husband the one who pleases her heart.
As she surveyed the flock of birds, she saw a peacock with a neck the color of jewels and variegated plumage;
seeing him, she declared, "Let this one be my husband. The flock of birds approached the peacock and said, "Friend..."
“O peacock, this princess, choosing from among so many birds, has conceived a desire for you as her husband.

Thinking, “Even now she does not see my strength,” the peacock, overcome with excessive joy, broke his sense of shame and modesty and began to dance in the midst of that great assembly of birds, spreading his wings; as he danced, he became completely uncovered.
The Golden Goose King was ashamed and thought, "In him there is no moral shame (*hirī*) arising from within, nor any dread of blame (*ottappa*) arising from without;
since his shame and dread of blame are destroyed, I will not give my daughter to him. Then, in the midst of the assembly of birds, he spoke this verse:
"His cry is charming, his back is beautiful, and his neck resembles the color of beryl;"
"And your tail-feathers are a fathom in length; because of this dance, I will not give you my daughter. In this context, *rudaṃ* is for *manuññaṃ*;
the letter *ta* has been changed to *da*. The meaning is: "the cry is pleasing," that is, the sound of the song is sweet.
And "your back is radiant" means that your back is both variegated and beautiful. It resembles the color of beryl.
They were like the color of beryl gems. "Byāmamattāni" means measuring one *vyāma* (the distance between the tips of the fingers when the arms are extended). "Pekhuṇāni" means tail-feathers.

"I will not give my daughter to you because of your dancing"—having thus spoken, breaking through his sense of shame and modesty (*hirī-ottappa*), saying, "I will not give my daughter to such a shameless man simply because of your dancing," the King of Swans, right there in the midst of the assembly, [addressed] his own nephew...
He gave his daughter to the young swan. The peacock, unable to obtain the young female swan and feeling ashamed, flew up from that very spot and fled.
The king of the swans also returned to his own dwelling place.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that this one, having broken his sense of shame and dread of blame, has fallen away from the precious Dispensation; formerly, too, he did so."
Having brought forward this teaching on the Dhamma, "He has indeed fallen away from the attainment of the Woman-Jewel," and having established the connection, he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time the peacock was Bahubhaṇḍika, while I myself was the king of the swans.
This is the second commentary on the Nacca-jātaka.
[33] 3. The Commentary on the *Sammodamāna-jātaka*. "Being in harmony" (*sammodamānā*):
this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at the Nigrodha Monastery near Kapilavatthu, concerning a dispute over a sandal.
This will be made clear in the *Kuṇāla-jātaka*. At that time, however, the Teacher addressed his kinsmen.
“Great King, it is not fitting for kinsmen to engage in mutual strife.
For even animals, when they were previously in harmony, overcame their enemies and attained safety; but when they fell into dispute, they met with great destruction.
Having said this, being requested by the royal kinsmen, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares,
the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a quail and lived in the forest surrounded by many thousands of quails. At that time, a quail-trapper went to their dwelling place,
imitated the cry of a quail, and having discerned that they had gathered together, he cast a net over them.
Gathering all those within reach, he would place them together, fill his basket, go home, sell them, and maintain his livelihood with the proceeds.
Then one day, the Bodhisatta said to those quails:
"This fowler is bringing destruction upon our kin; I know a stratagem by which he will not be able to capture us."
“From this moment on, as soon as he casts the net over you, each of you should place your head under one mesh, lift the net, carry it to the desired location, and throw it into a thicket of thorns.
When that is done, we shall escape from beneath by various routes. They all replied, “Very well.”

On the second day, when the net was cast over them, they lifted the net in the same manner as described by the Bodhisatta, threw it into a thicket of thorns, and fled from there in various directions by way of the lower part.
Even as the fowler was unfastening the net from the thicket, evening fell; he returned with empty hands.
From the following day onwards, the crows did exactly the same.
He too, releasing the net until sunset, returned home empty-handed, having obtained nothing. Then his wife, becoming angry, said:
"Day after day you return with empty hands; surely there is some other place abroad where you must support someone else?"
"I think so," she said. The fowler replied, "My dear lady, I have no other means of support;
moreover, these quails move about in harmony. As soon as I throw my net, they take it up and cast it into a thicket of brambles and depart.
However, they will not remain in harmony for all time; do not worry."
“When they fall into a dispute, I shall come taking them all with me, making your face smile,” he said,
and then spoke this verse to his wife:
“Birds go along in harmony, carrying their web together;”
"When they fall into dispute, then they will come under my power.

In this context, "when they fall into dispute" means at whatever time those partridges, having held various views and various opinions, shall fall into dispute—that is, they shall engage in quarreling. "Then they will come under my power" means at that time, all of them...
"They will come under my control; then, having captured them, I shall return while making you laugh," he reassured his wife.
But after only a few days had passed, one of the cranes, descending upon the feeding ground, failed to notice another.
He stepped on his head, and the other became angry, thinking, "Who has stepped on my head? Even when the first said, "I stepped on you unintentionally;
do not be angry," the other remained angry. As they spoke to one another again and again, they fell into a dispute, saying, "It seems it was you who threw the net!
While they were thus quarreling, the Bodhisatta thought, "There is no safety for those who quarrel."
"There is no safety for you now; they will not lift their net yet, but then you will meet with great destruction.
The fowler will find his opportunity; I cannot remain in this place.
Taking his own flock with him, he went elsewhere. After a few days had passed, the fowler returned and called out the quail's cry.
As they were gathered together, he threw a net over them. Then one quail said, "It is said that while you were throwing the net, feathers fell upon your head;
throw it now! Another said, "It is said that while you were throwing the net, wings fell upon both your sides; throw it now! Thus they said to one another, "You throw it! You [throw it]!"
Even as they were saying, "Lift it up!", the fowler lifted his net, gathered them all together, filled his basket, and went home making his wife laugh.
The Teacher said, "Thus, Great King, quarreling among kinsmen is not fitting; quarrel is indeed the root of destruction."
Having brought forth this teaching on the Dhamma and established the connection, he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the foolish Vaṭṭaka was Devadatta, while the wise Vaṭṭaka was none other than myself.
This is the third commentary, the Sammodamāna-jātaka.
[34] 4. The Commentary on the Fish Jātaka.
“Neither cold nor heat affects me”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the seduction by a former wife.
At that time, the Teacher asked that bhikkhu, “Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are weary of the religious life?”
The Teacher asked him, "Is it true, bhikkhu? "It is true, Blessed One," he replied. "By whom were you made despondent? "My former wife, venerable sir, has sweet hands and a sweet touch;
I am unable to abandon her. Then the Teacher said to him, "Bhikkhu, this woman is a bringer of harm to you.
In the past as well, because of her, you nearly met death, but by coming to me, you escaped from death."
Having said, "He is released," he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his domestic chaplain.
At that time, fishermen cast a net into the river. Then, one large fish, out of passion, [remained] with his own mate.
He came along playing. As he went, that female fish, moving ahead of him, smelled the scent of the net and avoided it.
But that greedy, lustful fish, intoxicated by sensual desire, entered right into the belly of the net.
When the fishermen realized that he had entered the net, they hauled it up, caught the fish, and without killing it, [placed it] on the surface of the sand.
Having thrown it down, they think, "We will cook this over coals and eat it," and they prepare the coals and carve the spit. The fish thinks:
"Neither this heating over coals, nor this piercing by the spit, nor any other suffering troubles me;
rather, it is that grief which this female fish falls into because she thinks, 'Surely he has gone elsewhere for pleasure,' that truly [troubles] me."
Lamenting, "It oppresses me," he spoke this verse:
"It is neither cold for me nor hot for me; the net does not oppress me.
But that which the female fish thinks of me, it has gone to another for pleasure."
In that regard, "it is not cold for me, it is not hot for me": when the fish are pulled out of the water, it is cold;
when that has passed, it is hot. Referring to both of these, he laments, "neither cold nor heat afflicts me.
And referring also to the suffering that will arise from being roasted on embers, he says, "it is not hot for me."
She laments. She laments, thinking: "The entanglement in the net does not oppress me;
even that oppression which was mine in the net no longer oppresses me. Regarding the passage beginning with "And what [of me]," this is the summarized meaning:
that female fish, unaware that I had fallen into the net and been seized by these fishermen, and not seeing me, [thought]: "That fish now [seeks] another..."
Thinking, “He will go to enjoy sensual pleasures with Mācchī,” he laments while lying on a bed of sand, distressed by her sorrowful thoughts.
At that time, the chaplain, surrounded by his servants, arrived at the riverbank for the purpose of bathing; he was one who understood the cries of all creatures.
It happened thus. Having heard the fish’s lamentation, it occurred to him: "This fish is lamenting under the influence of defilements;
indeed, with such a distressed mind as he dies, he will be reborn in hell. I shall be his refuge. Thinking this, he went to the fishermen and said:
"O sirs, [do not give] even a single day's worth of fish for our sauce..."
"Do not give it," he said. The fishermen replied, "What are you saying, sir? Take whichever fish pleases you and go.
"We have no other work; give us this one alone. "Take it, sir," they said.
The Bodhisatta took it with both hands, sat down on the riverbank, and said, "O fish, if today I [do not... "
“May you pass away; may you meet with the end of life. From this moment forth, do not be subject to the defilements.
Having thus exhorted him, he released him into the water, bathed, and entered the city.
After the Teacher had delivered this Dhamma instruction, he proclaimed the Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, the bhikkhu who was despondent—
He was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher, having connected the narrative thread, identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the female fish was the former wife; the fish was the discontented monk; and the chaplain was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Maccha Jātaka, the fourth.
[35] 5. The Commentary on the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka.
"There are wings, yet they do not fly"—this the Teacher spoke concerning the extinguishing of a forest fire while wandering on tour among the Magadhans.
For at one time, while the Teacher was wandering on tour among the Magadhans, he arrived at a certain village of the Magadhans.
Having walked for alms and returned from his almsround after the meal, the Blessed One set out on the road surrounded by a company of monks.

At that time, a great conflagration broke out; many monks were seen both ahead and behind him, and that fire, with a single column of smoke and a single crest of flame, was indeed advancing, spreading along its course. Thereupon, some monks who were worldlings...
Terrified by the fear of death, they thought, "We shall provide a counter-fire; thus, the other fire will not spread to the place already burnt.
Having brought out fire-sticks, they prepared a fire. Others said, "Friends, what are you doing?
[It is like trying to stop] the lunar disk situated in the midst of the sky, adorned with a thousand rays, as it rises from the eastern world-system."

“Just as those standing on the shore at the time of high tide do not see the ocean, or those standing near Sineru do not see Sineru itself, so too you do not look upon the Perfectly Enlightened One—the Supreme Person in the world with its devas—who is traveling together with you;
yet you say, ‘Let us give a counter-fire. You do not know what is called the power of a Buddha. Come, let us go into the presence of the Teacher.”
Both those going in front and those following, all together as one, approached the presence of the One of Ten Powers.
The Teacher, surrounded by a great community of bhikkhus, stood in a certain place. The forest fire was approaching, roaring as if overwhelming everything.
Having arrived and reached the spot where the Tathāgata was standing, that region—
Reaching a distance of sixteen cubits on all sides, it was extinguished like a grass torch dropped into water;
it was unable to spread beyond a distance of thirty-two cubits.
The bhikkhus began to speak of the Teacher’s virtues: "Oh, how great are the virtues of the Buddhas! For this [fire], though indeed insentient..."
“The fire is unable to spread through the place where the Buddhas stand; it is extinguished like a grass torch in water.
Oh, such is the power of the Buddhas! When the Teacher heard their talk, he said:
“Monks, this is not my power now, by which this fire is extinguished upon reaching this spot of ground. Rather, this is my ancient power of truth.”
"For in this place, throughout this entire aeon, fire shall not burn; this is called the 'aeon-lasting miracle,'" he said.

Then the Venerable Ānanda spread out his outer robe folded fourfold for the Teacher to sit upon, and the Teacher sat down, having crossed his legs in the lotus posture. The community of monks also paid homage to the Tathāgata and stood surrounding him.
He sat down. Then the Teacher, being requested by the monks, saying, "Venerable sir, this much is indeed manifest to us, but the past is hidden;
please make that manifest to us," brought forth a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Magadha, in that very same place, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of a quail.
Born from his mother’s womb, at the time he emerged after breaking out of the eggshell, he was a round young bird the size of a large ball.
Then his parents placed him in a nest and nourished him by bringing food with their beaks.
He possessed the power to travel through the air by spreading his wings, and the power to move on land by lifting his feet.
Or else there was none. That place was seized by forest fires year after year;

on this occasion as well, a great fire seized that place while roaring with a mighty roar. Flocks of birds, emerging from their respective nests and terrified by the fear of death, fled while crying out;
the parents of the Bodhisatta were likewise terrified by the fear of death.
They abandoned the Bodhisatta and fled. The Bodhisatta, still lying in his nest, raised his neck and, seeing the fire approaching while spreading out its wings, thought:
"If I possessed the power to fly through the air by stretching out my wings, I would leap up and go elsewhere. If I possessed the power to move by lifting my feet..."
"Perhaps, by taking a step in another direction, I might go elsewhere. My parents too, terrified by the fear of death, have fled, abandoning me alone to save themselves. Now I have no other refuge;
I am without protection and without shelter. What indeed should I do today?"
Then this thought occurred to him: "In this world there is such a thing as the quality of virtue (sīla); there is such a thing as the quality of truth (sacca).

In the past, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramitā) and sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree, they attained full enlightenment; they were perfected in virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
they were endowed with truth, compassion, pity, and patience; they cultivated loving-kindness (mettā) that radiated equally toward all beings; they were omniscient Buddhas."
There are indeed those [qualities] called the virtues of the Dhamma realized by them, and there is also one truth in me;
one existing phenomenon of intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma) is discerned.

Therefore, having recollected both the Buddhas of the past and the virtues realized by them, and having taken up the truth and the phenomenon of intrinsic nature existing within me, perform an act of truth (saccakiriya) toward the fire.
“Having made them retreat, it is fitting for me today to ensure the safety of both myself and the rest of the birds. Thus it was said:
“There is in the world the virtue of morality, truth, purity, and compassion;
by that truth, I shall perform an unsurpassed act of truth (saccakiriya).”
“Having reflected upon the power of the Dhamma and recalled the Conquerors of old,
and having relied upon the power of truth, he performed an act of truth.

Then the Bodhisatta, having reflected upon the virtues of the Buddhas who had attained final nibbāna in the past, uttered this verse while performing an act of truth concerning the true nature existing within himself:
“There are wings that do not fly; there are feet that do not run;
mother and father have departed; O Jātaveda, turn back!
Regarding this, “there are wings that do not fly” means: I indeed possess what are called wings, they are found, yet it is not possible [to fly].

"By these [means], to leap up and go through the air" means *apatanā*. "There are feet that do not deceive" means that although I have feet, it is impossible to deceive them by going on foot; thus they are "non-deceptive.
"And mother and father have departed" means that even those who would have led me elsewhere have themselves departed out of fear of death. "Jātavedas" refers to fire.
He speaks. For he, once born, feels and is conscious; therefore he is called "Jātavedo" (the Knower of Birth).
"Go back," he commands Jātavedo, meaning "depart" or "turn back.
Thus the Great Being thought: "If I have wings, and if, having spread them, I do not fall through the air..."

“The existence of my feet, the fact that they have not been cut off, and the truth that my parents abandoned me right there in the nest and fled—all this is real and of its very nature, O Jātaveda! By this truth, may you withdraw from here!
While still lying in the nest, he performed this act of truth (*saccakiriya*). Simultaneously with the performance of that act of truth, within an area of sixteen *karīsa*—
At that place, Jātaveda retreated. As he retreated, he did not go elsewhere while still burning;
rather, like a torch plunged into water, he was extinguished right there. Therefore it is said:
"As soon as my truth was spoken, the great, blazing flame..."
"He extinguished sixteen karīsas [of land], like a fire that has reached water.

Furthermore, because that spot could not be overcome by fire even throughout this entire eon (*kappa*), it became known as the "Eon-lasting Miracle" (*kappaṭṭhiya-pāṭihāriya*). Thus, having performed an act of truth (*saccakiriya*), the Bodhisatta passed away at the end of his life and went according to his karma.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it was not my power alone that prevented this forest from being overwhelmed by fire; rather—"
"This power of truth was mine even in the past, when I was a young crane," saying this, the Teacher brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths.
At the conclusion of the Truths, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some attained Arahatship.
The Teacher, having established the connection, identified the Jātaka.
—“At that time, the parents were none other than my own parents of the present day, while Vaṭṭaka the king was indeed myself.
The fifth, the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka, is concluded.
[36] 6. The Sakuṇa Jātaka Commentary.
"Depending on what": This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a monk whose leaf-hut had been burned down.

It is said that a certain monk, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, departed from Jetavana and dwelt in a forest lodging near a frontier village in the Kosala country. Then, in the very first month, [a fire broke out].
The leaf-hut caught fire. He informed the people, saying, "My leaf-hut has been burnt;
it is difficult for me to live here. The people said, "Now our field will dry up; we shall irrigate the furrows and work it. When it had been irrigated, they said, "We shall sow the seed.
When the seed had been sown, they said, "We shall build a fence. When the fence had been built, they said, "We shall sleep, reap, thresh, and trample [the grain]."
Thus they spent those three months merely making excuses for various acts.
That bhikkhu, having lived uncomfortably in the open air during the three months, was unable to develop his meditation subject and achieve any distinction.
But after the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side. The Teacher exchanged greetings with him.
Having done so, he asked, "Monk, did you spend the rains retreat happily? Has your meditation subject reached its culmination?
He explained the situation and said, "Because of the lack of a suitable dwelling, my meditation subject did not reach its culmination.
The Teacher said, "Monk, in the past even animals knew what was suitable and what was unsuitable for themselves."
Having said, "Why did you not know this?", he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a bird;
surrounded by a flock of birds, he lived in a forest region, depending upon a great tree endowed with branches and foliage.
Then one day, as the branches of that tree rubbed against one another, powder fell and smoke arose.
Seeing this, the Bodhisatta thought: "These two branches, rubbing thus together, will emit fire;
it will fall and catch the old leaves, and from then on it will burn this tree as well. He did not [wish for this].
“It is not possible for us to live here; it is better to flee from here and go elsewhere. Then he spoke this verse to the flock of birds:
“The fire that the birds who depend on this tree have released— O Vakkaṅga birds, seek out other directions!
Fear has arisen from the very place of refuge.”
In this context, "jagatiruha" means a tree; it is called "jagatī," which refers to the earth, and because it is born there, the tree is called a "jagatiruha.
"Vihaṅgamā" means birds; "vihaṃ" refers to the sky, and because they go there, winged creatures are called "vihaṅgamā.
"Disā bhajatha" means: having abandoned this tree and fled from here, take refuge in the four directions. "Vakkaṅgā" means...
He calls out to the birds. For they sometimes bend their necks—their upper limbs—crookedly; therefore they are called "crook-limbs" (*vakkaṅgā*).
Or else, because their wings are grown crooked on both sides, they are "crook-limbs.
"Fear has arisen from our refuge" means that fear has been produced from this very tree of ours, which was our place of shelter; "come, let us go elsewhere."
The wise birds, who obeyed the words of the Bodhisatta, flew up together with him at once and went elsewhere.
But those that were unwise, thinking, "In this very way he sees crocodiles even in a mere drop of water," did not accept his words and remained right there.
Then, before long, in the very manner intended by the Bodhisatta—
Once the fire had broken out, it seized that tree. When the smoke and flames arose, birds blinded by the smoke were unable to fly elsewhere;
falling again and again into the fire, they met their destruction.
The Teacher said, "In this way, monk, even in the past, those dwelling at the tops of trees among the animals [discerned] what was suitable and what was unsuitable for themselves."
Having brought forward this teaching on the Dhamma, "They know; why do you not know?", the Teacher proclaimed the Truths.
At the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher, connecting the sequence of events, identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the birds who followed the Bodhisatta's word were the assembly of the Buddha's followers, while the wise bird was none other than myself."
The Sixth: The Commentary on the Sakuṇa Jātaka.
7. The Commentary on the Tittira Jātaka.
"Those who do not honor their elders... This was spoken by the Teacher while traveling toward Sāvatthī, regarding the Elder Sāriputta’s refusal of a lodging.

He spoke concerning this. For after Anāthapiṇḍika had had a monastery built and dispatched messengers, the Teacher departed from Rājagaha, reached Vesālī, and having stayed there for as long as he desired, set out on the road with the intention, "I shall go to Sāvatthī.
At that time, the pupils of the group-of-six monks went ahead and [occupied] the lodgings of the elders.
Even while [the lodgings] were not yet taken, they made reservations over the dwellings, thinking, "This lodging is for our preceptor; this is for our teacher;
this one shall be ours alone. Consequently, the elder monks who arrived later did not obtain lodgings.
Even the disciples of the Elder Sāriputta, while searching for a lodging for their elder, could not find one. The elder—
Not obtaining a lodging, he spent the night sitting and walking at the foot of a tree not far from the Teacher’s lodging.
At dawn, the Teacher went out and coughed; the Elder also coughed. “Who is this?
“It is I, Bhante, Sāriputta. “Sāriputta, what are you doing here at this hour?”
Thus he reported that occurrence. Having heard the Elder’s words, the Teacher reflected:
"Even now, while I am still living, the monks dwell without mutual respect and deference; what indeed will they do when I have attained final Nibbāna?
As he pondered this, a profound sense of spiritual urgency arose within him.
Thus, when the night had turned to dawn, he had the community of monks assembled and asked the monks:
"Is it true, monks, that the group-of-six monks go ahead and preempt the lodgings for the elder monks?
"It is true, Blessed One. Then, having rebuked the group-of-six monks and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks.
“Monks, who indeed is worthy of the best seat, the best water, and the best alms-food? Some said, “One who has gone forth from a khattiya family.
Others said, “One who has gone forth from a brāhmaṇa family or a householder family.
Still others said, “One who is a master of the Vinaya, a preacher of the Dhamma, or one who has attained the first jhāna, the second, the third, or the fourth jhāna.”
“...an attainer. Others said, “A stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arahant, one possessing the threefold knowledge, one possessing the six direct knowledges.
When those bhikkhus had thus spoken according to their own inclinations regarding those worthy of the foremost seat and so forth, the Teacher said:
“Bhikkhus, in my teaching, one who has gone forth from a khattiya family is not the measure for receiving the foremost seat and so forth;”
“Monks, one who has gone forth from a brahmin family is not the measure; one who has gone forth from a householder family is not the measure;

nor is one who is a master of the Vinaya, a master of the Suttantas, or a master of the Abhidhamma; nor are those who have attained the first jhāna and so forth, or stream-enterers and so forth, the measure.
Rather, monks, in this teaching, salutation, rising up, joining of palms, and respectful service should be performed according to seniority.”
"The foremost seat, the foremost water, and the foremost alms-food should be received. This is the measure in this matter. Therefore, a more senior bhikkhu is the one worthy of these.
Now, however, bhikkhus, Sāriputta is my chief disciple, the turner of the wheel of the True Dhamma;
he deserves to receive a lodging immediately after me. Not having obtained a lodging for this night, he is staying at the foot of a tree."
“...he spent [the time]. Now that you are thus disrespectful and lacking in deference even now, what will you do as time goes on?
Then, for the purpose of giving them exhortation, he said: “Bhikkhus, in the past even animals thought:
‘It is not fitting for us to be disrespectful, lacking in deference, and to conduct ourselves in a manner inconsistent with our kind toward one another.’”
"Let us dwell here; having identified among us who is the eldest, we shall perform salutations and other duties toward him.
Having thus investigated thoroughly and recognized, "This one is our elder," they performed salutations and other duties toward him and departed, filling the path of the gods.
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in a region of the Himalayas, three companions—a partridge, a monkey, and an elephant—lived depending upon a great banyan tree.
They lived without mutual respect, without deference, and in a manner inconsistent with their status.
Then it occurred to them: "It is not fitting for us to live in this way; what if we were to [honor] whichever among us is the eldest?"
“Let us dwell together, performing such acts as salutations. Thinking, “Who among us is the eldest?
one day they thought, “There is a way to find out,” and all three sat at the foot of a banyan tree.
Then the partridge and the monkey asked the elephant, “Friend elephant, from how long ago have you known this banyan tree?”
He said, "Friends, when I was a young cub, I used to pass through this banyan grove between my thighs;
even now, when it stands spread out, its topmost branch does not touch my navel. Thus, from the time I first came to know this grove, I have known it.
Again, both men questioned the monkey in the same manner as before. He said, "I..."
“Friends, while still a young monkey, I sat on the ground and, without even raising my neck, ate the top sprouts of this young *nigrodha* tree;
it is from that time of its smallness that I have known it.
Then the other two questioned the partridge in the same manner as before. He said, “Friends, formerly, at such-and-such a place, there was a great *nigrodha* tree.”
"I was there; having eaten its fruits, I voided my excrement in this place, and from that this tree grew.
Thus, I have known this tree from the time it was unborn; therefore, I am older than you by birth.
When this was said, the monkey and the elephant said to the wise partridge, "Friend, you are older than us."
"From this day forward, we shall perform for you honor, respect, esteem, veneration, and worship, as well as salutations, rising from our seats, joining our palms in reverence, and acts of service;
we shall abide by your instruction. But you, from this day forward, should grant us your counsel and guidance.
From that time on, the partridge gave them his instruction and established them in the precepts (sīla), while he himself—
They undertook the precepts. Those three people, having established themselves in the five precepts, lived with mutual respect, deference, and harmony;
at the end of their lives, they were destined for the world of the gods. The undertaking of those three was known as the "Tittiriya Brahma-faring."
"Bhikkhus, even those animals live with mutual respect and deference toward one another;
why then, having gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, do you live without mutual respect and deference?
Bhikkhus, from this day forward, I allow you to pay homage and rise up for one another according to seniority."
"Salutation with joined palms, respectful service, and according to seniority: the best seat, the best water, and the best alms-food;
and from now on, one who is junior must not be preempted from a dwelling by one who is senior. Whoever should so preempt him incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Having thus delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher, having attained full enlightenment, spoke this verse:
“Those people who are skilled in the Dhamma honor the aged;
they are praised in this very life, and in the future life, a happy destination.
Herein, “those who honor the aged”: there are three kinds of aged—aged by birth, aged by years, and aged by virtue. Among these—
One endowed with birth is called "grown old by birth"; one established in age is called "grown old by age"; one endowed with virtues is called "grown old by virtue.
Among these, it is the one grown old by age who is intended here by the term "the aged.
"Honoring" means they worship them through the act of honoring the eldest. "Skilled in the Dhamma" means skilled in the Dhamma of honoring the eldest.
They are wholesome. "In this very life" means in this very personal existence (*attabhāva*).

"Praiseworthy" means worthy of praise. "And a happy destination in the future" means that even in the world beyond—having passed away and left this world to go to the next world—their destination is indeed a happy one.
This, then, is the summary of the meaning here: "Bhikkhus, whether they be Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras..."
Whether they be householders or renunciants, or even animals— whatever beings are skillful, proficient,
and endowed with virtue in performing acts of reverence toward their elders, they receive praise, commendation,
and eulogy as "those who honor their elders" in this very life, and upon the breakup of the body, they are reborn in heaven.
Having thus explained the virtue of the eldest brother’s act of veneration, the Teacher drew out the connection and identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the elephant king was Moggallāna, the monkey was Sāriputta, and the wise partridge was none other than myself.
This concludes the seventh narrative, the Tittira-jātaka.
[38] 8. The Commentary on the Bakajātakam:
"One whose wisdom is not entirely crooked. This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a monk who was a robe-maker.
It is said that a certain monk living at Jetavana performed whatever work was to be done for robes, such as cutting, smoothing, spreading out, and sewing.
He was highly skilled in that craft. Because of his skill, he increased the production of robes; therefore, he became known as "Cīvaravaḍḍhaka" (the Robe-Increaser).
What did he do? Having shown manual labor upon worn-out rags, he made robes that were smooth to the touch and pleasing;
then, at the conclusion of the dyeing process, having dyed them with alkaline water and rubbed them with a conch shell, they became brilliant.

Having made it pleasing, he sets it aside. Monks who did not know how to perform tailoring work took unwashed cloth, went to him, and said, "We do not know how to make robes; please make robes for us.
He replied, "Friends, a robe being made takes a long time to finish; I already have robes that I have made myself."
"Set these two cloths aside and take that one and go," he said, and having brought them out, he showed them.

Seeing only the excellence of its color and not knowing the internal condition, they gave the unwashed cloths to the robe-maker with the perception that it was "durable," and taking that one, they went away.
When it had become slightly soiled by them, it was washed with hot water and returned to its natural state.
He pointed these out, and here and there signs of decay became visible; consequently, they were filled with remorse.
Thus, deceiving people everywhere with rags as he went from place to place, that bhikkhu became notorious.
Just as he did in Jeta’s Grove, so too in a certain village there was a certain robe-maker who deceived the world.
His fellow monks reported to him, “Venerable sir, it is said that a certain robe-maker in Jeta’s Grove deceives the world in such a manner.
Then it occurred to him, “Well now, I shall deceive that city-dweller.
Having made a rag-robe look very pleasing and dyed it a beautiful color, he put it on and went to Jeta’s Grove. As soon as the other saw him, he—
Having conceived greed, he asked, "Venerable sir, was this robe made by you? "Yes, friend," [the monk replied].
"Venerable sir, give this robe to me; you will receive another. "Friend, we are village-dwellers for whom requisites are difficult to obtain;
having given this to you, what shall I wear myself? "Venerable sir, in my possession there are unwashed cloths..."
“There is; take them and make yourselves a robe. “Friend, I have already performed manual labor on this matter. But since you speak thus, what can I do?
Take it,” he said, and having given him his rag-robe and taken the new cloth garment, he deceived him and departed. After wearing that robe for a few days, the resident of Jetavana—
While washing it with hot water, he saw that it had become a worn-out rag and was ashamed, thinking, "It seems the resident of Jetavana has been cheated by a village tailor.
Thus, his state of being cheated became public knowledge in the midst of the Saṅgha.
Then one day, the monks sat in the Dhamma hall discussing this matter. The Teacher arrived and—
“Monks, for what discussion have you gathered here now? he asked. They reported the matter to him.
The Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that this robe-maker living in Jeta’s Grove deceives others; in the past, too, he deceived them.
Nor is it only now that this robe-maker living in Jeta’s Grove has been deceived by the village-dweller; in the past, too, he was deceived.”
Having said, “I have been deceived indeed,” he related a story of the past.
In the past, in a certain forest region, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity dwelling in a *varaṇa* tree standing near a certain lotus pond.
At that time, during the heat of the summer season, the water in a certain pond that was not very large...

It was shallow, and there were many fish there. Then a certain crane, seeing those fish, thought, "By some means I shall deceive these fish and eat them," and went to sit on the edge of the water, reflecting.
When the fish saw him, they asked, "Sir, why are you sitting here reflecting? He replied, "I am reflecting upon you."
“What are you thinking about us, noble lady? “I was sitting here thinking: ‘The water in this lake is scanty, the food supply is meager, and the heat is great; what indeed will these fish do now?
“Then what shall we do, noble lady? “If you would follow my advice, I shall [lead] each one of you...”
“Having seized you with my beak, I will lead you to a great lake covered with five-colored lotuses and release you.
“Noble sir, since the beginning of the first aeon, there has never been such a thing as a ‘fish-thinking heron’;
you wish to eat one of us. “I will not eat you as long as you trust me. “But if it is for the sake of the lake...”
“You do not believe my existence; send one fish with me to see the lake.
The fish, believing him, thought, “This man is capable both in water and on land,” and they gave him a large black fish, saying, “Take this and go.
He took it, led it there, released it into the lake, and showed him the entire lake.
Having brought them back again, he released them in the presence of those fish. He described to them the excellence of that lake.
Having heard his words, they desired to go and said, "Very well, noble sir, take us and go.
The crane first caught that very large black fish, led it to the shore of the lake, showed him the lake, and [stood] on the bank of the lake.
When the Varaṇa tree had grown, he would hide there, thrust the fish between its branches with his beak, and by pecking at them, bring them to their death;
then, having eaten the flesh and dropped the bones at the foot of the tree, he would go back again, thinking, "That fish has been released;
let another come. By this means, catching them one by one, he ate all the fish and returned once more.
He did not see even a single fish; however, one crab remained there.
The crane, desiring to eat that as well, said, "O crab, I have taken all those fish and released them into the great lake covered with lotuses;
come, I shall take you there too. "If you go taking me with you, how will you catch me? "I shall catch you by biting you."
“If you go taking me in this way, you will cause me to fall; I will not go with you.
“Do not fear,” said the crab, “I shall take hold of you firmly and go. The crab thought:
“Once he has led this fish to the lake, there will be no releasing him. But if he releases me at the lake, that would be well.”
"If he does not release it, we shall take his life by cutting off his neck.
Then he said to him: "Friend Baka, you will not be able to grasp it correctly;
our grasp, however, is a correct grasp. If I am permitted to seize your neck with my claws, [I shall take your life]. His neck—
“Having secured you well, I shall go with you. Not realizing that the crab intended to deceive him, he agreed, saying, “Very well.
The crab, having firmly seized his neck with its claws as if with a blacksmith’s tongs, said, “Now let us go.
He led him away, showed him the lake, and set out toward a *varaṇa* tree.
The crab said, "Uncle, this lake is this way; why then do you go that way? The crane replied, "I am not your uncle;
indeed, you are no nephew of mine! Having said this, he added, "I suppose you think, 'He is carrying me about, so he must be my slave.
Look at this heap of thorns at the foot of that *varaṇa* tree."
"All those fish have been eaten by you; I too shall eat you in the same way," he said. The crab replied, "Those fish were eaten by you because of their own foolishness.
But I will not allow you to eat me; rather, I shall bring about your destruction.
For you do not realize that you have been deceived by me through your own foolishness; both of us shall die together as we perish."
Having said, "I shall cut off your head and cast it upon the ground," he squeezed his neck with his jaws as if with a blacksmith's tongs.
Terrified by the fear of death, with tears streaming from his wide-open eyes, he cried out, "Master, I will not eat you;
give me my life! "If that is so, descend and enter into my body."
“Release it! He turned back, descended into the water, and placed the crab on the surface of the mud at the edge of the stream.
As if cutting a lotus stalk with a razor, the crab cut his neck and entered the water.
Seeing that marvel, the deity dwelling in the *varaṇa* tree, giving a cry of approval and making the forest resound, spoke this verse in a sweet voice:
“One whose wisdom is not ultimately deceitful does not thrive through deceit;
one whose wisdom is deceitful only succeeds as a crane catches crabs.
In this context, “one whose wisdom is not ultimately deceitful does not thrive through deceit”: *nikati* is said to mean deception (*vañcanā*); [thus,] one whose wisdom is deceitful...
A person of deceptive wisdom does not attain ultimate happiness through that trickery or deceit;
he is unable to remain established in happiness at all times, but rather inevitably meets with ruin—this is the meaning.
"Attains" (*ārādheti*) means "obtains. A person of deceptive wisdom is a wicked individual who has trained his intellect in the state of being a cheat (*kerāṭika*). By himself...
"He reaps, obtains, and finds the fruit of evil"—this is the meaning. How so?

"Like a heron [catching] a crab": just as a heron suffers the severing of its neck by a crab, even so does a person of evil deeds reap and obtain fear from the evil he has committed, whether in this very life or in a future state.
It was while elucidating this point that the Great Being went to the forest.
He taught the Dhamma with a loud voice.
The Teacher said, “Monks, it was not only now that this village-dwelling robe-maker deceived them; in the past, too, he deceived them.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma and established the connection, he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, that crane was...”
"The resident of Jetavana was the robe-maker, Kakkhaṭaka the village-dweller was the robe-maker,
and I myself was the tree deity.
Thus ends the eighth narrative, the Commentary on the Bakajātakaya.
[39] 9. The Exposition of the Nanda Jātaka:
"I imagine it is a heap of gold. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a co-resident disciple of the Elder Sāriputta.
It is said that this bhikkhu was easy to speak to and patient with words; with great effort on the part of the Elder—
He rendered assistance. Then, on one occasion, the Elder, having taken leave of the Teacher, set out on a journey and went to the region of Dakkhiṇāgiri.
When that monk arrived there, he became arrogant and stubborn;
he did not follow the Elder’s advice, and when the Elder said, "Friend, do this," he acted in opposition to him. The Elder [perceived] his disposition...

He did not know. Having wandered on his travels there, he returned again to Jetavana. From the moment that elder monk arrived at the Jetavana monastery, the other monk became just as he was before. The elder reported this to the Tathāgata:
"Venerable Sir, one of my co-residents acts like a slave bought for a hundred pieces in one place, yet in another place he is stiff with pride."
"Having made an offering, when told 'Do this,' he becomes an opponent," [the monk said]. The Teacher said, "Sāriputta, it is not only now that this bhikkhu has been of such character;
formerly too, when he went to one place, he was like a slave bought for a hundred coins, but when he went to another place, he became an opponent and an adversary.
Having said this, at the request of the Elder, he related the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in a certain householders’ family.
He had a friend who was a householder; he himself was old, but his wife was young.
Relying on him, she conceived a son. He thought: “This woman, because of her youth, after my passing, might [seek someone else]...”
“Suppose I were to take this man and destroy this wealth, so that he would not give it to my son;

what if I were to bury this wealth in the earth? Thinking thus, he took a slave named Nanda from his house, went to the forest, buried that wealth in a certain spot, informed him of its location, and said: “Dear Nanda, after my passing, this wealth—my...”
“Explain this to your son and do not abandon him,” she instructed, and then passed away.
In due course, her son reached maturity. Then his mother said to him, “Dear son, your father took the slave Nanda and buried wealth;
fetch that out and establish a household. One day, he...
He said to Nanda, "Uncle, has my father hidden any wealth away? "Yes, master," he replied. "Where was it hidden?
"In the forest, master. "Then let us go. Taking a spade and a basket, they went to the place where the treasure was buried.
"Where is the wealth, uncle? he asked. Nanda climbed up and stood upon the top of the treasure.
Having given rise to pride based on his wealth, he reviled the prince, saying, "Hey, you son of a slave-girl, servant! Where do you have any wealth in this place?
When the prince heard his harsh words, he acted as if he had not heard them and said, "In that case, let us go.
He took him and turned back; then, after two or three days had passed, he departed again, and Nanda did likewise.
He reviled him. Without speaking a harsh word in return to him, the prince turned back and said to the Bodhisatta:
“This slave goes about saying, ‘I will tell you of wealth,’ yet having gone, he reviles me; I do not know the reason for this.
However, I have a householder who is a friend of my father; I shall go and inquire of him and find out.”
Having gone into his presence and reported all that had occurred, he asked, "What, dear father, is the reason for this?
The Bodhisatta replied, "Dear son, in whatever place Nanda stands while reviling you, right there lies the wealth belonging to your father;
therefore, whenever Nanda reviles you, you should drag him by force, saying, 'Come here, you slave! Why do you revile me?'"
“Break open that place, take out the family wealth, have the slave released from bondage, and bring back the riches,” he said,
and then spoke this verse:
“I imagine there is a heap of gold, and Nandaka has a golden garland.”
"Where a slave born of a mother from the same caste stands and makes the large [drums] resound.
Therein, "I think" (maññe) means "I know thus. "Golden" (sovaṇṇaya) means those which have a beautiful color (sundara vaṇṇa);
what are they? Jewels such as silver, gems, gold, coral, and so forth. For in this context, all these are called "golden" (suvaṇṇāni).
These are intended; their heap is a heap of gold. "And a golden garland" means: I consider that the golden garlands belonging to your father are also right here.
"Where Nandaka is a slave" means: in whatever place Nandaka the slave stands. "Born of a slave-woman" (*āmajāta*) means:
the son of a female slave known as an *āmadāsī*—one who has entered into servitude by saying, "Yes, I am your slave. Standing.
“‘Thullāni gajjati’ means: ‘In whatever place he stands and utters harsh words, right there [is] that wealth belonging to the family;
thus do I consider it,’ the Bodhisatta explained this method for seizing the prince’s wealth.
The prince, having paid homage to the Bodhisatta, went home, took Nanda with him, and went to the location of the treasure as instructed.”
Having set out on that path, brought back that wealth, and established a household, he remained steadfast in the Bodhisatta’s advice;
performing meritorious deeds such as giving, he passed away at the end of his life according to his karma.
The Teacher, saying, "In the past, too, he was of such a character," delivered this Dhamma teaching and joined it to the relevant context.
He made the connection with the Jātaka: “At that time, Nanda was the co-resident disciple of Sāriputta, while I myself was the wise householder.
This concludes the commentary on the Nanda Jātaka, the ninth.
[40] 10. The Exposition of the Khadiraṅgāra Jātaka.
"I would rather fall into hell"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Anāthapiṇḍika.
For Anāthapiṇḍika, for the sake of the monastery alone, had renounced fifty-four koṭis of wealth for the Buddha’s Dispensation.

Having scattered [offerings] and established [his faith], and having produced no perception of other jewels apart from the Three Jewels, he went daily for three great audiences while the Teacher was dwelling at Jetavana:
once in the early morning, once after having eaten his breakfast, and once in the evening. There were also occasional intermediate audiences. And as he went,
Thinking, "If I were to come with nothing at all, would the novices or the young monks even look at my hands? he had never gone before with empty hands.
When going in the morning, he would go having had rice-gruel brought; after his breakfast, he would take along ghee, fresh butter, honey, molasses, and so forth;
and in the evening, he would have perfumes, garlands, and cloth in his hands. Thus, as he was giving away [his wealth] day after day, [the following occurred].
There was no limit to his generosity.
Many people who lived by trade took loans amounting to eighteen *koṭis* of wealth from his hand on written promissory notes, yet the Great Merchant did not have them brought back.
Furthermore, he had eighteen *koṭis* belonging to his family on the riverbank.
Having been buried and placed there, they entered the great ocean when the riverbank was breached by the waters of the Aciravatī;
they moved about within the interior of the eggshell like iron plates with their openings still sealed.
Furthermore, a regular meal for five hundred bhikkhus was constantly provided at the merchant’s house, for the merchant’s residence was like a crossroads for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
It was like a lotus pond dug out by hand, standing in the place of mother and father to all the bhikkhus.
Therefore, even the Fully Enlightened One went to that house, and the eighty great elders likewise went there. As for the other bhikkhus, however, there was no limit to those going and coming.
That house had seven stories and was adorned with seven gate-towers. Of it—
At the fourth gatehouse lived a deity of wrong view. When the Perfectly Enlightened One entered the house, she was unable to remain in her own celestial mansion;
taking her child, she descended and stood upon the ground.
She acted in exactly the same way when the eighty great elders and the remaining elders were entering or leaving.
She thought: "Whenever the ascetic Gotama and his disciples enter this house, I have no peace;
I shall not be able to remain on the ground, having to descend again and again at all times.
It is right for me to act in such a way that they do not enter this house. Then, one day, while he had just gone to his bed—
She went to the presence of the chief steward and stood there, pervading him with radiance.
When he asked, "Who is here?", she replied, "I am the deity reborn at the fourth gate-tower. He asked, "For what purpose have you come?
She said, "Do you not see what the merchant is doing? Without looking toward his own final hour, he is taking out his wealth and [giving it] to a recluse..."
“He honors only Gotama; he no longer engages in trade nor establishes his business operations.
Advise the merchant in such a way that he resumes his own work. And act so that the ascetic Gotama, along with his disciples, does not enter this house.
Then he said to her, “Foolish deity, the merchant has wealth...”
"By answering, one answers within the Buddha’s dispensation which leads to liberation;
if he were to seize me by the topknot and sell me, I would not say anything at all—go now!
On another day, she approached the merchant’s eldest son and advised him in the same manner, but he too rebuked her in the same way as before. However, together with the merchant...
He was not even able to speak.
As the merchant continued to give alms incessantly and ceased his business activities, his income diminished and his wealth came to an end.
Then, as he gradually fell into poverty, even his clothing, bedding, and food were no longer like they had been before.
They did not exist. Even though he gave alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus in such a manner, he was unable to give after having made it choice.
Then one day, as he was sitting after having paid homage to the Teacher, the Teacher asked him:
"Householder, is alms given in your family? He replied: "It is given, venerable sir, but it is only broken rice with sour gruel as the second course."
Then the Teacher said to him, “Householder, do not let your mind shrink back thinking, ‘I am giving coarse alms.
For when the mind is noble, an offering given to Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or disciples of the Buddha is not called coarse. Why?
Because of the greatness of its result. Indeed, for one who is able to make the mind noble, there is no such thing as coarse alms.
This should be understood thus:
"When the mind is serene, there is no gift that is small,
whether given to a Tathāgata, a Perfectly Awakened One, or to his disciple."
“There is indeed no service rendered to the Buddhas, those of peerless vision, that is insignificant.
Behold the fruit of a mere lump of millet, dry and saltless.
He further said to him: “Householder, you yourself, while giving such coarse alms, [have pleased] the eight types of noble persons...”

"Desi, at the time of the Velāma sacrifice, having made the entire land of Jambudīpa free of plows and distributing the seven treasures as if filling the five great rivers with a single flood, while I was bestowing such a great gift, I did not find anyone who had gone for refuge to the Triple Gem or who observed the five precepts;
indeed, persons worthy of offerings are so difficult to find. Therefore, [I thought], 'My gift is coarse.'"
"Do not let your heart shrink. Having said this, he then related the Velāma Sutta.

Then that deity, who previously had been unable even to converse with the merchant during his time of prosperity, thinking, "Now, because he is in a state of misfortune, he will heed my words," entered the bedchamber at the hour of midnight and emitted a radiance.
Having pervaded [the area], she stood in the air. Seeing her, the merchant asked, "Who is this? "I am the deity residing at the fourth gate-tower, O Great Merchant," she replied.
"For what purpose have you come? "I have come desiring to give you counsel. "Then speak it," he said.
"Great Merchant, you did not consider the time of your end; you did not look after your sons and daughters."
"In the teaching of the ascetic Gotama, much wealth was squandered;
because of your excessive distribution of that wealth, or perhaps because you did not engage in such occupations as trade, you have become impoverished through reliance on the ascetic Gotama.
Even being in such a state, you do not abandon the ascetic Gotama; even today, those ascetics still enter your house. As for what they said to you...
What has been taken cannot be recovered; let what is taken remain taken.
From now on, however, do not go yourselves into the presence of the ascetic Gotama, and do not allow his disciples to enter this house.
Even turning away from the ascetic Gotama and not looking back at him, carry on your own business and trade.
“Settle your family. Then he said to him, “This is the advice you must give me. “Yes, noble sir,” he replied.
“I have been made unshakable by the One Possessing the Ten Powers, even by a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand such deities.
For my faith is as immovable and well-established as Sineru; in this noble teaching of the jewels that leads to liberation, I am firm.”
"Wealth has been squandered; you have spoken what is improper; you have struck a blow against the Buddha's teaching.
There is no need for you to live in my house with such an immoral woman, of ill conduct and ill-omened;
depart quickly from my house and go elsewhere."
Having heard the words of the noble disciple who had attained the stream, she was unable to remain where she was;
she went to her own dwelling, took her children by the hand, and departed.
Having departed, and finding no other place to stay, she thought, "I shall ask the merchant for forgiveness and live right there," and [she approached] the son of a deity who protected the city.
Having approached him and paid homage, she stood before him. When he asked, "For what purpose have you come?
she replied, "My lord, out of my own foolishness and without due reflection, I spoke with the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika; he became angry and expelled me from my dwelling.
He has brought me to the merchant's presence to ask for my forgiveness and to restore my place of residence."
“Do so. “But what did you say to the merchant? “‘From this day forward, do not perform the service of attending upon the Buddha or the Saṅgha;
do not allow the ascetic Gotama entry into your house. ‘I spoke thus to him, Master. ‘What you have said is improper;
a blow has been struck at the Dispensation. I shall take you to the merchant’s presence—’”
“I am not able,” he replied. Having failed to receive favor from him, she went to the presence of the Four Great Kings.
Being likewise rejected by them as well, she approached Sakka, the King of the Gods, and having related these events, said:
“O Lord, finding no place to dwell, I wander about helpless with my children in my arms; [I have come] to you...”
“Please grant me a place to dwell with honor,” he entreated even more earnestly. He replied to him, “You have done what is improper;
you have dealt a blow to the teaching of the Conqueror. Because of you, I too am unable to speak with the merchant.
However, I shall tell you one means by which the merchant might forgive you. “Very well, Your Majesty, please speak,” he said. [To] the Great Merchant...
There is wealth numbering eighteen koṭis that has been taken from the hands of people after being entered upon documents; you,
assuming the guise of an official and without letting anyone know, should take those documents and, surrounded by several young yakkhas,
go to their houses holding a document in one hand and a pen in the other, and stand in the middle of the house.
Standing there by his own power as a *yakkha*, he terrified them and said, "This is your debt-bond.
When our merchant was in his time of prosperity, he said nothing to you; now that he has become poor, give us back the kahāpaṇas you took.
Having thus displayed his power as a *yakkha* and recovered all eighteen crores of gold, he—

Having filled the empty storehouse of the merchant, he used his own supernatural power to bring forth other wealth that had been buried on the bank of the Aciravatī River but entered the ocean when the riverbank collapsed;
having filled the empty storehouse with that as well, he further brought forth eighteen crores of ownerless wealth from a certain place.
"Bring that as well and fill the empty storehouse; having performed this punishment of filling the empty storehouse with these fifty-four koṭis, ask the Great Merchant for forgiveness.
She replied, "Very well, Your Majesty," and accepting his word, she brought all the wealth in the manner previously described.
Having filled the courtyard, at the hour of midnight she entered the treasurer’s bedchamber, pervaded it with radiance, and stood in the air.
When asked, "Who is this?", she replied, "I am the blind and foolish deity residing in the fourth gate-tower of you, Great Treasurer.
Being utterly deluded by great ignorance and not knowing the virtues of the Buddha, during the preceding days I— [...]"

There is something I have said together with [others]; please forgive that fault of mine. Indeed, by the word of Sakka, the king of the gods, having cleared your debt, I have brought back forty-five crores:
eighteen crores from the ocean, eighteen crores from the sea, and eighteen crores of ownerless wealth from various places—thus, by filling the empty storehouses, [I have fulfilled my task].
“The disciplinary action has been performed; all the wealth expended for the Jetavana Monastery has been accounted for.
Not finding a place to live, I am suffering. Great Merchant, please forgive what I said out of ignorance, disregarding it.
Having heard her words, Anāthapiṇḍika thought, “This deity says, ‘The disciplinary action against me has been performed.’”
“He speaks thus, and he confesses his own fault; the Teacher will discipline him and make his own virtues known.
We shall present him to the Perfectly Enlightened One. Then she said to him, “Mother, Devatā, if you wish to ask for my forgiveness, ask for it in the presence of the Teacher.
“Very well, I shall do so. But [bring] me into the presence of the Teacher.”

“Take it and go. He replied, “Very well,” and at the break of dawn, taking it early in the morning, he went into the presence of the Teacher and reported everything that had been done by her to the Tathāgata. Having heard his words, the Teacher said:
“In this world, householder, even a wicked person sees auspicious things as long as their evil has not yet ripened.”
"But when his evil ripens, then he sees only evil. Even a good person, as long as his goodness has not yet ripened, sees only evils. But when his goodness ripens, then he sees only what is good.
Having said this, he spoke these two verses from the Dhammapada:
“Even an evil person sees what is auspicious, as long as his evil does not ripen;
but when his evil ripens, then the evil person sees evils.
Even an auspicious person sees what is evil, as long as his auspiciousness does not ripen.”
“And when one is ripened, O blessed one, then the blessed one sees what is blessed.
At the conclusion of these verses, that deity was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
She prostrated at the Teacher’s feet, which were marked with the wheel-sign, and said: “Venerable sir, I was stained by lust, corrupted by hatred, deluded by ignorance, and blinded by nescience.”
“Having spoken evil words because I did not know your virtues, please forgive me,” she said, and after asking the Teacher for forgiveness, she also asked the Great Merchant for forgiveness.
At that moment, Anāthapiṇḍika spoke of his own virtues before the Teacher: “Venerable Sir, this deity—”
“Venerable Sir, even when she tried to stop me by saying, ‘Do not attend upon the Buddha and so forth,’ she was unable to restrain me;
and though I was forbidden by her saying, ‘You must not give alms,’ I gave the alms nonetheless. Surely, Bhante, this is my own virtue.
The Teacher said, “Householder, you are a stream-enterer, a noble disciple, with unshakable faith and purified vision. This deity of little power—[could she possibly shake you]?”

It is not surprising that she did not stop when being stopped. However, it was truly marvelous that in the past, when the Buddhas had not yet appeared and while still standing at a stage where her wisdom was immature,
she remained in the midst of a lotus calyx even though she had been forbidden by Māra—

the lord of the sense realm— who stood in the sky and showed her a pit of glowing coals eighty cubits deep, saying, "If you give this gift, you will roast in this hell," and thus tried to prevent her from giving.
"Standing there, they gave alms; this is wonderful," he said, and being requested by Anāthapiṇḍika, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into the family of the chief merchant of Bārāṇasī.
Being raised like a young god with various kinds of pleasant requisites, he gradually reached the age of discretion.
Having reached maturity in all the arts at the age of only sixteen, he took over the position of treasurer upon his father’s passing. He had six alms-halls constructed—
four at the city gates, one in the center of the city, and one at the door of his own residence—
and there he gave great gifts, observed the precepts, and performed the Uposatha rites.
Then one day, at the time for the morning meal, while various kinds of exquisite and delicious food were being served to the Bodhisatta,
a certain Paccekabuddha, having emerged from cessation after seven days and observing that it was the time for alms-round,
thought, "Today it is fitting for me to go to the gate of the house of the chief merchant of Bārāṇasī. Having thus chewed a betel-creeper tooth-stick, he set out.
Having performed his mouth-washing at the Anotatta lake, he stood upon a slab of emerald;
having put on his lower garment, fastened his girdle which resembled a flash of lightning, and donned his upper robe, he took a bowl made of magical clay and arrived through the air.
As soon as the food for the Bodhisatta had been brought, he stood at the door of the house. Upon seeing him, the Bodhisatta rose from his seat and paid him due honor.
Having shown this, he looked toward his attendant. When the attendant asked, "What shall I do, Master? he said, "Bring the noble one's bowl.
At that very moment, Māra the Evil One, trembling, rose up and thought, "This Paccekabuddha will receive food on the seventh day from now;
failing to obtain it today, he will perish, and I shall cause him to perish."
Thinking, “I shall create an obstacle to the merchant’s giving,” he arrived at that very moment and constructed a pit of coals eighty cubits deep within the inner courtyard.
Filled with acacia charcoal, blazing and glowing, it appeared like the great Avīci hell.
Having constructed it, he himself stood in the air. As [the merchant] was going to fetch the bowl—
A man, seeing it, was seized by great fear and turned back. The Bodhisatta asked, "Why have you turned back, dear one?
[The man replied,] "Sir, in this inner courtyard there is a great pit of glowing embers, blazing and aflame.
Then one after another, all those who had come and gone were overcome by fear and fled away in haste.
The Bodhisatta thought: "Today Māra Vasavattī must have exerted himself, desiring to create an obstacle to my giving;
yet he does not know my unshakable nature even by means of a hundred or a thousand Māras.
Today, indeed, I shall know the greatness of the power and the greatness of the majesty of either myself or Māra. Thus, [he remained] exactly as he had prepared himself.
Taking his own alms-bowl, he departed from his house, stood on the edge of the charcoal pit, looked up into the sky, and seeing Māra, asked, "Who are you?
"I am Māra," [Māra replied]. "Was this charcoal pit created by you? "Yes, it was by me.
"For what purpose? "To create an obstacle to your giving, and for the sake of the Paccekabuddha."
“...for the sake of ending my life. The Bodhisatta said, “I will neither create an obstacle to your own generosity nor an obstacle to the life of the Paccekabuddha;
today, let us both know the greatness of our strength and the greatness of our power.
Standing on the bank of the charcoal pit, he said, “Venerable Paccekabuddha, as for this charcoal pit...”
"Even though I am falling headlong, I shall not turn back; you need only accept the food given by me," he said, and uttered this verse:
"I would rather fall into hell, feet upwards and head downwards;”
"I shall not act unworthily; come, receive this alms-food.

Herein, the meaning of "alms" is this: "Venerable Sir, Pratyekabuddha Supreme One, even if, while giving you alms-food, I were to fall headlong into this hell with my feet up and my head down, nevertheless, this [act of] non-giving..."
Because it is not to be done by the noble ones (ariya) and is to be done by the ignoble ones (anariya), it is called "ignoble.
[He says: "I shall not do that which is ignoble; come now, accept this alms-food being offered by me.
And here, *handā* is a particle used in the sense of relinquishment (*vossagga*).
Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta took his alms-bowl with firm resolve and stepped over the charcoal pit;

at that very moment, a great paduma flower, eighty cubits deep, sprang up from the bottom of the charcoal pit, blooming with a hundred petals, and rose to receive the Bodhisatta’s foot. Then, dust the size of large gourds—
Having ascended and stood upon the head of the Great Being, it covered his entire body as if with gold dust.
Standing upon the pericarp of a lotus, he placed various kinds of exquisite food into the bowl of the Paccekabuddha.
Having accepted it and offered words of thanksgiving, he threw the bowl into the air while the great multitude looked on.
