He too, having ascended into the air, went back to the Himālayas as if crushing various rows of clouds.
Māra, defeated and overcome with dejection, returned to his own dwelling place.
But the Bodhisatta, while still standing upon the pericarp of the lotus, taught the Dhamma to the great multitude by praising generosity and virtue; and by that great multitude—
Surrounded by his retinue, he entered his own residence and, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving for the rest of his life, departed according to his karma.
The Teacher said, "Householder, it is not surprising that you, being thus endowed with vision, were not shaken by the deity now;
rather, it was precisely what the wise did in the past. Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, he established the connection [to the Jātaka].
Having thus connected the Jātaka, he identified it: "At that time, the Paccekabuddha attained final Nibbāna right there;
and as for the merchant of Bārāṇasī who, having defeated Māra, stood upon a lotus calyx and gave alms-food to the Paccekabuddha, it was none other than I myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Khadiraṅgāra Jātaka, the tenth.
The fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Bird’s Nest.
Its summary verse:
The bird’s nest, the dance, the friendly greeting, the fish, and the whirlpool.
The bird, the partridge, the crane, Nanda, and the charcoal of the acacia tree.
5. The Section on Those Desiring Welfare [41] 1. The Commentary on the Losaka Jātaka.
"Whoever desires welfare"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning the elder named Losaka Tissa.
But who was this elder Losaka Tissa? He was a son of a fisherman from the kingdom of Kosala, a monk who had brought ruin upon his own family and was one who obtained no gains.
It is said that after passing away from the place where he had been reborn, he was born in the kingdom of Kosala into a household of a thousand families...
He took rebirth in the womb of a certain fisherwoman in the village of Kevaṭṭa.
On the day he was conceived, that thousand families, searching for fish with their nets in rivers, ponds, and other waters, did not catch even a single small fish.
From that time on, those fishermen began to decline; indeed, while he was still in her womb, their [fortune] diminished.
The village was burned by fire seven times and punished by the king seven times. Thus, in due course, they became impoverished.
They thought, "In the past we did not have such misfortune; but now we are declining. There must be one ill-omened person among us;
let us divide ourselves into two groups. So five hundred families from each group came together.
Thereafter, wherever his parents lived, that very portion would decline while the other increased.
They divided that portion into two, and that again into two; thus, until the entire family became one [in fortune], they recognized their ill-fated nature, beat them, and cast them out.
Then his mother, having lived with great difficulty, gave birth to him in one place when her womb was fully matured.
It is impossible to destroy a being in his final existence; like a lamp inside a jar, the necessary condition for Arahantship burned within his heart.
After she had looked after that boy and he had reached the age of crawling about, she gave him a small bowl.
Having placed his hand [on the boy's head] and sent him off, saying, "Son, enter this house," she fled.
From then on, being all alone, he sought alms here and there and slept in various places;
he did not bathe, nor did he tend to his body, but like a dust-demon, he maintained his livelihood with great hardship. Gradually, he reached the age of seven years.
Having offered [the food], he would pick up and eat each grain of rice like a crow at a spot where the washing of a mortar had been discarded at the door of a house.
Then, while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, the Dhammasenāpati saw him and thought, "This being has reached a state of extreme wretchedness;
which village does he dwell in? Having extended a mind of loving-kindness toward him, he said, "Come here, you! He then approached.
Having paid homage to the elder, he stood before him. Then the elder asked him, “In which village do you live?
Where are your mother and father? “Venerable sir, I am destitute; my mother and father, saying ‘We are exhausted by supporting you,’ abandoned me and fled.
“But will you go forth into homelessness? “Venerable sir, I would indeed go forth; but one like me—”
"But who will ordain such a wretched person? "I shall ordain him," [the Elder replied]. "Very well, venerable sir, please ordain him.

The Elder gave him hard and soft food, led him to the monastery, bathed him with his own hands, ordained him, and when he had completed the full period of training, conferred upon him the higher ordination (*upasampadā*). In his old age, he became known as "Thera Losakatissa."
He was of little merit and received little gain. It is said that even when given an incomparable gift, he had never before obtained enough to fill his belly;
he received only what was necessary for his livelihood. For when a single lump of rice-gruel was poured into his bowl, it appeared as if the bowl were filled to the brim.
Then people, thinking, "His bowl is full," would pour more gruel into it from below. [Thus] the gruel in his bowl—
They say that at the time of giving, the rice-gruel would vanish from the bowls of people; the same principle applies to the cakes and other foods as well.
Although he later increased his insight (vipassanā) and established himself in the supreme fruit of Arahantship, he remained one who obtained little gain.
Then, as his life-forces gradually declined, the day of his final Nibbāna arrived. [Thus spoke] the General of the Dhamma.
Reflecting thus, he learned of the Elder’s impending Parinibbāna and thought, “Today this Losakatissa Thera will pass away;
today it is fitting for me to give him as much food as he requires. Taking him with him, he entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Relying upon him, the Elder did not even extend his hand to offer a mere salutation among the vast crowds of people in Sāvatthī.
He received nothing. Then the elder sent him away, saying, "Go, friend, sit down in the assembly hall," and departed. As soon as he arrived, the people, seeing him, said, "The venerable one has come!
They seated him on a seat and fed him. The elder also sent back the food he had obtained, saying, "Give this to Losaka.
But having taken it, they went and did not give it to the Elder Losakatissa; instead, they ate it themselves.
Then, as the Elder was rising and about to go to his monastery, the Elder Losakatissa came and paid homage to him.
The Elder turned back and, while still standing, asked, "Friend, have you received alms? "We shall receive them, venerable sir," they replied.
The Elder, overcome with a sense of urgency, looked toward the time; the time had already passed. The Elder said, "Let it be so, friend; let us stay right here."
Having seated the Elder Losaka in the assembly hall with the words, "Be seated," he went to the residence of the King of Kosala.
The king had the Elder’s bowl brought and, saying, "It is not yet time for the meal," had it filled to the brim with the four sweets.
Taking that, the Elder went and said, "Come, friend Tissa, eat these four sweets," and having taken the bowl—
He stood there, feeling shame and reverence, and would not eat. Then the Elder said to him, "Come, friend Tissa;
I shall stand holding this bowl while you sit and eat. If I were to let go of the bowl from my hand, nothing untoward would happen.
Thereupon, the Venerable Losakatissa Thera [addressed] the Chief Disciples...
While the Dhamma-Senāpati stood holding the bowl, [the Elder] partook of the fourfold sweet dish. By the power of the Elder’s noble psychic potency (*ariyiddhibala*), it did not reach exhaustion.
Then the Elder Losakatissa partook until his hunger was satisfied and his belly was full;
and on that very day, he attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*) in the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Having stood there, he caused his body to be laid down; they took his relics and erected a shrine.
Then, the monks gathered in the Dhamma hall and spoke among themselves: "Friends, alas!
The elder Losakatissa was of little merit and received few gains; how indeed could such a person of little merit and few gains attain the Noble Dhamma?"
They sat down. The Teacher went to the Dhamma Hall and asked, "Bhikkhus, about what talk are you gathered here now?
They reported, "It is this, venerable sir. The Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, this bhikkhu brought about his own state of non-attainment and his attainment of the noble Dhamma by his own hand.
For in the past, he created obstacles to the gains of others..."
"Having become one who gains little through the power of being devoted to insight (*vipassanā*)— contemplating ‘impermanence, suffering, and non-self’—
he became an attainer of the noble Dhamma,” he said, and then related a story from the past. It is said that in the past,
during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, a certain bhikkhu was living in a village monastery depending upon a certain householder.
A virtuous monk of purified nature, devoted to the practice of insight, was living there.
Now, a certain elder whose taints were destroyed, while traveling on his rounds for alms, eventually arrived at the village where that monk’s lay supporter lived.
The householder, having gained confidence in the elder merely by his deportment, took his bowl, led him into the house, and provided him with a meal with great care.
Having heard a brief discourse on the Dhamma, he paid homage to the Elder and said, "Venerable sir, please go to our own monastery;

we shall come and see you in the evening. The Elder went to the monastery, paid homage to the resident Elder, took leave of him, and sat down to one side. The resident Elder also exchanged greetings with him and said, "We have received..."
"Friends, have you received almsfood? he asked. "Yes, we have received it," they replied. "Where was it received?

"In the house of a householder in your village ahead. Having said this, he inquired about his own lodging, looked after it, put away his bowl and robes, and sat down, spending his time in the bliss of jhāna and the bliss of the fruit [of the path].
That householder, too, having taken perfumes, garlands, and lamps in the evening, went to the monastery.
Having paid homage to the resident elder, he asked, "Venerable sir, there is a visiting elder; has he arrived? "Yes, he has arrived.
"Where is he now? "In such-and-such a dwelling. He went to him, paid homage, and stood to one side.
Having sat down and heard the discourse on the Dhamma, and having worshipped both the shrine and the Bodhi tree at the cool hour, he lit lamps and went away after inviting both groups of people.
Meanwhile, the resident elder thought, "This householder has become estranged;
if this monk continues to dwell in this monastery, he will no longer take any account of me," and thus he felt displeasure toward the elder.

Having fallen into this state, he thought, "It is proper for me to show my displeasure toward him while staying in this monastery," and so he did not speak a word to him when the elder arrived at the time of attendance. The Elder Khīṇāsavatthera, knowing his intention, thought,
"This elder does not know that I am free from obstacles within my family or my group," and thus he went to his own dwelling place.
He spent his time in the bliss of meditation and the bliss of the fruit [of the path].
On the following day, the resident monk struck the gong with the back of his fingernail, knocked on the door with his nail, and went to the house of the householder.
The householder took his bowl, seated him on a prepared seat, and asked, "Where is the visiting elder?"
“Venerable sir,” he asked. “I do not know the news regarding your personal attendant; though I struck the gong and knocked on the door, I could not wake him.
Having eaten a sumptuous meal at your house yesterday, he will now have fallen fast asleep, unable to digest it. You, being full of faith, [should consider] such places as these.”

"Do you have faith? he asked. [The elder replied: "Even a *thera* whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), having observed his own time for alms-round and attended to his body, takes his bowl and robe, leaps into the air, and goes elsewhere.
That householder then fed the resident *thera* rice porridge prepared with ghee, honey, and sugar; he then rubbed the bowl with fragrant powders and once again—
Having filled it, he said, "Venerable sir, that elder will be exhausted from the journey; please take this for him," and gave it to him.

The other, without refusing, took it and as he was going along, he thought: "If that bhikkhu drinks this milk-rice, even if he were seized by the neck and dragged out, he would not leave. But if I give this milk-rice to people..."
"My deed will become manifest. If I throw it into the water, the ghee will appear on the surface of the water.
If I discard it on the ground, it will be revealed by the gathering of crows. Where, indeed, should I discard this?
While reflecting thus, he saw a burnt field; having spread out the embers and cast it there, he covered it over with embers.
Having covered [the bowl] and gone to the monastery, not seeing that bhikkhu, he thought:
"Surely that bhikkhu, having understood my intention, must have gone elsewhere; alas, for the sake of my belly, I have done what is improper.
At that very moment, great dejection arose within him. From that time forth, he became a hungry ghost (manussapeta) and no longer...
After a long time had passed, he died and was reborn in hell.

Having been boiled in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years, by the remaining residue of that karma, he was successively born as a *yakkha* for five hundred births, during which he did not obtain even a single day’s food to fill his belly. However, on one occasion, [he obtained] fetal impurity...
He obtained food to fill his belly. Again, for five hundred births, he was a dog;
even then, on one single day he obtained food to fill his belly from vomited meal, but at other times, he had never before obtained food sufficient to fill his belly.
Having passed away from that canine womb, he was reborn in a poor family in a certain village in the kingdom of Kāsi. From the moment of his birth...
That family became utterly destitute; from that time forward, they did not receive even a mere ladle of water or gruel.

He, however, was named Mittavindaka. His parents, unable to endure the suffering of hunger, beat him, saying, "Go away, you ill-omened one," and cast him out. Wandering without any refuge, he went to Bārāṇasī.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher in Bārāṇasī, instructing five hundred young brahmins in their craft.
At that time, the residents of Bārāṇasī would provide travel expenses for those of poor means so that they might learn the craft.
This Mittavindaka also learned his craft in the presence of the Bodhisatta. He was harsh and unable to endure correction. He—
Wandering about while striking him, he did not accept the advice even when being exhorted by the Bodhisatta.
Because of him, his own livelihood also became meager.
Then, after quarreling with the young students and refusing to accept their advice, he fled from there and, while wandering on, came upon one...
Having reached a border village, he lived by working for wages.
There, he entered into a union with a certain poor woman, and through him she gave birth to two sons.
The villagers, saying, "You should report our good news and bad news," provided Mittavindaka with his wages and had him live in a small hut at the entrance of the village. Him—

But because of their reliance on Mittavindaka, those inhabitants of the frontier village went to the royal court for punishment seven times, their houses were burnt down seven times, and their irrigation tank was breached seven times.
They thought, "Formerly, when this Mittavindaka had not yet come here, such things did not happen to us; but now, because of him..."
"Since the time you arrived, we have been declining," they said, and having beaten him, they cast him out.
Taking his children with him, he went elsewhere and entered a forest inhabited by non-human spirits (*amanussa*).
There, those non-humans killed both his children and his wife and devoured their flesh. He fled from there.
Wandering here and there, he reached a port town named Gambhīra on the very day ships were being dispatched;
becoming a laborer, he boarded a ship. After traveling across the ocean for seven days, on the seventh day, the ship came to a halt in the middle of the sea as if it had been driven to a standstill.
They drew lots for the "black-eared" curse (*kāḷakaṇṇi*), and for the seventh time...
It reached Mittavindaka himself. People gave him a bundle of bamboo, took him by the hand, and threw him onto the surface of the ocean;

as soon as he was thrown there, the ship departed. Mittavindaka lay down upon the bundle of bamboo and traveled across the surface of the ocean, and by the fruit of the virtue protected during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, [he arrived] at one spot upon the surface of the ocean.
Having obtained four celestial maidens in the crystal palace, he dwelt there for seven days experiencing happiness in their company.
Those palanquin-bearers of the celestial mansion experience happiness for seven days and suffering for seven days.
When they were about to go to experience the seven days of suffering, they said, "Stay right here until we return," and then they departed.
When they had departed, Mittavindaka lay down upon a bundle of reeds and, proceeding forward, obtained eight celestial nymphs (*devadhītara*) in a silver mansion.
Going further than that, he obtained sixteen in a jewel mansion and thirty-two celestial nymphs in a golden mansion.
Disregarding their words as well, he proceeded further and reached a city of *yakkhas* on an intermediate island.
He saw [them]. There, one female spirit (*yakkhinī*) was wandering about in the form of a goat.
Not knowing she was a spirit, Mittavindaka thought, "I shall eat goat's meat," and seized her by the foot. By the power of her spirit-nature, she lifted him up and threw him away.
Thrown by her, he traveled over the surface of the ocean and landed upon the top of a thicket of thorns on the edge of a moat in Bārāṇasī.
Having fallen and rolled along, he came to rest upon the ground. At that time, thieves were stealing the goats that were grazing on the bank of the moat belonging to the king.
The goat-herders stood hidden to one side, thinking, "We shall catch the thieves.
Having rolled down and come to a standstill on the ground, Mittavindaka saw those goats and thought, "In the ocean, at one..."
"In Dīpaka, I once caught a she-goat by its leg and threw it; it fell right here.
If I catch a she-goat by its leg now, it will throw me across to the surface of the ocean, into the presence of the deities of the celestial mansions.
Having thus applied his mind in an improper way, he caught the she-goat by its leg. As soon as it was caught, it bleated. The goat-herders came from this side and that.
Having seized him and beaten him, saying, "This thief has been eating goats in the royal palace for so long," they bound him and led him before the king.
At that moment, the Bodhisatta, surrounded by five hundred young brahmins, was departing from the city and going to bathe.
Seeing Mittavindaka and recognizing him, he said to those men, "Sirs, this is our pupil;
why have you seized him? "Noble sir, he is a goat-thief; he seized a goat by the leg, therefore he was caught.
"In that case, give him to us as a slave; he shall live supported by us. They replied, "Very well, noble sir," and [gave him to them].
Having dismissed him, they departed. Then the Bodhisatta asked him, "Mittavindaka, where have you been living all this time?
He related everything he had done. The Bodhisatta said, "By failing to follow the advice of those who wish one well, one encounters such suffering," and spoke this verse:
“He who, when exhorted by one who desires his welfare and is compassionate for his benefit, does not carry out the instruction—like Mittaka, he will grieve like the jackal hanging from the foot.
In this context, *atthakāmassa* means “of one desiring his prosperity”; *hitānukampino* means “of one who feels compassion through [the wish for] his benefit.”
"Being exhorted" means being advised with gentle and benevolent intent. "He does not follow the instruction" means he does not act upon what has been taught;

he is difficult to speak to and refuses correction. "He grieves like Mittaka" means that just as this Mittavindaka grieved and suffered after seizing the hind leg of a she-goat, so too does he grieve at all times. With this verse, the Bodhisatta taught the Dhamma.
Thus, throughout that entire period, that elder had previously obtained only enough to fill his own belly in three existences:
one day, as a *yakkha*, he received fetal impurity; one day, as a dog, he received vomit from food;
and on the day of his final *parinibbāna*, through the power of the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), he received the four sweet foods. Such is the obstructing of another’s gain.
It should be understood that this is indeed a great fault. At that time, both that teacher and Mittavindaka went according to their respective kamma.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, saying, "Thus, monks, he himself brought about his own state of meager gain and his attainment of the Noble Dhamma," and having established the connection, he identified the Jātaka.
—“At that time, Mittavindaka was the Elder Losakatissa, while I myself was the world-renowned teacher.
Thus ends the first commentary, the Losaka Jātaka.
[42] 2. The Commentary on the Kapota Jātaka.
"Whoever desires welfare..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning a certain greedy monk.
That monk’s greed will be made clear in the *Kākajātakam* of the *Navakanipāta*.
At that time, however, the monks informed the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, this monk is greedy. Then the Teacher said to him, "Is it true, monk?"
“Did you escape? he asked. “Yes, Bhante,” he replied. The Teacher said, “Monk, even in the past you were greedy, and because of your greed you met your death;
even wise men have been deprived of their dwelling places on account of you. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a pigeon.
At that time, out of a desire for merit, the inhabitants of Bārāṇasī hung straw baskets in various places for the birds to dwell in comfortably.
The steward of the merchant of Bārāṇasī also hung a straw basket in his own kitchen and set it there;
the Bodhisatta took up residence therein. Rising early in the morning, he went out to seek his food.

Having gone out and returned in the evening, he spent his time dwelling there. Then one day, a certain crow, flying over the kitchen, caught the scent of the smoke from the smoking of sour fish and meat;
conceiving a greedy desire, he sat down nearby and, while observing closely, thought, "By relying on whom shall I obtain this fish and meat? In the evening—
Seeing the Bodhisatta entering the kitchen, [the hunter] thought, "By means of this dove, I shall obtain fish and meat.
On the following day, he arrived early in the morning and followed right behind the Bodhisatta as he went out for his alms-round.
Then the Bodhisatta said to him, "Friend, why are you [following] with us?"
“Are you well? he asked. “Master, I find your service pleasing; from now on, I shall attend upon you,” she said.
“Friend, your range is one thing and ours is another; it would be difficult for you to serve us,” he replied.
“Master, when you go out to seek your food, I too will take my own food and go along with you,” she said.
“Excellent! You must simply be heedful,” the Bodhisatta advised the crow, and then, while wandering for his food, he ate grass seeds and the like.

However, at the time when the Bodhisatta went out to seek food, the crow would go ahead, remove clumps of cow dung, eat the insects therein until his belly was full, and then return to the Bodhisatta’s side, saying, “Master, you—”
"Go about for food at the proper time; it is not right to be one who eats excessively," he said.
Having taken his alms-round with the Bodhisatta, the crow entered the kitchen together with him as they returned in the evening.
The cook, thinking, "Our pigeon has come back bringing another," set out a basket for the crow as well. From then on, two birds lived there.
Then one day, they brought a great quantity of fish and meat to the merchant. Taking it, the cook hung it here and there in the kitchen.
Seeing this, the crow conceived a greedy desire and thought, "Tomorrow, instead of going to my usual feeding ground, I shall eat only this.
So he lay down that night groaning. On the following day, the Bodhisatta went out for his alms-round.
As he was going along, he said, "Come, friend crow! [The crow replied,] "Master, you go; I have a disease in my belly.
[The man said,] "Friend, a disease in the belly has never before occurred for crows. During the night, in each of the three watches, they become intoxicated;
however, when they swallow a lamp-wick, they are satisfied for a moment. You—this..."
“You will want to eat fish and meat; come now, that which is enjoyed by humans is difficult for you to enjoy.
Do not do such a thing; go with me for alms. “I cannot, Master,” he replied.
“In that case, you shall be known by your own deeds; do not fall under the power of greed, but be heedful,” he advised him.
The Bodhisatta had gone out for alms.
The cook, having prepared various kinds of fish and meat dishes, opened the vessels slightly to let the steam escape;
he then placed a straining bowl for the sauce upon the vessels and went outside.
He stood there wiping his sweat. At that moment, a crow perched [on a branch], raised its head, and looking toward the house where food was kept, realized that he had gone out.
Thinking, "Now is the time for me to fulfill my desire and eat some meat; shall I eat a large piece of meat, or rather, some small scraps? it considered, "With small scraps of meat..."
"Indeed, it is not possible to fill my belly quickly; I shall lie down while eating a large piece of meat that I have brought and placed in a basket.
Having leapt from the basket, he settled upon a soup-bowl. She let out a cry of "Kirī!
Hearing that sound, the cook entered wondering, "What is this? and seeing the crow, [thought], "This is a wicked crow..."
"The great merchant wishes to eat choice meat, yet I live by depending on the merchant and not on this fool;

what use have I for him? Having said this, he closed the door, seized the crow, plucked the feathers from its entire body, pounded fresh ginger, salt, cumin, and other spices, mixed them with sour buttermilk, and smeared it over the crow's whole body.
Having smeared it [with blood], he threw the crow into a basket. Overwhelmed by extreme pain, the crow lay down groaning.

The Bodhisatta, returning in the evening, saw that it had met with such calamity and said, “O greedy crow, because you did not do as I told you and relied instead on your greed, you have come to this great suffering,” and spoke this verse:
“He who, though being exhorted by one who desires his welfare and feels compassion for him, does not follow the instruction—”
"By not following the words of the pigeon, he lies like one who has fallen into the hands of his enemies.
In this context, "not following the words of the pigeon" means not acting upon the beneficial advice given by the dove.

"He lies like one who has fallen into the hands of his enemies" means [he lies] within the reach of the hands, that is, within the path of the hands, of enemies—those persons who cause harm and produce suffering.
“This person, like that crow, having fallen into great calamity, lies there lamenting.
Having spoken this verse, the Bodhisatta thought, “I can no longer dwell in this place,” and departed for another location.
The crow, too, met its end right there. Then the cook, along with his basket—
Having taken it, he threw it away in a place of refuse.
The Teacher also said, "Monk, you were not greedy only now; you were greedy even in the past.
And because of that greediness of yours, even wise men have been deprived of their own dwellings. Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, he proclaimed the Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths—
That bhikkhu attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala). The Teacher, having established the connection, identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the crow was the greedy bhikkhu, and I myself was the pigeon.
This is the second commentary on the Kapota-jātaka.
[43] 3. The Commentary on the Bamboo-Leaf Jātaka:
"He who desires one's welfare..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was difficult to speak to.
For the Blessed One, having asked him, "Is it true, monk, that you are difficult to speak to? he replied, "It is true."
When he had said, "Venerable Sir," [the Buddha] replied, "Monk, you were not only difficult to speak to just now; you were difficult to speak to even in the past.
And because of that very difficulty in speaking, by failing to follow the advice of the wise, you met your death in the mouth of a snake. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of great wealth in the kingdom of Kāsi.
Having been reborn and attained to maturity, he saw the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation;

abandoning sensual pleasures, he entered the Himalayas, went forth as an ascetic, performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*, and having developed the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments, he spent his time in the bliss of *jhāna*.
Later, accompanied by a great retinue of five hundred ascetics...
Surrounded by his followers, he lived as the Teacher of the community.
Now, a certain young snake, wandering according to its own nature, arrived at the hermitage of a certain ascetic.
The ascetic, having conceived a fatherly affection for it, laid it to sleep in a bamboo tube and looked after it. Because it slept in a bamboo tube, it was given the name "Veḷuka."
They gave him the name "Veḷuka-pitā" (Father of the Bamboo) because they raised him out of affection for their son.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having heard that "a certain ascetic is reportedly raising a venomous snake," summoned him and asked, "Is it true that you are raising a venomous snake?
When he replied, "It is true," [the Bodhisatta said], "A friendship with a venomous snake..."
“There is no such thing; do not hold such a view,” he said. “He is my teacher’s son; I shall not be able to live without him.

“In that case, you will meet your end at his very hands. The ascetic did not heed the Bodhisatta’s words, nor was he able to abandon the venomous snake. Then, after a few days had passed, all the ascetics—
Having gone for the sake of fruit and roots, they saw that fruit and roots were easily obtained at that place and stayed right there for two or three days.
Veḷuka’s father, also going with them, lay down a venomous snake right on a bamboo thicket, covered it over, and departed.
After two or three days had passed, he returned with the ascetics and [said], "Veḷuka’s grazing ground..."
Saying, "I will give it," he opened the bamboo joint and, calling out, "Come, my dear son, here is your food," he extended his hand.
The venomous snake, enraged by two or three days of hunger, bit the extended hand, bringing the ascetic to his death right then and there, and then entered the forest.
When the other ascetics saw this, they informed the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta [then addressed] him...
Having performed his bodily duties and sat down in the midst of the company of seers, he spoke this verse as an exhortation to the seers:
“He who, when exhorted by one who desires his welfare and is compassionate for his benefit,
does not follow the instruction— thus he lies struck down, just like the father of Veḷuka.”

"In that very place he lies thus struck down"—the meaning is this: whoever does not accept the advice of the seers, like this ascetic who, having reached a state of putrefaction in the mouth of a venomous snake, lies there struck down, even so he lies struck down after meeting with great ruin.
Having thus exhorted the company of seers and cultivated the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra), the Bodhisatta was reborn in the Brahma-world at the end of his lifespan.

The Teacher said, "Monk, it is not only now that you were difficult to speak to; formerly too you were difficult to speak to, and it was precisely because of this difficult speech that you met with putrefaction in the mouth of a venomous snake.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and established the connection, he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the monk Veḷuka-pitā was the difficult-to-speak-to monk, and the rest of the assembly was the assembly of Buddhas."
"But I myself was the leader of the host.
This concludes the third commentary, the Veḷuka Jātaka.
4. The Commentary on the Makasa Jātaka.
"Better is an enemy"—this was spoken by the Teacher while wandering on tour among the Magadhans, concerning certain foolish villagers of a particular small town.

It is said that at one time the Tathāgata, having departed from Sāvatthī for the kingdom of Magadha, reached a certain village while wandering there on tour. And that village was inhabited almost entirely by ignorant, foolish people.
[He was] elated. Then one day those foolish, blind men gathered together and said, "Friends, while we are working after entering the forest, mosquitoes bite us;
because of that, our work is interrupted. Let us all take up bows and weapons, go forth, fight with the mosquitoes, and pierce and cut every single mosquito."
Having deliberated thus, "We shall kill him," they went into the forest;

thinking, "We shall pierce the mosquito," they pierced and struck one another until they were overcome with pain, and having returned, they lay down inside the village, in the middle of the village, and at the village gate.
The Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, entered that village for alms. The remaining wise people [approached] the Blessed One...

Having seen them, they had a pavilion constructed at the village gate, offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, and after paying homage to the Teacher, they sat down. The Teacher, seeing the people fallen here and there, asked those lay followers:
"There are many of these sick people; what has been done for them? "Venerable Sir, these people [prepared] a 'battle of mosquitoes'..."
"Having gone there thinking, 'We shall kill them,' they pierced one another and became ill themselves.

The Teacher said, "It is not only now that foolish people strike themselves thinking, 'We shall strike the mosquitoes'; in the past as well, there were men who struck others thinking, 'We shall strike the mosquito.
Having said this, when requested by those men, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta made his living as a merchant.
At that time, in a certain frontier village in the kingdom of Kāsi, many carpenters lived.
There, a clumsy carpenter was hewing a tree; then, a mosquito settled upon his head, which resembled the surface of a copper iron cauldron.
As if striking with a spear, he pierced the head with his snout. He said to his son who was sitting near him, "Dear son, a mosquito is piercing my head as if striking it with a spear; ward it off!
"Father, endure it; I shall kill it in a single stroke. At that moment, the Bodhisatta also [spoke] to himself...
While searching for materials, he arrived at that village and sat down in the carpenter’s workshop.
Then the carpenter said to his son, “Dear boy, ward off this mosquito.
The son replied, “I will ward it off, father,” and raising a sharp, large axe, he stood behind his father’s back and split his father’s head in two, thinking, “I shall strike the mosquito.”
The carpenter met his death right there.
Having seen that deed of his, the Bodhisatta thought, "Even an enemy who possesses wisdom is better; for such a person will not kill people even out of fear of punishment," and he spoke this verse:
"Better is an enemy endowed with intelligence than a friend devoid of it."
“For ‘I shall kill my father,’ the mute and dull-witted son struck off his father’s head.
In this context, *seyyo* means excellent, preeminent, or supreme. *Matiyā upeto* means endowed with wisdom (*paññā*).
*Eḷamūgo* means one who is foolish and has saliva at the mouth. “The son struck off his father’s head” means that, due to his own folly, even though he was a son, he severed his father’s head.
Thinking, "I shall strike the mosquito," he split his own head in two.
Therefore, having spoken this verse—"Better indeed is a wise enemy than a foolish friend"—the Bodhisatta rose up and departed according to his karma.
The relatives of the carpenter also performed the funeral rites for his body.
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching— "O lay followers, even in the past there were men who struck others thinking,
'We shall strike the mosquito'"— and having established the connection, he identified the Jātaka, saying:
"And the wise merchant who departed after speaking the verse was none other than I myself."
The fourth *Makasa-jātaka* commentary.
[45] 5. The *Rohiṇī-jātaka* commentary:
"Better is an enemy... This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain female slave of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika.
He related the story. It seems that Anāthapiṇḍika had a female slave named Rohiṇī.
When she came to the place where the rice was being harvested, her elderly mother lay down there; flies swarmed around her and bit her as if piercing her with needles.
She said to her daughter, "Daughter, the flies are biting me; keep them away. She replied, "I will keep them away, Mother."

Lifting up a pestle, thinking, "I shall kill the flies on my mother's body and bring about her destruction," she struck her mother with the pestle and brought her to the end of life. Seeing this, she began to weep, saying, "My mother is dead.
They reported this occurrence to the merchant. The merchant, having had the funeral rites for her performed, went to the monastery and related the entire account.
He informed the Teacher. The Teacher said, "Householder, it was not only now that she killed her mother by striking her with a pestle, thinking, 'I will kill the flies on my mother's body';
she had killed her even before. Having been requested by him, he related a past event.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a merchant family, and upon the passing of his father...
He attained the status of a wealthy merchant. He too had a female slave named Rohiṇī.
She, having come to where her mother was lying after harvesting rice, was told by her mother, "Mother, ward off the flies for me.

Having spoken thus, she struck her mother with a pestle in that very manner, bringing her to the end of life, and then began to weep. The Bodhisatta, hearing of this occurrence, said: "Even an enemy..."
Thinking, "Indeed, in this world, only the wise man is better," he spoke this verse:
"Better is a wise enemy than one who is compassionate toward fools;
see how the wretched Rohiṇikā, having killed her own mother, now grieves."
In this context, "medhāvī" means wise, knowledgeable, and discerning. Regarding the phrase "yañce bālānukampako," here the word *yaṃ* has undergone a change of gender;

*ca* is a particle used in the sense of a name (*nāmatthe*). The meaning is: "A wise person is surely better—even if he is an enemy—than a fool who is compassionate, by a hundredfold or a thousandfold.
Alternatively, *yaṃ* is a particle used in the sense of negation (*paṭisedhanatthe*). No...
The meaning is: "this one who has compassion for fools. "Jamma" means base and dull-witted. "Having killed his mother, he grieves":
thinking, "I shall kill a fly," he kills his own mother; now this fool weeps and laments all by himself.
For this reason, [the Bodhisatta], praising the wise man, taught the Dhamma with this verse: "In this world, even an enemy who is wise is better."
The Teacher said, “Householder, it was not only now that she killed her mother thinking, ‘I will kill a fly’; she killed her even in the past.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and established the connection, he identified the Jātaka:
“At that time, the mother was indeed the mother, the daughter was indeed the daughter, and I myself was the great treasurer.”
The fifth is the Commentary on the Rohiṇī-jātaka.
[46] 6. The Commentary on the Ārāmadūsaka-jātaka.
"Truly, not with one unskilled in what is harmful... This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in a certain village of Kosala concerning a garden-ruiner.
The Teacher spoke concerning this. It is said that while wandering on tour among the Kosalans, the Teacher arrived at a certain village.

There, a certain householder invited the Tathāgata, seated him in his own garden, and having offered a great alms-giving to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he said: "Venerable Sir, please wander about in this garden as you please. The bhikkhus—
Having risen and taken the park-keeper with them, they wandered through the park;
seeing a certain open space, they asked the park-keeper, "Lay follower, this park has shade everywhere else, yet in this place there is neither any tree nor any shrub;
what could be the reason for this? [The park-keeper replied: "Venerable sirs, at the time this park was being planted..."
"A certain village boy, while sprinkling water, uprooted the young trees in this place and watered them according to the depth of their roots.
Those young trees withered and died; for this reason, this place became a courtyard.
The monks approached the Teacher and reported this matter to him. The Teacher said, "Monks, it was not by me..."
“This village boy is a garden-spoiler even now; in the past, too, he was a garden-spoiler,” he said, and related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, they proclaimed a festival in Bārāṇasī.
From the moment the sound of the festival drum was heard, all the inhabitants of the city went about occupied with the festival. At that time, in the king’s park...
Many monkeys lived there. The park keeper thought, "A festival has been proclaimed in the city;
I will have these monkeys water it and I myself will enjoy the festival.
He approached the senior monkey and said, "Friend, leader of the monkeys, this park is of great benefit to you as well; you should [tend] the flowers, fruits, and shoots here..."
"Eat! A festival has been proclaimed in the city; I shall enjoy the festival.
While I am away, you will be able to water the young trees in this park," he asked. "Very well, we shall water them," they replied.
"In that case, be diligent," he said, and for the purpose of watering, he gave them leather water-bags and—
Having given [the skins] to Dārukaṭa, he departed. The monkeys took both the leather tents and the wooden tents and sprinkled water upon the young trees.
Then the leader of the monkeys said to them: "Sirs, monkeys, water must be protected.
While you are sprinkling water on the young trees, you must pull up [the soil] again and again, examine the roots, and [water only those] that have gone deep."
“Pour much water on the roots that are deep, and little on those that have not gone deep; later, water will become scarce for us.
They agreed, saying, “Very well,” and did accordingly.
At that time, a certain wise man, seeing those monkeys acting thus in the royal garden, said: “Sirs, ...”
“Monkeys, why do you keep uprooting young trees and pouring water on them to the depth of their roots?
They replied, “The leader of our monkeys instructs us thus. Hearing those words, he thought, “Alas, these fools are unwise!
Desiring to accomplish what is beneficial, they instead bring about only harm,” and he spoke this verse:
“Indeed, for one skilled in what is harmful, conduct that aims at welfare does not bring happiness;
the fool ruins his own welfare, just like the monkey who was a monastery attendant.

In this context, *ve* is a mere particle. *Anatthakusalena* means skilled in what is harmful (*anattha*) and in what is not a [proper] sphere (*anāyatana*), [as opposed to] skilled in what is beneficial (*attha*) and in the [proper] sphere (*āyatana*).
The meaning is: "by means of unwholesomeness regarding the cause. *Atthacariyā* means the act of promoting welfare. "Bringing happiness" (*sukhāvahā*):

for one who is unskilled in what is beneficial in such a manner, an act of promoting welfare—consisting of physical and mental happiness—is not conducive to happiness; the meaning is that it is impossible to bring about such happiness.
Why is this? Because "the dull-witted person utterly ruins his welfare. A foolish person, thinking "I shall do what is beneficial," [proceeds in a way that destroys it].

Having lost what is beneficial, he does only what is harmful. "Just like the monkey who was a park-keeper" means that just as a monkey appointed to the park, a guardian of the park, intends "I shall do what is beneficial," yet does only what is harmful;
even so, whoever is skilled in what is harmful is unable to bring about beneficial conduct—he certainly causes the loss of benefit. Thus is that wise one.
The man, having rebuked the monkey chief with this verse, departed from the park taking his own retinue with him.
The Teacher also, saying, "Monks, it was not only now that this village boy was a defiler of the monastery;
even in the past he was a defiler of the monastery," brought forth this Dhamma teaching, established the connection, and identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the monkey chief..."
“The village boy who was the garden-destroyer was that one, while I myself was the wise man.
This concludes the sixth commentary, the Story of the Garden-Destroyer.
[47] 7. The Commentary on the Story of the Destroyer of Varuṇa’s Grove.
“Indeed, not by one skilled in what is harmful”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Vāruṇidūsaka.

It is said that a friend of Anāthapiṇḍika, a certain wine-merchant, having prepared sharp wine and taking gold, silver, and other goods to sell it, addressed a man in the midst of a great crowd of people:
“Dear sir, take the price and give me the wine.”
Having instructed his pupil, he went himself to bathe.
While the pupil was distributing the *vāruṇī* liquor to the crowd, he saw people bringing salt crystals from time to time and eating them. Thinking, "This liquor must be unsalted;
I shall add salt to it," he put a measure of salt about the size of a reed into the liquor jar and [offered] the liquor to them.
She gave it to them. Having filled their mouths one after another and spat it out, they asked, "What have you done?
She replied, "Seeing you drinking liquor and asking for salt, I mixed it with salt. "O fool! You have ruined such delightful *vāruṇī* liquor!
Having thus reviled her, they rose up repeatedly and departed. The merchant who sold the *vāruṇī* came and [saw] not even a single...
Seeing this, he asked, "Where have the drinkers of *vāruṇī* gone? and the other reported the matter to him.
Then the teacher, rebuking him, saying, "Fool, such liquor as that has been ruined by you," related this incident to Anāthapiṇḍika.
Anāthapiṇḍika, thinking, "Now I have a topic for conversation," went to Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and—
He reported this matter [to the Teacher]. The Teacher said, "Householder, this man was not only a destroyer of *vāruṇī* liquor now; in the past as well, he was a destroyer of *vāruṇī*.
Being requested by him, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a merchant in Benares.
Dependent upon him lived a certain liquor merchant. Having prepared sharp liquor and told his pupil, "Sell this," he went away to bathe.
As soon as the teacher had gone, the pupil added salt to the liquor and destroyed it in that very manner.
Then the teacher returned, and having understood what had happened, [he spoke] to the merchant...
He reported this. The merchant said, "Fools who are unskilled in what is beneficial do only harm even when they think, 'We shall do what is beneficial,'" and he spoke this verse:
"Indeed, for one unskilled in what is beneficial, conduct aimed at the good does not bring happiness."
“The fool ruins his own welfare, just as Koṇḍañña ruined the *vāruṇī*.
In this context, “just as Koṇḍañña ruined the *vāruṇī*” means:
just as this pupil named Koṇḍañña, thinking “I shall prepare a dish,” ruined, diminished, and destroyed the *vāruṇī* by adding salt to it, so too does anyone who is unskilled in what is beneficial.
"He ruins his welfare"—with this verse the Bodhisatta taught the Dhamma.
The Teacher also said, "Householder, this man was not only a ruinous consumer of *vāruṇī* liquor now; in the past, too, he was a ruinous consumer of *vāruṇī*.
Having thus established the connection, he identified the Jātaka: "The ruinous consumer of *vāruṇī* then was the ruinous consumer of *vāruṇī* even now."
"But as for the merchant of Bārāṇasī, he was none other than myself.
This concludes the seventh commentary, the Vāruṇidūsaka Jātaka.
[48] 8. The Commentary on the Vedabbha Jātaka.
"By one who lacks skillful means, though there be purpose..."—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a monk who was difficult to admonish.
Regarding that monk, the Teacher said: "Monk, you have not only been difficult to admonish now; formerly too you were difficult to admonish.
For that very reason, having failed to act upon the words of the wise, you were cut in two by a sharp sword and left on the road."
"Fall down! And by relying on that single [tree], a thousand men have met their end," he said, and then related a story from the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, in a certain village there was a certain brahmin who knew a spell called Vedabbha.
That spell, it is said, was priceless and of great value; when the conjunction of the constellations was obtained, one could [use] that spell...
Having turned it over and looked up into the sky, a rain of the seven treasures poured down from the heavens.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was learning his craft from that brahmin.
Then one day, the brahmin, taking the Bodhisatta with him on some business, departed from his own village and went toward Cetaraṭṭha; and along the way, in a certain forested spot—
There were five hundred so-called "errand-corps robbers" who waylaid travelers on the road. They seized both the Bodhisatta and the Brahmin Vedabbha.
Why, then, are they called "errand-corps robbers"? It is said that having captured two men, they would send one off for the purpose of fetching wealth;
therefore, they are called "errand-corps robbers. Having seized the father and son, they said to the father, "You..."
"Bring us our wealth and take our son and go," they said.
By this means, they took the mother and daughter and released the mother; they took the younger and the elder and released the elder brother;
they took the teacher and the pupil and released the pupil. At that time, they took the Brahmin Vedabbha and released the Bodhisatta.
The Bodhisatta, having paid homage to his teacher, said: "I shall return after one or two days have passed;
do not be afraid. However, you must follow my word: today there will be an astrological conjunction for the raining down of wealth.
Do not, out of inability to endure hardship, recite the mantra and cause the rain of wealth to fall. If you should cause it to rain, [the consequences would be grave]."
“Both you and these five hundred thieves shall meet with destruction,” he said, thus advising his teacher, and then departed for the sake of wealth.
When the sun had set, the thieves bound the brahmin and laid him down.

At that very moment, the full orb of the moon rose from the eastern world-system. As the brahmin was observing the constellations, [he saw] the conjunction of the constellation that causes rain of wealth.

Thinking, "I have obtained it; what is the use of my experiencing suffering? Having recited the mantra and caused a rain of jewels to fall, I will give the wealth to the bandits and go wherever I please," he addressed the bandits:
"Gentlemen bandits, for what purpose have you seized me? "For the sake of wealth, noble sir. "If you have need of wealth, quickly—"
“Release me from my bonds, wash my head, clothe me in new garments, anoint me with perfumes, adorn me with flowers, and set me down,” he said.
Having heard his words, the robbers did exactly so.
Then the brahmin, knowing the conjunction of the constellations, recited a mantra and looked up into the sky; at that very moment, from the sky—
The jewels fell down. The robbers gathered that wealth together, made it into bundles, placed them in their upper robes, and fled.
The brahmin also followed right behind them. Then, five hundred other robbers seized those robbers.
When asked, "For what purpose do you seize us? they replied, "For the sake of wealth. [The others said,] "If you have need of wealth, [take this brahmin]."
"Seize him! He looked up at the sky and caused rain to fall as wealth; this very wealth was given to us by him.
The robbers released their own companion and seized the brahmin, saying, "Give us wealth too!
The brahmin said, "I would give you wealth, but the astrological conjunction for causing rain to fall as wealth occurs only at the end of this year."
"It shall be so. If you have need of wealth, consent; then I shall cause a rain of wealth to fall," he said. The thieves, becoming enraged, cried out, "Ho!
Wicked Brahmin! Having caused wealth to rain for others this very moment, you make us wait for another year!
and having cut the Brahmin in two with a sharp sword, they cast him aside on the road.
Having pursued them with speed and fought with those thieves, he killed them all and took the wealth.
Then, dividing into two groups, they fought one another;
having slain two hundred and fifty men, by this same means they continued to kill each other until only two people remained. In this way, that thousand men met their destruction.
Those two men, having brought that wealth by means of a stratagem and concealed it in a thicket near a village, sat down;
one remained guarding it with a sword in hand, while the other entered the village taking rice to have a meal cooked.
Thinking, "Greed is indeed the root of destruction," he who was sitting near the wealth reflected: "In him..."
“When he has arrived, this wealth will be divided into two portions;
what if I were to strike him with my sword and kill him as soon as he arrives? He fastened his sword and sat waiting for his arrival.
The other also thought: “That wealth will be divided into two portions; what if I were to put poison in the food?”
“Having fed that man and brought him to the end of his life, I shall take the wealth all alone.
When the meal was finished, he ate himself, mixed poison into the remainder, took it with him, and went there.
As soon as the other had set down the food, the first man cut it in two with a sword and discarded it in a hidden place.
Having eaten that meal, he too met his death right there.
And so, because of that wealth, they all came to ruin.
Then the Bodhisatta, after one or two days had passed, returned with the wealth; not seeing his teacher in that place, he—
But seeing his wealth scattered about, he thought, "The teacher must have rained down this wealth because he did not follow my words;
surely they will all meet with ruin. So he set out along the great highway.
As he went, seeing the teacher cut in two on the great highway, he thought, "He has died because he did not follow my words. He gathered wood, built a funeral pyre, and—
Having cremated his teacher and honored him with forest flowers, he went forward.
Seeing five hundred men who had reached the end of their lives, then two hundred and fifty before him, and finally, at the very end, seeing two men who had reached the end of their lives, he thought:
"This thousand men minus two have met with destruction; there must be two other thieves."
“They will not be able to steady themselves; where indeed have they gone?
As he went along, taking their wealth, he saw the path leading into the dense forest.
Continuing on, he saw a heap of wealth tied in bundles, and having uncovered a bowl of rice, he saw one who was dead. Then he thought, “This must be what they have done.”
Having understood everything, he searched, thinking, "Where indeed is that man? Finding him too cast away in a hidden place, he thought:
"Our teacher, by not following my words and because of his own obstinacy, has met with destruction;
furthermore, a thousand men have been destroyed by him. Alas, he sought his own advancement through improper means and without cause!"
Thinking, "Desiring [this] from us, they will meet with great destruction just like our teacher," he spoke this verse:
"He who seeks his goal by an improper means is frustrated;
the Cetans killed Vedabbha, and they all met with disaster."

In this context, "he is frustrated" means that the person who, lacking skillful means, exerts effort at the wrong time thinking, "I desire my own welfare, progress, and happiness," becomes frustrated, grows weary, and meets with great ruin.
"Cetā" refers to the thieves dwelling in the country of Ceta. "They killed Vedabba" means they killed the brahmin who had received the name "Vedabba" on account of the Vedabba spell.
"All of them have met with disaster"—that is, they all, without exception, having caused one another to be slain, encountered and obtained ruin.

Thus the Bodhisatta thought: "Just as our teacher, by employing an improper means and exerting effort in the wrong place, caused the rain of wealth to fall and himself met his end, becoming the cause of destruction for others as well; even so, whoever..."
"Furthermore, anyone else who, desiring their own welfare, exerts effort by means other than the proper method will themselves be ruined and will become a cause for the ruin of others.
While the deities were giving shouts of "Well done! as he spoke these words, making the forest resound, he taught the Dhamma with this verse.
Then, having brought that wealth to his own home by means of the proper method, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving.
Having remained for the full span of his life and fulfilling the path to heaven, he passed away at the end of his life.

The Teacher, as well, said: "Monk, you were not only difficult to speak to just now; you were difficult to speak to in the past as well. It was because of that difficult speech, however, that you met with great ruin.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and established the connection, he identified the Jātaka: "At that time..."
"The Brahmin Vedabbha was the monk Dubbaca, while I myself was his pupil.
This concludes the eighth commentary, the Vedabbha Jātaka.
[49] 9. The Commentary on the Nakkhatta Jātaka.
"Waiting for the auspicious moment": This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain Ājīvaka.

It is said that in Sāvatthī, a young man from a certain family in the countryside had won the hand of a daughter from a family there and had fixed a date, saying, "I shall take her on such-and-such a day. When that day arrived, he—his own... [text truncated]
He asked a local Ājīvaka, “Venerable sir, today we shall perform an auspicious ceremony; is the lunar mansion (nakkhatta) favorable?
Becoming angry and thinking, “Without first asking me, he has already fixed the day and now asks me;
very well, I will instruct him,” he replied, “Today the lunar mansion is unfavorable; do not perform the auspicious ceremony today.”
“If you do so, or if you were to do so, there will be a great disaster,” he said. The people of that family, having placed their trust in him, did not go out on that day.
The city-dwellers, having performed all the auspicious rites, seeing that they had not arrived, thought, “They have set aside this day, yet they have not come; we too have much work to do.”
"What is the use of those things? We shall give our daughter to another," they said; and with the very same auspicious rites as before, they gave their daughter to another family.
On the following day, the others arrived and said, "Give us the girl. Then the residents of Sāvatthī said to the residents of the countryside:
“O householders, you wicked men did not come out of contempt by setting aside the day; go back by the very same path you came!
We have given our daughters to others,” they reviled them.
Having quarreled with them and failed to obtain the girl, they departed by the same path they had come. By that Ājīvaka as well, for those people...
The fact that the Ājīvaka had brought about an obstacle to the family’s auspicious ceremony became known among the monks.
Having assembled in the Dhamma Hall, those monks sat there conversing, saying, "Friends, the Ājīvaka has brought about an obstacle to the family’s auspicious ceremony.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, what conversation are you sitting here discussing now? They [replied].
“They said, ‘Indeed by this one. ‘Monks, it is not only now that the Ājīvaka has brought about an obstacle to the auspicious rites for that family;
in the past as well, he became angry with them and brought about an obstacle to their auspicious rites,’ and having said this, he related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the inhabitants of the city [took] the daughter of the inhabitants of the countryside..."
Having set aside the day and excluded their own personal attendant Ājīvaka, they asked him, "Venerable sir, today we have a ceremony for good fortune; is the lunar mansion auspicious?
He, thinking, "These people have chosen the day according to their own preference and are now asking me," became angry and thought, "Today I shall create an obstacle to their good fortune."
“Today is an inauspicious constellation; if you go, you will meet with great disaster,” he said.
Believing his words, they did not go. When the country-dwellers learned that they had not returned, they thought, “They have not come even today, which they had set aside;
what need have we for them? We shall give our daughters to others. And so they gave their daughters to others. The city-dwellers—
On the following day, they came and asked for the girl. The country-dwellers said, "You city-dwelling householders are indeed shameless;
you did not take the girl even after setting a date. Because of your failure to come, we gave her to others.
They replied, "We waited and consulted an Ājīvika, who told us, 'The constellation is not auspicious,' so we did not come."
“Give us the girl! [They replied: “Because you had not come, we gave her to others; now, how can we bring back a girl who has already been given away?
While they were thus quarreling with one another, a certain wise man living in the city, on account of some business...
Having gone to the countryside, he heard those city-dwellers saying, "We did not come because we had asked an Ājīvaka about the auspiciousness of the lunar mansion.
Hearing this, he said, "What is the use of a lunar mansion? Is it not the very fact that the girl has been obtained that constitutes the 'lunar mansion'?
and spoke this verse:
“The purpose passed by the fool who waited for the constellations;
purpose is the constellation for purpose—what will the stars do?
In this context, *patimānentaṃ* means looking out [expectantly], thinking, “Now the constellation will appear, now the constellation will appear.”
"Waiting. "The purpose has passed the fool": this means that for the foolish city-dweller, the purpose consisting of the acquisition of the girl has been surpassed.
"Purpose is the omen of purpose": whatever purpose one wanders about seeking, that very purpose once obtained is called the "omen of purpose.
"What will the stars do? refers, however, to the other stars in the sky.
"What will they do? What purpose will they accomplish? is the meaning. The city-dwellers, having quarreled, departed without even obtaining the girl.
The Teacher said, "Monks, this Ājīvaka has not only now caused an obstacle to the family's auspiciousness; in the past as well..."
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma and established the connection, he identified the Jātaka:
"The Ājīvaka of that time was the Ājīvaka of the present; those families were the very same families as they are now;
and the wise man who stood there after reciting the verse was none other than I myself."
The ninth is the commentary on the *Nakkhatta-jātaka*.
[50] 10. The commentary on the *Dummedha-jātaka*:

"Of the foolish ones"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning his conduct for the welfare of the world. This will be made clear in the *Mahākaṇha-jātaka* in the Twelfth Book (*Dvādasakanipāta*).
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of that king’s chief queen.
On the day his name was given upon his emergence from his mother’s womb, they named him Prince Brahmadatta.
When he reached the age of sixteen, having mastered the arts at Takkasilā, he became proficient in the three Vedas.
Having crossed over, he attained mastery in the eighteen branches of knowledge (*vijjāṭṭhāna*); then his father gave him the position of viceroy.
At that time, the inhabitants of Bārāṇasī were followers of the auspicious rites of the deities;
they worshipped the deities, and having slaughtered many goats, rams, chickens, pigs, and so forth, [they offered] various kinds of flowers, perfumes, meat, and blood.
And they performed the *bali* offering. The Bodhisatta thought: "Now these beings regard deities as auspicious and commit much slaughter of living beings;
for the most part, the great mass of people is settled in what is unrighteous (*adhamma*).

When I have obtained the kingdom upon my father’s passing, I shall not, even with a single person left unexhausted, allow the slaughter of living beings to continue by any means whatsoever. One day, he...
Having mounted his chariot and departed from the city, he saw a great multitude of people gathered at a large banyan tree.
At the foot of that tree, they were making various petitions before a deity who had been reborn there, seeking whatever they desired—sons, daughters, wealth, and so forth.
Seeing this, he descended from the chariot, approached the tree, and [offered] perfumes and flowers.
Having worshipped him, performed an ablution with water, circumambulated the tree, and— acting like one for whom the deities are his auspicious sign—
having paid homage to the deity, he mounted his chariot and entered the city. From that time forth, following this very routine,
he would go there from time to time and perform worship like one for whom the deities are his auspicious sign.

Then, at a later time, having established himself in the kingdom upon his father’s passing, he avoided the four courses of unrighteous conduct and, without violating the ten duties of a king, ruled the realm according to Dhamma. He thought:
"My heart's desire has reached its fulfillment; I am now established in sovereignty. That purpose which I previously contemplated has now reached its culmination."
Thinking, “I shall bring this about,” he summoned his ministers, brahmins, householders, and others, and addressed them:
“Gentlemen, do you know for what reason I obtained the kingdom? “We do not know, Your Majesty.
“Have you ever seen me before worshipping a certain fig tree named Asuka with perfumes and other offerings, while standing with palms joined in reverence? “Yes, indeed.”
"O gods! Then I made this aspiration: "If I attain the kingdom, I shall perform an offering for you.
"It is through the power of that deity that this kingdom was obtained; now I shall perform an offering for her.
Without making excuses, prepare the offering for the deity quickly. "What should we take? What?"

"O gods? "Sir, while making a petition to a deity, I prayed: 'Those who, during my reign, shall undertake and practice the five immoral acts beginning with the taking of life—the ten unwholesome courses of action—let me slay them and perform a sacrificial offering (balikamma) with their entrails, fat, flesh, blood, and so forth.
Therefore, you yourselves must cause this drum to be sounded: 'While we were still princes...'"
Thus he made this vow: "If I attain the kingdom, I shall execute all those who are immoral within my realm and perform a sacrificial offering with them.

Now, having taken up the fivefold immoral conduct and the tenfold path of unwholesome action, he has executed a thousand such immoral persons who were living according to those precepts, and has had their heart-flesh and other parts taken.
“Desiring to perform an offering to the deity, let the city-dwellers know this. Having spoken thus, and wishing to declare the following matter—
namely, “From now on, whoever shall engage in immoral acts, having had them executed by the thousands and having performed a sacrifice,
I shall be released from my vow through this invocation”— he spoke this verse:
“A sacrifice was requested of me by a thousand fools;
now indeed I shall sacrifice, for many people are unrighteous.
In this context, “by a thousand fools” refers to their state of not knowing, “This action ought to be done; this ought not to be done.”
Alternatively, those whose intelligence is corrupted by the habit of undertaking and practicing the ten unwholesome courses of action are called "dummedhā" (the witless);
for those witless ones, who lack wisdom and are foolish persons, [the sacrifice was offered] with a thousand that had been counted and taken.
"A sacrifice was requested by me" means that having approached a deity, I requested a sacrifice, thinking, "I shall sacrifice in this manner."
"Now indeed I shall perform a sacrifice. Because he had obtained the kingdom through this very prayer, he said, "Now I shall sacrifice.
For what reason? "For now there are many people who act contrary to the Dhamma; therefore, taking him [the elephant] right now, I shall perform the ritual offering (*balikamma*).
When the ministers heard the Bodhisatta's words, they replied, "Very well, Your Majesty," and throughout the city of Bārāṇasī, which was twelve *yojanas* in extent—
They caused a drum to be beaten. Upon hearing the proclamation by the drum, there was not even a single person who remained committed to an unvirtuous act.
Thus, for as long as the Bodhisatta reigned, not even one individual was seen to commit even a single act among the five or ten types of unvirtuous deeds.
In this way, without causing distress to even a single person, the Bodhisatta [governed] all the inhabitants of the kingdom.

Having caused others to guard their virtue and having himself performed meritorious deeds such as giving, at the end of his life he departed, filling the city of the gods while taking his own retinue with him.
The Teacher also said: "Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata acts for the welfare of the world; he has done so in the past as well."
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma and having established the connection, he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and the King of Bārāṇasī was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Dummedha Jātaka, the tenth.
The fifth chapter: *Atthakāmavagga*.
Its summary (*uddāna*) is as follows: Losaka, Tissa, Kapota, Veḷuka, and also Makasa;
Rohiṇī, Ārāmadūsa, Vāruṇī, Dūsava, Vedabbha, Nakṣatra,
Dummedha, and Dasa— these are the ten.
This is the first fiftieth section.
6. Āsīsavagga [51] 1.
Mahāsīlavajātaka Commentary:
"A man should indeed aspire..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who had slackened his effort.
The Teacher asked him, "Is it true, monk, that you have slackened your energy?
When he replied, "Yes, venerable sir," the Teacher said, "Monk, why have you slackened your energy after going forth in such a liberating dispensation?
In the past, even when wise men fell from their kingdoms, they remained steadfast in their own energy and [recovered] even lost glory."
Having said, "They produced [them] again," he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the king’s chief queen.
On the day his name was given, they named him Prince Sīlavā. When he was just sixteen years old...
Having attained mastery in all arts, later on, upon the passing of his father, he was established in the kingdom as the king named Mahāsīlava.

He was a righteous and dharma-observing monarch. Having caused six alms-halls to be built—four at the gates of the city, one in the center, and one at the gate of his own residence—he constantly bestowed gifts upon the poor and the destitute.

He guards his virtue, performs the Uposatha rites, and—endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion—he rules the kingdom according to the Dhamma, gladdening all beings as if he were comforting a son sitting on his lap.
Later, one of his ministers became corrupt within the inner palace and eventually became public knowledge. The ministers informed the king. The king, while investigating the matter...
Having known this through his own direct experience, he summoned that minister and said, "O blind fool, you have acted improperly;
you are not worthy to dwell within my kingdom. Take your own wealth, children, and wife, and go elsewhere.
Thus he banished him from the realm. Having departed and passed beyond the kingdom of Kāsī, he went to the province of Kosala and [approached] the King of Kosala.
While serving him, he gradually became an intimate and trusted confidant of the king.
One day, he said to the King of Kosala: "Your Majesty, the kingdom of Bārāṇasī is like a mass of honey free from flies;
the king there is exceedingly mild, so it is possible to seize the kingdom of Bārāṇasī with only a small force. The king [listened] to him.
Having heard these words, he thought, "The kingdom of Bārāṇasī is indeed great, yet this man says it can be seized with so little force and transport;
could he perhaps be a hired thief? Thinking thus, he said, "I suspect you are a hired agent.
"I am not a hired agent, Your Majesty; I speak the truth. If you do not believe me, send men..."
“Go and destroy the border village; when you have captured those men and brought them before me, he will give them their wealth and release them.
The king thought, “This man speaks as if he were exceedingly brave; I shall test him first,” and having dispatched his own men, he ordered the destruction of the border village.
The men captured those thieves and presented them to the King of Bārāṇasī. When the king saw them, he—

“Sirs, why are you plundering the village? he asked. When they replied, “We are unable to survive, Your Majesty,” the king said, “Then why did you not come to me? From now on, do not commit such an act.
Having given them wealth, he dismissed them. They went and reported this matter to the King of Kosala. Even with just that much...
Unable to proceed further, he had them executed again in the middle of the country. The king likewise gave those thieves wealth and released them.
When they still did not go, he sent them out once more and had them plunder the market streets;
the king again gave those thieves wealth and released them. At that time, the King of Kosala, realizing that he was "an exceedingly righteous king," [approached him].
Thinking, "I shall seize the kingdom of Bārāṇasī," he set out taking a powerful army with him.
At that time, however, even when the king of Bārāṇasī’s rutting elephants approached him, they were of such a nature that they would not turn back;

they were of such a character that they would not tremble even if a thunderbolt fell upon their heads. Yet, if the Great King Sīlavant so desired, the entire kingdom of Jambudīpa [was at his disposal].
There were about a thousand great warriors, peerless and brave, capable of seizing [the enemy].
Hearing that the King of Kosala was approaching, they went to the king and said, "Your Majesty, it is said that the King of Kosala is coming with the intention of seizing the kingdom of Bārāṇasī.
Let us go and strike him down before he has even entered our royal borders."
The king said, "Dear ones, there is no need for others to suffer on my account; let whoever desires the kingdom take it.
Do not go. Thus he forbade them. The King of Kosala, having crossed the boundary of the kingdom, entered the middle of the countryside.
The ministers again approached the king and spoke to him in the same manner, but the king forbade them in the very same way as before.
The King of Kosala, having stationed himself outside the city, sent a message to the Great King Sīlavat, saying: "Either give me the kingdom or give me battle.
When the king heard this, he sent a reply: "There shall be no battle with me; take the kingdom.
Again, the ministers approached the king and said: "Your Majesty, we do not [permit] the King of Kosala to enter the city..."
"Let us beat him and seize him right outside the city," they said.
The King, having restrained them in the same manner as before, had the city gates opened and sat upon the great terrace in the midst of his throne, together with a thousand ministers.
The King of Kosala entered Bārāṇasī with a vast army and retinue; seeing not even a single adversary, he—
Having gone to the gate of the king’s residence, surrounded by his retinue of ministers, he had the innocent and virtuous Great King—
seated upon the great terrace in the residence which had its doors thrown open and was fully adorned—
arrested along with a thousand ministers; then he commanded, "Go, bind this king and his ministers with firm bonds behind their backs."
"Take them to the raw charnel ground, dig a pit reaching up to their necks, and bury them by throwing earth over them in such a way that not even a single hand can be raised;
at night, jackals will come and do what is appropriate for them," he said.
When the people heard the command of the King of Thieves, they bound the king along with his ministers behind the back...
Having bound him with tight fetters, they departed. Even at that time, the Great King Sīlavanta did not harbor even the slightest resentment toward the robber-king.
While those ministers were being led away thus bound, not a single one among them was able to disobey the king’s command.
Indeed, his retinue was so well-disciplined. Then those royal officers [arrested] the Great King Sīlavanta together with his ministers.
Having led [the king] to the raw charnel ground, they dug a pit reaching down to his neck;
having lowered King Sīlavat into the center and the remaining ministers on both sides, they thus placed everyone into the pits, filled them with earth, and after stamping it firm, they departed.
