Then King Sīlavat addressed his ministers and exhorted them: "O dear ones, do not harbor anger toward the robber-king, but cultivate only loving-kindness."
Then, at the hour of midnight, jackals came, thinking, "We shall eat human flesh.
Upon seeing them, the king and his ministers raised a shout all at once; the jackals, terrified, fled.
Looking back as they turned, and perceiving that no one was following behind them, they returned once more. The others did exactly the same.
They made a sound. Having fled thus for a third time and looking back again, they realized that not even one of them had returned;
thinking, "These will meet their death," they became courageous, turned back, and did not flee even when those others made a sound.
The eldest jackal approached the king, while the remaining jackals went to the presence of the other ministers.
They arrived. The king, skilled in means, knowing that it had come into his presence, raised its neck as if giving it an opportunity to bite;
then, pulling back the one attempting to bite his neck with his jawbone, he seized it firmly as if throwing it into a mechanical trap.
By the strength of a nāga, the king pulled it back with his jawbone at the neck.
The jackal, firmly seized, being unable to free himself and terrified by the fear of death, let out a great cry.

The remaining jackals, hearing his cry of distress, thinking, "He must have been firmly seized by a man," and being unable to approach the ministers, all fled, terrified by the fear of death. By means of the king’s jawbone...
As the king moved back and forth while firmly clutching the jackal, the dust became loose.
The jackal, terrified by the fear of death, shoveled the dust over the king with all four of its feet. Knowing that the dust had become loose, the king released the jackal;
then, possessing the strength of an elephant and endowed with great power, he moved back and forth with both hands.
Having lifted himself up and clung to the rim of the pit’s mouth, he emerged like a cloud severed by the wind and stood there.
He reassured his ministers, cleared away the dust, and having rescued them all, he stood in the raw charnel ground surrounded by his ministers.
At that time, people were discarding a dead man in the raw charnel ground at the junction between two *yakkhas*.
They abandoned it. Those *yakkhas*, being unable to divide that dead man, said, "We cannot divide this;
this King Sīlavant is righteous (*dhammika*). He will divide it for us and give it to us. Let us go to him.
Grasping the feet of that dead man and dragging him along, they went into the presence of the king and said, "Your Majesty, this..."
“Divide the dead body and give it to us,” they said. “O yakkhas, I would divide and give this to you, but I am not yet purified;
let me first bathe. By their own supernatural power, the yakkhas brought scented water that had been prepared for the robber-king and gave it to the king for his bath.
After he had bathed and was standing there, [the water] that had been collected and set aside...
They brought robes for the king of thieves and gave them to him; when he stood there having put them on, they brought a casket of four kinds of fragrant scents and gave it to him;
when he stood there having anointed himself with the scents, they brought various flowers placed in golden caskets upon jeweled fans and gave them to him.
When he stood there having adorned himself with the flowers, [they asked], "What else shall we do?"
They asked. The king showed them his state of hunger; they went and brought back various kinds of choice food prepared by the robber-king and gave it to him.
The king, having bathed and anointed himself and being well-adorned and beautifully arrayed, ate the various kinds of choice food.
The yakkhas [brought] the scented water set aside by the robber-king, together with a golden pitcher and even a golden basin.

They brought it. Then, when he had drunk the water, rinsed his mouth, and washed his hands while standing there, they brought and gave him betel leaf—excellently prepared and perfumed with the five fragrant ingredients—which had been provided by the bandit-king.
When he had chewed that and was standing there, they asked, "What else shall we do? Having gone, [they fetched] the auspicious sword placed at the head of the bandit-king.

"Bring it! they said. They went and brought it back. The king took that sword, placed the dead man upright, struck him between the shoulders with the blade, divided him into two equal portions, and distributed them evenly between the two yakkhas.
Having given them away, he washed the sword, sheathed it, and stood there. Then those yakkhas...
Having eaten human flesh and being well-satisfied, they asked with joyful hearts, "What else, O Great King, shall we do for you?

He replied, "In that case, by means of your own supernatural power, cause me to descend into the inner chamber of the thief-king, and establish these ministers each in their own respective homes. They accepted, saying, "Very well, Your Majesty," and did exactly so.
At that time, the king of thieves was sleeping on a magnificent couch within the decorated inner chamber.
While he was thus heedlessly asleep, the king struck him in the belly with the blade of his sword. Terrified, he woke up;
seeing King Sīlavā by the light of the lamp, he rose from his bed, established mindfulness, and stood there, saying to the king:

“Great King, on such a night as this—when the palace is under guard, the doors are closed, and you have fastened your sword and prepared yourself in full regalia while standing in an unobserved spot among the guards—how indeed did you come to this bed?
The king related the entire manner of his arrival in detail. Upon hearing this, the robber-king’s heart was filled with awe.
“Great King, even though I am a human being, I did not know of your virtues;

yet your virtues were known by those fierce and harsh *yakkhas* who devour the blood and flesh of others. Therefore, O Lord of Men, I shall never again be unfaithful to you, who are so endowed with virtue.
Having spoken thus, he took up his sword, made an oath, and after asking the king for forgiveness, had him lie down upon a great couch.
Having lain down on a small couch himself, at the break of dawn when the sun had risen,
he had the drum beaten and assembled all the queens, ministers, brahmins, and householders; then, in their presence,
as if lifting the full moon into the sky, he spoke of the virtues of King Sīlavara, and right there in the midst of the assembly, he again asked the king for forgiveness.
Having handed over the kingdom, he said, "Great King, from this day forward, the burden of the danger posed by thieves that arises for you is mine;
rule the kingdom with protection provided by me," and after ordering the execution of the slanderer,
he took his own army and retinue and returned to his own country.
King Sīlava, too, having adorned himself and prepared for the occasion, sat upon a golden throne with legs of crystal beneath a white parasol.

Surveying his own prosperity, he thought: "Such prosperity as this, and the preservation of the lives of my thousand ministers—none of this would have come to pass had I not exerted effort. It is by the power of effort that I have recovered this lost glory."
"I have obtained [this], and I have granted the gift of life to a thousand ministers. Indeed, one should exert effort without cutting short one's hope.
For such is the fruit for one who has exerted effort," he thought, and as an inspired utterance, he spoke this verse:
"A wise man should surely aspire; he should not despair."
“I see myself as I have become, just as I desired.
In this context, “one should indeed hope” means that one should maintain hope through the power of one’s own energy, thinking: “By exerting such energy, I shall be liberated from this suffering.
“The wise person should not despair” means that the wise person, skilled in means, [should persevere] in the appropriate place.
While exerting effort, one should not become despondent, thinking, "I shall not obtain the fruit of this effort";
the meaning is that one should cut off hope [of success]. Regarding the phrase "I see myself," *vo* here is a mere particle; it means, "Today I see myself. As I wished, so it has come to pass:
for I, having been cast into a pit, have now been released from that suffering. And again...
"I desired the attainment of sovereignty for myself, and now I see myself having attained this very success.

Just as I wished before, so has my self become. Thus the Bodhisatta, having uttered this inspired utterance with the verse, "O, how indeed the fruit of energy succeeds for those endowed with virtue!", performed meritorious deeds for the rest of his life and departed according to his karma.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, proclaimed the Truths.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who had slackened his energy was established in Arahatship. The Teacher, connecting the present to the past, identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the corrupt minister was Devadatta; the thousand ministers were the Buddha’s retinue; and the virtuous Great King was none other than myself."
The First Explanation of the Mahāsīlavajātaka.
[52] 2. The Explanation of the Cūḷajanakajātaka:
"A man should indeed exert himself"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning one who had slackened his energy.
Whatever needs to be said regarding that matter will all be made clear in the Mahājanaka Jātaka.
However, while seated beneath the white parasol, King Janaka spoke this verse:
“A wise man should indeed exert himself; he should not become despondent.”
"I see myself as one who has been pulled from the water onto dry land.
In this context, "one should indeed strive" means one should exert effort. "Pulled from the water onto dry land" means I see myself having emerged from the water and established upon dry land.
Here too, a bhikkhu who had previously slackened his energy attained arahantship.
King Janaka was none other than the Perfectly Enlightened One himself.
This concludes the second commentary, the Cūḷajanakajātakavaṇṇanā.
[53] 3. The Commentary on the Puṇṇapātijātaka.
"Likewise, the bowl is full. The Teacher spoke this while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning Visavāruṇī.
On one occasion, some drunkards gathered in Sāvatthī and deliberated:
"Our supply of liquor is exhausted; where indeed shall we obtain more? Then a certain hard-hearted gambler said, "Do not worry; there is a way."
“What means, then, is there? “Anāthapiṇḍika goes to attend upon the king wearing his finger-ring and clothed in a smooth robe.
We shall prepare a drinking hall by putting a stupefying drug into a vessel of liquor, and having sat down, we shall call out, ‘Come this way, Great Merchant! at the time when Anāthapiṇḍika arrives.”
"Having made him drink that liquor, we shall take the ring and the cloak from him when he has lost consciousness and make them our own.
Having agreed, saying "Very well," they did so; and when the merchant arrived, they went out to meet him on the road, saying, "Master, please come this way for a moment.
This liquor of ours is most delightful; drink a little and then go on."
They said: "How could a stream-enterer, a noble disciple, drink liquor?

Even though he has no need for it, thinking, 'I shall catch these scoundrels,' he goes to their drinking place, observes their conduct, and having understood, 'This liquor was prepared by them for this specific purpose,' he thinks, 'From now on, I shall drive them away from this.'"
Having reflected, he said: "O wicked scoundrels! You have prepared the drinking hall with the intention:
'Having put medicine into the vessel of liquor and made those who come and go drink it, we will render them unconscious and plunder them.
Yet you sit there merely praising this liquor; not even a single person dares to lift it up and drink. If this [medicine] had not been mixed in..."
"Drink this yourselves! Having thus rebuked those rogues and driven them away from there, he went to his own home.
Thinking, "I shall report to the Tathāgata what was done by the rogues," he went to Jetavana and reported it.
The Teacher said, "Householder, for the time being these rogues have become intent on deceiving you; however, in the past, they [deceived] even the wise."
Having said, "They were desirous of deceiving him," when requested by him, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was the chief merchant of Bārāṇasī.
At that time, those rogues likewise conspired together, prepared liquor, and [waited] on the road leading toward the arrival of the chief merchant of Bārāṇasī.
Having gone there, they spoke in this very manner. Although the merchant was not interested, desiring to take them under his wing, he went and observed their conduct.
Thinking, "These men wish to do this; I shall drive them away from here," he said:
"Sirs, gentlemen, it is improper for you to go to the royal palace after drinking liquor. Having seen the king and returning again..."
“I shall find out; you sit right here,” he said, and having gone to attend upon the king, he returned.
The rogues said, “Come this way, master. He too went there, looked at the bowls of liquor mixed with medicine, and spoke thus:
“Gentlemen rogues, your conduct does not please me; your bowls of liquor remain exactly as they were filled.”
"You stand here merely praising the liquor, yet you do not drink it. If this were pleasing to you, you too would drink it;
therefore, it must be mixed with poison. Thus, shattering their desire, he spoke this verse:
"In the same way, the bowls are full; another conversation is underway."
“I know by inference, and this is not good liquor.
In that context, “just as before” means that just as these jars of liquor were seen by me at the time of my departure, they are now likewise full.
“This conversation concerns something else” means that this discussion of yours concerning the praise of liquor is something else entirely and untrue.
"It is not so. For if this liquor were pleasing, you too would have drunk it, and half-cups would have remained.
But not even one of you has drunk any liquor. I know by the manner of things;
therefore, I know by this reason that this is no good liquor—it cannot be good liquor, for it must be mixed with poison."
Having restrained the scoundrels so that they would not act in such a manner again, he threatened them and released them.
Having performed meritorious deeds such as giving for the rest of his life, he departed according to his karma.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "The scoundrels of that time were the scoundrels of the present day, while the merchant of Bārāṇasī was none other than myself."
The third *Jātaka* commentary, the *Puṇṇapāti-jātaka*.
[54] 4. The *Kiṃphala-jātaka* Commentary.
"This tree is not difficult to climb"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain lay follower who was skilled in fruits.

He spoke concerning this. It is said that a certain householder living in Sāvatthī, having invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, seated them in his own monastery, and given them rice gruel and solid food, commanded his park-keeper:
"After wandering in the park with the bhikkhus, give the masters various fruits, such as mangoes. Having assented with "Very well," he...
Taking the community of monks with him, as he was wandering through the park, he would look up at a tree and know:
"This fruit is unripe; this is not well-ripened; this is well-ripened. Whatever he said turned out to be exactly so. The monks went and reported it to the Tathāgata:
"Venerable Sir, this park keeper is skilled regarding fruits; even while standing on the ground, he [knows] the tree..."
"Having looked at them, he knows: 'This fruit is unripe; this is not well-ripened; this is well-ripened.
What he says is exactly so. The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only this park-keeper who is skilled regarding fruits;
in the past, wise men were also skilled regarding fruits," and having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of caravan leaders.
Having reached maturity, he engaged in trade with five hundred carts.
On one occasion, having entered the Mahāvattani forest and standing at its entrance, he gathered all his men together and said, "In this forest there are trees known as 'poison-trees' (visarukkha)."
“Indeed, there will be poisonous leaves, poisonous flowers, poisonous fruits, and poisonous honey;
whatever leaf, flower, fruit, or sprout you have not previously consumed, do not eat it without first asking me,” he said.
Having agreed, saying “Very well,” they entered the forest. And at the entrance of the forest, at the gate of a certain village—
There is a tree called the "What-Fruit Tree" (*kiṃphala-rukkha*);
its trunk, branches, foliage, flowers, and fruits all resemble mangoes. Not only in color and shape, but even in fragrance and taste, its raw and ripe fruits are exactly like mangoes;
however, once eaten, they cause the end of life at that very moment, like the *halāhala* poison. As they were walking ahead...
Some greedy men, perceiving it to be a mango tree, ate the fruits.
Others, thinking, "We shall eat only after asking the caravan leader," stood there holding them in their hands. When the caravan leader arrived, they asked him, "Sir, let us eat these mango fruits.
The Bodhisatta, knowing that "this is not a mango tree," [asked], "What kind of fruit tree is this?"

Having restrained them, saying, "This is not it; this is not the mango tree; do not eat! he made those who had eaten vomit, and having given them the four sweet substances (catumadhura) to drink, he rendered them free from disease.
Previously, however, people had established dwellings at the foot of this tree, and under the impression that they were "mango fruits," these—

Having eaten poisonous fruits, they meet their end. On the following day, the villagers go out, see the dead men, take hold of their feet, cast them away in a hidden place, and taking all their belongings along with their carts, they depart.
Even on that day, at the very time of sunrise, [they think], "My ox..."
Thinking, "This will be my cart; this will be my merchandise," they went in haste to the foot of that tree.
Seeing the men free from illness, they asked, "How did you know that this tree was not a mango tree?
They replied, "We do not know; our caravan leader knows. Then the men [approached] the Bodhisatta.
They asked, "O wise one, by doing what did you know that this tree was not a mango tree?
He replied, "I knew it by two reasons," and spoke this verse:
"This tree is not difficult to climb, nor is it far from the village;..."
"Without cause I know: this tree does not bear sweet fruit.
In this context, "this tree is not difficult to climb" means that this poisonous tree is not hard to ascend;

like a ladder set up and placed there, it can be climbed with ease—so he says. Nor is it "far from the village," meaning that even though it stands at a distance from the village, it is not [truly] far.
"He stands right at the village gate," he indicates. "I know by two kinds of reasons," means:
"By these two reasons I know this tree. What are they? "That this is not a tree with sweet fruit.
For if this were a mango tree (*amba*) with sweet fruit, then even though it is so easily climbed and standing nearby, not even a single fruit would remain, because of the people who eat the fruit.

"He would always have been surrounded [by them]. Thus, having determined for myself through my own knowledge that this was a poison-tree, I taught the Dhamma to the great multitude and departed in safety.
The Teacher also said, "Thus, monks, even in the past, the wise were skilled in discerning [the nature of things]," and he delivered this teaching on the Dhamma.
Having brought forward the connection and joined the narrative, he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly, and the caravan leader was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Kiṃphala Jātaka, the fourth.
[55] 5. The Commentary on the Pañcāvudha Jātaka.
"He who with an undaunted mind..."—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who had slackened his energy.
The Teacher addressed that monk, saying: "Is it true, monk, that you have slackened your energy?"
Having asked him, and being told by him, "It is true, Blessed One," [the Buddha] said, "Monks, in the past,
wise men exerted effort in the proper place for exerting effort and thereby attained the prosperity of kingship," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born as the chief queen of that king.
He was conceived in the womb. On the day of his naming ceremony, eight hundred brahmins were gratified with all their desires, and they inquired about his marks.
Seeing the perfection of his marks, the brahmins skilled in physiognomy said, "Great King, this prince is endowed with merit;
after you have passed away, he will attain the kingdom. He is renowned and famous for his skill in the five types of weaponry."

“He will become the foremost person in Jambudīpa,” they prophesied. Having heard the words of the brahmins, the king, while choosing a name for the boy, gave him the name “Pañcāvudhakumāra” (The Boy with Five Weapons).
Then, when he had reached maturity and was sixteen years old, the king addressed him, saying, “Dear son, learn a craft. “In whose presence shall I learn it, Your Majesty? he asked.
“Go, dear son, to the city of Takkasilā in the kingdom of Gandhāra and learn [the arts] from the preceptor who is renowned throughout the world;
give him this as his teacher’s fee. Having given him a thousand pieces of gold, he sent him forth.
He went there, mastered the craft, took the five weapons bestowed by the preceptor, and having paid homage to the preceptor, departed from the city of Takkasilā.
Having departed, equipped with his five weapons, he set out on the road to Bārāṇasī.
On the way, he reached a forest inhabited by a yakkha named Silesaloma.
Then, seeing him at the entrance of the forest, people said, "O young man, do not enter this forest; there is a yakkha here named Silesaloma."
"He brings death to every person he sees," they said, seeking to dissuade him.
But the Bodhisatta, mindful of his own purpose, entered the forest like a lion with an undaunted mane.
When he reached the middle of the forest, that *yakkha* became as tall as a palm tree, with a head the size of a gabled house, eyes the size of platters, and two [tusks] the size of *dakalima* buds.
Having fashioned his fangs and appearing with a white face, a brindled belly, and blue hands and feet, he showed himself to the Bodhisatta and said, "Where are you going?
Stop! You are my prey. Then the Bodhisatta said to him, "Yakkha, I entered here thinking myself safe; you should approach me with heedfulness. [With] poison-drunk..."
"Having pierced him with this arrow, I shall cause him to fall right here," he threatened;
then, having nocked an arrow smeared with *halāhala* poison, he released it, and it stuck fast in the yakṣa’s very hair.
Then another, then another—in this manner he released fifty arrows, and they all stuck fast in his hair. The yakṣa shook off all those arrows as well.
Having dropped it right at the Bodhisatta’s own feet, he approached him.
The Bodhisatta again threatened him and drew his sword to strike; the sword, thirty-three finger-breadths in length, stuck fast in the hair alone.
Then he struck with a spear, and that too stuck fast in the hair alone. Regarding its state of being stuck...
Knowing this, he struck him with a mallet, but that too stuck fast in his hair. Knowing it had stuck, he struck him with a spear, but that too stuck fast in his hair.
Knowing it had stuck, [the prince] said: "O yakkha, I have heard before that you are named 'The Boy with Five Weapons.
When I entered the forest presided over by you, I did not bring along bows and other such weapons."
"Having entered, I shall enter while taking him for myself; today, having struck him down, I will reduce him to dust!
Shouting thus, he took himself for the spirit and struck it with his right hand, but the hand stuck fast even to the hair.
He struck it with his left hand, and that too stuck fast. He struck it with his right foot, and that too stuck fast. With his left foot...
He struck him with his fist, but it stuck to him. Thinking, "I shall strike him on the head and crush him to pieces," he struck him on the head, but that too stuck to his hair.
Though suspended and bound at five points, he remained fearless and undaunted.
The yakkha thought, "This is a lion among men, a thoroughbred of a man, not merely an ordinary man; even by one such as I, he—"
“There will not be even the slightest terror for one seized by a *yakkha*;
never before have I seen such a person on this path as I destroy it—why, then, does he not fear?
Unable to bear devouring him, he asked, “Why, young man, do you not fear the fear of death? [The youth replied,] “For what reason, *yakkha*?”
"I shall not fear. For in one single existence, one death is inevitable; moreover, there is a thunderbolt weapon within my womb.
If you eat me, you will not be able to digest that weapon; it will cut your intestines into pieces and bring about the end of your life.
Thus, we both would perish. For this reason, I do not fear."
It is said that the Bodhisatta spoke this with reference to the weapon of wisdom within himself. Hearing this, the yakkha thought:
"This young man speaks the truth; not even a piece of flesh the size of a mung-bean from the body of this lion among men will be able to digest itself in my belly.
I shall release him," thus he was terrified by the fear of death.
Having released the Bodhisatta, he said, “Young man, you are a lion among men; I will not eat your flesh.
Today, like the moon released from the mouth of Rāhu, go forth from my hands, bringing joy to the circle of your kinsmen and friends.
Then the Bodhisatta said to him, “Yakkha, as for me, I shall indeed go; but as for you, you have previously committed unwholesome deeds...”
Having committed this, that hunter, with blood on his hands and a consumer of flesh and blood, was reborn as a *yakkha*.
If you remain here and continue to perform only unwholesome deeds, you will go from darkness to even greater darkness;
however, from the moment you have seen me, it is no longer possible for you to commit unwholesome acts—for the karma of taking life leads to hell or the animal realm.

Having explained the danger of the five types of unwholesome conduct and the benefits of the five precepts by way of such passages as, "One is reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts or among the asuras; and wherever one is reborn among humans,
it leads to a short lifespan," he then, through various means, rebuked the yakkha, taught him the Dhamma, tamed him, and rendered him harmless.
Having established them in the five precepts, he appointed a deity who received offerings in that very forest as their protector, advised them to be heedful, and departed from the forest.
Having informed people at the forest's entrance, he went to Bārāṇasī fully equipped with his five weapons.
There he saw his parents, and later, having been established in the kingdom, he ruled the realm according to the Dhamma.
Having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, he departed according to his karma.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and attained full enlightenment, spoke this verse:
“The man whose mind is unshaken, whose heart is unshaken, by means of an unshrinking mind...”
“He develops wholesome states for the attainment of security from bondage;
he shall gradually reach the destruction of all fetters.
This is the summary of the meaning here: that man who, with a mind that is neither sluggish nor constricted, is by nature one whose mind is not sluggish...
Having become one whose underlying intention is unshakable, he develops and increases the wholesome Dhamma—comprising the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—in its sense of being blameless;
with a broad mind, he applies himself to insight for the sake of attaining the security of Nibbāna through the four means of accomplishment.
Thus, having applied the three characteristics of "impermanence, suffering, and non-self" to all conditioned phenomena, he...
Cultivating the factors conducive to enlightenment that arise from the stage of nascent insight (taruṇa-vipassanā) onwards, one may gradually reach Arahantship—
which is designated as "the destruction of all fetters" because it arises at the conclusion of the fourth path that effects the total exhaustion of all fetters—
without leaving even a single fetter remaining.
Thus the Teacher, having taken up the peak of the Dhamma teaching through Arahantship, proclaimed the Four Truths at the very end;
at the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu attained Arahantship. The Teacher, having established the connection, identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the yakkha was Aṅgulimāla, but the youth with the five weapons was none other than I myself."
The fifth: The Exposition of the Pañcāvudha Jātaka.
[56] 6. The Exposition of the Kañcanakkhandha Jātaka.
"He who with a joyful heart..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain bhikkhu.

He related the story: It is said that a certain son of good family living in Sāvatthī, having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, entered the religious life, placing his breast upon the Jewel-like Dispensation.
Then his teachers and preceptors said to him: "Friend, virtue is of one kind;
it is of two kinds, three kinds, four kinds, five kinds, six kinds, seven kinds, eight kinds, nine kinds..."
"Virtue (sīla) is tenfold and manifold. This is called the minor virtue; this is called the intermediate virtue; this is called the major virtue.
This is called the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha; this is called the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties;
this is called the virtue of purity of livelihood; this is called the virtue of moderation in using the requisites. Thus they explain virtue.
He thought: "This so-called virtue is far too much; I will not be able to maintain it after having undertaken it all.
And what is the purpose of the going-forth for one who is unable to fulfill the precepts?
Being a householder, I shall perform meritorious deeds such as giving, and I shall support my wife and children. Having thought thus, he said: "Venerable sir, I..."
“I shall not be able to guard my virtue; and for one who cannot do so, what is the purpose of the going-forth? I shall return to the lower life;
take back your bowl and robe,” he said.
Then they said to him, “Friend, since that is the case, go after having paid homage to the One of Ten Powers. Taking him with them, they went to the Teacher.
They went into the presence of the Dhamma assembly. Upon seeing them, the Teacher asked, “Bhikkhus, why have you come taking this bhikkhu who is no longer interested?

They replied, “Venerable Sir, this bhikkhu said, ‘I will not be able to guard my virtue,’ and so he handed over his bowl and robes; therefore, we have come taking him with us. “But why, bhikkhus, did you [not stop him]?”
“Tell this bhikkhu about his many precepts; he will observe only as much as he is able to protect.
From now on, do not say anything to him; I know what must be done here.
Come, bhikkhu, what is the use of many precepts for you? You will be able to observe only three precepts.”

“I will guard them, Bhante. “In that case, from now on, you must guard the three doors—the door of the body, the door of speech, and the door of the mind—do not commit an evil deed by body, do not by speech, and do not by mind. Go;
do not turn back to the lower life, but guard these very three precepts. At this point, that bhikkhu, with a joyful heart, said: “Excellent!”
“Venerable sir, I shall observe these three precepts. Having paid homage to the Teacher, he departed together with his teachers and preceptors.
While fulfilling those three precepts, he realized: “The precepts taught to me by my teachers and preceptors were only this much;
however, because they were not yet Buddhas themselves, they were unable to bring me to full awakening. The Perfectly Enlightened One...”
"By virtue of his own perfect awakening as a Buddha and his sovereignty over the unsurpassed Dhamma, he has placed this much of the moral discipline within just three doors and caused me to grasp it;
truly, my Teacher has become my refuge. Having thus increased his insight, he was established in Arahatship within just a few days.
Having learned of that event, the monks assembled in the Dhamma hall and spoke of the Buddha’s qualities:

"Friends, it is said that when a certain monk was returning to the lower life, thinking, 'I am unable to guard many precepts,' the Teacher—having had him grasp all the precepts by condensing them into three groups—led him to Arahantship.
Oh, how wonderful is the power of the Buddhas! Thus they praised the virtues of the Buddha.
They sat there conversing. Then the Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, with what discussion are you sitting together now?
When they replied, "With this one," he said, "Monks, even a very heavy burden, when divided into portions and distributed, becomes as if light.
In the past, too, wise men, having obtained a great mass of gold..."
"Being unable to lift it, they divided it and then went away after lifting their respective portions," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a farmer in a certain village.
One day, he was plowing a field in a deserted village. Previously, in that village—
A certain wealthy merchant, possessing great riches, died after burying a mass of gold four cubits in length and as thick as a thigh.
That [gold] remained fixed, clinging to the Bodhisatta’s plough. Thinking, "This will be for the continuity of our root-lineage," he cleared away the soil;
but seeing it, he covered it back with earth and, having ploughed all day, when the sun had set—
Having set aside his plow, yoke, and other tools to one side, he thought, "I shall take the mass of gold and go," but he was unable to lift it up.
Being unable to do so, he sat down and reflected: "This much will serve for supporting my family;
this much I shall set aside as a store; with this much I shall engage in manual labor; and this much I shall use for meritorious deeds such as giving."
Thinking, “It will be,” he divided it into four portions. At the time he had thus divided it, that mass of gold became as light as a mere trifle.
Having lifted it up and brought it to his house, he divided it into four parts, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, and departed according to his karma.
Thus the Blessed One, having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma after attaining full enlightenment, spoke this verse:
“The person whose mind is joyful, with a heart full of joy,
who develops wholesome states for the sake of attaining security from bondage,
will gradually reach the destruction of all fetters.”

In that context, "with a clear mind" means with a mind free from hindrances (*vinīvaraṇa*). "With a clear heart" means having a mind made clear by that very state of being free from hindrances; the meaning is that he became one whose mind was radiant and shining like gold.

Thus the Teacher, having concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship and having established the connection, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the man who received the mass of gold was none other than myself.
This is the sixth commentary on the Kañcanakkhandha Jātaka.
[57] 7. The Commentary on the Jātaka of the Monkey King (Vānarinda-jātaka).
“Those four qualities which belong to one... This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana, concerning Devadatta’s attempt to bring about his own death.
For at that time, having heard that “Devadatta is plotting for his own destruction,” the Teacher said: “No, [it cannot be so].”
“Monks, it was not only now that Devadatta strove for my death; he strove even in the past, yet he was unable to do even so much as a hair’s breadth of harm.
Having said this, he related a story of the past:
“In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a monkey and grew up to maturity.”
Having the size of a young horse, endowed with strength, and wandering alone, he dwelt on the bank of a river.
In the middle of that river was an island, well-supplied with various kinds of fruit trees such as mangoes and jackfruits.
The Bodhisatta, possessing the strength of an elephant and endowed with vigor, leaped from the near bank of the river and alighted upon the island in the middle of the stream.
There was a flat rock; he would alight upon it, and from there, springing up, he would land on that island.
Having eaten various kinds of fruits there, he would return in the evening by the same means and stay in his own dwelling place.
On the following day as well, he did exactly the same. In this manner, he made his residence there.
At that time, a certain crocodile lived with his wife in that river.
His wife, seeing the Bodhisatta walking back and forth, conceived a craving for the heart-flesh of the Bodhisatta and said to the crocodile:
"My lord, a craving has arisen in me for the heart-flesh of this king of monkeys. The crocodile—
Saying, “Very well, Bhaddā; you shall have him,” he went and lay down on the back of the rock, thinking, “Today, I will seize you as you come from Dīpaka this very evening.
The Bodhisatta, having wandered about during the day, stood at Dīpaka at the time of evening and, looking toward the rock, said: “This—”
"The rock now appears higher; what could be the reason for this? he thought.
For it seems that both the level of the water and the size of the rock were well-established [in his mind]. Therefore, it occurred to him:
"Today the water of this river neither decreases nor increases, yet this rock appears to have become large. Could it be..."
"A crocodile is lying here for the purpose of seizing me.
Thinking, "I shall first test him," the monkey remained right there and, as if speaking with the rock, said, "O rock! Receiving no reply, he called out, "O rock!
a second and even a third time. What reply could the rock give? Again the monkey asked, "What..."
"O rock, today you do not give me an answer," he said. The crocodile thought, "Surely on other days this rock gave an answer to the lord of monkeys; I shall now give him an answer.
Having thought this, he said, "What is it, O lord of monkeys? "Who are you? "I am a crocodile. "For what purpose are you lying here?"
“‘Longing for the flesh of your heart’—the Bodhisatta thought, ‘There is no other way for me to go;
today I must deceive this crocodile. Then he said to him: ‘Friend crocodile, I shall surrender myself to you;
open your mouth and seize me when I have come into your presence.’”
For when the mouth of a crocodile is opened wide, its eyes close. Not noticing this reason, he opened his mouth, whereupon his eyes closed.
Having opened his mouth and closed his eyes, he lay down.
The Bodhisatta, perceiving this state of affairs, flew up from the island, alighted upon the crocodile's head, and stepped on it.
Then, leaping up like a flash of lightning, he stood radiant upon the opposite shore.
Seeing this marvel, the crocodile thought, "A truly extraordinary feat has been performed by this lord of monkeys," and said,
"O lord of monkeys, in this world, a person endowed with four qualities overcomes his enemies."
Having said, "I think all these qualities are within you," he spoke this verse:
"O Lord of Monkeys, he in whom these four qualities exist,
just as they do in you— truth, righteousness, fortitude, and generosity— he transcends even what has been seen."
In this context, "of whom" (*yassa*) means of any person whatsoever. "These" (*ete*) refers directly to those things that are about to be described.
"Four qualities" (*caturo dhammā*) means four virtues. "Truth" (*sacca*) is verbal truth;

having said, "I will come into your presence," one does not speak a falsehood but actually comes—this is your verbal truth. "Dharma" (*dhamma*) is the wisdom of investigation; when it has been done thus...
"This shall be my name"—you possess this wisdom of deliberation. "Fortitude" refers to uninterrupted energy; you also possess this.
"Generosity" means the relinquishing of oneself; you have come into my presence having relinquished yourself.
As for the fact that I was unable to accept you, that is my own fault. "Seen" refers to an enemy. He...
"He overcomes" means that the person in whom these four qualities exist, just as they do in you,
likewise overcomes and surpasses his own enemy, just as you have today surpassed me.
Having thus praised the Bodhisatta, the crocodile went to his own dwelling place.
The Teacher also, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching—"Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has striven for my death;
he has striven even in the past"—and having established the connection, he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, Devadatta was the crocodile, Ciñcamāṇavikā was his wife, and I myself was the lord of the monkeys."
The seventh: The Commentary on the Vānarinda Jātaka.
[58] 8. The Commentary on the Tayodhamma Jātaka:
"He for whom these three qualities... This was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana, concerning Devadatta’s efforts to bring about his own death.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, Devadatta was reborn in the womb of a monkey.

Living in the Himalayan region and leading a troop, he bit with his teeth and extracted the seeds of the young monkeys born of him out of fear that, once they had grown up, they might take over the leadership of the troop. At that time, the Bodhisatta also...
Dependent upon that very [act], he took rebirth in the womb of a certain female monkey.
Then, that female monkey, having realized that she was pregnant and wishing to protect her fetus, went to another mountain foot.
When her pregnancy had reached maturity, she gave birth to the Bodhisatta. As he grew up, he attained the state of discretion and became endowed with great strength.
It came to pass that one day he asked his mother, "Mother, where is my father?
"Dear son, he lives at the foot of such-and-such a mountain, leading a troop," she replied. "Mother, take me to him," he said.
"Dear son, it is not possible for you to go to your father's presence. For your father [is occupied with] the young monkeys born of himself..."
“Out of fear of being excluded from the herd, he bites with his tusks and uproots the seeds. “Mother, take me there;
I shall find out,” he said. Taking her son, she went into his presence.
As soon as that monkey saw his own son, he thought, “As this one grows, he will not allow me to remain in charge of the herd.”

"He must be killed this very moment! Thinking, "I will squeeze him tightly as if embracing him and bring about the end of his life," he pressed against the Bodhisatta as if embracing him, saying, "Come, dear one, where have you been for all this time?
But the Bodhisatta was possessed of the strength of a nāga and endowed with great power; he squeezed him back, until the man's bones reached the point of breaking.

They were there. Then this thought occurred to him: "As he grows, he will kill me; by what means might I kill him first? Then he reflected: "Not far from here there is a lake inhabited by a *rākṣasa*;
I shall have him devoured by that *rākṣasa*. Then he said to him: "Dear son, I am old; this herd belongs to you..."
“I entrust this to you; I shall make you king this very day.
In such-and-such a place there is a lake where two *kumudini* lilies, three *uppalini* lilies, and five *padumini* lilies are in bloom. Go, and bring those flowers from there.
He replied, “Very well, father, I shall bring them,” and having gone there, he did not descend hastily, but instead circumscribed his path all around.
He saw only the tracks of those who had entered, not the tracks of those who had emerged. He thought, "This lake must be possessed by a *rakkhasa*;
my father, being unable to kill me himself, will wish to have me devoured by the *rakkhasa*.
I shall not enter this lake, but I will take the flowers. Having gone to a place without water, he exerted his speed.
Having taken them and flown up, he went to the other side; standing in a place devoid of water, he took two flowers and landed on the opposite shore.
Returning from the opposite shore to this side, he took two more by that same means.
Thus, making a heap on both sides, he gathered the flowers and did not enter the place where the rākṣasa’s command was given.
Then, as he took those flowers and made a heap in one place, thinking, "I shall not be able to lift more than this," the rakkhasa thought:
"In all this time, I have never before seen such a wise and wonderful man;
he has taken as many flowers as he desired, yet he has not fallen under my command."

Splitting the water in two and rising from the water, he approached the Bodhisatta and said, “Lord of Monkeys, whoever possesses three qualities in this world overcomes their enemies; I believe all of these are present within you.
Having spoken thus, he uttered this verse in praise of the Bodhisatta:
“O Lord of Monkeys, he in whom these three qualities exist—just as they are in you:
skill, heroism, and wisdom—he transcends what has been seen.
In this context, *dakkhiyaṃ* means skillfulness; it refers to the supreme energy associated with the wisdom that knows how to dispel encountered danger.
“*Sūriya* means the state of being brave; it is a name for the state of fearlessness. *Paññā* is a name for the wisdom of skillful means (*upāyapaññā*), which is the foundation of wisdom.
Thus, having offered praise to the Bodhisatta with this verse, that water-demon asked: ‘What is the purpose of these flowers?’”
"Why do you carry [them]? he asked. "My father wishes to make me king; for that reason I carry them.
"It is not possible for such a supreme person as you to carry flowers; I shall carry them," she said, and lifting them up, she followed right behind him.
Then his father, seeing her from afar, thought: "I thought this girl would become food for a *rakkhasa*..."
"I sent him, and now he is coming back bringing flowers for the rākṣasa;
I am lost!"—thinking thus, his heart split into seven pieces and he met his death right there. The remaining monkeys gathered together and made the Bodhisatta their king.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher connected the narrative to the present and identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Devadatta was the leader of the herd, and I myself was the leader's son.
This concludes the eighth commentary, the Tayodhamma Jātaka.
[59] 9. The Commentary on the Bherivādaka Jātaka.
“Blow the bell! Blow the bell!”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning a certain monk who was difficult to speak to.

The Teacher asked that monk, “Is it true, monk, that you are difficult to speak to? When he replied, “It is true, Blessed One,” the Teacher said, “Monk, you have not only been difficult to speak to now;
in the past as well, you were difficult to speak to. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of drummers and lived in a village.
Hearing that a festival had been proclaimed in Benares, he thought,
"I shall earn wealth by playing the drum at the festival grounds," and taking his son with him, he went there, played the drum, and acquired much wealth.

He obtained it. Taking it with him as he was going to his own village, he reached a forest inhabited by bandits and forbade his son from beating the drum continuously, saying, "Son, do not beat it continuously;
beat it at intervals, like the drum of a lord traveling along the road.
Although he was thus forbidden by his father, the boy thought, "I shall drive away the bandits with the sound of the drum alone."
Having said this, he sounded it continuously. The thieves, having first heard the sound of the drum, thought, "This must be the drum of a lord," and fled;

but hearing the sound as it continued in an unbroken stream, they thought, "This cannot be the drum of a lord," and returning to investigate, they saw only two men and, having beaten them, plundered them. The Bodhisatta thought, "Alas, what a hardship for us!"...
"Having gathered the wealth he had obtained into one place, he played and lost it all," he said, and then spoke this verse:
"Blow, blow, but do not overblow; for what is overblown is ruined.
By blowing [once], what was gained by the hundred was lost by overblowing."
In this context, "one should blow the conch, one should not fail to blow it" means that one should strike the drum, one should not fail to strike it.
"One should not over-blow" means that one should not strike it continuously by exceeding the proper measure. Why is that?
Because "over-blown is evil"; for continuous drumming has now become evil and base for us. For by over-blown...
"He obtained a hundred [coins]" means that by sounding the drum in the city, he obtained a hundred *kahāpaṇa* coins.
"By over-sounding it, he lost it all" means that now, because my son did not follow my word and instead sounded it excessively in the wilderness,
through that excessive sounding, everything was lost.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and established the connection, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the son was the monk Dubbacca, but the father was none other than myself.
This concludes the ninth commentary, the Bherivādaka Jātaka.
10. The Commentary on the Saṅkhadhama Jātaka.
"Blow! Blow!"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning one who is difficult to speak with.
Long ago, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of conch-blowers.
When a festival for the constellations was proclaimed in Benares, he took his father and, through the work of blowing the conch, obtained wealth.
On the way back, in a forest inhabited by thieves, he forbade his father from blowing the conch shell continuously.
Thinking, "I will drive away the thieves with the sound of the conch," the father blew it incessantly; the thieves returned as before and plundered them.
The Bodhisatta spoke the verse in the same manner as previously:
“Blow, blow, but do not overblow; for what is blown too much is evil.
My father blew away those riches acquired by blowing [the conch]; I, therefore, blow them away.

In this context, “my father blew them away” means that after my father had blown the conch and obtained wealth, he blew it away—that is, he scattered, destroyed, and annihilated it—by blowing [the conch] again and again.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and established the connection, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the father was the monk Dubbaca, and his son was none other than myself.
The commentary on the *Saṅkhadhamajātaka*, the tenth.
The sixth chapter, the *Āsīsavagga*.
The summary verse for this is: Mahāsīla, Janaka, Puṇṇapāti, and Kiṃphala;
Pañcāvudha, Kañcanakkhandha, Vānarinda, and Tayodhamma.
They beat the kettledrums and blew the conchs.
7. The Chapter on Women [61] 1.
The Commentary on the Asātamanta Jātaka.
"Worldly women are indeed miserable"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who was despondent.
The story of that monk will be made clear in the *Ummādanti Jātaka*. Then the Teacher said to that monk:
"Monk, women are indeed unpleasant, unwise, base, and inferior; you have relied upon such a base woman."
Having asked, "Why are you despondent? he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in Takkasilā in the kingdom of Gandhāra.
Having reached maturity, he attained perfection in the three Vedas and in all the arts and sciences.

He was a preceptor renowned throughout the regions. At that time, in a certain brahmin family in Bārāṇasī, on the day their son was born, they took a fire and kept it burning without letting it go out. Then, when that brahmin youth reached the age of sixteen, his parents said to him:
"Son, on the day you were born, we took a fire and kept it. If you are destined for the Brahma-world..."
“If you wish to become [a world-renouncer], take fire, enter the forest, and by paying homage to the fire as the Blessed One, make the Brahma-world your goal.
But if you wish to live at home, go to Takkasilā, learn a craft from a world-renowned teacher, and establish a household.
The young man replied, “I shall not be able to [maintain] the fire in the forest...”

“I shall serve [him] and establish a household,” he thought. Having paid homage to his parents, he took a thousand pieces of money as the teacher’s fee, went to Takkasilā, mastered the craft, and returned.
However, his parents had no desire for a life of domesticity; they wished to have him tend the sacrificial fire in the forest. Then—
His mother, wishing to send him to the forest after showing him the faults of women, thought, "That teacher is wise and competent;
he will be able to explain the faults of women to my son," and said, "My dear, have you mastered your craft?
"Yes, mother. "Have you also mastered the *asātamanta* (the 'unpleasant' charm)? "I have not mastered it, mother. "My dear, if for you..."
“You have not mastered even the unpleasant [craft]; what craft have you learned? Go, and having learned it, come back!
Saying “Very well,” he set out once more toward Takkaśilā. That teacher’s mother was also elderly, being one hundred and twenty years old.
He personally attended to her, bathing, feeding, and drinking for her, looking after her. Other people saw him acting in that manner...
They felt disgust. He thought, "What if I were to enter the forest and dwell there, looking after my mother?

Then, having had a leaf-hut built in a secluded part of the forest at a place convenient for water, and having had ghee, rice, and other provisions brought, he carried his mother there, settled her, and made his dwelling while looking after her.
That young brahmin, having gone to Takkasilā and not seeing his teacher, asked, "Where is the teacher?
Upon hearing the news, he went there, paid homage, and stood before him.
Then the teacher said to him, "My dear son, why have you returned so quickly? Did I not have you learn the 'Asātamanta' [the charm for making others ill]?"
“But who taught you the unpleasant spells? “My mother, my teacher,” he replied.
The Bodhisatta thought, “There is no such thing as an ‘unpleasant spell. However, his mother must have intended to make him aware of this fault in women.
Then he said to him, “Very well, dear son, I shall teach you the unpleasant spells; starting from today—”

Standing in my place, bathe my mother with your own hands, feed her, give her drink, and attend to her; while massaging her hands, feet, head, and back, and so forth, you should speak of the beauty of her hands, feet, and other limbs at the time you are performing such services, saying:
"Noble lady, when your body was even now like this at the onset of old age, what must it have been like in your youth? And whatever...
“Tell me what my mother says; if you do so without shame or concealment, you shall receive what is unpleasant in its consequence, but if you do not, you shall not.
He replied, “Very well, teacher,” and having accepted his words, from then on he performed everything according to the prescribed method.
As that young man praised her again and again, the thought occurred to her—who was blind and aged—that "this man must desire to take pleasure with me," and thus a defilement arose within her.
One day, she said to the young man who was describing his own physical beauty, "Do you wish to take pleasure with me? "Noble lady, I certainly would wish so."
"But the teacher is heavy [to be killed]," he said. "If you wish for me, my son, then kill my teacher.
"Having learned such great skill from my teacher, how could I, out of mere defilement, kill my teacher?
"In that case, if you will not abandon me, I myself shall kill him. Thus, women indeed—
The woman was unpleasant, base, and of the lowest sort;

yet, standing at such an age, she had conceived a mind of lust and, following after her defilements, became desirous of killing her own helpful son. The young man reported all those words to the Bodhisatta.
The Bodhisatta said, "Well done, young man, for reporting this to me," and [he observed] the mother's life-force (*āyusaṅkhāra*).
Looking [at him], and knowing that "he will die this very day," he said, "Come, young man, let us test it.

Having cut down a single udumbara tree and fashioned a wooden figure of himself, he covered it with his own upper garment, laid it on its back in his own sleeping place, tied a rope to it, and said to his pupil: "Dear son, take an axe and go..."
“Give the signal to my mother. The young man went and said, “Lady, the teacher is lying down in his own sleeping place in the leaf-hut;
I have tied the signal-cord. Take this axe, go there, and if you can, kill him.
“But will you not abandon me? “For what reason would I abandon you? She took the axe.
Taking it up, trembling, she rose and went toward it, perceiving it as a rope.

Reaching out with her hand and touching it, she perceived, "This is my son," and removed the cloth from the mouth of the wooden figure. Taking an axe, thinking, "I shall kill him with a single blow," she struck it right on the neck;
when the sound "Dha! arose, she realized it was a tree. Then, by the Bodhisatta...
When he asked, "Mother, what are you doing?", she replied, "I have been deceived," and died right there, falling down.
Indeed, even as she lay in her own leaf-hut, she was destined to die at that very moment.
Having learned of her death, he performed the funeral rites, extinguished the funeral pyre, and honored her with wild forest flowers.
Taking the young man with him and sitting at the door of the leaf-hut, he said: "Dear son, there is no such thing as a 'limit of unpleasantness' that exists separately;

rather, women are themselves the unpleasantness. When your mother sent you to me saying, 'Learn the limit of unpleasantness,' she sent you for the purpose of making you understand the faults of women.
Now, however, you have seen for yourself the fault of my mother; for this reason—"
“You should know that women are indeed unpleasant, base, and inferior,” he said, and having thus instructed him, he dismissed him.
He too, having paid homage to his teacher, went into the presence of his mother and father. Then his mother asked him, “Dear son, have you mastered the spell for the unpleasant?
“Yes, mother,” he replied. “Now what will you do? Will you go forth and attend to the sacred fire?”
"Or will you live in the midst of a household? The young man, declaring his intention by saying, "Mother, I have personally witnessed the faults of women;
I have no need for the household life, I shall go forth," spoke this verse:
"Women of the world are indeed insatiable; no limit exists for them."
“Passionate and insolent, like a fire that devours everything—having abandoned them, I shall go forth and cultivate seclusion.
In this context, *asā* means non-pleasures (*asatiyo*), things that are base. Alternatively, *sāta* is said to mean happiness; that [happiness] is not found in them. Within oneself...
They are called *asā* because they give only what is unpleasant (*asāta*) to those whose minds are bound [to them]; the meaning is that they are suffering and the basis for suffering.
To establish this meaning, this sutta should be cited:
“Deceit and illusion, grief and disease, and calamity;”
“Harsh and binding, these are the snares of Death dwelling in the cave;
the man who places his trust in them is the lowest of men among men.
“Women of the world” means women in the world. “No limit exists for them,” O Mother, refers to the arising of defilements in those women.
Having reached [this state], there is no longer any boundary, restraint, limit, or measure. "Passionate and impudent" means that they have no boundary;

they are "passionate" because they are attached to and clinging to the five strands of sensual pleasure, and likewise they are "impudent" because they possess the threefold impudence of bodily impudence, verbal impudence, and mental impudence. For these women—
It shows that once they have reached the internal doors of the body and so forth, there is no such thing as restraint;

they are fickle, resembling crows. "Just as the fire named 'Sikhī' (the crested one) consumes everything, mother"—just as the fire known by the designation "Sikhī" due to its crest of flames consumes both the impure, such as excrement and the like, and the pure, such as clarified butter, honey, molasses, and the like, whether desirable or undesirable.
Whatever he obtains, he eats and devours it all; therefore, he is called "the all-devourer" (*sabbaghaso*).

In the same way, those women—whether they be elephants, rams, goats, and so forth, of low birth and low occupation, or whether they be Kṣatriyas and others, of noble birth and noble occupation—without considering their inferior or superior status, [engage] in the intimacy of defilements through the enjoyment of worldly pleasures.
Whatever they obtain when it arises, they indulge in all of it; thus they are like crows and partridges that devour everything.
Therefore, it should be understood: "Just as a crow-eating partridge [consumes all], so too am I.
"Having abandoned those, I shall go forth"—meaning, having abandoned those wretched women who are the basis for suffering, I shall enter the forest.

"I shall go forth into the ascetic life of the seers. Regarding "cultivating seclusion," there are three kinds of seclusion: seclusion of body, seclusion of mind, and seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhiviveka*).
Among these, both seclusion of body and seclusion of mind are appropriate here. This is what is meant:
"Mother, having gone forth and performed the preliminary work of the *kasiṇas*, I shall arouse the eight meditative attainments and the five direct knowledges (*abhiññā*)."
"Having separated my body from the crowd and my mind from defilements, by cultivating and increasing this seclusion, I shall become one whose ultimate destination is the Brahma-world;

enough for me with the household life. Having thus censured women and paid homage to his parents, he entered the Himalayas, went forth into homelessness, and by cultivating the aforementioned seclusion, became one whose ultimate destination was the Brahma-world.
The Teacher also, having explained the faults of women, saying, "In this way, bhikkhu, women are indeed unpleasant, base, inferior, and givers of suffering," proclaimed the Truths.
At the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
The Teacher, connecting the present to the past, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Bhaddakāpilānī was the mother, and the father..."
“Mahākassapa was the pupil, Ānanda was the student, and I myself was the teacher.
Thus ends the first commentary on the *Asātamanta-jātaka*.
[62] 2. Commentary on the *Aṇḍabhūta-jātaka*
"Regarding what the brahmin said": This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who was suffering from world-weariness (*ukkaṇṭhita*).
The Teacher asked him, "Is it true, monk, that you are indeed disenchanted? When he replied, "It is true," the Teacher said, "Monk, women are indeed unguardable;
in the past, even when wise men guarded a woman from the moment of conception..."
Having said, "They were unable to protect him," he related a story of the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen.
Upon reaching maturity and attaining proficiency in all arts, he established himself on the throne upon the passing of his father.
He ruled the kingdom according to the Dhamma. He played at dice with his court chaplain. While playing, however, he recited:
"All rivers flow crookedly; all forests are made of wood;
all women commit evil when they find a secluded place."
Singing this song of dice, he threw golden dice onto a silver board. Playing in this manner, the king always won, while the chaplain was always defeated.
As his household wealth gradually came to an end, he thought: "This being the case, all the wealth in this house will be exhausted;
I shall seek out and take into my home a woman who has not been with another man."
Then this thought occurred to him: "I will not be able to protect a woman who has previously seen another man;

however, having protected a woman from conception, established her under my control once she has reached maturity, made her devoted to a single man, and arranged for strict security, I shall bring wealth from the royal family.
He was also skilled in the science of bodily marks (*aṅgavijjā*).
Later, seeing a certain woman from a low-caste family who was pregnant, he realized she would give birth to a daughter.
He summoned her, gave her travel expenses, and had her live in his own house. When she gave birth, he gave her wealth and sent her away.
He did not allow that young girl to see other men, but placed her in the hands of women only to raise her until she reached maturity.
He brought her under his own control. As long as she was still growing up, she did not play dice with the king;
however, once he had brought her under his control, the brahmin said, "Great King, let us play dice. The king agreed, saying "Very well," and they played according to their previous custom.
When the royal chaplain, having sung for the king, was about to cast the dice, he said, "Except for my young woman."
From that time on, the chaplain was victorious and the king was defeated. The Bodhisatta,
having had the matter investigated and knowing for certain that there must be a single woman living alone in his house,
thought, "I shall cause him to break her virtue," and summoned a rogue, saying, "Will you be able to..."
“I shall break the virtue of the chaplain’s wife,” he said. “I am able, Your Majesty,” he replied.
Then the king gave him wealth and sent him away, saying, “In that case, complete this quickly.

Having taken the wealth from the king, he took perfumes, incense, powders, camphor, and so forth, and set up a shop for all kinds of perfumes not far from the chaplain’s house. The chaplain’s house, moreover, was seven stories high.
It had seven gate-towers, and at every gate-tower there was the guard of women alone.
Aside from the brahmin, no other man was permitted to enter the house;
even when disposing of refuse, they would only allow entry after first clearing it away. Only the family priest was permitted to see that young woman, and she had a single—
There was a female attendant. One day, as she was going along carrying scents and flowers, she passed near the shop of that rogue.
Recognizing her well as "that woman's attendant," he saw her approaching one day, rose from his shop, went over to her, and fell at her feet with both hands.
Grasping her hands and feet firmly, he lamented, "Mother, where have you been for all this time?
The remaining gamblers who were employed there also stood to one side and said, "By the shape of their hands, feet, and faces, and by their appearance, mother and son are exactly alike.
While they were speaking thus, that woman, not believing them, [thought], "This is my..."
“A son shall be born,” she said, and she herself began to weep. Both of them, having cried and wept, stood there embracing one another.

Then that rogue asked, “Mother, where do you live? “I live, dear father, serving as an attendant to the young wife of the chaplain, who dwells with the grace of a *kinnarī* and has attained the pinnacle of physical beauty. “Where will you go now? he asked.
“Mother? “For the sake of perfumes, garlands, and such for her. “Mother, what is the use of you going elsewhere?
From now on, bring them from me alone,” she said, and without taking any payment, she gave many betel leaves, cardamom seeds, and various flowers.
When the young woman saw the many perfumes, flowers, and so forth, she asked, “Mother, why is it that today our brahmin—”
“I am pleased,” he said. “Why do you say this? “Because I have seen the great quantity of these [flowers].
“The brahmin did not give me a high price; rather, I brought this from my own son.
From then on, she took whatever price was given by the brahmin herself and fetched the perfumes, flowers, and so forth from him alone. After a few days had passed, the rogue—
Having made a sickbed, she lay down. She went to the door of his shop; not seeing him, she asked, "Where is my son?

"Has your son become unwell? She went to the place where he was lying, sat down, and while massaging his back, asked, "What is it, dear, that makes you unwell? He remained silent. "Why [do you not speak]?"
“...and told his sons? [The son replied: “Mother, even if I were dying, I could not tell you. [The mother said: “Dear son, if you will not tell me, to whom would you tell it?
Tell me, dear son! [The son said: “Mother, I have no other ailment;
however, having heard the praises of that young woman, my heart has become bound to her. If I obtain her, I shall live; if I do not obtain her, right here—”
“I shall die. “Dear son, this is my burden; do not worry because of this,” she said, comforting him.
Then, taking many perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, she went to the young woman’s presence and asked, “Mother, my son has heard your reputation from me and has become infatuated with you.
What should be done? “If you can bring him here, I have already given you my consent.”
Having heard her words, from that time forward she gathered much refuse from the corners and eaves of that house and threw it upon the female guardian. Distressed by this, the guardian departed.
The other woman continued in that same manner, throwing refuse upon whoever said anything to her. From then on, however, she—whatever...
Whatever she brought or took away, no one was able to clear her of suspicion. At that time, having made the rogue lie down in the flower-basket, she brought him into the presence of the young woman.
Having violated the young woman’s virtue, the rogue remained in the palace for a day or two.
When the chaplain had gone outside, the two of them enjoyed themselves.
When he arrived, the rogue hid himself.
Then, after one or two days had passed, she said to him, "Husband, it is now time for you to go.
"I wish to go after striking the brahmin," he replied. She said, "So be it," and having caused the rogue to hide, when the brahmin arrived, she spoke thus:
“Noble sir, while you are playing the lute, I wish to dance. “Very well, dear lady, dance,” he said, and played the lute.
“I am ashamed while you are looking at me; however, I shall dance after covering your face with my garment.
“If you are ashamed, do so,” he replied. The young woman took a thick cloth and began to cover his eyes.
“Bind his mouth. The brahmin had his mouth bound and played the lute. After dancing for a moment, she said, “Noble sir, I wish to strike you once on the head.
The brahmin, who was lustful for women and did not understand the reason for her words, said, “Strike me!
The young woman gave a signal to the rogue. He approached the brahmin slowly...
Standing behind him, he struck him on the head with his knee; his eyes became as if about to fall out, and a swelling rose upon his head.
Overcome by pain, he said, "Bring me your hand.
The young woman raised her own hand and placed it in his. The brahmin remarked, "Your hand is soft, but the blow was hard."
He said: "The rogue struck the brahmin and hid himself.

While he was hiding, the young woman removed the cloth from the brahmin's face, took some oil, and massaged his head. When the brahmin went outside, that woman again had the rogue lie down in a basket and carried him out."
So he went into the presence of the king and reported all that had occurred.
The king said to the brahmin who had come to his court, "Shall we play at dice, brahmin? "Very well, Great King," he replied.

The king had the gaming board prepared and, singing the gambling song in the same manner as before, cast the dice. The brahmin [perceived] the state of the young woman's ascetic power having been broken.
Not knowing [the answer], he said, "Except for my young wife. Even though he spoke thus, he was indeed defeated.
Having won, the king said, "Brāhmaṇa, what do you say? Your asceticism has been shattered by your young wife.
You thought, 'I shall be able to protect a woman by guarding her in seven places from the time of conception,' yet a woman—"
"Even for one who places [a child] in the womb and carries it about, it is impossible to protect it; there is no such thing as a woman who belongs to a single man.

Your young wife, saying 'I wish to dance,' had your face bound with your own cloth while you were playing the lute, and having have her lover strike you on the head with a pestle, she sent him away. Now, what are you saying?"
Having spoken this, he recited the verse:
“What the brahmin said while covering his lute with his mouth—
‘A wife is like an egg’— who would ever trust in such women?”

In this context, "the Brahmin played the lute with his mouth covered" means that he did not know the reason why the Brahmin had played the lute while his mouth was covered along with his thick garment. For she, wishing to deceive him, had done so.
But the Brahmin, unaware of that woman’s great deceitfulness, [regarded] her as a woman...
Having placed his faith [in her], he formed the perception that "she is ashamed of me";
it was in order to reveal his state of ignorance that the king spoke thus—this is the intended meaning here. "A wife brought as an egg" (*aṇḍabhūtābhatā*): "egg" (*aṇḍa*) refers to the seed;

she was "brought" (*ābhatā*), meaning led from the mother's womb while still in the form of a seed, before having emerged; or alternatively, *bhata* means "nourished" or "reared. Who is she? The wife.
Pajāpati is the one who serves at the feet. She is called "bhariyā" (wife) because she is to be supported with food, clothing, and so forth; because her moral restraint (*saṃvara*) has been broken;
or because she is filled with worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*). Regarding them, who could ever trust? "Jātu" is a term for "ever" or "at any time.
Among those wives—who, even while being protected from the mother’s womb, fall into such a state of corruption—whom could one ever trust?
"What wise man indeed would place absolute trust [in her]? Who could believe, 'She is without change toward me'?"—this is the meaning.
For when there are those who address her and those who invite her, it is impossible to guard what is called "the womanfolk" by means of unrighteousness (*asaddhamma*).
Thus did the Bodhisatta teach the Dhamma to the brahmin. The brahmin [listened to] the Bodhisatta’s teaching of the Dhamma...
Having heard this, he went to his residence and said to that young woman, "Is it true that you have committed such an evil deed?
She replied, "Noble sir, who says such a thing? I did not do it; I alone struck him, no one else.
If you do not believe me, let me perform an act of truth: 'Except for you, I have never known the touch of another man's hand.'"

“Having prepared a fire and entered it, I shall make you believe. The brahmin said, “So be it,” and having had a great pile of wood prepared and a fire lit, he summoned her and said, “If you have faith in yourself, enter the fire.
The young woman first instructed her own attendant: “Mother, go there to your son...”
“Please say that you will take my hand when I enter the fire. She went and spoke thus.

The rogue came and stood in the midst of the assembly. Desiring to deceive the brahmin, that young woman stood in the middle of the great crowd and said, “Brahmin, apart from you, I have never known the touch of the hand of any other man; by this—”
"By truth, may this fire not burn me! she said, and began to enter the fire.

At that moment, the rogue went up and took hold of the young woman by the hand, saying, "Look, sirs! Behold the deed of this brahmin family priest; he is making such a woman as this enter the fire! She made him release her hand and said to the priest: "Noble sir,..."
“My act of truth has been broken; it is no longer possible to enter the fire. “For what reason?
“Today I performed such an act of truth, saying: ‘I know not the touch of another man’s hand except that of my husband.
But now I have been taken by the hand by this man. Realizing, “I have been deceived by her,” the brahmin—

Having beaten him, she had him expelled. Thus, these women, possessed of unrighteousness, even after committing such a great evil deed, remain of various minds—swearing oaths day after day, saying "I did not do such a thing"—only in order to deceive their own husbands. Therefore it was said:
“Among female thieves who possess many wiles, in whom truth is very difficult to find,
the disposition of women is hard to discern, like the path of a fish gone into the water.
For them, falsehood is as truth, and truth for them is as falsehood.”
“Like cattle grazing on grass, they pick out the very best for themselves.
‘These women are thieves, hard-hearted, fierce, and full of harsh words;
there is no deception among men that they do not know.’”
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, "Thus is the female sex to be guarded," proclaimed the Truths.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
The Teacher, having connected the present context to the past, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I myself was the King of Bārāṇasī."
The second commentary on the *Aṇḍabhūta-jātaka*.
[63] 3. The commentary on the *Takkapaṇḍita-jātaka*.
"Angry and ungrateful"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain dissatisfied bhikkhu.
The Teacher related the story. For the Teacher asked him, "Is it true, monk, that you are weary?
When he replied, "It is true," the Teacher said, "Monks, women are ungrateful and treacherous to their friends; why have you become weary on account of them? Having said this, he brought up the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta, having gone forth into the ascetic life, lived on the bank of the Ganges.
Having established a hermitage, he attained the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) and the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), and dwelt in the bliss of *jhāna*.
At that time, the daughter of the chief merchant of Bārāṇasī, named Duṭṭhakumārī, was fierce and cruel;
she reviled, insulted, and beat her slaves and laborers. Then one day, her attendants took her and [said], "To the Ganges..."
"Let us play," they said, and so they went. While they were still playing, the time for sunset arrived;
a cloud arose, and seeing the cloud, the people fled hither and thither with great speed.
The merchant’s daughter’s slaves and laborers thought, "Today it is right for us to see her back," and so they cast her into the water itself and climbed out.
