It rained, the sun had set, and darkness fell. They went home without her;
when asked, "Where is she?", they replied, "She has just emerged from the Ganges, and we do not know where she has gone. Although her relatives searched for her, they did not find her.
Crying out with a great lamentation, she was being carried away by the water until, at the hour of midnight, she reached the vicinity of the Bodhisatta’s leaf-hut.
She reached that place. Hearing her cry, [the Bodhisatta] thought, "This is the sound of a woman; I shall provide her protection.
Taking a torch, he went to the riverbank. Seeing her there, he comforted her, saying, "Do not fear, do not fear!
Then the Bodhisatta, possessing the strength of an elephant and endowed with fortitude, crossed the river, lifted her up, and brought her to his hermitage.
Having made a fire, he gave it to her. When the cold had passed, he offered her sweet fruits.
Having eaten them, he stood there and asked, "Where do you live, and how did you fall into the Ganges? She related that account to him.
Then, saying, "You must live right here," he had her dwell in a leaf-hut while he himself stayed out in the open air for two or three days.
"Now, let us go," he said. She, thinking, "I will take this ascetic after causing him to break his virtue," did not go.
Then, as time passed, she displayed feminine coquetry and dalliance, thereby breaking his virtue and causing his meditative absorption (*jhāna*) to vanish.
He took her and lived right there in the forest. Then she said to him, "Noble sir, why..."
“Why should we live in the forest? We shall go to the path of men. Taking him with him, he went to a certain frontier village and supported him by making his living through a trade in buttermilk.
Because he lived by selling buttermilk, they gave him the name “Takkapaṇḍita” (Buttermilk-Wise).
Then the villagers, giving him a maintenance allowance, said: “Explain to us what is well-reasoned and ill-reasoned.”
"Live here," they said, and so they lived in a hut at the village gate.
At that time, bandits would descend from the mountains and raid the border regions.
One day, having raided that village and having the villagers themselves carry up their bundles, they departed; taking that merchant’s daughter with them as well, they went on their way.
Having gone to their own dwelling place, they dismissed the rest of the people.
But the chief of the bandits, becoming infatuated with her beauty, made her his wife. The Bodhisatta asked, "Where is so-and-so?
Upon hearing that she had been seized by the chief of the bandits and made his wife, he thought, "She will not remain there without me; she will escape."
Thinking, "He will come," he remained right there, waiting for her arrival.
The merchant’s daughter also thought: "I am living here happily;
perhaps one day Takkapaṇḍita might come on some pretext, take me away from here, and then I would be deprived of this happiness. What if I were now..."
“Thinking as if she were full of affection for him, she will summon him and have him killed. She summoned a man and sent this message:
“I am living here in suffering; let Takkapaṇḍita come, take me with him, and depart.
Having heard that message and placing his trust in it, he went there and, standing at the village gate, sent word back to her. She came out...
Seeing him, they said, "Venerable sir, if we go now, the chief thief will pursue us and have both of us killed;

let us go during the night. Having brought him in, fed him, and seated him at the gateway, when the chief thief returned in the evening, drank liquor, and became intoxicated, they said, "Master, if at this time your enemy..."
“If you were to see him, what would you do? he asked. “I would do this and that,” he replied. “But is he far away?

Is he not sitting right there at the gateway? The chief robber took up a torch, went there, saw him, seized him, threw him down in the middle of the house, and beat him at will with a *kappara* and other weapons. Even as he was being beaten, he said nothing else.
"He is angry, ungrateful, slanderous, and a divider of friends"—he said only this much. The robber beat him, bound him, and made him lie down;
having eaten his evening meal, he went to sleep. When he woke up and the liquor had worn off, he began to beat him again, yet the other continued to recite those same four lines.
Coro thought, “Even though he is being beaten like this, he says nothing else but these same four phrases;
I shall question him. Realizing that she was asleep, he asked her, “Friend, even though you are being beaten like this, why do you say only these phrases?
Takkapaṇḍita said, “In that case, listen,” and explained the reason from the beginning.
He began to speak: "Formerly, I was a forest-dwelling ascetic who had attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).
Having rescued this woman from being swept away by the Ganges, I took care of her. Then, having seduced me, she caused me to fall away from those absorptions.
Consequently, abandoning the forest, I live in a frontier village supporting her. Now, she has been brought here by thieves. 'I am suffering...'"
“‘I shall dwell here; come and take me away’—having sent this message to me, she has now placed it in your hands.

For this reason, I speak thus. The robber thought: “She who has behaved so treacherously toward one as virtuous and helpful as this—what calamity indeed would she not bring upon me? She must be killed!”
Having thus comforted and awakened the logician, he took his sword and went out, saying, "I shall have this man executed at the village gate.
Having gone outside the village with her, he said, "Take him by the hand," and having had her take him by the hand,
he took up his sword and, as if striking the logician, cut him in two.
Having bathed him with lead [to remove his fever] and satisfied the wise Takkasilan for several days with excellent food, he asked, "Where will you go now?
The wise Takkasilan replied, "I have no need for the life of a householder;
having gone forth as an ascetic, I shall dwell right there in the forest. "In that case, I too shall go forth," he said, and so both of them went forth.
Having gone to that forest region, they developed the five higher knowledges (*pañca abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭha samāpattiyo*),
and at the end of their lives, they were reborn in the Brahma-world.
Having related these two accounts, the Teacher joined the connection, and having become fully enlightened, he spoke this verse:
“Angry and ungrateful, backbiting and divisive—practice the holy life, O bhikkhu, lest you dwell in suffering.
Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: Bhikkhu, these women are indeed angry; they do not restrain anger when it arises.
They are ungrateful and do not recognize even a very great service rendered to them. They are slanderers and speak only such words as create a void of affection.
They are dividers of friends; they split apart friends, being by nature prone to speaking words that cause division among friends.
Endowed with such evil qualities as these, what use have you for them? O bhikkhu, lead the holy life.
For this abstinence from sexual intercourse is called "the holy life" (*brahmacariya*) in the sense of being utterly pure; practice it. "You shall not abandon that happiness":
while dwelling in this way of living the holy life, you shall not abandon the happiness of *jhāna*, the happiness of the Path, and the happiness of the Fruit;
you will not forsake this happiness, nor will you fall away from this happiness—this is the meaning. "Na..."
There is also a reading, "parihāhisī," which has the same meaning.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher proclaimed the Truths;
at the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher then identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the chief thief was Ānanda."
“I was he, and it was I myself who was Takkapaṇḍita.
This concludes the third commentary, the Takkapaṇḍita Jātaka.
[64] 4. The Commentary on the Durājāna Jātaka.
"Do not desire delight," the Teacher said, while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain lay follower.
It is said that there was a lay follower living in Sāvatthī who was established in the three refuges and the five precepts;
he was devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dhamma, and devoted to the Saṅgha. However, his wife was immoral and of evil character. On a certain day, she committed misconduct.
On the day he visits her, she is like a slave-girl for hire; but on days when he does not commit misconduct, she is like a mistress—fierce and harsh.
He is unable to discern her true disposition, and then, oppressed by her, he does not go to attend upon the Buddha.
Then one day, as he had come bringing perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and was sitting after having paid his respects, [the Teacher spoke to him].
The Teacher said: “Why is it, lay follower, that you do not come to attend upon the Buddha for seven or eight days?
“Venerable sir, on one day my wife is like a slave bought for a hundred coins, and on another day she is like a mistress—fierce and harsh.
I am unable to discern her true disposition; thus, being oppressed by her, I [do not come].”

“I am not coming. Having heard his words, the Teacher said, “Lay follower, even in the past the wise have told you that ‘the nature of women is difficult to understand,’ yet because you have fallen into the confusion of worldly existence, you were unable to perceive it.
Having said this, at his request, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares,
the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher who instructed five hundred young brahmins in their craft. Then, a young brahmin from a foreign kingdom arrived and,
while learning his craft under him, became enamored with one of the women and made her his wife.
Having done so, while living in that very city of Bārāṇasī, he would not go to attend upon his teacher two or three times [a day].
Now, his wife was immoral and of evil character;
on days when she practiced misconduct, she was like a slave, but on days when she did not, she was like a mistress—fierce and harsh. Being unable to understand her true nature, he...
Harassed by her, his mind distracted, he did not go to attend upon his teacher.
Then, after seven or eight days had passed, when he had returned, the teacher asked him, "Why, young man, do you not appear?
He replied, "Teacher, my wife desires me one day and longs for me; she becomes humble like a slave. One day she is a mistress..."
"She is as stiff, fierce, and harsh as a stone; I am unable to understand her disposition.
Oppressed by her and with my mind distracted, I have not come to attend upon you. The teacher replied, "It is even so, young man.
Women, on a day when they have practiced misconduct, comply with their husbands, becoming humble like slaves. But on a day when they have not so practiced—"
"Having become arrogant with pride, they do not take account of their husbands. Such are these women—indeed, ill-behaved and immoral;
their true nature is difficult to discern. Whether they desire you or do not desire you, you must remain neutral toward them.
Having said this, he spoke this verse as an exhortation to him:
“Let her not desire me with joy; let her not grieve when she does not obtain me.
The state of a woman’s passion is difficult to discern, like that of a fish moving in the water.
In this regard, in the phrase “let her not desire me with joy” (*mā su nandi icchati maṃ*), the syllable *su* is merely a particle. [The meaning is: “This woman desires and longs for me.”
"Do not rejoice thinking, 'She feels affection for me. Do not grieve thinking, 'She does not desire me'—that is, do not grieve thinking, 'She does not want me.
By this he indicates that one should remain equanimous, without creating joy when she desires you and sorrow when she does not.
The state of women is difficult to understand; the nature of women is indeed difficult to comprehend because it is concealed by feminine guile."

Like what? "Like the movement of a fish in water. Just as the movement of a fish is difficult to discern because it is concealed by water, and for that very reason, when a fisherman approaches, it conceals its movement with the water and flees, not allowing itself to be caught;
even so, women, having committed even a great immoral act, [think], "We have done such a thing..."
"‘I did not do it’—thus, concealing the deed they themselves have committed through feminine guile, they deceive their husbands.
Such indeed are these women, evil-natured and difficult to understand; one who remains neutral toward them alone is happy.
In this way the Bodhisatta gave counsel to his pupil. From that time forth, he remained neutral toward her.
His wife, thinking, "It seems my lack of virtue has been discovered by the Teacher," refrained from immoral conduct from that time forward.
And the wife of that lay follower, thinking, "It seems my own misconduct has been discovered by the Perfectly Enlightened One," likewise ceased from that time forward to commit any evil deed.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, proclaimed the Truths.
At the conclusion of the Truths, that lay follower was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher, connecting the present to the past, identified the Jātaka:
"The husband and wife of that time were none other than the husband and wife of the present; as for the teacher, he was I myself."
The Fourth: The Commentary on the *Durājāna-jātaka*.
[65] 5. The Commentary on the *Anabhirati-jātaka*.
This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain lay follower who was likewise [discontented]. "Just as a river and a path... [etc.]
He spoke concerning this. However, while investigating the matter, he discovered her immoral conduct;

having been rebuked by her, his mind became disturbed, and for seven or eight days he did not come to attend upon him. One day, having gone to the monastery and paid homage to the Tathāgata, he sat down.
When asked, "Why have you not come for seven or eight days?", he replied, "Venerable Sir, my wife is immoral."

"Because my mind was distracted regarding her, I did not come," he said. The Teacher said, "Lay follower, wise men of old have told you that one should remain neutral toward women, without giving way to anger thinking, 'These women are immoral.
However, because you were obscured by another existence, you did not perceive that reason. Having said this, when requested by him, the Teacher related a past event.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was, as before, a world-renowned teacher.
A pupil of his, having perceived a fault in his wife, did not come for several days due to his troubled state of mind.
One day, when questioned by the teacher, he informed him of the reason. Then the teacher said to him, "Dear son,..."
"Women, indeed, are common property to all; therefore, the wise do not give way to anger toward them, thinking, 'These women are immoral,'" he said, and then spoke this verse by way of instruction:
"Just as a river, a road, a tavern, an assembly hall, and a watering place;"
"Thus, indeed, regarding those called 'women of the world,' the wise do not become angry.

In this context, "just as a river" means that just as a river with many fords is common to everyone who arrives seeking a bath—whether they be outcasts (*caṇḍāla*) or members of the noble class (*khattiya*)—and there is no one who cannot obtain the opportunity to bathe therein; so it is with the "path" and the other examples mentioned.
Just as a great highway is common to all, and no one is prevented from traveling upon it;
and as a tavern—a house for liquor—is common to all, so that whoever desires to drink may enter it;
and as an assembly hall built by those seeking merit for people to dwell in at various places is common to all, and no one is barred from entering it—
One does not obtain [it exclusively]. Water-cisterns placed along the great highway and constructed as public wells are common to all;

no one there is prevented from drinking water. "Thus are the women of the world"—in this very way, dear youth, women in this world are indeed common to all, and for that very reason of being common, they are like rivers, roads, drinking places, assembly halls, and crossroads.
Therefore, the wise do not become angry; having reflected that these women are "base, immoral, unvirtuous, and common to all," the wise—skillful and endowed with intelligence—do not become angry.
Thus the Bodhisatta gave this advice to his pupil, and having heard that advice, he became impartial.
His wife, thinking, "I have apparently been recognized by my teacher," did not commit any evil deed from that time forward.
That lay follower's wife, thinking, "I have apparently been recognized by the Teacher," likewise did not commit any evil deed from that time forward.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher proclaimed the Truths; at the conclusion of the Truths, the lay follower attained the fruit of stream-entry.
He established [the connection]. The Teacher, having linked the sequence of events, identified the Jātaka:
"The husband and wife of that time are the husband and wife of the present; as for the teacher-brāhmaṇa, he was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the *Anabhirati-jātaka*, the fifth.
[66] 6. The Commentary on the Mudulakkhaṇa Jātaka.
"In former times there was but one desire," etc.—The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this concerning moral defilement (saṃkilesa).

It is said that a certain son of good family from Sāvatthī, having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, embraced the jewel-like Dispensation with all his heart, went forth into homelessness, and...

A practitioner of yoga who was practicing his meditation subject without interruption once, while walking for alms in Sāvatthī one day, saw a woman fully adorned and prepared. Because of her beauty, he broke down his sense faculties and gazed at her.
Within him, the defilement stirred; he became like a milk-tree struck by an axe. From that moment on...
Being under the sway of defilements, he obtained neither satisfaction of body nor satisfaction of mind;
resembling a startled deer, he took no delight in the Teaching, with his hair, beard, and nails grown long and his robes soiled.
Then, seeing the change in his faculties, his fellow monks asked him, "Friend, why is it that your faculties are not as they were before?"
“I am dissatisfied, friends.
Then they led him into the presence of the Teacher. The Teacher asked, “Monks, why have you come taking a monk who does not wish to come?
“Venerable sir, this monk is dissatisfied,” they replied. “Is it true, monks? “It is true, Blessed One.”
“It is true, Blessed One. “Who made you weary? “Venerable sir, while wandering for alms, I saw a woman and looked at her with my faculties unrestrained;
then my defilement was stirred, and because of that I became weary.
Then the Teacher said to him, “It is not surprising, monk, that you looked at an unsuitable object with your faculties unrestrained.”
Looking with a base disposition, he was shaken by defilements; for even Bodhisattvas who had previously attained the five higher knowledges and the eight meditative attainments,
having suppressed defilements through the power of jhāna and possessed pure minds as they moved through the expanse of the sky,
broke their faculties and, looking upon objects of a discordant nature, fell away from jhāna and, shaken by defilements, experienced great suffering.
For the wind that uproots Mount Sineru does not take account of a mere elephant-sized mound of earth;
nor does the wind that uproots the great rose-apple tree take account of a shrub growing on a severed bank; nor does the wind that dries up the great ocean take account of a small pond.
In the same way, those things that produce ignorance in Bodhisattvas—who possess supreme intelligence and pure minds—do not affect them at all.
"What shame will the defilements feel toward you? Even pure beings become defiled; even those possessing supreme fame fall into disgrace.
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of great wealth in the kingdom of Kāsi.
Having been reborn in a brahmin family, he reached maturity and mastered all the arts.

Abandoning sensual pleasures, he went forth as an ascetic, performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*, and having developed the five supernormal powers (*abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he dwelt in the Himalayan region, spending his time in the bliss of *jhāna*. One day, he...
At the proper time, having descended from the Himālaya mountains for the purpose of partaking of salt and sour gruel, he reached Bārāṇasī and stayed in the royal park. On the following day,
after tending to his body and putting on a lower garment and upper robe made of red wool, placing a deerskin over one shoulder,
binding his mass of matted hair, and taking his alms-bowl, he went about Bārāṇasī for alms.

He arrived at the king’s palace gate. The king, having gained confidence in him merely by his deportment, summoned him, seated him on a magnificent throne, and gratified him with exquisite hard and soft foods.
After he had offered words of thanksgiving, the king requested that he dwell in the royal park. Having accepted, he ate at the royal residence and, while instructing the royal family, remained there.
He lived in the park for sixteen years.

Then one day, as the king was departing to pacify a rebellious border region, he said to his chief queen, named Mudulakkhaṇā, "Serve my lord with diligence," and went away. From the moment the king had departed, the Bodhisatta—
From that time on, she would go to the royal palace whenever she pleased.

Then one day, after Mudulakkhaṇā had prepared food for the Bodhisattva, thinking, "Today my noble lord is taking a long time," she bathed with scented water, adorned herself with all her ornaments, and having spread out a small couch upon the great terrace, lay down waiting for the Bodhisattva’s arrival. The Bodhisattva, too—
Having observed his own time, he emerged from meditation and went to the royal palace through the air.
Upon hearing the sound of the bark garment, Mudulakkhaṇā thought, "The noble one has arrived," and rose up in haste. As she rose so hastily, her smooth robe fell away.
Even as the ascetic was entering through the lion-window, the queen’s form presented itself as an object of discordant beauty to him.
Having broken his faculties, he looked out with a sense of well-being. Then, the defilement within him was stirred;
he became like a milk-tree struck by an axe. At that very moment, his meditative absorption vanished, and he became like a crow with clipped wings.
Still standing there, he took his food but did not eat it; shaken by defilement, he descended from the palace, went to the garden, and entered the leaf-hut.
Having entered and placed food beneath a bed spread with wooden planks,
bound by an incompatible object of perception and burning with the fire of the defilements, he lay upon those wooden planks for seven days,
wasting away due to lack of food. On the seventh day, the king, having pacified the border regions, returned and circumambulated the city, arriving at his residence.
Thinking, "I shall go see the noble one," he went to the park, entered the leaf-hut, and seeing him lying there, thought, "I suppose some ailment has arisen.

He had the leaf-hut cleaned, massaged the noble one's feet, and asked, "What is it that makes you unwell, noble sir? "Great King, I have no other ailment; however, on account of the defilements, I..."
“Your heart has become bound,” he said. “To whom is your heart bound, noble lady?
“To Mudulakkhaṇā, Great King. “Very well, noble lady; I shall give Mudulakkhaṇā to you.
Taking the ascetic with him, he entered his residence, adorned the queen with every ornament, and gave her to the ascetic. Even as he was giving her to Mudulakkhaṇā—
He gave her this instruction: “Noble lady, you must strive to protect yourself by your own strength. “Very well, Your Majesty, I shall protect myself,” she replied.
The ascetic took the queen and descended from the royal palace.
Then, as they were departing through the great gate, he said to her: “Noble lady, it is necessary for us to obtain a house; go now.”
“Go and ask the king for a house,” he said. The ascetic went and asked for one.
The king had him given a ruined house that was being used by people as a latrine. He took the queen and went there, but she did not wish to enter.
“For what reason do you not enter? “Because of its impurity. “What shall I do now? “Clean it up.”
Having said, "No," he sent for the king and instructed him, "Go, bring a spade; bring a basket.
Once they had brought them, he had the filth and refuse discarded, and having had the village brought there, he had it plastered. Then again, having instructed him one by one, "Go, bring a bed;
bring a stool; bring a rug; bring a bowl; bring a jar," he had each item brought.
Again, he commanded him to fetch water and perform other such tasks. Taking a jar, he fetched water, filled a basin, prepared bathing water, and spread out a bed.

Then, as the man sat on one side of the bed, [the king] seized him by the whiskers, saying, "You do not know what it means to be a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa," and leaning him over, he dragged him toward himself.
Thus, at that time he regained mindfulness; however, for all that time prior, he had been ignorant.
Such are the defilements called "causes of ignorance. In this regard, it should be said: "Monks, the hindrance of sensual desire is a maker of blindness, a maker of ignorance," and so forth.
Having regained his mindfulness, he reflected: "This craving, as it increases, will cause me to lose my head in the four states of misery."
"She will not give it; it is better that I hand her over to the king this very day and enter the Himālayas.
Taking her with him, he approached the king and said, "Great King, I have no need for your queen;
it was solely because of her that my craving increased," and he spoke this verse:
“There was once a single desire in me, not having obtained one of gentle fortune;
now that Aḷārakkhī has been obtained, let desire give birth to desire.
Herein, this is the summarized meaning: O Great King, previously, when I had not obtained this queen of yours, who possesses gentle fortune—
“O, that I might obtain her!”—thus there was one wish, and one craving alone arose.

But when I obtained this Āḷārakkhī, with her wide eyes and beautiful gaze, then that former wish gave birth to and produced another, manifold kind of craving after it: craving for home, craving for requisites, and craving for enjoyments.
She arose. But as this desire of mine grew in this way, it would not allow me even to lift my head out of the states of misery (*apāya*);
"Enough of this! You yourself take your own wife, but I shall go to the Himalayas.
At that very moment, having restored the lost meditative absorption (*jhāna*), sitting in the air, he taught the Dhamma, gave counsel to the king, and [departed] through the air.

Having gone to the Himālayas, he did not return again to the human realm; rather, having cultivated the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) and without falling away from his meditative absorption (jhāna), he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
After the Teacher had delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths (sacca), at the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu attained the fruit of Arahatship.
He established [the connection]. The Teacher, having linked the sequence of events, identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, Ānanda was the king, Uppalavaṇṇā was Mudulakkhaṇā, and I myself was the seer.
This concludes the commentary on the Mudulakkhaṇa Jātaka, the sixth.
[67] 7. The Commentary on the Ucchaṅga Jātaka:
"O King, my son is in my lap. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a certain woman from the countryside.
For at one time, three men were plowing in a certain forest clearing in the kingdom of Kosala.
At that time, thieves in the forest had plundered people and fled.
The people, having searched for those thieves and not finding them, came to that place and said, "After plundering in the forest, you now act like farmers!
Thinking, "These are those thieves," they bound them, brought them back, and presented them to the King of Kosala. Then a certain woman approached and said, "Clothing..."
“Give me [something], give me a garment! she lamented, wandering again and again around the royal palace.
Hearing her voice, the king said, “Go, give her a garment. The people took a cloth and gave it to her.
Seeing it, she said, “I do not ask for this garment; I ask for the garment of my husband.”
The people went and informed the king, saying, "It seems this woman does not speak of clothing for herself; she speaks of clothing for her husband.
Then the king summoned her and asked, "Is it true that you are asking for clothing for your husband?
She replied, "Yes, Your Majesty. For a woman, the husband is indeed what is called 'clothing'; for when the husband is absent, even a garment worth a thousand pieces [is of no use]."
A woman who is clothed is indeed called "naked. To establish this point, it is said:
"A river is naked when it is waterless; a kingdom is naked when it is without a king;
and even a woman with ten brothers is naked if she is a widow."
This sutta should be cited.
The king, pleased with her, asked, "Who are these three people? She replied, "One is my husband, O King, one is my brother, and one is my son.
The king said, "I am pleased with you; I shall give you one of these three. Which do you desire?"
She asked. She said, "O King, as long as I live, I shall have one husband and I shall surely have a son;
however, because my mother and father are dead, it is difficult for me to find even a brother. O King, give me my brother. The King, being pleased, released all three of them.
Thus, by depending on that single woman, those three people were liberated from suffering. This is the reason.

This became known throughout the community of monks. Then one day, having assembled in the Hall of Truth, the monks sat down discussing her virtues, saying, "Friends, by means of one woman, three people have been delivered from suffering.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now? and they replied, "About this very matter."
When he had spoken thus, [the Buddha] said, “Monks, this woman did not only now deliver these three people from suffering; she delivered them even in the past,” and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, three people were plowing at the edge of a forest;
everything else is exactly as before. Then, when the king asked, “Which one among the three do you desire? she replied, “All three.”
“O gods, you cannot give him? “Yes, we cannot. “If you cannot give three, then give me my brother.
When she was told, “Take a son or a husband; what use have you for a brother? she replied, “O King, these things are indeed easy to find, but a brother is hard to find,” and spoke this verse:
“O King, my son is in my lap while I am running along the path;
yet I do not see that place from which I might bring his sibling.
In this context, “O King, my son is in my lap” means: O King, my son is indeed right here in my lap. For just as in the forest...
Having entered [the forest], she placed him on her hip, gathered wild greens (*ḍāka*), and as she put them there, wild greens became easy to find on her hip;
in this way, a son is also easily obtained by a woman, just like the wild greens on the hip. Therefore it was said:
"O King, my son is on my hip. Regarding "running on the path": even though she was traveling alone after having set out upon the road, she ran along the path.
For a woman, a husband is indeed easy to find; he is found as soon as he is seen. Therefore it is said: "a husband for one running on the road.

And as for that place from which I might bring my uterine kin—since I have no mother or father, I now see no other place in the form of a mother’s womb from which I was born, being born from the same womb.
“I would bring back my brother, who is known as my sister’s husband; therefore, give me my brother alone.
The king, thinking, “She speaks the truth,” was pleased in heart and, having brought all three people out from the prison, gave them to her. She took those three and departed.
The Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that she has liberated these three people from suffering; she did so even in the past.”
Having brought forward this teaching on the Dhamma and having established the connection, he identified the Jātaka:
"In the past, these four were exactly as they are now; the king, however, was none other than myself.
This is the seventh commentary on the Ucchaṅga Jātaka.
[68] 8. The Commentary on the Sāketajātakam.
“In that wherein the mind dwells”—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing in the Añjana Grove near Sāketa, concerning a certain brahmin.
It is said that when the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, was entering Sāketa for alms, [he encountered him].
An elderly brahmin living in the city of Sāketa, while going out from the city, saw the One of Ten Powers at the inner gate;
falling at his feet and grasping them firmly by the ankles, he said, "Dear one, is it not true that when parents have grown old, they ought to be cared for by their children?
Why did you not show yourself to us for all this time? At least by me..."
“You have been seen; now come to see your mother,” he said, and taking the Teacher with him, he went to his own home.
The Teacher went there and sat down upon the seat prepared for him together with the community of monks.
The brahmin lady also came, prostrated at the Teacher’s feet, and said, “Dear son, where have you been for all this time? Is it not true that parents, when they are advanced in years...”
“He must be attended upon,” she lamented. Her sons and daughters also made her say, “Come, pay homage to your brother.
With hearts full of joy, they both gave a great almsgiving. After the Teacher had finished his meal, he preached the *Jarāsutta* (Discourse on Old Age) to them both.
At the conclusion of the discourse, they both were established in the fruit of Non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). The Teacher rose from his seat.
He went straight to the Añjana Grove.
While the bhikkhus were seated together in the Dhamma hall, they raised this discussion:
"Friends, the brahmin knows that Suddhodana was the Tathāgata’s father and Mahāmāyā his mother; and knowing this, he [approached] the Tathāgata together with his brahmin wife."
"He says, 'This is our son,' and the Teacher also accepts it. What indeed is the reason for this?
Having heard their words, the Teacher said, "Monks, both of them are calling their own son 'son,'" and he related a past event:
"Monks, in the past, throughout five hundred consecutive births, this brahmin was my father, and [the other] was my mother."
For five hundred births he was my father’s younger brother, and for five hundred births he was my father’s elder brother.
This brahmin woman also was, without interruption, my mother for five hundred births, my paternal aunt for five hundred births, and my great-aunt for five hundred births.
Thus, for one thousand five hundred births I was raised in the hands of a brahmin, and for one thousand five hundred births [I was raised] by a brahmin woman.
Having explained that he had been raised in his hand for three thousand births, and having attained full enlightenment, he spoke this verse:
“In whomsoever the mind settles and the consciousness finds confidence,
even if that person has never been seen before— one may indeed place trust in him.”
In this context, "in whom the mind settles" means that the consciousness becomes established as soon as that person is merely seen.
"And the mind becomes serene" means that upon merely seeing him, the mind becomes clear and gentle.

"He nurtures one never seen before" refers to a person who has not previously been encountered in that particular life-form (*attabhāva*). "One may indeed place trust even in such a person" is said because of a feeling of affection experienced in the past.
"In that person one should place absolute confidence; the meaning is that one indeed attains trust.

Having thus delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher connected the narrative sequence and identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the brahmin and the brahmin lady were these very two, while the son was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Sāketa Jātaka, the eighth.
[69] 9. The Commentary on the Visavantajāta­ka:
“Fie upon that vomited poison! This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta).
It is said that at the time when the Elder was eating a meal of flour-cakes, people brought a great quantity of flour-based food for the Saṅgha.
Having taken it, they went to the monastery; what remained after the Bhikkhu Saṅgha had taken their portions was very abundant.
People said, "Venerable sirs, please take some even for those who have gone into the village. At that moment, the Elder’s young pupil (saddhivihārika) was in the village;
having set aside a portion for him, [the Elder thought] that since he had not yet returned, it would be too late in the day.
They gave it to the elder. When the elder had consumed it, the junior monk arrived.
Then the elder said to him, "Friend, we have consumed the fresh food set aside for you. He replied, "Venerable sir, who would not like something sweet?
A sense of spiritual urgency arose in the great elder. From that time forward, [he resolved] regarding the fresh food made of flour...
“I will not eat it,” he resolved. From that time on, it is said, the Elder Sāriputta had never before eaten flour-based food (piṭṭhakhādanīya).
His abstention from eating flour-based food became well known throughout the Saṅgha of monks.
The monks sat in the Dhamma Hall discussing this matter. Then the Teacher approached and asked, “What is this...?”
“Monks, for what discussion have you gathered here now? he asked.
When they replied, “For this very one,” he said, “Monks, even though Sāriputta once gave up his life, he would never take it back again. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of snake-physicians.
He made his living by the practice of medicine. Now, a snake bit a man from the countryside;
his relatives, acting without negligence, quickly brought a physician. The physician said, "What is the use of medicine for now?

I shall extract the poison by means of a counter-poison (paribhāvita). I will summon the bitten snake and have it draw the poison back out from the site of the bite by means of that very [counter-poison]. "The snake..."
“Having summoned the snake, have it draw out the poison. He summoned the snake and said, “This person was bitten by you. “Yes, by me,” it replied.
“From the place where you bit him, you yourself must draw the poison out through your mouth.
“Once something has been abandoned by me, it is never taken back; I will not draw out the poison once it has been released by me. He [gathered] wood...
Having had it brought and having made a fire, he said, "If you do not draw back your own poison, enter this fire.
The snake said, "I will indeed enter the fire, but I shall never again bring back the poison once it has been cast out by me," and spoke this verse:
"Fie on that emitted poison which I have cast out for the sake of my life!"
"I shall take back what I have vomited; death is better for me than life.
In this context, *dhiratthu* is a particle used in the sense of reproach.
"That poison which I shall swallow back because of my desire for life—that vomited poison, shame upon it! 'Death is better for me than life'—[this refers] to that poison."
The meaning is that death by entering the fire for the sake of not returning [the debt] is better than my life.

Having spoken thus, he set out to enter the fire. Then the physician restrained him, freed the man from the poison and restored him to health by means of medicines and incantations, and having given the snake its precepts, said: "From this day forward, do not harm anyone..."
Having said, "He would not harm me," he released him.

The Teacher also, having delivered this Dhamma teaching—"Monks, Sāriputta, even when abandoning his life once cast away, does not take it up again"—and having established the connection, identified the Jātaka: "At that time..."
"Sāriputta was the snake, while I myself was the physician.
Thus ends the ninth story, the *Visavantajātaka*. [70] 10.
The *Kuddālajātaka* (The Spade Jātaka).
"This victory is not well won" was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Cittahattha Sāriputta.
It is said that he was once a young man of a certain family in Sāvatthī.
One day, returning from the fields, he entered the monastery and, having received smooth, sweet, and choice food from an elder’s alms-bowl, he thought:
“Even though we perform various kinds of work with our own hands day and night, we do not obtain such sweet food;
I too should become a recluse. Having gone forth, after the lapse of a month and a half, while attending to things in an improper manner and falling under the sway of the defilements, he disrobed.
Later, becoming weary from hunger, he returned, went forth again, and [studied] the Abhidhamma.
He mastered it. By this very means, having left the order six times, he went forth again.

Then, in his seventh monastic life, becoming a master of the seven books (*sattappakaraṇika*), while teaching the Dhamma to many bhikkhus, he increased his insight (*vipassanā*) and attained arahantship.
Then his fellow bhikkhus asked him, "Friend Cittahattha, why is it that now you are not as you were before?"
“The defilements do not increase! they said jokingly. “Friends, from this day forward, I am incapable of returning to the state of a householder.
When he had thus attained Arahatship, a discussion arose in the Hall of Truth:
“Friends, even though such a necessary condition for Arahatship existed, the Venerable Cittahattha Sāriputta went forth from the religious life six times.”
“Oh, how great is the fault of being an ordinary person! The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, the mind of an ordinary person is light and difficult to restrain;
it goes toward and clings to objects of perception. Once it has clung, it cannot be turned back.”
It is easy to release such a mind; therefore, the taming of such a mind is good. For it is only when tamed that it brings happiness:
"The taming of the mind, which is difficult to restrain, fickle, and falling wherever it pleases, is good; a tamed mind brings happiness."
"Because it is so difficult to restrain, in the past, wise men were unable to abandon it;
through the power of greed, they fell away from the homeless life six times, but on their seventh ordination, having developed jhāna, they subdued that greed.
Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of vegetable sellers and reached the age of discretion;
his name was "Kuddālapaṇḍita" (the Wise One with the Hoe).
Working the soil with a hoe, he planted garlic, bottle-gourds, pumpkins, cucumbers, and so forth, and by selling these, he maintained a humble livelihood. This was his...
Apart from that single spade, he had no other wealth. One day he thought, "What is the use of this household life?

I shall go forth and become a renunciant. Then one day, having placed his spade in a hidden spot and gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, he failed to sever his greed because he kept remembering that spade.

Relying on that blunt hoe, he went forth [into homelessness] and then returned to the world. In this way, for a second and a third time—thus six times—he placed that hoe in a hidden spot, having both gone forth and returned from the life of a recluse.
But on the seventh occasion, he thought: "It is because of this blunt hoe that I have repeatedly returned from the life of a recluse."
Thinking, "Now, having thrown it into the great river, I shall go forth," he went to the riverbank; however,
fearing that if he saw the spot where it had fallen, he might wish to return and retrieve it, he took the hoe by its handle with the strength and power of a nāga,
whirled it three times above his head, closed his eyes, and [threw it] into the middle of the river.
Having hurled it, he let out a lion’s roar three times, saying, “Victory! Victory is mine!
At that moment, the King of Bārāṇasī, having returned from suppressing the border regions, was bathing his head in the river;
adorned with all his ornaments and riding upon the back of an elephant, he heard that sound of the Bodhisattva and thought, “This man says, ‘Victory! Victory is mine!’”
"Who indeed has been conquered by him? Summon him! Having thus summoned him, he asked, "O man, as for me, I have already emerged victorious from battle;
now, having taken the spoils of victory, I am returning. But who has been conquered by you?
The Bodhisatta replied, "Great King, even for one conquering a hundred battles, a thousand battles, or a hundred thousand battles, it is truly difficult to be conquered."
"Because of not having conquered the defilements. But as he was saying, "I, however, am conquering the defilements by subduing greed within myself," he looked at the great river,
attained jhāna with the water-kasiṇa as its object, and, manifesting his supernormal power, sat in the air and,
teaching the Dhamma to the king, spoke this verse:
“That victory is not a good victory which, having been won, is lost again;
that victory indeed is a good victory which, having been won, is never lost.
In this context, “that victory is not a good victory which, having been won, is lost again” refers to [the case where], having defeated an enemy...
A kingdom that has been conquered and acquired is again defeated by those same enemies;
that victory is not called a "well-won" victory. Why? Because it is defeated once more. According to another method: "won" (*jita*) means victory.
A victory attained after fighting with enemies becomes a defeat when those very enemies conquer in turn; that is neither good nor—

It is beautiful. Why? Because there is no further defeat. "That victory is well-won, that victory is truly won, which, once won, is not lost again"—that which is won after crushing an enemy and is not subsequently defeated by them, or that victory once obtained which does not turn back into defeat—that victory is well-won, truly won, beautiful; such is victory.
It is called "good" or "excellent. Why? Because it does not decline again.
Therefore, O Great King, even if you were to conquer the front lines of battle a hundred times, a thousand times, or a hundred thousand times, you would still not be called a "warrior.
For what reason? Because you have not conquered your own defilements (*kilesa*). But he who, even once within himself...
"He who conquers the defilements is the supreme warrior at the head of battle"—saying this, while still seated in the air, he taught the Dhamma to the king with the grace of a Buddha.
Regarding the state of being a supreme warrior in battle here:
"He who, with a thousand [men], conquers a thousand men in battle among humans..."
"And one who should conquer only oneself—he indeed is the supreme warrior.
This sutta is the proof.

While the king was listening to the Dhamma, his defilements were abandoned through the method of abandoning by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*), and his mind [turned] toward the going-forth.
Nami. In the same way, the defilements were abandoned by Rājabala as well.
The king asked the Bodhisatta, "Where will you go now? "I shall enter the Himālaya mountains and go forth into the ascetic life, Great King," he replied.
"In that case, I too shall go forth," and so he departed together with the Bodhisatta, along with his army, brahmins, and householders.
"All the army" means that the entire great multitude of people assembled at that place set out together with the king.

Even the inhabitants of Bārāṇasī, thinking, "It seems our king, having heard the Dhamma teaching of Kuddālapaṇḍita, has turned toward the life of renunciation and has set out with his military forces; what shall we do here? [departed] from the twelve-league [city].
All the inhabitants of the city of Bārāṇasī went forth; the assembly was twelve yojanas in extent.
Taking them with him, the Bodhisatta entered the Himālaya mountains.
At that moment, the seat of Sakka, king of the gods, showed signs of heat. Reflecting on this, he [perceived]: "The wise Kuddāla..."
Having seen that [Kuddālapaṇḍita] had gone forth on the Great Renunciation, [the King] thought, "A great assembly will take place; it is necessary to obtain a dwelling place.
He addressed Vissakamma: "Dear one, Kuddālapaṇḍita has gone forth on the Great Renunciation;
it is necessary to obtain a dwelling place. Go to the region of the Himālayas and, on a level stretch of ground, [construct] a long [hall]..."
"Build an hermitage thirty yojanas in width and fifteen yojanas in length," he said. He replied, "Very well, Your Majesty," and having gone there, he did so.
This is the summary here; the detailed account, however, will be revealed in the *Hatthipāla Jātaka*.
For this [story] and that are indeed one single narrative. And in that hermitage, Vissakamma [constructed] a leaf-hut...
Having cleared away the deer, birds, and non-human beings that made noise, and having caused them to retreat,
he constructed a single-path track leading toward various directions and returned to his own dwelling place. The Wise Kuddāla, taking that assembly with him,
entered the Himālayas, went to the hermitage given by Sakka, and [found] what had been built by Vissakamma.
Having taken the requisites for renunciation, he first went forth himself, and afterwards caused the assembly to go forth as well;
having divided the hermitage grounds, he gave them away. The seven kings abandoned their seven kingdoms.

The hermitage grounds, thirty yojanas in extent, became filled. Having performed the preliminary practice (*parikamma*) on the remaining *kasiṇas* and cultivated the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), the wise Kuddāla [attained perfection].

He explained a meditation subject to the assembly. All of them became attainers of meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), and by developing the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), they were destined for the Brahma-world.
Those, however, who had performed service for them were destined for the world of the gods.
The Teacher said, "Monks, in this way, the mind that is attached through the power of the defilements is difficult to release; once arisen..."
“States of greed are difficult to abandon; even such wise men as these fall into ignorance. Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, he proclaimed the Truths (Saccāni).
At the conclusion of the Truths, some became stream-enterers (sotāpanna), some once-returners (sakadāgāmin), some non-returners (anāgāmin), and some attained arahantship.
The Teacher, having established the connection, identified the Jātaka.
“At that time, King Ānanda was the Buddha’s assembly, while the wise Kuddāla was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Kuddāla Jātaka, the tenth.
The seventh section, the Chapter on Women, is finished.
Its summary verse:
Asāta, Anta, Ḍabhūta, Takkapaṇḍi, Durājāna;
Anabhirati, Mudulakkhaṇa, Ucchaṅga, and Sāketa.
"A poisoned hoe. 8. The Varuṇa Chapter [71] 1.
The Commentary on the Varuṇa Jātaka.
"Those things which ought to have been done before"— this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Elder Tissa,
the son of a householder. It is said that one day, about thirty young men of good family from Sāvatthī, who were mutual friends,
took perfumes, flowers, garments, and other offerings, and surrounded by a great crowd, [set out] thinking, "We shall hear the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma."
Having gone to Jetavana and sat for a short while in the Nāga-maḷaka, the Sāla-maḷaka, and other such places, at the time of evening,
when the Teacher had emerged from the Fragrant Chamber perfumed with sweet scents and proceeded to the Dhamma Hall,

they went to the Dhamma Hall together with their retinue once the Teacher was seated upon the adorned Buddha-seat, and having honored the Teacher with fragrant flowers, [they stood] upon the soles marked with wheels.
Having prostrated at his feet, which were as beautiful as full-blown lotuses, they sat to one side and listened to the Dhamma.
Then it occurred to them: "In whatever way we understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, let us go forth.
When the Tathāgata had emerged from the Dhamma assembly hall, they approached the Tathāgata, paid homage, and requested the going-forth.

They requested [ordination], and the Teacher granted them the going-forth (*pabbajjā*). Having satisfied their preceptors and teachers and received full ordination (*upasampadā*), they lived in the presence of their preceptors and teachers for five years.

Having mastered the two matrices (*mātikā*), understood what is allowable and what is not, and learned the three thanksgiving discourses (*anumodanā*), they sewed and dyed their robes, thinking, "We shall now perform the duty of a recluse."
Having requested permission from their teachers and preceptors, they approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side.
They entreated him, saying, "Venerable Sir, we are weary of the realms of existence and terrified by the fear of birth, aging, sickness, and death;
please teach us a meditation subject for the sake of our liberation from saṃsāra. The Teacher [considered] which of the thirty-eight meditation subjects was suitable for them.
Having selected a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), he taught it to them.

Having received the meditation subject from the Teacher, they paid homage to the Teacher, circumambulated him keeping him to their right, and went to their respective dwellings. There, having looked upon their preceptors and teachers, they took up their bowls and robes and set out, thinking, "We shall practice the duty of a recluse."
Now, among them, there was one bhikkhu named the Elder Kuṭumbikaputtatissa, who was lazy, lacking in energy, and greedy for flavors.
He thought to himself: "I am not able to dwell in the forest, nor to exert myself in striving, nor to sustain myself by wandering for alms;
what is the use of my going? I shall turn back. Thus he [slackened] his energy.
Having dismissed those monks, he followed them for a short distance and then turned back. Those monks, while wandering on tour among the Kosalans, went to a certain frontier village;
depending upon it, they entered the rains retreat in a certain forest region.
Being diligent, striving, and exerting themselves throughout the three months, they brought forth the embryo of insight and caused the earth to resound.
Having attained arahantship and completed the rains retreat, they performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony and thought, "We shall report the qualities we have attained to the Teacher.
Departing from there, they gradually reached Jetavana; having put away their bowls and robes and seen their preceptors and teachers, they went into the presence of the Tathāgata, desiring to see him.
Having paid homage, they sat down. The Teacher [spoke] with them.
He exchanged pleasant greetings with them. Having been thus greeted, they reported to the Tathāgata the qualities they themselves had attained, and the Teacher praised those bhikkhus.

When the Elder Tissa, son of a householder, saw the Teacher speaking of their virtues, he too became desirous of practicing the duty of a recluse. Those bhikkhus, however, said: "Venerable sir, we..."
“Let us go and dwell in that very forest retreat,” they requested of the Teacher. The Teacher consented, saying, “Very well.
They paid homage to the Teacher and went to their respective cells.
Then, shortly after the first watch of the night, the Elder Tissa, son of the householder, exerted himself with excessive energy and with great haste—
While performing his duties as a recluse, during the middle watch of the night, he fell asleep while leaning against a wooden support board;
as he turned over, he fell down and broke his thigh bone, which caused intense pain.
Because those monks were tending to him, they were unable to go [to the Teacher]. Then, when they arrived at the time for attendance, the Teacher asked them:
“Did you not, monks, ask leave yesterday, saying, ‘We shall go tomorrow’? “Yes, venerable sir;

however, our companion, the elder Tissa, son of a householder, while practicing the ascetic’s duty with excessive haste at an improper time, was overcome by sleep, rolled over, and fell down. His thigh bone was broken, and because of that, we—”

“Your journey will not succeed. The Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that he, by his own state of deficient energy, exerts effort with excessive speed at the wrong time and creates an obstacle to your journey;
in the past as well, he created an obstacle to your journey. Having said this, being requested by them, he related the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Gandhāra at Takkasilā, the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher who instructed five hundred young brahmins in their crafts.
One day, those students went into the forest to fetch firewood and gathered some logs.
Among them, one indolent student, seeing a large varuṇa tree, [thought], "This is a dry tree..."
Thinking, "This is it," he spread out his upper garment, lay down, and fell asleep while scratching himself, thinking, "I will lie down for a moment first, and afterwards, having climbed the tree,
I will knock down the wood and take it away. Meanwhile, the other young men, having tied their bundles of wood and set off, struck him on the back with their feet.
Having awakened him, they departed. The young man Kusīta rose, wiped his eyes again and again, and while still drowsy, climbed the Varuṇa tree.
Grasping a branch, he pulled it toward himself and broke it;
as it snapped, the tip struck and pierced his eye. Covering it with one hand, he [took hold] with the other hand...
Having broken off pieces of *allakāra* wood, he descended from the tree, bound the bundle of wood, lifted it up,
and traveling with great speed, he dropped it upon the felled logs.
On that very day, in a village of the countryside, a certain family, thinking, "Tomorrow we shall perform the recitation for the brahmins," [invited] a teacher...
He invited them. The teacher said to the young men, “Sons, we must go to a certain village tomorrow;

however, you will not be able to go without food. Therefore, have rice-gruel cooked there early in the morning, and having gone there, return bringing with you both your own allotted portions and our own share from the bowl.
Early in the morning, they [sent] a maidservant for the purpose of cooking the gruel.
Having raised him up, they said, "Quickly cook us some rice-gruel. While she was gathering firewood, she took some fresh *varuṇa* wood that was standing above;
though she blew on it again and again with her mouth, she was unable to kindle the fire, so she caused the sun to rise.
The young students thought, "It has become too late; we cannot go now," and they went into the presence of their teacher. The teacher—
“Why, dear ones, have you not gone? “Yes, teacher, we did not go. “For what reason?
“A certain lazy youth went with us to the forest for the sake of wood;
he fell asleep at the foot of a *varuṇa* tree, and afterwards, having climbed the tree with speed, caused his eye to be pricked and brought back wet *varuṇa* logs, [while] we—”
“He threw them on top of the wood that had been brought. The cook, taking them for dry wood, was unable to kindle a fire until sunrise.
For this reason, an obstacle to our departure arose.
Having heard the deed committed by the youth, the teacher said, “Such a decline comes about through the actions of blind fools,” and uttered this verse:
“He who wishes to do later what ought to have been done earlier, like one who breaks a branch of the varuṇa tree, will later be filled with remorse.
In this context, “he will later be filled with remorse” refers to any person whatsoever who thinks, “This should have been done earlier; this should be done later.”
"Without first considering what ought to be done beforehand, he performs later those tasks that should have been performed first;
like this young man Varuṇakaṭṭhabhañja, such a foolish person later regrets, grieves, and laments.
Having thus explained this matter to his pupils, the Bodhisatta performed meritorious deeds such as giving and, at the end of his life, passed away according to his karma.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that this man has caused you an obstacle; he did so in the past as well.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and established the connection, he identified the Jātaka:

"The young brahmin who suffered the breaking of his eyes was the monk who suffered the breaking of his thigh; the other young brahmins were the Buddha’s assembly; and the teacher-brahmin was [the Buddha himself]."
"But it was I myself who was he.
The first commentary on the Varuṇa Jātaka is concluded.
[72] 2. The commentary on the Sīlavanāgarāja Jātaka.
"Of the person who is ungrateful"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Veḷuvana concerning Devadatta.
For in the Hall of Truth, the bhikkhus were sitting and discussing: "Friends, Devadatta is ungrateful; he does not recognize the virtues of the Tathāgata.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Bhikkhus, what discussion are you currently seated around?"
Having asked, "Is it indeed by her? and being told so, he said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta is ungrateful;
even in the past he was ungrateful, never once recognizing my virtue. Being requested by them, he related a story of the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born in the Himālaya region in the womb of an elephant.
He was born. Having emerged from his mother’s womb, he was entirely white, resembling a heap of silver;
his eyes were like polished gems, and his five physical excellences (*pasāda*) were clearly manifest.
His face was like red woolen cloth, and his trunk was like a silver wreath adorned with red gold spots. His four feet were as if treated with lacquer.
Thus his physical form became adorned with the ten perfections (pāramīs) and attained the pinnacle of beauty.
Then, when he reached the age of discretion, all the elephants in the Himālayas gathered together and roamed about attending upon him.
While he was thus living in the region of the Himālayas surrounded by a retinue of eighty thousand elephants, he later perceived the faults inherent in the herd.

Having left the community for the sake of physical seclusion, he dwelt all alone in the forest. Because of his virtuous conduct, he was known by the name "Sīlavanāgarāja" (The Virtuous Elephant King).
Now, a certain forest-dweller from Bārāṇasī, having entered the Himālaya mountains in search of provisions for his livelihood, became lost as he was unable to determine the directions.
Terrified by the fear of death, he raised his arms and lamented.

He wandered about. Having heard his powerful lamentation, the Bodhisatta, impelled by compassion with the thought, "I shall release this man from suffering," approached him. Upon seeing him, the man was terrified and fled.
Seeing him fleeing, the Bodhisatta stood right where he was. Seeing the Bodhisatta standing there, the man stopped.
The Bodhisatta came back again; having fled once more, he stood still when the elephant was standing and thought:
"This elephant stands when I am fleeing and comes forward when I am standing; he does not wish me harm, but must surely wish to rouse me from this suffering.
Resolving to be brave, he remained there. The Bodhisatta approached him...
“Why, good man, do you wander about lamenting? he asked. “Master, it is because I am lost, unable to determine the directions, and terrified by the fear of death.
Then the Bodhisatta led him to his own dwelling place, sustained him for several days with various fruits, and said, “Good man, do not be afraid; I shall lead you back to the path of men.”
Thinking, "I will carry him," he had the man sit upon his back and set out toward the path of men.
Then that treacherous man, thinking, "If anyone asks,
I must point it out," remained seated on the Bodhisatta’s back and traveled along, constantly observing the signs of trees and the signs of mountains.
Then the Bodhisatta, having led him out from the forest and placed him on the great road leading to the city of Bārāṇasī, dismissed him, saying, "Go by this path, my good man;
but whether asked or unasked, do not tell anyone of my dwelling place.
Having sent him away, he returned to his own abode. Then that man [proceeded] to Bārāṇasī.
Having gone there and wandered about, he reached the street of ivory-workers.
Seeing the ivory-workers fashioning various ivory objects, he asked, "But sirs, would you take even a living tusk? "Sir, what are you saying?
A living tusk is far more valuable than the tusks of a dead elephant. "In that case, I shall bring you a living tusk."
Taking provisions for his journey and carrying a coarse saw, he went to the place where the Bodhisatta was staying.
Upon seeing him, the Bodhisatta asked, "For what purpose have you come? He replied, "Sir, I am poor and destitute, unable to make a living.
Having requested a piece of your tusk, if you would grant it, I shall take it, go and sell it, and with that—"
“I have come thinking, ‘I shall live by means of his tusks. “Very well, sir;
I will give you the tusks, provided you have a saw for the purpose of cutting them. “I have come, Master, having brought a saw.
“In that case, cut the tusks with the saw, take them, and go,” said the Bodhisatta, who then drew up his legs and sat in the *goṇisinnaka* posture. He [the man] then took both the two front tusks...
He cut them off. The Bodhisatta took those tusks in his trunk and said, "O man, it is not because these tusks are dear or pleasing to me that I give them;

rather, the tusks of omniscient knowledge, which are capable of penetrating all phenomena, are hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands of times more dear to me than these. This gift of tusks is for him."
"May it be for the sake of penetrating all-knowing wisdom. Having thus honored the quest for omniscience, he gave him the pair of tusks.

Taking them and going away, he sold them; when the proceeds from that were exhausted, he went again to the Bodhisatta and said, "Master, the price I obtained by selling your tusks has only served to clear my debt; as for the remaining tusks—"
“Take them,” he said. The Bodhisatta, having consented with “Very well,” had them prepared in the same manner as before and gave him the remaining teeth.
That man sold those as well, and returning again, said, “Master, I am unable to live; give me my original tusks.
The Bodhisatta consented with “Very well” and sat down in the same manner as before. That wicked man [approached] the Great Being...
Trampling the trunk which resembled a silver garland, and mounting his forehead which was like a peak of Mount Kailāsa, he struck both tusks with his heels;
having torn away the flesh and mounted the frontal globes, he used a harsh saw to cut off the root-tusks and departed.
Even as that wicked man was still within the range of the Bodhisatta’s vision, [the earth]—which was two hundred and forty thousand yojanas in thickness—[shook].

Although the solid earth, Sineru, Yugandhara, and the other great mountains are capable of bearing immense weights—even foul-smelling and loathsome things such as excrement and urine—they were, as it were, unable to bear his heap of demerits; thus they split open and gave way.
At that very moment, flames of fire issued forth from the great Avīci hell and [seized] that man who had betrayed his friend, along with his family inheritance.
She took hold of him, wrapping herself around him as if covering him with a blanket.
Thus, at the moment that wicked man entered the earth, the tree deity dwelling in that forest grove said:
"A person who is ungrateful and treacherous toward friends cannot be satisfied even by giving him the sovereignty of a universal monarch," and she [spoke] to the forest...
Having raised his voice, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“For a person who is ungrateful, who always looks for flaws,
even if one were to give him the entire earth, one would never satisfy him.”
In this context, "to one who is ungrateful" means to one who does not recognize the benefit done for oneself. "To a person" (*posassa*) means to a man.
"One who looks for a rift" means one who watches only for a flaw or an opening.

"Even if he were to give the whole earth" means that even if one were to give such a person the entire sovereignty of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), or even the essence of the great earth by turning over this very earth.
"Neither can one please him"—the meaning is that even by acting in such a way, no one would be able to satisfy or gladden [him], for he destroys the merit of what has been done.
Thus that deity, having made the forest resound, taught the Dhamma. The Bodhisatta remained for as long as his lifespan lasted and then departed according to his karma.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta is ungrateful; in the past, too, he was ungrateful.
Having spoken thus, he delivered this Dhamma teaching, established the connection, and identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the person who betrayed his friend was Devadatta; the tree deity was Sāriputta; and I myself was the virtuous Nāga king."
The second [discourse], the Commentary on the Sīlavanāgarāja Jātaka.
[73] 3. The Commentary on the Saccaṅkīra Jātaka:
"They say this is indeed the truth"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning Devadatta’s attempt to bring about his own destruction.

He spoke concerning this. For while the community of monks was seated in the Dhamma Hall, they were discussing Devadatta’s faults, saying, "Friends, Devadatta does not know the virtues of the Teacher; he strives only for his murder.
When the Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what discussion are you sitting here having now?", and they replied, "This very one," [he spoke].
“Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has striven for my death; he strove for it even in the past,” he said, and related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, he had a son named Duṭṭhakumāra, who was cruel, harsh, and like a venomous snake that had been struck;
he would never speak to anyone or strike them unless they had first reviled him or attacked him.
He spoke thus. To his own people and to outsiders alike, he was as unpleasant and terrifying as a speck of dust fallen into the eye or a demon that had come to devour one;
he was loathsome and a cause for alarm. One day, desiring to play in the river, he went to the riverbank with a large retinue.
At that moment, a great cloud arose and the quarters of the sky became dark. He [sent] his slaves and servants...
He said, "Come, my men, take me, lead me to the middle of the river, bathe me, and bring me back.
They led him there and consulted among themselves, saying, "What will the king do for us? Let us kill this wicked man right here!
Saying, "Go away from here, you ill-omened one," they submerged him in the water. Having emerged and stood on the bank, [they asked], "Where is the prince?"
When this was said, they replied, "We do not see the prince; having seen a cloud arise, he must have submerged himself in the water and come forward.
The ministers went into the presence of the king. The king asked, "Where is my son? They replied, "We do not know, Your Majesty.
We came with the understanding that he would have come forward when the cloud arose. The king—
Having caused the gate to be opened, he had them search here and there, saying, "Go to the riverbank and search," yet no one saw the prince.
He too, while being carried away by the river during a rainstorm with blinding darkness, saw a log of wood;
sitting upon it and driven by the fear of death, he went along lamenting. At that time, however, a resident of Bārāṇasī...
A certain merchant, having buried forty crores of wealth on the bank of a river, died; through craving for that wealth, he was reborn as a snake upon the heap of treasure.
Another man, having buried thirty crores in that very same place, was reborn right there as a rat through craving for wealth.
Their dwelling place was flooded by water. Following the path by which the water had entered, they...
Having emerged and gone along cutting through the current, they reached the log of wood upon which the prince was sitting;
each mounting one end and the other the other, they lay down right on the back of the trunk.
Now, on the bank of that very river there was a *simbali* tree, where a young parrot lived. That tree, too, was [submerged] by the water.
With its roots washed away, it fell onto the riverbank; a young parrot, unable to fly away as the rain was falling, went and hid on one side of that very trunk.
Thus those four people proceeded, being swept along together.
At that time, the Bodhisatta had been reborn in the kingdom of Kāsi into a family of northern brahmins and had reached maturity.
Having gone forth into the ascetic life of a seer, he lived having constructed a leaf-hut at a bend in a river.
While walking up and down at the hour of midnight, he heard the sound of that prince’s intense lamentation and thought:
"While an ascetic such as myself, endowed with loving-kindness and compassion, is looking on, it is improper for this man to die; I shall lift him out of the water."
“I shall grant him the gift of life. Having comforted him, saying, “Do not fear, do not fear,” he went along cutting through the current of the water;

seizing that log by one end and pulling it, the elephant-strong and powerful man reached the shore in a single stroke, lifted the prince up, and set him down on the bank. Seeing those snakes and other creatures as well, [he...]
Having lifted him up and brought him to the hermitage, he lit a fire;
thinking, "These are weaker," he first steamed the bodies of the snakes and others, and afterwards steamed the body of the prince, making him healthy as well.
Even when giving food, he first gave it to the snakes and others, and afterwards offered various fruits to him. The prince said, "This..."
The false ascetic harbored resentment toward the Bodhisatta, thinking, "Disregarding me, he shows honor to mere animals.

Then, after a few days had passed and all of them had regained their strength and the river's flood had subsided, the snake paid homage to the ascetic and said, "Venerable sir, you have done me a great service; however, I am not poor."
"I have buried forty crores of gold coins in such-and-such a place;
if you have need of wealth, I am able to give all this money to you. Come to that spot and call out, 'Dīgha!
Having said this, he departed. The rat likewise invited the ascetic, saying, "Standing in such-and-such a place, call out, 'Undūra!'"
Having said, "You may summon him," he departed. But the young parrot, having paid homage to the ascetic, said, "Venerable sir, I have no wealth;
however, if you have need of red rice, my dwelling place is called such-and-such.
Go there and summon me by crying 'Parrot! and I shall inform my kinsmen and [provide] red rice filling many wagons."
Having said, "I am able to have it brought and give it to you," he departed.
But the other, the betrayer of friends, thought, "It is improper to depart without saying something regarding the excellence of the Dhamma; I shall kill him when he comes into my presence.
He then said, "Venerable sir, please come when I am established in the kingdom; I shall attend upon you with the four requisites."
Having spoken thus, he departed. He went and before long was established in his kingdom.
The Bodhisatta, thinking, "I shall first test them," went to the presence of the snake; standing not far away, he called out, "Dīgha!
At the mere word, the snake emerged, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, and said, "Venerable sir, in this..."
"Take all those forty crores of gold that are in the treasury and bring them out," he said. The Bodhisatta replied, "So be it;
I shall know when the need arises," and having dismissed him, he went to the mouse and made a sound.
The mouse did exactly the same. The Bodhisatta dismissed him as well and went to the crow, saying, "Crow!"

He called out. He too, descending from the top of the tree with a single word, paid homage to the Bodhisatta and asked, "Venerable sir, shall I go to my kinsmen and have them bring for you the *sayañjāta* rice from the Himalayan region?
The Bodhisatta replied, "I shall know when the need arises," and having sent him back as well, he thought, "Now I shall examine the king."
Having gone and stayed in the royal park, on the following day he prepared his proper appearance and entered the city according to the practice of alms-gathering.
At that moment, King Mittadubbhi, mounted upon the back of a magnificent, adorned state elephant and accompanied by a great retinue, was performing a circumambulation of the city.
Seeing the Bodhisatta from afar, he thought, "This is that fraudulent ascetic..."
“Having eaten in my presence, he has come desiring to dwell here;

as long as he does not proclaim his own merits performed for me in the midst of the assembly, I shall have his head cut off! Thus he looked toward his men. When they asked, “What shall we do, Your Majesty?
he said, “I think this fraudulent ascetic has come wishing to ask something of me; [be on guard against] this ill-omened ascetic.”

“Without allowing him to see me, seize this man, bind his hands behind his back, strike him at every crossroads, drive him out of the city, and having cut off his head at the place of execution, impale his body on a stake! he said.
They agreed, saying, “Very well,” and went; they bound the Great Being, who was innocent, and [struck him] at every crossroads.
As they began to lead him away to the place of execution, the Bodhisatta, instead of crying out "Mother! Father!
at every spot where he was struck, remained unperturbed and spoke this verse:
"Truly, as some men here have said:"
"A piece of wood that has floated away is better than some men here.
Regarding this, "they say truly indeed" means they speak thus without falsehood. "Some men here" refers to certain wise persons here.
"A piece of wood that has floated away" refers to dry timber being carried along by a river.
"It is better and more excellent that it be brought ashore and placed on dry land.
If those men were speaking thus, would they indeed be speaking the truth? Why so? Because it serves as a benefit for the purpose of cooking rice porridge, boiled rice, and the like;
