for the purpose of warming those suffering from the cold; and for the purpose of warding off other dangers. But not so, O man, does a certain person [serve such a purpose].
"But that treacherous friend, the ungrateful wicked man, who was being carried away by the flood—having been seized by the hand and rescued—is not at all better off.
For indeed, having rescued this wicked man, he brought this suffering upon himself.
Thus, at each spot where he had struck [the tree], he spoke this verse.
Having heard that, the wise men there said, "But, O renunciant, what benefit have you done for our king?

The Bodhisatta, having related those events, said, "In this way, while rescuing him from the great flood, I have brought suffering upon myself; indeed, I have not acted according to the words of the ancient sages."
"Having recollected this, I speak thus," he said. Hearing that, the kshatriyas, brahmins, and other city-dwellers cried out, "This king is a betrayer of friends!
He does not recognize even a fraction of the virtue of one who bestowed his very life upon him;

how can there be any prosperity for us depending on such a man? Seize him! Thus incensed, they rose up from all sides and, with blows from spears, javelins, stones, clubs, and other weapons, [assailed him].
Having had him killed while still on the back of the elephant, they seized him by the feet, dragged him away, and cast him onto the bank of the moat;
then, having consecrated the Bodhisatta, they established him in the kingdom.
While he was ruling the kingdom according to Dhamma, one day, desiring to capture the snakes and other creatures, he set out with a great retinue.
Having gone to the snake’s dwelling place, he called out, “Dīgha! The snake came forward, paid homage, and said, “Lord, take this wealth of yours.
The king entrusted forty crores of gold to his ministers and went to the rat’s presence;
calling out, “Undūra! the rat also came, paid homage, and presented thirty crores of wealth.
The king entrusted him also to his ministers, went to the parrot’s dwelling place, and called out, “Parrot!
He too came, prostrated at the king’s feet, and asked, “What is it, my lord? Shall I fetch the rice? The king said, “You shall fetch it when there is need for rice;
come, let us go. Having had those three people taken along with seventy million pieces of gold, he departed from the city.
Having gone to the great terrace of the excellent palace and secured his wealth, he had a golden tube made for the snake’s dwelling,
a crystal cave for the mouse, and a golden cage for the parrot; and for the food of the snake and the parrot,
he caused sweet rice-pudding to be served daily on a golden platter, while for the mouse, he provided fragrant *śāli* rice.

He also performed meritorious deeds such as giving. Thus, those four people lived together in harmony and mutual affection for as long as they lived, and at the end of their lives, they departed according to their respective kamma.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has striven to kill me; in the past, too, he strove to do so."
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, and having established the connection, he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the wicked king was Devadatta; the snake was Sāriputta; the rat was Moggallāna; the bird was Ānanda;
and the righteous king who later attained the throne was none other than I myself."
The third [story], the commentary on the *Saccaṅkara-jātaka*.
4. The commentary on the *Rukkhadhamma-jātaka*:
"Excellent, many kinsmen!"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning his own kinsmen who were engaged in a water-quarrel.
Knowing that a great destruction was imminent, he traveled through the air, sat cross-legged above the Rohiṇī River, and emitted blue rays.
Having stirred his kinsmen to a sense of urgency, he descended from the sky and sat on the riverbank;
there, concerning that quarrel, he spoke. This is the summary here; the detailed account, however, will be revealed in the Kuṇāla Jātaka. At that time...
Then the Teacher addressed his kinsmen: “Great kings, you are my kinsmen; it is fitting for kinsmen to be harmonious and to live in mutual affection.
For when there is harmony among kinsmen, enemies find no opportunity; let alone human beings, even insentient trees ought to attain harmony. For in the past, in a region of the Himalayas...”

A great wind struck the sāla grove; however, because that sāla grove was interconnected with one another by means of trees, shrubs, thickets, and creepers, it was unable to topple even a single tree and passed right over their very tops.
But a great tree standing in an open space, though possessed of branches and foliage, was uprooted because it was not connected to other trees.
Having said, "He cast it upon the ground; for this reason, it is fitting that you also remain in harmony and in mutual affection," he related a story of the past when requested by them.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, Vessavaṇa the Great King first appeared.
When Sakka passed away, he appointed another as Vessavaṇa. After this change of Vessavaṇa, the newly born Vessavaṇa sent forth a message:
"Let the deities of trees, shrubs, thickets, and creepers take up their celestial mansions (vimānas) in whatever places they each prefer.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in a certain sāla grove in the Himalayan region.
He said to his kinsmen, "When you take your palaces, do not take those standing on trees in the courtyards;
instead, take the palaces that stand surrounding the palace I have taken in this sāla grove.
Thereupon, the wise deities who followed the Bodhisatta's word took the palaces standing around the Bodhisatta’s palace.
But the foolish deities thought, "What use have we for forest palaces? We shall take our palaces on the paths frequented by humans—at the gates of villages, market towns, and royal capitals.
For deities who dwell depending upon villages and such places attain the highest gain and the highest glory.
Thus they took their palaces among the great trees that had grown in open spaces along the human pathways.

Then one day a great storm of wind and rain arose. Because of the extreme force of the wind, even the preeminent forest trees with firm roots fell down, their branches and boughs shattered along with their very roots.
However, when that wind reached the grove of sal trees standing there joined together by one another, though it struck here and there, it was unable to topple even a single tree.
The deities, whose celestial mansions were destroyed, were left without refuge.
Taking the children by the hands, they went to the Himālayas and related their own situation to the deities of the Sāl forest.
Those deities, in turn, informed the Bodhisatta that they had come in such a manner.
The Bodhisatta said, "Those who do not heed the words of the wise end up in such a state of utter helplessness," and while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“Excellent, O many kinsmen! Even trees born in the forest, and even a vast forest tree, are carried away by the wind when they stand alone.
In this context, “many kinsmen” refers to four or more, even up to a hundred thousand.
In this way, many kinsmen dwelling in dependence upon one another are "good"—meaning they are beautiful, praiseworthy, and unassailable by others.
Let alone trees born in the forest; even trees grown in the wilderness, when standing in great numbers through mutual support, are indeed good.
For even among trees, the state of having supporting conditions is to be found.

It is fitting. "The wind carries away that which stands alone" means that the wind, blowing in its various directions such as the east and so forth, carries away even a great forest tree—a massive tree endowed with branches and spreading boughs—that stands all by itself in an open space;
the meaning is that it uproots and fells it. Having explained this reason, the Bodhisatta passed away according to his karma when his life-span was exhausted.
The Teacher also, having delivered this Dhamma teaching—"Even so, Great King, it is right first to obtain harmony among kinsmen;
being united and in mutual affection, dwell only in pleasant companionship"—and having established the connection, he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the deities were the Buddha’s assembly, but the wise deity was I myself."
The Fourth: The Exposition of the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka.
[75] 5. The Exposition of the Maccha Jātaka:
"O Pajjunna, do not thunder! This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the rain he himself had caused to fall.
He related [the story]. It is said that once, in the kingdom of Kosala, the rain did not fall;
the crops withered, and in various places the tanks, lotus ponds, and lakes dried up. Even the water in the Jetavana lotus pond near the gatehouse of Jetavana was cut off.
Fish and turtles, having entered the thick mud and lying there, were [attacked] by crows, owls, and other birds with beaks like the points of spikes.
Having crushed them with their snouts and repeatedly dragged them out, they devour them as they writhed.
Seeing that calamity of the fish and turtles, the Teacher’s heart was stirred by great compassion, and thinking,
"Today it is fitting for me to cause the rain to fall," he attended to his physical needs at dawn and, at the time for the alms-round—
Having observed this, surrounded by the great community of bhikkhus, he entered Sāvatthī for alms with the grace of a Buddha.
After his meal, having returned from the alms round, while going from Sāvatthī to the monastery, he stood at the steps of the Jetavana lotus pond and addressed the Elder Ānanda:
"Ānanda, bring me my bathing robe; [we shall bathe] in the Jetavana lotus pond."
“I shall bathe. “But, Bhante, has not the water in the Jetavana lotus pond run dry, with only mud remaining?
“Ānanda, the power of a Buddha is indeed great; bring me my bathing robe. The Elder brought it and gave it to him.
The Teacher, having dressed in one part of the bathing robe and covered his body with the other part, [proceeded].
Thinking, "I shall bathe in the lotus pond of Jeta’s Grove," he stood upon the steps. At that very moment, the stone seat of Sakka, made of pale sandalwood, showed signs of heat.

Wondering, "What could this be? he reflected and, understanding the cause, summoned the divine king Vassavalāhaka and said, "Dear son, the Teacher stands at the main steps, thinking, 'I shall bathe in the lotus pond of Jeta’s Grove.'"
"Quickly, having made the entire kingdom of Kosala into a single cloud, cause it to rain!
He accepted this, saying "Very well," put on one cloud-cloth as an undergarment and another as an upper robe, and while singing the song of the clouds, he leapt toward the eastern world-system.
In the region of the eastern direction, a single mass of cloud arose the size of a threshing floor, and then a hundredfold mass.

Becoming a canopy of a thousand [clouds], emitting flashes of lightning and raining down like water-jars placed with their mouths turned downward, it overwhelmed the entire kingdom of Kosala as if with a great flood.
Raining in an unbroken stream, the deity filled the lotus pond of Jetavana in a mere moment;
the water stood reaching up to the main staircase.
The Teacher, having bathed in the lotus pond, put on his bright red inner robe, fastened his waistband,
and draped the great robe of the Sugata over one shoulder; surrounded by the community of monks, he went to the courtyard of the Fragrant Chamber, sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared there,
and when the community of monks had performed their duties, he rose, stood upon the jeweled stair-tread, and [addressed] the community of monks.

Having given his exhortation and dismissed them, he entered the fragrant Perfumed Chamber, lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture, and in the evening time, to the bhikkhus assembled in the Dhamma Hall, said:
"Behold, friends, the perfection of the Ten-Powered One’s patience, loving-kindness, and compassion; even while various crops were withering and various reservoirs of water were drying up..."
Out of compassion for the fish, turtles, and sea-monsters who were undergoing great suffering, and thinking,
"I shall liberate the multitude from their pain," he put on his water-cloak, stood at the main staircase of the Jetavana lotus pond,

and caused the rain to fall until it was as if the entire kingdom of Kosala were being submerged by a great flood in an instant; thus, having liberated the multitude from both physical and mental suffering, [he departed].
While this conversation was taking place, [the Buddha] emerged from the Fragrant Chamber, came to the Dhamma Hall, and asked, "Bhikkhus, about what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "About this very one," he said, "Bhikkhus, it is not only now that the Tathāgata causes rain to fall when the great multitude is suffering; formerly, while in the animal realm..."
"Having been reborn, she indeed caused it to rain even during the time of King Maccha," he said, and then related a story of the past:

"In the past, in this very Kingdom of Kosala, in this very city of Sāvatthī, in this very place where the Jetavana lotus pond now stands, there was a mountain cave surrounded by a thicket of creepers. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a fish."
Surrounded by a multitude of fish, he dwelt there. Just as it is now, even so at that time, rain did not fall in that kingdom;
the crops of the people withered, the water in the irrigation ponds, caves, and other places was cut off, and the fish and turtles entered the thick mud.
In this cave as well, the fish and turtles [entered] the thick mud.
Having entered, they hid themselves in various places. Crows and other birds pecked at them with their beaks, drove them out, and ate them.
The Bodhisatta, seeing that calamity befalling his kinsmen, thought: "There is no one else capable of delivering them from this suffering except me;
I shall perform an act of truth (*saccakiriya*) to make the rain-god send down rain, and thus save my relatives from the suffering of death."

Thinking, "I shall release them," he pushed aside the black-colored mud on both sides, emerged, and—being a great fish with the color of the heartwood of an *añjana* tree—opened his eyes, which resembled well-polished red coral gems, looked up at the sky, and addressed the divine king Pajjunna:
"O Pajjunna, I am suffering because of my kinsmen; while I, who am virtuous, am thus distressed..."
"Why did you not cause the rain to fall? he asked. [The boy] replied: "There is no fish, even the size of a grain of rice, that I have ever eaten since being born among my own kind;
nor has any other living being ever been deprived of life by me.
By this truth, may you cause the rain to fall and deliver my circle of kinsmen from suffering. Having said this, he [addressed] the servant-boy...
As if commanding the divine king Pajjunna, he addressed him with this verse:
“Thou rain-cloud, thunder forth! Destroy the hoard of the crow!
Subject the crow to sorrow, and release me from my grief.”
In this context, "Pajjunna" refers to the rain-cloud;
however, he is here addressing the divine king Vassavalāhaka, who has received that name by virtue of his clouds. His intention is as follows:
a deity does not shine even when raining if he does not thunder or flash lightning; therefore, you, thundering and flashing lightning...

"Causing them to pour out, make it rain. "Destroy the treasure of the crows": when crows enter the mud and peck with their beaks at fish staying there, they pull them out and eat them; therefore, those fish within the mud are called "treasure" (*nidhi*).
By making the god rain, you should destroy that treasure of the flock of crows by concealing it with water. [Make] the crow [suffer] grief.
"Cook them! [He said: "The flock of crows, finding no fish in this cave filled with water, will grieve;
therefore, filling this cave for that flock of crows, cook them for the sake of their grief—that is, cause the god to rain so that there may be comfort for the fish instead of grief.
Act in such a way that they reach the state of grief characterized by internal brooding."
"And release me and my kinsmen from sorrow"—here the word *ca* has the sense of inclusion, meaning "release both me and all my relatives from this sorrow of death.

Thus, having addressed Pajjunna as if commanding a servant or attendant, the Bodhisatta caused a great rain to fall throughout the entire kingdom of Kosala; having liberated the great multitude from the suffering of death, he passed away at the end of his life according to his karma.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata causes the rain to fall; even when he was reborn in the womb of a fish in the past, he caused it to fall.
Having spoken thus, he delivered this Dhamma teaching, established the connection, and identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the shoals of fish were the assembly of the Buddha; Pajjunna the king of the gods was Ānanda; and as for the king of the fish, that was I myself."
The fifth: The Commentary on the Maccha-jātaka.
[76] 6. The Commentary on the Asaṅkiya-jātaka.
"I am not suspected in the village"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a lay follower from Sāvatthī.

He spoke concerning this. It is said that a certain noble disciple who had attained the stage of stream-entry (sotāpanna), while traveling along a road with a certain caravan leader for some business, halted the wagons at a certain forest spot.
When the camp was pitched, he was walking up and down at the foot of a tree not far from the caravan leader. Then, having observed the time for his own [passing], he...
Five hundred thieves, thinking, "We shall plunder the military camp," surrounded that place with bows, clubs, and other weapons in their hands.
The lay follower was walking his meditation walk (caṅkama) right there. When the thieves saw him, they thought, "Surely this man must be the protector of the camp;
we shall plunder it when he has fallen asleep. Unable to overwhelm him, they remained right where they were.
They stood there. That lay follower also remained standing, pacing back and forth during the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch.
When dawn broke, the thieves, finding no opportunity, abandoned the stones, clubs, and other weapons they had seized and fled.
The lay follower, having completed his task, returned again to Sāvatthī and approached the Teacher.
“Venerable sir, those who protect themselves protect others,” he asked. “Yes, lay follower, one who protects oneself also protects others;
one who protects others also protects oneself. He said, “How well this was spoken by the Blessed One!
Once, while traveling with a certain caravan leader, I was walking back and forth at the foot of a tree.”

"I shall protect myself," he said, and thus protected the entire body of teachings. The Teacher said, "Upāsaka, even in the past, the wise, while protecting themselves, protected others," and being requested by him, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family.

Having reached maturity and seen the peril in sensual pleasures, he went forth into the ascetic life of a seer (*isipabbajjā*). While dwelling in the Himalayas, he came to the inhabited lands for the sake of partaking of salt and sour food;
wandering on a journey through the countryside, he set out on the road together with a certain caravan leader.
When the caravan had encamped in a certain forest region, he remained not far from the caravan, passing his time in the bliss of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) in a certain place.
He stood walking back and forth at the foot of a tree. Then five hundred thieves, thinking, "We shall plunder that caravan when it has finished its evening meal," arrived and surrounded it.
Seeing the ascetic, they thought, "If he sees us, he will inform those staying with the caravan; we shall plunder it while he has fallen asleep."
They remained right there. The ascetic continued to walk his meditation path throughout the entire night.
Finding no opportunity, the thieves discarded the clubs and stones they had seized and called out to the caravan dwellers, saying, "Sirs, caravan dwellers!
Had this ascetic who walks at the foot of the tree not been here today, you all would have suffered a great plunder."
"Having paid great honor to the ascetic," they said, and then they departed.
When night had turned to dawn, they saw the clubs, stones, and other implements discarded by the bandits;
terrified, they went into the presence of the Bodhisatta, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable sir, were the thieves seen by you? "Yes, friends, they were seen," he replied.

“Venerable sir, having seen so many robbers, did fear or trepidation not arise in you? The Bodhisatta replied, “Friends, fear arises for one who possesses wealth; but I am without wealth, so why should I be afraid?
For whether I dwell in the village or in the forest, there is no fear or trepidation for me,” and he taught them the Dhamma.
Declaring this, he spoke this verse:
“I am free from fear in the village; in the forest there is no danger for me.
I have ascended the straight path through loving-kindness and compassion.”
In this context, "I am unsuspected in the village" means: one who is connected with or established in suspicion is "suspected"; one who is not so is "unsuspected.
This indicates that even while living in a village, because he is not established in suspicion, he is unsuspected—fearless and free from apprehension.
"In the forest" means in a place distinct from both the village and its vicinity. "Having ascended the straight path" refers to [the path] of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*).

He says: "By means of loving-kindness and compassion consisting of the third and fourth jhānas, I have ascended the straight path leading to the Brahma-world, which is free from crookedness of body and so forth.

Alternatively, having shown: "By virtue of perfectly pure morality, I have ascended the straight path to the deva-world, which is free from crookedness of body, speech, and mind," he further shows that because he is established in loving-kindness and compassion, he has also ascended the straight path to the Brahma-world.

He also shows that he has ascended. For those whose jhāna is not lost are destined for the Brahma-world with absolute certainty; thus, loving-kindness, compassion, and so forth are called the "straight paths.

Having thus taught the Dhamma with this verse, the Bodhisatta was honored and worshipped by those people with joyful hearts; and having cultivated the four divine abodes (brahmavihāras) throughout his life, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and established the connection, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the caravan leaders were the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples, and the ascetic was none other than myself.
This concludes the sixth narrative, the Commentary on the Asaṅkiya Jātaka.
[77] 7. The Commentary on the Mahāsupina Jātaka.
"The gourds are sinking"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning sixteen great dreams.
One day, it is said, the Great King of Kosala, having fallen asleep at night, saw sixteen great dreams during the last watch;
terrified and trembling, he woke up and thought, "What will become of me now that these dreams have been seen?"
Terrified by the fear of death, he spent the night sitting right there on the back of his bed.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, the brahmin chaplains approached him and asked, "Did you sleep well, Great King?
"How could I have slept well, teachers? This morning at the break of day, I saw sixteen great dreams."
“Ever since I saw them, I have been overcome with fear. “Speak, O Great King; having heard it, we shall know,” he said.
When the king had related the dream he had seen, he asked, “What indeed will come of this for me because of what they have seen?
The brahmins shook their hands. When asked, “Why do you shake your hands? they replied, “You are cruel...”
“Great King, they are dreams. “What will be their outcome?
“One of these three obstacles: an obstacle to sovereignty, an obstacle to life, or an obstacle to wealth. “Are they remediable or irremediable?
“Granted, these dreams are so extremely harsh that they are irremediable; nevertheless, we shall make them remediable.”
“What will our state of being trained avail us if we are unable to make them turn back? [The brahmins asked:
“But what must be done to make them turn back? [The king replied: “We shall perform a sacrifice with every fourfold set, Great King.
The king, terrified and trembling, said: “In that case, teachers, let my life be in your hands; quickly bring me safety!”
"Perform [the sacrifice]," he said. The brahmins, delighted and joyful, thinking, "We shall receive much wealth;
we shall have much food and drink brought," reassured the king, saying, "Do not worry, Great King.
Having departed from the royal palace, they constructed a sacrificial enclosure outside the city, brought many herds of four-footed animals to the sacrificial posts, and gathered flocks of birds.
“This and that ought to be obtained,” they kept saying as they moved back and forth.

Then Queen Mallikā, having understood the reason for this, approached the King and asked, “Why is it, Great King, that the brahmins keep moving back and forth? “You are fortunate, my lady; [I shall tell you] in your ear.”
“You do not know that a venomous snake is wandering about. “What is this, Great King? “I have seen such bad dreams, O Brahmins.

Having said, ‘One of three calamities is foreseen,’ they keep circulating again and again, saying, ‘We shall perform a sacrifice to ward them off. But what, Great King, [is there] in the world with its devas...”
“Has the foremost brahmin been asked about the interpretation of the dream? “But who, Bhaddā, is the foremost brahmin in the world with its devas?
“You do not know the Supreme Person in the world with its devas—the All-Knowing One, the Pure One, the Stainless Great Brahmin.
For that Blessed One would know the meaning of the dream; go, Great King, and ask him.”
“Very well, O Queen,” the King replied. He went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down.
The Teacher, emitting a sweet voice, said: “Why have you come so early, Great King?
“Venerable Sir, at the time of dawn, having seen sixteen great dreams, I was terrified and reported them to the brahmins. The brahmins—”
“O Great King, dreams are harsh; for the sake of averting them, we shall perform a sacrifice with every fourfold set,” they said, and prepared the sacrifice.
Many living beings were terrified by the fear of death. And you are the Supreme Person in the world together with its devas;
from the past, the future, and the present, there is no object of knowledge that does not come within the range of the opening of your wisdom.
“Tell me, Blessed One, the fulfillment of these dreams. “It is even so, Great King.
In this world with its devas, there is no one else besides me who is capable of knowing the meaning or the fulfillment of these dreams.
I shall tell you; however, you should relate the dreams exactly as they appeared to you.”
“Excellent, venerable sir,” the king said, speaking according to his own established method:
“The bull, the trees, the cows, and the cow;
the horse, the bronze vessel, the female jackal, and the water-pot.”
And the lotus pond and the white sandalwood:
“Gourds sink, stones float; female frogs swallow black snakes;
golden birds surround a crow; and timid wolves flee in fear of rams.”
Having set forth this outline, he spoke:
(1) "Venerable sir, first of all, I had such a dream:

four black bulls, the color of collyrium, came from the four directions into the royal courtyard saying, 'We shall fight,' while the great multitude gathered, thinking, 'We shall watch the bull-fight.'"
Having assembled, they displayed the manner of fighting, roared, and thundered, but without actually fighting, they retreated.
This was the first dream I saw; what will be its fruition? "Great King, the fruition of this will occur neither in your time nor in mine;
rather, in the future, it will be for unrighteous and wretched kings and for unrighteous men."
At a time when the world was undergoing transformation, when the wholesome had declined and the unwholesome had increased, at a time of the world’s decay, the rain-god did not rain properly;
the bases of the clouds were cut off, the crops withered, and there would be famine.
Clouds, as if desiring to rain, arose from the four quarters for women who were spreading out [clothes] in the sun.

When the rice and other grains were being brought inside for fear of spoilage, and while men carrying spades and baskets had gone out to bind the straw-fences, I displayed the appearance of rain, thundered, and flashed forth lightning;
thus, like bulls that do not fight but flee without shedding their strength, they will escape.
This is its ripening. But as for you, no obstacle shall arise on account of it.
“There is none; this dream was seen concerning the future, but the brahmins spoke based on their own livelihood.
Having thus explained the fulfillment of the dream, the Teacher said, “Tell the second one, Great King.
(2) “Venerable Sir, for the second time I saw this: small trees and shrubs, having split the earth...”
They flower and bear fruit without even extending a *vidatthi* or a *ratana*. This was the second thing I saw;
what is its result? "Great King, the result of this too will occur at a time when the world is declining and the lifespan of human beings is short.
For in the future, sentient beings will possess intense passion, and even while they have not yet reached maturity—"
"The maidens, having gone to other men, will become subject to their seasons and pregnant, and they will increase with sons and daughters.
For their state of being subject to the seasons will be like the flower of small trees, and their sons and daughters will be like the fruit.
You have no cause for fear on this account either; tell me the third thing, Great King."
(3) "Venerable sir, I saw cows drinking the milk of their calves born on that very day. This is my third dream;
what will be its result? "The result of this too will come about in the future, at a time when people have lost the practice of honoring their elders.
For in the future, beings will feel no shame toward their mothers and fathers, or toward their mothers-in-law and fathers-in-law."

Without providing for them, while managing the household themselves, they may wish to give even a mere measure of food and clothing to their elders, yet if they do not wish to give, they will not give.
Thus the elders will live dependent on their children, being without a protector and lacking self-mastery, like great cows drinking the milk of calves born that very day. On account of this as well—
“They have no fear; tell me the fourth thing, Great King.
“Venerable sir, I saw people yoking young, untrained bullocks to the yoke in succession instead of great oxen that were full-grown and possessed of perfect proportions.
Being unable to pull the yoke, they stood there having abandoned it, while the carts [remained stuck].”
They did not turn back. "This is my fourth dream; what will be its fruition?
"The fruition of this too will come about only in the future, during the time of unrighteous kings.
For in the future, unrighteous and stingy kings will not grant honor to wise ministers who are skilled in tradition and capable of accomplishing their tasks. In the Hall of Justice..."
They will not appoint wise, experienced ministers skilled in legal procedure to positions of judicial authority;
instead, they will grant honors to those who are the opposite—those who are very young—and appoint such individuals to the judicial offices.
Being ignorant of both royal affairs and what is appropriate or inappropriate, they will be unable to uphold that honor.
They will not be able to complete their royal duties. Being unable to do so, they will abandon the burden of their work.
Even the elder and wise ministers, though capable of completing their tasks, will receive no honor; thinking, "What use have we for these? We are outsiders;
the young men of the inner circle will know [how to handle it]," they will not perform the duties that have arisen. Thus...

"In every respect, there will only be decline for those kings; it will be like the time when young oxen unfit to bear the burden are yoked to the yoke, and unlike the time when great draft-oxen capable of bearing the burden are yoked in succession.
You have no cause for fear on this account either. Tell me the fifth thing, Great King."
(5) “Venerable sir, I saw a horse with two heads; they give fodder to it from both sides, and it eats with both mouths. This is my fifth dream; what is its result?
“Even this will find its fulfillment only in a future time of unrighteous kings. For in the future, unrighteous, foolish kings will, in an unrighteous manner...”
“They will establish themselves as judges over frivolous people;

those fools, being indifferent toward both evil and merit, will sit in the court and, while handing down judgments, take bribes from the hands of both the plaintiff and the defendant and eat them like a horse eating barley from two mouths.
You have no danger arising from this source either; speak the sixth, Great King.”

(6) "Venerable Sir, a great multitude of people swept a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and offered it to an old jackal, saying, 'Empty your bladder here. I saw him emptying his bladder there.
This is my sixth dream; what will be its result? "The result of this one, too, will come to pass only in the future."

For in the future, unrighteous kings of low birth, out of suspicion toward sons of noble family who are well-born, will not grant them honor, but will grant it only to those of low lineage. Thus, great families will become impoverished, while base families will become powerful.
And those men of noble family, unable to make a living, will say, "We shall live by depending on these [base ones]," and thus [they will serve] the low-born.

"They will give their daughters in marriage; thus, for those daughters of noble family, cohabitation with men of low birth will be like a golden bowl being used as a chamber-pot by an old jackal. You have no cause for fear on this account either. Tell me the seventh.
"Venerable Sir, a man repeatedly winds a rope and places it at his feet; by means of that [rope], he [pulls] the stool upon which he sits..."
"I saw this: while he was unaware, a hungry female jackal lying beneath him was devouring him.
This is my seventh dream; what will be its fruition? "The fruition of this too will occur only in the future.
For in the future, women will become lustful for men, lustful for liquor, lustful for ornaments, lustful for the streets, and lustful for food; they will be immoral."
Those women of evil conduct, having performed labors such as farming and tending cattle for their husbands,
would drink liquor with their paramours using the wealth they had accumulated with great difficulty and toil; wearing garlands, perfumes, and ointments,
they would disregard even urgent duties within the house and keep watch for their paramours even from above the enclosure walls or through openings in the house.

"They will even grind the seeds suitable for sowing in their own fields and, having prepared rice gruel, boiled rice, hard foods, and so forth, they will plunder you—just like a hungry female jackal lying beneath a bench, circling again and again over the rope placed at her master's feet.
You have no cause for fear on this account; tell me the eighth."
(8) "Venerable sir, at the king’s gate I saw a single large jar filled with water standing surrounded by many empty jars.
The four castes, bringing water from the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions in their jars, were filling that very jar again and again;
yet as soon as it was filled, the water would overflow and run away, and they [continued to pour]."
"Again and again they pour water right there, yet even when looking at the empty jars, none are to be found.
This is my eighth dream; what will be its fruition? "The fruition of this too will occur only in the future.
For in the future, the world will decline; the kingdom will become devoid of essence, and kings will become destitute and wretched."
Whosoever shall become the lord, there shall be in his treasury a hundred thousand kahāpaṇas;
all these people, being thus impoverished, shall make their own subjects perform labor for them.
Oppressed, the people, abandoning their own work, shall plant, guard, reap, and thresh grain—both early and late—for the sake of the kings alone.
Plowing the fields of sugarcane, constructing machines, operating those machines, boiling molasses and other products,
and establishing flower and fruit orchards, they will bring back the rice and other crops produced here and there to fill the king’s granaries alone;
they will not even have to look into their own empty storehouses at home.
“Without looking at an empty jar, one will find that a full jar is exactly like filling [it].
You have no fear on this account; tell me the ninth.
(9) “Venerable Sir, there is a deep lotus pond, covered with five-colored lotuses, which has a landing-place on every side.”
I saw it. Bipeds and quadrupeds had descended from all sides and were drinking the water there.
In its deep center, the water was turbid; but in the areas near the banks, where bipeds and quadrupeds stepped upon it, the water was clear, serene, and undisturbed.
This is what I saw. This is my ninth dream; what will be its fruition?
The result of this too will come about only in the future. For in the future, kings will be unrighteous;
following wrong courses through the influence of desire and other passions, they will exercise their rule.

They will not administer justice according to the Dhamma, but will be greedy for bribes and covetous of wealth. Among the inhabitants of the kingdom, they will have no patience, loving-kindness, or compassion.
There will be no harsh or cruel people who, like stalks of sugarcane being crushed in a sugarcane mill, oppress the people, exacting various kinds of taxes and seizing their wealth.

Oppressed by these taxes, the people—unable to give anything further—will abandon their villages, towns, and other settlements to go and make their homes in the border regions; thus, the central provinces will become empty.
“The border region is densely populated, just like the water in the middle of a lotus pond being turbid while the periphery is clear.
You have no danger arising from this source; tell me the tenth.
(10) “Venerable sir, I saw rice being cooked in a single pot that was not yet cooked; having investigated it, I thought, ‘It is uncooked.’”
"It was as if it had been set aside after being divided, cooking in three different ways:
in one part it was overcooked, in another it was undercooked, and in another it was well-cooked. This is my tenth dream; what will be its fruition?
"The fruition of this too will occur only in the future. For in the future, kings will become unrighteous; while they are unrighteous..."
“Even the brahmins and householders associated with the king, as well as those from the towns and the countryside—in short, all human beings including ascetics and brahmins—will become unrighteous.

Consequently, their guardian deities, the deities who receive offerings, the tree deities, and the deities dwelling in the sky—all such deities will likewise become unrighteous. And of these unrighteous kings...”
In your kingdom, violent and harsh winds will blow; they will shake the celestial palaces situated in the sky.
When those are shaken, the deities will become angry and will not grant rain. Even if it does rain, it will not fall all at once over the entire kingdom;
and even when it rains, it will not be beneficial for the work of plowing or sowing everywhere.
It will not rain. Just as it will not rain in the kingdom, so too in the province, in the village, in a single irrigation pond, or in a single lake—it will not rain all at once.
Raining on the upper part of the pond, it will not rain on the lower part; raining on the lower part, it will not rain on the upper part.
In one area the crop will be destroyed by excessive rain, while in another it will be destroyed by the lack of rain.
"It will come together; when it rains properly at one time, it will succeed.
Thus, in the kingdom of a single king, there will be three kinds of crops, like rice cooked in a single pot. You have no fear on this account either; speak the eleventh.
(11) "Venerable Sir, I saw people selling the finest sandalwood, worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], for rotten sour gruel. This—"
"This is my eleventh dream; what will be its fruition? "The fruition of this too will occur only in the future, when my dispensation is declining.
For in the future, there will be many shameless monks who are greedy for requisites;
they will preach the Dharma that I have taught by crushing out my own teaching on greed for requisites for the sake of others' robes and the other four requisites."

Being infatuated with material requisites and remaining on the side of non-renunciation, they will not be able to teach while directing their minds toward Nibbāna; rather, they will teach only in this way:
"Having heard the perfection of the words and phrases and the sweet sound [of the teaching], one will give costly robes and other requisites.
Others, sitting in the middle of streets, at crossroads, at royal gates, and so forth, [will teach].
They will teach by relying even on coins, half-coins, quarters, māsakas, rūpakas, and so forth.
Thus, they will sell and teach the Dhamma—which I have taught as being worth the value of Nibbāna—for the sake of the four requisites and for the sake of coins, half-coins, and the like;
they are like those who sell the finest sandalwood, worth a hundred thousand, for rotten tallow.
“There will be [others]. You have no fear on account of this either; tell me the twelfth.
(12) “Venerable Sir, I saw empty gourds sinking in the water. What is the ripening of this?
“Even for this, the ripening will occur only when, in the future, the world has turned toward a time of unrighteous kings. For at that time, kings [will favor] those of noble birth...”
They will not grant honor to sons of noble family, but will grant it only to those of low birth;

they themselves will become masters, while others will be poor. Even in the presence of the king, at the palace gate, in the presence of ministers, and in the courts of justice, the speech of those of low birth—who are like empty gourds—will remain as if submerged, motionless, and firmly established. This shall be so even in assemblies of the Saṅgha.

"In matters of formal acts of the Saṅgha and the community, as well as in decisions regarding alms-bowls, robes, and monastic courtyards, only the talk of immoral and wicked persons will lead to deliverance, not that of modest bhikkhus;
thus, in every respect, it will be like the time when a hollow gourd sinks. You have no fear on this account either—speak the thirteenth."
(13) "Venerable Sir, I saw very large solid rocks, the size of gabled houses, floating upon the water like ships.
What is the karmic result of this? "The result of this will likewise occur at a similar time.
For then, unrighteous kings will bestow honor upon those of low birth; they will become lords while those of noble birth fall into poverty. Among them, no one will show respect."

They will do so only among others. Whether in the presence of the king, or in the presence of ministers, or at a place of legal judgment, the speech of those noble sons—who are skilled in adjudication and resemble solid rocks—will not sink in and find its footing.
While they are speaking, the others will merely mock them, wondering, "What are these people saying? This will happen even in assemblies of bhikkhus.

"In the places described, they will not regard even the well-behaved bhikkhus as worthy of respect, nor will their discourse be established after being thoroughly investigated; it will be like the time when stones float.
You have no danger arising from this cause either; speak the fourteenth."

(14) "Venerable Sir, I saw small female frogs, about the size of madhuka flowers, swiftly pursuing large black snakes, cutting them like lotus stalks one after another, and swallowing them after devouring their flesh.
What will be the result of this? "The result of this will also come to pass in the future, when this world is declining. At that time..."
For humans are by nature prone to intense passion; following after their defilements, they will come under the power of their very young wives.
Even the slaves, laborers, and others in the household, as well as the cattle, buffaloes, and so forth, and all the gold and silver, will be dependent upon them alone.
[They will ask: "Where is such-and-such gold or silver, or this collection of clothing and other goods?"
Having said, “Let it be here or there; what business is it of yours?

You have become one who wishes to know whether I have anything in my house or not,” they will revile him in various ways, strike him with the weapons of their mouths, bring him under their own control like slaves and servants, and exercise their sovereignty over him. Thus, [they treat those] who are the size of *madhuka* flowers...
"It will be like the time when a young frog swallows a venomous black snake. You have no fear on this account;
tell me the fifteenth.
(15) "Venerable Sir, regarding the crow that frequents the village and possesses ten unrighteous qualities, because of its golden color..."
“I saw golden royal swans, known by the name ‘Suvaṇṇā,’ flying about; what will be the result of this?

“The result of this too will come to pass only during a future period of weak kings. For in the future, kings will be unskilled in the arts of elephants and so forth, and lacking confidence in battle;
fearing the ruin of their own kingdoms, they [will seek out] those of their own kind...”
Without granting authority to sons of noble family, they will bestow it upon their own foot-attendants, bathers, barbers, and the like;
and when sons of noble family endowed with birth and lineage fail to find a footing in the royal court and become unable to maintain a livelihood,
they will wander about attending upon those of low birth and ignoble origin who hold positions of power— just as a crow [is surpassed] by golden royal swans.
"It will be as if you are surrounded by them. You have no cause for fear on this account; speak the sixteenth.
(16) "Venerable Sir, formerly it was the leopards that ate the goats. But I saw leopards chasing the goats and devouring them with a 'murumuṛu' sound.
Then other trembling crabs, seeing the goats from afar, became terrified and seized with fear."
"Fleeing out of fear of the sheep, they entered thickets and dense groves and hid themselves; thus did I see them.
What will be the result of this? "The result of this too will come about only in a future time when there are unrighteous kings.
For then, those of low birth who are favorites of the king will become powerful, while those of noble birth will be unknown and destitute. Those royal favorites [will treat] the king..."
Having caused their own claims to be accepted, they become powerful in places of legal adjudication and the like;
they then bring charges against those of noble lineage regarding fields, lands, and so forth inherited through family tradition, asserting, "These belong to us.

When these [nobles] come to the places of adjudication and the like to dispute, saying, "These are not yours, they are ours," [the claimants] have them beaten with rattan canes and the like, and seize them by the neck.
Having dragged them out, they will threaten them, saying: "You do not know your own measure; you quarrel with us!
Now we shall report this to the king and have your hands, feet, and so forth cut off!
Out of fear of them, they will hand over their own property, saying, "Take these yourselves," and then enter their own homes.
They will lie down in fear. Even wicked bhikkhus will harass the well-behaved bhikkhus according to their pleasure;
those well-behaved bhikkhus, finding no refuge, will enter the forest and hide in dense thickets.
Thus, for those sons of noble birth and well-behaved bhikkhus who are oppressed by those of low birth and by wicked bhikkhus...
It will be like a time of flight for sheep and wild beasts out of fear; even on account of this, there is no danger for you.
For this dream, too, was seen concerning the future alone. However, the brahmins did not speak out of affection for you because of the excellence of the Dhamma;
rather, they spoke out of a desire for material gain, seeking their livelihood with the thought, "We shall receive much wealth."
"Relying upon [this], they spoke.
Thus the Teacher, having explained the fulfillment of the sixteen great dreams, said: "Great King, it is not only you who have seen these dreams now;
ancient kings also saw them. The brahmins likewise [interpreted] them in this very same way."
"Having seized these dreams, they cast them before the sacrificial altar; then, having gone according to the method given by the wise men, they questioned the Bodhisatta.
Even the ancient wise men, when explaining these dreams to them, spoke in this very same manner.
Having said this, being requested by him, he related the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of northern brahmins.

Upon reaching maturity, he went forth as a seer, and having attained both the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he dwelt in the Himalayan region sporting in the play of jhāna.
At that time, in Benares, Brahmadatta likewise had these dreams in this very manner.
Having seen this, he questioned the brahmins. The brahmins then began to perform the sacrifice in that very manner.
Among them, a wise and competent young student who was a pupil of the family priest said to his teacher: "Teacher, we have been made to learn the three Vedas by you;
is there not, among them, a single passage stating that one should not kill another for the sake of performing a rite for safety?"
“Dear son, by this means much wealth will accrue to us; however, you seem to think only of protecting the king’s wealth.
The young brahmin thought, “In that case, teacher, you do your work; what shall I do in your presence?
and wandering about, he went to the king’s park.
On that very day, the Bodhisatta, having understood the reason for this, thought, "Today, when I have gone to the path of men, there will be the release of the great multitude from their bonds.
Traveling through the air, he descended into the park and sat upon the auspicious stone slab like a golden statue.
The young brahmin approached the Bodhisatta, paid homage, sat down to one side, and exchanged friendly greetings with him.
The Bodhisatta also exchanged pleasant greetings with him and asked, "Young man, does the king rule according to the Dhamma?
"Venerable sir, the king is indeed righteous; however, the brahmins cause him to leap over the proper ford.
The king, having seen sixteen dreams, reported them to the brahmins. The brahmins said, "We shall perform a sacrifice."
“[The dream] has been undertaken. Venerable sir, is it not fitting that you inform the king—‘This indeed is the outcome of these dreams’—and thus release your great multitude from fear?
“Māṇava, we do not know the king, nor does the king know us.
However, if he were to come here and ask, we would tell him. The Māṇava…
“Venerable sir, I shall bring him; please sit for a moment while you await my return,” he said, having thus obtained the Bodhisatta’s consent.

He then went into the presence of the king and said, “Great King, a sky-walking ascetic has descended into your park and is calling for you, saying, ‘I shall tell you the fulfillment of the dreams you have seen.’”
Having heard his words, the king immediately went to the park with a large retinue.
After paying homage to the ascetic, he sat to one side and asked: "Venerable sir, you say that you know the outcome of the dreams I have seen?
"Yes, Great King. "Then please tell me. "I shall tell you, Great King, regarding the dreams as they were seen..."
“Teach me,” [he said]. “Very well, venerable sir,” the king replied:
“The bull, the tree, the cow, and the ox;
The horse, the bronze vessel, the female jackal, and the jar.”
And the lotus pond and the yellow sandalwood:
“Gourds sink, stones float; female frogs swallow black snakes;
golden birds surround a crow; and timid wolves flee in fear of rams.”
Having spoken thus, he related the dream exactly according to the method explained by King Pasenadi.
The Bodhisatta, having now explained the detailed fulfillment of those dreams according to the method taught by the Teacher, at the conclusion spoke this himself:
"Inversion prevails; it does not exist here."
In this regard, O Great King, this is the fulfillment of these dreams.
As for that sacrificial rite which is performed for the purpose of counteracting them, it is said to proceed by way of perversion, to proceed erroneously, and to proceed through distortion.
For what reason? Because the fulfillment of these occurs at a time when the world is undergoing a revolution, and when there is no [proper] cause.
It will be a cause at the time of grasping, but not a cause at the time of discarding;

it will be real at the time of grasping what is unreal, but unreal at the time of abandoning what is real; it will exist during the period when the shameless are prevalent and the modest have declined.
But as for the phrase "it does not exist here," this refers to the present time, during the current human generation, whether in your time or mine.
"There is no fulfillment of these things; therefore, the sacrificial ritual performed for their sake proceeds by way of perversion—enough with that!
You have no fear or trepidation arising from this cause.
Having thus reassured the king, the Great Man released the great multitude from their bonds, stood once more in the air, and gave the king further instruction.

Having established him in the five precepts, he taught the Dhamma, saying, "From this day forward, Great King, do not join with the brahmins to perform animal sacrifices," and then departed through the air for his own dwelling place.
The king, abiding by his advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms and passed away according to his karma.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "You have no fear on account of the dream; let the sacrifice proceed.
Having thus allowed the sacrifice to go forward and granted the gift of life to the great multitude, he connected the present context to the past and identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, King Ānanda was the king, the young brahmin was Sāriputta, and the ascetic was none other than myself."

When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, the compilers of the collection, having incorporated the three phrases beginning with “Like a bull” into the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), composed the four phrases beginning with “Like a gourd” into a single verse and included them in the Pāḷi of the Ekakanipāta.
This concludes the seventh commentary, the Mahāsupinajātakavaṇṇanā.
8. Illisajātakavaṇṇanā (The Commentary on the Illisa Jātaka)
"Both are lame"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the merchant Macchariya-Kosiya.
It is said that not far from the city of Rājagaha there was a market town named Sakkara;
there lived a merchant named Macchariya-Kosiya, possessing a fortune of eight hundred million. He would not give even a drop of oil on the tip of a blade of grass to others.

He gives it away, but does not enjoy it himself. Thus, that wealth of his serves neither the purpose of his children, wife, and others, nor that of recluses and brahmins; like a lotus pond possessed by a rākṣasa, it remains unused.
One day, at the time of dawn, the Teacher emerged from the attainment of great compassion and [surveyed] the entire world-system.
Looking for those among his kinsmen who were ready to be enlightened, he saw that the merchant and his wife, who lived forty-five yojanas away,
possessed the necessary potential (*upanissaya*) for the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti*). On the previous day, however,
having gone to the royal palace to attend upon the king and having performed his duties as a courtier, he was returning when he encountered a man from the countryside who was hungry and famished.
Seeing him eating a bowlful of *kummāsa* and *kapallapūva*, he conceived a longing for them;
returning to his own home, he thought: "If I say, 'I wish to eat *kapallapūva*,' many will want to eat with me, and thus my store of rice, ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth will be exhausted."
“They will go away; I shall not tell anyone,” thinking thus, he wandered about enduring his craving.
As time passed, he became pale and yellowish, and his body became covered with visible veins.
Then, unable to endure the craving any longer, he entered a hut, approached a bed, and lay down. Even in that state, out of fear of losing his wealth, he said nothing to anyone.
Then his wife approached him, massaged his back, and asked, "What is it, my lord, that makes you unwell?
"I have nothing that makes me unwell," he replied. "Is it perhaps that the king is angry with you? "The king is not angry with me either.
"Then has something unpleasant been done to you by your sons or daughters, or by your slaves, laborers, and so forth?"
“There is nothing like that either. “But do you have craving for anything?
Even when this was said, he remained silent and lay down, saying nothing out of fear of losing his wealth. Then his wife said to him, “Speak, master; what is it you crave?
As if swallowing back his words, he replied, “I have one craving. “What is it you crave, master? she asked.
“I wish to eat a *kapallapūva*. “Then why did you not say so before? Are you poor?
Now I shall bake enough *kapallapūvas* for all the inhabitants of Sakkāra village.
“What use have I for them? They will eat after doing their own work. “In that case, I shall bake enough for those living on one street. “I know that.”
“You have great wealth. “In that case, I shall cook enough for everyone in this entire household.
“I know your great ambition. “In that case, I shall cook enough for you and your wife and children alone.
“But what use have you for them? “In that case, I shall cook enough for both you and me.”
“I am cooking it. “What will you do with it? “In that case, I shall cook enough for you alone. “Many people expect what is being cooked in this place;

therefore, leave aside all the whole grains, take the broken grains, the hearth, the potsherds, and so forth, and taking a small amount of milk, ghee, honey, and molasses, [go] to the seventh floor...”
“Having ascended to the upper floor of the palace, I shall sit there alone and eat.
She replied, “Very well,” and having had what was to be taken gathered, she ascended the palace, dismissed the female servants, and summoned the merchant.
Starting from the beginning, he closed the doors and fitted bolts as small as needle-eyes at all the entrances.
Having ascended to the seventh floor, he sat there after closing the door.
His wife, for her part, lit a fire on the hearth, placed a pan upon it, and began to bake cakes.
Then, early in the morning, the Teacher addressed the Elder Mahāmoggallāna: "Moggallāna, this [is the situation] in the city of Rājagaha..."
Not far away, in the town of Sakkara, the merchant Macchariya-Kosiya, fearing that others might see him,
was having pan-cakes baked in a seven-storied palace, thinking, "I shall eat them alone. Go there, subdue that merchant, strip him of his stinginess,
and cause both husband and wife to take the cakes, milk, ghee, honey, molasses, and other provisions.
"Bring Jetavana by your own power. Today, together with five hundred bhikkhus, I shall sit right here in the monastery;

we shall perform the meal-offering with these very cakes. The Elder, having accepted the Teacher’s word with "Very well, Bhante," went at that very moment to that town by the power of his psychic potency and stood properly dressed at the lion-window door of the palace.
Well-protected, he stood there like a gem-image suspended in the sky.
As soon as the great merchant saw the Elder, the flesh of his heart trembled.

Thinking, "It was out of fear of just such a person that I came to this place, and yet here he is, having arrived and standing at the window," and seeing no way to seize him, [he turned] toward the fire.
Fuming with anger like salt thrown into a wound, he said, “Ascetic, what will you gain by standing in the air?
Even if you were to walk back and forth, displaying footprints in the trackless sky, you would gain nothing. The Elder walked to and fro at that very spot.
The merchant said, “What will you gain by walking? [Even if you were to sit] cross-legged in the air...”
"Even if you sit down, you will certainly not obtain it," he said. The Elder sat down, folding his legs crosswise in the *pallaṅka* posture.
Then [the other] said to him, "What will you obtain by sitting? Even if you come and stand at the threshold of the window, you will not obtain it.
Then the Elder stood at the threshold. Then [the other] said to him, "What will you obtain by standing at the threshold? Even if you smoke [incense], you will certainly not obtain it."
The Elder emitted smoke, and the entire palace became filled with smoke; it was as if the merchant’s eyes were being pierced by needles.
Fearing that his house might burn down, he did not say to him, "Even if you set fire to it, you shall not escape," but thought instead, "This ascetic is very persistent;
he will not leave until he has obtained what he seeks. I shall have one cake given to him. [He said this to] his wife.
He said, "Bhadde, bake a single small cake, give it to the ascetic, and send him away.
She put only a little flour into a shallow pan; it became a large cake, filling the entire pan and rising up.
Seeing this, the merchant thought, "You must have taken a great deal of flour," and he himself took a small amount with his finger.
Taking some dough, he threw it [into the oven], and the cake became larger than the previous one. In this way, whatever he baked, each one became increasingly large.
Becoming weary, he said to his wife, "My dear, give me one of these cakes.
As she was taking one from the stack, they all stuck together as one solid mass. She [reported this] to the merchant.
He said, "Master, all the cakes are stuck together; I cannot separate them.
"I will do it," he replied, but he too was unable to do so. Both men, grasping the edges and pulling, were still unable to separate them.
Even as he continued striving with the cakes, sweat broke out from his body and his thirst was quenched.
Then he said to his wife, "My dear, I have no need for the cakes; give them all to this monk along with the basket.
She took the basket, approached the elder, and gave all the cakes to him.
The elder taught the Dhamma to both of them, spoke of the virtues of the Three Jewels, and [taught] regarding giving and the rest, saying: "There is what is given; there is what is sacrificed."
The fruit appeared in the sky like the full moon.
Hearing this, the merchant, with a clear and confident heart, said, "Venerable sir, please come, sit upon this couch, and partake of the cakes.
The Elder replied, "Great merchant, the Sammasambuddha [has already declared], 'I shall eat the cakes,' together with five hundred bhikkhus..."
“Sitting together in the monastery, if it pleases you, have the merchant’s wife bring some cakes, milk, and other provisions;
we shall go into the presence of the Teacher,” he said. “But, venerable sir, where is the Teacher now?
“Fifty-four yojanas from here, at the Great Monastery of Jetavana. “Venerable sir, without letting the time pass by—”
"How shall we travel such a distance? "Great merchant, if it pleases you, I will carry you by the power of my own psychic potency (*iddhibala*).
The top of the staircase in your palace shall remain in its original place, but the bottom of the staircase shall be at the gatehouse of Jetavana;
it will take no more time than it takes to descend from the upper palace to the lower one."
“I will lead you to Jetavana. He replied, “Very well, venerable sir.
The Elder made the top of the staircase remain right there and resolved, “Let the base of the staircase be at the gatehouse of Jetavana,” and it became exactly so.
Thus, the Elder [arrived] even sooner than the time when the merchant and the merchant’s wife descended from the upper palace.
He brought them to the Jeta Grove. Both of them approached the Teacher, paid homage, and announced the time.
The Teacher entered the refectory and sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared for him, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
The great merchant offered water of welcome to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and the merchant’s wife [offered it] to the Tathāgata.
He placed the cakes upon the alms-bowls. The Teacher took only as much as was necessary for his own sustenance, and the five hundred bhikkhus likewise took only enough for themselves.
The merchant continued on his way, giving milk, ghee, honey, molasses, sugar, and other provisions.
The Teacher, together with the five hundred bhikkhus, finished the meal. The great merchant, along with his wife, [provided] as much as they required.
As they ate, the end of the cakes could not be seen; even when given to the monks and the scavengers throughout the entire monastery, no limit was reached.
They reported to the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, the cakes do not reach exhaustion.
He said, "In that case, discard them at the gateway of the Jeta Grove. Then, not far from the gateway, they [discarded them].
They discarded it on a mountain slope. Even today, that place is known as “Kapallapūvapabbhāra” (the Slope of the Cake Pans).
The great merchant, together with his wife, approached the Blessed One and stood to one side. The Blessed One gave a discourse of thanksgiving.
At the conclusion of the thanksgiving, both of them were established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and [they paid homage] to the Teacher.
Having paid homage at the gatehouse and ascended the stairs, they established themselves in their own palaces.
From that time forth, the Great Merchant distributed eighty koṭis of wealth solely for the sake of the Buddha’s dispensation.
On the following day, after the Perfectly Enlightened One had wandered for alms in Sāvatthī and returned to Jetavana, [he addressed] the bhikkhus...

Having given the Sugata’s exhortation and entered the fragrant chamber to dwell in seclusion, at the time of evening, the monks assembled in the Dhamma Hall said: "Behold, friends, the power of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna!
Without violating the merchant Macchariya’s faith and without violating his wealth, he has, in a mere moment, tamed him and rendered him free from stinginess, and had him take up cakes."
Having brought him to Jeta’s Grove and placed him before the Teacher, he established him in the fruit of stream-entry.
"Oh, how great is the power of this Elder! they said, sitting there as they spoke in praise of the Elder's virtues.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now? When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Monks, by one who tames a family..."
"A monk should approach a family like a bee gathering pollen from a flower—without causing them distress or fatigue—and thus make known the virtues of the Buddha.
Having said this, he praised the Elder:
"Just as a bee, without harming the color or fragrance of the flower..."
"Taking the essence, it departs; thus should a sage wander in the village.
Having spoken this verse from the *Dhammapada*, and in order to further manifest the Elder’s virtue, [the Buddha] said:

"Monks, it was not only now that Moggallāna subdued the merchant Macchariya; in the past as well, having subdued him, he made him understand the connection between action and its fruit," and then he related the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, there lived in Benares a merchant named Illisa, possessing a fortune of eight hundred million.
He was possessed of human defects: he was lame, crooked, and had uneven eyes; he was faithless, lacking conviction, and miserly.
He gave nothing to others, nor did he enjoy anything himself. [He was like] a lotus pond inhabited by a rākṣasa.
His house became one of poverty. However, for seven generations back, his parents had been givers and masters of charity.

Having attained the position of a wealthy merchant, he destroyed his family lineage; he burned down the hall of giving and, having beaten and driven away the supplicants, he established himself solely in the accumulation of wealth.
Thus, one day, having gone to attend upon the king and returning to his own home, he saw a countryman exhausted from the road carrying a jar of liquor.

Seeing him sit on a bench, filling his mouthful after mouthful of sour liquor with pickled fish as an accompaniment, and drinking it, the prince, desiring to drink the liquor himself, thought: "If I am to drink this liquor..."
“When I drink, many will desire to drink as well; thus my wealth will be exhausted.

Enduring that craving, he wandered about, but as time passed, being unable to endure it any longer, his body became pale like bleached cotton and his limbs grew covered with scales. Then one day, having entered a cave—
Having embraced his couch, he lay down. His wife approached him, massaged his back, and asked, "What is it that makes you uncomfortable, my lord?
Everything is to be understood according to the sequence already explained below.
When she said, "In that case, I shall brew enough liquor for you alone," he replied, "When liquor is being brewed in the house, many..."
“They expect [wine] back; even if one were to have it brought from the market, it would not be possible to drink it while sitting here.
Having given a mere māsaka coin, he had a wine-jar brought from the market and had a servant take hold of it.
Then, departing from the city and going to the riverbank, he entered a grove near the main road, had the wine-jar set down, and said, “Go now.”
Having had the servant sit at a distance and filled the vessel, he began to drink the liquor.
Meanwhile, his father, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, was reborn in the world of the gods as Sakka.
At that moment, reflecting, "Is my supreme generosity still proceeding, or has it ceased?", he perceived its cessation.
Having seen that [the son] had destroyed his family lineage, burned down the hall of giving, driven away the supplicants, and established himself in a state of stinginess;
and having seen that out of fear—thinking, "I shall have to give to others"—he had entered the forest thicket and was drinking liquor all alone, [the father thought]:
"I shall go, agitate him, subdue him, and make him understand the connection between action and its fruit."
Thinking, "Having caused [him] to give alms, I shall make him worthy of rebirth in the world of the gods," he descended to the human realm.
Having fashioned for himself a physical form resembling that of the merchant Illisa—one who was lame, withered, and possessed of uneven eyes—he entered the city of Bārāṇasī.
Standing at the gate of the king’s palace, he had it announced that he had arrived; when told, "Enter," he went inside.
Having entered and paid homage to the king, he stood before him. The king said, "What is it, Great Merchant?
Why have you come at such an unusual hour? "Indeed, Your Majesty, I have come; there is eighty million in wealth in my house, and may Your Majesty have it brought and fill your own treasury.
"Enough, Great Merchant; there is more wealth in our palace than in your wealth."
“If, O King, you have no business of your own, I shall take as much wealth as you desire and give it as alms.
“Give it, Great Merchant,” he replied. Saying, “Very well, Your Majesty,” he paid homage to the king and departed.
He went to the house of the merchant Illisa, surrounded by all his attendants; there was not a single person capable of recognizing him, thinking, “This is not Illisa.”
Thus, having entered the house and stood at the threshold, he summoned the doorkeeper and said,
"If anyone else who resembles me comes and enters, saying 'This is my house,' you must strike him on the back and drive him out.
Having spoken thus, he ascended the palace, sat upon a magnificent throne, and summoned the merchant’s wife with a smile.

Having shown [the food], he said, "Bhadde, let us give alms. Upon hearing those words, the merchant’s wife, his sons and daughters, and the slaves and laborers said, "For so long a time there was not even the thought to give alms;
but today, having drunk liquor and become soft-hearted, he must have become desirous of giving. Then the merchant’s wife—
“Give it as you please, Master,” he replied. Thereupon, he summoned the drum-beater and said, “Have the drum beaten throughout the entire city, proclaiming:
‘Let those who require gold, silver, jewels, pearls, and so forth, go to the house of the merchant Illisa.
He did exactly so. The great multitude gathered at the door of the house, taking baskets, bags, and other containers. Then Sakka...
Having caused the chamber filled with the seven treasures to be opened, he said, "I give this to you; take as much as you desire and depart.
The great multitude brought out the wealth, made it into a heap upon the great floor, filled their brought vessels, and departed.
A certain person from the countryside yoked the oxen of the merchant Illisa to his own chariot and [departed] with the seven treasures.
Having filled [the chariot] and departed from the city, he set out upon the great highway. Driving the chariot not far from that grove, he said:
"Live for a hundred years, Master Illisa the merchant! By depending on you, it has now become possible for me to live my life without performing labor.
The chariot is yours alone; the oxen are yours alone; the seven treasures in the house are yours alone. Not even...
"Given by my mother, not by my father; obtained through her support, my lord," he said, going along while speaking in praise of the merchant's virtues.
Hearing that sound, he was terrified and thought, "He is mentioning my name and saying this and that;
has the King perhaps given my wealth to the world? Emerging from the thicket, he [saw] the oxen and...
Recognizing the chariot, he said, "Hey, Ceṭaka! These oxen are mine; this chariot is mine! and went forward to seize the oxen by their nose-ropes.
The householder, alighting from the chariot, cried out, "Hey, you wicked servant!
The great merchant Illisa is giving alms to the entire city; what have you become? and lunging at him, he struck him on the shoulder like a falling thunderbolt.
Having struck him, he took the chariot and departed. He rose up again, trembling, wiped away the dust again and again, and ran with speed to seize the chariot.

The householder descended from the chariot, seized him by the hair, bent him over, beat him with blows of his palm, grabbed him by the neck, threw him toward the path he had come, and departed. At that point, his intoxication from the strong drink [subsided].
He was struck and, trembling, hurried to the gate of his residence. Seeing the great crowd departing with the wealth, he cried out, "Ho!

What is this? Is the King having my wealth plundered? As he ran here and there seizing people, each person he caught would strike him and hurl him right down at his own feet. Overcome by pain, he began to enter his house.
The gatekeepers said, "Ho there, wicked householder! Where are you going? and having beaten him with bamboo splints and seized him by the neck, they cast him out.
He thought, "Now that the King has been set aside, I have no other refuge," and went into the presence of the King, saying, "Your Majesty, you are causing my house to be plundered.
[The King replied: "I am not having the merchant plundered; is it not you yourself who..."
Having arrived, he had a drum beaten through the city, saying, "If you do not take it, I shall give my own wealth as a gift," and thus he gave the gift.
"I will not come into your presence, O King; do you not know my stinginess?
I would not give even a drop of oil on the tip of a blade of grass to anyone. As for one who gives a gift...
“Summon him and investigate, Your Majesty. The king summoned Sakka; neither the king nor his ministers could discern the difference between the two men.
The merchant Macchariya said, “Your Majesty, who is this merchant, and who am I? “We do not recognize [the distinction];
is there anyone who can identify you? “My wife, Your Majesty,” he replied.
Having summoned his wife, they asked her, "Who is your husband? She stood right beside Sakka and said, "This one.
They summoned their sons and daughters, as well as their slaves and laborers, and questioned them; all of them likewise stood beside Sakka.
Then the merchant thought, "I have a boil on my head, hidden by my hair; however, the barber..."
“Whoever knows him, I shall summon him. He replied, “Your Majesty, the barber knows me;
summon him. At that time, the Bodhisatta was his barber. The king summoned him and asked, “Do you know Illisa the merchant?
“I shall know him by looking at his head, Your Majesty. “In that case, look at the heads of both,” he said.
At that moment, Sakka caused a boil to appear on his head.
The Bodhisatta, looking at the heads of both, saw the boils and said, "Great King, there is indeed a boil on the heads of both;
I am not able to perceive any difference between them," and he spoke this verse:
“Both are lame, both have withered hands, both have squinting eyes;
pustules have grown on both of them—I do not see Illisa.
In this context, “both” means two people. “Lame” means having crippled feet. “Withered hands” means having crippled hands. “Squinting eyes” means—
"Visamakkhimaṇḍalā" means squint-eyed. "Piḷakā" means that on the very same spot of the head, both had grown pustules of identical shape.
"'I do not see'—I do not see which one among these is named Illisa;
I do not know the nature of Illisa even for one of them," he said.
Having heard the Bodhisatta’s words, the merchant, trembling and unable to regain his composure due to the grief over his wealth, fell down right there.
At that moment, Sakka stood in the sky with great Sakkan-like splendor, saying, "Great King, I am not Illisa; I am Sakka.
They wiped Illisa’s face and sprinkled him with water; he then rose up.
Having paid homage to Sakka, the king of the gods, he stood there. Then Sakka said to him: "Illisa, this wealth belongs to me, not to you.
For I am your father and you are my son. By performing meritorious deeds such as giving, I attained the status of Sakka;
but you, having cut off my lineage, have become one who does not give, remaining established in stinginess regarding the gift-halls."
