Having burned [the alms-hall] and driven out the beggars, he established only the wealth itself. You neither enjoy it yourself nor give it to others;
it remains as if possessed by a demon. If you restore my hall of giving and provide alms, that would be well. If you do not, I shall cause all your wealth to vanish and, with this—
“With my thunderbolt, I shall sever your head and bring about the end of your life!
Terrified by the fear of death, the merchant Illisa gave his promise, saying, “From this day forward, I shall give alms.
Having received his promise, Sakka, while remaining seated in the air, taught him the Dhamma, established him in the precepts, and returned to his own abode.
They too, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, became destined for heaven.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Moggallāna has tamed the merchant Macchariya; in the past, he was tamed by him as well.
Having spoken thus, he delivered this Dhamma teaching, established the connection, and identified the Jātaka.
“At that time, Illisa was the merchant Macchariya, Sakka the king of the gods was Mahāmoggallāna, King Ānanda was [the king],
and the barber was none other than myself.
This concludes the eighth commentary, the Illisajātakavaṇṇanā.
[79] 9. The Commentary on the Kharassara Jātaka:
"Since the cattle have been plundered and slain... This was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain minister.
It is said that a certain minister of the King of Kosala, having gained the king's favor, received royal tribute from a frontier village.
Having joined together with the bandits, he said, "I will enter the forest taking people with me;

you should plunder the village and give half of it to me. Having assembled the people early in the morning and gone to the forest, when the bandits had arrived, slaughtered the cows, eaten the meat, plundered the village, and departed, [the king] was surrounded by a great crowd at the time of evening.
He arrived. Before long, that deed of his became public knowledge. People informed the king.
The king summoned him, established his guilt, and having punished him with a fitting reprimand, dispatched another village overseer.
Then, going to Jetavana, he reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "Great King, it is not only now that this man..."
"Having such virtue, he was indeed of such virtue even in the past. Having said this, when requested by him, [the Buddha] related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, he gave a border village to a certain minister.
Everything else was exactly as before. At that time, however, the Bodhisatta, traveling through the border regions on business, [arrived] there.
He made his dwelling in that village. When the village headman was approaching in the evening, accompanied by a great retinue with drums being beaten, [the monk] thought:
"This wicked village headman has conspired with thieves to plunder the village;
now that the thieves have fled and entered the wilderness, he is acting as if perfectly calm while the drums are being beaten."
Having said, "He is coming," he spoke this verse:
"Since the cows have been stolen and slaughtered, the houses burnt down, and the people led away,
then has come the son of a woman whose sons were slain, beating a loud-sounding drum."
In this context, "when" (*yataḥ*) means *yadā* (at which time). "Plundered and slain" (*viluttā ca hatā ca*) means they were plundered and bound, and then led away;

or they were slain for the purpose of eating their flesh. "Cows" (*gāvo*) refers to bovine animals. "Burnt" (*daḍḍhāni*) means set on fire and consumed by flames. "And the people were led away" (*jano ca nīto*) means they were taken away after being seized as prisoners of war (*karamaraggāha*).

"The son of one whose son was slain" (*puttahatāya putto*) means the son of a woman whose child has been killed; the sense is that he is shameless (*nillajjo*). [This refers to] one who has severed both moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*).

For there is no such thing as a mother; thus, even while he was still living, he stood in the place of a slain son to her, and so he became known as "the son of a woman whose son was slain. "Harsh-voiced" means having a harsh sound. "Ḍiṇḍima" refers to a *paṭaha* drum.
Thus the Bodhisatta rebuked him with this verse. Before long, that deed of his became manifest, and then the king inflicted upon him a punishment proportionate to his offense.
The Teacher said, “Great King, it is not only now that he is of such a character; formerly, too, he was of exactly the same character.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and established the connection, he identified the Jātaka:
“At that time, the minister was none other than the present minister, and the wise man who recited the verse was I myself.”
The ninth: The Exposition of the Kharassara Jātaka.
[80] 10. The Exposition of the Bhīmasena Jātaka:
"That which you boasted of in the past... This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain boastful person.
He spoke concerning a certain bhikkhu. It is said that a certain bhikkhu thought: "Friend, there is no one with a birth equal to ours, nor anyone with a clan equal to ours.
We were born into such a great kṣatriya family; by clan, wealth, or lineage, there is no one equal to us.
Within our possession of gold, silver, and so forth, there is no end."
"Even our slaves and laborers eat rice with meat, wear Kāsī cloth, and anoint themselves with Kāsī perfumes.
Yet because of our state of having gone forth, we now eat such coarse food and wear such coarse robes," he said,
boasting among the elder, junior, and middle-ranking bhikkhus on account of his birth and other such matters.
He wandered about insulting, reviling, and disparaging others. Then, one monk, having observed his conduct regarding families, reported this boastful behavior to the monks.
The monks assembled in the Dhamma hall and said, "Friends, such-and-such a monk, having gone forth in this liberating dispensation, wanders about boasting, insulting, and disparaging others."
They spoke of his lack of virtue. The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Monks, that monk does not wander about boasting, reviling, and disparaging only now;
formerly, too, he wandered about boasting, reviling, and disparaging. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a prominent brahmin family in a certain market town.
Upon reaching maturity, he studied the three Vedas and the eighteen branches of knowledge under a world-renowned teacher at Takkasilā;
having attained perfection in all arts and sciences, he became known as the wise Cūḷadhanuggaha (the Junior Archer).
...was his name. Having departed from Takkasilā, while seeking mastery in all the arts of every school, he arrived in the kingdom of Mahimsaka.
In this Jātaka, however, the Bodhisatta was somewhat short and of a stooping appearance. He thought:
"If I approach any king, he will say, 'Since you have such a short body, what work can you do for us?'"
"He will say, 'Will you do it? What if I were to make a plank out of a man endowed with height and girth, handsome to look upon, and maintain my livelihood by living in his shadow?
While searching for such a man, he went to the weaving shed of a weaver named Bhīmasena and exchanged greetings with him.
Having done so, he asked, "Friend, what is your name? "I am named Bhīmasena," he replied.
"But why, having been so handsome and endowed with such physical excellence, do you perform this lowly work? "Because I am unable to earn a living," he said.
"Friend, do not do this work; there is no archer in all of Jambudīpa who is my equal."
"But if I were to see some king, he might become angry with me, thinking, 'What work will this man of such short stature do for us?
When you see the king, you should say, 'I am an archer. The king will give you a travel allowance and provide you with a regular livelihood.
I shall earn my living by performing the work that arises for you, while remaining in the shadow of your back."
"In this way, both of us shall be happy. Do as I say," he said. "Very well," he replied and accepted.
Then, taking him with him, he went to Bārāṇasī; acting as his junior attendant himself and placing him in front, he stood at the king's gate and announced their arrival to the king.
When the king said, "Let them enter," they both went inside, paid homage to the king, and stood there.
When it was asked, “For what purpose have you come? Bhīmasena replied, “I am an archer; there is no archer like me in all of Jambudīpa.
“But what will you receive in exchange for attending upon me? “I shall attend upon you, O Lord, receiving a thousand [pieces of gold] every half-month.
“And what is this man here? “He is my junior attendant, O Lord.”
“Serve him well,” he said. From that time forth, Bhīmasena attended upon the king.
However, whenever any business arose, the Bodhisatta alone resolved it.
Now at that time, in a certain forest in the kingdom of Kāsi, there was a path frequented by many people.
A tiger was causing people to be abandoned; seizing many men one after another, it devoured them. They reported this occurrence to the king.
The king summoned Bhīmasena and said, "My son, will you be able to capture that tiger?
"Your Majesty, am I not called an archer? If I cannot capture a tiger," [he replied]. The king gave him his travel expenses...
Having given it, he sent him away. He went home and told the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta said, "Very well, friend, go.
"But will you not go? "Yes, I shall not go; however, I will tell you a stratagem. "Tell me, friend," [he replied].
"Do not go alone and in haste to the tiger's dwelling; [inform] the people of the countryside..."
However, having assembled [the people] and caused one or two thousand bowmen to take up their positions there, you should go there;
then, upon learning that the tiger has risen, you should flee, enter a thicket, and lie down on your chest.
The local people themselves will strike and capture the tiger; once the tiger has been captured by them, you should cut a single creeper with your teeth.
Taking hold of the end [of the vine], you should go into the presence of the dead tiger and say: "Sir, by whom was this tiger killed?
I intended to bind this tiger with a vine like an ox and carry him to the king;
I had entered the thicket for the sake of the vine. Since the vine had not yet been brought back by me, by whom was he killed? Then you...
The country folk, terrified and trembling, said, "Master, do not tell the king; they will give you much wealth.
You will have captured a tiger, and from the king as well, you will receive much wealth.
Having agreed, saying "Very well," he captured the tiger according to the method explained by the Bodhisatta, made the forest safe, and was surrounded by a great multitude of people.
Having arrived at Bārāṇasī and seen the king, he said, "Your Majesty, the tiger has been captured by me; the forest has been made safe.
The king, being pleased, gave him much wealth. On another day, they reported, "A buffalo is causing people to abandon the single path.
The king sent Bhīmasena there in the same manner. He too, following the method given by the Bodhisatta, [dealt with] the tiger...
Taking him along as well, he returned; the king again gave him much wealth, and great power arose for him.

Intoxicated by the pride of that power, he held the Bodhisatta in contempt and would not accept his advice, speaking harsh words such as, "I do not live depending on you; are you the only man? and so forth.

Then, after a few days had passed, a neighboring king arrived and, having besieged Bārāṇasī, sent a message to the king saying, "Either surrender the kingdom or give battle. The king replied, "Fight," and dispatched Bhīmasena.
Fully equipped with all his armor and assuming the royal guise, he mounted the back of a well-armored elephant. The Bodhisatta, out of fear for his life, [also set out].
Fully armored, he sat upon the hindquarters of Bhīmasena.
Surrounded by a great multitude, Vāraṇa emerged through the city gate and reached the front of the battlefield. Upon hearing the sound of the war drums, Bhīmasena began to tremble.
The Bodhisatta, thinking, "Now he will fall from the back of the elephant and die," [leapt] from the elephant's shoulder.
To prevent him from falling, they bound Bhīmasena with a rope and seized him.
Seeing the place of combat, Bhīmasena, terrified by the fear of death, defiled the back of the elephant with the filth of his body. The Bodhisatta said:
"Bhīmasena, your former conduct does not match your latter; formerly you were like a warrior in battle, but now [you have defiled] the back of the elephant."
Having said, "You are a defiler," he spoke this verse:
"What you boasted about before, now your festering wounds are oozing after.
Both do not match, Bhīmasena: your talk of battle and this affliction of yours."
In this regard, that which you boasted of previously—namely, that boastful and contemptuous speech you uttered earlier, saying, "Are you alone a man? I am no man;
I too am a warrior in battle"—that is one thing. Then, as for the phrase "your festering wounds flow afterwards":
these are called "festering wounds" (*pūtisarā*) because of their state of putrefaction and their nature of oozing.
*Sarīravaḷañjadhārā* means they resound, they flow, they drip. *Pacchā* means after that;
having boasted previously, subsequently, now—at this head of the battle—this is the meaning. *Ubhayaṃ na sameti bhīmasena*:
O Bhīmasena, these two do not coincide. Which two? The talk of battle and this [state] of yours which afflicts you. And...
"The story of battle has been told purely; and as for this distress and exhaustion you now experience, it has reached the point of defiling the back of an elephant—this is the meaning.
Having thus rebuked him, the Bodhisatta said, "Do not fear, friend; why do you suffer while I am standing here?
He then helped Bhīmasena down from the back of the elephant, sent him away with the words, "Go home after bathing," and declared, "Today, by me being manifest..."

"It is fitting that I become such," he thought; and having entered the battle, raised a great shout, broken through the enemy's ranks, and captured the rival king alive, he went into the presence of the King of Bārāṇasī. The king, being pleased, bestowed great honor upon the Bodhisatta.
From that time forth, he became renowned throughout all Jambudīpa as "the wise Cūḷadhanuggaha."
Having given Bhīmasena his travel expenses and sent him back to his own place, and having performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, he departed according to his karma.
The Teacher said, "Monks, this monk does not boast only now; in the past, too, he was a boaster.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and established the connection, he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Bhīmasena..."
The boastful monk was [the other], while I myself was the clever Cūḷadhanuggaha.
This concludes the tenth story, the Bhīmasena Jātaka.
The eighth chapter, the Varuṇa Vagga, is finished.
Its summary verse:
Varuṇa, Sīlavanāga, Saccaṃkira, Rukkhadhamma;
Maccharājā, Asaṅkiya, Mahāsupina, and Illisa.
“With a harsh voice, like Bhīmasena. 9.
The Chapter on the Non-Drinkers [81]. 1.
The Commentary on the Surāpāna Jātaka.
"We have drunk [the Dhamma]; we have danced!"—this was said by the Teacher while residing at Ghosita’s Monastery near Kosambī, concerning the Elder Sāgata.

For when the Blessed One, having spent the rains retreat at Sāvatthī, arrived at a market town named Bhaddavatikā on his journey, the cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers saw the Teacher, paid homage to him, and...

“Venerable sir, do not go to Ambatittha; at the hermitage of the matted-hair ascetic in Ambatittha there is a venomous snake named Ambatitthaka, a serpent of fierce poison, who might harm the Blessed One,” they tried to dissuade him.
But the Blessed One, as if not hearing their words, went on his way even though they continued to try to stop him up to three times.
There the Blessed One was dwelling in a certain grove not far from Bhaddavatī.
Now at that time, the elder named Sāgata, an attendant of the Buddha who possessed the supernatural power of an ordinary person,
approached that hermitage and prepared a grass mat in the place where the royal nāga dwelt.
He sat down cross-legged. The nāga, unable to endure the insult, emitted smoke; the Elder also emitted smoke.
The nāga blazed up; the Elder also blazed up. The nāga’s fiery power did not afflict the Elder, but the Elder’s fiery power afflicted the nāga.
Thus, having subdued that king of nāgas in an instant and established him in the refuges and the precepts, he went into the presence of the Teacher.
The Teacher, having dwelt at Bhaddavatikā for as long as he desired, went to Kosambī.
The fact that the Elder Sāgata had tamed the Nāga spread throughout the entire country. The inhabitants of the city of Kosambī went out to meet the Teacher;
having paid homage to him, they approached the Elder Sāgata, paid their respects, and stood to one side.
They said, “Venerable sir, please tell us what is difficult for you to obtain; we shall prepare that very thing.
The Elder remained silent. But the group of six said, “Friends, for those who have gone forth, ‘dove-colored’ liquor is both rare and pleasing.
If you have faith in the Elder, prepare some ‘dove-colored’ liquor.”
Having accepted [the invitation] by saying, "Very well," and having invited the Teacher for the following day, they entered the city.

Thinking, "We shall give it to the Elder," each person in their own house prepared clear *kāpotika* liquor and, having invited the Elder, gave him the clear liquor from house to house. Having drunk it, the Elder, intoxicated by the liquor, was departing from the city.
Falling through the doorway, he lay down lamenting.
When the Teacher had finished his meal and was departing from the city, he saw the elder lying in that manner;
saying, "Monks, take Sāgata," he had him taken up and went to the monastery. The monks [placed] the elder's head toward the Tathāgata.
Placing him at the base of his feet, they laid him down; he turned over and lay down with his feet directed toward the Tathāgata.
The Teacher asked the bhikkhus, “Bhikkhus, does Ambatitthaka the Nāga King still possess that same reverence for me as he did before?
“No, Bhante,” they replied. “Bhikkhus, who [could have restrained] Ambatitthaka the Nāga King?”
“Damesī? “He has been tamed, Bhante. “But now, monks, would Sāgata be able to tame even a water-snake? “Certainly not, Bhante.
“Monks, would it be proper to drink such a thing, having drunk which one becomes so devoid of right perception? “It would not be proper, Bhante. Then the Blessed One [addressed] the Elder...
Having rebuked them and addressed the monks, he laid down the training rule: "In drinking fermented liquor and spirits, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Then, rising from his seat, he entered the Fragrant Chamber.
The monks assembled in the Hall of Truth spoke in dispraise of drinking fermented liquor, saying, "How great indeed is the fault in this!"
"Friends, regarding this drinking of liquor: even one so endowed with wisdom and possessed of psychic power acted in such a way that he did not know even a fraction of the Teacher's virtues.

The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you sitting together here now? When they replied, "For this very discussion," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that [one who drinks] liquor..."
"Having drunk it, those who have gone forth become unconscious; this has indeed been so even in the past," he said, and related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a family of learned brahmins in the kingdom of Kāsī.
Upon reaching maturity, he went forth as an ascetic, and having developed the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he...
Sporting in the play of meditation, he dwelt in the Himalayan region surrounded by five hundred pupils.
Then, when the rainy season had arrived, the pupils said to him, "Teacher, let us go to the path of men, partake of salt and sour flavors, and return.
He replied, "Friends, I shall remain right here; you, however, go and nourish your bodies."
“Spend the rains retreat and then return,” he said. Saying, “Very well,” they paid homage to their teacher and went to Bārāṇasī.
Staying in the royal park, on the following day they went for alms in a village just outside the gate; having eaten their fill, on the next day they entered the city.
The people, filled with affection, gave them alms. After a few days had passed, it was also the king’s turn...
They reported: "Your Majesty, five hundred seers have come from the Himālayas and are dwelling in the park;

they are performers of terrible austerities, with faculties perfectly subdued, and possessed of virtue. Having heard of their virtues, the king went to the park, paid homage, and after exchanging greetings, he requested them to stay right there for the four months of the rains and invited them. From then on, they resided in the royal palace itself.
Having eaten, they dwelt in the park.
Then one day, there was a festival called the Surā-nakkhatta in the city. The king, thinking, "Liquor is difficult for those who have gone forth to obtain," had much of the finest liquor provided.
Having drunk the liquor, the ascetics went to the park and became intoxicated with the madness of wine.
Some rose up and danced, others sang; having danced and sung, they lay down to sleep after spreading out straw mats and other coverings.
When the intoxication of the liquor had worn off and they woke up, they saw their own disgraceful state.

Weeping and lamenting, they thought, "We have not acted in a manner befitting those who have gone forth into homelessness," and added, "Because we were separated from our teacher, we committed such evil deeds."
At that very moment, leaving the park and going to the Himalayas, they took up their requisites, paid homage to the teacher, and sat down.
Being asked, "Dear ones, did you dwell happily on the human path without being fatigued by seeking alms, and did you dwell in harmony? they replied, "Teacher, we dwelt happily; however—"
“Having drunk that which was unfit for drinking, we became unconscious; unable to maintain mindfulness, we danced and sang.
Reporting this matter, they uttered this verse and said:
“We drank, we danced, we sang, and we wept;”
"Having drunk the intoxicant that causes loss of consciousness, we monkeys were no longer seen.
In this context, *apāyimha* means "we drank liquor. *Anaccimha* means "having drunk it, we danced, flailing our hands and feet.
*Agāyimhā* means "opening our mouths, we sang with long-drawn-out notes. And *rudimha* means "furthermore, being filled with remorse..."
“We have done such a thing! they cried, and wept. Having drunk the intoxicant that causes loss of consciousness, they said, “We were not seen as monkeys,” because it destroyed their perception;
having drunk that liquor which causes the loss of awareness, they thought, “It is well indeed that we are no longer monkeys.
In this way, they spoke of their own lack of virtue.

The Bodhisatta, having reproached those ascetics, saying, "Such is indeed the state of those who lack the company of a teacher," and having given them this admonition, "Do not act in such a way again," remained possessed of his meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and was destined for the Brahma-world.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka:

"From this point forward, we shall no longer provide the connection by saying 'having joined the context. At that time, the group of seers was the assembly of the Buddha, and I myself was the leader of the group."
The First: The Surāpāna Jātaka Commentary.
[82] 2. The Mittavindaka Jātaka Commentary.
"Beyond the delightful [grove]"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who was difficult to speak with.
He related it. The background story for this Jātaka belongs to the time of Kassapa Sammāsambuddha;
it will be made clear in the Mahāmittavindaka Jātaka in the Dasaka Nipāta. At that time, however, the Bodhisatta spoke this verse:
“Having passed beyond Ramaṇaka, Sadāmatta, and Dūbhaka;”
“Svāsi pāsāṇamāsīno, yasmā jīvaṃ na mokkhasī” (You sit upon a stone; for you shall not escape with your life).
Therein, “Ramaṇaka” was the name of a palace at that time; it indicates that he has passed beyond the Phalika Palace.
“Sadāmatta” was the name of a silver [palace]; it indicates that he has passed beyond the Silver Palace. “Dūbhaka”...
This indicates that you have surpassed even the name of a gem and the jeweled palace. "Svāsī" means you are such a sword.
"Pāsāṇamāsīno" refers to what is called a *khuracakka* (razor-wheel); it may be made of stone, silver, or gemstone, but this one is indeed made of stone.
And he is seated upon it—firmly settled and completely covered by it. Therefore, because he is seated upon stone, he is called "pāsāṇāsīno."
In what should be said, the letter *m* is taken by way of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*) of consonants, and thus it is stated as "pāsāṇamāsīno.
Alternatively, the meaning is: "seated upon a stone," that is, having approached and reached that razor-wheel, he stands there. As for "because you shall not escape alive":
because as long as your evil is not exhausted, even while still living you shall not be released; therefore, "you are seated upon it."

Having spoken this verse, the Bodhisatta went back to his own dwelling place. Mittavindaka, too, having raised the wheel of razors and experiencing great suffering until his evil karma was exhausted, departed according to his destiny.
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma instruction, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Mittavindaka was the monk of harsh speech, and I myself was the king of the gods.
This is the second commentary on the Mittavindaka Jātaka.
[83] 3. The Commentary on the Kāḷakaṇṇi Jātaka:
"A friend indeed is one who follows for seven paces. The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this concerning a certain friend of Anāthapiṇḍika.
It is said that he had played in the dust together with Anāthapiṇḍika, having been a pupil of the same teacher.

He was one who had learned his craft in the presence [of the teacher], known by the name Kāḷakaṇṇī. As time passed, having become impoverished and unable to make a living, he went into the presence of the merchant.
The merchant comforted him, gave him a travel allowance, and entrusted him with his own household.
Acting as a benefactor to the merchant, he performed all the necessary tasks for him. To that merchant...
Whenever she came into his presence, they would say, "Stop, you ill-omened one! Sit down, you ill-omened one! Eat, you ill-omened one!
Then one day, the merchant's friends and ministers approached the merchant and said to him, "Great merchant, do not keep her near you;
do not say to her, 'Stop, you ill-omened one! Sit down, you ill-omened one! Eat, you ill-omened one!'"
"Indeed, even a *yakkha* would flee at this sound; moreover, he is not your equal—he is wretched and ill-favored. What have you to do with him?
Anāthapiṇḍika replied, "A name is merely a conventional designation; the wise do not take it as an authority.
It is not fitting that I should be called 'Sutamaṅgalika' [Fortunate by Hearing]. I cannot, on account of a mere name, [deny my kinship] with one who played in the dust with me."
Disregarding their words, saying, "I shall abandon my companion," one day, while going to his own village of wealth, he left that house-guardian behind and departed.
The thieves, thinking, "The merchant has indeed gone to the village of wealth; we shall plunder his house," took up various weapons in their hands during the night.
Having arrived, they surrounded the house. The other man, fearing the arrival of the thieves, remained sitting without sleeping.

Knowing that the thieves had arrived, he made the entire residence resound with a single noise—as if holding a great festival—to awaken the people, saying, "You blow the conch! You beat the drum! The thieves—
“The house is empty! We have been badly deceived; the great merchant is indeed still here! Crying out thus, they abandoned their stone clubs and other weapons right there and fled.
On the following day, people saw the stone clubs and other items discarded here and there, and were moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
"If such a wise steward had not been present today, the thieves would have entered as they pleased and plundered the entire house;
it is by relying on this Daḷhamitta that the merchant’s prosperity has increased.
Having thus praised him, when the merchant returned from his village of wealth, they reported all those events to him. Then they...
The merchant said, "You have driven out such a friend as this guardian of my house;
had he been driven out by me at your word, today my entire household would have perished. Indeed, a mere name is no authority;
only a heart of goodwill is authoritative. Having given him even more travel expenses, [the merchant thought], "I now have this gift of conversation."
Having gone into the presence of the Teacher, he reported the entire occurrence from the beginning.
The Teacher said, "Householder, it is not only now that one who bears the mark of ill-fortune protects the household of his friend; in the past, too, he protected it.
Being thus requested by him, the Teacher related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a highly renowned merchant.
He had a friend named Kāḷakaṇṇī; everything else was exactly as in the present-day story.
When the Bodhisatta returned from the village of his wealth and heard of that occurrence, he thought, "If such a friend had been driven out by my word, [it would have been a great loss]."
Having said, "Today my family will no longer exist," he spoke this verse:
"A friend indeed is formed by walking seven paces; a companion is formed by twelve paces;
one becomes a kinsman after a month and a half-month; but beyond that, one is even as oneself."
"So how could I, for the sake of my own happiness, abandon one who has long been familiar, though she be ill-fated?
In this context, *ha* is merely a particle. *Mettāyati* means "a friend" (*mitto*); it means he establishes loving-kindness (*mettaṃ*) or shows affection.
Furthermore, this [friendship] occurs through the seven steps; the meaning is that it occurs by the mere act of walking seven steps together.
"But a companion [sahāya] is one who stays for twelve days": he is called a companion because he goes along with [another] in all postures (iriyāpatha) by performing all duties together.
Furthermore, "he is one who stays for twelve days" means he dwells together for twelve days.
"Or for a month or half a month" means either for a month or for half a month. "He becomes a kinsman" means he becomes equal to a kinsman. "Beyond that" means...
Beyond that, by living together, he even became like himself. Regarding the words "one should abandon," he spoke of the friend's virtue, thinking, "How could one abandon such a companion?
From that time on, there was no one at all who could speak against him.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was the ill-omened one, and I myself was the merchant of Bārāṇasī."
The third: The Commentary on the Kāḷakaṇṇi Jātaka.
[84] 4. The Commentary on the Atthassadvara Jātaka.
"One should desire health and supreme gain"—the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this regarding a certain man skilled in what is beneficial (atthakusala).
He spoke concerning a young man of good family. In Sāvatthī, there was the son of a very wealthy merchant who was seven years of age, wise, and skilled in matters of meaning.
One day, he approached his father and asked a question regarding the "gateways to meaning" (*atthadvārapañha*).
The father did not know it. Then it occurred to him: "This question is exceedingly subtle; setting aside..."
“Within this world-system, delimited above by the peak of existence and below by the Avīci hell, there is no one else capable of answering this question except the Omniscient Buddha.
Taking his son with him and having many garlands, perfumes, and ointments prepared, he went to Jetavana;
having honored and paid homage to the Teacher, he sat down to one side and addressed the Blessed One:
He said this: “Venerable sir, this boy is wise and skilled in the meaning; he asked me a question regarding the gateway to the meaning.
Not knowing that question, I have come into your presence. It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would explain that question to me.
The Teacher said: “Upāsaka, in the past, too, I was asked this very question by this same youth.”
"I told him then, and he knew it; however, because he has now entered the cycle of existence (*bhava-saṅkhapa*), he does not recognize it," he said.
When requested by him, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a very wealthy merchant.
Now his son was seven years old by birth, wise and skilled in the meaning.
One day he approached his father and asked the question regarding the door to prosperity: "Father, what is the door to prosperity?
Then his father, explaining that question to him, spoke this verse:
“One should desire health as the supreme gain, virtue approved by the Buddhas, and learning;
following the Dhamma and lack of dejection—these six are the foremost doors to prosperity.
In this context, regarding the phrase “one should desire health as the supreme gain,” the word *ca* is merely a particle. My dear, first of all, that which is termed health...
He spoke thus while illustrating this meaning: "One should desire the supreme gain.
In this context, "health" (*ārogya*) refers to the state of being free from disease and the absence of affliction in both body and mind.

For when the body is afflicted by disease, one is unable either to acquire unobtained gains of wealth or to enjoy those already acquired; however, when it is free from disease, one is capable of both. As for the mind...

Furthermore, when one is afflicted by defilements, one is unable to produce gains such as the various meditative absorptions (jhāna) not yet obtained, nor is one able to enjoy those already obtained by means of repeated attainment.
When this lack of health exists, even a gain not yet obtained is not gained, and even one already obtained becomes useless;
however, when this [lack of health] is absent, even a gain not yet obtained is gained, and even one already obtained becomes purposeful.
"It is well" means that health is called the supreme gain; this should be desired first of all. "This is one door to welfare"—this is the meaning here.
"And virtue" refers to the virtue of conduct (*ācāra-sīla*); by this, he shows worldly propriety.
"Approved by the elders" means approved by those who are elders in virtue, the wise; by this, he shows the instruction of venerable ones endowed with knowledge.
"And what has been heard" (*sutañca*) refers to learning based on a cause; by this, he shows the abundance of learning (*bāhusacca*) in this world that is grounded in purpose.
"And conformity with the Dhamma" (*dhammānuvattī ca*) means following the threefold Dhamma of good conduct;
by this, he shows the state of following the Dhamma of good conduct while avoiding the Dhamma of misconduct. "And lack of dejection" (*alīnatā ca*) refers to the mind’s lack of dejection.
"Anīcatā" (non-lowliness). By this, he shows the mind's lack of contraction, its state of refinement, and its state of excellence.
"The six doors are the foremost for the goal"—the meaning is that "goal" (*attha*) refers to prosperity;
these six doors or means, which are the foremost and supreme for attaining that prosperity known as mundane and supramundane, are the gateways to realization.

Thus the Bodhisatta explained the "Door-Questions" for the sake of his son. From that time forth, the son practiced those six principles. The Bodhisatta, too, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, departed according to his karma.
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the son was the present son, and the Great Merchant was none other than myself.
This is the fourth commentary on the *Atthassa-dvāra-jātaka*.
[85] 5. The Exposition of the Kiṃpakkajāta­ka.
“Not knowing the fault in the future”—this the Teacher spoke while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain dissatisfied bhikkhu.
It is said that a certain son of good family, having entered the Buddha’s teaching with sincere resolve, went forth; one day, in Sāvatthī...
While wandering for alms, he saw a woman adorned with ornaments and became discontented.
Then his teachers and preceptors brought him into the presence of the Teacher. The Teacher asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?
When he replied, "It is true," the Teacher said, "Monk, these five strands of sensual pleasure are delightful at the time of enjoyment. However, their enjoyment..."
Because it bestows rebirth-linking in the hells and other realms, it is like the consumption of the *kiṃpākaphala* fruit.
The *kiṃpākaphala* is endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and taste; however, once eaten, it tears the intestines apart and brings about the end of life.
Previously, many foolish people, failing to see its danger and becoming attached to its color, fragrance, and taste, consumed that fruit.
Having said, "They reached the end of their lives," he was requested by them to relate a past event.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, being a caravan leader, was traveling from the eastern to the western region with five hundred carts.
Upon reaching the entrance of a forest, he assembled his men and said: "In this..."
“There is a tree in the forest called the poison-tree; do not eat fruits you have never eaten before without first asking me,” he advised them.
Having passed through the forest, the people saw at its entrance a *kiṃpākka* tree, its branches bowed down by the weight of its fruit.
Its trunk, branches, leaves, and fruit were identical in shape, color, taste, and fragrance to those of a mango.
Among them, some, being attached to the color, fragrance, and taste, ate the fruits under the perception that they were mangoes;
others, thinking, "We will eat them after asking the caravan leader," took them and stood aside.
When the Bodhisatta reached that place, he had those who stood with their fruits taken away discard them, and he had those who stood eating them undergo emetics.
He gave them medicine. Among them, some were cured and recovered; however, those who had already consumed it first met their end.

The Bodhisatta, having reached his desired destination safely and obtained his reward, returned once more to his own place, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and departed according to his karma.
Having related this story, the Teacher, having attained full enlightenment, spoke this verse:
“He who indulges in sensual pleasures without knowing the future danger—
when the result ripens, it destroys him, like eating the fruit of the *kiṃpāka* tree.”
In that context, "not knowing the harm in the future" means not having known the harm in the future; the meaning is "having failed to understand.

"He who indulges in sensual pleasures" means he who indulges in both objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*) and defilement-sensual pleasures (*kilesakāma*). "At their ripening, they strike him down":

those sensual pleasures strike that person with various kinds of suffering when he has arisen in the hells and other realms at the end, which is to say, at the stage of their own ripening (*vipākante*).
They kill by binding [one to suffering]. How so? "Like eating the *kiṃpākā* fruit.

Just as the *kiṃpākā* fruit is pleasing at the time of consumption due to its excellence of color, fragrance, and taste, yet when eaten without seeing its future danger, it kills in the end and brings about the destruction of life;
even so, sensual pleasures, though pleasing at the time of enjoyment, kill at the time of their ripening. This is the teaching according to the sequence of the discourse.
Having brought them to the truths, he proclaimed the Truths; at the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was weary attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Among the rest of the assembly, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some became arahants.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly, and the caravan leader was none other than myself."
The fifth is the commentary on the Kiṃpakkajāta­ka.
6. The commentary on the Sīlavīmaṃsaka­jāta­ka:
"Virtue alone is indeed good"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain brahmin who tested virtue.
[The Buddha] spoke concerning him. It is said that he lived supported by the King of Kosala;
he had gone for refuge, maintained the five precepts unbroken, and was a master of the three Vedas. The king, thinking "this man is virtuous," accorded him exceptional honor. He thought:
"This king accords me greater honor than other brahmins, holding me in exceedingly high esteem."
He thought, "I see; does he show me this honor because of my success in birth, clan, family, region, or craft, or is it because of my success in virtue? I shall investigate this for now.
One day, having gone to attend upon the king and returning home, he took a single kahāpaṇa from a money-changer’s board without asking permission.
He arrived; out of respect for the brahmin, the money-changer said nothing and sat down. On the following day, he took two kahāpaṇas, and the money-changer likewise consented.

On the third day, he took a handful of kahāpaṇas, whereupon the money-changer said to him, "Today is the third day you have been plundering the royal household! and [addressed him as] "the thief who plunders the royal household."

“I have been caught! he cried out three times. Then people came from here and there and, saying, “For a long time now you have been wandering about as if you were virtuous,” they struck him two or three blows, bound him, and presented him to the king.
The king, feeling remorseful, said, “Brāhmaṇa, why did you commit such an act of immorality? and added, “Go—”
“Give him the king’s command,” he said. The brahmin replied, “Great King, I am not a thief.
Then [the king asked], “Why did you take the kahāpaṇas from the merchant’s board? [The brahmin said], “When you were showing me such great honor, I wondered:
‘Is it because of my birth and other qualities that the king shows me such great honor, or is it because of my virtue?’”
This was done for the sake of investigation; however, I have now known it with certainty.

That you have shown me such honor based solely on my virtue (*sīla*), and not on my birth or other factors—since you have now commanded me to rule as king—I have reached the conclusion that "in this world, virtue alone is supreme; virtue is foremost. And as for this...
"Remaining at home and enjoying the defilements would not allow me to act in a manner befitting my virtue;
this very day I shall go to Jetavana and go forth in the presence of the Teacher. Grant me the going-forth, O King!
Having said this, he took leave of the king and set out toward Jetavana.
Then his kinsmen, friends, and relatives, having gathered together, were unable to dissuade him and turned back.
He went into the presence of the Teacher, requested the going forth, and having received both the going forth and full ordination, he developed insight without neglecting his meditation subject.
Having attained arahantship, he approached the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, my going forth..."
"has reached the summit," he thus declared his own realization. This declaration of his attainment became well known throughout the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

Then one day, the bhikkhus assembled in the Dhamma Hall and said, "Friends, that brahmin who was the king’s attendant, having tested his own virtue and having requested permission from the king, went forth and attained Arahantship."
As they sat there, speaking of his virtues, saying, “He is firmly established,” the Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “For this very discussion,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that this brahmin, having tested his own virtue, went forth and made himself firm; in the past as well, he did so.”
"Having examined their own virtue and gone forth, the wise established themselves," he said,
and being requested by them, he related a story of the past. In the past,
when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his chaplain, devoted to giving.
One whose inclination is toward virtue is one who possesses the five precepts unbroken. The king honored him even more than the other brahmins;

everything else was exactly as before. However, while the Bodhisatta was being bound and led into the presence of the king, snake-charmers playing with snakes in the middle of the street seized them by the tails, seized them by the necks, and coiled them around their throats.
The Bodhisatta, seeing them, said: "Sons, do not seize this snake by the tail;
do not seize it by the neck; do not wrap it around your throat. For if it bites you, it will bring about the end of your lives. The snake-charmers replied:
"Brahmin, this snake is virtuous and possessed of good conduct; he is not such a person of evil character as you are through your own lack of virtue."
“They say you are a thief who plundered the royal household through improper conduct;
you must be bound and led away. He thought: “Even snakes that do not bite and cause no harm receive the name ‘virtuous’;
how much more so those who have become human! Virtue alone is supreme in this world; there is nothing higher than it. Then—
Having led him there, they presented him to the king. The king asked, "What is this, my sons? "He is a thief, Your Majesty, one who plunders the royal household.
"In that case, let the king's command be carried out against him. The brahmin said, "I am not a thief, Great King.
When it was further asked, "Then why did you take the coins? he related everything in the same manner as before, saying, "As for me..."
"For this reason, he reached the firm conclusion: 'In this world, virtue alone is supreme; virtue is preeminent.
Having said this, and further praising virtue by saying, "Let this matter rest for now; even a venomous snake, so long as it does not bite or cause harm, is worthy of being called 'virtuous.
For this reason too, virtue alone is supreme; virtue is excellent," he spoke this verse:
“Virtue alone, it is said, is beautiful; virtue is unsurpassed in the world.
Behold: though he be a serpent of deadly venom, one who is virtuous is not slain.

In this context, “virtue alone” refers specifically to the virtue of conduct (*ācārasīla*), which consists in non-transgression by way of body, speech, and mind. “It is said” (*kira*) indicates by way of oral tradition.
He speaks. "Excellence" (*kalyāṇa*) means most beautiful. "Supreme" (*anuttara*) means the eldest, the giver of all virtues.
"Behold" (*passa*) he says, speaking while pointing toward the reason he himself has seen. "One who is virtuous" (*sīlavā*) is not harmed:
even though he may possess a terrible venom, by merely refraining from biting and causing injury, he receives the praise of being "virtuous"; thus he is neither harmed nor afflicted.
"For this reason also, virtue alone is supreme.

Thus the Bodhisatta, having taught the Dhamma to the king with this verse, abandoned sensual pleasures, went forth as an ascetic, entered the Himalayas, and after developing the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments, became destined for the Brahma-world.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was the king; the king's retinue was the Buddha’s retinue; and the chaplain was none other than myself."
The sixth: The Exposition of the Sīlavīmaṃsaka Jātaka.
7. The Exposition of the Maṅgala Jātaka:
"He whose auspicious signs have been eradicated... This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning a certain Brahmin who possessed the marks of a clothed man.
He spoke concerning this. It is said that there was a certain brahmin living in Rājagaha who was superstitious about omens and auspicious signs;
he had little faith in the Three Jewels and held wrong views. He was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments. A pair of garments kept in his casket had been eaten by mice.
Then, after he had bathed his head and at the time he said, "Bring the garments," [he realized] they had been eaten by a mouse.
They reported it. He thought: "If this pair of garments bitten by a rat remains in this house, there will be a great disaster.
For this is an inauspicious thing, like a black ear-mark; it cannot be given to sons, daughters, or even to slaves and laborers.
Whoever takes this, for all of them there will be a great disaster at the raw-corpse cemetery."
“I shall have it discarded; however, it cannot be placed in the hands of slaves, laborers, and the like.
For they, having conceived greed for it, might seize it and meet with ruin. I will give it into the hand of my son.
Having summoned his son and explained the matter to him, he said: “My dear son, you too must not touch it with your hand, but [take it] with a stick...”
"Take it, discard it in the raw charnel ground, wash your head, and then come back," he sent him.
On that day, at the time of dawn, the Teacher, surveying those kinsmen who were ready to be enlightened, saw the necessary condition for these father and son to attain the fruit of stream-entry;
he took the path to the deer park and went like a deer-hunter to the gate of the raw charnel ground.

He sat down, emitting rays of the six-colored light of a Buddha. The young man, having accepted his father’s words, took that pair of garments with the tip of a staff like a python and reached the gate of the raw charnel ground.
Then the Teacher said to him, "What are you doing, young man? "Master Gotama, this pair of garments has been bitten by mice; it is like a bringer of misfortune."
“Friends, my father sent me away out of fear, thinking, ‘If anyone else were to discard this, they would give rise to greed.
I have come here thinking, ‘I shall discard this and wash my head,’ O Gotamas. “In that case, discard it,” [said the Teacher].
The young brahmin discarded it; then the Teacher, thinking, “Now it is fit for us,” [acted] right before him.
He took it. “This is an ill omen, Master Gotama; it is like a black ear of corn. Do not take it, do not take it!
Even as he was thus forbidding him, [the Buddha] took it and set out toward the Veḷuvana.
The young man ran quickly and informed his father: “Father, a recluse has taken a pair of garments that I had discarded in the raw charnel ground.”
"Even though I forbade him, saying, 'Gotama, this will not do for us,' he took it and went to Veḷuvana.
The brahmin thought: "That pair of garments is inauspicious, like a black ear;
by using it, even the ascetic Gotama will perish, the monastery will perish, and consequently we shall be censured. [This is] of the ascetic Gotama..."
“By giving many other cloths, we shall cause him to cast that one aside. Having had many cloths brought, he went with his son to Veḷuvana;

seeing the Teacher, he stood to one side and said, “Is it true, Master Gotama, that you took a pair of cloths from the raw charnel ground? “It is true, brahmin,” [the Teacher replied]. “Master Gotama, as for that pair of cloths—”
“It is an ill omen! While you are using it, you will perish, and the entire monastery will perish as well.
If you do not have enough for a lower garment or an upper robe, take these two cloths and discard that one.
Then the Teacher said to him, “Brāhmaṇa, we are indeed called renunciants; for us, [there is nothing] in the raw charnel ground, in the middle of the street, or in the place of refuse...”
"Rags discarded or fallen in places such as bathing ghats or on great highways are permissible;
moreover, you have not held this view only now, but you have held it even in the past. Having said this, being requested by him, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, in the kingdom of Magadha, in the city of Rājagaha, a righteous King of Magadha reigned. At that time, the Bodhisatta..."
Having been reborn in a certain northern brahmin family, he reached maturity, went forth as a seer, and attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*).

While dwelling in the Himalayas, at one time he departed from the Himalayas and, having reached a royal park in the city of Rājagaha, stayed there; on the following day, for the purpose of almsround, he entered the city.
He entered. The king, seeing him, summoned him, seated him in the palace, fed him, and obtained his promise to reside in the very garden.
The Bodhisatta, having eaten at the king’s residence, lived in the garden. At that time, there was in the city of Rājagaha a brahmin named Dussalakkhaṇa.
All else—such as the pair of garments placed in his casket—is exactly as described previously.

As the young man was going to the charnel ground, the Bodhisatta went there first, sat down at the entrance of the charnel ground, and taking the pair of garments discarded by him, he went to the park. The young man arrived and informed his father.
The father, thinking, "The ascetic who is a frequent visitor to the royal family might have been lost," went to the Bodhisatta and said, "Ascetic, regarding the pair of garments taken by you..."
"Throw it away; let it not be lost," he said. The ascetic taught the Dhamma to the brahmin, saying: "Rags discarded in our charnel grounds are sufficient for us;
we are not seekers of curiosity and omens. Indeed, this pursuit of curiosity and omens has not been praised by the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or Bodhisattvas;
therefore, one who calls himself wise should not be a seeker of curiosity and omens."
Having heard the Dhamma, the brahmin shattered his wrong views and went for refuge to the Bodhisatta.
The Bodhisatta, too, without falling away from his jhāna, became destined for the Brahma-world.
The Teacher, having brought up this past event and having attained full enlightenment, spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma to the brahmin:
“He for whom auspicious signs have been uprooted—omens, dreams, and bodily marks—he has transcended the fault of auspicious signs;
having attained the yoke of the pairs, he does not come to birth again.
In this context, “for whom auspicious signs have been uprooted” refers to the Arahant whose taints are destroyed, for whom there are no more auspicious signs seen or heard.
"Mutamaṅgala": these auspicious signs have been eradicated. Regarding "portents, dreams, and bodily marks":

such as "there will be an eclipse of the moon of this kind," "there will be an eclipse of the sun of this kind," "there will be an eclipse of a lunar mansion of this kind," "there will be a meteor-fall of this kind," and "there will be a conflagration of the quarters of this kind"—these are the five great portents, as well as various other kinds.
The marks of dreams, the mark of good fortune, the mark of misfortune, the mark of a woman, the mark of a man,
the mark of a female slave, the mark of a male slave, the mark of a sword, the mark of an elephant, the mark of a horse, the mark of a bull, the mark of a weapon, the mark of cloth—
these and other such marks, as well as these bases of views, have been uprooted by him; he is not [defined] by them.
One perceives one's own good fortune or misfortune through such signs as earthquakes and the like.
"He has transcended the faults of auspiciousness" means that he, having exhausted the taints (*khīṇāsava*), stands having abandoned and gone beyond all faults of auspiciousness.
"Attained through paired conjunctions" refers to the defilements that come together in pairs according to the method beginning with: "Anger and resentment, and contempt and spite," and so forth.
"Yokes" (yuga) refers to the following: the yoke of sensual desire, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance.

These are called the four yokes because they bind one to the cycle of existence (saṃsāra). A bhikkhu who has reached, overcome, transcended, and passed beyond these "yokes and bonds" (yugayoga)—one whose taints are exhausted—does not come to birth again;
that is, by way of rebirth-linking, he certainly does not return to this [existence].
"He does not go to the world; he does not come back.
Thus the Teacher, having taught the Dhamma to the brahmin with this verse, proclaimed the Truths.

At the conclusion of the Truths, the brahmin, together with his son, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher then identified the Jātaka: [The Buddha said: "At that time, the brahmin was Moggallāna, and his son was Sāriputta. I myself was the Teacher."
“Then those very father and son were now father and son, and the ascetic was none other than myself.
This concludes the seventh commentary, the Maṅgala Jātaka.
8. The Commentary on the Sārambha Jātaka.
"One should release only what is wholesome"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the training rule on abusive speech (*omasavāda*).
Both stories are identical to those told below in the *Nandivisāla Jātaka*.
However, in this *Jātaka*, the Bodhisatta was the ox named Sārambha belonging to a certain brahmin in Takkasilā in the kingdom of Gandhāra.
It came to pass. Having related this past event, the Teacher, having attained full enlightenment, spoke this verse:
“One should release only what is good; one should not release what is evil.
Release from the good is excellent; having released it, one regrets the evil.”
In this context, "one should utter only what is auspicious" means that one should utter, release, and speak only speech that is auspicious—beautiful, blameless, and free from the four faults.
"One should not utter what is evil" means that one should not utter or speak what is evil, base, unpleasant to others, and disagreeable.
"The release of the auspicious is good" refers precisely to the utterance of auspicious speech.
"In this world, that which is good, beautiful, and auspicious is [praised].
Having uttered, released, and spoken evil, harsh speech, one burns"—meaning that person who has let loose such words burns, grieves, and suffers.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the brahmin was Ānanda, the brahmin woman was Uppalavaṇṇā, and Sārambha was none other than myself."
The eighth: The Commentary on the Sārambha Jātaka.
[89] 9. The Commentary on the Kuhaka Jātaka.

"It was only speech, it is said, that you had..."—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain hypocritical monk. The account of the hypocrite will be made clear in the Uddālaka Jātaka.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, there lived a fraudulent ascetic, a false matted-hair ascetic, depending on a certain village.
A certain householder had a leaf-hut built for him in the forest and, while providing him with lodging there, maintained him with choice food from his own home.
Trusting that this false matted-hair ascetic was "virtuous," he...
Out of fear of thieves, he took a hundred gold coins to the ascetic’s leaf-hut, buried them in the ground, and said, "Venerable sir, please keep an eye on this.
Then the ascetic said to him, "Friend, it is not proper for those who have gone forth to speak in such a manner;
moreover, we have no greed for the property of others. He replied, "Very well, venerable sir," and accepted his words.
Having placed his faith [in him], he departed. The wicked ascetic, thinking, "One can live on this much," waited for several days;
then, taking that gold and placing it in a certain spot along the road, he returned and stayed right there in the leaf-hut.
On the following day, having performed his meal-duty at the man's house, he said: "Friend, we have lived long depending upon you..."
"We have lived here for too long; for those dwelling in one place for a very long time, there is social contact with laypeople, and such contact is indeed a stain for those who have gone forth.
Therefore, we shall depart. Having said this, even though he was entreated by him again and again, he did not wish to turn back.
Then he [the host] said to him, "If that is the case, go, venerable sir," and escorted him as far as the village gate.

Having followed him, he turned back. The ascetic, too, having gone only a short distance, thought, "It is fitting that I deceive this householder," and placing a blade of grass among his matted locks, he turned back. The householder asked, "Why have you turned back, venerable sir?
"Friend, a blade of grass from the roof of your house became caught in my matted locks; indeed, it is called 'taking what is not given'."

"It is not permitted for those who have gone forth; we have come taking it with us. The householder said, "Discard it and go, venerable sirs," and thinking, "He does not take even a blade of grass belonging to another;
oh, how conscientious my noble master is! he gained faith, paid homage, and sent them on their way.
At that time, however, the Bodhisatta was staying at that residence while traveling to the frontier on business.

It was taken. As soon as he heard the ascetic’s words, [the king thought], "Surely something must have been taken from this man by that wicked ascetic," and he asked the householder, "My good man, do you have anything deposited with this ascetic?
"I have, my lord, a hundred gold coins. "In that case, go and fetch it."
“Bring it back! Having gone to the leaf-hut and not seeing him, he returned in haste and said, “She is not here, my dear.
“The gold was not taken by anyone else; it was taken by that very same deceitful ascetic. Come, let us pursue him and seize it!
Running with speed, they caught the fraudulent ascetic, beat him with their hands and feet, and [took] the gold.

Having had it brought, they took it. When the Bodhisatta saw the gold, he said, "While carrying a hundred *nikkhas*, you did not stumble even over a mere blade of grass," and reproaching him, he spoke this verse:
"Indeed, your speech alone was soft, O you who speak with such courtesy."
“You did not touch even a blade of grass, nor did you take a hundred pieces of gold.

Regarding this, it is said that your speech alone was gentle, for you spoke with kindly words: “For those who have gone forth, it is not permitted to take even a blade of grass that has not been given”—thus, as you spoke such kind and soft words, your speech alone was indeed gentle.

"It was," meaning it was merely a word; "you were attached to a mere blade of grass" means, O fraudulent ascetic, that you were a being who clung and adhered by feeling remorse over a single blade of grass.
"But they carried off a hundred coins"—however, while carrying off this hundred coins, you have become unattached and entirely free from clinging.
Thus the Bodhisatta, having rebuked him and given this admonition, “Do not do such a thing again, you fraudulent ascetic,” departed according to his kamma.
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, said, “Monks, it is not only now that this monk was a deceiver; in the past, too, he was a deceiver.
Having spoken thus, he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the fraudulent ascetic was the deceitful monk, and the wise man was [the Bodhisatta].”
"But it was I myself who was he.
Thus ends the ninth commentary, the *Kuhaka-jātaka*. [90] 10.
The Commentary on the *Akataññu-jātaka* (The Story of the Ungrateful One).
"He who has done good in the past"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Anāthapiṇḍika.
It is said that he had a certain merchant from the borderlands with whom he had no prior acquaintance.
On one occasion, having filled five hundred carts with merchandise for export to the borderlands, he said to his workmen: "Go, sirs, with this merchandise..."
"Take him to Sāvatthī, sell him to our friend, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, for his full value, and bring back the proceeds.
They agreed to his words, saying, "Very well," and having gone to Sāvatthī, they saw the great merchant, presented the gift, and reported what had happened. The great merchant said, "Welcome to you."
Having provided them with lodging and travel expenses, and having inquired after his friend's welfare, he had the goods sold and the proceeds used to purchase merchandise in return.
They went to the border region and reported the matter to their own merchant.
Later, Anāthapiṇḍika likewise dispatched five hundred carts there. The people there—
Having gone there and taken the gift, they saw the merchant living in the border region. He asked, "Where have you come from?
When they replied, "From Sāvatthī, from your friend Anāthapiṇḍika," he joked, "Anāthapiṇḍika must be the name of some man," and after taking the gift, he said, "Go."
Thus he dismissed them, providing neither lodging nor travel expenses.
They themselves sold their goods, took the merchandise in exchange, and having returned to Sāvatthī, reported the matter to the merchant.
Then that frontier dweller once again dispatched five hundred carts to Sāvatthī in exactly the same manner.
People, taking gifts, went to see the Great Merchant.
When they saw him, Anāthapiṇḍika’s men said, “Master, we shall provide for their lodging, food, and travel expenses.
Having had their carts unloaded at a suitable place outside the city, they said, “You may stay right here; we shall provide you with rice-gruel and meals in our own homes.”
Thinking, “There will also be a reward,” they went and assembled their slaves and laborers;

then, during the middle watch of the night, they plundered five hundred carts, stripped them of their lower and upper garments, drove off the oxen, overturned the carts, set them on the ground, and having even seized the wheels, they departed. The border-dwellers—
Not being the owners even of their own undergarments, they fled in fear and went straight to the borderlands.

The merchant’s men reported this matter to the great merchant. Thinking, "Now there is a story worth telling," he went into the presence of the Teacher and related the entire incident from the beginning. The Teacher said, "Householder, that border-dweller..."
"Having said, 'He was of such a character even in the past,' when requested by him, he related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a very wealthy merchant in Bārāṇasī.
He had a merchant friend living in a border region with whom he had never met. The entire story of the past is exactly like the present story."
But when the Bodhisatta’s men reported, "Today we have done this and that," he said,
"Only after first failing to recognize the help they themselves have rendered do they later receive such as this. Then,
teaching the Dhamma to the assembled multitude, he spoke this verse:
“He who has previously performed good deeds, but having accomplished his purpose does not realize it, finds no one to assist him when a need subsequently arises.
Herein, this is the summarized meaning: any man whatsoever among the kṣatriyas and others who has previously, at an earlier time, had good deeds performed for him by another...
Having performed the service, having accomplished the purpose, and having fulfilled his duty, he does not recognize the excellence and the benefit that another has conferred upon him;
later, when his own need arises, he does not find—that is, he does not obtain—the one who performed that service for him.
Thus the Bodhisatta, having taught the Dhamma with this verse, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and departed according to his karma.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “The border-dweller of that time was indeed a border-dweller even now; as for the merchant of Bārāṇasī, he was none other than myself.
This concludes the tenth discourse, the Commentary on the Jātaka of the Ungrateful.
This is the ninth chapter, the Apāyimha Vagga.
Its summary verse:
Drinking liquor, winning friends, the black-eared one, the door of wealth;
testing character with the *kiṃpākka* fruit, auspiciousness, and also the destruction of life.
The deceitful one and the ungrateful one.
10. The Chapter on the Smeared (Littavagga). 1. The Commentary on the Smeared Jātaka (Littajātakavaṇṇanā).
"Anointed with supreme splendor"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the use of requisites without prior reflection.
It is said that at that time, monks, having received robes and other requisites, for the most part used them without reflecting upon them.
By using the four requisites without such reflection, they were for the most part reborn in the realms of hell or the animal womb.
They were not released. The Teacher, having understood the reason for this, gave a discourse on the Dhamma to the bhikkhus in many ways;

then, showing the danger in using requisites without reflection, he said: "Bhikkhus, it is not proper for a bhikkhu, having obtained the four requisites, to use them without reflecting. Therefore, from now on, regarding the four requisites—"
Having reflected, you should consume [them]. Thus, showing the method of reflection, he established the tradition by means of the sequence beginning with:
“But here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, uses the robe for protection against cold,” and so forth;
[he then said]: “Monks, it is proper to consume the four requisites after reflecting in this way, and not without reflecting.”

"Enjoyment [of such things] is like the enjoyment of the hālāhala poison. For in the past, those who consumed poison without reflecting and without knowing its danger experienced great suffering at the time of its ripening. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a certain family of great wealth.
Having been reborn, he reached maturity and became a gambler.
Now, another was a fraudulent gambler who, while playing with the Bodhisatta, would not break up the gaming circle when his own victory was imminent;
however, at the moment of defeat, he would put a die in his mouth, break up the gaming circle saying, "The die is lost," and depart. The Bodhisatta [reflected] upon him...
Having understood that reason, [the man] thought, "Very well; we shall find a suitable pretext here.
Taking some dice, he dyed them with *halāhala* poison in his own house, dried them repeatedly, and taking them with him, went into the other's presence and said, "Come, friend, let us play with dice.
The other replied, "Excellent, friend," and having prepared the gaming circle, he played together with him.
While playing, at the moment of his own defeat, he thrust a die into his mouth.
Then, seeing him doing so, the Bodhisatta spoke this verse to reproach him, saying, “Swallow it for now; later you will know what this is”:
“A man who has smeared himself with the highest glory does not realize that he has swallowed a die.”
"Swallow it, O swallower of evil tricksters; later it will become bitter for you.
In this context, *littaṃ* means smeared, stained, or colored. *Paramena tejasā* means by the most powerful poison, *halāhala*.
*Gilā* means swallowing. *Akkhaṃ* means a die. *Na bujjhati* means [he does not realize]: "This thing being swallowed by me will do such-and-such to me."
He does not know. "Gila," "reti," and "gilāhi" are [imperatives]. "Gilāti" is said by one who is urging him again.
"Pacchā te kaṭukaṃ bhavissati" means that once this die has been swallowed by you, this poison will later become sharp.
Even as he was speaking to the Bodhisatta, the man, overcome by the force of the poison, rolled his eyes and [fell] upon his shoulder.
Having thus addressed him, the Bodhisatta thought, "Now it is fitting to grant him the gift of life.
He gave him a medicinal emetic prepared with herbs; once he had vomited, he fed him ghee, molasses, honey, sugar, and other such things, restoring him to health.
He then exhorted him, saying, "Do not do such a thing again," and having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, he departed according to his karma.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, what is called 'enjoyment without reflection' is like the enjoyment of food prepared without prior inspection," and having spoken thus, he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I myself was the clever gambler;
the fraudulent gambler is not mentioned here, and as it is here, so it is everywhere. But as for whoever..."
“At this time, it is not known; therefore, it is not even mentioned.
The first commentary on the Littajātaka.
[92] 2. The commentary on the Mahāsārajātaka.
“One seeks a hero in Ukkaṭṭha. This was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Venerable Ānanda Thera.
For on one occasion, the women of King Kosala thought: “The arising of a Buddha is indeed rare;
likewise is the attainment of human birth and the possession of complete faculties. And we have encountered this rare convergence of conditions.”
Even though we have obtained [this opportunity], we are unable to go to a monastery at our own pleasure to listen to the Dhamma, to perform worship of the Buddha, or to give alms;
we live as if placed inside a casket. Having informed the King, we shall have him summon a monk suitable to teach us the Dhamma, and we will listen to the Dhamma in his presence. Then...
"Whatever we are able to master, we shall learn; and we shall perform meritorious deeds such as giving. In this way, this attainment of the opportune moment will become fruitful for us.
All of them approached the king and explained the reasons they had each considered.
The king accepted their proposal, saying, "Excellent."
Then one day, the king, desiring to enjoy a pleasure excursion in the park, summoned the park-keeper and said, "Cleanse the park.
While cleansing the park, the park-keeper saw the Teacher seated at the foot of a certain tree;
he went to the presence of the king and said, "The park is clean, O King, but there is someone here at the foot of a certain tree..."
"The Blessed One is seated," he said. The king replied, "Excellent, my friend; we shall hear the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher.
Ascending his decorated chariot, he went to the park and approached the presence of the Teacher.
At that time, a certain lay follower named Chattapāṇi, a non-returner (anāgāmī), was listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher.
He was sitting there. When the king saw him, he stood for a moment apprehensive;
then, thinking, "If this man were an evil person, he would not sit near the Teacher and listen to the Dhamma;
he must be a virtuous man," he approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side. Out of reverence for the Buddha, the lay follower did not rise to greet the king.
He did not perform either the greeting or the salutation; because of that, the king was displeased.

The Teacher, perceiving his displeasure, spoke of the lay follower’s virtues: “Great King, this lay follower is learned, one who has mastered the traditional teachings, and is free from passion for sensual pleasures.
The king thought, “This man cannot be insignificant, since the Teacher praises his virtues.”
“Lay follower, tell him what you need,” he said. The lay follower accepted, saying, “Very well.
Having heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, the king paid homage to the Teacher by keeping him to his right and departed.
One day, while standing on the upper terrace with the great window open, he saw that lay follower after he had finished his breakfast.
Seeing him going to Jetavana with his sunshade, he had him summoned and said this: "It is said, lay follower, that you are very learned;
our women wish both to hear and to learn the Dhamma. It would be well indeed if you were to recite the Dhamma to them.
[The man replied: "Your Majesty, for householders to teach the Dhamma within the royal palace—"
“...or to recite [the Dhamma], it is not appropriate for me; it is appropriate only for the noble ladies.

The king, thinking, “What he says is true,” sent him away, summoned the women, and said: “Ladies, I am going to the Teacher’s presence for the purpose of receiving a teaching on the Dhamma and for the purpose of having the Dhamma recited;
I request one bhikkhu from among you. Which one among the eighty great disciples should I request?”
He said: Having consulted among themselves, they all reported the matter to the Elder Ānanda, the keeper of the Dhamma-treasury.
The king went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and sitting to one side, spoke thus:
"Venerable sir, the women in our household wish to hear and learn the Dhamma from the Elder Ānanda; it would be well indeed if the Elder [would grant their request]."
“May he teach and recite the Dhamma in our home. The Teacher consented, saying, “Very well,” and commanded the Elder.
From that time forth, the king’s women listened to the Dhamma from the Elder and mastered it.
Then one day, the king’s crest-jewel was lost. When the king heard of its disappearance, he gave orders to his ministers.
“Seize all the men who are householders and bring back the crest-jewel,” he commanded. The ministers, beginning with the women of the palace, searched for the crest-jewel;
not finding it, they caused great distress among the people. On that very day, the Elder Ānanda entered the royal residence.
Just as those women, upon seeing the Elder previously, had become joyful and glad to hear the Dhamma—
They both heard and learned [the news], yet failing to act accordingly, they all became overcome with dejection.

Then, when the Elder asked them, "Why have you become like this today?", they replied: "Venerable sir, we thought, 'Let us search for the king's crest-jewel,' and so we have been harassing the womenfolk starting from the inner apartments; we do not know what will happen to whom."
“Because of that, we have fallen into grief. The Elder, saying “Do not worry,” comforted them and went into the presence of the king.
Sitting on the prepared seat, he asked, “Great King, it is said that your jewel has been lost? “Yes, venerable sir.
“But were you able to have it brought back? “Venerable sir, even though we have exhausted all our household people, we have not been able to find it.”
“I am able to have it brought,” [he said]. “Great King, there is a way to have it brought without causing distress to the multitude.
“Which one, venerable sir? “The gift of a morsel, Great King. “What kind of gift of a morsel, venerable sir?
“Great King, take those who are suspected and give each of them a single morsel of straw or a single lump of clay, saying: ‘This—’”
