One should say: "Bring it at dawn and throw it in such-and-such a place.
Whoever has taken it will put it there and bring it back. If they throw it down on the very first day, that is well;
if they do not throw it down, the same should be done on the second and third days as well. In this way, the great multitude will not...
“He will become weary, but you shall obtain the jewel,” having said this, the Elder departed.
The king caused [the search] to be conducted for three days in the same manner as described, yet they did not bring the jewel. On the third day, the Elder returned and asked, “What is it, Great King?
Has the jewel been dropped? “They do not find it, venerable sir. “In that case, Great King—”
“Having had a large vat placed in a concealed spot right on the ground floor, filled with water, and surrounded by a curtain, tell them:
‘All the people who frequent the interior and the women must put on their upper robes;
then, one by one, enter within the curtain, wash your hands, and come out. Having explained this expedient, the Elder—

He departed. The king acted accordingly. The jewel-thief thought, "It is impossible that the Dharma-treasurer would withdraw from this legal matter without showing the jewel; it is now time to drop it.
Concealing the jewel, he took it, entered the inner tent, dropped it into a water-jar, and went out. When everyone had departed, [he left].
Having discarded the water, they saw the jewel. The king was delighted, thinking, "Relying on this elder, I have obtained my jewel without causing the great multitude any fatigue.
The people of the inner palace were also delighted, thinking, "By relying on this elder, we have been liberated from great suffering.
Because the king’s crest-jewel had been obtained through the power of the elder, the elder’s majesty became known throughout the entire city.
He became well-known both among the King and within the Saṅgha of monks.
As the monks sat gathered in the Dhamma Hall, they praised the virtues of the Elder, saying:
"Friends, the Elder Ānanda, through his great learning, wisdom, and skill in means, has—without causing hardship to the multitude—by means of skillful methods alone [instructed] the King..."
“...showed him the jewel. The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that Ānanda has shown property that had fallen into another’s hands;
in the past as well, wise men, without causing the great multitude any hardship, recovered property that had fallen into the hands of animals by means of skillful methods.”
Having said, "They caused [them] to see," he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, having attained perfection in all arts, was his very minister.
Then one day, the king, accompanied by a great retinue, went to a pleasure grove and [wandered] through the forest thickets.
Having wandered about and desiring to play in the water, he descended into the auspicious lotus pond and summoned the women of the harem.

The women removed their various ornaments, such as those for the head and neck, placed them in their upper robes, set these aside on the tops of caskets, and having entrusted them to female slaves, they descended into the pond. Then, a certain female monkey from the pleasure garden—

Seeing her sitting on the branch, having removed her ornaments, placed them in her upper robe, and setting them down on the surface of a casket, [the queen]— desiring to wear a pearl necklace herself—
sat watching for the maid’s negligence; the maid, too, while guarding her, sat looking here and there and began to doze off.
The female monkey, perceiving her state of negligence, descended with the speed of the wind, fastened a great pearl necklace around her neck,
and leaped back up with the speed of the wind. Sitting within the branches, out of fear of being seen by the other female monkeys,
she placed it in a hollow of a tree and sat there guarding it as if it were perfectly secure.
The maidservant, too, having woken up and not seeing the pearl necklace, began to tremble;
seeing no other recourse, she cried out with a great clamor, "A man has taken the queen's pearl necklace and fled!
Then the guardsmen, gathering from here and there, heard her words and reported them to the king. The king said, "Seize the thief! The men—
Having emerged from the park, they looked here and there, crying out, "Catch the thief! Catch the thief!
Then a certain villager, a tax-collector, hearing that sound, fled in trembling.
Seeing him, the king’s men thought, "This must be the thief," and pursuing him, they seized him and beat him, saying, "Hey, you wicked thief, in this way..."
“You shall steal the ornament named Mahāsāra,” they reviled him.
He thought, “If I say, ‘I will not take it,’ I shall have no life today; they will surely kill me by beating me. I accept it.
He said, “Yes, sir, it has been taken by me. Then, having bound him, they brought him into the presence of the king.
The king also asked him, "Was your precious jewelry taken? "Yes, Your Majesty," he replied. "Where is it now?
"Your Majesty, I have never before seen even a bed or a chair made of such great value;
however, the merchant had me take that precious jewelry and give it to him, and he alone knows where it is."
The king summoned the treasurer and asked, "Did you receive this highly valuable ornament from his hand?
"Yes, Your Majesty," he replied. "Where is it? "It was given by me to the chaplain. The king then summoned the chaplain and questioned him in the same manner;
he too admitted it and said, "It was given by me to the musician. The king then summoned the musician as well...
“Did you take those ornaments of great value from the hand of the chaplain? he asked. “Yes, Your Majesty,” he replied. “Where are they?
“Out of defilement, I gave them to my maidservant. He had her summoned as well and questioned her, but she said, “I did not take them.
While they were questioning these five people, the sun went down. The king thought, “It is now the wrong time.”
“Once born, we shall know it for ourselves. Having entrusted those five men to the ministers, he entered the city.
The Bodhisatta thought: “This jewelry was lost within the inner precincts; this householder is outside the precincts, and there is heavy guard-duty at the gate.
Therefore, even those belonging to the inner precincts would not be able to take it and escape.”
Thus, no means of seizing those who frequent the gardens—neither those outside nor those within—is seen.
By this man of low birth saying, “It was given to me by the merchant,” it must have been said for the sake of his own liberation;
and by the merchant also saying, “It was given to me by the chaplain,” [it must have been said] thinking, “Let us escape together.”
Having reflected, the chaplain must have said, "She has been given to me by the musician," thinking,
"We shall dwell happily in the prison thanks to the musician. And the musician, having said,
"She has been given to me by the courtesan," must have said it thinking, "We shall certainly be free from longing."
Having reflected, he thought, "It must have been said [by someone else]; it cannot be these five thieves.
There are many monkeys in the park; it must have been placed in the hand of one monkey by means of the jewelry.
He approached the king and said, "Great King, hand over the thieves to us, and we shall clear ourselves of that matter. The king replied, "Very well."
“Learned one, examine them,” he said, and handed him over.
The Bodhisatta summoned his own servants and had those five men stay in one place;
having established a guard all around and provided an ear, he said, “Whatever they say to one another, report it to me.”
Having said this, he departed. They did exactly as instructed. Then, at the time when the people had gathered together, the merchant said to that householder:
"Hey, wicked householder! Where have you ever seen me before? Or where have I ever seen you?
When did I ever give you my jewelry? He replied: "Master, great merchant, [I saw] a bedstead with legs made of *mahāsāra* heartwood..."
“I did not even know of the bed and chair; I did not say, ‘Relying on this, I shall obtain liberation.
Do not be angry with me, Master,” he said. The chaplain then said to the merchant, “Great merchant, you have given me a report concerning what was not even given by him.
[The merchant replied,] “We two are both masters; when we stand together as one, our work—”
“It will be accomplished quickly,” they said. The *gandhabba* also said to the chaplain, “Brāhmaṇa, when did you give me my ornaments?
“I told you, ‘Relying on you, I shall live happily in my dwelling place,’” he replied.
The courtesan also said to the *gandhabba*, “O wicked *gandhabba*, when did I ever come to your side?”
“Have you been here before? Or have you ever come to me before?
When was my jewelry given to you? “Sister, why are you angry? We said, ‘If we five live together as one, there will be a household life;
living without longing, we shall dwell in happiness. [Thus spoke the Bodhisatta] from the presence of the men he had dispatched.
Having heard this and understood from the facts that they were not thieves, he thought, "I shall cause the ornaments taken by the female monkey to be dropped by means of a stratagem.

He had many ornaments made of *geṇḍu* (a type of wool or soft material) fashioned, had monkeys caught in the park, and having had the *geṇḍu* ornaments fastened upon their hands, feet, and necks, he released them.
The other female monkey, guarding her own ornaments, remained right there in the park.
The Bodhisatta commanded the men: "Go, search for all the female monkeys in the park;
when you see that ornament on any of them, frighten her away and take the ornament.
Those female monkeys, delighted and overjoyed at the thought, "We have obtained the ornament," were wandering about in the park when they came into her presence.
“Look at our jewelry,” they said. The female monkey, unable to endure it, thought, “What is the use of this head-ornament?
and, having put on a pearl necklace, she went out. Then those men, seeing her, made her discard the ornament, brought it back, and gave it to the Bodhisatta.
He took it, showed it to the king, and said, “This, O King, is your jewelry.”
“Those five were not thieves; however, this was brought by a female monkey in the park,” he said.
“But how, O wise one, did you know that it had been taken from the hand of the female monkey, and how was it seized? He explained everything.
The king, with a joyful mind, offered praise to the Bodhisatta, saying: “Indeed, heroes and the like are required at the head of battle and in such situations.”
Speaking this verse, he said:
“In times of crisis, they desire a hero; among counselors, one free from curiosity;
one dear for providing food and drink; and when a matter arises, a wise man.”
In that context, *ukkaṭṭhe* means "when it has drawn near," that is, when a battle is joined on both sides and a conflict is taking place.
*Sūramicchanti* means they desire a hero who does not flee even when a thunderbolt is falling upon his head; at such a moment, a warrior of this kind must be sought.
Regarding *mantīsu akutūhalaṃ*: when the time has come for deliberating on what ought and ought not to be done, [one should be] free from curiosity among the counselors.
Among counselors, they desire one who is free from curiosity, whose speech is not scattered, and who does not betray a secret; such a person should be sought for those positions.
And "a beloved one regarding food and drink": when sweet food and drink are presented, they seek a beloved person to enjoy them together with;
such a person should be sought at that time. And "a wise man when a matter has arisen."
"When some matter profound in meaning or profound in Dhamma arises—whether a cause or a question—they desire one who is wise and discerning;
for such a person is to be sought at such a time.
Having thus praised and extolled the Bodhisatta, the king, like a great cloud raining down a heavy shower, [honored him] with seven...
Having honored him with jewels and abiding by his advice, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving and departed according to his karma; the Bodhisatta also departed according to his karma.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and praised the Elder’s virtue, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, King Ānanda was the king, and the wise minister was none other than myself.
This is the second commentary on the Mahāsāra Jātaka.
[93] 3. The Commentary on the Vissāsabhojana Jātaka (The Story of the Meal of Trust).
"Do not trust the untrustworthy"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a meal given in trust.
It is said that at that time, most of the monks were thinking, "This was given by our mother; this was given by our father; this was given by our brother..."
"Given by our sister, Cūḷamātā, Cūḷapitā, our maternal uncle, and our maternal aunt. These are worthy of being given both during our time as householders and during our time as monks.
Thus, they accepted the four requisites given by their relatives with confidence and consumed them without reflecting upon them.
The Teacher, knowing this situation, [thought]: "I shall give a Dhamma teaching to the monks..."
“It is proper to do so. Having thus addressed the monks, he said: “Monks, a monk must indeed consume the four requisites—whether given by relatives or by strangers—only after reflecting upon them.
For a monk who dies having consumed them without reflection is not released from the state of a *yakkha* or a *peta*; such is the consequence of consuming things without reflection.”
"This is like the consumption of poison. For poison kills indeed, whether it is given by one who trusts you or by one who does not trust you.
In the past, people have met their end after consuming poison given in good faith," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a very wealthy merchant.
A certain cowherd, having taken his cattle into the forest at the time when the pastures were overgrown with weeds, built a cow-pen there and lived guarding them.
He brought dairy products to the merchant from time to time.
Then a lion took up residence not far from that cow-pen. Because of their fear of the lion, the cows became emaciated, and their milk became thin.
Then one day, when he had returned bringing ghee, the merchant asked him, "My good Gopālaka, why is the ghee so thin?
He explained the reason to him. "But, my good man, does that lion have any attachment to anyone?
"He does, master; he has a connection with a certain doe. "Is it possible, however—"
“Have him catch it. “It can be done, Master,” he replied.
“In that case, having caught it, dye its body repeatedly with poison starting from its forehead, dry it, and after two or three days have passed, release that doe.
Out of affection for her, it will lick her body and meet its death. Then, for it—”
“Take her hide, claws, teeth, fat, and flesh, and then return,” he said, and having given him *halāhala* poison, he sent him away.
The cowherd cast his net and, by a clever stratagem, captured that mother-deer and did as he was told.
As soon as the lion saw her, out of intense affection he licked her body and met his death. The cowherd also [took] the hide and the other parts...
Having taken it, he went into the presence of the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta, understanding the reason for this, said: "One should not harbor affection for others;

thus, even though he was endowed with such strength, Sīha, the king of beasts, fell into death through the influence of the defilements, having relied on intimacy and licked the body of the doe, thereby consuming poison. Having spoken thus to the assembled multitude...
While teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
"Do not trust the untrustworthy, nor trust even the trustworthy;
from trust comes danger, as the lion does to the deer."
Herein, this is the meaning in brief: one should not place trust even in that person who was previously fearless and trustworthy toward oneself;
nor should one place trust in him who was previously fearful and untrustworthy toward oneself. Why is that?
Because fear follows from trust. For wherever there is trust—whether in a friend or in an enemy—from that very source comes fear.

He approaches. How so? Like a lion following a doe: just as fear follows a lion from the presence of a doe with whom he has established intimacy through familiarity, meaning that she has approached and come near him;
or alternatively, it means that the doe, out of confidence, has followed and approached the lion.
Thus the Bodhisatta, having taught the Dhamma to the assembled company and performed meritorious deeds such as giving, departed according to his karma.
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma instruction, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I myself was the great merchant.
This is the third commentary on the Vissāsabhojana Jātaka.
[94] 4. The Exposition of the Lomahaṃsa Jātaka:
"Thirsting and parched with thirst..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at the Pāṭikārāma near Vesālī, concerning Sunakkhatta.
For on one occasion, Sunakkhatta, having been an attendant of the Teacher, took his bowl and robe and departed.
While wandering about, finding pleasure in the doctrine of the Koliyan Khattiya, he offered his bowl and robes to the One of Ten Powers and lived in dependence upon the Koliyan Khattiya.
When that [Koliyan] was reborn in the asura realm of the Kālakañjas, [Saccaka] remained a householder and declared:
"There is no superhuman state, no distinction in noble knowledge and vision, in the ascetic Gotama; the ascetic [Gotama] is merely beaten out by logic..."
“Gotama teaches a Dhamma that follows after inquiry and is based on his own inspired intuition;
yet for whatever purpose he teaches that Dhamma, it does not lead the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.
Thus he spoke in dispraise of the Teacher as he wandered between the three walls of Vesālī.
Then, as the Venerable Sāriputta was walking for alms, he heard that person speaking such dispraise.
Having returned from his almsround, he reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, “Sāriputta, Sunakkhatta the misguided man is angry;
he spoke thus out of anger. Yet even out of anger, he could not say, ‘That does not lead one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.’”
"Even though he speaks without knowing it, he is merely praising my own virtues. Yet that foolish man does not truly know my virtues.
For I, Sāriputta, possess what are called the six direct knowledges (*cha-abhiññā*); this too is a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*) of mine.

I possess the ten powers of knowledge (*dasabala-ñāṇa*), the four grounds of self-confidence (*caturvesārajja-ñāṇa*), and the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth (*catuyoni-paricchedaka-ñāṇa*)."
"I possess the knowledge that discerns the five destinies; this too is a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) of mine.

Now, if anyone were to say of me, who is thus endowed with a superhuman state, 'There is no superhuman state in the ascetic Gotama,' then without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that thought, and without relinquishing that view, he would be cast down just as if carried [to his burial place]."
“...and likewise in hell. Having thus spoken of the qualities of his own superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*) as it actually exists, he said:
“Sāriputta, it is said that Sunakkhatta has placed his faith in the false asceticism of the Kora kṣatriya’s practice of austerities.
But one who places faith in such false asceticism ought rather to place faith in me. For ninety-one eons ago from now, I declared: ‘There is—’”
"Was there indeed any essence here? Thus, while investigating the wrong asceticism of outsiders, I lived the holy life endowed with its four factors.
Indeed, I was an ascetic, a supreme ascetic; indeed, I was coarse, a supreme coarse one; indeed, I was loathsome, a supreme loathsome one;
indeed, I was secluded, a supreme secluded one. Having said this, when requested by the Elder, he related the past.
In the past, ninety-one aeons ago, the Bodhisatta, thinking, "I shall test external asceticism," went forth into the Ajīvaka order.
He became naked, smeared with dust and dirt, living in seclusion and dwelling alone. Upon seeing people, he would flee like a deer;
he consumed gross, repulsive food, such as cow dung from calves and the like, for the sake of abiding in heedfulness.
He dwelt in a certain terrifying forest grove in the wilderness.

While dwelling there, during the season of snowfall in the month of Antaraṭṭhaka, he would emerge from the forest grove at night, dwell in the open air, and upon the rising of the sun, re-enter the forest grove.
Just as he had been drenched by the cold water of the snow at night while in the open air, so too during the day [he was drenched] by the water dripping from the forest grove.
He is drenched by drops of water. In this way, he experiences the suffering of cold day and night.
However, in the last month of the summer, having spent the day in the open air, he enters the forest thicket at night.

Just as he had reached a state of burning heat from the sun during the day in the open air, so too does he reach a state of burning heat at night in the windless forest thicket; [this occurs] from his body.
Streams of sweat were released. Then, this verse, never heard before, occurred to him:
“Thirsting and parched, alone in the terrifying forest, naked and not sitting by a fire—the sage is intent on his search.”
In this context, "well-heated" means thoroughly heated by the sun's heat. "Well-soaked" means thoroughly soaked or drenched by cold water.

"Alone in a terrifying forest" indicates that he was solitary and without a second companion in such a terrifying thicket of woods where, for the most part, the body hairs of those who enter it stand on end.
"Naked and not sitting near a fire" means he was naked... [and so forth].
And he did not sit by a fire. This indicates that even when oppressed by cold, he neither took up a lower garment nor an upper robe, nor did he sit down near a fire.
"Devoted to seeking" means that even regarding that which is not the holy life, he perceived it as the holy life, thinking:
"This very seeking and searching is the means for the Brahma-world. Thus, by means of that seeking for the holy life—
This shows that he was devotedly intent and made a diligent effort. "The Sage" (Munī) indicates that he was thus esteemed by the world as one who had practiced for the sake of silence (mona).
Having lived the holy life endowed with these four factors, at the time of death, the Bodhisatta—[who was] standing before him—

Having seen the signs of hell and realizing, "Alas, this undertaking of vows is useless," he immediately broke that adherence at that very moment, adopted right view, and was reborn in the world of the gods.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, I was that Ājīvaka."
The Fourth: The Exposition of the Lomahaṃsa Jātaka.
[95] 5. The Exposition of the Mahāsudassana Jātaka.
"Impermanent indeed are conditioned things"—this was said by the Teacher while lying on his deathbed to the Elder Ānanda: "Do not, Ānanda..."
He spoke concerning the words beginning with, "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One [resided] in this small town.
For while the Tathāgata was dwelling at Jetavana, on the full moon day of the month of Kattika, the Elder Sāriputta attained final nibbāna in his birthplace at Nāḷaka village;
and on the new moon day of the dark fortnight of that same month of Kattika, Mahāmoggallāna did likewise. Thus, when the pair of chief disciples had attained final nibbāna...
“I too shall attain final Nibbāna at Kusinārā,” he said.
Traveling by stages on his journey, he arrived there and lay down between the twin sāla trees on a couch with its head toward the north, in the posture of one who does not rise again.
Then the Venerable Ānanda Thera said to him, “Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One not pass away in this small town, this uneven, desolate, and barren town.”
He entreated, saying, "Let the Blessed One attain final Nibbāna in one of the great cities such as Campā or Rājagaha, rather than in this minor town of Sākhā.
The Teacher said, "Do not, Ānanda, call this a 'minor town,' a 'desolate town,' or a 'branch town.
For in the past, during my time as the universal monarch Sudassana, I dwelt in this very city."
"Then this great city, surrounded by a rampart of jewels twelve *yojanas* in extent, came into being.
Having said this, when requested by the Elder, he related the *Mahāsudassanasutta*, bringing forth the past.
At that time, however, Mahāsudassana, having descended from the Sudhamma Palace, was in a grove of palm trees made of the seven precious gems not far away.

Having seen him lying on his right side in the posture of one who will not rise again upon a prepared lawful couch, Queen Subhaddā said, "Your Majesty, here are these eighty-four thousand cities, with the royal capital Kusāvatī as their chief; take pleasure in them!
To this, Mahāsudassana replied, "Do not speak thus, O Queen; rather, [take pleasure] in this..."
"Discard [this attachment], do not harbor longing," thus he exhorted me. When asked, "For what reason, O Lord?
he replied, "Today I shall pass away. Then the queen, weeping and wiping her eyes, spoke those words with great difficulty and distress, and she wept and lamented.
The remaining eighty-four thousand women also wept and lamented.
Not even a single one among his ministers and others was able to restrain their grief; they all wept. The Bodhisatta, having restrained them all by saying, "Enough, sirs!
Do not make a noise," addressed the queen: "Do not weep, O Queen; do not lament.
For there is not even a thing as small as a sesame seed that is called permanent; all things are indeed impermanent and subject to dissolution."
Having spoken thus, while instructing the goddess, he uttered this verse:
“Impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena, subject to the nature of arising and passing away;
having arisen, they cease—their pacification is bliss.”

In this regard, "Impermanent indeed are formations," O Bhaddā Subhaddā-devī: whatever formations—such as the aggregates, bases, and so forth—are produced by the coming together of various conditions, all of them are indeed called impermanent. For among these, form is impermanent...
[and so on] ...consciousness is impermanent. The eye is impermanent... [and so on] ...mental objects are impermanent. Whatever is with consciousness or without consciousness, [all is impermanent].
All that is a treasure is indeed impermanent. Thus, grasp this: "Conditioned phenomena are indeed impermanent. Why? Because they are "of the nature of arising and passing away";
all these are subject to arising and subject to passing away, having the very essence of appearing and perishing;
therefore, they should be understood as "impermanent. And because they are impermanent, they cease after having arisen, and having arisen, they pass away.
Even after reaching [their peak], they simply cease. All these phenomena, when being produced, are said to "arise"; when breaking up, they are said to "cease.
Only when there is arising does there come to be "stability," and only when there is stability does there come to be "dissolution.
For that which has not arisen cannot have stability, nor is there such a thing as the dissolution of what has already stood still. Thus, all conditioned formations (saṅkhārā) [are of this nature].
Having reached their three characteristics, they cease right there;

therefore, all these are impermanent, momentary, fleeting, unstable, subject to dissolution, shifting, stirred, non-enduring, passing away, devoid of substance. In the sense of being merely temporary, they are like an illusion, a mirage, or a bubble.
O Bhaddā, Queen Subhaddā, why did you conceive the perception of happiness regarding them? Thus...
"But take it up: their stilling is bliss. Because it is the stilling of the entire cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), "their stilling" is indeed *nibbāna*;
that alone is absolute bliss, and there is no other bliss besides it.

Thus, having reached the pinnacle of his teaching with the great *nibbāna* of the Deathless, Mahāsudassana gave instruction to the rest of the multitude, saying, "Give gifts, guard your virtue, and observe the Uposatha rites," and he became one whose destination was the world of the gods.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Queen Subhaddā was Rāhula’s mother;
the Jewel of the General was Rāhula; the rest of the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly; and Mahāsudassana was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Mahāsudassana Jātaka, the fifth.

[96] 6. The Commentary on the Telapatta Jātaka "Full to the brim, without remainder"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in a certain grove near the town named Sedaka in the kingdom of Sumbha, concerning the Janapadakalyāṇī Sutta. For there the Blessed One said: "Just as, monks, if a great crowd of people were to say, 'The Janapadakalyāṇī, the Janapadakalyāṇī!'"... [text continues] ...Thus, monks, the Janapadakalyāṇī is not the most beautiful in the world.

At that time, a certain monk approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down at one side. As he was sitting there, the monk said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, it is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous how well-spoken was this statement by the Blessed One: 'Monks, even if a great crowd of people were to say, "The Janapadakalyāṇī, the Janapadakalyāṇī! yet, monks, the Janapadakalyāṇī is not the most beautiful in the world. Monks, the most beautiful woman in the world is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. When this was said, the Blessed One told that monk: "Monk, it is not because of her physical beauty that the Janapadakalyāṇī is called 'the Janapadakalyāṇī. Rather, monks, she is called 'the Janapadakalyāṇī' because she is the most excellent among the women of the country regarding her skill in conversation, her grace, her charm, and her deportment. But the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the most beautiful in the world because he is supreme in virtue, supreme in concentration, supreme in wisdom, supreme in liberation, and supreme in the knowledge and vision of liberation. Then the monk said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason why, when the Blessed One speaks thus, some of those present feel inspired and others do not? "Monk, it is because of the diversity of dispositions and inclinations of beings. Just as, monk, when a man strikes a gong with a mallet, some hear the sound as sweet, some as harsh, and some as neutral; so too, monk, when the Tathāgata speaks thus, some of those present feel inspired and others do not. This is the cause, this is the reason. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, suppose there were a bowl full to the brim with water, without any remaining space. If someone were to pour more water into it, the water would overflow. Even so, monks, if a person is full of lust, hatred, and delusion, and does not abandon them, they will be overwhelmed by suffering. But if a person abandons lust, hatred, and delusion, they will be freed from suffering. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall abandon lust, hatred, and delusion. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves. This is the commentary on the Telapatta Jātaka.
A great crowd would gather; moreover, that beauty of the land would be supremely skilled in dancing and supremely skilled in singing.
Thinking, "The beauty of the land is dancing and singing," monks, an even greater multitude of people would gather.
Then a man might come who desires life, does not desire death, desires happiness, and is averse to suffering.

One might say to him: "Good man, you must carry this bowl of oil filled to the brim between a great crowd of people and Janapadakalyāṇī, while a man with a raised sword follows closely behind you, thinking:
'Wherever you spill even a little of it, right there I shall strike off your head!'"
“What do you think, monks? Would that man, neglecting that oil-bowl, bring about negligence regarding something external?
“Certainly not, Bhante. Monks, this simile has been used by me for the purpose of making the meaning known.
This is the meaning here: “The oil-bowl filled to the brim,” monks, is a term for mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*).
"It is a designation for mindfulness. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'Mindfulness directed to the body shall be developed by us and well undertaken.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus he spoke this Janapadakalyāṇī Sutta, complete in meaning and phrasing.
Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: "The beauty of the land" means she is beautiful, supreme, and free from the six defects of the body, being endowed with the five excellences.
For she is neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too stout, neither too dark nor too fair;
thus, because she has transcended the human form but has not yet reached the divine form, she is free from the six defects of the body.

She is called "endowed with the five excellences" because she possesses these five excellences: excellence of skin, excellence of flesh, excellence of sinews, excellence of bones, and excellence of youth. For her, there is no need for the function of adventitious light;
by the radiance of her own body alone, she creates light within a space twelve cubits around. She is the color of yellow *piyaṅgu* flowers.

Or it may be the color of gold. This is her excellence of skin. Furthermore, her four hands and feet, as well as the area around her face, are like red coral or red woolen cloth, as if treated with lac dye. This is her excellence of flesh.
Her twenty nails—where they are not detached from the flesh—are as if filled with lac dye, while where they are detached, they resemble streams of milk.
This is her excellence of sinews. Her thirty-two teeth appear perfectly polished, like a row of well-cleaned diamonds;

this is her excellence of bones. Even though she is a hundred and twenty years old, she appears as if she were sixteen years of age, being free from wrinkles and grey hair; this is her excellence of youth.
Regarding the term *paramapāsāvinī*: here, *pasava* means "flowing forth," which is to say, "occurrence. *Pāsāva* is simply another term for *pasava*.

*Paramapāsāva* (supreme flowing) means the highest occurrence; one who possesses that is *paramapāsāvinī*. It refers to the supreme occurrence or the most excellent activity in both dancing and singing.
What is meant is that she dances the very best dance and sings the very best song.
"Now, a man might come" does not mean he would come of his own accord; rather, this is the intended meaning here:
while the Janapadakalyāṇī was dancing in the midst of the great crowd and the shouts of "Well done! Well done!
were occurring, along with the snapping of fingers and the waving of garments, the king, having heard of that occurrence, [released] a certain criminal from the prison.

Having summoned him, she had his shackles broken off, gave him a bowl of oil filled to the brim and perfectly full, and making him grasp it firmly with both hands, she commanded a man with a sword in hand:
"Take this man and go to the festival grounds where Janapadakalyāṇī is. Wherever he, through negligence, spills even a single drop of oil..."
"If you abandon her, I shall cut off your head right there. That man, raising his sword and threatening him, led him there.
Terrified by the fear of death and desiring to live, he neglected her through negligence;
even once opening his eyes, he did not look at that Janapadakalyāṇī. This is indeed a story from the past.
However, it should be understood that this was stated in the Sutta by way of a hypothetical supposition (*parikappa*).
As for the phrase "This simile occurs to me," the correlation of the oil-bowl with mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) has already been made.
Herein, action (*kamma*) should be regarded as like the king, the defilements (*kilesa*) as like the sword, and the man with the drawn sword...
Like Māra, the practitioner of insight (vipassaka-yogāvacara) who cultivates mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati) is like the man with the oil-filled bowl in his hand.

Thus, the Blessed One, having cited this sutta, demonstrated: "A bhikkhu who wishes to develop mindfulness directed to the body should develop it with diligence, without letting go of mindfulness, just as that man did with the oil-filled bowl in his hand."
Having heard this sutta and its meaning, the bhikkhus said:
"Venerable sir, difficult was the deed done by that man who, without even looking back at such a woman, the most beautiful in the land, went on his way carrying the bowl of oil. The Teacher said:
"Bhikkhus, it was not a difficult thing done by him; it was indeed easy. Why? Because he was pursued by a man with a raised sword."

"Because he was being led away after being terrified. But that which the wise men of old achieved—having practiced with diligence and not relaxing their mindfulness—even when presented with celestial forms, they proceeded without breaking their sense-faculties or looking back, and thus attained kingship; this is difficult to do. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was among the hundred sons of that king.
He was reborn as the youngest of all, and in due course he reached the age of discretion.
At that time, Pacceka Buddhas were eating in the king’s palace, and the Bodhisatta performed services for them. One day he thought, “I have many brothers;
shall I obtain the kingdom belonging to my family in this city, or not? Then to him—
It occurred to him, "I shall find out by questioning the Paccekabuddhas.
On the following day, when the Paccekabuddhas had arrived, he took a water vessel, strained water, washed their feet, and anointed them with oil.
While they were sitting and eating their midday meal, he paid homage to them, sat down to one side, and asked about that matter.
Then they said to him: "Prince, you will not obtain the kingdom in this city. However, two hundred yojanas from here there is a city named Takkasilā in the kingdom of Gandhāra;
if you are able to go there, you will obtain the kingdom on the seventh day from now.
But along the way, there is an obstacle in the Mahāvattania forest; [cross] that forest..."
For one traveling by way of detours, the path is a hundred yojanas long, but for one going straight, it is fifty yojanas;
for that is what is called the "wilderness inhabited by non-human beings.
There, yakkhinīs construct villages and rest-houses along the road, and having prepared magnificent couches with canopies variegated with golden stars, they spread out cloths of various colors.

Having surrounded herself and adorned her body with celestial ornaments, she sat in the pavilions and, winning over the men who were approaching with sweet words, beckoned them, saying, "You appear as if you are weary; come here, sit down, drink some water, and then depart.
As they arrived one after another, she gave them seats and [fascinated them] with the playful charms of her own beauty.

Having enticed them and brought them under the power of the defilements, when they commit an act of transgression with them, [the spirits] devour them right there while blood flows profusely, bringing about the end of their lives. They seize a being whose range is form by means of form itself;
one whose range is sound, by means of sweet sounds of song and instrumental music; one whose range is fragrance, by means of divine scents; and one whose range is taste—
They will provide you with divine food of various exquisite flavors, and they will offer you divine couches with red woolen covers on both sides as objects for the sense of touch.
If you go there having broken your senses, not looking at them, and establishing mindfulness,
you will obtain the sovereignty there on the seventh day.
The Bodhisatta said, "Very well, venerable sirs; having accepted your instruction, what need is there for me to look at it?

Having had the Paccekabuddhas perform a protective recitation (*paritta*), he took the protective sand and the protective thread, paid homage to the Paccekabuddhas and his parents, and went to his residence.
There he addressed his men: "I am going to Takkasilā to seize the kingdom."
“I am going; you stay right here. Then those five men said to him, “We too shall follow you.
“It is not possible for you to follow,” he replied. “For along the way, it is said, there are female spirits (*yakkhinīs*) who prey upon forms and such;
they entice people with various forms and other charms and seize them. It is a great obstacle. I, however, go having fortified myself.”
“But why, O King, should we look upon our own dear forms and so forth while going with you?
We too shall go in that very same manner. The Bodhisatta said, “In that case, be heedful,” and taking those five people with him, he set out on the path.
The yakkhinīs established villages and other settlements and sat there. Among them was a man whose range of perception was limited to forms;
having looked at those yakkhinīs, his mind became bound to the object of their beauty, and he lagged behind for a short while. The Bodhisatta said, "Why, sir, do you lag behind?
"Your Majesty, my feet are aching; I shall sit down in a hall for a short while before I come. "Ho there! These..."
“O yakkhinīs, do not desire me. “Whatever may be, I cannot help it, O gods,” she replied. “In that case, you shall be known for it!
Having said this, she took the other four and departed. He too, whose range was forms, went into their presence.
When they committed misconduct with him, they caused him to meet his end right there and continued on ahead.
Having built another hall and taken up various musical instruments, they sat down singing; there, the one whose range was sound remained behind.
Having devoured him as well in the same manner as before, they moved forward, filled various kinds of perfume caskets, set up a shop, and sat down;
there, the one whose range was fragrance remained behind. Having devoured him too, they moved forward.
They filled vessels with various choice flavors of divine food and sat down, having set up a rice shop;
there, the one whose range was flavor remained behind. Having eaten that as well, they went forward and sat down after arranging divine couches;
there, the one whose range was touch remained behind. They ate that too, and the Bodhisatta was left all alone.
Then a certain female spirit (*yakkhinī*), thinking, "This man possesses truly fierce spells;
I shall turn back only after devouring him," followed closely behind the Bodhisatta.

When the forest workers and others saw the female spirit at the far end of the forest, they asked, "Who is this man walking ahead of you? She replied, "He is my husband, noble sirs. They said, "Oh!"...
“This maiden, so delicate, like a garland of flowers, golden-hued, has left her own family and gone forth out of devotion for you;
why do you not take her away without causing her distress? [He replied:
“She is not my wife, noble lady; she is a *yakkhinī*, and five men have been devoured by her. [The other said: “Noble sir, men...”
“Indeed, even at times of anger, one’s own wives may become *yakkhinīs* or *petīs*.

As she went along, she displayed the appearance of being pregnant, and then again, having assumed the appearance of having recently given birth, she followed the Bodhisatta, carrying her son on her hip;
whenever she was seen, she questioned him in the same manner as before. The Bodhisatta, speaking in that very same way, continued on his way.
She reached Takkasilā. Having caused her son to vanish, she pursued him alone.
The Bodhisatta, having gone to the city gate, sat down in a certain hall. Unable to enter because of the Bodhisatta’s splendor, she assumed a celestial form and stood at the door of the hall.
At that time, as the King of Takkasilā was going to his pleasure garden, he saw her and became infatuated with her.
He sent a man, saying, “Go and find out whether she has a husband or not. The man approached her and asked, “Are you married?
“Yes, noble sir; this man sitting here in the hall is my husband,” she replied. The Bodhisatta thought, “She is not my wife.”
"This is a *yakkhinī*; five men have been devoured by her," he said.
She replied, "Noble sirs, when men are angry, they say whatever they wish. He reported the words of both to the king.
The king, thinking, "Property without an owner belongs to the king," summoned the *yakkhinī*, had her sit upon the back of an elephant, and [led her] into the city.
Having performed a circumambulation, he ascended the palace and established her in the position of chief queen.
Having bathed and anointed himself, and having eaten his evening meal, he ascended the couch of glory (*sirisayana*).
That *yakkhinī* also, having brought food suitable for herself and being adorned and prepared, lay down upon the couch of glory with the king; and by reason of the king’s passion—
While she was lying down, having been granted comfort, she turned onto her side and wept.
Then the king asked her, "What is it, lady, that you weep? "Your Majesty, I was seen by you on the road and brought here;
yet there are many women in your house. Living among my rivals, when conversation arose, [they asked], 'Who is your mother?'"
“Whether it be my father, my clan, or my birth—when you see me on the road and say, ‘This woman was brought here by you,’ I will become dejected as if being crushed while held by the head.
If you were to grant me sovereignty and authority over the entire kingdom, no one would be able to speak to me with a provoked mind. “Bhadde,” he said.
“The inhabitants of my entire kingdom belong to no one; I am not their master. However, I am the master only of those who, having provoked the King’s anger, do what ought not to be done.
For this reason, it is impossible for me to grant you sovereignty or authority over the whole kingdom or the city.
“In that case, Your Majesty, if in the kingdom or the city—”
“You cannot give me orders; however, give me authority over those who are part of the inner household and the inner retinue, so that I may exercise my power over them.

Bound by divine touch, the king was unable to disregard her words and said, “Very well, lady, I grant you authority over the members of the inner household; you may bring them under your own control.”

She replied, "Very well," and accepted the task. When the king had fallen asleep, she went to the city of the *yakkhas*, summoned the *yakkhas*, and having caused the king to meet his end, she left nothing but his bones; she devoured all his sinews, skin, flesh, and blood.
The remaining *yakkhas* then began from the great gate and proceeded through the interior of the residence, starting with the cocks and dogs.
Having devoured everything, they left nothing but bones. On the following day,
seeing that the door was closed just as before, the people pounded the panels with axes, entered within,
and seeing the entire residence strewn with bones, said, "Truly, that man spoke the truth when he said, 'This is not...'"
"She is my wife; she is a yakkhinī. But the king, knowing nothing of the matter, took her and made her his own wife.
They said, "She will summon the yakkhas and go away after devouring everyone.
On that very day, the Bodhisatta also placed a small amount of sand on his head and wrapped a protective thread around himself in that same hall.
Standing there with sword in hand, he caused the dawn to rise.

The people, having cleansed the entire royal palace, smeared it with green plaster, anointed it above with perfumes, scattered flowers, hung garlands of blossoms, and offered incense, fastened new wreaths, and deliberated: "O sirs, that man who has manifested a divine form..."
“He did not even cast a glance at the female spirit (yakkhinī) coming from behind him, having broken his senses;
he is an exceedingly noble being, steadfast and endowed with wisdom. While such a man rules the kingdom, the entire realm will become happy;
let us make him the king. Then all the ministers and the citizens, becoming of one mind, [acted accordingly].

Having approached the Bodhisatta and said, "Your Majesty, please rule this kingdom," they escorted him into the city, placed him upon a heap of jewels, and consecrated him, making him the King of Takkasilā.
Avoiding the four wrong courses and not violating the ten duties of a king, he ruled the kingdom righteously; performing meritorious deeds such as giving, he passed away according to his karma.
The Teacher, having related this past event and having attained full enlightenment, spoke this verse:
"Just as one would carry a bowl of oil filled to the brim and without spilling a drop,
so should one guard one's own mind, aspiring for the direction never before reached."
In this context, "filled to the brim" means filled level with the rim of the mouth of the vessel. "Without leaving anything behind" means without spilling or straining out any of it.
"A bowl of oil" means a bowl into which sesame oil has been poured. "Should carry around" means he should carry it, taking it with him as he goes.
"Thus one protects one's own mind" means that one's own mind is like that bowl filled with oil.

Having placed it between these two—the objective field of mindfulness directed to the body and the mindfulness associated with it—the wise practitioner should guard and protect it so that it does not waver for even a moment toward an external object.
For what reason? Because of this:
“The mind is difficult to restrain, fickle, and falling wherever it pleases;
the taming of the mind is good, for a tamed mind brings happiness.
Therefore—
“The wise person should guard the mind, which is very difficult to see, extremely subtle, and which falls wherever it desires; a guarded mind brings happiness.
For this—
“Those who will restrain the mind— which travels far, wanders alone, is bodiless,
and dwells in the cave— will be released from the bonds of Māra.
But for the other:
“For one whose mind is unsteady, who does not understand the true Dhamma,
and whose confidence wavers, wisdom does not reach fulfillment.
But for one who has a companion in a firm meditation subject—
“For one whose mind is not defiled, whose heart is unassailed,
who has abandoned both merit and evil— there is no fear for the vigilant.
Therefore, this—
“The flickering mind is restless, difficult to guard and hard to restrain;
the wise man makes it straight, just as a fletcher straightens an arrow-shaft.
Thus, making his own mind straight, he should protect it.

"Longing for a direction never gone before": having begun the work in this meditation subject of mindfulness occupied with the body, the meaning is that one should guard one's own mind according to the method described, longing for and yearning for a direction never gone before in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
But what is this so-called "direction"?—
“Parents are the eastern quarter; teachers are the southern quarter;
children and wife are the western quarter; friends and colleagues are the northern quarter.
Servants and laborers are below; ascetics and brahmins are above.”
“One should honor these directions; such is sufficient for a householder in his family.”—In this context, children, wife, and so forth are called “directions.
“The four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below—these are the ten directions.”
"In which direction does the Naga king stand, whom he saw in his dream as having six tusks?"— here,
"direction" (*disā*) refers specifically to the directions distinguished as east and so forth.
"Householders who give food, drink, and clothing, and those who invite [others], they call that too a 'direction'."
“This is the supreme direction, O Seta-keṭu, reaching which those who were suffering become happy.
Here, however, Nibbāna is called “the direction. In this context as well, that alone is intended. For it is seen and designated by such terms as “destruction” and “dispassion”;
therefore, it is called “the direction. But in the beginningless cycle of existence (saṃsāra), by some foolish worldlings—
It is said that even in a dream, a direction never before reached is called "unreached. One who aspires to that must apply himself to mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*).

Thus, having taken the pinnacle of his teaching with Nibbāna, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the king’s retinue was the Buddha’s retinue, and the prince who attained the kingdom was none other than I myself.
This concludes the sixth commentary on the Telapatta Jātaka.
[97] 7. The Explanation of the Nāmasiddhi Jātaka:
"And having seen Jīvaka dead"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was successful merely by name.
It is said that there was a son of good family named Pāpaka; he went forth into homelessness, having committed himself wholeheartedly to the Teaching.
When the monks said to him, "Come, friend Pāpaka! Stop, friend Pāpaka!
he thought, "In the world, 'Pāpaka' is called something base, unlucky, and ill-omened; I shall have them choose for me another name associated with auspiciousness.
He approached his teachers and preceptors and said, "Venerable sirs, my name is inauspicious; please give me another name."
"Give it to me," he said. Then they replied to him, "Friend, a name is merely a designation;
there is no accomplishment of any purpose through a name. Be content with your own name alone. Yet he continued to beg for it again and again.
This man's obsession with the attainment of a name became well known throughout the Saṅgha of monks. Then one day, in the Hall of Dharma—
The monks, having sat down together, raised this discussion: "Friends, it is said that such-and-such a monk, who is supposedly accomplished in names, causes [people] to choose an auspicious name.
Then the Teacher, having come to the Hall of Truth, asked: "Monks, with what discussion are you sitting here now?
When they replied, "With this one, sir," he said: "Monks, it is not only now that he..."
“Even in the past, he was one whose name brought ill fortune,” he said, and related a story from the past.
In the past, at Takkasilā, the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher who taught the mantras to five hundred young brahmins.
Among them was one young brahmin named Pāpaka. Whenever he was addressed, he was told, “Come, Pāpaka! Go, Pāpaka!”
He thought, "My name is inauspicious; I shall have another name bestowed upon me. He approached his teacher and said, "Teacher, my name is inauspicious; please give me another name.
Then the teacher said to him, "Go, dear boy, travel through the countryside and choose for yourself one auspicious name that pleases you."
“Take this and come; once you have arrived, I will change your name and give you another.
Saying, “Very well,” he took his provisions and set out. Traveling from village to village, he reached a certain city.
There, a man named Jīvaka had recently passed away. Seeing him being carried to the cremation ground by his kinsmen, [he asked], “What...?”
“What is this man’s name? he asked. “His name is Jīvaka. “Does even Jīvaka die? “Jīvaka dies too, and one who is not Jīvaka dies too;
‘name’ is merely a designation. You seem to be a fool,” he replied.
Having heard those words, he became indifferent toward the name and entered the city.
Now, there was a certain maidservant who did not give her wages; her masters made her sit at the door and beat her with a rope.
Her name was Dhanapālī. As he was walking along the street, he saw her being beaten and asked, "Why are you beating this woman?
"She is unable to give her wages. "But what is her name? "Dhanapālī."
"By name. Even though she was named Dhanapālī, she was unable to provide even a mere pittance; thus, both those who were "Dhanapālīs" and those who were not "Dhanapālīs" became destitute.
A name is merely a designation. "You think you are a fool," he said.
Becoming more indifferent toward the name, he departed from the city and set out on the road; on the way, seeing a man who had lost his path, he said: "O friend!"
“What are you doing as you wander about? he asked. “I am lost on the road, sir,” he replied. “But what is your name? “My name is Paṇṭhaka.
“Does even Paṇṭhaka get lost on the road? “Both Paṇṭhaka and Apanṭhaka get lost on the road;
‘name’ is merely a conventional designation. But you, sir, seem to think that a name is something substantial. Having become indifferent toward his own name, he [approached] the Bodhisatta.

Having gone into his presence, when he was asked, "My dear son, having chosen what name have you come?", he replied: "Teacher, those called 'Jīvaka' (living) die just as those called 'Ajīvaka' (non-living) do;
those who protect wealth become poor just as those who do not protect wealth do; those on the path become lost just as those who are off the path do.
A name is merely a designation; there is no accomplishment through a name, for accomplishment comes only through action."
“Enough with another name for me; let that very same name be mine,” he said. The Bodhisatta, correlating what had been seen and what had been done, spoke this verse:
“Having seen Jīvaka dead and Dhanapāli in misery;”
“And Panthaka, who was lost in the forest, has returned again, though he was wicked.
In this context, “returned again” means that he came back after seeing these three reasons; the letter *r* is used here for the sake of euphonic junction (*sandhi*).
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher said: “Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, this man was one whose name brought success.”
Having spoken thus, he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Nāmasiddhika was indeed Nāmasiddhika even now;
the teacher’s assembly was the Buddha’s assembly, and I myself was the teacher.
This concludes the seventh commentary, the Nāmasiddhi Jātaka.
[98] 8. The Commentary on the Kūṭavāṇija Jātaka:
"It is indeed good to be wise. This was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a fraudulent merchant.
For in Sāvatthī, two men who were trading together took their goods in a cart and went to the countryside.
Having gone and obtained their profit, they returned. Among them, the fraudulent merchant thought: "This man has been exhausted by poor food and miserable sleep for many days;
now, having eaten as much fine food as he desires with various delicious flavors at his own home, he will die from indigestion.
Then I shall divide this merchandise into three portions and give one to his children."
“I will give [you a share], but I shall take two portions for myself. Thus he did not wish to divide the goods, saying, “We shall divide them today; we shall divide them tomorrow.

Then the wise merchant, having pressured him against his will until he was made to divide them, went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and after the customary exchange of greetings, said: “You have caused excessive delay; even though you have come here—”
When he was told, "It has been a long time since you last came to attend upon the Buddha," he reported that occurrence to the Blessed One.
The Teacher said, "Lay follower, this man was not only a fraudulent trader now; in the past, too, he was a fraudulent trader.
But now he has become intent on deceiving me, whereas in the past he was capable of deceiving even the wise. Having said this, at his request, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a merchant family in Bārāṇasī;

on the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name “Paṇḍita. When he reached maturity, he engaged in trade together with another merchant, and that man’s name was “Atipaṇḍita. From Bārāṇasī, the two of them—by means of five...
Taking their goods on hundreds of carts, they went to the countryside, engaged in trade, and having acquired profit, they returned again to Bārāṇasī.
Then, at the time of dividing the merchandise, the Over-wise One said, "I should receive two shares. "For what reason? he asked.
"Because you are wise and I am over-wise. A wise man deserves one share; an over-wise man..."
"Two? "But surely even the price of our two goods, including the oxen and so forth, was exactly equal;
why do you deserve to receive two portions? "Because of my extreme cleverness. Thus they increased their dispute through such talk.
Then the "extremely clever" one, thinking, "There is a certain stratagem," caused his father to enter a hollow tree.
Having said, “When we have arrived, you should say, ‘He is exceedingly wise;
he deserves two portions,’” they approached the Bodhisatta and said, “Friend, this tree deity knows whether my receiving two portions is appropriate or inappropriate.
Come, let us ask her. Having led him there, they said, “Noble tree deity, ...”
“Settle our dispute,” he said. Then his father, turning over the dice, said, “In that case, speak.
[The other replied: “Noble lady, this man is wise, while I am exceedingly wise. We have made a transaction together; therein, what should be obtained by whom?
One portion should be obtained by the wise one, but two portions by the exceedingly wise one.”
When the Bodhisatta heard the judgment thus pronounced, he thought, "Now I shall know whether he is a deity or not a deity," and having brought straw,
he filled the hollow and set it on fire. When the flames touched the exceedingly wise man,
his father climbed up with his body half-burnt, grasped a branch while hanging there, and falling to the ground, he uttered this verse:
“It is indeed good to be wise, but not to be over-wise;
for by a son who is over-wise, I have been overwhelmed.
In this context, “It is indeed good to be wise” means one who is endowed with wisdom in this world, knowing what is the right course and what is the wrong course.
The person was good and handsome. "Extremely wise"—merely by this name he was called extremely wise, yet he was not truly a superior man.
"He has been scorched in my presence" means he has been slightly burned; the sense is that he escaped with only half-burnt.
Both of them, having split the middle and taken an equal portion, departed according to their karma.

The Teacher, thinking, "In the past, too, this man was a fraudulent merchant," brought forth this past event and identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the fraudulent merchant was the same as the fraudulent merchant of the present, while the wise merchant was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Kūṭavāṇija Jātaka, the eighth.
[99] 9. Commentary on the Parosahassa Jātaka.
“Even if they have gathered by the thousands”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the five questions asked by worldlings (*puthujjana*).
The story will be made clear in the *Sarabha Jātaka*. On one occasion, however, the monks, having assembled in the Hall of Truth (*dhammasabhā*), said:
“Friends, that which was spoken in brief by the One of Ten Powers, the General of the Dhamma...”
Sāriputta explained it in detail,” they said, sitting there while recounting the Elder’s virtues.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that Sāriputta explains in detail what has been spoken by me in brief.”
"Even in the past he would have explained it," he said, and then he related a story of the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of northern brahmins.
Having mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, he renounced sensual pleasures, went forth as an ascetic, and attained the five supernormal powers (pañca-abhiññā).
Having attained the eight meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he dwelt in the Himalayas. His retinue consisted of five hundred ascetics.
Then, during the rainy season, his senior disciple took half of the group of seers and went to the inhabited world to subsist on salt and sour gruel.
At that time, the time for the Bodhisatta’s passing away arrived. Then his disciples...
“Teacher, what spiritual quality have you attained? they asked, inquiring about his realization. He replied, “There is nothing at all,” and was reborn in the Ābhassara Brahma-world.
For even though Bodhisattas may have attained the formless absorptions, they are not reborn in the formless realms because such places are unfitting for them.
The pupils, thinking that their teacher had no realization, did not perform the funeral honors at the cremation ground.
The senior pupil came and asked, "Where is the teacher? Upon hearing that he had passed away, he asked, "Did you ask the teacher about his realization?
"Yes, we did," they replied. "What did he say? "He said, 'There is nothing,' and so we did not offer him the funeral honors," they said. The senior pupil [said], "You [have failed] the teacher..."

“You do not understand the meaning of the words; your teacher has attained the meditative absorption of the base of nothingness,” he said. Although he spoke thus again and again, they did not believe him.
The Bodhisatta, understanding the reason for this, thought, “These blind fools do not believe the words of my senior disciple.
I shall make this matter clear to them. Having said this, he descended from the Brahma-world.
Standing in the sky with great majesty at the edge of the hermitage, praising the power of wisdom of his senior disciple,
he spoke this verse:
“Even if more than a thousand who lack wisdom were to gather together and cry out for a hundred years;”
“Better than a thousand people is that one wise man who understands the meaning of what is spoken.
In this context, “even more than a thousand” means exceeding a thousand. “Of those assembled” refers to fools gathered together who are unable to understand the meaning of what is spoken.
“They might cry out for a hundred years, being devoid of wisdom” refers to those very people thus assembled.

This indicates that these people, being devoid of wisdom, might weep and lament for even a hundred years or a thousand years—just like foolish ascetics—but even while weeping, they would know neither the goal nor the reason.
"Better than a thousand such fools is one wise man" means that even compared to more than a thousand such fools, a single wise man is better and more excellent. What kind of person is "wise"?
"He who understands the meaning of what has been spoken is like the senior pupil.

Thus the Great Being, while remaining in the sky, taught the Dhamma, awakened the company of ascetics, and departed for the Brahma-world itself. Those ascetics, too, at the end of their lives, became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, Sāriputta was the senior pupil, and I myself was the Great Brahmā."
The ninth: The Commentary on the Parosahassa Jātaka.
[100] 10. The Commentary on the Asātarūpa Jātaka:
"The unpleasant as pleasant"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Kuṇḍadhāna Forest near the city of Kuṇḍiya.
He spoke concerning the female lay follower Suppavāsā, the daughter of the Koliyan king.
At that time, having carried a fetus in her womb for seven years, she had been suffering from a difficult labor for seven days, and extreme pains were occurring.
Although she was thus overwhelmed by such extreme pain, [she thought]: "Truly, the Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One, who..."
"He teaches the Dhamma for the abandoning of such suffering. Well-practiced indeed is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, who has practiced for the abandoning of such suffering.
Truly, Nibbāna is most blissful, wherein even the suffering of form does not exist.
With these three reflections she consented. She then called her husband and [told him] about herself...
She sent [a messenger] to the presence of the Teacher to announce her welfare and to deliver a message of greeting.
Upon hearing the message of greeting, the Teacher said, “May Suppavāsā the Koliyan daughter be well; may she be healthy and give birth to a healthy son.
At the very moment these words were spoken by the Blessed One, Suppavāsā the Koliyan daughter became well and healthy, and gave birth to a healthy son.
She gave birth. Then her husband, having gone home and seeing that she had given birth, exclaimed, "How wonderful!
and was filled with a sense of amazement and wonder due to the Tathāgata’s extraordinary power.
Suppavāsā, too, having given birth to her son, desired for seven days to give alms to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
He sent him again for the purpose of inviting [the Sangha]. Now at that time, the Sangha headed by the Buddha had been invited by Mahāmoggallāna’s attendant.
The Teacher, in order to grant Suppavāsā the opportunity to give her gift, sent the Elder to him;
having thus informed him, he accepted her gift for seven days along with [the rest of] the Sangha.
...with the community of bhikkhus. On the seventh day, however, Suppavāsā, having adorned her son Prince Sīvali, had him pay homage to both the Teacher and the community of bhikkhus.
When he was led into the presence of the Elder Sāriputta in due order, the Elder exchanged greetings with him, saying:
"I hope it is bearable for you, Sīvali? He replied: "How could it be so, venerable sir?..."
“‘It was happy, Svāha; for seven years I dwelt in a copper cauldron,’ she said, engaging in such conversation with the Elder.
Upon hearing his words, Suppavāsā attained a state of joy, thinking, ‘My son, only seven days old, is conversing with the Dhamma-Senāpati who has awakened.
The Teacher said, ‘Suppavāsā, are there others like this?’”
"Do you wish for sons? he asked. "Venerable sir, if I could obtain seven such sons as these, I would certainly wish for them.
Having uttered this inspired utterance and offered words of thanksgiving, the Teacher departed.

Prince Sīvali, at the age of only seven years, having placed his heart in the Dispensation and gone forth, received full ordination when he had reached the full age, and being possessed of merit, attained the pinnacle of gain.
Having made the offering, caused the earth to resound, and attained Arahatship, he reached the foremost position among those possessed of merit.
Then one day, the monks having assembled in the Dhamma Hall, said: "Friends, the Elder named Sīvalī is such a person of great merit;
having fulfilled his aspirations, this being in his final existence lived for seven years in a copper vessel filled with blood."
They raised the discussion, saying, "She remained in a state of obstructed labor for seven days; oh, what great suffering both mother and child experienced!

What deed must they have committed? The Teacher, having arrived there, asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now? When they replied, "For this very one," he said, "Monks, regarding Sīvalī..."
"Both the seven-year residence in a copper vessel and the seven days spent as a child in the womb were rooted in deeds performed by Mahāpuñña himself;
likewise, both the seven years of suffering from carrying the fetus in her womb and the seven days of suffering from a difficult labor were rooted in deeds performed by Suppavāsā herself.
Having said this, at their request, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of his chief queen.
Upon reaching maturity, he mastered all arts at Takkasilā;
after his father’s passing, he ascended the throne and ruled according to the Dhamma. At that time, the Great King of Kosala arrived with a vast army.
Having seized Benares and killed the king, he made that very king’s chief queen his own chief queen.
But the son of the King of Benares, having fled through the drainage gate at the time of his father’s death, gathered an army and returned to Benares;
sitting down not far away, he sent a letter to the king saying, "Give me either the kingdom or battle."
Thus, he dispatched a messenger who had set out with the intent: "I shall give battle. But when the prince’s mother heard that message, she said:
"There is no need for battle; cut off all movement in every direction and surround the city of Bārāṇasī.
Then, by the exhaustion of its fuel, water, and food, you will capture the city even without a fight, once its people are worn out."
He sent a letter. Having heard his mother’s message, he cut off all movement for seven days and besieged the city.
The citizens, unable to find a way out, on the seventh day took the head of that king and gave it to the prince.
The prince, having entered the city and taken over the kingdom, passed away at the end of his life and went according to his karma.
Thus, having now cut off all movement for seven days and besieged the city,
as a result of that deed he lived for seven years in a vessel of blood and entered upon a state of obstructed labor for seven days. However,
because he had given a great alms-offering at the feet of the Blessed One Padumuttara, thinking, "May I become the foremost among those who receive gains," [he attained this preeminence].
Because she had made a formal aspiration (paṭṭhāna) during the time of Vipassī Buddha— having offered sugar and curd worth a thousand pieces of gold together with the citizens—
she became the foremost among those who receive gains through the power of that merit. As for Suppavāsā, because she had been sent with the command, "Seize the city,
my dear," she carried the fetus in her womb for seven years and was born with the fetus still obstructed for seven days.
The Teacher, having brought up this past event and having attained full enlightenment,
spoke this verse: “Disagreeable things in the form of the agreeable, The unlovely in the form of the lovely,
And suffering in the form of happiness— These overcome the heedless.”
In this context, "the disagreeable in the form of the agreeable" means that which is not sweet [appears] in the likeness of what is sweet.

"The heedless one is overcome" means that these three types—the disagreeable, the unlovely, and suffering—overcome, master, and overwhelm the heedless person by way of the absence of mindfulness through such modes as the appearance of the agreeable; this is what was stated by the Blessed One.
Those mother and son were overwhelmed by this experience— consisting of the protection of the womb and dwelling in the womb— which was unpleasant and the like, yet appeared as pleasant and so forth,
just as their previous confinement in the city had appeared as pleasant and the like; and now that laywoman has likewise been overwhelmed seven times over by such unpleasantness,
disagreeableness, and suffering, which, though consisting of the protection of the womb and dwelling in the womb, appeared as pleasant and the like because her son was the object of her affection.
It should be understood that all of this was spoken with reference to him.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the prince who captured the city and obtained the kingdom was Sīvali; his mother was Suppavāsā, and his father, the King of Bārāṇasī, was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Asātarūpa Jātaka, the tenth.
The Tenth Chapter: The Littavagga.
Its summary (uddāna) is as follows: Littateja, Mahāsāra, Vissāsa, and Lomahaṃsana.
Sudassana, the oil-bowl, Nāmasiddhi, the fraudulent merchant,
and the more than thousand forms of the unpleasant—
thus ends the Middle Fifty.
11. Parosata-vagga [101] 1.
Parosata-jātaka-vaṇṇanā “Even if more than a hundred have gathered together, if they should meditate for a hundred years without wisdom...”
“Better than a thousand men is one wise man who understands the meaning of what is spoken.
This Jātaka is identical in its narrative background (*vatthu*), its exposition (*veyyākaraṇa*), and its synthesis (*samodhāna*) with more than a thousand other Jātakas;
the only difference here is the single word “they should meditate” (*jhāyeyyuṃ*). Its meaning is as follows: even for a hundred years, those lacking wisdom...
They might meditate upon it, look into it, and investigate it; yet even while looking thus, they do not perceive the meaning or the reason.
Therefore, he alone who knows the meaning of what has been spoken is truly wise and superior.
This concludes the first commentary on the *Parosata-jātaka*.
[102] 2. The Commentary on the Paṇṇika Jātaka:
"Who might be a refuge for one touched by suffering. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain lay follower who was a vendor of leaves.
It is said that this lay follower, a resident of Sāvatthī, [dealt in] various kinds of roots, leaves, and so forth.
He made his living by selling gourds, pumpkins, and other such items.
He had a daughter who was beautiful, pleasing, endowed with good conduct and virtue, possessed of a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, and always had a smiling face.
When suitors from families of equal status arrived seeking her hand in marriage, he thought: "It is time for her marriage, yet she always has a smiling face."

Furthermore, if the maiden’s virtue is lacking, there will be reproach from her parents once she has gone to another family, thinking, "I shall investigate whether or not this maiden possesses the virtue of a maiden.
One day, having had his daughter take a basket, he went into the forest for the sake of gathering leaves; then, as a means of testing her, he acted as if he were dependent upon defilement.
Having offered the sacrifice and spoken in secret, he took her by the hand.
As soon as she was seized, she wept and cried out, "This is improper, father; it is like fire appearing from water! Do not do such a thing!
"My dear child," he said, "I have taken your hand for the sake of testing you, not out of defilement. Tell me, do you now..."
“...the conduct of a maiden. “Yes, father, there is. For I have never before looked upon any man with lustful intent.
Having comforted his daughter, he brought her home, performed the auspicious rites, and sent her to her husband’s family.

Then, thinking, “I shall pay homage to the Teacher,” he went to Jetavana with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in his hands; having paid homage to the Teacher and made offerings, he sat down to one side.

When he was told, "It has been a long time since you last arrived," he reported that matter to the Blessed One. The Teacher said, "Lay follower, this young woman has long been endowed with virtuous conduct;
it is not only now that you examine her in this way, but you have examined her even in the past.
Having been thus requested by him, the Teacher related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in the forest.
Now, there was a certain lay merchant in Benares; the background story is exactly like the present one.
