But when she was merely grasped by him for the sake of testing her, she, lamenting, spoke this verse:
“He who would be a refuge for one touched by suffering—he, my father, acts with cruelty in the forest.
To whom shall I cry out in the midst of the woods? He who was my protector now acts with violence.
In this context, “one who would be a refuge for one touched by suffering” means a protector for one touched by physical and mental sufferings.
"She would have been my protector and support. "My father, that betrayer, acts thus in the forest"—the meaning is:
my father, who was my protector from suffering, now commits such an act of treachery against a friend in this forest;
he thinks to transgress against his own daughter. "To whom shall I cry out?"—to whom shall I weep? Who will be my support?
"He illuminates. "He who is my protector commits a violent act"—the meaning is: he who ought to be my protector, my guardian, and my refuge, that very father commits a deed of violence.

Then the father, having comforted her, asked, "Daughter, is your person protected? "Yes, father, my person is protected. He led her home, adorned her, performed the auspicious rites, and sent her to the other family.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the lay follower was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
"At that time, the father was the father of today; the daughter was the daughter of today; and as for the tree deity who witnessed the event firsthand, she was none other than myself.
This is the second commentary on the Paṇṇika Jātaka.
[103] 3. The Commentary on the Verijātaka.
"Wherever an enemy dwells..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning Anāthapiṇḍika.
It is said that Anāthapiṇḍika, having gone to his village of wealth and returning along the road, saw bandits there and thought, "On the road..."

"It is not proper for me to stay; I shall go to Sāvatthī itself. Having urged his oxen forward with speed, he returned to Sāvatthī and went to the monastery on the following day, where he reported this matter to the Teacher.
The Teacher said, "Householder, in the past as well, wise men, upon seeing bandits along the way, did not linger but proceeded directly to their own place of residence."
Being thus requested, he brought forth a story of the past:
"In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a very wealthy merchant.
Having gone to a certain village to eat at an invitation, while returning on the road, he encountered bandits."
Having stayed on the way, he hurriedly drove his oxen, returned to his own home, ate various choice delicacies,
and while seated on a great couch, spoke this verse as an utterance of joy: "I have escaped from the hands of the thieves and have come to my own home, a place of safety."
“Where an enemy dwells, there a wise person should not live;
for one night or two nights, one who has an enemy dwells in suffering.
In this context, “enemy” (*verī*) refers to a person possessing the volition of enmity. “Dwells” (*nivisati*) means to settle. “There a wise person should not live” means:
In whatever place that hostile person is established and dwells, a wise person endowed with wisdom should not dwell there.
Why is that? Because "one dwells in suffering among enemies for one night or two nights";
the meaning is that while dwelling among enemies, one dwells in nothing but suffering even for a single day or two days.
Thus the Great Being, having uttered this inspired utterance and performed meritorious deeds such as giving, departed according to his karma.
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, I myself was the merchant of Bārāṇasī.
This is the third commentary on the Verijātaka.
[104] 4. The Commentary on the Mittavindaka Jātaka:
"From four, eight were obtained. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was difficult to speak to.
The narrative should be related in detail according to the method already stated below in the Mittavindaka Jātaka. However, this Jātaka—

This was during the time of the Buddha Kassapa. At that time, a certain being in hell, who was being cooked in hell after having been cast up by his chest-wheel, asked the Bodhisatta: "Venerable sir, what evil deed did I commit?
The Bodhisatta, saying, "You committed this and that evil deed," spoke this verse:
“From four he attained eight, and from eight, sixteen;
from sixteen, thirty-two. The wheel of one who is insatiate rolls upon his head;
for the person overcome by desire, the wheel turns upon his crown.”

Regarding the phrase *catubbhi aṭṭhajjhagamā*: having obtained four celestial nymphs (*vimānapeti*) in the midst of the ocean, being dissatisfied with them, he went further due to his lack of contentment;
the meaning is that he attained another eight. The same method applies to the other two lines as well.
Regarding *atricchaṃ cakkamāsadoti*: thus, being dissatisfied with his entire acquisition, seeking here and there, he went further...
"Longing for gain from others, you have now come under the wheel; you have reached this breast-wheel.
For you, a man thus struck by desire, struck and ruined by craving, the wheel revolves upon your head.
Between these two—the stone wheel and the iron wheel—it is the razor-edged iron wheel that revolves repeatedly upon your head by way of falling down."
Having seen this, he spoke thus; and having spoken, he departed for his own celestial realm.
That being in hell also, when his own evil karma was exhausted, departed according to his destiny.
Having brought forth this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Mittavindaka was the monk of harsh speech, and I myself was the son of the gods."
The Fourth: The Commentary on the Mittavindaka Jātaka.
[105] 5. The Commentary on the Dubbalakaṭṭha Jātaka:
"There is much wood here in the forest. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain terrified bhikkhu.
He related the story: it seems there was once a son of good family living in Sāvatthī who, having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, went forth into homelessness.

However, he was fearful of death; whether at night or by day while standing in his watch-post, whenever he heard the wind blowing, or a dry branch falling, or the sound of birds or quadrupeds, he was so terrified by the fear of death that he would let out a great cry.
He flees. For he does not possess even a mere measure of mindfulness that "I must die.
If he were to know, "I shall die," he would not fear death. It is precisely because he has not cultivated the meditation subject of mindfulness of death that he fears it.
This state of his, being terrified of death, became well known throughout the community of monks.
Then one day, in the Hall of Dharma, the monks initiated a discussion: "Friends, such-and-such a monk is afraid of death;
he fears dying. It is fitting for a monk to develop the meditation subject of mindfulness of death, thinking: 'I must certainly die.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you sitting gathered here now?"
Having questioned him, when it was said, "It is indeed she," he had that monk summoned and asked, "Is it true, as it seems, that you are afraid of death?
When he replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," [the Buddha] said, "Monks, do not be displeased with this monk;
it is not only now that he is afraid of death, but even in the past he was afraid of death. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in the Himalayas.
At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī gave his state elephant to the elephant trainers to train it in the art of *āneñja* (immovability).
Having bound it immovably to its post, men with lances in their hands surrounded it.

They subjected him to the "immovable" torture. While undergoing that torture, being unable to endure the sensation, he broke his tethering post, frightened away the men, and entered the Himalayas. The men, unable to capture him, turned back.
There, he became fearful of death; hearing the sounds of the wind, trembling and terrified by the fear of death, he [raised] his trunk...
Having shaken it off, he flees with speed; having been tied to a post, it is as if it is time for him to perform the act of immovability.
Failing to obtain either physical refreshment or mental refreshment, he wanders about trembling.
Seeing him, a tree deity standing upon a branch spoke this verse:
“Much indeed is this wood in the forest that the wind breaks, being weak;
if you fear it, O Naga, you will surely become emaciated.
Herein, this is the summarized meaning: that weak wood which the wind—divided into the eastern and other directions—breaks.
"That [meat] is abundant and easily obtained in this forest; it is found here and there.
If you are afraid of it, then, being constantly afraid under such circumstances, you will surely become emaciated after the depletion of your flesh and blood.
But in this forest, there is no cause for fear for you; therefore, from now on, do not be afraid."
Thus the deity gave him this advice, and from that time forth he was free from fear.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. "At that time, the Nāga was this bhikkhu, and the tree-deity..."
"But it was I myself who was he.
The commentary on the *Dubbalakaṭṭha Jātaka* is the fifth.
[106] 6. The commentary on the *Udañcanī Jātaka*.
“‘May they indeed live happily!’—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the seduction of Thullakumārikā.
The story will be made clear in the *Cūḷanāradakassapa Jātaka* of the *Terasakanipāta*.
Then the Teacher asked that bhikkhu, ‘Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are disenchanted? and he replied, ‘It is true.’”
When he replied, “Lord,” the Blessed One asked, “To whom is your mind bound? He said, “To a certain young woman.

Then the Teacher said to him, “This woman has brought you harm; in the past as well, by relying on her, you fell into ruin regarding your virtue and wandered about trembling, but by relying on the wise, you obtained happiness. Having said this, he related the past.
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī"—this past narrative will also be made clear in the Cūḷanāradakassapa Jātaka.

At that time, however, the Bodhisatta, having returned in the evening with various fruits, opened the door of the leaf-hut, entered, and said this to his son, the young ascetic: "Dear son, on other days you [would gather] wood..."
“You bring food, you bring drinking water and water for rinsing, and you tend the fire;
yet today, having done none of these, why are you lying there with a dejected face, brooding? “Father, while you had gone out for fruit, a woman came, seduced me, and began to take me away.
But I thought, ‘I shall go only when dismissed by you.’”
“I did not go; rather, having seated him at such-and-such a place, I have returned. Now I am going, dear father.
The Bodhisatta, realizing that it was impossible to turn him back, said, “In that case, dear father, you may go.
But when she wishes to eat fish, meat, and so forth, or when she desires ghee, salt, rice, and the like—”

"When there is need, then you will weary yourself by saying, 'Bring this and bring that. At that time, remembering my virtue, you should flee and come back right here," he dismissed him. He went with her to a human settlement.
Then, having brought him under her control, she said to him, "Bring meat! Bring fish! whenever she had need of anything.

When he had become so, he would have various things brought for him. Then, thinking, "This man oppresses me as if making me his own slave or a laborer," he fled, went to his father’s presence, and while standing there after bowing to his father, he spoke this verse:
"Happy indeed am I while living, though the water-drawing ladle cooks me!"
“Under the pretext of being a thief, she begs for oil and salt.
Regarding that, “May I indeed live happily” means, dear one, may I live happily in your presence.
“Cooking” means heating, pressing, or whatever it is they desire to eat, they cook that very thing. They draw water.
"Udañcanī" means a water-lifting device; it is the name for a small jar used for drawing water from a well or a cistern.
The meaning is that, like a water-lifting device, like water, and like a jar, it draws toward itself whatever one has need of. "By a female thief under the pretext of being a wife":
a certain female thief, having enticed me there with sweet words under the name of "wife,"...
He spoke of her fault, saying: "She demands oil, salt, and whatever else she desires;
treating him like a slave or a laborer, she makes him bring it.
Then the Bodhisatta comforted him, saying: "Be at ease, dear one; come, you must cultivate loving-kindness (mettā) and cultivate compassion (karuṇā)."
He taught the four divine abidings (brahmavihāra), and having taught them, he taught the preliminary practice for the kasiṇas.

Before long, having produced the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and the meditative attainments (samāpatti), and having cultivated the divine abidings, he was reborn in the Brahma-world together with his father.

Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths (sacca), the Teacher identified the Jātaka; at the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti).
“Then the elder maiden was indeed the elder maiden of today; the junior ascetic was the dissatisfied bhikkhu, and my father was none other than myself.
The sixth: The Commentary on the Udañcanī Jātaka.
7. The Commentary on the Sālittaka Jātaka.
“Excellent indeed is what is called a craft!”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was a swan-shooter.
It is said that there was a son of good family living in Sāvatthī who had attained mastery in the craft of *sālittaka*.
“The craft of *sālittaka*” refers to the craft of shooting pebbles. One day, having heard the Dhamma, he [entered] the Teaching...
Having given his breast [in marriage] and gone forth, he received full ordination; however, he was not desirous of training, nor was he a practitioner of the path.
One day, taking a young bhikkhu with him, he went to the Aciravatī River, bathed, and stood on the riverbank.
At that time, two white swans were traveling through the air. He said to the young bhikkhu: "This..."
“Having struck the last swan in the eye with a pebble, I shall cause it to fall at my feet.
The other said, “How will you make it fall? You will not be able to strike it. The other replied, “Let its eye remain on this side for now; I shall strike it in the eye on that side.
But now you are speaking what is untrue. [The first said: “In that case, then test it. He took a sharp pebble.
Having taken it, he placed it at the tip of his finger and threw it behind that swan.
It made the sound "ru," and the swan, thinking, "There must be some danger," turned back and began to listen for the sound.
At that moment, the other took a round pebble and struck the eye of the one who had turned back to look at the rear.
The pebble, having pierced the other eye as well, passed through. The swan, crying out with a great cry, fell right at the Master’s feet.
Then, monks coming from here and there, rebuking him and saying, "What you have done is unbecoming," led him into the presence of the Teacher.
They reported the matter, saying, "Venerable Sir, this man has done such-and-such. The Teacher rebuked that monk.
“Monks, it is not only now that he was skilled in this craft; in the past, too, he was indeed skilled. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his minister.
At that time, the king’s domestic priest was extremely talkative and a great chatterer; while he had begun to speak, others had no opportunity [to speak].
They could not find anyone. The king thought, "When indeed shall I find someone who can interrupt his speech?
From that time on, he wandered about searching for such a person.
At that time, there was a certain cripple in Bārāṇasī who had attained mastery in the craft of throwing pebbles. Village boys placed him upon a cart and...
Dragging it along, they brought it to the foot of a great banyan tree with many branches near the gate of the city of Bārāṇasī;
having surrounded it there and given him a farthing and other such coins, they said, "Make the form of an elephant!
Make the form of a horse! Throwing pebble after pebble, he displayed various forms upon the leaves of the banyan tree—indeed, all of them.
The leaves were completely perforated with holes.
Then the King of Bārāṇasī, while proceeding to the pleasure garden, arrived at that spot. Out of fear of the royal proclamation, all the children fled, but the cripple remained lying right there.
Having reached the foot of the banyan tree, the king sat in his chariot and [looked at] the leaves.
Seeing the variegated shadows cast by the gaps [in the bowls], he looked closely; seeing that all the alms-bowls had holes, he asked, "By whom were these made thus?
"By a cripple, Your Majesty," they replied. The king thought, "With the help of this man, it will be possible to cut off the Brahmin's speech," and he asked, "Where is the cripple, my good man?"
The neighbors, seeing him lying between the roots, said, "This is he, Your Majesty.
The king summoned him, cleared the assembly, and asked, "There is a certain talkative brahmin in our presence; will you be able to make him silent?
"If I receive as much as a reed-measure of *ajalaṇḍika* beans, I shall be able to do so, Your Majesty," he replied. The king [sent] the cripple to his house...
Having led him inside and made him sit down, she had a hole made in the screen and arranged a seat for the brahmin facing toward the hole.
She then had some dried *ajalaṇḍika* fruit, about the size of a reed, placed near the lizard.
When the brahmin arrived at the time of his visit, she had him sit on that seat and initiated a conversation. The brahmin [asked] others...
Without giving him an opportunity to speak with the king, he began to talk.
Then the cripple, as if inserting a single frog at a time through a hole in a winnowing basket, caused them to fall right upon the surface of his palate;
the Brahmin swallowed each one as it arrived, like pouring oil into a tube until they were all exhausted. This quantity was merely the size of a tube.
The *ajalaṇḍikā* fruits that had entered their stomachs amounted to half an *āḷhaka*.
When the king realized they were exhausted, he said:

"Teacher, because of your excessive talkativeness, you swallowed as many as half a reed-bundle of *ajalaṇḍikā* fruits without realizing anything; from now on, you will not be able to digest any more."
"Go, drink the piyaṅgudaka water, and having discarded [the illness], make yourselves healthy.
From that time on, the brahmin became as if he had his mouth covered; even when spoken to, he was one who would not speak with him.
The king, thinking, "He has brought pleasure to my ears," gave four villages in the four directions, each worth a hundred thousand coins, to the cripple.
He gave [the money]. The Bodhisatta approached the king and said, “Your Majesty, a craft indeed must be learned by the wise in this world;
even by a cripple, through merely making earthenware pots, this prosperity was obtained. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Excellent indeed is a craft, whatever it may be;”
"Behold, by the strike of a cripple, four villages were obtained in the four directions.

Therein, "Behold, by the strike of a cripple," means: "Behold, Great King, how by this strike of a cripple—a cripple who was a bed-snake—four villages in the four directions were obtained; what limit can there be to the benefits of other crafts? Thus he spoke of the excellence of the craft.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the cripple was this very bhikkhu; the king was Ānanda; and the wise minister was none other than myself.
This concludes the seventh narrative, the Sālittaka Jātaka.
8. The Bāhiya Jātaka Narrative:
"One should train in what ought to be trained"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest near Vesālī, concerning a certain Licchavi.

It is said that this Licchavi king, being faithful and confident, invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha and hosted a great almsgiving at his own residence. His wife, however, had stout limbs and members.
She appeared like a bloated corpse and was devoid of proper decorum.

At the conclusion of the meal, the Teacher gave his blessing, went to the monastery, and after giving exhortation to the bhikkhus, entered the fragrant chamber. Thereupon, the bhikkhus initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth:
"Friends, even for such a handsome Licchavi king, how can he have such a wife?"
“With his limbs and members so gross and lacking in decorum, how could he take delight with her?
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now? When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, he took delight only with a woman who was gross-bodied.”
Having spoken thus, being requested by them, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his minister.
Now, a certain country woman, stout of body and lacking in decorum, was working for hire not far from the royal courtyard.
As she was walking along, being oppressed by the discharge from her body, she covered herself with her lower garment, sat down, and released the bodily waste; having done so, she rose up immediately.
At that moment, the King of Bārāṇasī, looking out at the royal courtyard through a window, saw her and thought: "This woman is discharging bodily waste in such a public place."
"Having cast aside shame and fear of blame, she uncovered herself with only her lower garment, exposed her private parts, and quickly stood up.
She must be free from disease; her womb will surely be pure.
When a son is conceived in a pure womb, he will be pure and meritorious. Therefore, I shall appoint her as my chief queen."
"It is fitting to do so. Having learned that she was unattached [to another], he had her brought and appointed her to the position of chief queen.
She became dear and pleasing to him, and before long, she gave birth to a son.
That son of hers became a universal monarch (cakkavatti-rāja).
The Bodhisatta, seeing her prosperity and finding such an opportunity for speech, said:
"Your Majesty, why should one not train in the arts that ought to be learned?

For indeed, it was by training in them that this woman of great merit, without abandoning shame and fear of wrongdoing, attained such prosperity after pleasing you while performing bodily services in a concealed manner."
Having spoken thus, while praising the crafts that ought to be learned, he recited this verse:
“One should train in those things that ought to be trained; there are people who possess the desire [to learn].
For by means of a good shave, Bāhiya pleased the king.”
In that regard, "there are people who have a desire" means there are indeed people who have a desire for various crafts.
"Bāhiyā" refers to a woman born and raised in the Bāhīka country. "By means of a 'suhanna'"—*hanna* means what is struck down;

*suhanna* is that which is struck down while not abandoning shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*), and it is by means of that *suhanna*. "She gratified the king" means having gratified the lord, she [presented] this...
"He attained prosperity. Thus the Great Being spoke of the excellence of the crafts suitable for training.

Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the husband and wife were the husband and wife of the present day; as for the wise minister, he was none other than myself.
This is the eighth narrative, the Bāhiya-jātaka.
[109] 9. The Commentary on the Kuṇḍakapūva Jātaka:
"Whatever kind of person one is..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Sāvatthī concerning a man of great poverty.
For at times in Sāvatthī, only a single family would give alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Sometimes three or four people would come together; sometimes they would do so in groups; sometimes by neighborhood;
and sometimes the entire city would collect alms. On that occasion, however, it was known as a "street-meal.
Then, after the people had given rice-gruel to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, they said, "Bring some solid food! At that time—
A certain poor man who worked for hire, living on that street, thought:
"I will not be able to give rice-gruel, but I shall give some food.
Having prepared very fine broken rice, moistened it with water, wrapped it in a leaf, and roasted it over hot embers, he thought, "I will give this to the Buddha," and [offered] it.
Having taken it and gone to stand in the presence of the Teacher, as soon as the Teacher had spoken the single word,
"Bring some solid food," he went first of all and placed that cake into the Teacher’s bowl; the Teacher,
not accepting the solid food being offered by others, consumed that very cake.

At that very moment, a great clamor arose throughout the entire city: "It is said that the Perfectly Enlightened One, without revulsion, has consumed the *kuṇḍaka* porridge of the Great Poor Man as if it were the Deathless (*amata*).
Then the king, the royal ministers, and all others, down to the doorkeepers, gathered together, paid homage to the Teacher, and approached the Great Poor Man.
“Come now, sir! Take one hundred, take two hundred, take five hundred, and give us our share,” they said.
He replied, “I shall find out after consulting the Teacher,” and went into the presence of the Teacher and reported the matter to him.
The Teacher said, “Whether you take the wealth or not, give the share to all sentient beings.”
He said, "He began to take the wealth. As people gave according to double, quadruple, octuple, and so forth, they presented nine crores of gold.
Having offered the blessing of thanksgiving (*anumodana*), the Teacher went to the monastery;
when the monks had performed the duties, he gave them the exhortation of the Sugata and entered the Fragrant Chamber (*gandhakuṭī*). At evening time, the King summoned the Great Poor Man.
He honored him with the position of a treasurer.
In the Dhamma Hall, the monks initiated a discussion: "Friends, the Teacher consumed the *kuṇḍaka* cakes given by Mahāduggata without revulsion, as if they were the Deathless;
and Mahāduggata, too, having obtained great wealth and the position of a treasurer..."
“...attained great prosperity. The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that I have eaten that *kuṇḍaka*-cake without feeling disgust;
formerly, when I was a tree deity, I ate it as well, and even then he—”
"By relying on me, he indeed obtained the position of a treasurer," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in an eraṇḍa tree in a certain place.
At that time, the people in that village were devoted to propitiating deities for good fortune. Then, one day—
When the festival arrived, people performed offerings to their respective tree deities.
Then, seeing those people tending to the tree deities, a certain poor man tended to a castor-oil tree (*eraṇḍa-rukkha*).
Those people [offered] various kinds of garlands, perfumes, ointments, and so forth, as well as foods to be chewed and eaten, for their respective deities.
And they took [the offerings] and departed. But he, having taken a *kuṇḍaka* cake and a bowl of water, went and stood not far from an *eraṇḍa* tree and thought:
"Devas eat divine snacks; this deva will not eat my *kuṇḍaka* cake. Why should I throw it away for no reason? I myself shall eat it."
Then he turned back. Standing on the branch of the tree, the Bodhisatta said, "O man, if you were a lord, you would give me sweet snacks.
But you are poor; if I do not eat your cake, what else shall I eat?
Do not deprive me of my portion. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“As a man’s food is, so is his deity’s food.
Bring this *kuṇḍapūva* cake; do not ruin my portion.
In this context, “as a man’s food is” means whatever kind of food he eats; “so is his deity’s food” means that the deity of that man likewise eats that same kind of food.
[The man] said, "Bring this *kuṇḍapūva*. [The Bodhisatta replied,] "Bring this cake baked in a *kuṇḍa* [pot]; do not ruin my portion.
He turned back, looked at the Bodhisatta, and performed the offering ceremony (*balikamma*). Having consumed the essence from that, the Bodhisatta asked, "Man, for what purpose do you attend upon me?
[The man replied,] "I am poor, sir; it is by depending on you that I am released from poverty."
“I am looking after this for the sake of my desire for liberation. “O man, do not worry;
you have performed an act of worship toward one who is grateful and mindful of favors. Surrounding this castor-oil plant, there stand treasure jars, each touching the neck of the next.
Inform the king, have him bring wealth by means of carts, and pile it up in the royal courtyard; the king, being pleased with you, will—”
“...he will grant you the position of treasurer,” said the Bodhisatta, and then he vanished. He did exactly as instructed, and the king granted him the position of treasurer.
Thus, by relying on the Bodhisatta, he attained great prosperity and departed according to his karma.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the poor man was none other than the present poor man, and the deity of the castor-oil tree was I myself.”
The ninth: The Explanation of the Kuṇḍakapūva Jātaka.
[110] 10. The Explanation of the Sabbasaṃhāraka Question:
"There is no one who can gather everything"—this Sabbasaṃhāraka question will be made clear in every respect in the Umaṅga Jātaka.
The commentary on the *Sabbasaṃhāraka-pañha-jātaka* is the tenth.
The eleventh chapter is the *Parosatavagga*.
Its summary verse (*uddāna*) is as follows:
The merchant Parosata, the enemy Mittavindaka,
the weak Udañcanī, Sālitta, Bāhiya, and Kuṇḍakapūva the all-devourer.
12. The Chapter on the Haṃca [111]. 1. The Commentary on the Ass’s Question Jātaka.
Regarding the verse, “If you indeed think thus,” this question of the ass will also be made clear in the Mahā-umaṅga Jātaka itself.
The first commentary: the Gadrabhapañhajātakavaṇṇanā.
[112] 2. The second: the Amarādevīpañhajātakavaṇṇanā.
The verse beginning with "Yena sattubilaṅgā ca" is also known as the Amarādevīpañha; it will be explained in that very same place.
The second commentary on the Amarādevīpañha Jātaka.
[113] 3. The Commentary on the Siṅgāla Jātaka:
"He believed the jackal"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Veḷuvana concerning Devadatta.

At that time, the bhikkhus, having assembled in the Dhamma Hall, said: "Friends, Devadatta has gone to Gayāsīsa taking five hundred bhikkhus with him, and having caused those bhikkhus to adopt his own view by saying, 'What the ascetic Gotama does is not the Dhamma;
what I do is the Dhamma,' he has committed a deliberate lie and [separated] the Saṅgha."
Having broken [the unity of] a single boundary, they sat down discussing Devadatta’s lack of virtue, saying, "Two Uposathas have been performed.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you sitting here now?
When they replied, "About this very one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta is a liar; in the past, too, he was a liar. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in a charnel ground forest.

At that time, a festival was proclaimed in Benares. Thinking, "We shall perform the offering to the *yakṣas*," people scattered fish, meat, and other offerings at various crossroads and street corners, and filled skull-bowls with much liquor.
They set it aside. Then, at the hour of midnight, a certain jackal entered the city through a drain;
having eaten fish and meat and drunk liquor, he entered the midst of a *punnāga* grove and fell asleep until the rising of the sun.
Upon waking and seeing the light, thinking, "It is no longer possible to go out now," he went toward the road and remained there, invisible.
Having lain down, even upon seeing other people he said nothing; but when he saw a certain brahmin going for the purpose of washing his face, he thought:

"Brahmins are indeed greedy for wealth. I shall entice this man with money so that he will carry me out of the city, having placed me under his arm and covered me with his upper robe. Then, in the language of men...
“Brahmin,” he said. He turned back and asked, “Who is calling me? “I am, Brahmin. “For what reason?
“Brahmin, I have two hundred kahāpaṇas. If you can take me by the armpits, cover me with your upper robe, and carry me out of the city so that no one sees you, then those [coins] are yours.”
“I will give you a kahāpaṇa coin. Out of greed for wealth, the brahmin agreed, saying, “Very well.
Having done so, he took it and, departing from the city, went a short distance. Then a jackal asked him, “To what place are you going, brahmin?
“To such-and-such a place,” he replied. “Go to another place a little further on,” the jackal said. Speaking thus again and again, [he led him away].
Having reached the great charnel ground, he said, "Bring me down here. He brought him down there.
Then the jackal said, "In that case, Brahmin, spread out your upper garment. Out of greed for wealth, he agreed, saying, "Very well," and spread it out.
Then, having directed him toward the digging of the earth by saying, "Dig at this foot of the tree," [he took] the Brahmin's upper garment...
Having mounted [the chariot], he let his bodily fluids flow from five places—on the four corners and in the middle—smearing and drenching it, and thus entered the charnel forest.
Standing on the branch of a tree, the Bodhisatta spoke this verse:
“You believed the jackal, O Brahmin drunk on liquor!”
“There is not even a hundred of craftsmen; how could there be two hundred of bronze?

In this context, *saddahāsī* means “you believe,” or rather, it is read as *saddahāsi*, which has the meaning “you trust. “There is not even a hundred of craftsmen” means that he does not even have a hundred craftsmen.
“How could there be two hundred of bronze? means: how indeed could he have two hundred kahāpaṇa coins?
Having spoken this verse, the Bodhisatta said, “Go, brahmin; wash your garment, bathe, and perform your own work,” and then he vanished.
The brahmin, having done so, departed filled with dejection, thinking, “I have been cheated.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction, identified the Jātaka: “At that time Devadatta was the jackal, and I myself was the tree deity.”
The third is the commentary on the Siṅgālajāta­ka.
[114] 4. The commentary on the Mitacintījātaka:
"He who thinks much, he who thinks little"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning two elder monks who were advanced in years.

He related this. It seems that those people, having spent the rainy season retreat in a certain forest dwelling in the countryside, prepared provisions for the journey, thinking, "We shall go to see the Teacher.

But as they delayed for a month, saying, "We shall go today," or "We shall go tomorrow," and then again prepared provisions for another month, and yet another month—thus, due to their own state of indolence...

Having stayed for three months out of regard for their place of residence, they departed from there, went to Jetavana, and after settling their bowls and robes in a suitable location, they saw the Teacher.
Then the monks asked them, "Friends, it has been a long time since you last attended upon the Buddha; why did you stay away so long? They related the matter to them.
Then that state of indolence and laziness of theirs became manifest within the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Even in the Hall of Truth (Dhammasabhā), they initiated a discussion based on the very laziness of those bhikkhus.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Bhikkhus, about what talk are you sitting here gathered now? When they replied, "About this indeed," he summoned them.
"Is it true, monks, that you are lazy and indolent? Having asked this, and being told, "It is true, venerable sir," he said, "Monks, these are not only lazy now;
formerly they were also lazy, and they were attached and longing for their dwelling place. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there were three fish in the river at Bārāṇasī.
Their names were Bahucintī (Much-Thinking), Appacintī (Little-Thinking), and Mitacintī (Measured-Thinking). They came from the forest to a human settlement.
There, Mitacintī said to the other two, “This place called a human settlement is full of danger and fear;
fishermen cast various nets, traps, and the like to catch fish. Let us go back to the forest.”
The other two men, due to both laziness and greed for bait, let three months pass by, saying, "We will go today; we will go tomorrow.
Then the fishermen cast their nets into the river.
Bahucintī and Appacintī were walking ahead, gathering their catch, when through their own foolishness they failed to notice the scent of the net.
They entered the honeycomb itself. As Mitacintī was coming from behind, he noticed the scent of the honey and, knowing that they had entered the honeycomb, thought:
"I shall grant the gift of life to these lazy, blind fools.
Thinking thus, he went to the spot of the honeycomb by way of the outer opening, split open the honeycomb, and appeared as if he had emerged from within.

Having offered himself, he fell before the net while churning the water; then, entering back into the belly of the net, he appeared as if he had emerged after splitting it open at the rear. Churning the water again, he fell at the rear.
Thinking, "The fish have split the net and gone," the fishermen seized the edge of the net and hauled it up. Both those fish [were then released] from the net.
Having been released, they fell into the water. Thus, by relying on Mitacintī, they regained their lives.
Having brought up this past event, the Teacher, having attained full enlightenment, spoke this verse:
“The one who thinks much and the one who thinks little—both were caught in the net.”
“Mitacintī released them; both met there.
In this context, *bahucintī* is one who has acquired that name due to having many thoughts and an abundance of discursive thinking (*vitakka*). The same principle applies to the other two as well.
*Ubho tattha samāgatā* means that those who had obtained their livelihood by depending on Mitacintī met there in the water.
Furthermore, the meaning is that both men met with Mitacintin.
Thus the Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the elder monks were established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, Bahucintin and Appacintin were these two [monks].
There were two others, but I myself was Mitacintī.
This concludes the commentary on the Mitacintī Jātaka, the fourth.
[115] 5. Commentary on the Anusāsika Jātaka.
"He who instructs others rightly"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain instructing bhikkhunī.
It seems that she was a daughter of a noble family living in Sāvatthī who had gone forth;
from the time of her full ordination, however, she did not apply herself to the duties of a recluse, but became greedy for material gain, going to places where other bhikkhunīs would not go.
She wandered for alms in a certain part of the city. Then people gave her choice almsfood. Bound by craving for flavors, she thought:
"If other bhikkhunīs also wander for alms in this place, my gains will diminish.
It is right for me to act in such a way that others do not come to this place. Having thought thus—

Having gone to the nuns' quarters, she instructs the nuns, saying: "Venerable ladies, in such-and-such a place there wanders a fierce elephant, a fierce horse, a fierce ram, and a fierce dog; it is a dangerous place, do not go there for alms.
Having heard her words, not even a single nun turns her neck toward that region.
She looked around. One day, while she was walking for alms in that place, as she was entering a certain house with haste, a fierce ram struck her and broke the bone of her thigh.
People ran up quickly, bound the split bone together on one side, and taking the bhikkhunī on a litter, they carried her to the bhikkhunīs’ dwelling.
The bhikkhunīs made jokes, saying, "This other bhikkhunī, having instructed [the first], has herself come back after having that thigh-bone broken while walking in that place.
Before long, the reason for what she had done became known throughout the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Then one day, in the Dhamma Hall, the bhikkhus said, "Friends, such-and-such an instructing bhikkhunī, having instructed another..."
“While she herself was walking in that place, a fierce ram gored her thigh,” they said, speaking ill of her.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, she instructed others while remaining herself [unrestrained].”
"But it is not right; one experiences only suffering at all times," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the forest in the womb of a bird.
Having reached maturity, he became the leader of the birds and, surrounded by many thousands of birds, entered the Himālaya mountains. To him—
There, at the time of dwelling, a certain fierce bird would go along the Great Vattani Road to seek its food.

Having found there grains of rice, mung beans, and other seeds dropped by carts, she thought, "I shall act in such a way that other birds do not come to this place again," and she gave this instruction to the flock of birds: "The Great Vattani Road..."
"It is indeed dangerous; elephants, horses, and the like, as well as vehicles drawn by fierce oxen, pass through there, and one cannot even suddenly spring away;
therefore, you must not go there. The flock of birds gave her the name "The Instructor" (Anusāsikā).
One day, while she was walking along the great highway, she heard the sound of a vehicle approaching with excessive speed.
Having heard this, she turned back and looked, but as she was still traveling, thinking, "It is still far," the vehicle reached her with the great speed of the wind;
she was unable to rise, and having been split in two by the wheel, she passed away.
The elder of the birds, while gathering the other birds together, not seeing her, said, "The instructor is not to be seen; search for her! And so the birds searched.
Seeing that it had been cut in two on the main road, they informed the leader of the birds.
The leader of the birds said, "That was another female bird who, having forbidden me, was herself walking there when she was cut in two," and he spoke this verse:
"She who instructs others, while she herself behaves with greed;..."
"She lies down in the evening with her wings destroyed, struck by the discus like a quail.
In this regard, in the phrase "yāyaññe manusāsatī," the letter *y* serves as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*); the meaning is "she who instructs others.
"Sayaṃ loluppacārinī" means being herself one who behaves with greed. "Sāyaṃ vipakkhikā setī" means that very same one, her wings having been destroyed...
Having sacrificed herself, she lay upon the great highway. "Struck by the wheel of the *sāsikā*": this means she was struck by the wheel of a vehicle; she was a *sāsikā*, a female bird.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the female bird who was the instructor was this nun Anusāsikā, while the elder of the birds was none other than myself.
This is the fifth commentary on the Anusāsikā Jātaka.
[116] 6. The Commentary on the Jātaka of the Ill-Mannered One (*Dubbaca-jātaka*).
"The Teacher who made the crocodile his pupil"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain ill-mannered monk.
The background story for him will be revealed in the *Gijjha-jātaka* of the *Navaka-nipāta*. However, the Teacher addressed that monk...
Having addressed him, he said, "Monk, it is not only now that you are difficult to speak to; even in the past you were difficult to speak to.
Because you did not follow the advice of the wise due to your very nature of being difficult to speak to, you met your end by the stroke of a spear. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of a trapeze artist.
Having taken it up, he reached maturity and became wise and skilled in means.
Having learned the art of leaping seven spears from a certain leaper, he wandered about demonstrating the craft together with his teacher.
However, that teacher knew the art of leaping only four spears, not five. One day, in a certain village, he [demonstrated] the craft...
Intoxicated by liquor, the man set up five spears in succession, thinking, "I shall leap over them.
Then the Bodhisatta said to him, "Teacher, you do not know the art of leaping over five spears; remove one spear.
If you leap, you will be pierced by the fifth spear and die. Because he was so thoroughly intoxicated, he replied, "But you—"
Disregarding his words, "You do not know my measure," he leaped over four spears and was impaled on the barb of the fifth like a *madhuka* flower; writhing in lamentation, he lay there.
Then the Bodhisatta, saying, "Because you did not act upon the words of the wise, you have met with this calamity," spoke this verse:
“O Teacher who has done what was beyond measure, this does not please me either;
having leaped over the fourth, you have become stuck on the fifth.
In that context, “Teacher who has done what was beyond measure” means: O Teacher, today you have performed an act of exceeding measure—something more than your own usual performance.
"Karaṇaṃ akari" means "he did the deed. "Mayhampetaṃ na ruccati" means: "Even though you are my pupil, this deed of yours does not please me;
therefore, I spoke to you about it right from the beginning"—this is what he indicates. "Catutthe laṅghayitvāna" means:
having leaped over the fourth, that is, without falling into the seventh place. "Pañcamāyasi āvuṭo" means... [text fragment] ...woven into the fifth.
“Not heeding the words of the wise, you are now pierced by this fifth spear. Having said this, he removed the teacher from the spear and performed what was appropriate to be done.
The Teacher, having brought forth this past event, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, this ill-behaved one was the teacher, while I myself was the pupil.”
The sixth: The Commentary on the Duvaca Jātaka.
[117] 7. The Commentary on the Tittira Jātaka.
"Exceedingly lofty and exceedingly powerful"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning Kokālika. Regarding him...
The background story will be made clear in the *Takkāriyajātaka* of the *Terasakanipāta*. However, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Kokālika has been ruined by his own words;
he was ruined even in the past," and having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of northern brahmins.

Having reached maturity, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā; then, abandoning sensual pleasures, he went forth into the ascetic life and developed the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments.
In the Himalayan region, the entire community of seers gathered together, made him their preceptor and teacher, and surrounded him.
Acting as the preceptor and teacher to five hundred seers, he engaged in the play of meditative absorption (*jhānakīḷa*).
He lived in the Himalayas, sporting about. At that time, there was a certain ascetic afflicted with jaundice who, having taken an axe, was splitting wood.
Then a talkative ascetic sat down near him and provoked that ascetic, saying, "Strike here! Strike here!
He became angry and said, "Now you are no longer my teacher for training me in the craft of splitting wood."
Raising a sharp axe, he brought him to his death in a single stroke. The Bodhisatta performed the funeral rites for his body.
At that time, a partridge lived at the foot of an anthill not far from the hermitage.
Every evening and morning, it would stand upon the top of that anthill and utter a loud cry. Hearing this, one...
The hunter, thinking, "It must be a partridge," went there guided by the sound, killed it, and took it away.
Not hearing its cry, the Bodhisatta asked the ascetics, "A partridge lives in such-and-such a place; why is its cry not heard?
They explained the matter to him, and he [considered] both of those causes.
Having addressed the assembly of seers, he spoke this verse:
“Speech that is excessively loud, exceedingly powerful,
and spoken at the wrong time destroys the witless man, just as excessive rain destroys the partridge.”
In this context, *accuggatā* means excessively elevated. *Atibalatā* means having an exceedingly powerful nature due to being spoken again and again.
*Ativelaṃ pabhāsitā* means spoken beyond the proper time, that is, by transgressing the limit of measure.
*Tittiraṃ vātivassitaṃ* means just as excessive rain destroys a partridge, so too such speech destroys a foolish person of dull wit.
Thus the Bodhisatta, having given this advice to the company of seers and having cultivated the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), became destined for the Brahma-world.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it was not only now that Kokālika was ruined by relying on his own words; he was ruined even in the past.
Having spoken thus, he brought forth this Dhamma teaching and identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the ascetic Mukhara was Kokālika."
“The flock of partridges was the assembly of the Buddha, but I myself was the teacher of the group.
The commentary on the Tittira Jātaka is the seventh.
[118] 8. The commentary on the Vaṭṭa Jātaka.
"Not one who does not reflect is a man"—this was said by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning the son of the merchant Uttara.
It is said that in Sāvatthī there was a merchant named Uttara of great wealth.
Into the womb of his wife, a meritorious being who had passed away from the Brahma-world took rebirth; and when he reached maturity, he was handsome and pleasing.

He possessed the appearance of a Brahmā. Then one day, when the Kattika festival was proclaimed in Sāvatthī and the entire world was intent upon the festival, his friends—the other sons of merchants—were accompanied by their wives.
However, because the son of the merchant Uttara had dwelt for a long time in the Brahma-world, his mind did not cling to the defilements.

Then his friends, having deliberated, saying, "Let us bring a woman for the son of the merchant Uttara as well and celebrate the festival," approached him and said, "Friend, the Kattika festival has been proclaimed in this city;
let us bring a woman for you too and celebrate the festival. Even when he replied, "I have no need for a woman," they continued.

Having bound her over and over again and made her agree, they adorned a certain courtesan with all kinds of ornaments, led her to his house, and sent her into the bedchamber, saying, "Go to the merchant’s son.
Even when she had entered that bedchamber, the merchant’s son neither looked at her nor spoke to her. She—
She thought, "He does not even look at me, nor does he speak to me, though I have attained such excellence of physical beauty and am endowed with the highest grace.
Now, I shall cause him to look at me by means of my feminine coquetry. Displaying her feminine charms, she opened her front teeth with a joyful expression and laughed.
The merchant’s son looked at her and took a mental sign from the row of her teeth.
Then the perception of bones arose within him, and his entire body appeared like a skeleton.
Having given her her travel expenses, he dismissed her, saying, "Go.
As she was descending from his house, a certain wealthy man saw her in the middle of the street, gave her his own travel expenses, and [led her] to his own house.
When seven days had passed, the auspicious constellation had shifted. The mother of the courtesan, not seeing her daughter return, went to the sons of the merchant and asked, "Where is she?
They went to the house of the son of the northern merchant and asked, "Where is she?
[He replied,] "At that very moment, I gave her her fee and sent her away."
Then her mother, weeping, took the son of the merchant Uttara and went before the king, saying, "I do not see my daughter;
bring back my daughter. The king, adjudicating the legal case, asked, "These sons of merchants brought a beauty-maid and gave her to you, did they not?
"Yes, Your Majesty," she replied. "Where is she now? "I do not know; at that very moment—"
“He dismissed him. “Are you able to bring him back now? “I am not able, Your Majesty,” he replied. The king said, “If you cannot bring him back, then carry out the royal command against him.
Then, having bound him by his two arms, they took him away, saying, “We shall carry out the royal command.
[The people said: “They say they are taking the merchant’s son to bring him back to the courtesan Vaṇṇadāsī.”
“Since he is unable [to comply], the king shall enforce his royal command. Thus, the entire city was filled with a single clamor.
The great multitude, placing their hands upon their chests, lamented: “What is this, Master? You have received what is utterly unworthy of you!
The merchant also went along behind his son, lamenting.
The merchant’s son thought: “This suffering of mine has arisen because of living at home.
If I am released from this, I shall go forth into homelessness in the presence of the Great Sammasambuddha Gotama.
Then that courtesan, hearing that tumultuous noise, asked, “What is this sound? and having heard what was happening, she went in haste.
Having descended, he called out, "Help me, help me, master! Let me see the king’s men! and thus revealed himself.
When the king’s men saw him, they allowed his mother to withdraw, released the merchant’s son, and departed.
Surrounded by his companions, he went to the river, bathed including his head, returned home, and after eating breakfast, [approached] his parents.
Having paid homage and requested permission for the going-forth, he took his robes and garments and went into the presence of the Teacher with a great retinue.
Having paid homage and requested the going-forth, he received both the going-forth and full ordination.
Without neglecting his meditation subject, he developed insight and before long was established in Arahantship.
Then one day, the monks gathered in the Dhamma Hall spoke of his virtues:
"Friends, when fear arose for himself, the son of the merchant Uttara recognized the excellence of the Teaching;

thinking, 'If I am released from this suffering, I shall go forth,' he was liberated from death by that very right thought, and having gone forth, he has established himself in the highest fruit. Thus they discussed his virtues.
They spoke. The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?

When they replied, "About this very one," he said, "Monks, it was not only the son of the merchant Uttara who, when fear arose within him, thought, 'By this means I shall be freed from this suffering,' and was thus released from the fear of death; in the past, wise men likewise [were released] from their own..."
"Having thought, 'When fear arises, by this means we shall be freed from this suffering,' they indeed were freed from the fear of death," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, wandering through the cycle of rebirths by way of death and rebirth-linking, was born into the womb of a quail.
At that time, a certain quail-trapper brought many quails from the forest to his house.
Setting aside his own food, he provided fodder and took the roots for himself, sustaining his life by selling the balls of grain into the hands of whoever came along.
One day, he brought the Bodhisatta along with many of the other balls.
The Bodhisatta thought: "If I consume the fodder and the water given by this man, he will take me [and sell me]."
"I will show it to people who come. But if I do not consume it, I shall wither away;
and seeing me withering away, people will not take it. In this way my safety will be secured; I shall employ this stratagem.
Acting accordingly, he became so withered that he was nothing but skin and bone. When people saw him, they...

They did not take him. When the other quails had been exhausted, except for the Bodhisatta, the hunter took out the basket, placed it at the door, and holding the Bodhisatta in the palm of his hand, thought, "What kind of quail is this?
and began to look at him. Then, perceiving the hunter's moment of negligence, the Bodhisatta spread his wings and flew up.
He went straight to the forest. Other quails, seeing him, asked, "Why do you not appear? Where have you gone?
When he replied, "I was captured by a hunter," they asked, "By doing what were you released?
The Bodhisatta said, "Without taking the food given by him and without drinking water, I was released through the application of a stratagem," and he spoke this verse:
“A man who does not reflect does not attain distinction;
behold the fruit of reflection: I am released from execution and bondage.
Herein, this is the summarized meaning: having encountered suffering, a person reflects, “By such-and-such a means I shall be freed from this suffering.”
"One who does not reflect does not attain the distinction known as liberation from one's own suffering.
But now, behold the fruit of the deed I have reflected upon! By that very means, I am released from slaughter and bondage;
I am freed from death and from captivity. Thus the Bodhisatta explained the reason for his own actions.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: “At that time, it was I myself who was the quail that escaped death.
This concludes the eighth narrative, the Vaṭṭa-jātaka.
9. The Narrative of the Untimely Crier (Akālarāvi-jātaka)
"Raised by no mother or father"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who cried out at improper times.
It is said that this son of good family from Sāvatthī, having gone forth in the Dispensation, did not learn either the duties (*vatta*) or the training (*sikkhā*).
He thought, "At this time I must perform the duties; at this time I must attend upon [the teacher]; at this time..."
He does not know that "this should be learned at this time" or "this should be recited at this time.
Even during the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch of the night, he makes a great noise every single moment he wakes up; thus, the monks cannot obtain sleep.
In the Hall of Truth, the monks said, "Friends, such-and-such a monk, having gone forth under such a jewel-like dispensation..."
"He knows neither the proper conduct, nor the training, nor the right time, nor the wrong time," they said, speaking in dispraise of him.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "About this very one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that he is a night-crier; formerly too he was a night-crier. [He does not know] the right time or the wrong time."
"Because he did not know [the way] and his neck was twisted, he met his death," he said, and then related a story of the past:
"In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of northern brahmins.
Upon reaching maturity, he mastered all the arts and became a world-renowned teacher in Benares, [instructing] five hundred..."
He taught a craft to some young brahmin students. Among those students, there was a cock that crowed at dawn;
they would rise by the sound of its crowing and practice their craft. That cock died. Searching for another cock, they wandered about.
Then, one young student, while gathering firewood in a charnel ground forest, saw a cock; he brought it back, placed it in a cage, and—

He looked after it. Because he had grown up in a charnel ground, not knowing "it should be rained upon at such-and-such a time," sometimes it rained past midnight, and sometimes at the rising of the dawn.

When the young men were learning their craft while it was raining past midnight, they were unable to continue learning until the rising of the dawn; falling asleep, they could not even maintain their positions.
They were watching. During the time of excessive early dawn rain, they could not even find an opportunity for their recitation.
The young students thought, "It rains too late at night or too early in the morning; because of this bird, our craft will not reach completion.
Having seized it and wrung its neck until it reached the end of its life, they said, "The cock that crows at the wrong time has been killed by us."
They told it to the teacher. The teacher, saying, "He has met his death because he was raised without receiving instruction," spoke this verse:
"Rearing him not as a mother and father would, Living in a family where no teacher dwells..."
“The cock does not know the proper time or the improper time.
In this context, “not raised by mother and father” means he was raised without depending on his mother and father and without receiving their instruction.
“Living in a family without a teacher” means that even though he did not live in a family with a teacher, he lived without depending on anyone to instruct him in proper conduct (*ācāra*).

The meaning is this: "He does not know the right time or the wrong time" means that this cock does not recognize the appropriate time for crowing or the wrong time, thinking, "One should crow at this time;
one should not crow at this time. Because of his very lack of such knowledge, he met his death.
Having shown this reason, the Bodhisatta remained for the duration of his lifespan and then passed away according to his karma.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the cock who crowed at the wrong hour was this very bhikkhu; the pupils were the Buddha’s retinue, and the teacher was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Akālarāvī Jātaka, the ninth. 10. Commentary on the Bandhanamokkha Jātaka.
“Those who are not bound there become bound”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the young woman Ciñcā.
The story of her case will be revealed in the Mahāpaduma Jātaka of the Dvādasakanipāta. At that time, however, the Teacher said:
“Monks, it is not only now that the young woman Ciñcā has misrepresented me with what is untrue; formerly, too, she did so.”
Having said, "He has indeed slandered me," he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into the household of the chief priest.
Upon reaching maturity, after his father passed away, he became that very man’s chief priest. He then granted a boon to the queen consort.
“‘My dear lady, say whatever you wish,’ he said. She replied, ‘I have no other boon that is difficult to obtain;
however, from this day forward, you must not look upon another woman with a mind defiled by passion.
Though he rejected her request, being pressured again and again and unable to override her words, he finally consented. From then on, regarding the sixteen [women]...”
Among thousands of dancing women, he did not look upon even a single one due to the influence of the defilements. Then his border region rose in revolt;

the warriors stationed at the border fought two or three battles with the bandits and sent a letter to the king, saying, "We are unable to go beyond this point. The king, desiring to go there, [prepared] the army...
Having withdrawn [the army] and summoned her, he said, "Bhadde, I am going to the borderlands;
there are various kinds of battles there, and victory and defeat are uncertain. In such places, it is difficult to attend to a woman;
you should remain right here. She replied, "It is not possible for me to turn back, Your Majesty," and she spoke thus again and again to the king.
Being refused, he said, "In that case, having traveled one *yojana* each, you should send one man from each [station] so that I may know my own pleasure and pain.
The King, accepting this with the words "Very well," left the Bodhisatta behind in the city and set out with a great military force;
as he went, at every *yojana* he appointed one man, saying, "To us..."
"Having announced my health and learned of the Queen's well-being and suffering, please return," he sent [the messenger].
Each time a man arrived, she would ask, "For what purpose has the King sent you?

When they replied, "To learn of your well-being and suffering," she would say, "In that case, come," and engage in unrighteous conduct with him. As the King traveled along the thirty-two-league road, he...
She sent thirty-two men, and she acted in exactly the same way with all of them.
When the king, having pacified the border region and reassured the countryside, was returning, he again sent thirty-two men;
she likewise misconducted herself with them as well. Upon his arrival at the site of the victorious camp, the king—
Having stopped, he sent a letter to the Bodhisatta, saying, "Have the city repaired.
The Bodhisatta, having had the entire city repaired, went to the place where the queen resided while overseeing the repair of the royal palace.
Upon seeing the Bodhisatta’s body, which had reached the pinnacle of physical beauty, she was unable to restrain herself and said, "Come, Brahmin, ascend the bed."
He said: “Do not speak thus. The king is also venerable, and I am afraid of unwholesome action; it is not possible for me to do such a thing.
“The sixty-four foot-soldiers neither revere the king nor fear unwholesome action.
Only you revere the king, and only you fear unwholesome action. “Yes, Queen. If even they were to think thus...”
“They would not do such a thing. “But I, knowing this, will not commit such a reckless act.
“Why do you prattle so much? If you do not do as I say, I shall have your head cut off!
“Let alone one lifetime—were my heads to be cut off even in a thousand lifetimes, it would still not be possible for me to [do such a thing].”

She replied, "Very well, I shall find out. Having thus threatened the Bodhisatta, she entered her own chamber, showed the marks of fingernails on her body, anointed her limbs with oil, put on soiled garments, and feigning illness, she commanded her handmaidens:
"If the King asks where the Queen is, you must say she is ill."
The Bodhisatta also went out to meet the king. Having circumambulated the city and ascended his palace, the king, not seeing the queen, asked, "Where is the queen?
"She is ill, Your Majesty," they replied. He too entered the bedchamber and, massaging her back, asked, "What is it that makes you unwell, my lady? She remained silent.
On the third occasion, looking at the king, she said, "Great King, you too are indeed called 'living,' and women like me are likewise called 'having a husband.

"What is this, lady? he asked. She replied, "The chaplain appointed by you for the protection of the city came here saying, 'I shall look after your residence,' and having struck me because I did not do as he said—"

"Thinking, 'He has departed having fulfilled his own desire,' the king, seething with anger like salt-crystals cast into a fire, emerged from the inner chamber, summoned the doorkeepers, footmen, and others, and said: 'Go, men!
Bind the chaplain by his two arms behind his back, subject him to the death penalty, lead him out of the city, take him to the execution ground, and cut off his head.'"
“Cut them off! he said. They went quickly, bound him by the back of his arms, and caused the drum of execution to be beaten.
The Bodhisatta thought: “Surely the king has already been alienated by that wicked queen;
today, therefore, I shall liberate myself by my own strength alone. He said to those men: “Sirs, do not kill me.”

“Kill him only after showing him to the king. “For what reason? “I am a royal official; much work has been done by me, and I know many locations of great treasures. I have managed the king’s household.
If you do not show me to the king, much wealth will be lost. Once I have pointed out the king’s property, you may do as you wish afterwards.”
They showed him to the king. As soon as the king saw him, he said, "Why, O brahmin, did you not feel shame before me?
Why have you committed such an evil deed? [The man replied: "Great King, I was born into a family of physicians;
I have never before taken the life of even a tiny ant, nor have I ever taken so much as a blade of grass that was not given."
Out of greed, she had never before looked upon the wives of others even by opening her eyes; out of mirth, she had never before spoken a falsehood;
and even with the tip of a blade of kusa grass, she had never before drunk intoxicants. I am innocent toward you.
But that foolish woman, out of greed, took hold of me by the hand; when I refused her, she threatened me and [confessed] the evil deed she herself had committed.
“Having turned it face up and explained it to me, she entered the inner chamber. I am innocent;
however, those sixty-four people who came taking the letter are guilty. Summon them, Your Majesty, and ask: ‘Was your word carried out by her, or not?
The king had those sixty-four people bound and summoned the queen, saying: “By you—”
He asked, "Was the evil deed committed with these people, or not?
When it was replied, "It was committed, Your Majesty," he had their hands tied behind their backs and commanded, "Cut off the heads of these sixty-four men!
Then the Bodhisatta said to him, "There is no fault in these, Great King; it was the Queen who acted according to her own will."
"These men are innocent; therefore, forgive them. There is no fault in her either, for women are by nature insatiable in sexual desire.
This is simply their innate character. It is only right that she should be forgiven. Therefore, forgive her as well.
Having thus persuaded the king in various ways, he had all sixty-four people and that fool released, and for everyone—
He had them released to their respective places. Having thus liberated them all and restored them to their own positions, the Bodhisatta approached the king and said:
"Great King, it was indeed the mark of blind fools that wise men—who ought not to have been bound—were bound with their hands behind their backs on the basis of groundless words;
whereas wise men, even when bound with their hands behind their backs on the basis of reasoned arguments,"
“Oysters [are released]. Thus, fools indeed cause those who ought not to be bound to be bound, while the wise release even those who are bound.
Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“In that place where fools boast, those who are unbound there are bound.”
“Even those bound there are liberated where the wise shine forth.
In this context, *abaddhā* means “not fit to be bound. *Pabhāsare* means they shine forth, speak, and explain.
Thus, having taught the Dhamma to the king with this verse, the Great Being [reflected]: “This suffering has come upon me because of living in a household.”
"I have received [all this]; now I have no further need for the household life. Grant me permission to go forth, O King!

Having thus obtained permission to go forth, he abandoned his tearful kinsmen and his great wealth, and having entered the ascetic life of an *isi*, while dwelling in the Himalayas, he developed the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), becoming destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the wicked queen was Ciñcā Māṇavikā, the king was Ānanda, and the chaplain was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Bandhanamokkha Jātaka, the tenth.
The twelfth chapter, the Haṃsa Vagga, is finished.
Its summary verse:
The donkey-question, Amarā, the jackal, and Mitacintin;
the instructor, the ill-spoken, the partridge, and again the quail.
"Unseasonable crying is a bond. 13.
The Kusa-reed Chapter [121]. 1.
The Commentary on the Kusa-reed Jātaka.
"Kare sarikkho" (He is like unto you): This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a friend of Anāthapiṇḍika.

For Anāthapiṇḍika’s friends, companions, kinsmen, and relatives had gathered together and said to him repeatedly, "This great merchant is neither equal to you in terms of birth, lineage, wealth, grain, and so forth, nor is he superior; why do you maintain intimacy with him? Do not do so!"
They tried to dissuade him. But Anāthapiṇḍika, thinking, "Friendship must indeed be maintained even with those who are inferior, equal, or superior," did not heed their words.
As he was going to Bhoganagara, he took that guardian of his household with him;
all this is to be understood according to the method already explained in the Kāḷakaṇṇi-vatthu. Here, however, by Anāthapiṇḍika himself—
When the news was reported as it had occurred at home, the Teacher said: "Householder, there is no such thing as a 'small' friend;
rather, the capacity to protect the nature of friendship is the measure here. A friend—whether equal, inferior, or superior—should be accepted.
All of them indeed carry across the burden placed upon them. Now, for your part, [regard] your own lowly friend..."
"By relying on [such people], one becomes the master of a household; however, in the past, by relying on low companions, people became masters of celestial mansions.
Having said this, when requested by him, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was in a clump of *kusa* reeds in the king's pleasure garden."

Having offered oblations to the deity, he was reborn there. And in that very garden, near the Maṅgala stone, there was a tree called Rucamaṅgala—also known as "Mukhaka"—which had straight trunks and was endowed with well-rounded branches and foliage, having received honor from the king.
In that tree, a powerful king of the gods was reborn. By him, [the Bodhisatta’s... the Bodhisatta’s...
He became close friends with him. At that time, the king was living in a palace with a single pillar, and that pillar shook.

They reported the fact of its shaking to the king. The king summoned the carpenters and said, "Sirs, the pillar of my auspicious palace, which has but a single pillar, has shaken; [bring] a pillar of solid heartwood..."
"Bring it here and make it motionless," he said. They replied, "Very well, Your Majesty," and accepting the king's command, they searched for a tree suitable for that purpose.
Not finding one elsewhere, they entered the royal garden and saw that mukhaka-tree;
then, returning to the king, they were asked, "My sons, have you seen a tree suitable for that? and they replied:
“It has been seen, Your Majesty; however, we do not dare to cut it down,” they said. “For what reason?
“Because we entered the park without seeing any other tree elsewhere, and even there we saw no other tree except for this auspicious tree.
Thus, because it is an auspicious tree, we do not dare to cut it down. “Go then, and cut it down.”
“Make the palace firm; we shall make another auspicious tree,” they said. Saying, “Very well,” they took offerings and went to the garden.
Having performed the offering ceremony for the tree with the thought, “We will cut it down tomorrow,” they departed.
The deity of that tree, knowing this matter, thought, “Tomorrow they will destroy my mansion; taking the children, where—”
"I shall go," she said; but seeing no way to go, she took her two little sons by the neck and wept.
A tree deity who was her close friend and companion came to her, asked, "What is this?
and upon hearing the reason, and herself seeing no means for the carpenters to depart, she embraced her and began to weep. At that moment, the Bodhisatta...
Thinking, "I shall see the tree deity," he went there and, having heard the reason, comforted those deities, saying: "Be at ease; do not worry.
I will not allow the tree to be cut down. Tomorrow, when the carpenters arrive, you shall see my stratagem.
Then, on the following day at the time the carpenters were due to arrive, he assumed the guise of a *kakaṇṭaka* bird.
Going ahead of the carpenters, he entered the hollow at the base of the auspicious tree;
having made that tree appear as if it were hollow, he climbed up through the middle of the trunk, emerged from the top of the bole, and lay down shaking his head.
When the master carpenter saw the woodpecker, he struck the tree with his hand and said, "This is a hollow tree."
"This is the lack of discernment; yesterday we performed the offering without even considering [the recipient]," she said, and having rebuked the great tree as a single mass, she departed.
By relying on the Bodhisatta, the tree deity became the mistress of the celestial mansion (*vimāna*).
For the sake of welcoming her, many deities who were friends and companions gathered together. The tree deity...
Thinking, "I have obtained a celestial mansion," her heart filled with joy, she spoke of the Bodhisatta’s virtues in the midst of those deities:
"O deities, although we were of great power, because of our dull-wittedness we did not know this stratagem;
yet the deity of the kusa-reed, through the excellence of her own wisdom, has made us the owners of these mansions—for even a friend who is equal or superior [should be honored]."
“Even one who is inferior must act [to help]; for all, according to their own strength, indeed rescue their friends from arisen suffering and establish them in happiness.
Having thus praised the nature of friendship, he spoke this verse:
“A peer, or even a superior, or even one who is inferior—anyone at all may act [for a friend].”
"May these people perform their duties toward me just as I do toward Kuśanāḷi.
In this context, "one who is similar" (*sarikkha*) means one who, though equal in birth and other such factors, would practice the duty of friendship;
