or alternatively, "one who is superior" (*seṭṭha*) means one who, though superior in birth and other such factors, would practice it; or "one who is inferior" (*nihīnaka*) means even one who is inferior in birth and other such factors would practice the duty of friendship.
One should act [in this way]. Therefore, he shows that all these indeed should be made friends. For what reason?

Because "these would accomplish the highest good in times of misfortune. When misfortune has arisen for a companion, all these—carrying their respective shares of the burden—would accomplish the highest good;
the meaning is that they would surely liberate that companion from bodily and mental suffering. Therefore...
Even an inferior friend should indeed be made so, let alone others. Here is an illustration:
just as I, Rucā, and this deity Kusanāḷī—though we were both of little power—engaged in friendship;
there, although I was one of great power, through my foolishness and lack of skill in means, I [experienced] the suffering that arose for me.
"I was unable to rescue myself; yet, although I am of little power, by relying on this wise deity, I have been liberated from suffering.
Therefore, others who also desire to be freed from suffering should, without regarding whether they are equal or superior, make even an inferior person a wise friend."

Having taught the Dhamma to the assembly of devas with this verse, the deity Rucā remained for as long as her lifespan lasted and then, together with the deity Kusanāḷī, departed according to their respective karma.
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma instruction, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the deity Rucā was Ānanda, while the deity Kusanāḷī was none other than myself.
This is the first commentary on the Kusanāḷī Jātaka.
[122] 2. The Commentary on the Dummedha Jātaka.
Having acquired fame, the fool... This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Veḷuvana concerning Devadatta.
For in the Hall of Truth, the monks said, "Friends, Devadatta [has disparaged] the Tathāgata’s face, which is as beautiful as the full moon..."

When he beholds his own person— adorned with the eighty minor marks and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, encircled by a fathom-wide aura, and emitting dense Buddha-rays that form continuous, overlapping garlands—
and yet is unable to gladden his heart but instead feels only envy, [he reflects: "The Buddhas indeed possess such virtue..."

They spoke of Devadatta’s lack of virtue, saying, "When it is said that he is 'endowed with concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation,' he is unable to endure the praise and instead acts out of envy.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now? and they replied, "About this very one."
Having said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta felt envy while my praise was being spoken;
he did so even in the past," he related a story of the past.
Long ago, when a certain king of Magadha was reigning in the city of Rājagaha in the kingdom of Magadha, the Bodhisatta—
Having been reborn in the womb of an elephant, he was entirely white and endowed with a perfection of physical form similar to what was described above.
Then, thinking, "This one is possessed of the auspicious marks," the king made him his state elephant (*maṅgalahatthi*).
Then, on a festival day, having caused the entire city to be decorated like the city of the gods, [he paraded] the state elephant adorned with every ornament.
Having mounted [the elephant], the king, with great royal majesty, performed a circumambulation of the city.
Great crowds of people stood here and there, and seeing the body of the auspicious elephant, which had reached the pinnacle of physical beauty, they exclaimed: "Oh, what beauty!
Oh, what gait! Oh, what grace! Oh, what perfection of marks! Such a truly white, excellent war-elephant is indeed worthy of a Universal Monarch."
He praised the elephant Maṅgala.
Having heard the praise of the elephant Maṅgala, the king was unable to endure it;
conceiving envy, he thought, “This very day I shall cast him down at the foot of a mountain and bring about his death. He summoned the elephant trainer and said, “What [should be done]?”
"Having done so, this elephant has been trained by you," he said. "He is well-trained, Your Majesty," [the trainer] replied.
"Is he not well-trained? He is poorly trained! "He is well-trained, Your Majesty. "If he is well-trained, will you be able to make him climb to the summit of Mount Vepulla?
"Yes, Your Majesty. "Then come along," [the king said]. Having himself descended and mounted the elephant trainer, [he proceeded] to the foot of the mountain.

Having gone there, the elephant trainer sat upon the back of the elephant and, once the elephant had been made to ascend the summit of Mount Vepulla, he himself, surrounded by his retinue of ministers, also climbed to the mountain top; then, having directed the elephant toward the precipice, he said:
"You claim, 'I have trained this one well'; now, stand on it with only three feet!"
He said: The elephant trainer, sitting upon the back, gave a signal with his heel, saying, "Sir, stand on three feet.
The Great Being did so. Again the king said, "Stand on two front feet alone," and the Great Being lifted his two hind feet and stood on his front feet. "On the hind feet alone! [he commanded].
Even when told "two," he lifted his two front feet and stood on his hind feet;
even when told "one," he lifted three feet and stood on one alone. Then, knowing that he would not fall, [the king] said, "If you are able, place him in the air.
The teacher thought: "In all of Jambudīpa, there is no elephant so well-trained as this; without a doubt—"
"He must intend to throw this man over the precipice and kill him. He whispered into his ear, "Dear friend, this king intends to throw you over the precipice and kill you; you are not worthy of him.
If you have the power to travel through the air, take me as I am seated and fly up into the sky, then go to Bārāṇasī."
Endowed with the power of merit (*puññiddhi*), the Great Being stood in the air at that very moment. The elephant trainer said, "Great King, this elephant is endowed with the power of merit;
he is not suited for one of such meager merit and dull intellect, but is suited for a wise king possessed of merit. Such men of meager merit as you are unfit for a vehicle of this kind."
"Having obtained his merit, those who do not recognize it will surely destroy both that very vehicle and the rest of his glorious prosperity," he said,
and while still seated upon the elephant's back, he spoke this verse:
"Having gained fame, the foolish man acts for his own disadvantage."
“He proceeds toward the harming of both himself and others.
Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: O Great King, such a foolish and witless person, having obtained the excellence of a retinue, acts for his own detriment.
For what reason? Because he, intoxicated by the pride of fame, [fails to distinguish] between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
Not knowing [the truth], he proceeds to the harming of both himself and others. "Harming" (hiṃsā) is said to be exhaustion and the production of suffering;
he proceeds for that very purpose.
Having thus taught the Dhamma to the king with this verse, saying, "Now, stop!", he sprang up into the air.
Having gone to the city of Bārāṇasī, he stood in the air over the royal courtyard.
The entire city was thrown into agitation, and a great clamor arose: "A noble white elephant has come through the air and stands in our king's courtyard!
They reported this to the king with great haste. The king went out and said, "If you have come for my use, [stand] upon the ground."
"Set foot [upon it]," he said. The Bodhisatta set his foot upon the ground; the teacher descended, paid homage to the king, and when asked, "Where have you come from, dear?
replied, "From Rājagaha," and related the entire account.
The king, delighted and joyful, saying, "Dear, you have done well in coming here," had the city prepared and placed the elephant in the position of a state auspicious elephant.
Setting aside his entire kingdom and dividing it into three portions, he gave one to the Bodhisatta, one to the teacher, and took one for himself.
From the very moment the Bodhisatta arrived, however, the entire kingdom of Jambudīpa came into the king's hands.
Having become the supreme king of Jambudīpa, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving and departed according to his karma.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, Devadatta was the King of Magadha, Sāriputta was the King of Bārāṇasī, Ānanda was the elephant trainer, and I myself was the elephant.
This concludes the second commentary, the Dummedha Jātaka.
3. The Commentary on the Naṅgalīsa Jātaka.
"Speech that does not lead anywhere"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Elder Lāḷudāyin.
It is said that when he preached the Dhamma, he did not know what was appropriate or inappropriate, thinking, "In this place this should be spoken; in this place this should not be spoken.
Speaking what was auspicious as inauspicious, he would say: "They stand beyond walls, at crossroads, and at junctions..."
And so, having turned this inauspiciousness into an auspicious sign, he delivers a discourse of thanksgiving.

While offering thanks for such inauspicious things, he says, "Many gods and humans have contemplated these auspicious signs," and adds, "May you be capable of performing even a hundred or a thousand such auspicious rites. Then one day, in the Hall of Dharma, the bhikkhus—
“Friends, Lāḷudāyī does not know what is appropriate and what is inappropriate; he speaks words that should not be spoken on every occasion,” they said, thus initiating the discussion.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, “Monks, with what discussion are you sitting here gathered now?
When they replied, “With this one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that Lāḷudāyī is slow in his efforts.”
"He does not know what is appropriate or inappropriate; he was like this even in the past; he is always just a beggar," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of great brahmin householders.
Upon reaching maturity, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā and became a world-renowned teacher in Benares.
Having performed the sacrifice, he taught the craft to five hundred young men. At that time, among those young men, there was one young man named Lāḷaka who was slow-witted;
he became a religious pupil and sought to learn the craft, but because of his slowness, he was unable to master it.
However, he was helpful to the Bodhisatta and performed all duties like a slave. Then, one day—
Having eaten his evening meal, the Bodhisatta lay down on his bed and said to the young man who was departing after massaging his hands and feet,
"Dear son, go after propping up one of the bed-legs. The young man,
having propped up one leg but finding no support for the other, spent the night placing it upon his own thigh.
The Bodhisatta rose at dawn, and seeing him, asked, "What is it, dear son, that you are sitting here?
"Teacher, not finding a support for one leg of my bed, I have placed it upon my thigh and am sitting," he replied.
The Bodhisatta, his heart filled with emotion, thought, "This man has been of great service to me; yet, among all these young brahmins—"
"This man is so dull-witted that he cannot even learn a craft; how indeed can I make him wise?
he thought. Then it occurred to him: "There is a certain stratagem.
When this young man has returned from going to the forest for wood and leaves, I will ask him, 'What did you see today? What did you do? Then he will say to me, 'This..."
"Today I have seen something; he will explain what was done.
Then I shall ask him, 'What was it that you saw and what was done? He will describe it with similes and reasons, saying, 'It was like this.
Thus, by making him speak ever-new similes and reasons through this means, I shall make him wise."
So, having summoned him, he said: "Dear young man, from now on, whenever you go for the sake of wood or leaves,
whatever you see, hear, eat, drink, or chew in that place, you must come and report it to me."
Having assented with "Very well," one day he went to the forest with his young students for the purpose of gathering wood.
There, having seen a snake, he returned and reported, "Teacher, I have seen a snake. "What is a snake like, dear?
"It is just like a ploughshare. "Excellent, dear! You have brought a pleasing simile. As for snakes—"
“...they would be just like plow-shafts. Then the Bodhisatta thought, “The young brahmin has brought a pleasing simile;
I shall be able to make him wise. One day, having seen an elephant in the forest, the young brahmin said, “Teacher, I have seen an elephant.
“What is an elephant like, my dear? “Just like a plow-shaft, Teacher.”
The Bodhisatta remained silent, thinking: "An elephant's trunk is like a plough-handle; its tusks and other features are of such and such a kind.
But this man, out of ignorance, was apparently unable to distinguish them and spoke while referring only to the trunk.
Then one day, having received sugarcane at an invitation, he said: "Teacher, today we ate sugarcane."
He asked, "What is this thing called sugarcane like? When told, "It is just like a plowshare," the teacher remained silent, thinking, "He has given a somewhat appropriate reason.
On another day at an invitation, some of the young brahmins ate molasses with curds, while others ate it with milk. He...
Having arrived, he said, "Teacher, today we ate curds and milk. When asked, "What are curds and milk like?
he replied, "They are just like a plowshare. The teacher thought, "This young man has spoken very well when saying that 'a snake is like a plowshare';
even one who says 'an elephant is like a plowshare' [would be speaking well] regarding its trunk..."
"It was spoken with an underlying intention (*sandhāya*). Even in the statement, 'Sugar-cane is like a plough-handle,' there is an underlying intention;
however, he did not state the simile in its entirety here by saying, 'But curds and milk are always white and take the shape of the vessel into which they are poured.
[The Teacher said: 'It is impossible to train this brat,' and having said this, he recited this verse:"
“The fool speaks everywhere a word that does not apply everywhere:
‘This is not curd, nor is it a ploughshare; he mistakes the curd for a ploughshare, and the ploughshare for curd.
Herein, this is the summary meaning: that speech which, by way of analogy, does not apply everywhere—that is ‘speech that does not go everywhere’ (asabbatthagāmin).”
A foolish person of dull wit speaks indiscriminately on all matters; even when asked, "What is curd like?
he replies, "It is just like a ploughshare. Speaking thus, he knows neither the curd nor the ploughshare. Why is this?
Because he conceives the curd to be the ploughshare, since he perceives the curd as being nothing other than the ploughshare. Or alternatively, *dadhi* simply means curd.
They prepare milk, curds, and "curd-milk" (a mixture of both). Because this man regards even curds and milk as being like a plowshare, he is such a fool;
what is the use of him? Having thus delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to his pupils and given them their travel expenses, he dismissed him.
The Teacher, having brought forth this teaching of the Dhamma, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the young Brahmin Lāḷaka was Lāḷudāyī, and the world-renowned teacher was none other than myself."
The third *Naṅgalīsājātaka-vaṇṇanā*.
[124] 4. The *Ambajātaka-vaṇṇanā*:
"A man should indeed exert himself"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was perfect in his observance of the rules.

He spoke with reference to this. It is said that he was a son of good family living in Sāvatthī who had gone forth, having dedicated his heart to the Dispensation, and was endowed with proper conduct.
He performed well the duties toward his teachers and preceptors, as well as the duties regarding water for drinking and rinsing, the Uposatha hall, the bathhouse, and so forth;
indeed, he was one who fulfilled all fourteen great rules and eighty minor rules of the Khandhaka.
He swept the monastery, swept the courtyard, the thought-hall, and the path to the monastery, and provided drinking water for people.
People, having gained confidence in his excellence in performing these duties, gave him about five hundred regular meals;
thus, great gain and honor arose for him. By means of that, a comfortable living was established for many. Then, one day—

In the Dhamma hall, the monks started a discussion: "Friends, a certain monk named so-and-so has produced great gain and honor through his excellence in fulfilling his duties; because of him alone, the comfortable dwelling of many has come about.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Monks, with what discussion are you sitting here gathered now? [They replied: "With this one..."
When he said, "It is his name," [the Blessed One] replied, "Monks, it is not only now; formerly this monk was also perfect in his duties.
Formerly, relying on him alone, five hundred seers would not go into the forest for the sake of fruits and roots, but sustained themselves with the fruits and roots brought by him himself.
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of northern brahmins.
Upon reaching maturity, he went forth as an ascetic and, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred ascetics, dwelt at the foot of a mountain.
At that time, there was a fierce heat in the Himalayas; the water sources dried up here and there, and the animals [sought] water.

Not obtaining [water], they grew weary. Then, among those ascetics, one ascetic, seeing their suffering from thirst, cut down a tree, fashioned a trough, drew up water, filled the trough, and gave them water to drink.
As many gathered together and drank the water, the ascetic had no opportunity to go for the sake of gathering fruits.
Thus, even though he was without food, he continued to give them water. The herds of deer thought, “While this man gives us water, he finds no opportunity to go in search of fruits;
because of his lack of food, he is exceedingly exhausted. Come now, let us make an agreement.
They made an agreement: “From now on, by whoever comes here for the sake of drinking water, according to their own strength...”

"You must return having taken various fruits and foods. From then on, each of the animals returned after gathering very sweet mangoes, rose-apples, jackfruits, and so forth, according to its own strength.
The fruit and food brought for the sake of one person amounted to the measure of two and a half cartloads. Those five hundred ascetics consumed that very same amount.
The surplus was thrown away.

Seeing this, the Bodhisatta said, “By relying on even one person who is perfect in his duties, such a livelihood has arisen for so many ascetics that they do not have to go out for fruit and roots; indeed, energy must be exerted,” and he spoke this verse:
“A man should strive indeed; the wise person should not despair.”
“Behold the fruit of effort: the mangoes have been eaten, not by mere hearsay.
Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: A wise person should indeed exert himself in his duties, such as fulfilling his obligations, and should not grow weary.
Why? Because there is no lack of fruit from effort. Thus the Great Being said: “This so-called effort...”
Addressing the company of seers, he said, “Behold the fruit of effort,” as if saying, “It has indeed become fruitful. Of what kind? “Mangoes have been eaten, not according to hearsay.
In this context, “mangoes” is merely a term of illustration; for they had brought various kinds of fruits and fruits.
It was called “mangoes” by way of those that were most excellent or most abundant among them. These were [the fruits] brought by these five hundred seers.
"Without having gone to the forest myself, mangoes brought for the sake of one person were eaten; this is the fruit of effort.
Furthermore, that fruit is not based on mere tradition—that which must be grasped through hearsay such as 'thus he said' or 'thus he spoke.
Rather, see that fruit as something directly perceived. In this way, the Great Being gave counsel to the company of seers.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the ascetic who was perfect in his duties was this very Bhikkhu, while I myself was the leader of the group.
This concludes the commentary on the Amba Jātaka, the fourth.
[125] 5. The Commentary on the Kaṭāhaka Jātaka.
"He might boast even more"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain boastful monk. The background story for him is the same as that told previously.
However, in the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a very wealthy merchant.
His wife gave birth to a son, and on that very same day, his female slave also gave birth to a son. They were both born together.

They prospered. While the sons of the merchant were learning writing, the slave, carrying his wooden slate, went along with them and learned writing and arithmetic; he engaged in two or three types of business.
Gradually, he became skilled in speech, proficient in commerce, a youth, handsome, and was known by the name Kaṭāheka. He performed the work of a storekeeper in the merchant’s house.
As he worked, he thought: "These people will not have me perform the work of a storekeeper for all time;
once they find some fault, they will beat me, bind me, brand me with a mark, and even use me as a slave.
Now, there is a merchant who is a friend of the merchant in the border region; what if I were to take a letter by the merchant's word and go there?"
"Having gone there, let me deceive that merchant by saying 'I am the merchant's son,' take his daughter, and live happily.
He himself took a letter and wrote: "I have sent my son, named so-and-so, to you;
indeed, there is a marriage alliance between me and you, and between you and me."
"He is worthy; therefore, give your own daughter to this boy and have him dwell right there.

As for me, I too shall come once I have found an opportunity. Having written this and having it sealed with the merchant’s own seal, he took as much travel provisions as he desired, along with perfumes, garments, and other necessities, and went to the border region. Upon seeing the merchant, he paid homage and stood before him.
Then the merchant asked him, "Where have you come from, dear? "From Bārāṇasī," he replied. "Whose son are you? "The son of the merchant of Bārāṇasī.
"For what purpose have you come? At that moment, Kaṭāhaka gave him a letter, saying, "Upon seeing this, you will know.
The merchant read the letter and, with a heart full of joy, thinking, "Now indeed I am truly alive," [addressed] his daughter...
Having given it, he established [the practice]. His retinue became large.

When rice gruel, solid food, and so forth, or robes, perfumes, and so forth, were brought to him, he would criticize the rice gruel and other items, saying, "They actually cook rice gruel like this! Solid food like this! Rice like this!
Oh, how they are called 'frontier dwellers'! He thought, "It is precisely because of their status as frontier dwellers that these people do not use unwashed robes."
“They know how to grind perfumes, but they do not know how to weave cloth or string flowers,” he said, thereby censuring the weavers and others.
The Bodhisatta, not seeing the slave, dispatched men in all directions, saying, “The potter is not to be seen; where has he gone?
Search for him! Among them, one man went there, saw him, and recognized him, yet without revealing his identity, he...
Having arrived, he reported it to the Bodhisatta. Upon hearing the news, the Bodhisatta thought, "He has done what is improper;
I shall go, seize him, and bring him back. Having taken leave of the king, he set out with a great retinue.
It became known everywhere that "the merchant is going to the border region. Kaṭāhaka heard that "the merchant is coming."
Having heard this, she thought: "He will not come for any other reason; his coming must surely be on account of me.
If, however, I were to flee, it would be impossible for him to return again. But there is a means:
I shall go to meet my husband, perform the work of a slave, and thus win him over. From that time forth...

In the midst of the assembly, he speaks thus: "Other foolish people, through their own foolishness, not knowing the virtues of their parents, fail to perform acts of veneration at the time of their meal and eat together with them.
We, however, at the time our parents eat, bring forward a receiving bowl, we bring forward a spittoon, and [we provide] vessels."

"Let us attend upon him, taking both water and a fan," she said; thus, from the time of the body's cleansing until the carrying of the water-jar to the private chamber, she demonstrated to the slaves every duty that servants must perform for their masters.
Having thus instructed her retinue, when the Bodhisatta arrived near the border region, she spoke to her father-in-law.
“Father, it is said that my father is coming to see you; please have hard and soft foods prepared.
I shall take a gift and go out to meet him on the road. “Very well, dear,” he replied.
Then Kaṭāhaka, taking many gifts and accompanied by a large retinue, went forth to meet the Bodhisatta.

Having paid homage, he presented a gift. The Bodhisatta, having accepted the gift and exchanged greetings with him, encamped his army at the time of breakfast and entered a secluded place for the purpose of bathing his body.
Kaṭāhaka, having dismissed his own retinue, took a water-pot and approached the Bodhisatta.
Having gone there and finished his business with the water, he fell at [the Bodhisatta’s] feet and said, “Master, I will give you as much wealth as you desire;
do not let my reputation perish. The Bodhisatta, being pleased by his excellence in conduct, comforted him, saying, “Do not fear;
there shall be no obstacle for you from my side,” and then [departed for] the frontier city.
He entered. There was great honor shown to him; Kaṭāhaka performed for him every service that a slave ought to do without interruption.
Then, on one occasion, while he was sitting comfortably, the border-town merchant said to him, "Great merchant, as soon as I saw your letter, I gave my daughter to your son.
The Bodhisatta, treating Kaṭāhaka as his very own son, [responded].
Having spoken words of affection appropriate to the occasion, he delighted the merchant. From that time forth, there was no one capable of even looking at the mouth of the cauldron.
Then one day, the Great Being summoned the merchant’s daughter and said, "Come, mother, search for lice on my head."
Having spoken thus, she returned, took the *ūkā* (a small vessel), and after speaking words of endearment to him who was standing there, she asked:
"Tell me, mother, is my son diligent in matters of pleasure and pain? Do you two live in harmony, living together in mutual affection?
She replied: "Dear one, Great Merchant, your son has no other fault; he merely censures food."
“Mother, he is always of a harsh disposition; however, I shall give you a spell for binding his mouth.
Having mastered it thoroughly, when my son is eating and speaking abusively, you should stand before him and speak according to the method you have learned.
Having thus caused her to learn the verse, he stayed for a few days and then departed for Bārāṇasī itself.
Kaṭāhaka also took a great deal of hard and soft food and followed along the road; having given him much wealth and paid homage, he turned back.
From the moment the Bodhisatta departed, Kaṭāhaka became excessively conceited.
One day, after bringing various kinds of choice food to the merchant’s daughter, he took a spoon and began to criticize the meal as she was serving it.
The merchant’s daughter, having already mastered the method in the presence of the Bodhisatta, recited this verse:
“Though he may boast much, having gone to another country, He might come back and defile me;
Enjoy your pleasures, Kaṭāhaka!”
In this regard, he might boast much: "He has gone to another country"—meaning one who has gone from his own birthplace to another country where they do not know his birth;
such a person might boast much, speaking words of disparagement or words of deception. "Having followed after, he might defile" means, for this time, [he follows] against the path of the husband.
"Having gone [there], because you performed the duty of a slave, you were released from being struck with whips, from having the skin of your back torn away, and from being branded.
If you commit misconduct, then on your next visit, your master will come after you and defile you;
by coming to this house, you will be subjected to blows from whips, branding, and the disclosure of your birth-status."
And he might corrupt and ruin it. Therefore, Kaṭāhaka, abandon this improper conduct and enjoy your wealth;
do not later make your own state of slavery manifest and then be full of remorse—this was the intention of the merchant here.
But the merchant’s daughter, not understanding this matter, merely repeated the literal words according to the method she had learned.
Kaṭāhaka thought, "Surely the merchant has told her everything after mentioning my family," and from that moment on, he was no longer able to criticize the food.
With his pride humbled, he ate whatever he received and departed according to his karma.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the boastful monk was Kaṭāhaka, and I myself was the merchant of Bārāṇasī."
The fifth: The Commentary on the Kaṭāhaka Jātaka.
[126] 6. The Commentary on the Asilakkhaṇa Jātaka.
"In the same way, for one person it is auspicious..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a reader of sword-omens for the King of Kosala.
He spoke concerning a certain brahmin. It is said that when the smiths brought swords for the king, he would sniff them and describe their characteristics.
To those from whose hands he received a gift, he would say of their sword, "It is endowed with auspicious marks and possesses good fortune.
To those from whose hands he did not receive a gift, he would say of their sword, "It has inauspicious marks."
He reproached him. Then a certain smith, having fashioned a sword and placed fine pepper powder inside its scabbard, brought the sword to the king.
The king summoned the brahmin and said, "Examine the sword.
As the brahmin drew the sword and sniffed it, the pepper powder entered his nose and caused a desire to sneeze to arise. As he was about to sneeze—
His nose was struck by the blade of the sword and split in two. Thus, the fact that his nose had been cut off became known throughout the community of monks.

Then one day, in the Hall of Dharma, the monks initiated a discussion, saying, "Friends, it is said that the king’s expert in the marks of swords, while sniffing the sword, had his own nose cut off. The Teacher arrived and asked, "What is this talk? [The monks replied: "Venerable Sir, the monks were discussing how the king’s expert in the marks of swords had his nose cut off while sniffing the sword. The Teacher said:
“Monks, for what discussion have you gathered here now? he asked.

When they replied, “For this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that this brahmin suffered the cutting off of his nose while sniffing at a sword; he suffered it in the past as well. Having said this, he related a story of the past:
“In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, there was a brahmin who was an expert in the science of sword-marks.”
Everything else was exactly as in the present-day account.
However, the king, having given him physicians and had the tip of his nose made comfortable, had a new nose fashioned for him out of lacquer and once again made him his attendant.
But the King of Bārāṇasī had no son; he had only a daughter and a nephew. He kept both of them right in his own presence.
He raised them. As they grew up together, their hearts became bound to one another.
The king, having summoned his ministers, said, "My nephew is indeed the rightful owner of this kingdom; I shall give my daughter to him alone and perform his consecration.
Having spoken thus, he thought further: "In every respect, my nephew is my own kinsman; for him, no other..."
“Having brought the king’s daughter and performed her consecration, I shall give my daughter to another king;
thus our kinsmen will become numerous, and we alone shall be the masters of both kingdoms.
Having consulted with his ministers, he decided, “It is fitting to separate these two,” and he had his nephew live in one residence and his daughter in another.
When they reached the age of sixteen, their hearts became exceedingly attached to one another.
The prince, reflecting, "By what means might it be possible to have my maternal uncle’s daughter led away from the royal palace? thought, "There is a certain expedient.
He summoned a great procuress, gave her a bundle of a thousand pieces of gold, and asked, "What must I do?"
When he had spoken thus, she said, "Mother, there is no failure in what you do;
however, state some pretext so that my maternal uncle, the king, may have his daughter removed from the inner apartments.
"Very well, master," she replied, "I will approach the king and say, 'Your Majesty, there is an ill omen upon the princess.'"
Even looking back for such a long time, there was no one; on such-and-such a day, I placed the princess upon a chariot,
took men with many weapons in their hands, and accompanied by a great retinue, went to the cemetery,
laid a dead man upon a bed beneath a circular platform, placed the princess upon the upper bed, and [prepared] jars of scented water...
"Having bathed her with one hundred and eight [pots of water], we shall cast out the ill-omened one," he said; and having spoken thus, he continued: "I will take the princess to the charnel ground.

On the day of our departure there, you must go to the charnel ground before us, taking a small amount of powdered black pepper, and mounting your chariot surrounded by your own men with weapons in hand. Then, having gone to the charnel ground, [he mounted] the chariot.

Having stationed men with weapons in hand at one spot at the entrance to the charnel ground and sent them into the forest of the cemetery, you yourself should spread out a circular seat in the cemetery and lie down prostrate like a corpse.
When I arrive there, I will spread a couch over you, lift up the princess, and have her lie down upon that couch; you, meanwhile, [should remain] therein.
"At the moment, you should place powdered black pepper in your nose and blow it out two or three times.
When you have blown it out, we shall abandon the princess and flee.
Then, having bathed the princess's head and having bathed your own head as well, you may take her and go to your own home. He accepted this, saying, "Excellent! This is a beautiful stratagem."
She too went and reported the matter to the king, and the king accepted it. She explained this secret to the princess as well, and she too accepted it.

On the day of her departure, having given a signal to the prince, she said—while proceeding to the charnel ground with a great retinue in order to inspire fear in the guards: "By me, on the bed of the princess..."
"When it is set down, a dead man will be thrown beneath the bed;
having been thrown, he will emerge from beneath the bed and seize whoever he first sees. You must be vigilant!
The prince went ahead and lay down there in the manner described. The chief executioner lifted up the princess and [placed her] at the spot where the circular seat stood.
As she was departing, he reassured her, saying, "Do not be afraid," and placed her upon a couch.
At that moment, the prince threw a powder of black pepper into his nose and spat it out.
As soon as it was spat out, a great female monkey abandoned the princess and fled first, crying out with a loud roar; from the moment she fled, not a single one remained.
He was no longer capable; they all abandoned the weapons they had seized and fled.
The prince, having performed everything as he had planned, took the princess and went to his own residence.
The fortune-teller went and reported the matter to the king. The king said, "By nature, she was intended by me for him alone..."
Having accepted [the omen], thinking, "When asked, it has become like ghee thrown away in milk-rice," he later gave the kingdom to his nephew and made his daughter Mahādevī his queen.
Living in harmony with her, he ruled the kingdom according to the Dhamma.
That same interpreter of sword-omens remained his personal attendant. One day, while he was attending upon the king...
Having returned and stood facing the sun to attend to him, the lac dissolved and his nose fell to the ground.
Out of shame, he stood with his face cast down. Then the king, joking with him, said: "Teacher, do not be distressed;
what is thrown is auspicious for one person and inauspicious for another. By what was thrown by you, your nose has been severed."
"But we, by throwing [the dice], obtained our maternal uncle's daughter and attained the kingdom," he said, and spoke this verse:
"Likewise for one there is good fortune; likewise for one there is misfortune.
Therefore, not everything is auspicious, nor is everything indeed inauspicious."
In that context, *tathevekassa* means *tadevekassa*. Or rather, this is the reading itself. The same method applies to the second word as well.
Thus, having brought forward that reason with this verse, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving and departed according to his karma.
By means of this teaching, the Teacher revealed the non-uniformity of the good and evil deeds esteemed by the world.
He made the connection with the Jātaka: "At that time, the one who read the marks on swords was none other than the sword-mark reader of today, while the nephew-king was I myself.
This concludes the sixth commentary, the Asilakkhaṇa Jātaka.
[127] 7. The Commentary on the Kalaṇḍuka Jātaka.
"Those countries, those places"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain boastful bhikkhu. In this regard, two stories are similar to the Kaṭāhaka Jātaka.
Here, however, he was a slave named Kalaṇḍuka belonging to the chief merchant of Bārāṇasī. Having fled, he [entered the service] of a chief merchant living in a border region...
When he had taken his daughter and was living there with a great retinue, the merchant of Benares, though having searched for Kalanduka, did not know where he had gone;
therefore, he sent the young white parrot he himself had raised, saying, "Go and search for Kalanduka.
The young parrot, wandering here and there, reached that city. At that time, Kalanduka was engaged in playing in the river.
Desiring to play, he had much garland, perfume, and ointment, as well as various kinds of food and drink, brought;
then, having gone to the river and boarded a boat with the merchant’s daughter, he sported in the water.
In that place, those of noble birth who were sporting in the river drank milk infused with a potent medicinal drug, by which they remained [vigorous] even for the duration of the day.
For those playing in the water, the cold does not trouble them. But this Kalanduka, having taken a mouthful of milk and rinsed his mouth, spat it out.
Even as he spat, instead of spitting into the water, he spat upon the head of the merchant’s daughter.
The young parrot, too, went to the riverbank and sat upon a branch of an udumbara tree.
Having looked and recognized Kalaṇḍuka, and seeing him spitting on the head of the merchant’s daughter, [the king said]: "Hey, slave Kalaṇḍuka!

Remember your own birth and your place of residence! Having taken a mouthful of milk and rinsed your mouth, do not spit on the head of the merchant’s daughter, who is of noble birth and raised in comfort! Do not overstep your own measure!"
Having said, "Do you know?", he spoke this verse:
"They know those places and those grounds, and I am one who roams the forest;
having investigated thoroughly, they would take hold of you—drink the milk, O Kalandaka!"
In this context, "those regions" and "those sites" refer to the mother's womb. This is the intended meaning:

those regions where you dwelt were not the regions of the wombs of daughters of the Khattiya caste and so forth; nor were those sites where you were established the sites of the wombs of daughters of the Khattiya caste and so forth.
Rather, it was in the womb of a slave-girl that you both dwelt and were established.
"And I am one who roams the forest"—by this he indicates that even as a creature of the animal realm, he knows this matter.

"Having investigated, they would surely take you"—this means that when I have gone and reported on you while you were practicing such improper conduct, your masters, having investigated and ascertained the truth, would beat you, brand you with marks, and take you away; having taken you, they will depart.
Therefore, knowing your own measure, do not peck at the head of the merchant’s daughter; drink the milk. He addresses him by the name Kalaṇḍuka.
Kalaṇḍuka, recognizing him as the young parrot, said out of fear, "Come, master! When did you arrive?
The parrot thought, "He does not call me out of a desire for my welfare; rather, he wishes to kill me by twisting my neck."
Realizing, "I have no need for her," he flew up from there and went to Bārāṇasī, where he related everything he had seen in detail to the merchant.
The merchant said, "What he has done is improper," and having gone there himself,
he issued an order for him to be brought back to Bārāṇasī, where he enjoyed his use as a slave.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Kalaṇḍuka was this bhikkhu, and the merchant of Bārāṇasī was none other than myself.
This concludes the seventh narrative, the Commentary on the Kalaṇḍuka Jātaka.
[128] 8. The Commentary on the Biḷāravata Jātaka.
"He who makes the Dhamma his banner"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning a certain hypocritical monk.
At that time, when the Teacher’s attention was drawn to that monk’s hypocrisy, he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past, too, this man was a hypocrite," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of a mouse.
Upon reaching maturity, he became large-bodied, resembling a young boar, and lived in the forest surrounded by many hundreds of mice.
Then, a certain jackal, wandering here and there, saw that troop of mice and [thought]: "These..."
Thinking, "I shall deceive the mice and eat them," he stood not far from the mice's dwelling, facing the sun and inhaling the wind on one leg.
As the Bodhisatta was wandering for alms and saw him, he thought, "This one must be virtuous," and approaching him, he asked, "Venerable sir, what is your name? "I am Dhammika."
“Why do you stand on only one foot instead of placing all four feet on the ground?
“If I were to place all four feet on the earth, the earth would not be able to support me; therefore, I stand on only one.
“Why do you stand with your mouth open? “We eat nothing else; we eat only wind.”
“Then why do you stand facing the sun? “I am paying homage to the sun.
Having heard his words, the Bodhisatta thought, “This one must be virtuous,” and from then on he went to attend upon him morning and evening together with the group of mice.

Then, when it was time for him to depart after having attended to him, the jackal took the very last mouse, ate the flesh, swallowed it, wiped his mouth, and stood there. Gradually, the group of mice became thin.
The mice thought, "Previously this dwelling place of ours was not sufficient; we stood packed together. Now it has become spacious, yet even so—"
"The nest is not being filled at all; what could this mean? they reported that occurrence to the Bodhisatta.
The Bodhisatta, reflecting, "For what reason have the mice become so few?", became suspicious of the jackal and thought, "I shall investigate this.
At the time of attendance, he placed the other mice in front and himself remained behind. The jackal [beheld] him...
The Bodhisatta leapt upward; seeing him leap up in order to seize him, he turned back and said, "Ho, jackal!

This undertaking of yours is not for the sake of the Dhamma being well-proclaimed as Dhamma, but rather you wander about making the Dhamma a banner for the purpose of harming others. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“He who, having made righteousness his banner, secretly practices evil, and having inspired confidence in living beings—that one, alas, is called a ‘cat’.
In this context, “he who” refers to anyone at all among the kṣatriyas and so forth. “Having made righteousness his banner” means having taken the ten courses of wholesome action as his banner.
"Having made it a banner" means raising it up and displaying it as if making a peak.
"Having inspired confidence" means having caused others to develop trust through the perception that "this person is virtuous.

"They call that the 'cat-vow'" means that for one who makes such a doctrine their banner and commits evil deeds in secret, that practice is called the "cat-vow" (*kerāṭika-vata*); this is the meaning.
Even as he was speaking, the King of the Mice sprang up, fell upon his neck, bit him below the jaw inside the throat-pipe, tore through the throat-pipe, and brought about his death.
The troop of mice turned back, devoured the jackal with "murū murū" cries, and departed.
It is said that those who arrived first obtained the meat, while those who arrived later did not.
They did not obtain it. From that time forth, the mouse community became fearless.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the sly jackal was the deceitful bhikkhu, but the king of the mice was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Biḷāravata Jātaka, the eighth.
[129] 9. The Commentary on the Aggikabhāradvāja Jātaka.
"This crest is not for the sake of merit"—the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain hypocritical monk.
For in the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta, having become a king of mice, lived in the forest.
He lived there. Now, one day a jackal, unable to escape when a forest fire broke out, stood pressing his head against a tree.

The hair on his entire body was burned away, but at the spot where he had remained pressed against the tree, a small amount of hair remained on his head like a tuft. One day, while he was drinking water from a pond—
Looking at his shadow and seeing the tuft of hair, [the rat] thought, "Now my capital has been recovered.
Wandering through the forest, he saw that mouse-hole and, thinking, "I shall deceive these mice and eat them," stood not far away in the manner described above.
Then the Bodhisatta, while wandering for food, saw him and, perceiving him to be virtuous, approached him.
“Who are you by name? he asked. “I am named Aggikabhāradvāja,” he replied. “Then for what purpose have you come?
“For the sake of protecting you. “By doing what will you protect us?
“I know a method called ‘counting on the fingers. When you go out early in the morning to seek alms, I shall count how many there are, and when you return, I shall do the same.”
“I will count them; by counting them every morning and evening in this way, I shall protect them. “In that case, protect them, uncle,” he said.

He consented, saying, “Very well,” and at the time of going out, he counted, “One, two, three,” and upon returning, he likewise counted them in the same way and ate the very last one. The rest was exactly as before.

Then the mouse-king turned back and stood there, saying, "O Aggikabhāradvāja, this crest has not been placed upon the top of your well-proclaimed Dhamma; rather, it was placed there for the sake of food. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
"This crest is not for the sake of merit; this crest is for the sake of food.
It does not count as a finger-ring; enough of you, O fire-worshipper!"
In this context, "finger-counting" (*aṅguṭṭhigaṇanā*) refers to counting by means of the thumb, as in the phrase "it goes to finger-counting.
This mouse-heap does not go to, does not reach, and does not fill the count of the thumb; the meaning is that it reaches exhaustion.
"Enough for you, O fire-eater!"—he spoke thus, addressing the jackal by name. "By this much, enough for you; no further than this."
"You will eat the mouse. Or, "Enough of our living together with you; we shall not live with you from now on"—this is also the meaning. The rest is exactly as before.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the jackal was this monk, and the king of mice was none other than I myself."
The ninth: The Commentary on the Aggikabhāradvāja Jātaka.
[130] 10. The Commentary on the Kosiya Jātaka:
"May you eat according to your word. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain woman in Sāvatthī.
He spoke concerning this. It is said that there was a certain brahmin lay follower endowed with faith whose wife was immoral and of evil character.
Having committed adultery with another man at night, she would do no work during the day, but instead would lie down feigning illness and groaning.
Then the brahmin asked her, "What is it that makes you unwell, my dear? She replied, "The winds are piercing me."
“What is it that she needs? he asked. “Soothing and sweet foods, both excellent and ordinary, such as rice-gruel, boiled rice, oil, and so forth.
Whatever the woman desired, the brahmin would bring and give it to her; like a slave, he performed all her tasks.
Yet, whenever the brahmin entered the house, she would lie down, and whenever he went out, she would spend her time with her paramours.
Then the brahmin, thinking, "The end of these piercing winds within her body is not apparent," went one day to Jetavana taking perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.
Having approached the Teacher, he paid homage, worshipped him, and sat down to one side.
When [the Teacher] asked, "Brahmin, why is it not apparent? he replied, "Venerable sir, it is said that piercing winds are striking the body of my brahmin wife."
“Indeed, I seek out for her ghee, oil, and other such things, as well as the most excellent foods;
yet her body has become stout and her complexion clear, though no end to her wind-disease is seen.
While I am thus attending to her, I find no opportunity to come here,” he said. The Teacher [perceived] the wicked nature of the brahmin woman.
Having understood this, he said, "Brāhmaṇa, even before now the wise have told you that 'when a woman lying thus does not recover from her illness, these and those medicines should be administered';
however, because you were caught up in the cycle of existence, you did not take it to heart.
Having said this, at his request, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a prominent brahmin family.
Upon reaching maturity, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā and became a world-renowned teacher in Benares.
From among the princes and brahmin youths in one hundred royal capitals, almost all were his pupils.

They were learning their crafts in his presence. Then, a certain Brahmin youth from the countryside, having learned the three Vedas and the eighteen branches of knowledge under the Bodhisatta, established a household right there in Bārāṇasī;
he came into the presence of the Bodhisatta two or three times every day. His Brahmin wife was immoral.
The phrase "she was of evil character" is entirely similar to the present-day account.
However, when [the man] said, "For this reason, I do not find an opportunity to receive his advice," the Bodhisatta,
knowing that "this young woman is lying there having deceived him," thought, "I shall prescribe medicine suitable for her illness."
Having reflected, he said: "Father, from now on, do not give her ghee, milk, juice, or similar things.
Instead, having placed five leaves and various fruits into cow's urine, grind them, place the mixture in a vessel of new brass, and let her take up the smell of the metal.
Then, taking a rope, a cord, a tree, or a creeper, say: 'This is for your illness.'"
"Take this appropriate medicine, or drink this, or having risen, perform some task suitable for one who has finished eating"—
having said this, you should recite this verse. "If he does not drink the medicine, then,
having struck him several times with a rope, a cord, a tree, or a creeper, and having seized him by the hair..."
“Having pulled it out, you should rub it with a stone; it will rise up at that very moment and perform its work.
He agreed, saying, “Very well,” and having prepared the medicine according to the instructions given, he said, “My dear lady, drink this medicine.
“By whom was this told to you? “By my teacher, my dear lady. “Remove him! she said.

“I shall drink. The young man said, “You will not drink of your own free will,” and taking a rope, he said, “Drink medicine suitable for your illness, or perform work suitable for rice gruel and food,” and spoke this verse:
“Act according to what you say, and speak according to what you have done.”
"Both of these do not agree for you, O Kosiya: your words and your eating.
In this context, "you should eat according to your words" means that you should eat in accordance with what you have said;
the sense is that you should eat only in a manner consistent with your statement, "The winds are piercing me. The reading "yathāvācaṃ vā" (or "according to your words") is also appropriate.
They also read it as *yathāvācāya*, and in all cases the meaning is the same. *Yathābhuttañca byāharā* means:
speak in accordance with what has been eaten by you; that is to say, having said, "We are well," perform whatever must be done in the house.
There is also the reading *yathābhūtañca*; alternatively, it means having spoken exactly as it is, namely, "We are well."

The meaning is: "Perform work. "Both do not agree for you, O Kosiya"—that is, both this speech of yours, "The winds pierce me," and this fine food that has been eaten by you, these two do not agree with you;
therefore, rise up and perform work. He addresses him by his clan name, "O Kosiya."
When this was said, the daughter of the Kosiya brahmin thought, "Since the time my teacher began to exert himself on my behalf, it has not been possible for me to deceive him;
I shall rise up and perform the work. Thinking, "My teacher has discovered my immoral conduct;
henceforth, I can never do such a thing again," she rose up and performed the work out of reverence for her teacher.

Having desisted from evil deeds, she became virtuous. That brahmin woman, thinking, "I have indeed been recognized by the Perfectly Enlightened One," out of reverence for the Teacher did not commit misconduct again.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "The husband and wife of that time are now this very husband and wife; as for the teacher, it was I myself."
The commentary on the *Kosiya-jātaka* is the tenth.
The thirteenth chapter, the *Kusanāḷi-vagga*.
Its summary verse (*uddāna*) is as follows:
Kusa-nāḷi and Dummedha, Naṅgalīsa and Amba-kaṭāha;
Asilakkhaṇa and Kalaṇḍuka, Biḷāraggi and Kosiya—these are the [discourses] of the Chapter on Non-Conferral (Asampadāna-vagga). 14. Asampadānavaggo.
[131] 1. The Commentary on the *Asampadāna-jātaka*.
"By not sharing with one another," etc.—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning Devadatta.
At that time, the monks in the Hall of Truth raised this discussion: "Friends, Devadatta is ungrateful."
“He does not know the virtues of the Tathāgata. The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta is ungrateful;
in the past as well, he was ungrateful. Having said this, he related a story of the past.

In the past, when a certain Magadhan king was ruling in Rājagaha in the kingdom of Magadha, the Bodhisatta was his very own treasurer, a man of eighty crores of wealth known by the name Saṅkha-seṭṭhi.
In Bārāṇasī, there was likewise a treasurer named Pīḷiya-seṭṭhi, also possessing eighty crores of wealth.
They were friends with one another. Of them, [this is the account] of Pīḷiya-seṭṭhi in Bārāṇasī...
For some reason, a great fear arose and all his wealth was lost.
Having become poor and destitute, he took his wife and, making the merchant Saṅkha his refuge, departed from Bārāṇasī on foot.
Upon reaching Rājagaha, he went to the residence of the merchant Saṅkha. As soon as the merchant saw him, he said, “Friend...”
Having embraced him, saying, "Welcome," he paid him honor and respect, and after they had spent several days together, one day he asked, "Friend, for what purpose have you come?
"Fear has arisen for me, friend; all my wealth is exhausted;
be my support. "Very well, friend, do not fear," he said, and having opened the storehouse, [he gave] forty...
Having caused ten million pieces of gold to be given away, he divided all his remaining possessions— both animate and inanimate—
right down to his personal belongings, and gave away exactly half. Taking that wealth, he returned once more to Bārāṇasī and established his residence there.
In the course of time, a similar fear arose for Saṅkha the merchant as well.
Seeking a refuge for himself, he thought, "My friend has done me a great service and given me half his wealth; he will not abandon me upon seeing me, so I shall go to him.
Having thus reflected, he took his wife and traveled on foot to Bārāṇasī, and there [he left] his wife...
He said, "Bhadde, it is not proper for you to travel with me through the middle of the street;
you shall come later, riding in a carriage sent by me and accompanied by a large retinue. Stay right here until I have sent the carriage.
Having spoken thus, he left her in the hall and entered the city himself. Going to the house of the merchant, [he said], "From the city of Rājagaha..."
“Your friend, the merchant Saṅkha, has arrived,” he announced.
The king said, “Let him come,” and having summoned him, upon seeing him, neither rose from his seat nor offered any greeting;
he merely asked, “For what purpose have you come? “I have come to see you. “Where have you taken up residence? “Not yet.”
“There is a place for you to stay; we have even left the merchant’s wife standing in the hall before we came.
“You have no place to stay here. Take the bait, cook it in one spot, eat it, and go;
do not enter our house again,” he said, and having bound my companion by the hem of his garment...
"Give the slave a basketful of husks," he commanded. It is said that on that very day, having caused a thousand cartloads of red rice to be unloaded, he had filled his storehouse;
yet this ungrateful great thief, having received forty million in wealth, gave only a basketful of husks to his friend.
The slave, having placed one basketful of husks in a carrying-basket, [set out].
He went into the presence of the Bodhisatta.
The Bodhisatta thought: "This wicked man, having received forty million pieces of wealth from me, now demands a mere gourd-pot; shall I take it or not? Then this occurred to him: "First of all..."
Ungrateful and treacherous toward friends, he broke our friendship by his act of destruction.
If I do not accept this hollow gourd given by him because it is of poor quality, I too shall break the friendship.
For foolish blind people destroy friendship when they refuse to accept even a small thing they have received; however, as for me, what has been given by him—
“Taking this gourd vessel, I shall establish a friendship with him on my own terms.
Binding the gourd vessel to the hem of his garment, he descended from the palace and went to the hall. Then his wife asked him, “Noble sir, what have you obtained?
“My dear, our friend Seṭṭhi Pīḷiya gave us a gourd vessel and has released us this very day.”
She began to weep, saying, "Noble sir, for what purpose did you take this? Is this worthy of one worth forty million?
The Bodhisatta said, "My dear, do not weep. I took it out of fear that our friendship might be broken by him;
I took it so that our friendship would remain established through my influence. For what reason are you weeping? Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Through not providing for one another, the friendships of fools turn into strife;
therefore, I shall remove my excessive pride, lest my friendship with you perish forever.

In this passage, *asampadānena* means through non-provision. The elision of the vowel *a* is a grammatical euphonic combination (*sandhi*); the meaning is “through non-acceptance. *Itarītarassa* means...

“Of anyone, however lowly. The phrase “the friend of a fool becomes a source of misfortune” means that the friends of one who is dull-witted and lacking in wisdom become like *kalī*—that is, like those with ill fortune (*kāḷakaṇṇi*)—and thus break apart; this is the meaning. Therefore, he shows: “So I carry away the half-measure of chaff,” meaning:
for that reason, I am carrying away and taking the single *palāpa*-measure given by my companion. “A measure (*māna*)”—this refers to the measure.
Indeed, eight *nāḷīs* are called a *māna*, and four *mānas* plus four *nāḷīs* are called a *tumba*.
Therefore it is said, "a *palāpa*-tumba. "May my friendship with my friend not decay for eternity" means:
may my friendship with my companion not be broken; let this remain eternal—this is the meaning.

Even when this was said, the merchant’s wife continued to weep. At that moment, a laborer belonging to Saṅkha the merchant, who had been given to Pīḷiya the merchant as a slave for his work, arrived through the door of the hall. Hearing the sound of the merchant’s wife weeping, he entered the hall;
seeing his own master, he fell at his feet, wept and wailed, and asked, "For what purpose have you come here?"
“Master,” he asked. The merchant related everything. The slave said, “Let it be so, Master;

do not worry,” and after comforting both of them, he led them to his own house. Having bathed them with scented water and fed them, he gathered the remaining slaves together, saying, “Your masters have arrived,” and showed them to them.
After spending a few days there, he took all the slaves and went to the royal courtyard.
Having gone there, he made a loud noise. The king had him summoned and asked, "What is this? They reported the entire incident to the king.
Having heard their words, the king summoned both merchants and asked Saṅkha-seṭṭhi, "Is it true that you gave forty million pieces of wealth to Mahāseṭṭhi as a loan? "Yes, Your Majesty."

"He gave not only wealth, but having divided his entire fortune—both animate and inanimate—into two equal portions, he gave it all to my companion who came to Rājagaha thinking it was me. The King, thinking "Is this true?", asked the merchant Pīḷiya:
"Yes, Your Majesty," he replied. "But did you give that to him when he came thinking it was you?"

“Did you offer him any hospitality or show him any respect? He remained silent. “But did you have even a single gourd-soup bowl’s worth of cloth tucked into his robe and given to him? Hearing that as well, he remained silent.
The king, consulting with his ministers on what should be done, rebuked him and said, “Go; [seize] everything in the house of the merchant Pīḷiya.”
“Give the wealth of Saṅkha the treasurer! he said. The Bodhisatta replied, “Great King, I have no need for another’s property;
however, please cause only what was given by me to be returned. The king had the Bodhisatta’s property restored to him.
Having recovered all the wealth that had been given to him, the Bodhisatta, surrounded by his servants, went back to Rājagaha.
Having gone home, he established his family, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and departed according to his karma.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the merchant Pīḷiya was Devadatta, while the merchant Saṅkha was none other than myself.
This is the first commentary on the Asampadāna Jātaka.

[132] 2. The Commentary on the Bhīrukajātaka "‘In the instruction on what is wholesome, through firmness of resolve’—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Sutta on the Temptation by the Daughters of Māra at the Ajapāla Banyan tree. For the Blessed One, starting from the beginning, said:
‘Tanhã, Arati, and Ragā came forth, shining brilliantly...’"
“There the Teacher dispelled them, like the wind blowing away a tuft of cotton.
Thus, when the Teacher had finished reciting that sutta up to its conclusion, the monks gathered in the Dhamma Hall initiated this discussion:
“Friends, the Perfectly Enlightened One [subdued] even the hundreds of Māra’s daughters, though they possessed divine forms...”
Even when women approached him for the sake of seduction, he did not look at them, even opening his eyes; "Oh, how wonderful is this so-called power of a Buddha!
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that, having exhausted all taints, I have [remained detached]."
"It is indeed marvelous that even one who has attained omniscience does not look upon the daughters of Māra; for previously, while seeking the knowledge of enlightenment,
even when I was still possessed of defilements, I went away without looking upon a fashioned divine form created by the power of my senses under the influence of defilements,
and thus I attained great sovereignty," he said, and related the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was the youngest of a hundred brothers;
all of this should be detailed in the same manner as described below in the Takkasilā Jātaka.

At that time, however, the inhabitants of the city of Takkasilā approached the Bodhisatta at a hall outside the city, made their request, and having had him accept the kingship, performed his consecration.
Then the inhabitants of the city of Takkasilā adorned the city like a city of the gods and the royal palace like the abode of Indra.
At that time, the Bodhisatta entered the city and, having ascended a precious couch beneath a raised white parasol upon the great terrace of the palace,
sat there with the majestic bearing of a king of the gods, while the ministers, brahmins, householders, and others [surrounded him].
And the young kṣatriyas, adorned with every ornament, stood surrounding him;
sixteen thousand dancing women, resembling celestial nymphs, skilled in dance, song, and instrumental music, and endowed with supreme grace, performed dances, songs, and instrumental music.
With the sound of that singing and instrumental music, the royal palace was like the interior of the great ocean filled with the thundering of clouds.
There was a single cry. The Bodhisatta, gazing at his own splendor and beauty, thought:
"If I had looked upon the divinely fashioned forms created by those yakkhinīs, I would have met my death; therefore, I shall not look upon this splendor and beauty.
It is because I stand firm in the instruction of the Paccekabuddhas that this has come to pass for me."
"‘I have attained! Having thought thus, and uttering this inspired exclamation (udāna), he spoke this verse:
‘Through the instruction in what is wholesome, through firmness of resolve, and through not turning back out of fear or cowardice, we have not fallen under the power of the ogresses;
this safety has come to me amidst great danger.’"
In that context, "instruction in the wholesome" (*kusalūpadesa*) means instruction in what is wholesome; the meaning is the exhortation of the *paccekabuddhas*.
"And with firm fortitude" (*dhitiyā daḷhāya ca*) means with firm fortitude; the meaning is with steadfast, uninterrupted, and continuous energy.
"And because of not turning back due to fearfulness" (*anivattitattā bhayabhīrutāya ca*) means because of the state of not turning back due to fearfulness. In that context, "fear" (*bhaya*)—
“Mere mental trepidation” is limited fear; “timidity” is great fear that has reached the point of bodily trembling.
Neither of these occurred to the Great Being even upon seeing the terrifying object [of] “these are indeed yakkhinīs who devour humans.
Therefore he said: “Because of his non-retrogression and because of the absence of timidity. Precisely due to the absence of timidity, the terrifying object—
The meaning is: "even having seen [them], because of our state of non-retrogression.
"We did not fall under the power of the rākṣasīs" means that in the wilderness of the yakṣas, we did not come under the control of those rākṣasīs.

Because our fortitude was firm in following the instruction in wholesome states, and because we were by nature non-retrogressive due to the absence of fear and timidity, therefore we did not fall under the power of the rākṣasīs.

This is what was said: "That safety of mine through great fear"—meaning, "Today, this state of safety, security, and joy for me, which would otherwise have been reached in the presence of the ogresses through great fear and the suffering and dejection resulting therefrom, has indeed come to pass.

Thus the Great Being, having taught the Dhamma with this verse, having ruled the kingdom according to the Dhamma, and having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, departed according to his karma.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, I was the prince who went to Takkasilā and attained the kingship.
This concludes the second commentary, the Bhīruka-jātaka.
3. The Commentary on the Ghaṭāsana-jātaka.
"Where there is safety"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain bhikkhu.
That bhikkhu, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, went to the borderlands and entered the rains retreat in a forest lodging near a certain village.
As soon as the first month had passed, while he had gone out for alms, his leaf-hut...
He meditated. Being distressed by the lack of a dwelling place, he informed his attendants. They spent the three months saying things such as, "Very well, venerable sir;
we shall build a leaf hut; let us first plow, let us first sow," and so forth.
Due to the lack of a suitable resting place, he was unable to bring his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) to its consummation. He did not even attain the mere sign (*nimitta*).
Having completed his rains retreat without having produced [any higher attainment], he went to Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side.
The Teacher exchanged greetings with him and asked, "Bhikkhu, what subject of meditation has become suitable for you?
He explained from the beginning how it had been unsuitable. The Teacher said, "In the past, bhikkhu, even animals..."
"Having understood what was suitable and what was unsuitable for themselves, they dwelt during the time it was suitable and, abandoning the dwelling place when it became unsuitable, went elsewhere;
why did you not know what was suitable and what was unsuitable for yourself? Having said this, being requested by him, he related a story of the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a bird."
Having attained maturity and reached the height of fortune, he became a king of birds.
He took up residence with his retinue, depending upon a great tree in a certain forest region on the bank of a lake—a tree endowed with branches and boughs and thick with leaves and foliage.
Many birds, dwelling on the branches spreading over the surface of the water of that tree, left behind their bodily refuse.
They dropped it into the water. Now, a fierce nāga king lived in that lake. It occurred to him:
"These birds are dropping bodily refuse into my dwelling, the lake; what if I were to produce fire from the water, burn the tree, and scatter these [birds]?
With a mind full of anger, during the night, he [acted] toward all the birds.
Having gathered together and settled upon the branches of the tree, at the first instance he caused the water to boil as if it were placed on a hearth;
at the second instance, he raised smoke; and at the third instance, he produced a flame as high as the trunk of a palmyra tree.
Seeing the flame rising from the water, the Bodhisatta said: "O birds, that which is set ablaze by fire is extinguished by water."
"But now it is the water itself that is ablaze. We cannot remain here; we shall go elsewhere," he said, and spoke this verse:
"Wherever there is safety, even if an enemy is raised up there—where the fire-god blazes in the midst of the water."
"Today there is no dwelling on the earth or in the trees; seek refuge in the directions today, for neither [of these] is secure.
In this context, "where there is safety" means where there is a state of security and fearlessness;
yet in that very place, an enemy—an adversary—has arisen. "Of water" (*dakassa*) means of water. "The consumer" (*ghatāsano*) is fire. It...
Indeed, he eats from a pot; therefore, he is called "the pot-eater" (*ghatāsana*). "Not today is our dwelling" means that today we have no place to stay.
"A tree on the earth" is called *mahīruha*; the meaning is: a tree born upon this earth.
"Take refuge in the quarters" means: go and take refuge in the directions. "Today there is fear for us from our refuge" means: today we have fear arising from our place of refuge.
"Fear has arisen; the meaning is that fear has arisen from the very place of refuge.
Having said this, the Bodhisatta took with him those birds who had followed his word and flew away elsewhere. Those birds who remained without accepting the Bodhisatta’s advice met their end.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths (*saccāni*), identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu was established in Arahatship.
At that time, the birds who carried out the Bodhisatta’s word became the assembly of the Buddha, while the king of the birds was none other than myself.
This concludes the third narrative, the Ghaṭāsana Jātaka.
[134] 4. The Jhānasodhana Jātaka Narrative.

"Those who possess perception"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the detailed explanation given by the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) to a question he had asked in brief at the gate of Saṅkassa City. Herein is the story of the past:
it is said that in the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta passed away in a forest region.
When questioned by his pupils, he replied, "Neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. ... [and so on] ... The ascetics did not accept the words of the eldest pupil.
The Bodhisatta, having come from the Ābhassara realm, stood in the air and spoke this verse:
"Those who possess perception are ill-fated; those who are without perception are also ill-fated."
"Avoiding both these, that is the stainless bliss of attainment.
Therein, "those who possess perception" indicates all sentient beings with consciousness, excluding those who have attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
"They too are miserable" means that because they do not attain that meditative attainment, they are indeed called miserable. "And those who are non-percipient" refers to...

It shows that in the non-percipient realm (*asaññabhava*), beings are without consciousness. "They too are miserable" means that they too are indeed called miserable because of their failure to obtain this very attainment.
"Avoiding both of these" means that he advises the pupil to avoid and abandon both of these:
the realm of perception (*saññibhava*) and the non-percipient realm (*asaññibhava*). That bliss of attainment is free from blemish (*anaṅgaṇa*).
For one who has attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, that meditative bliss—which is reckoned as "bliss" in the sense of peace—is free from blemish (*anaṅgaṇa*) and faultless;
it is called "free from blemish" because its essential nature is powerful one-pointedness of mind.
Thus, after the Bodhisatta had taught the Dhamma and praised the virtue of his pupil, he returned to the Brahma-world. Then the remaining ascetics placed their faith in the senior pupil.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Sāriputta was the senior pupil, and I myself was the Great Brahmā.
This concludes the commentary on the Jhānasodhana Jātaka, the fourth.
[135] 5. The Commentary on the Candābha Jātaka.
"Candābham" (The Moon's Radiance): This was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Elder’s own answer to a question at the gate of Saṅkassa city.
It is said that in the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, while dying in a forest glade, was asked by his pupils;
having replied, "The moon’s radiance, the sun’s radiance," he was reborn among the Ābhassara devas.
The ascetics did not believe the senior pupil. Then the Bodhisatta, having come from the Ābhassara realm, stood in the air and spoke this verse:
“He who here gains a foothold through wisdom in the radiance of the moon and the radiance of the sun, Through jhāna free from applied thought, becomes one who has reached the Ābhassara realm.”
Therein, "moonlight" indicates the white kasiṇa; "sunlight" indicates the yellow kasiṇa.

"Who here finds a foothold with wisdom" refers to that person who, in this world of beings, finds a foothold in these two kasiṇas through wisdom—taking them as an object, entering into them, and becoming firmly established therein.
Alternatively, [it refers to] moonlight and sunlight, who here [finds a foothold] with wisdom...

Regarding the phrase "he gains a footing": to whatever extent the radiance of the moon and the radiance of the sun pervade a certain place, having expanded the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-kasiṇa*) to that same extent and taking that as the object, one who generates jhāna is said to "gain a footing" in both types of light through wisdom.
Therefore, this too is the meaning here: by means of jhāna without applied thought (*avitakka*), that person becomes one whose form is luminous (*ābhassara-rūpa*).
"Having done so, by means of the second jhāna thus attained, he becomes one who goes to the Ābhassara Brahma-world.
Thus the Bodhisatta, having awakened the ascetic and spoken of the virtue of his senior pupil, went back to the Brahma-world itself.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Sāriputta was the senior pupil, and I myself was the Great Brahmā."
The fifth: The Commentary on the Candābhajātakavaṇṇanā.
[136] 6. The Commentary on the Suvaṇṇahaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā.
