"One should be content with what one has received"—this [verse] the Teacher spoke while residing at Jetavana concerning the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
He spoke with reference to this. For in Sāvatthī, a certain lay follower, having invited the community of bhikkhunīs to partake of garlic, commanded his field-guard:
"If bhikkhunīs come, give two or three bulbs to each bhikkhunī.
From then on, the bhikkhunīs went to both his house and his field for the sake of garlic.

Then, on a festival day, the garlic in his house was completely exhausted. The nun Thullanandā, together with her retinue, went to the house and said, "Friends, we have need of garlic. When they replied, "Venerable lady, there is none; as much as was brought has been entirely consumed;
please go to the field," she went to the field and, not knowing moderation, [took] garlic...
He had it brought. The field-guardian complained, “How can these bhikkhunīs take garlic without knowing moderation?
Having heard his words, those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires also complained;
having heard them, the bhikkhus also complained. And having complained, they reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One...
Having rebuked the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, [the Buddha said]: "Bhikkhus, a person of great desire is disliked and displeasing even to his own mother;

he is unable to inspire confidence in those without confidence, or to increase the confidence of those who already have it, nor can he produce unarisen gain or stabilize gain that has already arisen."

“However, a person of few desires is able to inspire confidence in those who lack it, to produce even greater confidence in those who already have it, to bring about unarisen gain, or to make established gain firm.
Having spoken to the monks on this and other such lines regarding the Dhamma appropriate for them, [the Blessed One said]: “Monks, it is not only now that Thullanandā...
"Having great desire, even in the past he had great desire," he said, and then related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a certain brahmin family.
When he reached maturity, they brought him a wife from a family of equal status. Her names were Nandā and Nandavatī.
Sundarīnanda had three daughters. While they were still unmarried, the Bodhisatta passed away and was reborn in the womb of a golden goose;
the knowledge of recollecting his past births (*jātissara-ñāṇa*) arose within him.
Upon reaching maturity, seeing his own great body covered in gold and endowed with supreme beauty, he thought: "From where have I passed away to be reborn here?"
Reflecting thus, he recognized, "They are from the human world. Then, considering further, "How indeed do my brahmin wife and daughters live?
he perceived, "They live in hardship, working as servants for others. He thought, "In my body there are golden bowls that can be struck and beaten;
I shall give one bowl each to them from this, and by means of that—"
“May my wife and daughters live happily. Having gone there, he hid at the tip of the rear pole;
and when the brahmin woman and her daughters saw the Bodhisatta, they asked, “From where have you come, Master?
He replied, “I am your father, who, having passed away, was reborn in the womb of a golden goose; I have come to see you.”
“From this day forward, you have no need to live a life of suffering by working for hire for others;
I shall give each of you a bowl. By selling it, you may live in comfort. Having given one bowl, he departed.
In this very manner, he would come from time to time and give them each a bowl, while the brahmin lady and her daughters [continued their lives].
They became wealthy and happy.
Then one day, that brahmin woman addressed her daughters: "Daughters, the minds of animals are indeed difficult to fathom.
It may happen that your father does not come here; therefore, while he is currently present, let us pluck all the feathers and take them."
Thinking, "In this way our father will suffer," they did not consent.
But the brahmin woman, out of great greed, on another day when the golden swan king arrived, said, "Come here first, my lord.
When he had approached her, she seized him with both hands and plucked all his feathers. Those feathers, however, were to the Bodhisatta's liking...
Because he had been taken by force, all his feathers became like those of a crane (*baka*).
The Bodhisatta was unable to fly away with his wings spread; then she placed him in a large jar and nourished him.
When his feathers grew back, they turned white. Having regained his feathers, he flew up and went to his own dwelling place, never to return again.
The Teacher, having related this past event, said: "Monks, it is not only now that Thullanandā was of great desire;
in the past, too, she was of great desire, and because of her great desire, she was deprived of gold. Now, however, because of her own great desire, she will be deprived even of garlic;
therefore, from this time forward, she shall not be allowed to eat garlic."
"Just as it was with Thullanandā, so it was for the other bhikkhunīs who relied upon her. Therefore, even when receiving much, one must know the proper measure;
but when receiving little, one should be content with what has been obtained and not aspire for more.
Having said this, he recited this verse:
“One should be content with what one has obtained, for excessive greed is evil;
by seizing the king of swans, you have fallen away from your golden state.
In this context, *tuṭṭhabbaṃ* means one should be satisfied.

Having said this, the Teacher rebuked her in many ways and, having laid down the training rule: "Should any bhikkhunī eat garlic, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)," he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the brahmin woman was this Thullanandā;
the three daughters were these very same three sisters; and the golden swan king was none other than myself."
The sixth is the commentary on the Suvaṇṇahaṃsa Jātaka.
[137] 7. The commentary on the Babbu Jātaka:
"Where one finds a bat... This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the training rule regarding Kāṇamātā.
He related the story. For in Sāvatthī there was a female lay follower named Kāṇamātā, well-known by her daughter’s name, who was a stream-enterer and a noble disciple.
She gave her daughter Kāṇā in marriage to a man of the same caste in a certain village.
On one occasion, Kāṇā went to her mother’s house on some business. Then, after a few days had passed, her husband sent a messenger...
He sent word, saying, “Let Kāṇā come; I desire the arrival of Kāṇā. When Kāṇā heard the messenger’s words, she asked her mother, “Mother, I shall go.
Kāṇā’s mother said, “Having lived here for so long, how can you go away empty-handed?
and she baked some cakes. At that very moment, a certain monk wandering for alms arrived at her house.
She arrived, and having had that laywoman seat him, she had her give him a bowl full of cakes. That monk went out and told another;
she likewise had her give him one. He too went out and told another; she likewise did the same for him.
In this way, she gave to four people. The cakes she had prepared were completely exhausted.
The journey did not succeed for the one-eyed woman. Then her husband sent a messenger a second time and a third time.
When sending the third time, he sent him saying, "If the one-eyed woman does not come, I shall bring another wife.
On all three occasions, the journey did not succeed by that very same means; the husband of the one-eyed woman brought another wife. The one-eyed woman—
Having heard that news, she stood there weeping.

The Teacher, knowing the reason for this, dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, went to Kāṇamātā’s residence, sat down on the prepared seat, and asked Kāṇamātā, “Why is this Kāṇā weeping? [She replied: “By this...”
Having heard these words, “...for such a reason,” he comforted Kāṇamātā, delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, and rising from his seat, went to the monastery.
Then, after those four monks had taken the prepared cakes three times, the fact that Kāṇā’s departure was cut short became known throughout the Saṅgha of monks. Then one day, the monks—

In the Dhamma Hall, they raised this discussion: "Friends, after four monks had eaten three times the fried cakes prepared by Kāṇamātā and caused Kāṇā to go off with them, they have, on account of a daughter abandoned by her husband, caused great distress to arise in the Great Laywoman.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, what is it that you are discussing now?"

Having asked, "Sitting for what conversation? and being told, "For this one indeed," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that those four monks, having consumed what belonged to Kaṇamātā, gave rise to grief in her; they gave rise to it even in the past. Having said this, he related the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of stone-cutters.
Having reached maturity, he became one whose craft was perfectly refined.
In a certain town in the kingdom of Kāsī, there was a merchant of great wealth who possessed forty crores of gold stored in his treasuries. Then his wife passed away;
out of attachment to her wealth, she went and was reborn as a mouse upon the surface of that hoard. In this manner, by degrees—
The entire family perished; the lineage was cut off. That village too was abandoned and fell into desolation.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was splitting rocks and pounding them at the site of that old village.
Then, as she was wandering about for food, the mouse saw the Bodhisatta again and again, and having developed affection for him, she thought:
“Much of my wealth will perish for no reason; if I join together with this man, give him this wealth, and have him sell the meat, we shall eat it.
One day, she bit a kahāpaṇa coin with her mouth and went into the presence of the Bodhisattva.
Seeing her, he addressed her with affectionate words: “What is it, indeed?”
“Mother,” he said, “you have come having taken a kahāpaṇa. “Father, take this and enjoy it yourself;
bring some meat for me as well. He consented, saying, “Very well,” and taking the kahāpaṇa, went home.
Having bought meat with one māsaka and brought it back, he gave it to her. She took it, went to her own dwelling place, and according to her desire...
"Eat. From that time forth, she gave a kahāpaṇa to the Bodhisatta every day according to this very routine, and he would bring her meat.
Then one day, a cat seized that mouse. She said to him, "Friend, do not kill me!"
“For what reason will I not kill him? For I am hungry and desire to eat meat; it is not possible for me not to kill him.
“But do you desire to eat meat only for one day, or at all times? “If I obtain it, I desire to eat it at all times.
“If that is so, I shall give you meat at all times; release him.”
Then the cat said to her, "In that case, be careful," and released her.
From then on, she would divide the meat she had brought into two portions, giving one to the cat and eating one herself.
Then one day, another cat seized her; she likewise persuaded him in the same manner and caused him to release her. From then on...
They divided it into three portions and ate it. Again another seized it; he too, having convinced him in the same manner, freed himself.
From then on, they divided it into four portions and ate it. Again another seized it;
he too, having convinced him in the same manner, freed himself. From then on, they divided it into five portions and ate it.
As she was eating the fifth portion, she became exhausted from eating so little, emaciated, and devoid of flesh and blood.
When the Bodhisatta saw her, he asked, "Mother, why are you so withered? When she replied, "For this reason," he said, "Why did you not tell me for all this time?
I shall know what must be done here. Having thus comforted her, he...

Having fashioned a cave out of a smooth-surfaced stone and brought it there, he said, "Mother, having entered this cave and lain down, you should frighten everyone who comes with harsh words. She entered the cave and lay down.
Then a certain cat came and said, "Give me some meat today! Thereupon the mouse said to him, "Hey, you wicked cat!..."
"Am I a meat-stealer to you? Do I eat the flesh of my own children? she rebuked him.
The cat, unaware that he was lying within the crystal cave, rushed forward impulsively with the thought, "I will seize the mouse," and struck the crystal cave with his chest.
At that very moment, his heart burst, and his eyes bulged out.
They were born. Having met their end right there, they fell to one side in a hidden place.
In this manner, one after another, all four individuals reached the end of their lives.
From then on, the mice became fearless and gave two or three kahāpaṇas to the Bodhisatta every day. In this way, gradually, all the wealth—
He gave it to the Bodhisatta alone. Both of them, having maintained their friendship for as long as they lived, passed away according to their respective kamma.
Having related this past event, the Teacher, now fully enlightened, uttered this verse:
“Where one cat gains [a mouse], a second is born there.”
"The third and the fourth—this, O baboon, is your hole. In this context, "where" means in whatever place. "Babū" means a cat.
"A second is born there" means that in whatever place one [cat] finds a mouse or meat, a second cat is also born and arises there; likewise for the third and the fourth.
And so, at that time, there were those four cats. Having become such, they ate meat day after day;
and those mongooses, striking this crystal cave with their chests, all met their end.

Thus the Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the four cats were the four monks; the mouse was Kāṇamātā; and the stone-cutter jeweler was none other than myself."
The Seventh: The Commentary on the Babbu Jātaka [138].
8. The Commentary on the Godhā Jātaka.

"What use are matted locks to you, O witless one?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain hypocritical bhikkhu. The story of the present is exactly as told below.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of a lizard.
At that time, a certain ascetic endowed with the five supernormal powers and great austerity lived in a leaf-hut in a forest grove near a frontier village;
the villagers attended upon the ascetic with great devotion. The Bodhisatta [became] his...

At the edge of the walkway, he lived in a certain anthill; while living there, he would approach the ascetic two or three times every day, and having heard words connected with the Dhamma and beneficial to his welfare, he would pay homage to the ascetic and return to his dwelling place.
Later on, the ascetic took leave of the village dwellers and departed. As he was departing...
Furthermore, while that ascetic was endowed with virtue, another fraudulent ascetic arrived and took up residence in that hermitage.
The Bodhisatta, perceiving that "this one too is virtuous," approached him in the same manner as before.
Then one day, during the heat of the summer season, when an unseasonable cloud had rained, flies emerged from the anthills; of these—

The iguanas roamed about for the purpose of eating. Villagers went out, caught the flies-eating iguanas, prepared the iguana meat—which was combined with smooth ingredients and was both sour and non-sour—and gave it to the ascetic.
Having eaten the iguana meat, the ascetic, bound by craving for flavor, said: "This meat is exceedingly sweet; what kind of meat is this?"
Having asked, "What is it? and hearing that it was "monitor lizard meat," he thought, "A large monitor lizard is coming toward me;
I shall kill it and eat its meat. Having so reflected, he had a vessel and items such as ghee and salt brought and set aside in a corner;
then, taking a club and concealing it with his saffron robe, he stood at the door of the leaf-hut.
Waiting for the Bodhisatta’s arrival, he sat there appearing as if perfectly tranquil and composed.
At evening time, the Bodhisatta thought, "I shall go into the presence of the ascetic," and having set out, as he was approaching, he observed the ascetic’s disturbed state of mind and reflected:
"This ascetic is not sitting in the same manner as on other days; even as he looks at me today..."
Having become one with corrupted faculties, he looked about, thinking, "I shall seize him.
Standing downwind from the ascetic, he caught the scent of the iguana meat and thought, "This fraudulent ascetic must have eaten iguana meat today;
therefore, being bound by craving for its flavor, he will strike me with a club as I approach him today."
Thinking, "He will cook the meat and wish to eat it," he did not approach the ascetic but turned back and wandered away.
The ascetic, realizing that the Bodhisatta was not coming, thought: "This man must have realized, 'He wishes to strike me,' and for that reason he does not come;
and for one who does not come, how can there be any escape? He [grasped] a club...
Having pulled it out, he threw it away. It struck the very tip of his big toe.
The Bodhisatta quickly entered the anthill, raised his head through another opening, and said: "Ho, fraudulent ascetic!
When I approached you, I did so with the perception that you were 'virtuous. But now I have discovered your fraudulent nature; for one such as you, a great thief—"
"What is the use of this outward mark of renunciation? he said, and rebuking him, he spoke this verse:
"What use have you for matted hair, O dull-witted one? What use have you for a deerskin garment?
Your inner self is a thicket, yet you polish only the outside."
In this context, "What use have you for matted hair, O dull-witted one? means: "O dull-witted one, O one lacking wisdom, these matted locks ought to be worn by one who has gone forth;
what use have you for those matted locks, you who are devoid of the virtues of the religious life? "What use have you for the deer-skin garment? means:
since the time when you lacked the self-restraint appropriate for wearing a deer-skin garment, what use have you for that deer-skin garment? Internally, you...
"Thicket" means that your inner heart is a thicket, obscured by the thicket of greed, hatred, and delusion.
"You polish the outside" means that while your interior is a thicket, you polish the exterior with baths and the like, as well as with the concealment of outward marks;
while polishing it, you are like a gourd filled with sour gruel, or a bowl filled with poison, or a termite mound filled with venomous snakes.
"You are like a jar filled with excrement that appears smooth on the outside; what is the use of you, a thief, living here?
Flee from here quickly! If you do not flee, we shall inform the village dwellers and have you punished.
Having thus threatened the false ascetic, the Bodhisatta entered the anthill, and the false ascetic departed from there as well.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the fraudulent ascetic Kūṭatāpasa was this deceiver; the virtuous ascetic Purima was Sāriputta; and the wise lizard was none other than myself.
This concludes the eighth story, the Commentary on the Godhājātaka.
9. The Commentary on the Ubhatobhaṭṭhajātakavaṇṇanā.
"His eyes are ruined, his cloak is lost"—this was said by the Teacher while staying at Veḷuvana concerning Devadatta.
At that time, it seems, the monks in the Dhamma Hall raised this discussion:
"Friends, just as a brand of dung, burning at both ends and smeared with excrement in the middle, serves neither for firewood in the forest nor for firewood in the village..."

"It spreads; even so, Devadatta, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, has become fallen from both sides and excluded from both, he has lost the enjoyments of a householder and does not fulfill the goal of recluseship.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what talk are you sitting here now? and they replied, "About this very thing."
When this was said, [the Blessed One] remarked, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has fallen away from both sides;
in the past, too, he fell away from both sides," and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity.

At that time, fishermen lived in a certain village. Then, one fisherman took his hook and, together with his young son, went to a pool where fishermen naturally caught fish; having arrived there, he cast his hook.
The hook became snagged on a stump hidden by the water. Unable to pull it out, the fisherman—
He thought, "This net will catch a large fish; I shall send my son to his mother and cause him to quarrel with the neighbors, so that no one from here will expect a share.
He said to his son, "Go, dear son, and inform our mother that we have caught a large fish, [saying], 'With the neighbors...'"
“Go and say to him, ‘Engage in a quarrel with him! Having sent his son, and being unable to pull in the fishhook, he placed his upper garment on the bank for fear of breaking the line;
then, descending into the water and searching for fish out of greed for them, he struck against stumps and broke both his eyes. The thief [then took] the garment he had placed on the bank...
Hari, having fallen into such pain, took hold of his eyes with his hand and pressed them;
then, emerging from the water, he searched for his garment while trembling.
His wife, thinking, "I shall create a quarrel so that no one will have any hope of him," [did so] at that very moment.

Having fastened a palm leaf to one ear, anointed one eye with collyrium from a mortar, and taking her dog in her arms, she went from house to house among her neighbors. Then a female companion said to her:
"A palm leaf is fastened to only one of your ears, one eye is anointed, and you have taken a dog in your arms as if he were a beloved son."
“You are going away; have you gone mad? “I am not mad, but you insult and revile me without cause.
Now I shall go to the village headman and have you fined eight kahāpaṇas.
Having thus quarreled, they both went into the presence of the village headman. While the quarrel was being settled, [the story continues:]
The staff fell right upon her head. Then, having bound her, they began to beat her, saying, "Pay the fine!

Seeing this occurrence in the village and that calamity of hers in the forest, the tree deity stood between their shoulders and said, "O man, your business has failed both in the water and on the land; you have met with ruin on both sides."
Having spoken thus, he recited this verse:
“The eyes are ruined, the cloth is lost, and there is a quarrel in my friend’s house;
on both sides my undertakings have failed, both in the water and on the land.”
"In that regard, 'quarrels at the friend’s house' means: a 'friend' (sakhī) is a female companion; at her house, a quarrel was started by your wife.
Having quarreled, she will be bound, beaten, and made to pay a fine. 'Both undertakings ruined' means:
thus, in both places, your undertakings are indeed ruined and broken. Which two? [The two mentioned above]."
"In the water and on the land": by the piercing of the eyes and by the falling [of the net], the operations in the water were ruined;
by the quarrel in the house of the friend, the operations on the land were ruined.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, Devadatta was the fisherman, but I myself was the tree deity."
The ninth: The Commentary on the Ubhatobhaṭṭha Jātaka.
[140] 10. The Commentary on the Kāka Jātaka.

"Always with a heart full of anxiety"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the conduct for the benefit of kinsmen. The story of the present will be made clear in the Bhaddasāla Jātaka of the Dvādasakanipāta.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a crow.
Now one day, the king’s court chaplain, having bathed in a river outside the city, anointed himself with perfumes, adorned himself with garlands, and dressed in fine garments, entered the city.
Two crows were perched upon the gateway arch of the city. One of them said to the other: “Friend,
"I shall let my bodily excrement fall upon the head of this brahmin. The other said, "Do not let this please you;
this brahmin is a lord, and enmity with a lordly person is evil. For if he were angry, he might destroy all the crows.
"I cannot help but do it," [the first crow replied]. "In that case, you will be found out," said the other. Then the other—
The crow fled. When the brahmin reached the lower part of the gateway, the crow, as if shaking a hanging ornament, dropped excrement upon his head.
The brahmin, becoming angry, conceived a grudge against all crows.
At that time, a hired female slave who was threshing rice spread the grain out in the sun at the door of her house and was guarding it.
She fell asleep while still sitting. Perceiving her negligence, a long-haired goat came and ate the rice.
When she woke up and saw it, she drove it away. The goat came and ate the rice again, and a third time as well, while she was sleeping in that same manner.
After driving it away three times, she thought: "This [creature] comes again and again..."
"If he eats half the rice, he will eat more; there will be much waste for me. Now I shall do something so that he will not come back again.
Taking a firebrand, she sat down as if sleeping.
When the sheep arrived for the purpose of eating the rice, she stood up and struck a sheep with the firebrand; the wool caught fire. As it burned on its body—
Thinking, "I shall extinguish the fire," he went with speed and rubbed his body against a certain grass hut near the elephant stable;
it caught fire. The flames rising from there seized the elephant stable.
While the elephant stables were burning, the backs of the elephants were scorched, and many elephants had their bodies wounded. The physicians set about making the elephants healthy again.
Being unable [to cure him], they informed the king. The king said to the chaplain, “Teacher, the elephant physicians are unable to treat the elephant;
do you know of any medicine? “I know one, Great King. “What is required to obtain it? “Crow fat, Great King.
The king said, “In that case, kill crows and bring the fat. From that time on—
Having killed the crows but failing to obtain possession of them, they piled them up right there; thus a great danger arose for the crows.
At that time, the Bodhisatta lived in the great charnel ground surrounded by eighty thousand crows. Then one crow went and reported the danger that had arisen for the crows to the Bodhisatta.
He thought: "Apart from me, no one else [can protect] my kinsmen."
"There is no one capable of removing this arisen fear; I shall remove it!

Having thus reflected upon the ten perfections (*pāramī*) and made the perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī*) his precursor, he sprang forward with a single impulse, entered through the wide-open great window, and descended beneath the king’s seat.
Then, a certain man desired to seize him. The king said, "For refuge..."

“Do not seize him! he cried, and stopped him. Having rested for a short while and reflecting upon the perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī*), the Great Being descended from his seat and said to the king:

“Great King, it is fitting for a king to rule his kingdom without being led by desire and the like. Whatever task must be performed, all of it should be done with careful reflection and deliberation.”
It is proper to do that which, when performed, succeeds; one should do only that, and not otherwise.
For if kings perform that which, when performed, does not succeed, a great danger arises for the populace, culminating in the fear of death.
The chaplain, being under the power of enmity, spoke a falsehood, saying: "The fat of crows..."
Having heard this, the king, with a mind full of faith, had a golden *bhadda*-throne prepared for the Bodhisatta.
Once he was seated upon it, the king had his wings anointed with oils refined a hundred and a thousand times;
then, having fed him with excellent food worthy of a king from a golden platter and given him water to drink, he attended to the Great Being until he was satisfied and free from fatigue.
He said this: "O wise one, you say that 'there is no such thing as the fat of crows'; for what reason do they have no fat?
The Bodhisatta, making the entire household raise a single cry of agreement, spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma: "For this and that reason..."
“‘Their hearts are constantly anxious, and they harass the entire world;
therefore, we have no power over them, just as crows have no power over us, their kin.
Herein, this is the summarized meaning: Great King, those called crows always dwell with agitated minds, perpetually overcome by fear.”
Furthermore, these kṣatriyas and others who cause harm to the entire world wander about merely tormenting and afflicting people—men, women, boys, girls, and so forth;
therefore, for these two reasons, there is no such thing as "the fat of our kinsmen, the crows.
It has never existed in the past, nor will it ever exist in the future.
Having thus made this matter clear, the Great Being enlightened the king, saying, "Great King, a king indeed must not perform any action without careful reflection and deliberation.
The king, being satisfied, honored the Bodhisatta with the kingship.
The Bodhisatta returned the kingdom to the king alone, established the king in the five precepts, and [established] all beings...
He begged for safety. Having heard his discourse on the Dhamma, the king granted safety to all beings and established a regular almsgiving for the crows.
Day after day, a meal of rice and bean curry was cooked, seasoned with various choice flavors, and given to the crows;
however, for the Great Being alone, the king’s own food was provided.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī was Ānanda, and the king of the crows was none other than myself.
This concludes the tenth narrative, the Kāka-jātaka.
This is the fourteenth chapter, the Chapter on Non-Generosity.
Its summary verse:
Asampadāna, Bhīruka, Ghaṭa, Āsana, Jhāna, Sodha;
Candābha, Suvaṇṇahaṃsa, Babbu, Godhu, Abhatobhaṭṭha.
"Kākarāja and others—these are ten.
15. The Section on Kakaṇṭaka. 1.
The Commentary on the Godhā Jātaka.

"Not associating with evil people": this was spoken by the Teacher while staying at Veḷuvana concerning a certain monk who associated with adversaries. The present-day account is identical to what was told in the Mahiḷāmukha Jātaka.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of a lizard.
Upon reaching maturity, he made his dwelling in a great hole on a riverbank, surrounded by a retinue of many hundreds of lizards. To him...
The young lizard, having formed a friendship with a certain scorpion and dwelling in mutual affection with him,
would cover him over, thinking, "I shall embrace the scorpion. When they reported his intimacy with that creature to the king of the lizards,
the king summoned his son and said, "Dear son, you have placed your trust in an unworthy place."
"You are doing wrong; those known as Kakaṇṭakas are of low birth, and one should not place trust in them.
If you establish friendship with him, this entire family of geckos will come to ruin because of that Kakaṇṭaka.
From now on, do not make friends with him," he said. Yet, he continued to do exactly that.
Although the Bodhisatta spoke again and again, he was unable to prevent the man from forming a bond of intimacy with him;
thinking, "Surely this danger will arise for us because of this kakaṇṭaka bird, and when it arises,
it is necessary to prepare a path for escape," he had a wind-cave constructed on one side.
In due course, the boy’s body became large, while Kakaṇṭaka remained the same size as before.
The other [the boy] would repeatedly press against Kakaṇṭaka, thinking, "I shall embrace Kakaṇṭaka," and it was like the time when he was being pressed by the mountain peak.
Becoming weary, he thought: "If this one continues to embrace me in this way for several more days..."
“I have no means of livelihood; by joining together with a single hunter, we shall exterminate this family of lizards.
Then one day, during the heat of the summer season, when a cloud had rained, ants swarmed up from an anthill, and lizards emerged from here and there to eat them.
A certain lizard-hunter took up a spade for the purpose of breaking open the lizard’s burrow.

Taking [the dog], he entered the forest with the dogs. Seeing him, Kakaṇṭaka thought, "Today I shall fulfill my own desire," and approaching him, he lay down not far away and asked, "O man, why do you wander in the forest?
He replied, "For the sake of iguanas. [Kakaṇṭaka said,] "I know the lair of many hundreds of iguanas, and I also [know how to use] fire..."

"Take straw and come! Having led him there, he said, "Throw straw in this place, set fire to it, create smoke, station dogs all around, and taking a great club yourself, strike and kill each lizard as it comes out;
then make a heap of them and go. Having spoken thus, [he added], "Today, against the enemy..."
Thinking, “I shall see his back,” he lay down with his head raised in one spot. The hunter also made smoke from the straw;
the smoke entered the hole, and the lizard, blinded by the smoke and terrified by the fear of death, emerged and began to flee.
The hunter struck each one as it came out and killed it, until the dogs escaped from his hands.
They seized them. A great calamity befell the iguanas.
The Bodhisatta, realizing that "this danger has arisen because of Kakaṇṭaka," thought:
"One must not associate with wicked men; there is no benefit or happiness to be found by relying on the wicked. By the power of this single wicked Kakaṇṭaka..."
“Such a destruction has come upon so many iguanas! While fleeing through the rat-hole, he spoke this verse:
“One who associates with evil people does not enjoy ultimate happiness;
like the *kakaṇṭāva* bird, the iguana family brings misfortune upon itself.”
Herein, this is the meaning in brief: A person who associates with evil people does not attain, find, or obtain what is called absolute happiness, unalloyed happiness, or uninterrupted happiness.
How so? Like a family of geckos from a *kakaṇṭaka* tree.
Just as a family of geckos finds no happiness from a *kakaṇṭaka* tree, so too a person who associates with evil people finds no happiness.
He obtains [misfortune]. However, by associating with evil people, one brings about ruin for oneself with absolute certainty; "ruin" (kali) is said to mean destruction.
One who associates with the wicked brings about the destruction of both himself and others living together with him.
In the canonical text (Pāḷi), however, it is written as “phalaṃ pāpeyya. That phrasing does not exist in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), nor is its meaning [there].
That is not tenable. Therefore, one must accept exactly what was stated above.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Kakaṇṭaka was Devadatta;
the disobedient monk Godhāpillaka, who associated with adversaries, was the son of the Bodhisattva; and the king of the mongooses was [the Bodhisattva himself]."
"But it was I myself who was he.
The first commentary on the Godhā Jātaka [142].
2. The commentary on the Siṅgāla Jātaka.
"Indeed, this is difficult for you to understand. The Teacher spoke this while staying at Veḷuvana, concerning Devadatta’s attempt to kill him.
Having heard the conversation among the monks in the Hall of Truth, the Teacher said:
"Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has attempted to kill me; he attempted to do so in the past as well, yet he was unable to slay me."
Having said, "He was able [to do so], but he himself became exhausted," he related a story of the past.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a jackal and, having become a king of jackals, dwelt in a charnel ground forest surrounded by a pack of jackals. At that time, there was a festival in Rājagaha.
At that time, for the most part, people drank liquor; it was indeed a festival of liquor.
Then, many rogues there had much liquor and meat brought in, and being adorned and decorated, they sang again and again while drinking the liquor and eating the meat.
At the end of the first watch of the night, their meat was exhausted, but the liquor remained in great abundance.
Then a certain rogue said, "Give me a piece of meat. When it was replied, "The meat is exhausted," he said, "While I am here, there can be no such thing as a depletion of meat.

Saying, "I will kill the jackals that have come to the raw charnel ground to eat the flesh of dead men and bring you meat," he took a club, went out from the city by the drainage ditch, and reached the charnel ground.
Having gone there and seized a club, he lay down flat on his back like one who was dead. At that moment, the Bodhisatta, surrounded by a pack of jackals, arrived at that place;

seeing him, he recognized, "This is not dead," yet thinking, "I shall examine it more thoroughly," he went downwind of him, smelled the odor of his body, and knowing for certain that he was indeed not dead, [he said], "Having put him to shame..."
Thinking, "I will drive him away," he went and bit the tip of the club and pulled it;
the rogue did not let go of the club, and even as [the Bodhisatta] approached, he did not look at him but gripped him more tightly.
The Bodhisatta stepped back and said, "O man, if you were dead, you would not have gripped me more tightly while I was pulling the club."
"For this reason, whether you are dead or not dead is difficult to discern," he said, and then recited this verse:
"This indeed is hard for you to understand, that you lie there in the posture of the dead;
yet as you are being dragged along, the staff does not slip from your hand."
In this regard, "for this is difficult for you to understand" means that this reason is hard for you to discern.
"That you lie down as one who is dead" means that by which reason you lie down like a corpse, sleeping as if you were dead.
"While you are being dragged" means that while you are being pulled by the hand, the staff does not slip from your grasp as it is seized by the tip of the stick; such as you are—
“Thus, you are not called the Deathless One.
When this was said, the rogue thought, “This man knows my state of being the Deathless One,” and rising up, he threw his staff;
the staff missed its mark. The rogue said, “Go, you have been missed by me now! The Bodhisatta turned back and said, “O sir...”
"Man, even though you have missed me, you have not failed to fall into the eight great hells and the sixteen secondary hells," she said, and then she departed.
Having received nothing at all, the rogue emerged from the cemetery, bathed in the moat, and entered the city by the same way he had come.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the rogue was Devadatta, but I myself was the king of the jackals."
The second [section], the commentary on the Siṅgālajāta-ka.
[143] 3. The commentary on the Virocajātaka:
"Your discharge has flowed out. This was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Veḷuvana concerning Devadatta’s construction of a Sugata-shrine at Gayāsīsa.
He spoke concerning the state of having been shown [the path]. For Devadatta, having fallen away from meditative absorption and being deprived of gain and honor, thought,
"There is a certain means," and having requested five points from the Teacher and not obtaining them,
he took with him five hundred bhikkhus— recently ordained disciples of the two chief disciples who were unskilled in the Dhamma and Vinaya— and departed.
Having gone to Gayāsīsa and split the Saṅgha, he performed a formal act of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*) independently within a single boundary.
The Teacher, knowing that the time for the ripening of those monks' wisdom had come, dispatched the two chief disciples. Upon seeing them, Devadatta was delighted in mind;
thinking, "I shall display the play of a Buddha," he showed the abode of the Sugata while preaching the Dhamma during the night.
“Friend Sāriputta, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is free from sloth and torpor; let a discourse on the Dhamma occur to you for these bhikkhus.
My back aches, so I shall stretch it,” he said, and then he fell asleep.
The two chief disciples, having taught the Dhamma to those bhikkhus and awakened them to the paths and fruits, took them all and returned to the Veḷuvana itself.

Seeing the monastery empty, Kokālika went to Devadatta and said, "Friend Devadatta, having split your assembly, the two chief disciples have gone and left the monastery empty; yet you simply continue to sleep!
Having said this, he pulled off Devadatta’s upper robe and struck him with his heel as if feeling for his backbone against the wall.
He struck him in the heart. At that very moment, blood gushed from his mouth, and from then on he became ill.
The Teacher asked the Elder, "Sāriputta, what did Devadatta do while you were away?
"Venerable Sir, upon seeing us, Devadatta thought, 'I shall display the play of a Buddha,' and after showing the Sugata’s dwelling, he met with great destruction."
The Teacher said, "Sāriputta, it is not only now that Devadatta has met his destruction by imitating me; he did so even in the past.
Having said this, at the request of the Elder, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a maned lion living in the Himalayan region.
He made his dwelling in a golden cave. One day, having emerged from the golden cave, he stretched his limbs, looked toward the four quarters, and let out a lion’s roar;
then, setting out for his prey, he killed a great buffalo, ate its choice meat, descended into a lake, filled his belly with water the color of jewels, and headed back toward the cave.
He went forth. Then a certain jackal, intent on foraging, suddenly saw the lion;
unable to flee, he fell at the lion’s feet and lay down before him. When asked, "What is it, jackal? he replied, "I wish to serve your feet, my lord.
The lion said, "Very well, come; serve me, and I shall have you fed with choice meats," and he took the jackal [with him].
Taking [the meat], he went to the golden cave. From then on, the jackal ate the lion’s leftovers. After a few days, his body became stout.
Then one day, while the lion was lying down in the cave, he said to him: "Go, jackal;
standing on the mountain peak, look at the elephants, horses, buffaloes, and other creatures wandering at the foot of the mountain, and identify whichever one you wish to eat."
"Having come here, say: 'I wish to eat such-and-such meat. After paying homage to me, say: 'Be radiant, Master!
Then I will kill it, eat the sweet flesh myself, and give some to you as well.
The jackal climbed to the mountain peak, surveyed various kinds of wild animals, and [approached] whichever one he desired to eat. He went to the golden cave...
Having entered, he informs the lion of this, falls at his feet, and says, "Be gracious, Master. The lion springs forward with speed;
even if it be a noble, rutting elephant, he brings it to its death right there, eats choice meat himself, and gives some to the jackal as well.
Having eaten his fill of meat, the jackal enters the cave.
Having entered, he fell asleep. As time passed, his pride increased: "I too am a four-footed creature;
for what reason do I live being fed by others day after day? From now on, I too shall kill elephants and other animals and eat their flesh.
Even the lion, the king of beasts, relied solely upon the very words spoken to him: "Be radiant, my lord."
“Kill the excellent elephant! I too, having had the lion say to me, ‘Shine forth, jackal,’ shall kill an excellent elephant and eat its flesh.
He approached the lion and said this: “Master, for a long time I have [seen] the excellent elephants killed by you...”
"Meat has been eaten; I too desire to kill an excellent elephant and eat its flesh.
Therefore, I shall lie down in the Golden Cave at the place where you are lying.
When you see an excellent elephant wandering at the foot of the mountain, come to me and say, 'Viroca, Jambuka!'—there is no stinginess in this much."
"Do not do it! Then Sīha said to him, "No, jackal, you were not born into a lion family capable of killing elephants;
there is no such thing as a jackal in this world capable of killing an elephant and eating its flesh. Do not let this please you;
live by eating only the flesh of choice elephants killed by me. Even when this was said, he—
He did not wish to desist, but begged again and again. Unable to dissuade him, Sīha consented and said, "In that case, enter my dwelling and lie down.

Having had the jackal lie down in the Golden Cave, Sīha himself went to the foot of the mountain to look at his excellent, intoxicated elephant, then returned to the entrance of the cave and called out, "Viroca, jackal!"

He said: The jackal, having emerged from the Golden Cave, stretched his limbs, looked toward the four quarters, and after letting out three cries, leaped forward thinking, "I shall land upon the forehead of the noble elephant," but he missed his mark and fell at the elephant's feet.
The elephant raised its right foot and trampled the jackal's head; the bones of its skull were crushed to powder.
[They] were there. Then an elephant, having trampled his body with its foot, made it into a heap, dropped dung upon it, and entered the forest while letting out a trumpeting cry.
Having seen this occurrence, the Bodhisatta said, "Now shine forth, jackal," and spoke this verse:
“The brain has flowed out, your skull is split open, and all your ribs are broken;
today you truly shine forth. Therein, *lasī* means the brain matter (*matthaluṅga*).
*Nipphalitā* means it has emerged. Having spoken this verse, the Bodhisatta remained for the duration of his lifespan and then departed according to his karma.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Devadatta was the jackal, but I myself was the lion.
This concludes the third narrative, the Viroca-jātaka.
[144] 4. The Naṅguṭṭha-jātaka (The Tail-Jātaka) Narrative.
"Bahumpetaṃ asabbhi jātavedo. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the wrong asceticism of the Ājīvakas.

At that time, it is said, the Ājīvakas were practicing various kinds of wrong asceticism on the back of the Jetavana, such as the squatting posture, strenuous exertion, hanging from trees, lying on beds of thorns, and exposure to the five fires.
A number of bhikkhus [observed] these various practices...
Seeing this wrong austerity, they asked the Blessed One, "Venerable sir, is there indeed any wholesome result or progress to be gained by relying on this wrong austerity?
The Teacher replied, "Bhikkhus, there is no wholesome result or progress to be gained by relying on such wrong austerity as this;
in the past, the wise did not think that 'by relying on such austerity, wholesome result or progress will come to be.'"

"Having taken the fire from consciousness, they entered the forest; seeing no increase whatsoever through the offering of fire and other such rites, they extinguished the fire with water, performed the preliminary exercises for the kasiṇas, and having produced the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, they became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of northern brahmins.
On the day of his birth, his parents took a birth-fire and preserved it. Then, when he reached the age of sixteen, they said to him:
"My son, on the day you were born, we took up the fire for you. If you wish to live the household life, [take] three..."
“Study the Vedas! If you desire to go to the Brahma-world, take the sacred fire, enter the forest, and by attending to the fire, win over Mahābrahmā and become destined for the Brahma-world.
He replied, “I have no need for the household life,” and taking the fire, he entered the forest, established a hermitage, and dwelt in the wilderness while tending the fire.
Thus, one day, having received a cow as a gift in a frontier village, he led that ox to his hermitage and thought, "I will have the Blessed One Aggika eat beef.
Then it occurred to him: "There is no salt here; the Blessed One Aggika will not be able to eat it without salt. I shall bring salt from the village and [feed] the Blessed One Aggika..."
“I will have him fed salt. Having tied the ox right there, he went to the village for the sake of salt.
When he had gone, many hunters came to that place. Seeing the ox, they killed it, cooked the meat, and ate it;
then, having discarded the tail, the shanks, and the hide right there, they took the remaining meat and departed.
The brahmin, having arrived and seen nothing more than the tip of the tail and so forth, thought:
"This Blessed One Aggika is not even able to protect what belongs to himself; when then will he protect me? This service to the fire must be useless;
there is no merit or progress resulting from this. Thus, his desire for the service of the fire vanished.
“O venerable Aggibhagavā, when you yourself are unable to protect even what belongs to you, when will you ever protect me?
There is no meat; be satisfied with this much. Saying this, as he threw his tail and other parts into the fire, he spoke this verse:
“O Jātaveda, it is much that we honor you with our tails, though you are unrighteous.”
“There is no meat today for one who craves meat; may your honor accept even the tail.
In this context, *bahumpetaṃ* means “even this much is much. *Asabbhī* means a person who is not a true man (*asappurisa*), one of ignoble character.
*Jātavedo*: he addresses the fire. For fire, as soon as it is born, is felt, becomes manifest, and appears; therefore, it is called “born-knower” (*jātavedo*).
It is said: "That which we honor with our tail" means: "Today we honor the Blessed One, whom even we ourselves are unable to protect, with our tail; even this is of great value to you"—thus he shows.
"Worthy of meat": there is no meat for you today who are worthy of meat. "May your lordship accept even the tail" [refers to] himself...
“Being unable to protect what belongs to me, may you, sir, accept even this body with its legs and skin, down to the tail.

Having said this, the Great Being extinguished the fire with water, went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, and having realized the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he became destined for the Brahma-world.
The Teacher, having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, I myself was the ascetic whose fire had been extinguished.”
The Fourth: The Commentary on the Naṅguṭṭha Jātaka.
[145] 5. The Commentary on the Rādha Jātaka:
"O Rādha, you do not understand," this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning the seduction by his former wife.
He spoke concerning this. The story of the present will be revealed in the Indriya Jātaka.
However, the Teacher addressed that bhikkhu, saying: "Bhikkhu, womenfolk are indeed unprotected;
even those who provide protection are unable to protect them. You too, in the past, though you provided protection for her, were unable to protect her."
"You were not able [to protect it before]; how will you protect it now? Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a hawk.
In the kingdom of Kāsī, a certain brahmin raised both the Bodhisatta and his younger brother, treating them as his own sons. Among them—
The Bodhisatta’s name was Poṭṭhapāda, and the other’s was Rādha. Now, that brahmin’s wife was unchaste and immoral.
When he was about to go on business, he said to both his sons, “Sons, if your mother, the brahmin woman, practices misconduct, you must restrain her. The Bodhisatta said, “Very well.”

“Father, if we are able to restrain him, we shall do so; if we are unable, we shall remain silent. Thus the brahmin entrusted the female parrots to the brahmin woman and departed for the sake of business.
From the day he left, however, the brahmin woman began to commit adultery with those who entered and those who departed.
There was no end to it; seeing her conduct, Rādha said to the Bodhisatta:
"Brother, our father went away after saying, 'If your mother practices unchaste behavior, you must restrain her. Now that she is practicing such behavior, let us restrain her.
The Bodhisatta replied: "Dear one, you speak thus because of your own incompetence and childishness."
"Even those who wander about lifting up women are unable to protect them.
That which is impossible to do should not be done," he said, and then recited this verse:
"You do not understand, Rādha, that even when midnight has not yet come..."
“You lament for what is imperishable; you are disenchanted with Kosiya’s son.
To that he replied: “You do not understand this, Rādha;
you do not know, dear Rādha, that even though it is not yet midnight, so many people have already arrived during the first watch of the night. Now who knows how many more will still come?”
"You lament what is not to be lamented" means that you utter an improper lamentation.
"Kosiyāyanī has become dispassionate" means our mother, the brahmin woman Kosiyāyanī, has become dispassionate toward us and has grown devoid of affection for our father.
By these words he made clear this meaning: "If she still possessed any attachment or love for him, she would not commit such an act of misconduct."
Having thus made this disclosure, he did not permit Rādha to speak with the brahmin woman. She, too, wandered about as she pleased until the brahmin’s return.
When the brahmin arrived, he asked Poṭṭhapāda, "Dear boy, what kind of mother do you have?
The Bodhisatta told the brahmin everything exactly as it had happened, saying, "What use have you for such a mother, dear boy?"
Having said, "She is immoral," [the monk] prostrated at the brahmin’s feet, saying, "Father, from the moment we spoke of our mother's fault, it is no longer possible for us to live here.
Together with Rādha, he sprang up and went into the forest.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction, proclaimed the Truths (Saccāni). At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was despondent—
He was established in the fruit of stream-entry. "At that time, the brahmin and the brahmin lady were these very two people;
Rādha was Ānanda, and Poṭṭhapāda was none other than myself.
This is the fifth, the Commentary on the Rādha Jātaka.
[146] 6. The Commentary on the Samuddakāka Jātaka.
"Are the jaws still there?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a number of senior bhikkhus.
It is said that in their time as householders, they were wealthy and affluent family men in Sāvatthī who were friends with one another.
Having become one and performing meritorious deeds, they heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma and thought, “We are old; what is the use of household life for us?
Having gone forth in the delightful Buddha-sāsana in the presence of the Teacher, we shall make an end of suffering.
Thus, having given away their entire property to their sons, daughters, and others, and having abandoned their tearful circle of kinsmen, they requested the Teacher for the going-forth.
Having made their request, they went forth. But once gone forth, they did not practice the ascetic’s duty (samaṇadhamma) in accordance with their renunciation;

due to their advanced age, they were unable to master even the Dhamma. Just as in their time as householders, even during their period of renunciation, they had leaf huts built on the outskirts of the monastery and lived together.
Even when wandering for alms, they generally did not go elsewhere, but [stayed] right where their own sons and wives were.
Having gone home, they ate. Among them, one elder had a former wife who was helpful to all the senior elders;
therefore, the others also took the food they had received and sat down to eat right there in her house.
She gave them whatever curries and condiments she had on hand. One day, she was afflicted by a certain illness.

passed away. Then those elder monks went to the monastery and, walking about the outskirts of the monastery while weeping and holding one another by the necks, cried out, "The female lay devotee with such sweet hands has passed away!
Hearing their sound, monks gathered from here and there and asked, "Friends, why are you weeping? They replied, "Our companion..."
“Our former wife was sweet in her touch and very helpful to us;
we weep for this reason, thinking, ‘Now, from where shall we find another such as she?
Having seen their distress, the monks raised the discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying, “Friends, by this [monk]...”
“Indeed, because of that very reason, the elder monks are walking about at the edge of the monastery, weeping and holding one another by the neck.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, with what discussion are you sitting here gathered now?
When they replied, “With this one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that these men are wandering about weeping over her death; formerly, too, they were so.”
"Having been reborn in this womb of a crow, by relying on one who had died in the ocean and striving with the thought,
'We shall empty out the water of the ocean and carry him away,' they obtained life by relying on the wise," he said, and then related a story of the past. In the past,
while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a deity of the ocean.
Then a certain crow, taking his wife the female crow, went to the seashore while searching for food.
At that time, people had performed a nāga-offering on the seashore with milk-porridge, fish, meat, liquor, and other offerings, and had departed.
Then that crow went to the place where the offering had been made; seeing the milk and other things, together with his wife, [he ate] the milk-porridge, fish, meat, and so forth.
Having eaten much, they drank wine. Both of them, intoxicated by the wine, sat on the shore thinking, "We shall play in the sea," and began to bathe.
Then a wave came and carried the female crow into the sea.
A fish, having eaten her flesh, swallowed it. The crow cried out and lamented, "My wife is dead!"
Then, hearing the sound of her lamentation, many crows gathered together and asked, "For what reason do you weep?
She replied, "Your friend, while bathing at the seashore, was swept away by a wave. They all wept, crying out with one voice.
Then it occurred to them: "What power does this so-called ocean water have over us? Let us bale out the water!"
“Having emptied the ocean, we shall bring out our companion. Filling their mouths again and again, they spat out the water;
and whenever their throats grew parched with salt water, they would rise up repeatedly, go to dry land, and rest.
When their jaws were weary, their mouths were dried up, and their eyes were bloodshot, they became dejected and exhausted, and [addressed] one another.
Having addressed them, they said, "Friends, let us take the water of the ocean and cast it outside;
yet each place from which we take it fills up again with water, so we shall not be able to empty the ocean," and they spoke this verse:
"Though our jaws ache and our mouths grow parched..."
“We cannot reach the near shore, for the great ocean only fills up.
In this context, “api nu hanukā santā” means “are our jaws indeed weary?
“Oramāma na pārema” means “we draw in and pour out the water of the great ocean by our own strength, yet it remains empty.”
"We cannot do it; for this great ocean is indeed filling up.
Having spoken thus, all those crows said, "That female crow had such a beak, such round eyes, such a shape of skin, and such a sweet voice. She [could cross] this sea of thieves for us..."
"Relying on him, we have been lost," they lamented at great length. While they were thus lamenting, a sea-deity displayed a terrifying form and drove them away;
in this way, their safety was secured.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the female crow was this former wife."
"The crow was the Elder Mahallaka; the other crows were the other Elders; and as for the ocean deity, she was none other than myself.
The commentary on the *Samuddakāka Jātaka* is the sixth.
[147] 7. The commentary on the *Puppharatta Jātaka*.
"This is not suffering; that is suffering"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain dissatisfied monk.
For when the Blessed One asked him, "Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied? he replied, "It is true. And when asked, "By whom have you been made dissatisfied?
he said, "By my former wife. [The Buddha continued: "She has hands as sweet as nectar..."
“Venerable sir, she is that woman; I cannot live without her,” he said. Then the Teacher said to him, “Monk, this woman has brought you harm.
In the past as well, because of her you were impaled on a stake; having died with a longing for her alone, you were reborn in hell.
Why do you long for her again now? Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a deity dwelling in the sky.
Then, when the festival of the full moon in the month of Kattika arrived in Benares, they decorated the city like the city of the gods.
All the people were intent on their festive sports; however, a certain poor man possessed only a single pair of thick cloths.
It was so. Having had it thoroughly washed and bleached, he had it woven into cloth with a hundred threads and a thousand threads, and he set it aside.

Then his wife said to him, "Husband, I wish to spend the Kattika full-moon night wandering about, wearing one garment dyed with safflower and another draped over me, clinging to your neck. He replied, "My dear, from where would we have such [cloth]?"
“Wear a saffron-dyed cloth and play! she replied, “If I cannot obtain saffron-dyed cloth, I will not play at the festival;
you may take another woman and play. He said, “My dear, why do you distress me? Where would we get saffron?
She said, “Master, when a man has a desire, what indeed is there that does not exist? Is it not true of the king?”
“In the place where the safflower grows, there is much safflower. “My dear lady, that place is like a lotus pond occupied by a rākṣasa;
it is well-guarded and cannot be approached. Do not let this please you; be content with what you have already obtained.
“Master, when it is the dark of night, there is no place that is inaccessible to a man. Thus he spoke.
As she spoke again and again, he took her words under the influence of defilement and, consoling her by saying, "Be at ease, my lady;
do not worry," he surrendered his life during the night. Having departed from the city and gone to King Kusumbha’s estate, he broke down the enclosure wall and entered the inner grounds.
Hearing the sound of the wall being broken, the guards cried out, "A thief! A thief!"
Having surrounded him, seized him, reviled him, beaten him, and bound him, they presented him to the king at daybreak.
The king said, "Go, impale him on a stake! Then, having bound his arms behind his back while the drum of execution was being beaten, they led him out of the city and impaled him on a stake.
Intense pains arose, and crows [settled] upon his head.
Hiding themselves, they pecked at his eyes with their beaks, which were like needles;
yet, disregarding such suffering, he kept recollecting that woman alone.
Thinking, "I have been deprived of the nights of the Kattika full moon while she was dressed in garments of thick, red flowers and her two arms were thrown around my neck," he spoke this verse:
“This is not suffering, that is suffering: the pain that the crow inflicts upon me;
for Sāmā shall not enjoy the red flower of Kattika.
Therein, “this is not suffering, that is suffering: the pain that the crow inflicts upon me” refers to the suffering caused by being impaled on the stake.

"Physical and mental suffering, and even that which the crow pecks at with its beak as if it were made of iron—all this is not suffering for me; rather, that [other] suffering alone is my suffering. What is that?
It is what Sāmā, with her safflower-red garment, will not enjoy during the month of Kattika—that is, my beloved wife Piyaṅgu-Sāmā, who [wore] a single garment dyed with kusumbha.

"Having dressed in one [robe] and wrapped myself in another, thus covered by this pair of garments dyed with thick red flowers, I shall not experience the Kattika full-moon night while holding my mother’s neck; this is my suffering, for it alone torments me.
While lamenting thus concerning his mother, he passed away and was reborn in hell.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "The husband and wife of that time are the husband and wife of the present; as for the deity dwelling in the sky who stood there having witnessed that event, she was none other than myself.
This concludes the seventh narrative, the Puppharatta Jātaka.
8. The Siṅgāla Jātaka Narrative.
"I do not purify, nor do I cause others to purify"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the subduing of the defilements.

It is said that in Sāvatthī, about five hundred wealthy friends, sons of merchants, having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, placed their full trust in the Dispensation, went forth, and dwelt in the Jetavana on a mat spread within a corner. Then, one day...
At the hour of midnight, a thought based on defilement arose in them.
Becoming dissatisfied, they conceived the intention to take up again those defilements they had previously abandoned.

Then, immediately after midnight, the Teacher raised the staff of omniscient knowledge and, considering the inclinations of the monks, [asked]: "With what kind of delight do the monks dwell in Jeta’s Grove?"
Looking within those monks, he recognized that a thought of sensual desire had arisen.
For the Teacher protects his disciples as a woman with an only son protects her son, or as a man with one eye protects his only eye.
At whatever time—whether in the morning or at other times—their defilements arise, he [perceives] them.
Not allowing the defilements to increase beyond that point, he suppressed them at each respective moment. Therefore, it occurred to him:
"This situation is like the time when thieves arise within the inner city of a wheel-turning monarch;
I shall now give them a teaching on the Dhamma, suppress those defilements, and grant them the state of Arahatship. From his fragrant Perfumed Chamber...
Having gone out, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda, the Elder Dhamma-bhaṇḍāgārika, with a sweet voice, saying, “Ānanda!
The Elder approached, paid homage, and stood aside, asking, “What is it, Bhante?
[The Buddha replied: “Ānanda, assemble all the bhikkhus who are dwelling within the inner enclosure of Koṭisanthāra in the Gandhakuṭi courtyard. This was indeed his intention.

He thought, "If I summon only those five hundred bhikkhus, they will be so moved by the thought, 'The Teacher has known the arising of defilements within us,' that they will not be able to receive the teaching on the Dhamma with a composed mind.
Therefore, he said, "Have them all assemble. The Elder replied, "Very well, Bhante," and taking his key, [went] through the monastery grounds.
Having wandered through the monastery grounds, he gathered all the bhikkhus together in the courtyard of the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī) and prepared the Buddha’s seat.
The Teacher sat upon the prepared Buddha’s seat, having crossed his legs in the full lotus posture and set his body erect;
standing as if upon the rocky earth like Mount Sineru, the six-colored, dense rays of the Buddha’s light streamed forth in continuous, interlacing waves.
As he released them, those rays—measuring a palm, a parasol, and the height of a gabled house—broke off again and again and moved through the vault of the sky like streaks of lightning.
Having agitated the depths of the great ocean, it became as if at the time of the rising of the young sun.
The community of monks also, having paid homage to the Teacher and manifested a mind of reverence, [covered him] with a red woolen cloth...
He sat surrounding him as if encircling him. The Teacher, emitting the Brahma-voice, addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, it is not fitting for a bhikkhu to entertain these three unwholesome thoughts—thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty.
For a defilement that has arisen within should not be disregarded as 'insignificant.'"
It is not permissible; defilement (kilesa) is like an enemy. There is no such thing as a minor enemy;
once he gains an opportunity, he brings about total destruction. In the same way, even a slight defilement, having arisen, leads to great ruin if it is allowed to increase.
This defilement is comparable to deadly halāhala poison, like a tumor with its skin torn away, and similar to a venomous serpent.
Like a thunderbolt or fire, it is not fit to be approached or relied upon; it should be suspected.

At every moment it arises, by the power of reflection and the power of meditation, one must abandon it so that it does not remain in the heart for even a moment, but rolls away like a drop of water on a lotus leaf.
Even the ancient sages, having censured even a slight defilement, [acted] so that it would not arise again...
"Thus they should restrain it so that it does not arise within," he said, and then related a story of the past.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of a jackal and made his dwelling in a forest on a riverbank. Then, an old elephant died on the bank of the Ganges.
A jackal, intent on foraging, saw that dead elephant’s body and thought, “A great feast has appeared before me! He went over and bit it on the trunk;
it was as if he had bitten a plow-pole. Thinking, “There is nothing here fit to eat,” he bit it on the tusks;
it was as if he had bitten a wooden post. He bit it on the ear; it was as if he had bitten the tip of a winnowing fan.
When he bit his belly, it was as if he had bitten into a granary. When he bit his foot, it was as if he had bitten into a mortar.

When he bit his tail, it was as if he had bitten into a pestle. Thinking, "There is nothing here fit to eat," and finding no satisfaction anywhere, he bit his anus; it was as if he had bitten into soft cakes. Thus he proceeded.
Thinking, "Now I have found within this body a soft place fit to be eaten," he began to eat from that point;
having entered the interior of the belly and devoured the kidneys, heart, and other organs, he drank the blood when thirsty,
and when wishing to lie down, he spread himself out across the stomach and lay there.
Then it occurred to him: "This elephant's body is like a house for the comfort of my dwelling;
since there is abundant flesh when there is a desire to eat, what need have I now to go elsewhere? Without going anywhere else, he remained right there in the elephant's belly, eating the flesh.
As time passed, during the heat of the summer, by the touch of the wind and the scorching heat of the sun's rays...
As that corpse dried up, its folds began to shrink; the opening through which the jackal had entered became closed, and the interior of the belly became dark.
It was as if the jackal had come to dwell in the intermediate space between worlds (*lokantarika*).
As the corpse dried, the flesh withered and the blood was cut off. Finding no way out, he became overcome with fear and ran about.
Striking here and there, he wandered about searching for an exit door.
While he was thus being cooked within the belly like a lump of dough in a frying pan, after the lapse of a few days, a great rain cloud poured down.
Then that corpse, having been soaked, stood up and remained in its natural form. The anus opened up, and stars appeared.

It appeared as such. Seeing that opening, the jackal thought, "Now my life is saved," and drawing back as far as the elephant's head, he rushed forward with speed, struck the anus with his head, and emerged.
Because his body was covered [with hair], all his fur clung to the anus; thus, with his hairless body resembling the trunk of a palmyra tree, he was filled with terror.
Having run for a moment and then turned back to sit down, he looked at his body and thought: "This suffering was not caused by anyone else;
rather, it was done by me because of greed, on account of greed, and depending upon greed. From this day forward, I shall no longer be a slave to greed;
I will never again enter the body of an elephant. Thus, with a heart deeply moved, he felt a sense of spiritual urgency.
Having offered this, he spoke this verse:
“Neither once, nor twice, nor even again and again shall I enter the elephant-stable; for I am terrified by fear.”
In this context, the word *na* (not) and *ca* (and) are merely particles; *apunaḥpunaḥ* (again and again) is formed with the syllable *a-* as a mere expletive.

Now, the meaning of this entire verse is as follows: "For I shall not enter again from here, nor again from there—meaning, after the manner already described—and not again and again into the elephant-body known as the 'elephant-bondage.
For what reason? Because I am terrified by fear; for in this very [state]..."
"Terrified by the fear of death, he was struck with alarm and agitation at the moment of entering.

Having spoken thus, he fled from that very spot; even when he turned back toward that elephant’s body or another, he did not look at it again. From that time forth, he was no longer under the sway of greed.
The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma instruction, said: "Monks, it is impossible for a defilement that has arisen within to increase..."
"Without giving it away, it is right to restrain it right there," he said, and having proclaimed the Truths, he identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, those five hundred monks were established in Arahatship;
among the remainder, some became Stream-enterers, some Once-returners, and some Non-returners. "At that time, I myself was the jackal."
The eighth is the Commentary on the Siṅgālajātakavaṇṇanā.
[149] 9. The Commentary on the Ekapaṇṇajātakavaṇṇanā:
"This tree has but a single leaf. This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest near Vesālī.
He spoke concerning a wicked Licchavi youth from Vesālī. At that time, the city of Vesālī was surrounded by three walls at intervals of one *gāvuta* each;
it possessed gate-towers and watchturrets in three locations and had attained the highest degree of splendor.
Therein resided seven thousand seven hundred kings who ruled the kingdom at all times.
There were seven kings, just as many vice-kings, just as many generals, and just as many treasurers.
Among those princes, there was one named the wicked Licchavi prince, who was irascible, fierce, harsh, and violent;
like a venomous snake struck by a staff, he was constantly ablaze with anger. Before him, two...
There was no one capable of making him speak even three words. Neither his parents, nor his kinsmen, nor his friends and companions were able to train him.
Then his parents thought: "This boy is exceedingly harsh and violent;
there is no one else capable of disciplining him except for the Perfectly Enlightened One. He is one who must be guided by a Buddha."

"It must be so. Taking him with them, they went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and said, "Venerable Sir, this prince is fierce, harsh, and ablaze with anger; please give him instruction.
The Teacher instructed the prince: "Prince, among these very beings, one who is fierce, harsh, and violent..."
One should not be of a nature to cause harm. For one who is harsh in speech is disliked and displeasing even to his own mother, father, children, wife, brothers, sisters, wife, friends, and kinsmen;
he is as terrifying as a snake coming to bite, a bandit rising up in the forest, or a yakṣa coming to devour.
Having performed [an act of anger], one is reborn in the hells and other realms during the second moment of consciousness.

Furthermore, in this very life, a person who is prone to anger becomes ugly even if adorned and well-ornamented; though his face possesses the splendor of the full moon, it becomes misshapen and unsightly, like a lotus struck by fire or like a golden mirror-disk covered in grime. It is on account of anger that...
For indeed, beings take up a weapon and strike themselves with it, consume poison, hang themselves with a rope, or throw themselves down from precipices.
Thus, having died through the influence of anger, they are reborn in the hells and other lower realms.

Those of a harmful nature, having incurred reproach even in this very life, are reborn in the hells and other lower realms after the breakup of the body; and thereafter, [they may attain] the human state.
From the time they are born, they are indeed full of disease.
Among diseases such as eye-disease, ear-disease, and so forth, they rise up together and fall upon one another; being never free from disease, they remain constantly suffering.
Therefore, one should maintain a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*), a mind of welfare, and a gentle mind toward all beings. Such a person...
“Indeed, such a person is not liberated from the fears of hell and the other realms. Having heard the Teacher’s exhortation, that youth, by that very instruction, had his pride subdued;
he became tamed, free from worldly attachments, possessed of a mind of loving-kindness, and a gentle heart.
Even when others reviled him or struck him, he did not turn back to look at them, like a snake with its fangs extracted, like a crab with its claws cut off, or like one whose horns have been severed.
And he was like a bull.
Having learned of his conduct, the monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth:
"Friends, although they had exhorted him for a very long time, neither his parents nor his relatives and friends were able to subdue the wicked Licchavi youth; [only] the Perfectly Enlightened One—"
But having tamed it with a single instruction and rendered it free from stubbornness, he made it grasp the cause of non-wavering like a noble elephant in rut.

How well said indeed is this: "Monks, when an elephant to be tamed is trained by an elephant-tamer, it runs in only one direction—either east, west, north, or south. When a horse to be tamed... [and so on]."

“By a well-tamed horse... [or] by a well-tamed ox... or even by a well-tamed human being... By the Tathāgata, bhikkhus, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, when the tameable person is guided, it runs in eight directions: possessing form, one sees forms; this is one direction... [and so on].
He is called ‘the unsurpassed charioteer of tameable persons among those who practice the way. For it is not by the Perfectly Enlightened One, friend...”
