“There is no one like me, a charioteer of men to be tamed. The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “For this very discussion,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that I have tamed him with a single word;
in the past as well, I tamed him with a single word. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of northern brahmins.
Upon reaching maturity, he studied the three Vedas and all the various arts at Takkasilā.

After living as a householder for some time, following the passing of his parents, he went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*. Having attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he dwelt there.
He made his dwelling in the Himavat mountains. Having lived there for a long time, he went to the countryside to partake of salt and sour gruel;

upon reaching Bārāṇasī, he stayed in the royal park. On the following day, well-robed and well-clad, endowed with the appearance of an ascetic, he entered the city for alms and reached the royal courtyard. The king, looking out from the lion-window, saw him.
Having gained confidence in his deportment, he thought, "This ascetic has tranquil faculties and a tranquil mind;
he looks only the distance of a yoke ahead. At every step, he moves like one setting down a thousand pieces of gold.
If there is such a thing as the 'Dhamma of Peace,' it must exist within him. Having reflected thus, he looked toward a certain minister.
Thus he said, "What shall I do, O King? [The king replied,] "Bring that ascetic here. He said, "Very well, Your Majesty," and approached the Bodhisatta.
Having paid homage and taken the alms-bowl from his hand, when asked, "What is it, O one of great merit?
he replied, "Venerable sir, the king summons you. The Bodhisatta said, "We are not attendants of the royal court; we are dwellers of the Himalayas."
"I am not," he said. The minister went and reported that matter to the king. The king said, "We have no other personal attendant;
bring him here. The minister went, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, and having made his request, led him into the royal residence.
The king paid homage to the Bodhisatta, had him sit upon a golden couch beneath a raised white parasol, and [addressed] himself...
Having served them various kinds of choice food that had been prepared, he asked, "Where do you dwell, venerable sirs?
"We are from the Himalayan region, Great King. "Where are you going now? "We are seeking a dwelling suitable for the rainy season, Great King.
"In that case, venerable sirs, please stay in our very own park," he said, and having obtained their consent, he himself—
Having eaten, he took the Bodhisatta and went to the park;

there he had a leaf-hut constructed, established places for standing by day and night, provided the requisites for one who has gone forth, and having entrusted him to the park-keeper, entered the city.
From that time on, the Bodhisatta lived in the park, and the king went to attend upon him two or three times every day.
That king had a son named Duṭṭhakumāra, who was fierce and cruel; neither the king nor his other relatives were able to subdue him.
Even the ministers and the brahmin householders, having gathered together and speaking with indignation, saying, "Sire, do not act thus;
it is not right to act in this way," were unable to make him accept their advice.
The king thought, “Apart from my noble master, the ascetic of the Himalayas, there is no one else capable of taming this prince;

he alone shall tame him. Taking the prince with him, he went into the presence of the Bodhisatta and said, “Venerable sir, this prince is fierce and harsh; we are unable to tame him. May you [tame] him by means of a single...”
“Teach him by means of skillful methods,” he said, and having handed the prince over to the Bodhisatta, he departed.

Taking the prince with him, the Bodhisatta wandered through the park; seeing a single nimba sapling growing between two footprints—one from one side and one from the other—he said to the prince, “Prince, first eat a leaf of this young tree and find out its taste.”
Having eaten one of its leaves and perceived its taste, he cried out, "Alas! and spat it onto the ground along with his saliva.
When asked, "What is this, young man? he replied, "Venerable sir, even now this tree is like the *halāhala* poison;
as it grows, it will kill many people. Having uprooted that young neem tree and crushed it in his hands, he spoke this verse:
“This tree has but a single leaf, not even four finger-breadths above the ground;
with fruit [only] at the end of a hundred thousand aeons, what will this great thing become?
In this context, “having but a single leaf” means having one leaf on each side. “Not even four finger-breadths above the ground” means not even the measure of four fingers from the earth.
"Not grown. "By its fruit" means by the taste of its fruit. "By a poison-like appearance" means it is like the *halāhala* poison.
The meaning is: although it is small, it is possessed of such a bitter leaf. "What will this great one become? means:
when it has reached maturity and becomes large, what indeed will it become? Surely, it will be a destroyer of men.
"It will become [bitter]," he said, and having uprooted it and crushed it, he threw it away.
Then the Bodhisatta said this to him: "Prince, you uprooted, crushed, and threw away this young neem tree, thinking: 'It is bitter only now;
what will it be like when it is full-grown? From where could there be growth depending on this?'"

Just as you have acted in this matter, so too will the inhabitants of your kingdom think: "This prince was already so fierce and cruel even in his youth; what will he do when he attains the kingship in old age?
From where shall we derive any prosperity through him? Thus, instead of giving you the kingdom that belongs to your family, they will uproot you like a young neem tree.

“They will carry out the formal act of banishment from the kingdom; therefore, abandoning your resemblance to the *nimba* tree, from this day forward be endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion.
From that time on, having subdued his pride and become free from malice, he remained established in the Bodhisatta’s counsel, endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion.
Upon his father’s passing, he attained the kingship, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and so forth.
He departed according to his karma.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it was not only now that I tamed this wicked Licchavi youth;
in the past as well, I tamed him. Having said this, he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the wicked prince..."
"This Licchavi youth was King Ānanda, while the ascetic who gave him counsel was none other than myself.
This concludes the ninth narrative, the Commentary on the Ekapaṇṇa Jātaka. [150] 10. The Commentary on the Sañjīva Jātaka.
"He who upholds what is non-existent"— this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Veḷuvana concerning King Ajātasattu’s support of the non-existent.
For having placed his confidence in Devadatta, who was a thorn in the side of the Buddhas,
immoral, and of evil nature, the king took hold of that non-existent, unworthy person and, thinking, "I shall pay him honor," bestowed much wealth upon him.
Having had a monastery built at Gayāsīsa and having followed his advice, he caused his father, the Dhamma-king, to be killed—
an Arahant and a Sotāpanna noble disciple— thereby destroying the necessary condition for his own attainment of the path of stream-entry and meeting with total ruin.
Indeed, upon hearing that "Devadatta has sunk into the earth," he thought, "I wonder if the earth will [swallow] me too?"
Thinking, “He might swallow me,” he is terrified and trembling; he does not obtain the pleasure of kingship, nor does he find the gratifying happiness of his bed.
Like a young elephant struck by a sharp goad, he wanders about quivering.
It is as if the earth were crushing him, as if the flames of Avīci were issuing forth, as if the earth were swallowing him up, or as if he were lying face-up on a blazing iron ground.
He perceived himself as if being impaled on iron spikes; thus, like a cock that has been struck, he was unable to stand still for even a moment.

Desiring to see the Perfectly Enlightened One, desiring to ask for forgiveness, and desiring to pose a question, he was nevertheless unable to approach because of the magnitude of his own transgression.

Then, when the full moon of the month of Kattika had arrived and the city of Rājagaha was adorned like a city of the gods, the King sat upon a golden throne on the great terrace surrounded by his assembly of ministers.
Seeing Jīvaka Komārabhacca seated nearby, he thought: "I shall take Jīvaka and go into the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One."
However, it would not be straightforward for me to say, "Friend Jīvaka, I am unable to go myself;
come, lead me to the presence of the Teacher. Instead, by way of praising the excellence of the night, I shall say:
"What ascetic or brahmin might we visit today, such that our minds would find confidence upon visiting him?"
“I shall speak; having heard it, the ministers will each praise their own teachers, and Jīvaka too will praise the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Then, taking him with us, we shall go into the presence of the Teacher.
Thus he praised [the night] during the night with five phrases: “O, how auspicious is this moonlit night! O, how beautiful...”
"O, what a moonlit night! Indeed, O, what a beautiful moonlit night! Indeed, O, what a serene moonlit night!
Indeed, O, what a delightful moonlit night! Whom indeed might we attend upon today—whether a recluse or a brahmin—so that our minds might find confidence while attending upon him?"

Then one minister spoke in praise of Pūraṇa Kassapa, another of Makkhali Gosāla, another of Ajita Kesakambalin, another of Pakudha Kaccāyana, another of Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, and another of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.
Having heard their words, the king remained silent; for he expected the speech of the chief minister Jīvaka alone.
Jīvaka, thinking, “I shall know when the King speaks specifically concerning me,” sat in silence not far away.
Then the King said to him, “But you, dear Jīvaka, why are you silent?
At that moment, Jīvaka rose from his seat, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said, “Sire, this is the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, our—”
He was dwelling in the Mango Grove together with twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus.

Having thus stated the nine qualities beginning with "arahant," and having proclaimed the majesty of the Blessed One—beginning from his birth and including the various portents and signs—the [deity] said:
"Let the deity attend upon that Blessed One; let him hear the Dhamma."
“Let him ask a question,” he said.
The king, his heart’s desire fulfilled, replied, “In that case, my dear Jīvaka, prepare the elephant-vehicles.
Having prepared the vehicles, he went with great royal splendor to Jīvaka’s mango grove, where [he saw the Blessed One] surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus in the pavilion.
Having seen the Tathāgata and observed the community of monks— immovable like a great ship in the midst of calm waters—
he looked here and there and thought, "Never before have I seen such an assembly as this.
Confident simply by their deportment, he raised his joined palms toward the Saṅgha, offered praise, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down to one side.
He asked about the question on the fruits of the ascetic life. Then the Blessed One preached to him the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, adorned with two recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*).
At the conclusion of the discourse, being satisfied, he asked the Blessed One’s forgiveness, rose from his seat, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and departed.
Not long after the king had left, the Teacher addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, this man has been ruined.”

“Monks, this king is ruined. Monks, had this king not, for the sake of power, deprived his father—the righteous Dhamma-king—of life, the dustless, stainless Eye of Dhamma would have arisen in him right here on this very seat.
But by relying on Devadatta and exerting himself toward what is unreal, he has fallen away from the fruit of stream-entry,” he said.
On the following day, the bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall:

"Friends, it is said that Ajātasattu, having exerted himself improperly and relying on the immoral and evil-natured Devadatta, has fallen away from the fruit of stream-entry because he committed the deed of patricide;
the king has been led astray by Devadatta. The Teacher, having arrived, asked: "Bhikkhus, what is it that you are discussing now?"

Having asked, "Sitting for what discussion? and being told, "For this one indeed," [the Buddha] said, "Monks, it is not only now that Ajātasattu has met with great ruin through his lack of self-restraint;
formerly, too, he destroyed himself by his very lack of self-restraint. Having said this, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of great wealth among the brahmins.

Having been reborn and reached maturity, he went to Takkasilā and, after mastering all the arts, became a world-renowned teacher in Bārāṇasī, where he taught the craft to five hundred young men. Among those students was a young man named Sañjīva;
the Bodhisatta gave him a charm for raising the dead. He [used] only that charm for raising [the dead].
However, without having taken up the warding-off charm, one day he went to the forest with some young brahmins for the sake of firewood.
Seeing a dead tiger there, he said to the brahmins, "Friends, I shall raise this dead tiger.
The brahmins said, "You will not be able to do it. He replied, "I shall raise it right before your very eyes. "If [you can]..."
“Young man, can you? Try to raise him up. Having said this, those young men climbed the tree.
Sañjīva recited his mantra and struck the dead tiger with pebbles.
The tiger rose up, rushed forward with great speed, bit Sañjīva in the throat, brought him to the end of his life, and fell down right there; Sañjīva also fell down right there.
The husband and wife both lay dead in one and the same place.
The young men, having taken firewood, returned and reported what had happened to their teacher. The teacher addressed the young men, saying:
"Sons, those who practice misplaced zeal—those who bestow honor and respect in an inappropriate place—suffer such misery."
Having said, "They indeed obtain it," he spoke this verse:
"He who exerts himself for what does not exist, and serves that which does not exist,
makes a meal of that very person, just as a tiger does of a living doll."
In this context, "one who is non-existent" refers to one who is immoral and of evil character, possessed of the three types of misconduct.

"Whoever supports him" means that anyone among the kṣatriyas and so forth—whether a renunciant by providing robes and other requisites, or a householder by providing positions such as viceroy or general—supports such an immoral person; the meaning is that they show him honor and respect.
"He cultivates what is non-existent" means that whoever cultivates, associates with, and attends upon such a non-existent person who is immoral—him alone he makes his food;
that is to say, that immoral, evil person devours, consumes, and brings to ruin that one who supports the non-existent. How so?
"Like a tiger and a snake-charmer": just as by the young man Sañjīva, through [the power of] a spell...
Having turned back, the tiger Sañjīvika, who had been favored by the gift of his life, took the very Sañjīva who was the giver of his own life and deprived him of life right there, casting him down.
Thus, anyone else who favors the unworthy is an immoral person who destroys the very one who favored him. In this way, those who favor the unworthy meet with destruction.
Having taught the Dhamma to the young brahmins with this verse, the Bodhisatta performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms and departed according to his karma.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma instruction, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the young brahmin who caused the dead tiger to rise was Ajātasattu, while the world-renowned teacher was none other than myself.
This concludes the commentary on the Sañjīva Jātaka, the tenth.
The fifteenth chapter, the Kakaṇṭaka-vagga.
Its summary verse (uddāna) is as follows: Godha, Siṅgāla, Virocana, Naṅguṭṭha, Rādha, and Kāka.
The Flower-Red Jackal, the Single-Leaf, and the Sañjīva.
Now, the summary of the Vaggas:
The Apaṇṇaka and Sīla Vaggas, the Kuruṅga and the Kulāvaka.
*Atthakāma*, *Āsīsa*, and *Itthivimāna*;
*Varuṇa*, *Pāyāsi*, and *Litta*; *Parosata*, *Haṃsa*, and *Kusanāḷi*;
*Sampadāna*, *Kakaṇṭaka*, and the fifteen *Jātaka*s ending with *Satapaññāsa*.
The commentary on the Ekaka-nipāta is finished.
(The first part is finished.)
